c.h: Our promise: checked knowledge, no fuss
c.x: our promise: checked knowledge, no fuss facts are checked against an official document, a standard or a well-sourced reference, and every page lists what it was checked against. where an official source could not be reached, the page says so and those claims are being re-checked. code examples are run before they go on a page. some sections already link to a repository of runnable code ("run the code"); more repositories and runnable samples are being built so that every section has something you can run. what is memory or opinion says so ("as i remember it"), and what is planned is called planned. no ads, no tracking, no sign-up. read in peace, and save any page as a pdf. when something is wrong, it gets fixed: every page ends with a link to report it in the open. no guide can promise to be perfect. this one promises to show its sources and correct its mistakes.

what well-rounded means here the base: character and thinking. honesty, curiosity, care for people, and clear reasoning grounded in mathematics, the scientific method and philosophy. ai can generate code; it cannot supply judgement or integrity. see behaviours and the thinking & character tabs. the foundation: shared fundamentals. every engineer needs these: sql, one language well (java or python), linux, docker, networking and the web, git and ci/cd, testing, security basics, and reading logs. breadth across the system. enough of data, services, design, cloud and operations to read the code, follow a design discussion, and find the right person or doc. depth where you choose. real expertise in one or two areas. many engineers on this kind of system go deep in data (bigquery, dbt, pipelines) or platform (cloud, kubernetes, delivery), or both; the shape is sometimes drawn as a t or a y. ai across all of it. you build features on models and use assistants to work faster, with the same discipline as everything else. "know enough" below is the bar for breadth: what any engineer should manage without help. "go deep" is what a specialist in that area owns.

not only for engineers we get one life, and whatever job we do, we can make the journey beautiful. the tabs under thinking & character ( mathematics , science & method , philosophy , being a good human and body, mind & nature ) and the behaviours page are written for engineers, but they hold for anyone: a nurse, a teacher, an accountant, a builder. read them that way. the engineering tabs show what "fundamentals first" looks like in one craft; every craft has its own.

from data to wisdom there is more information within reach today than ever, but information is not understanding. a useful way to think about learning is a ladder of four steps, often called dikw: data: raw facts. a stack trace, a column of numbers, a snippet of code. information: data with meaning. this error happens when that field is empty. knowledge: understanding how and why. the field is empty because the upstream system sends dates in another format. wisdom: knowing what to do, and what not to do. validate at the boundary, and design so this whole kind of error cannot happen again. a search result or an ai answer can hand you information, sometimes even text shaped like knowledge. wisdom only comes from understanding the fundamentals and applying them yourself, again and again. nobody can learn everything; the aim is enough foundations to climb from data to wisdom in whatever you take on. this guide is here to help you climb.

c.h: Fundamentals first: be the site manager, not a vibe coder
c.x: fundamentals first: be the site manager, not a vibe coder ai hands every engineer a bulldozer. a bulldozer on a building site is only safe with a site manager who knows how buildings stand up: the foundations, the materials, the regulations, and what to inspect before anyone moves in. "vibe coding", accepting whatever the model produces because it looks right, is a bulldozer with nobody in charge of the site. it feels fast until the first thing breaks and nobody can say why. on a building site in software where to learn it foundations and ground operating systems, networking, how the web works, databases and sql linux , networking , web fundamentals , sql skills , database design materials and how they behave a language well, its data structures and concurrency, the libraries you depend on java , python , data libraries plans and structure requirements, architecture, data models, system design architecture , system design building regulations security, privacy, licences, compliance security , oauth & oidc inspections and sign-off tests, reviews, checks that must be green testing , devops running the finished building deploying, monitoring, incidents, cost observability , sre vibe coder site manager starts with a prompt starts with the problem, the constraints and what "done" means cannot tell good output from plausible output knows the fundamentals well enough to spot what is wrong stuck when the ai is stuck debugs from first principles: logs, queries, packets, stack traces ships what runs once ships what is tested, secure, observable and maintainable learns little from each task gets better with every task, and so gets more out of the tool how to learn this way: do it by hand once. write the loop, the sql query, the dockerfile, the deploy, the test yourself before asking ai to do it for you. then you can judge its version. use ai as a tutor keep going back to basics: when something surprises you, the gap is almost always in a fundamental, not in the tool. ai raises the floor of what anyone can produce. fundamentals raise the ceiling of what you can be trusted with.

c.h: An engineer who uses AI, not a prompt engineer
c.x: an engineer who uses ai, not a prompt engineer writing a good prompt is one skill among many, and the smallest one. what makes ai work in production is engineering: data: the model is only as good as what you retrieve and feed it. that is sql, pipelines, chunking and freshness, the data tabs of this guide. evaluation: a test set and a score, so a change to the prompt or model is measured, not judged by eye. systems: timeouts, retries, caching, cost limits, logging, and a fallback when the model is down or refuses. security: untrusted text can carry instructions (prompt injection). least-privilege tools, no secrets in prompts, output treated as untrusted input. judgement with assistants: ai-written code gets the same review, tests and doc checks as yours. you stay responsible for what ships. the ai tab covers each of these. a prompt engineer stops at the prompt; a well-rounded engineer ships, measures and operates the whole feature.

c.h: The four levels used on every tab
c.x: the four levels used on every tab 1 foundation can use it with examples and guidance. reads it, runs it, makes small changes safely, and knows when to ask. 2 practitioner works independently. builds and ships features with it, tests them, debugs ordinary problems, follows the team's standards. 3 senior designs with it. makes trade-offs, reviews others' work, handles the hard incidents, and mentors. 4 expert sets direction across teams. knows the internals, writes the standards and blueprints, and leads migrations and decisions. where a well-rounded engineer aims: senior in the one or two areas they go deep in; practitioner in the foundations, testing, security, and the thinking and character tabs; at least foundation everywhere else. expert in one or two areas comes with time and is not expected of everyone. each tab ends with its own level expectations and an "explore further" card of official docs, books and topics to study next.

self-check: the foundations you should be able to do all of these without asking: explain what a query will cost before you run it. read a stack trace or a job log and name the line that failed. say why a service cannot reach another: dns, firewall, or auth. read a terraform plan and spot a destroy or a replace. write a test that fails before your fix and passes after it. roll back a bad deploy. get a shell in a running container and find why it exited. say what a prompt-based feature returns when the model is down, and how you would know.

self-check: ai return validated json from a model instead of parsing free text. build a small eval set and show a change improved the score. explain how retrieved documents could smuggle instructions into a prompt, and how you limit the damage. estimate the monthly cost of a feature from tokens per call and calls per day. reject an ai-suggested change because a test or the docs show it is wrong.

self-check: depth in data design a partitioned, clustered table for a given query pattern. choose between merge, insert_overwrite and microbatch for a dbt model, and explain why. make a dag rerun for one date without duplicating data. find rows a parse silently turned into null, and stop it happening again. explain a bigquery bill from information_schema.jobs.

self-check: depth in platform write the terraform for a cloud run job, its service account, its iam and its schedule. give a service a fixed egress ip and private access to cloud sql. ship a canary revision and move traffic in steps. size memory and cpu for a jvm container and justify the numbers. debug a crashloopbackoff or a "failed to listen on port" from logs alone.

c.h: The tills are a good picture
c.x: the tills are a good picture supermarkets once had a long row of tills, each with a person behind it. over the years most have moved to a few staffed tills and a bank of self-service ones. fewer people do the scanning. but the shop still needs people: someone approves an age check, clears a jammed scanner, helps the customer who is stuck, and knows what to do when the system goes down. software is going the same way. fewer people will type routine code by hand, but people are still needed to manage the work, and managing it well takes a good understanding of what is being built. the people who stay most useful are the ones who understand what the machines are doing, and can take over when they stop.

c.h: We have been here before: CAD and CAM
c.x: we have been here before: cad and cam engineering design went through this once already. drawings used to be made by hand at drawing boards, by teams of draughtsmen. then computers took over the drawing and the machining: 1940s and 1950s: the first numerically controlled machine tools follow points fed into them, instead of a person guiding every cut. 1963: ivan sutherland writes sketchpad for his phd thesis, an early program for drawing on a computer screen. 1982: autocad is released for desktop computers, and computer-aided design (cad) spreads to ordinary offices. computer-aided manufacturing (cam) then turns those designs into instructions for the machines that cut and shape the parts. the drawing board disappeared, and many drafting jobs changed or went. but engineering did not end: it grew. the people who did well learned the new tools and kept the judgement the tools could not supply: whether a part would be strong enough, whether it could be made, whether it was safe. cad made drawing faster; it never decided what was worth drawing. ai is the same kind of shift for writing code and documents, faster and wider. the lesson carries over: learn the tool, keep the understanding, and own the decisions. checked against (wikipedia): computer numerical control ; sketchpad ; autocad ; computer-aided design ; computer-aided manufacturing .

c.h: The risk of a team that can only prompt
c.x: the risk of a team that can only prompt picture a team whose only skill is asking an ai to do the work. everything is automated. then something fails, and the only thing they know how to do is ask the ai to fix it. if the ai is wrong, unavailable, or part of what failed, nobody in the room can help. we have seen what large automated failures look like. on 19 july 2024 a faulty update to a widely used security product crashed about 8.5 million windows computers, by microsoft's estimate, and many had to be repaired by hand, one machine at a time. people with hands-on skills were the way out.

c.h: Keep a hand on the controls
c.x: keep a hand on the controls the boeing 737 max accidents of october 2018 and march 2019 carry a lesson worth remembering. official investigations found that a new automated flight-control feature, mcas, contributed to both crashes, and references to it had been removed from the pilots' flight manual. when it misbehaved, the crews did not have what they needed to take back control. agents that heal themselves are useful. but every automated system needs a documented manual override , and people who have practised using it. in an emergency, a person should be able to step in and fix things directly, not only through another agent.

c.h: We will use it more than we meant to
c.x: we will use it more than we meant to nobody knows for sure where this goes. but rightly or wrongly, most of us will end up using ai more than we intended. that can be good or bad. my view: it is good for someone who has the idea and knows the specification but could never find the hundreds of hours to build it. for people with that experience, it is a genuinely useful tool, and solo builders who want to make a product should start: doing something beats waiting. it is bad when it becomes a habit of prompting and never going back to check. a mind that stops checking slowly stops being able to. so use the time it gives back well. if ai saves you hours, spend some of them reading the foundation books you never had time for. the other view: some argue that building with ai before you understand the foundations produces products you cannot maintain or debug, and that learning first is the better start, even if it means waiting.

c.h: More with fewer, or more with the same
c.x: more with fewer, or more with the same come back to the bulldozer. companies may expect the same work from fewer engineers, or more work from the same number. we can already see some reduction across the industry, and there will be disruption, though no one can say yet how much. the people who come through it best will be the ones who can direct the machine and still understand the ground it is moving.

seven ways people use ai to automate without learning. fast today, fragile tomorrow: when it breaks, nothing was learned. to learn. ask it to explain, then check the explanation against the docs. as a tester and reviewer. ask it to find the cases you missed, try to break your code, and review your writing, designs and pull requests. as a tutor and mentor. ask it to quiz you, review your reasoning, and say what to read next. to explore and research. summarise a long document, compare options, brainstorm, draft something new; then check what comes back against the real sources. as a builder. use it to build what you design and understand: frameworks, tools, products, reusable blueprints for your team. you set the architecture and the standards; ai speeds up the making. see frameworks vs ai . to automate, with oversight. let it, or an agent, run routine work you understand. watch what it does, keep the logs, and keep the off switch. see "keep a hand on the controls" above and agent harness . only the first makes you weaker; the rest make you stronger, as long as you stay the one who understands.

c.h: You may not read every line, but you must understand it and test it
c.x: you may not read every line, but you must understand it and test it with ai writing more of the code, we may not read every line it produces. that can be acceptable, on two conditions: we understand most of it, how it is shaped, what it depends on, and where it can fail; and we can test all of it in the right way , even the lines we did not read. tests, types, reviews and monitoring become how we know the code works. see testing and observability .

c.h: Every role is changing, not only engineering
c.x: every role is changing, not only engineering in a large company the change reaches everyone: business analysts, journey managers, product owners, software engineers, solution architects, enterprise architects, data engineers, data analysts, testers, and engineers who have spent careers on mainframes and are now learning cloud and ai. none of us is finished learning, whatever the job title says. many people are worried simply because they do not yet know what is changing. there will be work, in some capacity, for people who are ready to use ai in the right way. what helps most is not one course or one tool. it is the will to adapt : understanding what is changing, trying it, and changing how we work. it will be hard, and some days it will feel slow. learning one small thing every day still adds up: a command, a concept, a page of this guide, a question asked out loud. analysts, journey managers and product owners: learn enough of how ai works to write requirements it can meet, and to spot where it should not be trusted. your knowledge of customers and rules is what checks its answers. software engineers: ai can write more of the code, so the job moves towards design, review, testing and running it in production. keep the foundations sharp enough to judge what it produced. see testing and claude code & cowork . solution architects: ai becomes another component to design around: where it sits, what data it may see, how it fails, what it costs, and where a person must stay in the loop. see architecture and agent harness . enterprise architects: set the guard rails across the organisation: which models and tools are approved, how data is governed, how agents are given access, and how the estate changes without a big-bang rewrite. see frameworks vs ai . data engineers and analysts: ai is only as good as the data it reads. quality, lineage and access control matter more, not less. see data engineering . engineers coming from mainframes and older platforms: what you know about reliability, batch, transactions and running systems for decades is exactly what new platforms often lack. bring it with you; learn the new tools on top of it.

whatever your role learn what it is and is not. ai predicts likely text; it can be fluent and wrong. ai for engineers and llms are written plainly. use it on your own work, and check it. you learn its strengths and its mistakes fastest on things you already know well. keep your domain knowledge. knowing your customers, your trade and your rules is what tells you when an answer is wrong. invest in people skills. explaining, listening and deciding together are hard to automate. see being a good human .

if you are an engineer be able to fix it without the agent. read the logs, follow a request through the system, roll back a release. linux , networking and observability are where that starts. write runbooks a person can follow at 3 a.m., and keep them next to the automation they cover. see sre . build the off switch. every agent gets a kill switch, a manual fallback and limits on what it may touch. see agent harness and agents on gcp . practise the bad day. rehearse an outage with the automation turned off, so taking over is a habit, not a hope.

keep your own memory as ai does more of the work, what you have learned (how your systems behave, why decisions were made, what worked and what did not) becomes more valuable, not less. keep it in a form you own, so it stays useful to you over the years and goes with you from job to job. that is what we are building with headworks , penstock and cistern running together: a self-hosted ai agent that runs on your own machine with a model you pick. its memory is plain files you own and can read, change or delete, and it reads only the data you choose to share, with a receipt for every read. what you build up stays yours, and you decide what to share with others. see our open source .

a journey, not a fight when change feels threatening, the body reacts as if to danger: the fight-or-flight response. it helps in a real emergency and hurts in a long change, because a mind in that state reacts instead of thinking. the change ai brings will take years, not days, so treat it as a journey rather than a fight. it is a journey, and we are in competition with no one: not our colleagues, not the machines. step back from the headlines. ask what is actually changing in your own work this month, not what the loudest voice predicts. learn something new every day. one thing learned each day compounds; atomic habits calls it getting about 1% better each day. see the reading list . look after the basics. sleep, movement and time away from screens keep you calm enough to think. see body, mind & nature . keep doing the work. good things happen to people who are ready and keep going, day after day, long after the headlines move on. think above the ordinary. when everyone is anxious, the person who stays calm, learns steadily and helps others becomes the one people turn to.

understanding before opinion every day brings millions of posts about ai, and everyone has an opinion. we have come to find more satisfaction in expressing a view than in understanding the thing itself, and we miss the experience of learning it. that is why this guide is a quiet, static site: no feed, no comments, no tracking. come, find a section, read it in peace, try the code, and save it as a pdf if you like. understanding first; the opinion can wait.

believe in yourself "when you are inspired by some great purpose, some extraordinary project, all your thoughts break their bonds: your mind transcends limitations, your consciousness expands in every direction, and you find yourself in a new, great and wonderful world. dormant forces, faculties and talents become alive, and you discover yourself to be a greater person by far than you ever dreamed yourself to be." a passage often attributed to patanjali whoever wrote it, the idea is true: the limits we feel are often limits in how we see ourselves. in times of change, belief in yourself is what lets you start learning something new instead of waiting to be told you can. belief is built, not found. the psychologist albert bandura called it self-efficacy: your belief that you can succeed at a particular task. he found the most effective way to build it is mastery experiences, small successes of your own. so start small and finish. run one command, fix one bug, read one chapter. each thing you complete is evidence you can do the next. watch your self-image. "i am not technical" or "i am too old to learn this" become true only if you act on them. psycho-cybernetics and as a man thinketh on the reading list are about exactly this. find a purpose bigger than the worry. as the passage says, a purpose you care about wakes up abilities you did not know you had. checked against: self-efficacy (wikipedia) .

harness it, and keep control like every technology before it, ai is worth using for what it gives us, and worth controlling for what it can break. use it every day. keep the foundations, keep the manual override, and keep people who know how to use both.

the short answer our view: the path from idea to production has not changed in shape: find out whether the idea is worth building, build it in small steps, check it, release it safely, run it, and learn. what has changed is how much of the building agents can do. that moves people’s value towards the ends of the path, deciding what is worth doing and judging whether it worked, and towards the foundations that let you check an agent’s work. the other view is in the cards below: some expect the division of work, and even the shape of the path, to keep shifting.

the path from idea to production, and back eight stages in two rows joined by arrows. top row: idea, test the idea, specify, build. bottom row, right to left: verify, release, operate, learn. an arrow from learn returns to idea, so the path is a loop. a note says people decide at every stage and agents can help at every stage. idea test the idea specify build learn operate release verify feedback people decide at every stage; agents can help at every stage. the path drawn as a loop: production is where you learn whether the idea was right, and that feeds the next idea. the stage names are ours ( analysis ); the practices at each stage are sourced in the table below.

the launch checklist in google’s sre book asks about canaries under live traffic and staged rollouts when to release, and to whom preparing release notes and rollout steps devops operate before launch, the same sre-book checklist asks what happens when a machine, rack or data centre fails, how the service is monitored, and whether there are backups, so operating it is planned before it starts on-call judgement, and talking to users watching signals, drafting incident timelines sre , observability learn measure delivery: dora uses change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate deciding what the evidence means for the next idea gathering the numbers and the feedback devops (measuring delivery) the practices in the second column are sourced (below), except where marked as our view; the “people own” and “agents can help” columns are our view, and how much you hand to agents is a choice by requirement on humans & agents .

a checklist that has lasted google’s sre book prints the company’s original launch coordination checklist, from about 2005. its headings are still a fair list of what production asks of an idea: architecture; machines and data centres; volume, capacity and performance; reliability and failover; monitoring; security; automation and manual tasks; growth; external dependencies; and schedule and rollout. the book says checklists like it are used to reduce failure and ensure consistency, as in aviation and surgery. analysis: an agent can work through such a list quickly; deciding which answers are good enough for your users is still a person’s call.

one ecosystem, not two camps our view: people and agents work best as one system with clear roles: people set direction, own decisions and stay accountable; agents do well-briefed work quickly and report what they did and how they checked it. the guide’s humans & agents page has how to brief an agent and how it should report back. the other view: some argue roles will keep moving towards agents, so drawing fixed lines now may age badly; on that view the skill that matters most is adapting the division of work as tools change.

c.h: In harmony with what is happening
c.x: in harmony with what is happening our view: the change is real and it is not stopping, and fighting it costs energy that learning would use better. being in harmony with it does not mean accepting everything: it means seeing clearly what is changing, keeping what still matters, and choosing where to put your effort. the guide’s philosophy page has more on nothing being permanent, and on being at peace with what happens; worried about ai? has more on the worry itself. the other view: some changes deserve resistance, not harmony: when a tool is unsafe, unfair or simply wrong for the job, saying so is part of the work, and acceptance can become passivity.

upskilling on foundations our view: when agents write more of the code, the foundations matter more, not less: you cannot judge an agent’s database migration without understanding transactions, or its retry logic without understanding failure. the foundations change slowly; the tools on top of them change every year. that is why this guide starts where it does, and why start here argues for being the site manager rather than a “vibe coder”. if you can’t yet… start with explain what happens when two requests change the same data at once concurrency , database design say why a call to another service can be slow or fail networking , distributed systems judge whether an agent’s tests prove anything testing , test strategy choose where data should live choosing a data store read what an agent changed and explain it to a colleague writing & code review the other view: some argue that, as tools improve, more people will build useful software without deep foundations, and that learning on the job, with an agent explaining as it goes, can replace much up-front study.

c.h: Why this belongs in a software guide
c.x: why this belongs in a software guide a new generation of engineers needs the whole foundation, not only the top layers. today a small number of companies design and make most of the world's advanced chips: tsmc alone accounts for roughly 70% of the global foundry market. when knowledge sits in so few places, everyone else depends on them for every device, data centre and ai model. learning electronics does not mean everyone builds a fab. it means more people understand what their software runs on, can repair and reuse hardware instead of throwing it away, and can take part in open hardware. that is how the foundations stay shared, and how technology becomes more sustainable.

from switch to chip the transistor is an electrically controlled switch. the first, a point-contact transistor, was invented in 1947 at bell labs by john bardeen, walter brattain and william shockley, who shared the 1956 nobel prize in physics. logic gates (and, or, not) are built from transistors; everything a computer does is built from gates. the integrated circuit puts many transistors on one piece of semiconductor: credited to jack kilby (1958) and robert noyce (1959). moore's law is the observation that the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years, which drove decades of cheaper, faster computing.

how chips are designed hardware description languages such as verilog and vhdl describe circuits as code, which is then tested in simulation like software. fpgas are chips that can be reprogrammed after manufacture, so you can try your own digital designs on real hardware without making a chip. instruction sets define what a processor understands. risc-v is a free and open standard instruction set, started at the university of california, berkeley: anyone can design a risc-v processor without paying royalties. open manufacturing kits exist too: skywater's 130 nm process design kit (sky130) is available under the apache license, so a chip design can be taken to real silicon with open tools. from binary and gates to an adder you can run, and every step of the design flow: from binary to gpus .

sustainability e-waste is one of the fastest-growing waste streams: about 62 million tonnes in 2022, of which only 22.3% was formally collected and recycled; it is projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030. repair before replace. the right-to-repair movement argues that people should be able to fix what they own. engineers who understand electronics can design for repair and keep devices in use longer. efficient software is green software. code that does less work needs less hardware and less power. see performance and body, mind & nature .

where to start learn basic circuits: voltage, current, resistance, and how a transistor switches. build logic gates and a small adder in a free simulator, then in verilog. program a microcontroller board to read a sensor and drive a motor. see robotics . put a small design on an fpga board, then a simple risc-v core. read how chips are made, and repair one device instead of replacing it.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain voltage, current and how a transistor switches explain logic gates and how they add numbers explain what an instruction set is 2 practitioner build a microcontroller project with sensors and motors write and simulate a small design in verilog or vhdl run a design on an fpga board 3 senior design a simple processor or peripheral on an fpga read datasheets and choose components for a product design hardware for repair and long life 4 expert lead hardware and software co-design take a design towards silicon with an open process kit shape open hardware and sustainability practice each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

risc and cisc an instruction set is the list of operations a processor understands: the contract between hardware and software. cisc (complex instruction set computer): instructions can do several things at once, such as load from memory, calculate and store, with many addressing modes. x86, in most pcs and servers, is the best-known cisc family. risc (reduced instruction set computer): fewer, simpler instructions that each do one thing, so the chip can run them quickly and efficiently. the ideas came from projects such as ibm's 801 in the late 1970s and work at berkeley and stanford. arm (originally acorn risc machine, 1985) and risc-v are risc. today the line is blurred: modern x86 chips translate complex instructions into simpler internal steps, and risc chips have grown richer. the practical difference now is mostly power efficiency, licensing and the software ecosystem.

programming devices microcontrollers are small computers on one chip: processor, memory and inputs and outputs. they run washing machines, cars, sensors and robots. firmware is the software built into a device, usually stored in flash memory. you "flash" new firmware to update it. device drivers let the operating system control hardware: a driver turns "play this sound" or "print this page" into the device's own commands. try it: program a microcontroller board to blink a light, read a sensor and drive a motor. it teaches timing, memory limits and the hardware underneath every abstraction. see robotics .

a short cpu history when what why it mattered 1971 intel 4004 often called the first microprocessor: a whole processor on one chip. 1978 intel 8086 the start of x86, still the instruction set of most pcs and servers. 1985 arm (acorn risc machine) a risc design that later came to power most phones and tablets. 2003 amd64 (x86-64), first in amd's opteron 64-bit x86: far more memory, while running older 32-bit software. mid-2000s multi-core processors in ordinary pcs clock speeds stopped climbing fast, so chips added cores instead; software had to learn to do work in parallel. see java threads. 2020 apple m1 an arm system on a chip in mainstream laptops: cpu, gpu and more on one chip with shared memory.

c.h: How a modern laptop is built
c.x: how a modern laptop is built system on a chip (soc): cpu cores, a graphics processor, ai and media engines and security functions on one chip, often with memory packaged right beside it and shared between them. storage: a solid-state drive on the pci express bus, spoken to with the nvme protocol: no moving parts, far faster than a spinning disk. power and heat: the battery and cooling decide how hard the chip can work and for how long; thin laptops trade peak speed for quiet and battery life. firmware first: when you press the power button, firmware checks the hardware and starts the operating system.

media and sound cards midi (standardised 1983) lets instruments and computers exchange notes and controls rather than recorded sound. sound cards gave early pcs real audio: adlib (founded 1987) and then creative's sound blaster (1989), which became the de facto standard for pc audio until windows 95 and audio built into the motherboard took over. integrated audio: today sound is part of the motherboard or chip, following intel's ac'97 and high definition audio (2004) specifications. the pattern repeats: a separate card proves a need, then the function moves onto the main chip. graphics went the same way in laptops.

from gaming graphics to ai 1995 to 1999, 3d for games: 3dfx's voodoo graphics chip (to manufacturing in november 1995) brought fast 3d to pc gaming. in 1999 nvidia marketed the geforce 256 as "the world's first gpu", popularising the term. why gpus are different: drawing a frame means doing the same small calculation on millions of pixels at once, so gpus have thousands of simple cores built for parallel arithmetic, where a cpu has a few complex ones. 2007, cuda: nvidia's cuda let ordinary programs use the gpu for general-purpose computing, opening it to science and engineering. 2012, alexnet: a neural network for image recognition, trained on two nvidia gtx 580 gaming gpus, entered the imagenet challenge and showed that gpus made deep learning practical. 2015 to 2017, chips for ai: google introduced its tensor processing unit (tpu), a chip designed only for neural networks, and nvidia's volta gpus (first product announced may 2017) added tensor cores for deep learning. neural networks are mostly large matrix multiplications, exactly the parallel arithmetic that games had already paid to make fast and cheap. see llms and mathematics . why gpus work the way they do, built up from gates: from binary to gpus .

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain what an instruction set is, and risc versus cisc explain firmware and device drivers explain why gpus suit graphics and ai 2 practitioner program a microcontroller to read a sensor and drive an output read a laptop or server spec sheet and know what each part does run a workload on a gpu and compare it with the cpu 3 senior choose hardware for a workload: cores, memory, storage, accelerators profile where time goes between cpu, memory, disk and gpu plan for arm and x86 in the same estate 4 expert set hardware strategy for a platform or data centre co-design software with accelerators lead a move between processor architectures each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the short answer if you have ever written an if statement, you already understand most of what a chip does. a computer is a very large number of tiny switches, arranged so that switches control other switches. group a few of them and you get a logic gate ; group gates and you can add numbers; group adders and memory and you have a processor. no single step is mysterious. what makes chips impressive is the scale, billions of transistors, and the care taken at every layer. this is also why hardware matters more now, not less. software has become so dependent on what chips can do, from the phone in your pocket to the gpus that train ai models, that knowing roughly how they work helps you write better software and judge the hype. the basics, from the first transistor to moore’s law, are on electronics & chips and how computers are built ; this page goes one level deeper, with something you can run. from transistors to software, one layer at a time six layers, from top to bottom: software; cpu and gpu; alu and registers; adders; logic gates; transistors. each layer is built only from the one below it. software your program, compiled to instructions cpu and gpu fetch, decode, execute, billions of times a second alu and registers add, compare, remember, on every clock tick adders full adders chained bit by bit logic gates nand alone can build all the others transistors switches turned on and off by voltage built from below every layer is made only from the one beneath it. the program below builds the middle three for you, from nand gates up to an 8-bit adder.

c.h: Binary and hex, without the fear
c.x: binary and hex, without the fear a binary number uses only two symbols, 0 and 1, and each digit is called a bit . thomas harriot studied the modern system and gottfried leibniz is credited with inventing it, though related systems appeared much earlier in several cultures. why only two symbols? because a switch has two states, on and off, and that is all a transistor needs to represent. binary works exactly like the decimal you already know, just with 2 instead of 10. in decimal, the places are ones, tens, hundreds. in binary, they are ones, twos, fours, eights, and so on. so 0100 0001 is 64 + 1 = 65. hexadecimal is simply a shorthand for binary that people can read. one hex digit stands for four bits (a nibble ), so a whole 8-bit byte is exactly two hex digits: 0100 0001 is 41 , and 0010 1100 is 2c . that is why hex appears everywhere engineers look at raw data: colours like #5980a6 , memory addresses, network packets, hash values. decimal binary hex 9 1001 9 10 1010 a 15 1111 f 65 0100 0001 41 255 1111 1111 ff

c.h: Logic gates: decisions made of switches
c.x: logic gates: decisions made of switches a logic gate takes one or two bits in and gives one bit out, following a simple rule. you know these rules already from programming: gate output is 1 when… in code and both inputs are 1 a and b or at least one input is 1 a or b not the input is 0 not a xor the inputs differ a != b nand not both inputs are 1 not (a and b) here is the remarkable part. nand on its own is functionally complete : any boolean expression at all can be rebuilt using nothing but nand gates. not(x), for example, is just nand(x, x). (nor has the same property; and and or together do not, because they cannot make not.) so in principle, a whole computer can be built from one kind of gate, repeated.

c.h: Run it: an adder built only from NAND
c.x: run it: an adder built only from nand adding two bits is where gates start to do arithmetic. a half adder takes bits a and b and gives a sum (a xor b) and a carry (a and b); join two half adders with an or gate and you get a full adder , which also accepts a carry from the column to its right. chain eight full adders and you can add two bytes, exactly as you add numbers on paper, column by column, carrying as you go. the program below builds all of it from nand alone, then checks itself against python’s own + : """build an adder from one kind of gate, nand, and check it against python's own +.""" def nand(a, b): return 0 if (a and b) else 1 # the only gate we are given def not(a): return nand(a, a) def and(a, b): return not(nand(a, b)) def or(a, b): return nand(not(a), not(b)) def xor(a, b): return and(or(a, b), nand(a, b)) def full_adder(a, b, carry_in): s1 = xor(a, b) total = xor(s1, carry_in) carry_out = or(and(a, b), and(s1, carry_in)) return total, carry_out def add_8bit(x, y): """ripple-carry adder: eight full adders in a row, like the first stage of an alu.""" carry, result = 0, 0 for i in range(8): # lowest bit first bit, carry = full_adder((x >> i) & 1, (y >> i) & 1, carry) result |= bit << i return result, carry for x, y in [(23, 42), (200, 100), (0b1111_0000, 0x0f)]: total, overflow = add_8bit(x, y) print(f"{x:3} + {y:3} = {total:3} binary {total:08b} hex {total:02x} carry out {overflow}") assert all(add_8bit(x, y) == ((x + y) & 0xff, (x + y) >> 8) for x in range(256) for y in range(256)) print("checked all 65,536 pairs: the nand-only adder agrees with python") what it printed when we ran it: 23 + 42 = 65 binary 01000001 hex 41 carry out 0 200 + 100 = 44 binary 00101100 hex 2c carry out 1 240 + 15 = 255 binary 11111111 hex ff carry out 0 checked all 65,536 pairs: the nand-only adder agrees with python look at the second line: 200 + 100 came out as 44, with a carry of 1. eight bits can only hold 0 to 255, so 300 overflowed; the carry bit is the hardware telling you so. that single bit is the root of every integer overflow bug you will ever meet in software. a real processor’s arithmetic logic unit (alu) is this idea grown up: a combinational circuit that performs arithmetic and bitwise operations on whole binary numbers. add registers to hold values and a clock , a steady signal that tells every part of the chip when to take its next step, and you have the heart of a cpu.

how chips are designed today nobody draws billions of transistors by hand. modern digital design starts as code. engineers describe the circuit at register-transfer level (rtl), the usual starting point for designers, in a hardware description language such as verilog or vhdl. here is the full adder from the program above, written the way a chip designer would: // a full adder in verilog: the same circuit as full_adder() in the python above module full_adder (input a, input b, input carry_in, output sum, output carry_out); assign sum = a ^ b ^ carry_in; assign carry_out = (a & b) | ((a ^ b) & carry_in); endmodule from there, the journey to silicon is a series of steps, most of them done by software tools: how a digital chip goes from idea to silicon seven steps: specify what the chip must do; write it at register-transfer level in verilog or vhdl; simulate and test it; synthesise the rtl into logic gates; place and route the gates; tape out, sending the final layout; and fabricate it at a foundry. specify what it must do rtl verilog or vhdl simulate test like code synthesise rtl to gates place, route lay out gates tape-out send layout fabricate at a foundry the shaded steps are code and software tools: they feel much like building any other program a digital chip’s journey. only the last step needs a factory; everything before it happens on a computer, and much of it can be done with open-source tools. simulate: run tests against the design before anything is built, just as you test software. synthesise: a synthesis tool turns the rtl into an implementation made of logic gates, called a netlist. place and route: physical design decides where each gate sits on the silicon and how the wires connect them. tape-out: the point at which the final layout for the photomasks is sent to the fabrication plant. the name comes from the days when the data went on magnetic tape. it is closer to normal software than most people think. openroad, an open-source project, describes itself as delivering an automated flow from rtl to the final layout (gdsii) with a 24-hour turnaround. with skywater’s open 130 nm process kit (sky130) and projects such as tiny tapeout, where many small designs, some drawn in a browser simulator, share one manufactured chip, students and hobbyists can now have their own circuits made in real silicon. before committing to a chip at all, an fpga lets you load your design onto reprogrammable hardware and try it on a desk.

c.h: Why GPUs, and why AI runs on them
c.x: why gpus, and why ai runs on them a cpu has a small number of powerful cores, each able to follow its own complicated path through a program. a gpu makes the opposite trade: thousands of simpler cores that all apply the same instruction to different data at once. nvidia introduced the model it calls simt , single instruction, multiple threads, with its g80 chip in the tesla architecture. a single control unit broadcasts one instruction to many processing units, each working on its own data. that shape suits drawing graphics, where the same calculation runs on millions of pixels, and it turned out to suit neural networks too, which are mostly enormous matrix multiplications: the same multiply-and-add, repeated across huge grids of numbers. the history, from 3d gaming to cuda, alexnet and ai chips, is on how computers are built , and the maths behind it is on mathematics . analysis: simt also explains a gpu’s weakness. because only the control unit has a program counter, threads that take different branches have to wait for each other, so code full of if statements runs poorly on a gpu. the best gpu code is the same simple work, done to a great deal of data.

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: every software engineer should build an adder from gates once, in code, as above. it takes an afternoon, it makes binary, overflow and performance feel physical rather than abstract, and it shows that the most complex machine you use is ordinary ideas, stacked very high. the other view: modern chips are far beyond this picture. timing, power, heat, manufacturing variation and verification take most of a chip team’s effort, and the abstractions exist precisely so that most engineers never need to think about them. knowing the ladder is a foundation, not a qualification.

the short answer for twenty years the career advice for engineers pointed one way: towards software. hardware looked slow, expensive and finished. ai has changed that. every model is trained and served on chips, the companies that make them have become some of the most valuable in the world, and governments are spending large sums to build chip industries at home. that creates jobs at every level, from technicians in a fab to engineers who write the code that runs on a gpu. if you studied electronics, you already hold the foundation many software engineers lack: you know what a transistor, a clock and a signal really are. the rest of this page is about how to build on that, whether you want a job or a company. if binary, gates and chip design are still hazy, start with from binary to gpus .

c.h: Why chips are a job for the AI era
c.x: why chips are a job for the ai era the clearest numbers come from the united states, where the semiconductor industry association commissioned a study from oxford economics in 2023. it projected that the industry’s us workforce would grow from about 345,000 jobs to about 460,000 by 2030 , and that roughly 67,000 of the new jobs risk going unfilled at current graduation rates. of those unfilled jobs, 39% are technicians, most with certificates or two-year degrees; 35% are engineers with four-year degrees or computer scientists; and 26% are engineers at master’s or phd level. so this is not only a field for phds. governments are paying for the build-out: united states: the chips and science act (2022) includes $39 billion in subsidies for chip manufacturing. india: the semicon india programme began with an outlay of ₹76,000 crore for fabs, packaging plants and a design linked incentive scheme for chip design companies. its next phase, semicon 2.0, was approved with ₹1,27,500 crore, and talent development is one of its pillars. europe has its own european chips act. analysis: subsidies build factories, but factories need people, and people take years to train. that gap is the opportunity for anyone willing to learn now.

the jobs, layer by layer “working in chips” covers very different work. some of it is about making the chip; some of it is about programming a chip someone else made. here is the map, from the factory floor up: role what you do what to learn fab or test technician run and maintain the equipment that makes and tests wafers a certificate or two-year course; cleanroom practice; the equipment itself design engineer (rtl) describe the chip’s logic in verilog, systemverilog or vhdl digital logic, computer architecture, a hardware description language verification engineer prove the design does what the spec says, before it is manufactured simulation, test benches, coverage; a lot like testing software, with higher stakes physical design engineer turn logic into a layout: placement, routing, timing, power eda tools, timing analysis, the foundry’s process rules fpga engineer program a chip whose logic can be rewired after manufacture the same hdls; high-level synthesis lets you start from c or c++ gpu kernel programmer write the code that makes ai models run fast on gpus parallel programming, cuda, or triton, which lets you write gpu kernels as python functions compiler and tools engineer build the software that turns models and designs into something a chip can run compilers, computer architecture, and usually a lot of c++ analysis: the bottom rows are where software engineers cross over most easily. triton, for example, was released by openai in 2021 and is now the default gpu code generator behind pytorch’s torch.compile . the top rows are where an electronics degree counts most.

will ai design the chips? it already helps, and the honest picture is more interesting than the headlines. commercial tools use it. synopsys, a chip design software company listed in 2024 as the world’s 12th largest software company, introduced dso.ai in 2020, which uses reinforcement learning to make logic synthesis and place-and-route decisions; it added ai tools for verification and test in 2023, and a generative ai assistant built with microsoft the same year. the famous research result is disputed. in 2021 google researchers reported in nature that a reinforcement learning system, later called alphachip, placed parts of a chip “in under six hours” and beat human-made layouts, and google used it in designing its tpus. since then, independent researchers at uc san diego re-implemented the method and found it did not consistently beat established placement methods; in their comparisons it never produced shorter wiring than a commercial placer. in 2023 nature added an editor’s note saying the claims had been called into question, and the accompanying commentary was retracted. google’s authors reject the criticism. our view: designing chips still needs human intelligence today: deciding what to build, what to trade away, and what “good enough” means for a product. but at some point ai is going to design chips. the steps are already being automated one at a time, from placement to verification, and each one that falls makes the next easier. the other view: chip design is unforgiving in a way most software is not. a mistake found after manufacture can cost a new mask set and months, so the industry adopts new methods slowly and demands proof; the alphachip dispute shows how hard that proof is to get. on this view ai becomes a powerful assistant inside the tools, while people stay accountable for the design for a long time yet. analysis: either way, the safest career bet is the same: understand the fundamentals well enough to direct the tools and to check their answers.

c.h: Starting a GPU company: the bottlenecks
c.x: starting a gpu company: the bottlenecks suppose you want to build a company that makes gpus or ai accelerators. the good news first: you do not need your own factory. almost every chip company today, nvidia included, is fabless : it designs chips and pays a foundry to make them. that is just as well, because a modern fab costs tens of billions of dollars. what it takes to ship a gpu, and where the bottlenecks are seven layers, from the top: software such as drivers, compilers and libraries, where nvidia’s cuda has been building since 2007; architecture and rtl design, which needs people who have done it before; verification, most of the effort and risk; physical design with eda tools; masks and wafers at a foundry, which need money and a production slot; lithography machines, where only asml makes euv machines; and memory and packaging, where three companies make hbm memory. five of the layers are highlighted as bottlenecks. the layers of a gpu company what makes it hard software: drivers, compilers, libraries nvidia's cuda has been building since 2007 architecture and rtl design people who have done it before verification most of the effort, and the most risk physical design (eda tools) commercial tools and experience masks and wafers at a foundry money, and a slot at tsmc or similar lithography machines only asml makes euv machines memory (hbm) and packaging three hbm makers; scarce advanced packaging a gpu is not only a chip. the highlighted layers are the usual bottlenecks; the two at the bottom are owned by a handful of companies worldwide, and the one at the top, software, is where most challengers have struggled. even without a factory, five things stand in the way: software, the biggest moat. a gpu is only useful if people’s code runs on it. nvidia released cuda in 2007, and nearly two decades of libraries, tools and habits have grown around it. a new chip needs drivers, a compiler and libraries good enough that customers do not have to rewrite their models. money for each attempt. a complete mask set can need as many as 30 masks, and each attempt at an advanced process means a new set and wafers before you know whether the chip works. manufacturing that a few companies control. leading-edge chips are made by a small number of foundries, tsmc above all, and asml is the world’s only manufacturer of the euv lithography machines those foundries need for the most advanced chips. memory and packaging. ai chips need high-bandwidth memory (hbm), made by sk hynix, samsung and micron, joined to the chip with advanced packaging that is itself in short supply. rules and people. export controls decide who may buy what: in 2023 the us added the chinese gpu maker moore threads to its entity list. and the engineers who have taken a big chip to production before are few and much sought after.

what happened to the challengers real companies show how these bottlenecks play out: company what it tried what happened nvidia founded in 1993 by three engineers; released the geforce 256, the first product it marketed as a gpu, in 1999 built cuda in 2007 and became the company everyone else is measured against graphcore a new kind of processor for ai, founded in 2016 in the uk valued at $1.7 billion in 2018; softbank agreed to buy it in 2024 for around $500 million groq an inference chip, founded in 2016 by former google engineers including one of the tpu’s designers in december 2025 nvidia agreed to license its technology in a deal reportedly worth about $20 billion cerebras one chip the size of a whole wafer, to avoid the cost of connecting many gpus revenue of $510 million in 2025, though 62% of it came from one customer tenstorrent ai chips; jim keller, who designed processors at amd, apple and tesla, joined as cto in 2020 keller became ceo in 2023: a sign of how much one proven chip architect is worth to a young company analysis: the chips were often good. what decided outcomes was usually software, customers and money, which is why the founders who succeed tend to think about those first.

c.h: Choosing where to start, by requirement
c.x: choosing where to start, by requirement nobody starts by taping out a rival to nvidia’s best chip. there are smaller first steps, and which one suits you depends on what is true for you: if this is true for you it leans towards you want to learn and prove an idea cheaply an fpga: real hardware, reprogrammable, no factory needed you want your own design in real silicon, as a first step tiny tapeout: a small tile on a shared chip, built on the open-source skywater 130 nm process; a tile holds about 1,000 logic gates you need a working prototype chip a multi-project wafer service, where several designs share the cost of masks and wafers your strength is architecture, not manufacturing selling your design as licensable ip, as imagination technologies does: its business is designing powervr gpus that other companies build into their chips your strength is software compilers, kernels and tools for existing chips, the layer every new chip needs most you have a narrow workload that gpus serve badly a specialised accelerator for that one job, rather than a general-purpose gpu

c.h: What an electronics engineer needs to learn
c.x: what an electronics engineer needs to learn if you studied electronics, here is what you bring and what to add. analysis , drawn from the roles and bottlenecks above: you probably have add next circuits, transistors, digital logic a hardware description language (verilog or systemverilog) and simulation microprocessors and microcontrollers computer architecture at depth: pipelines, caches, memory bandwidth, and why gpus run thousands of threads at once (see from binary to gpus ) signals and systems, maths the maths of ai workloads: matrix multiplication and how neural networks use it (see neural networks ) some c programming parallel programming with cuda or triton, so you understand what customers will run on your chip lab work and testing verification: test benches and coverage, where most design effort goes engineering judgement the business side: who buys accelerators, what they pay for, and why software decides sales (see how companies are valued )

who makes what, and where it is often said that chips are “made in asia”, and for manufacturing that is largely true. but the chain has many links, and different countries lead different ones: country what it leads in a number to know taiwan making the most advanced chips, for others (tsmc) tsmc produces over 50% of the world’s advanced semiconductors south korea memory (samsung, sk hynix) 60.5% of the global memory market and 70.5% of dram in 2022 china buying chips, and a fast-growing industry of its own (smic, hua hong, jcet) the largest chip market by consumption: 53.7% of worldwide chip sales in 2020, much of it imported japan manufacturing equipment (tokyo electron); it led memory in the 1980s in 2007 taiwan’s chip industry passed america’s, ranking second only to japan’s singapore assembly and test since 1968, wafer fabs since 1984; mostly lower-end chips texas instruments and national semiconductor opened assembly and test plants there in 1968 netherlands lithography machines (asml) the world’s only maker of euv machines united states chip design, design software (eda) and equipment its share of global fab capacity fell from 37% in 1990 to 10% in 2022; it is projected to rise to 14% by 2032 india design talent, and new fabs and packaging under the semicon india programme ₹76,000 crore, then ₹1,27,500 crore for semicon 2.0 analysis: two things follow for anyone outside east asia. manufacturing jobs cluster where the fabs are, and new fabs are being built in the us, europe, japan and india with government money, which is why technician roles are opening in new places. design, verification and chip software are not tied to a fab: fabless companies such as nvidia design chips without owning a factory.

c.h: If AI designs chips, how do people get in?
c.x: if ai designs chips, how do people get in? this is the natural worry: why learn chip design if ai will do it? analysis , from the roles and evidence above, of where people stay valuable even as ai does more: deciding what to build. a chip is a bet on a workload, a market and a price. ai can explore designs, but someone has to set the goal and the trade-offs. checking the ai’s work. verification, proving a design does what is intended, already takes up to 70% of design and development time on large projects; ai-generated designs make it more important, not less. the alphachip dispute shows how hard it is to prove that an automated result is really better. physical work. running fabs, testing wafers and bringing up new silicon in a lab are hands-on jobs; 39% of the us jobs at risk of going unfilled are technicians. building the ai tools. companies such as synopsys are putting ai into design software, and that needs people who understand both chips and machine learning. a way in, step by step, using free tools: learn binary, gates and the adder on from binary to gpus . write verilog and simulate it with free, open-source simulators such as icarus verilog or verilator, which turns verilog into fast c++ models. put the same design on an inexpensive fpga board, so it runs on real hardware. join a tiny tapeout workshop and design a tile that is manufactured on a shared chip. use an ai assistant to draft verilog, then prove it with your own test bench; that habit is the job in miniature. apply for verification, fpga or gpu-kernel roles, or train as a technician near a new fab. our view: ai will design more and more of each chip, and the people who thrive will be those who can tell it what to build and prove that what it built is right. the other view: automation may shrink the number of entry-level design roles, so the safest entry points may be the physical and verification jobs that ai touches least.

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: chips are one of the best bets an engineer can make in the ai era, and an electronics background is a real advantage, not a relic. start small, with an fpga or a tiny tapeout tile, and grow towards the software that every chip needs. the other view: the industry is cyclical and capital-hungry, the big prizes are concentrated in a few companies, and ai tools may shrink some design roles. learning chips is valuable, but building a gpu company is one of the hardest things in technology; most attempts so far have ended in sale or licensing rather than independence.

c.h: From Unix to Linux: a short history, with BSD and Solaris
c.x: from unix to linux: a short history, with bsd and solaris the commands on this page are older than most of the people who type them. ls , pipes, “everything is a file” and the shell all come from unix, started at bell labs in 1969. knowing the family tree explains why linux, macos and the bsds feel alike, and why a script written on one often runs on another. when what happened 1960s bell labs, mit and general electric build multics, an ambitious time-sharing system. bell labs, frustrated by its size and complexity, pulls out. 1969 at bell labs, ken thompson, dennis ritchie and colleagues start unix , first written in assembly language for a pdp-7. 1973 version 4 unix is rewritten in c, a high-level language. a system written in a high-level language can be moved to new machines far more easily, and unix spreads. 1978 the first bsd (berkeley software distribution) release, from the university of california, berkeley, after thompson spent a sabbatical there installing unix; bill joy led early development. 1983 at&t sells unix system v commercially. richard stallman announces the gnu project , to build a complete free unix-compatible operating system. 1988 the first posix standard (ieee 1003.1) defines a common interface, so programs can run on many unix-like systems; its shell and tools are based on system v. 1991 linus torvalds releases the linux kernel on 17 september. gnu had the tools but no working kernel; together they make a complete free system. 1993 sun microsystems’ solaris , based on system v, replaces its bsd-based sunos. solaris becomes known for scaling on sparc servers, and for originating dtrace and zfs. 2005 sun releases most of solaris as open source (opensolaris). 2007 apple’s mac os x 10.5 is certified as unix 03 compliant: macos is a certified unix. 2010 oracle buys sun and discontinues opensolaris. the community continues it as illumos . today linux is the leading operating system on servers, and through android has the largest installed base of any general-purpose operating system. solaris is now oracle solaris, a proprietary unix. family where you meet it now linux (a unix-like kernel, with gnu and other tools) cloud servers, containers, android phones, chromebooks (see docker and kubernetes ) bsd descendants freebsd, openbsd and netbsd; macos’s kernel draws on mach and bsd, and macos is a certified unix commercial unix oracle solaris, ibm aix and hp-ux, still used in certain fields, often on dedicated hardware solaris’s open-source line illumos; zfs and dtrace also reached other systems our view: learn the unix ideas, not one distribution’s quirks: small tools that do one thing, text streams joined by pipes, and files and permissions as the common language. they work on every system in the table, and posix is why. the other view: in practice most engineers now meet only linux, in containers and cloud machines, so time is better spent on linux specifics such as systemd, cgroups and the distribution your servers run.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation navigate, read and search files and logs run, stop and inspect processes understand permissions well enough to fix 'permission denied' 2 practitioner write safe bash scripts with set -euo pipefail, traps and quoting diagnose disk, memory and cpu problems with df, free, top, dmesg manage services with systemd and read journalctl 3 senior tune a host or container for a workload (file limits, memory, i/o) debug with strace, lsof and tcpdump decide when a script should become a real program 4 expert understand kernel mechanisms behind containers (namespaces, cgroups) set the team's base images and hardening standards lead performance investigations end to end each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

dns, step by step where a dns answer comes from four boxes left to right: browser cache, operating system, resolver, authoritative servers. a lookup asks each in turn and stops at the first one that holds a fresh answer. the answer travels back, and each layer keeps it for the record's ttl, which is why a changed record takes up to one ttl to be seen everywhere. browser cache operating system resolver authoritative ask in turn until one has a fresh answer the answer comes back, and each layer caches it for the ttl lower the ttl a day before a planned change a dns lookup stops at the first cache with a fresh answer, and every layer keeps the answer for the record’s ttl. that is why a change can take up to one ttl to reach everyone.

http & tls status classes: 2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx your request is wrong (401 no/invalid credentials, 403 authenticated but not allowed, 404 missing, 429 rate limited), 5xx the server failed (502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 upstream timeout). http/1.1 one request at a time per connection; http/2 multiplexes streams on one tcp connection (grpc uses it); http/3 runs over quic on udp. tls proves the server's identity with a certificate chain to a trusted root, then encrypts. sni sends the hostname so one ip can serve many certificates. mtls : the client also presents a certificate. common inside service meshes. a proxy that terminates tls can read and route on the request; one that passes it through (l4) cannot. openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null \ | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates curl -vi https://example.com # handshake, headers curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns %{time_namelookup} connect %{time_connect} tls %{time_appconnect} ttfb %{time_starttransfer} total %{time_total}\n' https://example.com

troubleshooting commands ping -c 3 10.0.0.5 # icmp reachability (often blocked; not proof) nc -vz db.internal 5432 # is the tcp port open? traceroute -n host / mtr host # where packets stop curl -v http://svc:8080/health # app-level answer ss -tulpn # what is listening locally ip addr; ip route # my addresses and routes cat /etc/resolv.conf # which resolver am i using getent hosts db.internal # resolve the way apps do sudo tcpdump -i any -n port 5432 -c 20 # see packets

"cannot connect": read the error could not resolve host / nxdomain: dns. wrong name, wrong resolver, or a private zone not visible from here. connection refused: the host answered but nothing listens on that port, or the app binds to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0 . connection timed out: packets are dropped. firewall, security group, missing route, or no nat for egress. tls / certificate error: name mismatch, expired certificate, missing intermediate, or a corporate proxy re-signing traffic. 403 from a proxy or website: first suspect your own egress (datacentre ip, proxy policy) before blaming the far side. works locally, fails in the cloud: compare egress path, dns resolver and credentials, not code.

nat, proxies, load balancers nat lets private hosts reach the internet through a shared public ip. inbound connections are not possible through it. forward proxy acts for clients going out (egress control, allowlists). reverse proxy acts for servers taking traffic in (nginx, envoy, cloud lbs). load balancer health checks decide which backends get traffic. a failing check looks like a 502/503 to clients. stateful firewalls allow the reply to an allowed connection automatically; you write rules for the initiating direction only. bastion / iap tunnel reaches private hosts without giving them public ips.

gcp networking map piece what it does vpc global private network. subnets are regional and carry the ip ranges. firewall rules / policies stateful allow/deny, ingress or egress, targeted by network tag or service account. default: deny ingress, allow egress. cloud nat outbound internet for vms, gke nodes and cloud run (with vpc egress) that have no public ip. gives a fixed egress ip to allowlist. private google access lets private-only hosts reach google apis (bigquery, gcs) without a public ip. private service connect / private services access private ips for managed services such as cloud sql, reachable only from the vpc. direct vpc egress / serverless vpc access connector connects cloud run and cloud functions to private ips in the vpc. cloud load balancing global external http(s) (l7), regional internal, and network (l4) load balancers. managed certificates. cloud armor waf and ip allow/deny in front of an external http(s) load balancer. cloud dns public and private zones; private zones resolve only inside chosen vpcs. vpc service controls a perimeter around google apis so data cannot be copied out to another project. gcloud compute networks list gcloud compute networks subnets list --network=default gcloud compute firewall-rules list --format="table(name,direction,sourceranges.list(),allowed[].map().firewall_rule().list(),targettags.list())" gcloud compute routers nats list --router=my-router --region=asia-south1 gcloud compute ssh vm-1 --tunnel-through-iap # no public ip needed

l: How the Internet Is Tied Together

c.x: the pieces piece what it does autonomous systems each internet provider, cloud or large company runs its own network, an autonomous system, with its own block of addresses. bgp (border gateway protocol) how autonomous systems tell each other which addresses they can reach. it is the internet's map, and every network trusts the others to describe it honestly. internet exchange points buildings full of switches where many networks connect directly and exchange traffic, instead of sending it the long way round. submarine cables fibre-optic cables on the sea bed carry the great majority of data between continents. dns and the root servers dns turns names into addresses. at its top are thirteen well-known root server addresses, served by many copies around the world. content delivery networks akamai, cloudflare and others keep copies of websites close to users and absorb attacks, so a large share of the web passes through them. cloud regions huge data centres run by a few providers, where much of today's software and data live. see how the cloud is built .

when a shared piece fails 4 october 2021, bgp: facebook withdrew the routes to its own name servers in a burst of bgp updates, and its services were unavailable worldwide for six to seven hours. 20 october 2025, a cloud region: services in aws's northern virginia region (us-east-1) failed, taking down sites such as roblox, fortnite, snapchat and duolingo. 18 november 2025, a cdn: a cloudflare outage took down major platforms, including x and chatgpt. each one is a single shared dependency that many companies chose independently. see kubernetes dr and sre on designing for it.

what engineers can do know your dependencies: dns provider, cdn, cloud region, identity provider, payment gateway. write them down. avoid one region for everything that must stay up; test failing over before you need it. lower dns ttls before planned changes, and keep a way to switch providers. show an honest status when a dependency is down, rather than a confusing error. see observability .
