c.h: What happens when you open a URL
c.x: what happens when you open a url parse the url and check the browser cache, including a cached hsts rule that forces https. dns resolves the host name to an ip address (browser cache → os → resolver → authoritative servers). connect: tcp handshake (or quic over udp for http/3), then the tls handshake proves the server's identity and agrees keys. http request with method, path, headers and cookies, usually reaching a cdn or load balancer first. server side: load balancer → reverse proxy → application → database or cache → response. http response : status, headers (caching, cookies, security), and the body (html, json, images). render: parse html into the dom, css into the cssom, run javascript, lay out, paint, and fetch the sub-resources the page references. after load: javascript calls apis ( fetch ), updates the page, and may open websockets or server-sent events. every step can fail or be slow. browser devtools (network tab: timing, headers, initiator) shows which. what happens when you open a url a sequence diagram with four lifelines: the browser, dns, a cdn or load balancer, and the application with its database or cache. 1: the browser asks dns for the host name's ip address and 2: gets it back. 3: it opens a tcp connection, or quic for http/3, and 4: the tls handshake proves the server's identity and agrees keys. 5: the browser sends the http request, which reaches the cdn or load balancer first. 6: that passes it to the application, which 7: reads the database or cache. 8: the response comes back with status, headers and body. 9: the browser renders the page and fetches what it references. browser dns cdn / lb app + data 1 ip address of shop.example? 2 the address (cached for its ttl) 3 tcp handshake (or quic) 4 tls handshake: identity, keys 5 get / + headers, cookies 6 forward the request read db or cache 7 8 200, headers, html render, fetch css, js, images 9 the list above, drawn as a uml sequence diagram, one arrow per step. every arrow can fail or be slow; the network tab in devtools shows which.

anatomy of a url https://shop.example.com:443/v1/orders/123?store=1_05&page=2#items └─┬─┘ └──────┬───────┘└┬─┘└─────┬──────┘└───────┬────────┘└─┬──┘ scheme host port path query fragment origin = scheme + host + port. it is the browser's security boundary. path names the resource; query parameters filter or modify it. fragment ( #… ) never reaches the server; the browser uses it to scroll or route. encoding: special characters are percent-encoded ( space → %20 , + in a query can mean a space). encode parameters with a library, not by hand.

http request and response get /v1/orders/123 http/1.1 host: shop.example.com accept: application/json accept-encoding: br, gzip authorization: bearer eyj… if-none-match: "a1b2c3" http/1.1 200 ok content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 content-encoding: br cache-control: private, max-age=60 etag: "a1b2c3" strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000; includesubdomains {"id":"123","order_ref":"ord-2024-000123", …} content negotiation: accept / content-type for format, accept-language for language, accept-encoding for compression. compression: brotli or gzip for text; never for already-compressed images or video. mime types tell the browser what it received; a wrong one breaks scripts or opens security holes.

status codes you will see code means 200 / 201 / 204 ok / created / ok with no body 301 / 308 moved permanently (308 keeps the method) 302 / 307 temporary redirect (307 keeps the method) 304 not modified: use your cached copy 400 malformed or invalid request 401 not authenticated (missing or bad credentials) 403 authenticated but not allowed 404 / 410 not found / gone for good 409 / 422 conflict / valid syntax but semantically invalid 429 too many requests; see retry-after 500 server error 502 / 503 / 504 bad gateway / unavailable / gateway timeout (usually a proxy talking to a sick backend)

cookies, sessions and tokens http is stateless. state across requests comes from cookies or tokens the client sends each time. cookie : set by set-cookie , sent back automatically to the same site. flags that matter: secure (https only), httponly (javascript cannot read it), samesite=lax|strict|none (whether it goes on cross-site requests), domain , path , max-age . server session: the cookie holds a random id; data lives on the server (or redis). easy to revoke. token (jwt): the client sends authorization: bearer … ; the server validates it without a lookup. harder to revoke; keep it short-lived. see oauth & oidc . browser storage: localstorage and sessionstorage are readable by any script on the page, so never keep secrets there; indexeddb for larger client data.

same-origin policy and cors by default, a script on https://app.example.com cannot read responses from another origin such as https://api.example.com . cors lets the api opt in with response headers: access-control-allow-origin: https://app.example.com . preflight: for non-simple requests (custom headers, json bodies, put/delete) the browser first sends options and checks access-control-allow-methods and -headers . credentials (cookies) cross-origin need access-control-allow-credentials: true and an exact origin, never * . cors protects users in browsers; it is not server-side access control. curl ignores it. serving the app and api from the same origin (e.g. /api on the same host) avoids cors entirely.

caching on the web header effect cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable cache everywhere for a year; for fingerprinted assets like app.3f2a9c.js cache-control: private, max-age=60 only the user's browser may cache, for 60 s cache-control: no-cache may store, but must revalidate before each use cache-control: no-store never store (sensitive data) etag + if-none-match revalidate cheaply; server answers 304 if unchanged vary: accept-encoding cache separate copies per header value layers: browser cache → cdn → reverse proxy → application cache → database. fingerprint static files so you can cache them forever and still deploy changes instantly.

rendering models model how good for trade-offs server-side rendering (classic) server returns full html per request content sites, seo, simple apps full page reloads; server does the work single-page app (spa) browser loads js once, renders and routes on the client, calls json apis rich interactive tools (react, vue, angular) slower first load, seo effort, more client code ssr + hydration server renders html, then js takes over on the client fast first paint with interactivity (next.js, nuxt) complexity; double rendering work static site generation (ssg) html built at deploy time, served from a cdn docs, marketing, blogs content changes need a rebuild progressive web app (pwa) web app with a manifest and service worker for offline and install app-like experiences without an app store platform differences, caching complexity native wrapper web app inside a native shell (capacitor, cordova) store presence and device apis from one codebase native build and signing still required

how the browser renders html parsed into the dom ; css into the cssom . combined into a render tree; layout computes sizes and positions; paint draws pixels; composite layers them. render-blocking resources (css, synchronous scripts in <head> ) delay the first paint. use defer or type="module" for scripts. javascript runs on one main thread; long tasks block input. move heavy work to web workers.

performance: core web vitals metric measures good lcp (largest contentful paint) when the main content appears ≤ 2.5 s inp (interaction to next paint) how quickly the page responds to input ≤ 200 ms cls (cumulative layout shift) how much the layout jumps ≤ 0.1 serve from a cdn; compress; cache fingerprinted assets. send less javascript; split bundles by route; lazy-load below-the-fold images. size images correctly; use modern formats (webp, avif) and give width and height to avoid shifts. measure with lighthouse in the lab and real-user data in the field.

web security essentials https everywhere plus hsts , so browsers never fall back to http. xss (cross-site scripting): untrusted data rendered as html runs as script. escape output (frameworks do it by default), avoid innerhtml with user data, and add a content-security-policy . csrf : another site makes the user's browser send a cookie-authenticated request. use samesite cookies and csrf tokens for cookie-based sessions. clickjacking : your page framed invisibly. use frame-ancestors in csp. mixed content : http resources on an https page are blocked or warned. subresource integrity ( integrity= ) for scripts from cdns. more on the security tab. content-security-policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; frame-ancestors 'none' x-content-type-options: nosniff referrer-policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

accessibility basics semantic html first: <button> , <nav> , <main> , headings in order, <label> for every input. keyboard: everything usable with tab, enter and space; visible focus outlines. text alternatives: alt on meaningful images; empty alt="" on decorative ones. contrast: at least 4.5:1 for normal text (wcag aa). aria only when html has no native element for the job. test with a screen reader and automated checks (axe, lighthouse); they catch different things.

servers on the web web server / reverse proxy (nginx, envoy): tls, static files, compression, routing to apps. application server : runs your code (spring boot with tomcat or netty, quarkus with vert.x, gunicorn or uvicorn for python). cdn : caches content near users and absorbs traffic spikes and attacks. real-time : websockets (two-way) and server-sent events (server to browser, simpler, works over http). http versions : http/1.1 (one request at a time per connection), http/2 (multiplexed streams), http/3 (over quic, better on lossy networks).

devtools habits network: status, timing waterfall, request and response headers, "disable cache", throttling, "copy as curl". console: javascript errors and cors failures, which say exactly which header is missing. application: cookies with their flags, storage, service workers. performance and lighthouse: long tasks, layout shifts, core web vitals. elements: live dom and css, accessibility tree.

the short answer a search engine does most of its work before you ever type anything. it is constantly exploring the web, reading pages and filing what it finds in an enormous index, a bit like the index at the back of a book that says which pages mention which words. when you search, it is not reading the web at that moment; it is looking up your words in that index and deciding which of the matching pages deserve to be at the top. google describes this in its own documentation as three stages: crawling, indexing and serving , and says plainly that not every page makes it through each one. in the last two years a fourth layer has been added on top, ai that writes a summary answer, and the same ai is now moving into the browser itself. how a search engine answers a query four stages from left to right: crawl, where googlebot follows links and renders pages with chrome; index, where duplicate pages are clustered and words and signals are stored; rank and serve, where the query is matched and hundreds of factors are weighed; and an ai layer, where ai overviews and ai mode summarise results. before you search when you search crawl follow links, render with chrome index cluster duplicates, store words and signals rank and serve match the query, weigh hundreds of factors ai layer ai overviews and ai mode summarise crawling and indexing run all the time; ranking and the ai layer run when you press enter google describes search in three stages, crawling, indexing and serving. the ai layer sits on top of the third: ai overviews still draw on pages that went through all three.

stage one: crawling there is no central register of all web pages, so google has to keep looking for new and changed ones. it calls this url discovery . some pages it already knows; others it finds by following a link from a page it knows; others are listed by site owners in a sitemap . the program that fetches pages is googlebot . an algorithm decides which sites to crawl, how often and how many pages to fetch, and the crawler deliberately slows down so it does not overload a site; an http 500 error, for example, means “slow down”. while crawling, google renders the page and runs its javascript using a recent version of chrome, just as your browser would, because many sites build their content with javascript. site owners can keep crawlers out of parts of a site with a robots.txt file.

stage two: indexing next google works out what each page is about, reading its text and key tags such as the <title> element and image alt attributes. it also groups pages with similar content into a cluster and picks the most representative one as the canonical , the version that may be shown in results; the others are kept as alternates, for example for mobile. it collects signals about the canonical page, such as its language, the country it is relevant to and how usable it is, and stores all this in the google index, a large database spread over thousands of computers. again, indexing is not guaranteed: low-quality content or a noindex rule can keep a page out. the core data structure behind any index like this is an inverted index : instead of storing “page → words”, it stores “word → pages”, so looking up a word is instant however many pages there are.

stage three: ranking and serving when you search, google’s machines look up the matching pages in the index and return the ones it judges most relevant and of the highest quality. google says relevance is decided by hundreds of factors , including your location, language and device: “bicycle repair shops” gives different results in paris and in hong kong. it also says it does not accept payment to rank pages higher; ads are shown separately. google publishes a guide to its ranking systems. a few that show how search has evolved: system what it does pagerank judges a page’s importance by the number and quality of links to it. it was one of google’s core systems at launch; google says it has evolved a lot and is still part of the core rankbrain a machine learning system, confirmed in 2015, that helps google understand how words relate to concepts bert a language model applied to english searches in the us from october 2019, and to over 70 languages by december that year; it helps understand how combinations of words change meaning neural matching matches the concepts in a query with the concepts in pages, even when the words differ passage ranking identifies individual sections, or passages, of a page, so one useful section of a long page can be found freshness and spam systems prefer newer pages when a query needs them, and keep spam out

c.h: Run it: a search engine in forty lines
c.x: run it: a search engine in forty lines the real thing runs on thousands of computers, but every stage fits in a small python program. this one crawls four pages by following links, builds an inverted index, computes pagerank with the usual damping factor of 0.85, and ranks results by combining matching words with pagerank: # a search engine in about 40 lines: crawl, index, rank, serve. import math, re from collections import defaultdict # 1. the "web": four pages and the links between them. web = { "home": ("bicycle repair guide and shop list", ["tyres", "brakes", "shops"]), "tyres": ("how to fix a flat bicycle tyre", ["home"]), "brakes": ("adjusting bicycle brakes safely", ["home", "tyres"]), "shops": ("bicycle repair shops near you", ["home"]), } # 2. crawl: start from one page and follow links, like googlebot. seen, queue = set(), ["home"] while queue: url = queue.pop(0) if url not in seen: seen.add(url) queue += web[url][1] # 3. index: an inverted index maps each word to the pages that contain it. index = defaultdict(set) for url in seen: for word in re.findall(r"[a-z]+", web[url][0].lower()): index[word].add(url) # 4. pagerank: a page is important if important pages link to it. d, rank = 0.85, {u: 1 / len(seen) for u in seen} for _ in range(50): rank = {u: (1 - d) / len(seen) + d * sum(rank[v] / len(web[v][1]) for v in seen if u in web[v][1]) for u in seen} # 5. serve: score pages by matching words (rarer words count more) times pagerank. def search(query): scores = defaultdict(float) for word in query.lower().split(): pages = index.get(word, set()) for url in pages: scores[url] += math.log(len(seen) / len(pages)) + 0.1 return sorted(((s * rank[u], u) for u, s in scores.items()), reverse=true) print("crawled:", sorted(seen)) print("index['bicycle']:", sorted(index["bicycle"])) print("pagerank:", {u: round(r, 3) for u, r in sorted(rank.items())}) for q in ["bicycle repair", "flat tyre"]: print(f"search {q!r}:", [(u, round(s, 3)) for s, u in search(q)]) what it printed when we ran it: crawled: ['brakes', 'home', 'shops', 'tyres'] index['bicycle']: ['brakes', 'home', 'shops', 'tyres'] pagerank: {'brakes': 0.163, 'home': 0.442, 'shops': 0.163, 'tyres': 0.232} search 'bicycle repair': [('home', 0.395), ('shops', 0.145), ('tyres', 0.023), ('brakes', 0.016)] search 'flat tyre': [('tyres', 0.69)] look at the search for “bicycle repair”. the home page and the shops page both contain both words, so on words alone they tie. the home page wins because three pages link to it, so its pagerank is highest. that is the idea that set google apart in its early years: links are votes , and votes from important pages count for more.

c.h: AI on the results page: AI Overviews and AI Mode
c.x: ai on the results page: ai overviews and ai mode google first tested ai-written answers as the search generative experience in may 2023. at google i/o in may 2024 it renamed them ai overviews and launched them in the united states, then globally by october 2024. they use google’s gemini models. ai mode goes further, for questions that need more exploration and reasoning. google’s documentation says both may use a query fan-out technique: issuing several related searches across subtopics and data sources to build an answer. they are built on the same index: to appear as a supporting link, a page must already be indexed and eligible to show a snippet, and google says there are no extra requirements beyond normal search best practice. site owners can limit what is shown with nosnippet , data-nosnippet , max-snippet or noindex . what it changes: a december 2024 study by botify and demandsphere found that when an ai overview and a featured snippet appear together, they take up about 67% of the screen on desktop and 76% on mobile, so even the top-ranked page may not be visible without scrolling. google says people have been visiting a greater diversity of websites with ai overviews. analysis: those two statements can both be true, and which matters more depends on whether you are a reader looking for an answer or a publisher who depends on visits.

how browsers are adding ai the browser is where we read, shop, work and sign in, so it is a natural home for an ai assistant. browsers are adding ai at three levels: level what it does examples assistant in a sidebar summarises the page, answers questions about it, rewrites text microsoft edge added bing chat, now copilot, in february 2023; brave added leo in november 2023; chrome added the gemini chatbot, at first for us users on windows in english; firefox lets you pick a chatbot provider such as chatgpt, claude, copilot, gemini or le chat a model on your own device runs ai locally, without sending the page to a server in 2026 chrome installed gemini nano, a 4 gb local model, on an unspecified number of desktops; it was criticised for doing so without telling users agentic browser takes actions for you: navigates, fills in forms, sends emails, buys things perplexity’s comet (july 2025, free from october 2025); openai’s chatgpt atlas (october 2025, macos only); opera neon (2025); dia the new agentic browsers, comet, atlas and opera’s, are built on chromium , the open-source project behind chrome, so the ai is what sets them apart, not the engine. the field is moving fast and not every attempt lasts: openai folded atlas into a single desktop app with chatgpt and codex, and the browser shut down on 9 august 2026.

c.h: The risks: injection, publishers and competition
c.x: the risks: injection, publishers and competition prompt injection. an ai that reads web pages can be steered by text hidden in them, and an agentic browser can then act on those instructions with your logged-in accounts. researchers at layerx security described an attack on comet they called “cometjacking” that could send a user’s personal data to an attacker’s server. the wider problem is covered on agentic ai security . publishers. when the answer appears on the results page or in the browser’s sidebar, fewer people may click through to the site that wrote it. the associated press noted at atlas’s launch that this could reduce referrals to online publishers. competition. in august 2024 a us federal judge, amit mehta, ruled that google held an illegal monopoly in search. in september 2025 he ruled that google would not have to sell chrome or android, but barred it from exclusive search contracts and required it to share some data with competitors; parts of that ruling are under appeal by both sides.

c.h: Choosing how much AI you want, by requirement
c.x: choosing how much ai you want, by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards you want answers quickly and will check important ones ai overviews or a sidebar assistant, following the cited links when it matters you must not send page content to a third party on-device models, or a browser that lets you choose or bring your own model you want repetitive web tasks done for you an agentic browser, used first on accounts where a mistake is cheap you are signed in to banking, email or work systems keep agent features off in that browser profile; prompt injection is not solved you run a website the same basics as always, crawlable, indexable, useful pages, plus the snippet controls if you want to limit what ai shows

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: search is becoming an answer engine, and the browser is becoming an assistant. understanding the old machinery, crawling, indexing and links as votes, is the best way to judge the new layer, because the ai still stands on that index. the other view: some see ai answers as a threat to the open web that search was built on, since they keep readers away from the sites that did the work; others see them as the biggest improvement to search in years. both sides point to real evidence, and the outcome is not settled.

mental model image: a read-only stack of layers plus metadata (entrypoint, env, user). built from a dockerfile, named registry/repo:tag , pinned exactly by @sha256:digest . container: a running process from an image, with its own filesystem layer, network and process namespace. not a vm: it shares the host kernel. layer cache: each instruction is a layer. a change invalidates that layer and every one after it, so put what changes least first. volume: storage that outlives the container. anything written elsewhere disappears with it. tag vs digest: a tag can be moved to a new image; a digest cannot. deploy by digest or by an immutable tag such as the commit sha.

the layer cache, drawn how the layer cache decides what to rebuild two copies of the same dockerfile, five instructions each, from from at the top to cmd at the bottom. on the left, only the source code changed: the first three layers come from the cache and only copy of the source and the layers after it are rebuilt. on the right, the requirements file changed: that layer and every layer after it are rebuilt, including the slow dependency install. putting what changes least first keeps rebuilds short. you changed src/ from python:3.13-slim cached copy requirements.txt cached run pip install cached copy src/ rebuilt cmd [...] rebuilt you changed requirements.txt from python:3.13-slim cached copy requirements.txt rebuilt run pip install rebuilt copy src/ rebuilt cmd [...] rebuilt a change rebuilds its own layer and every layer after it: put what changes least first the same five-line dockerfile twice. changing your code rebuilds two layers; changing the dependency list rebuilds four, including the slow install. order the instructions from least to most often changed.

everyday commands docker build -t api:dev . docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -e app_profile=local api:dev docker run -d --name db -e postgres_password=pw -p 5433:5432 postgres:16 docker ps -a docker logs -f --tail=100 db docker exec -it db psql -u postgres docker stop db && docker rm db docker images docker image inspect api:dev --format '{{.config.user}} {{.size}}' docker history api:dev # layer sizes docker inspect db --format '{{.state.exitcode}} {{.state.oomkilled}}' docker stats # live cpu and memory docker tag api:dev asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:3f2a9c1 gcloud auth configure-docker asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev docker push asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:3f2a9c1 docker system df # what uses disk docker system prune # stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, unused build cache docker builder prune # build cache

a good dockerfile # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 from python:3.12-slim as base env pythonunbuffered=1 pythondontwritebytecode=1 workdir /app # dependencies first: cached until requirements change copy requirements.txt . run --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt # then the code, which changes often copy src/ ./src/ run useradd --uid 1001 --no-create-home app user 1001 expose 8080 entrypoint ["python", "-m", "src.main"] # .dockerignore: keeps the build context small and secrets out .git .venv __pycache__/ *.pyc .env node_modules/ target/ build/

multi-stage builds # build with the full toolchain, ship only the result from eclipse-temurin:21-jdk as build workdir /src copy gradle/ gradle/ copy gradlew settings.gradle.kts build.gradle.kts ./ run ./gradlew dependencies --no-daemon # cache dependencies copy src/ src/ run ./gradlew bootjar --no-daemon -x test from gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian13 # no shell, no package manager copy --from=build /src/build/libs/app.jar /app.jar user nonroot entrypoint ["java", "-xx:maxrampercentage=75", "-jar", "/app.jar"] # build one stage only docker build --target build -t api:build . distroless images have no shell, which makes them smaller and safer but harder to debug. keep a -debug variant or use an ephemeral debug container.

c.h: Base images as a template: update once, like a parent POM
c.x: base images as a template: update once, like a parent pom in maven, every project inherits from a parent pom (ultimately the super pom), so shared settings live in one place and a project picks up a change by moving to a new parent version. container images can work the same way: one organisation base image holds what every service needs, and every service’s dockerfile starts from it. maven containers parent pom, with shared plugins and settings base image, with the jre, ca certificates, a non-root user, time zone and shared jvm settings the <parent> version a project points at the base image tag (and digest) in from releasing a new parent version rebuilding and publishing the base image a bot or a person bumping the parent version in each project dependabot (or a similar bot) opening a pull request to bump the base image in each service 1. one base image, built in one place. # java-runtime/dockerfile: the organisation's base image, built and published by one pipeline from eclipse-temurin:21-jre@sha256:<digest> # pinned; dependabot proposes updates run groupadd --system app && useradd --system --gid app app copy certs/company-root-ca.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/ run update-ca-certificates env tz=utc user app 2. services take the base image as an argument. docker allows arg before the first from , and from can use that value, so the base image is a default you can override at build time. # orders-service/dockerfile: every service starts from the base image arg base_image=registry.example.com/platform/java-runtime:21 from ${base_image} workdir /application copy target/orders-service.jar app.jar entrypoint ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"] # normal build: the default base image docker build --pull -t orders-service:dev . # try a new base image without editing the dockerfile docker build --build-arg base_image=registry.example.com/platform/java-runtime:21-rc -t orders-service:test . 3. let a bot keep every service current. docker’s best-practice guide recommends pinning base images to a digest, because tags are mutable, and using dependabot’s docker ecosystem to raise pull requests that update tags and digests on a schedule: you stay in control, with an audit trail. it also recommends rebuilding images often, with --pull , so security fixes in the base reach your images. # .github/dependabot.yml in each service repository version: 2 updates: - package-ecosystem: "docker" directory: "/" schedule: interval: "weekly" our view: a pinned organisation base image, updated by pull requests that run each service’s tests, gives the control of a parent pom without surprise changes at build time. the other view: some teams prefer no dockerfiles at all and let a buildpack builder choose and patch the base (spring boot’s build-image , below); that centralises the base even further, at the cost of less control over what is inside it.

c.h: Images for Spring Boot, Quarkus and Dataflow jobs
c.x: images for spring boot, quarkus and dataflow jobs kind ways to build the image where the base image is chosen spring boot service a dockerfile using spring boot’s layer extraction (below), or mvn spring-boot:build-image , which builds an oci image with cloud native buildpacks and runs it as a non-root user the from lines; for buildpacks, the plugin’s builder and runimage settings, which can live in the parent pom quarkus service a container-image extension: jib (dependencies cached in their own layer, no docker daemon needed to build), docker or podman (using the dockerfiles quarkus generates under src/main/docker ), openshift, or buildpack the generated dockerfiles, or the extension’s configuration; with jib, a red hat ubi openjdk runtime image unless you change it dataflow pipeline a custom sdk container, starting from an apache beam sdk image, and a flex template image that launches the job (below) the beam sdk image tag, which must match the java version you launch the pipeline with, and the google-provided template launcher base image spring boot, layered. spring boot’s documentation shows extracting the jar into four layers (dependencies, the loader, snapshot dependencies, your application), so docker only re-ships the layer that changed. # spring boot: split the jar into layers so a code change does not re-ship the dependencies from bellsoft/liberica-openjre-debian:25-cds as builder workdir /builder arg jar_file=target/*.jar copy ${jar_file} application.jar run java -djarmode=tools -jar application.jar extract --layers --destination extracted from bellsoft/liberica-openjre-debian:25-cds workdir /application copy --from=builder /builder/extracted/dependencies/ ./ copy --from=builder /builder/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./ copy --from=builder /builder/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./ copy --from=builder /builder/extracted/application/ ./ entrypoint ["java", "-jar", "application.jar"] dataflow. google recommends that, if a pipeline needs a custom container, the flex template uses the same image, so the launcher has the same dependencies as the job. the image copies the template launcher binary from a google-provided base image and names the main class. # dataflow flex template for a java pipeline: one image that launches the job from gcr.io/dataflow-templates-base/image_name:tag as template_launcher # a google-provided base image from apache/beam_java11_sdk:beam_version # the pipeline's runtime image; match the java version you launch with copy --from=template_launcher /opt/google/dataflow/java_template_launcher /opt/google/dataflow/java_template_launcher copy target/my-pipeline-bundled.jar /template/ env flex_template_java_main_class="com.example.mypipeline" env flex_template_java_classpath="/template/*" with the base-image pattern above, the runtime stages of all three can start from images your platform team owns and pins, so one update reaches every service and job through ordinary pull requests.

instructions that trip people up entrypoint vs cmd : entrypoint is the program; cmd supplies default arguments that docker run image … replaces. exec form ["java","-jar","app.jar"] runs your process as pid 1 so it receives sigterm . shell form java -jar app.jar wraps it in /bin/sh , which may not forward signals. copy over add : add also unpacks archives and fetches urls, which surprises people. arg vs env : arg exists only at build time; env persists into the running container. neither is a safe place for secrets: use run --mount=type=secret . one run per logical step, cleaning up in the same command: apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* . pin base images to a version ( python:3.12-slim ) or a digest, never latest .

docker compose for local stacks # compose.yaml services: db: image: postgres:16 environment: postgres_password: pw postgres_db: shop ports: ["${db_port:-5433}:5432"] volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data] healthcheck: test: ["cmd-shell", "pg_isready -u postgres"] interval: 5s retries: 10 api: build: . ports: ["${app_port:-8080}:8080"] environment: db_host: db # service name is the hostname depends_on: db: { condition: service_healthy } volumes: dbdata: docker compose up -d --build docker compose logs -f api docker compose exec db psql -u postgres shop docker compose down # keep volumes docker compose down -v # also delete volumes (data gone) docker compose -p wt2 up -d # second copy with its own project name

multi-platform & build secrets # apple silicon builds arm64 by default; cloud run and most servers need amd64 docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 -t registry/api:3f2a9c1 --push . docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t registry/api:3f2a9c1 --push . docker image inspect api:dev --format '{{.os}}/{{.architecture}}' # secret available during one run, never stored in a layer docker build --secret id=pip_token,env=pip_token . run --mount=type=secret,id=pip_token \ pip_index_url="https://__token__:$(cat /run/secrets/pip_token)@pypi.example.com/simple" \ pip install -r requirements.txt

debugging containers symptom check exits immediately docker logs ; docker inspect … .state.exitcode . 137 = killed (often oom), 139 = segfault, 1 = app error, 127 = command not found. "exec format error" wrong cpu architecture: rebuild with --platform linux/amd64 . port works inside, not from host app binds to 127.0.0.1; bind 0.0.0.0. or a missing -p host:container . cannot reach another container use the service name on a shared network, not localhost . permission denied on a volume container user's uid does not own the host directory. image is huge docker history ; move build tools to a build stage; add a .dockerignore . build ignores code change cached layer: check copy order, or --no-cache once. docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh api:dev # look inside the image docker run --rm -it --network container:db nicolaka/netshoot # debug its network

image security run as a non-root user ( user 1001 ). start from a minimal base (slim, distroless, or alpine where musl is fine). fewer packages, fewer cves. scan images in ci: trivy image registry/api:tag , or artifact registry's built-in scanning. never bake secrets into an image or a layer; anyone who can pull it can read them with docker history or by unpacking layers. rebuild regularly so base-image security fixes reach you. generate an sbom ( docker buildx build --sbom=true or syft ) so you can answer "are we affected?" quickly.

the short answer our view: pick the structure that makes your most frequent operation cheap. looking things up by key: a hash table. keeping things in order: a sorted array or a balanced tree. always taking the smallest or most urgent next: a heap. then estimate the cost with big o, and measure, because constants and hardware matter too.

c.h: Time and space complexity, in plain words
c.x: time and space complexity, in plain words time complexity asks: if the input gets ten times bigger, how much longer does the work take? space complexity asks the same about memory. neither measures seconds or megabytes; they describe how the cost grows , which is what decides whether code that is fine on 100 test rows survives a million real ones. shape an everyday picture in code constant , o(1) collecting your coat with a numbered ticket: one step, however many coats there are reading array[i] ; looking up a key in a hash map logarithmic , o(log n) finding a word in a dictionary by opening it in the middle and halving each time binary search; a lookup in a sorted index linear , o(n) reading every name on a list to find one person one loop over the data n log n sorting a deck of cards well good general-purpose sorting quadratic , o(n²) everyone at a party shaking hands with everyone else a loop inside a loop over the same data reading your own code: one loop over the input is n; a loop inside it is n times n; cutting the problem in half each step is log n; a fixed number of steps is constant. keep the biggest term and drop the rest: 3n + 50 is just o(n). the trap is the hidden loop. a call that looks like one step can be a loop of its own. cpython’s lists are arrays, so x in some_list checks the items one by one; java’s documentation says arraylist runs most operations in linear time, while hashset offers constant-time contains (if the hash function spreads the items well). # slow: `in` on a list checks the items one by one, inside a loop -> o(n²) def has_duplicate(orders): seen = [] for o in orders: if o in seen: # a hidden loop return true seen.append(o) return false # fast: a set looks up by hash -> o(n) time, at the cost of o(n) extra memory def has_duplicate(orders): seen = set() for o in orders: if o in seen: return true seen.add(o) return false // the same trap in java: arraylist.contains is linear, hashset.contains is constant time list<string> slow = new arraylist<>(); // slow.contains(o) walks the list set<string> fast = new hashset<>(); // fast.contains(o) jumps straight to it space is often the price of time. the fast version above remembers everything it has seen: it uses more memory to do less work. our view: that trade is usually worth it, and caches, indexes and hash maps all make it; when memory is tight, sorting in place or streaming the data one item at a time can be the better choice. try it: the slow duplicate check drill in the labs is exactly this bug, in python and java, with a test that fails until the code is fast enough. the table below puts numbers on each shape.

big o: how cost grows big o notation describes how a function grows as its input gets large, as an upper bound, and is used for both time and memory. it ignores constant factors, so it tells you how an approach scales, not how fast it runs today. notation name n = 1,000 n = 1,000,000 typical example o(1) constant 1 1 array access by index; hash table lookup on average o(log n) logarithmic about 10 about 20 binary search; balanced tree lookup o(n) linear 1,000 1,000,000 scanning a list o(n log n) linearithmic about 10,000 about 20 million good general-purpose sorting o(n 2 ) quadratic 1,000,000 10 12 comparing every pair the columns are rough step counts (log 2 ), worked out for illustration. the jump from n to n 2 is why a nested loop that is fine on test data can stall in production.

c.h: The structures you meet every day
c.x: the structures you meet every day structure good at watch out for array constant-time access by position inserting in the middle shifts everything after it dynamic array (such as java’s arraylist) appending: it grows by a large factor such as doubling, so each append costs constant time on average (amortised) the occasional resize copies everything linked list inserting or removing where you already are no random access: reaching item k means walking k links stack and queue last in, first out, and first in, first out only the ends are cheap to reach hash table (dict, map) lookup by key in about constant time on average, independent of size collisions; the worst case is linear balanced binary search tree ordered data with lookups, inserts and deletes in o(log n) more work per operation than a plain sorted array that rarely changes ( analysis ) b-tree sorted data on disk: wide nodes keep the tree shallow, so few blocks are read. used in databases and file systems usually provided by your database rather than written by hand ( analysis ) heap a priority queue: always the smallest (or largest) next not for searching arbitrary items trie (prefix tree) prefix lookups: autocomplete, spell checking, ip routing memory per node graph relationships: networks, dependencies, routes algorithms are more involved bloom filter (burton bloom, 1970) a small, probabilistic “have i seen this?” that answers “possibly yes” or “definitely no” false positives are possible; false negatives are not

inside a hash table a hash table with separate chaining three keys, ana, ben and cyd, pass through a hash function that maps each to one of five buckets numbered 0 to 4. ana goes to bucket 1. ben and cyd both go to bucket 3, a collision, so bucket 3 holds a short linked list of two entries. keys hash function buckets entries hash(key) mod 5 ana ben cyd 0 1 2 3 4 ana → 7 ben → 3 cyd → 9 collision: a chain a hash table with separate chaining. the hash function turns each key into a bucket number; two keys that land in the same bucket (a collision) share it as a short linked list. with few collisions, a lookup costs about the same however many entries there are. each entry is key → value.

searching binary search finds a value in a sorted array by halving the range each step, so a million items take about 20 comparisons. python’s bisect module does this for you, and a set does hash lookups. from bisect import bisect_left def linear_steps(items, target): for steps, value in enumerate(items, start=1): if value == target: return steps return len(items) def binary_steps(items, target): lo, hi, steps = 0, len(items) - 1, 0 while lo <= hi: steps += 1 mid = (lo + hi) // 2 if items[mid] == target: return steps if items[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid - 1 return steps items = list(range(1_000_000)) # already sorted target = 999_999 print("linear:", linear_steps(items, target), "steps") print("binary:", binary_steps(items, target), "steps") print("bisect finds index", bisect_left(items, target)) print("set lookup:", target in set(items)) linear: 1000000 steps binary: 20 steps bisect finds index 999999 set lookup: true run as shown with python 3; the second block is its real output.

sorting merge sort (john von neumann, 1945): divide and conquer, o(n log n), and most implementations are stable , keeping equal items in their original order. quicksort (tony hoare, 1959): efficient in practice; its worst case, o(n 2 ), is rare when the pivot is chosen well, but a naive pivot makes already-sorted input the worst case. timsort (tim peters, 2002): a stable hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort that uses runs already in order. it was python’s standard sort from 2.3 until 3.11 replaced it with powersort, and java se 7 uses it for arrays of objects. analysis: in everyday code, call your language’s built-in sort; knowing how they work tells you when stability or the worst case matters. the other view: a hand-written sort can win when the data has a known shape, but measure first.

graphs and harder problems breadth-first search explores all nodes at one depth before the next: the fewest hops between two nodes in an unweighted graph. depth-first search goes as far as possible along each branch before backtracking: cycles, dependency order. dijkstra’s algorithm (conceived in 1956) finds shortest paths in a weighted graph, such as a road network, with non-negative weights. dynamic programming (richard bellman, 1950s) solves a problem from the stored answers to overlapping subproblems, instead of recomputing them.

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) most operations look things up by an exact key a hash table (dict, map, set) you need items in order, or ranges (“everything between a and f”) a sorted array if it rarely changes; a balanced tree if it changes often you always want the most urgent or smallest item next a heap (priority queue) data lives on disk and must be found with few reads a b-tree index, which your database already uses you must check membership in a huge set with little memory, and an occasional false “maybe” is acceptable a bloom filter in front of the real lookup prefix search or autocomplete a trie the data is small (hundreds of items) whatever is simplest to read ( our view ): big o ignores constant factors, and at that size they can dominate

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: every engineer should be able to estimate the big o of their own code and know the common structures well enough to pick one. it prevents the nested loop that only fails at production scale. the other view: libraries, databases and frameworks already embody these choices, and interview-style puzzles test something different from day-to-day work. measuring real code with a profiler often teaches more than theory.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation read and compare o(1), o(log n), o(n), o(n log n) and o(n^2) explain arrays, lists, hash tables, stacks and queues write a binary search 2 practitioner pick a structure for the most frequent operation spot an accidental o(n^2) loop and fix it use heaps, sets and sorted collections from the standard library 3 senior explain b-tree indexes, tries and bloom filters, and where systems use them choose graph algorithms: bfs, dfs, dijkstra solve problems with dynamic programming 4 expert design data layouts for scale and hardware (cache, disk) review designs for algorithmic risk teach and interview for these skills fairly each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the short answer concurrency means several computations in overlapping time periods; parallelism means running at the same physical instant, on separate processors, usually to speed a computation up. wherever two threads share data that one of them changes, you need a rule for who may touch it when.

race conditions: the lost update a race condition is when a system’s behaviour depends on the sequence or timing of events it does not control. they are hard to reproduce, because the result depends on timing between threads, and they can disappear when you add logging or run in a debugger. a lost update between two threads a uml sequence diagram with three lifelines: thread a, the shared balance, and thread b. the balance starts at 0. thread a reads 0. thread b reads 0. thread a writes 0 plus 100, so the balance is 100. thread b writes 0 plus 100, also 100. two deposits of 100 leave a balance of 100: one update is lost. thread a balance thread b {balance = 0} read sees 0 read sees 0 write 0 + 100 write 0 + 100 {balance = 100} balance = 100, not 200: one update lost a lost update, as a uml sequence diagram. both threads read the balance before either writes it back, so the second write overwrites the first. the code below forces exactly this order, then fixes it with a lock. import threading balance = 0 both_have_read = threading.barrier(2) lock = threading.lock() def deposit_unsafe(amount): global balance seen = balance # 1. read both_have_read.wait() # (force the bad interleaving: both threads read first) balance = seen + amount # 2. write, based on a stale read def deposit_safe(amount): global balance with lock: # read and write as one step balance = balance + amount def run(worker): global balance balance = 0 threads = [threading.thread(target=worker, args=(100,)) for _ in range(2)] for t in threads: t.start() for t in threads: t.join() return balance print("two deposits of 100, unsafe:", run(deposit_unsafe)) print("two deposits of 100, locked:", run(deposit_safe)) two deposits of 100, unsafe: 100 two deposits of 100, locked: 200 run as shown with python 3; the second block is its real output, the same on every run because the barrier forces the bad order. in real code the order is not forced, which is why the bug comes and goes.

deadlock a deadlock is a set of threads each waiting for a resource another holds. edward coffman described four conditions in 1971; all four must hold for a deadlock: mutual exclusion: a resource can be used by only one at a time. hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another. no preemption: a resource is released only voluntarily. circular wait: each waits for the next, in a cycle. most prevention breaks one condition, especially the circular wait. analysis: the everyday fix is to take locks in one fixed global order. the other view: a fixed order is hard to keep across a large code base, so some teams use timeouts or lock-free structures instead.

tools for shared data mutex (lock): only one thread at a time runs the protected section. semaphore: a counter that limits how many may enter, invented by edsger dijkstra in 1962 or 1963. compare-and-swap: an atomic processor instruction that updates a value only if it still holds what you last read; the basis of lock-free structures. optimistic concurrency: do the work, then check for conflicting changes at commit and retry if there were any; common in databases. memory models define when one thread’s writes become visible to another. in java, everything before releasing a lock is visible to the next thread that acquires it (the happens-before order).

models of concurrency model the idea where you meet it threads and locks threads share memory; locks guard it java, c#; python’s threading module lightweight threads many cheap threads managed by the runtime; a blocked one does not hold an operating-system thread java’s virtual threads, stable since java 21 event loop and async/await one thread runs many tasks, switching at each wait javascript, python’s asyncio communicating sequential processes (tony hoare, 1978) share data by sending it over channels between processes go, whose channels follow the csp idea (see go ) actors (1973) each actor has private state and reacts to messages: it can decide, create actors and send messages erlang, akka in cpython, a global interpreter lock lets only one thread run python code at a time, so threads help with waiting on i/o more than with cpu work. python 3.13 added an experimental free-threaded build without it (pep 703).

c.h: How much parallelism helps: Amdahl’s law
c.x: how much parallelism helps: amdahl’s law gene amdahl’s law (1967) predicts the speed-up from more processors. if a fraction p of the work can run in parallel on s processors, the speed-up is 1 / ((1 − p) + p / s). p = 90% parallel speed-up 2 processors 1.82× 8 processors 4.71× 64 processors 8.77× unlimited 10×, never more worked out from the formula. the serial 10% sets the ceiling, however many processors you add.

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) many requests that mostly wait on i/o (databases, other services) virtual threads, or async/await, or an event loop: many waits, few cpu cores cpu-heavy work that can be split parallel workers or processes, sized by amdahl’s law; in cpython, processes rather than threads a small piece of shared state updated by several threads a lock, or an atomic or concurrent collection from the standard library components that should not share memory at all channels or actors: pass messages instead rows that many users may change at once the database’s transactions, with optimistic concurrency (a version column) where conflicts are rare your team already uses one model well stay with it unless a requirement above forces a change: switching has a cost

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: share as little mutable state as you can, and where you must share it, use a higher-level tool your platform offers (a concurrent collection, a database transaction, a channel) before reaching for raw locks. the other view: high-level abstractions hide costs and can make performance harder to predict; for latency-critical code, some teams prefer explicit locks or lock-free structures that they can measure and reason about directly.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation tell concurrency from parallelism explain a race condition with an example use a lock around shared state 2 practitioner spot and fix a lost update explain the four conditions for deadlock and avoid one choose threads, async or processes for a task 3 senior choose a concurrency model by requirement use optimistic concurrency in a database estimate parallel speed-up with amdahl's law 4 expert set concurrency standards for a platform review designs for shared mutable state diagnose timing bugs in production each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

c.h: Practice schema used on this tab
c.x: practice schema used on this tab orders(order_id string, order_ref string, store_id string, order_date date, order_year int64, items array<string>, raw_date string, _landed_at timestamp) stores(store_id string, name string, state string) practise for free in the bigquery sandbox (no billing account needed) against bigquery-public-data , for example bigquery-public-data.stackoverflow.posts_questions or bigquery-public-data.new_york_taxi_trips . always dry-run first and select only the columns you need.

c.h: The order SQL really runs in
c.x: the order sql really runs in from and join : build the row set where : filter rows group by : form groups aggregates computed having : filter groups window functions computed qualify : filter on window results select expressions, then distinct order by limit this explains most errors: you cannot use a window function in where (it does not exist yet; use qualify ), and where cannot filter on an aggregate (use having ). the order a sql query really runs in two columns. on the left, the order you write a query in: select, from, where, group by, having, qualify, order by, limit. on the right, the order it runs in, numbered: 1 from and join build the rows, 2 where filters rows, 3 group by forms groups and aggregates are computed, 4 having filters groups, 5 window functions are computed, 6 qualify filters on them, 7 select and distinct, 8 order by, 9 limit. select is written first but runs late, which is why where cannot use a window function or an aggregate. how you write it how it runs select from … join where group by having qualify order by limit 1 from, join: build rows 2 where: filter rows 3 group by + aggregates 4 having: filter groups 5 window functions 6 qualify: filter windows 7 select, distinct 8 order by 9 limit written first, runs 7th the list above beside the order you type. each step can only use what earlier steps produced: where runs before aggregates and windows exist, so it cannot filter on them; having and qualify can.

c.h: Write it so it reads top to bottom
c.x: write it so it reads top to bottom with landed as ( -- 1. narrow the input early select order_id, store_id, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date between '2024-01-01' and '2024-12-31' ), per_store as ( -- 2. aggregate at one grain select store_id, count(*) as n from landed group by store_id ) select c.name, coalesce(p.n, 0) as n -- 3. join for labels last from `p.ref.stores` as c left join per_store as p using (store_id) order by n desc; one cte per step, named for what it holds. state each cte's grain in a comment when it is not obvious. filter and aggregate before joining wide tables.

c.h: NULL: the source of quiet bugs
c.x: null: the source of quiet bugs null = null is null, not true. use is null , or a is not distinct from b to compare nullable values. count(*) counts rows; count(col) skips nulls. avg , sum , min ignore nulls too. x not in (subquery) returns no rows if the subquery yields a single null. use not exists . where status != 'x' drops rows where status is null. sum of no rows is null, not 0: wrap in coalesce(…, 0) . safe_cast and safe.parse_date turn bad input into null. count those nulls, or the failure is invisible. select count(*) as total_rows, count(order_date) as with_date, countif(raw_date is not null and order_date is null) as failed_parse from `p.analytics.orders`;

joins without surprises know the grain of both sides before joining. joining one-to-many multiplies rows; a sum afterwards is inflated (fan-out). aggregate first, then join when you need totals from two child tables. a filter on the right table in where turns a left join into an inner join. put it in on . check row counts before and after each join while developing. -- wrong: stores with no 2024 orders disappear select c.store_id, count(o.order_id) n from stores c left join orders o using (store_id) where o.order_year = 2024 group by 1; -- right: the filter belongs to the join select c.store_id, count(o.order_id) n from stores c left join orders o on o.store_id = c.store_id and o.order_year = 2024 group by 1; -- did my join fan out? keys should be unique on the "one" side select store_id, count(*) from stores group by 1 having count(*) > 1;

semi-joins and anti-joins -- semi-join: stores that have at least one order (no duplicates) select * from stores c where exists (select 1 from orders o where o.store_id = c.store_id); -- anti-join: stores with no order select * from stores c where not exists (select 1 from orders o where o.store_id = c.store_id); -- same anti-join with left join select c.* from stores c left join orders o using (store_id) where o.store_id is null; -- set operations (columns by position) select order_ref from a except distinct select order_ref from b; -- in a, not in b select order_ref from a intersect distinct select order_ref from b; select order_ref from a union all select order_ref from b; -- keeps duplicates, cheaper

aggregation toolkit select store_id, count(*) as n, count(distinct order_ref) as orders_n, countif(order_date is null) as undated, safe_divide(countif(order_date is null), count(*)) as undated_share, min(order_date) as first_d, max(order_date) as last_d, any_value(order_ref having max order_date) as latest_order_ref, -- value at the max string_agg(distinct cast(order_year as string), ',' order by cast(order_year as string)) as years, approx_quantiles(date_diff(date(_landed_at), order_date, day), 100)[offset(50)] as median_lag_days, logical_and(order_date is not null) as all_dated from `p.analytics.orders` group by all; -- groups by every non-aggregated column -- subtotals in one pass select state, store_id, count(*) n from orders join stores using (store_id) group by rollup (state, store_id); -- per store, per state, grand total

window functions, properly a window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows, without collapsing them . three parts: partition by (which rows are related), order by (their sequence), and the frame (which of them count for this row). select store_id, d, n, row_number() over w_date as rn, -- 1,2,3 no ties rank() over (partition by store_id order by n desc) as rnk, -- 1,1,3 dense_rank() over (partition by store_id order by n desc) as drnk,-- 1,1,2 lag(n) over w_date as prev_day, lead(n) over w_date as next_day, sum(n) over (partition by store_id order by d rows between unbounded preceding and current row) as running_total, avg(n) over (partition by store_id order by d rows between 6 preceding and current row) as avg_7_rows, avg(n) over (partition by store_id order by unix_date(d) range between 6 preceding and current row) as avg_7_days, n / sum(n) over (partition by store_id) as share_of_store, first_value(d) over w_date as first_day, last_value(d) over (w_date rows between unbounded preceding and unbounded following) as last_day from daily window w_date as (partition by store_id order by d); rows vs range: rows 6 preceding means six rows back, even if days are missing. range on a numeric day number means six calendar days back. fill gaps with a date spine or use range. default frame trap: with order by and no frame, the frame ends at the current row, so last_value returns the current row. give an explicit frame. ties: row_number picks arbitrarily among ties. add a tie-breaker column to order by so results are repeatable.

pattern: top n per group -- 3 most recent orders per store select store_id, order_ref, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null qualify row_number() over ( partition by store_id order by order_date desc, order_id -- tie-breaker ) <= 3; use rank instead of row_number if ties should all be included.

pattern: deduplicate -- find duplicates first: never dedupe blind select order_ref, count(*) as copies, count(distinct _landed_at) as loads from `p.raw.orders` group by order_ref having count(*) > 1 order by copies desc limit 20; -- keep the latest copy of each key select * from `p.raw.orders` qualify row_number() over (partition by order_ref order by _landed_at desc) = 1; -- exact duplicate rows only select distinct * except (_run_id) from t; -- leave out the column that differs on every load

c.h: Pattern: date spine and missing days
c.x: pattern: date spine and missing days with days as ( select d from unnest(generate_date_array('2025-01-01', '2025-03-31')) as d ), grid as ( -- every store × every day select c.store_id, days.d from `p.ref.stores` c cross join days ), actual as ( select store_id, order_date as d, count(*) as n from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date between '2025-01-01' and '2025-03-31' group by 1, 2 ) select g.store_id, g.d, coalesce(a.n, 0) as n from grid g left join actual a using (store_id, d) order by 1, 2; without the spine, days with zero rows simply do not appear, and averages and lags are computed over the wrong set.

pattern: gaps and islands -- streaks of consecutive days on which a store took orders with d as ( select distinct store_id, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null ), tagged as ( select *, date_sub(order_date, interval row_number() over (partition by store_id order by order_date) day ) as island -- constant within a run of consecutive days from d ) select store_id, min(order_date) as start_d, max(order_date) as end_d, count(*) as days from tagged group by store_id, island order by days desc; the trick: a date minus its row number stays the same while dates are consecutive and jumps at each gap.

pattern: change vs previous period with yearly as ( select store_id, order_year, count(*) as n from `p.analytics.orders` group by all ) select * from ( select *, lag(n) over (partition by store_id order by order_year) as prev_n from yearly ) where safe_divide(n - prev_n, prev_n) < -0.2; -- fell by more than 20% lag takes the previous row . if a year is missing for a store, "previous" is two years back. use a spine when that matters.

pattern: arrays (one-to-many in one row) -- top 3 items per store by number of orders with per_item as ( select store_id, trim(item) as item, count(*) as n from `p.analytics.orders`, unnest(items) as item group by all ) select * from per_item qualify row_number() over (partition by store_id order by n desc, item) <= 3; -- filter rows by array content without exploding select order_ref from `p.analytics.orders` where exists (select 1 from unnest(items) i where i like '%umbrella%'); -- array size, and rows whose array is empty or null select array_length(items) as n_items from t; select countif(array_length(items) = 0 or items is null) from t; the comma before unnest is a cross join: rows with an empty array vanish. use left join unnest(items) as item to keep them.

pattern: pivot and unpivot -- one row per store, a column per year select * from ( select store_id, order_year, order_id from `p.analytics.orders` where order_year between 2023 and 2025 ) pivot (count(order_id) for order_year in (2023 as y2023, 2024 as y2024, 2025 as y2025)); -- conditional counts without pivot (countif is bigquery; elsewhere use count(case when … then 1 end) or filter) select store_id, countif(order_year = 2023) as y2023, countif(order_year = 2024) as y2024, countif(order_year = 2025) as y2025 from `p.analytics.orders` group by store_id; -- columns back to rows select * from wide unpivot (n for year in (y2023, y2024, y2025));

pattern: recursive hierarchy -- every category under x, directly or through a chain (max depth 5) with recursive chain as ( select category_id, parent_id, 1 as depth from `p.analytics.categories` where parent_id = 'x' union all select c.category_id, c.parent_id, chain.depth + 1 from `p.analytics.categories` c join chain on c.parent_id = chain.category_id where chain.depth < 5 -- always bound the recursion ) select category_id, min(depth) as depth from chain group by category_id;

pattern: point-in-time join (scd type 2) -- which store name was valid on the order date? select o.order_ref, o.order_date, s.name from `p.analytics.orders` o join `p.snapshots.store_snapshot` s on s.store_id = o.store_id and o.order_date >= date(s.dbt_valid_from) and (s.dbt_valid_to is null or o.order_date < date(s.dbt_valid_to)); half-open intervals ( >= from and < to ) never match two versions for one date.

reusable logic -- temporary sql function for this script create temp function parse_any_date(s string) as ( coalesce(safe.parse_date('%y-%m-%d', s), safe.parse_date('%d-%m-%y', s)) ); select raw_date, parse_any_date(raw_date) from t; -- persistent function in a dataset create or replace function `p.util.safe_ratio`(a float64, b float64) as ( if(b = 0 or b is null, null, a / b) ); -- table function: a parameterised view create or replace table function `p.util.store_year`(c string, y int64) as select * from `p.analytics.orders` where store_id = c and order_year = y; select count(*) from `p.util.store_year`('1_05', 2024);

making bigquery fast and cheap habit why select named columns bytes billed = bytes of the columns you read. one wide text column can be most of a table. filter on the partition column with literals or parameters lets bigquery skip partitions before reading. wrapping the column in a function can prevent it. filter on clustered columns skips blocks inside partitions; benefit shows in "bytes processed" after the run. dry-run before running shows bytes to be scanned for free. set a maximum bytes billed on risky jobs. aggregate early, join late shuffling fewer rows between stages is the main cost in slot time. avoid order by without limit on huge results sorting a very large result can fail with "resources exceeded"; put order by in the outermost query and add a limit . use approx_count_distinct for exploration exact distinct counts on billions of rows are expensive; the approximate version returns a statistical estimate and uses fewer resources. materialise reused intermediate results a cte referenced several times may be computed several times. write it to a table (or temp table in a script) when it is big. read the execution graph in the console's execution details: look for a stage with skewed time (one huge key), large shuffle, or spill to disk. avoid self-joins for running totals a window function does in one pass what a self-join does quadratically.

c.h: Mistakes that give wrong answers quietly
c.x: mistakes that give wrong answers quietly fan-out from a one-to-many join before a sum . a right-table filter in where after a left join . not in against a column that contains null. integer division in other engines ( 1/2 = 0 ); bigquery's / returns float64, but div() is integer. between on timestamps: between '2025-01-01' and '2025-01-31' misses most of the 31st. use >= start and < next_day . time zones: date(ts) is utc unless you pass a zone ( date(ts, 'asia/kolkata') ). row_number without a tie-breaker: a different row "wins" on each run. limit without order by : an arbitrary sample, not the top rows. averaging averages, or averaging percentages, instead of recomputing from totals. safe-parsing into null and never counting the nulls.

check your own query grain: what does one output row mean? is the key unique? ( count(*) vs count(distinct key) ) totals: does the sum across groups equal the ungrouped total? rows in vs out: did a join drop or multiply rows you did not expect? edges: empty groups, nulls, the first and last day, ties. one example by hand: pick one key and check its row against the source. cost: dry-run bytes reasonable for the question?

exercises (open each for a solution) try each on the practice schema, or adapt it to a public dataset. solutions are one good answer, not the only one. 1. orders per store in 2024, including stores with none. select c.store_id, c.name, count(o.order_id) as n from `p.ref.stores` c left join `p.analytics.orders` o on o.store_id = c.store_id and o.order_year = 2024 group by all order by n desc; filter in on , and count a column from the right table so empty stores give 0. 2. the most recent order per store, with ties broken consistently. select store_id, order_ref, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null qualify row_number() over (partition by store_id order by order_date desc, order_id) = 1; 3. what share of each store's rows failed to parse their date? only stores above 1%. select store_id, count(*) as n, countif(raw_date is not null and order_date is null) as failed, safe_divide(countif(raw_date is not null and order_date is null), count(*)) as failed_share from `p.analytics.orders` group by store_id having safe_divide(countif(raw_date is not null and order_date is null), count(*)) > 0.01 order by failed_share desc; 4. daily counts for one store with a 7-day moving average, including days with zero. with days as ( select d from unnest(generate_date_array('2025-01-01', '2025-06-30')) d ), daily as ( select order_date as d, count(*) n from `p.analytics.orders` where store_id = '1_05' and order_date between '2025-01-01' and '2025-06-30' group by 1 ) select days.d, coalesce(n, 0) as n, avg(coalesce(n, 0)) over (order by days.d rows between 6 preceding and current row) as ma7 from days left join daily using (d) order by d; the spine makes rows equal to days, so the moving average is over seven calendar days. 5. stores whose yearly count fell by more than 20% compared with the previous year. with y as ( select store_id, order_year, count(*) n from `p.analytics.orders` group by all ), c as ( select *, lag(n) over (partition by store_id order by order_year) as prev_n, lag(order_year) over (partition by store_id order by order_year) as prev_year from y ) select *, safe_divide(n - prev_n, prev_n) as change from c where prev_year = order_year - 1 -- only compare adjacent years and safe_divide(n - prev_n, prev_n) < -0.2; 6. find duplicate keys, then build the deduplicated table keeping the latest load. select order_ref, count(*) copies from `p.raw.orders` group by order_ref having count(*) > 1; create or replace table `p.scratch.orders_dedup` as select * from `p.raw.orders` qualify row_number() over (partition by order_ref order by _landed_at desc) = 1; -- verify: should return 0 select count(*) - count(distinct order_ref) from `p.scratch.orders_dedup`; 7. the longest run of consecutive trading days for each store. with d as ( select distinct store_id, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null ), t as ( select *, date_sub(order_date, interval row_number() over (partition by store_id order by order_date) day) as grp from d ), runs as ( select store_id, min(order_date) s, max(order_date) e, count(*) len from t group by store_id, grp ) select * from runs qualify row_number() over (partition by store_id order by len desc, s) = 1; 8. each store's share of all 2024 orders, and its rank within its state. with n as ( select c.state, o.store_id, count(*) n from `p.analytics.orders` o join `p.ref.stores` c using (store_id) where o.order_year = 2024 group by all ) select *, n / sum(n) over () as share_all, rank() over (partition by state order by n desc) as rank_in_state from n order by state, rank_in_state; 9. stores present in the reference table but absent from the landed data, and the reverse. (select 'missing_data' as issue, store_id from `p.ref.stores` except distinct select 'missing_data', store_id from `p.analytics.orders`) union all (select 'unknown_store', store_id from `p.analytics.orders` except distinct select 'unknown_store', store_id from `p.ref.stores`); parenthesise when mixing different set operators; bigquery requires it. 10. median, 90th percentile and maximum lag (days) between order and landing, per store. select store_id, approx_quantiles(lag_d, 100)[offset(50)] as p50, approx_quantiles(lag_d, 100)[offset(90)] as p90, max(lag_d) as max_lag from ( select store_id, date_diff(date(_landed_at), order_date, day) as lag_d from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null ) group by store_id order by p90 desc; 11. upsert a day's new rows into a target table without creating duplicates. merge `p.mart.serving` t using ( select * from `p.analytics.orders` where date(_landed_at) = @run_date qualify row_number() over (partition by order_id order by _landed_at desc) = 1 ) s on t.order_id = s.order_id when matched then update set order_date = s.order_date, order_ref = s.order_ref when not matched then insert row; deduplicate the source first: merge fails if two source rows match one target row. 12. explain why this returns no rows: select * from stores where store_id not in (select store_id from orders) . if any orders.store_id is null, x not in (…, null) evaluates to null for every x, never true, so no row passes. use not exists , or add where store_id is not null inside the subquery.

a plan to get better week 1: the evaluation order, nulls and joins. redo exercises 1, 9 and 12 until they feel obvious. week 2: window functions. exercises 2, 4, 5 and 8; then rewrite one self-join you have seen as a window. week 3: patterns. gaps and islands, date spines, dedup, pivots (6, 7). week 4: bigquery cost and plans. dry-run everything, read the execution graph of your slowest query, and cut its bytes in half. ongoing: before sharing any number, run the self-check list on this tab. read other people's sql: dbt models in your repo, and the queries behind dashboards you use. ask "what is the grain?" of each.
