modelling rules start normalised (third normal form): each fact stored once, in the table it describes. denormalise later, on purpose, for a measured read need. every table has a primary key. surrogate ( bigint identity or uuid) for internal identity; natural keys (order reference, email) get a unique constraint. never reuse or renumber a key that others store: urls, foreign systems, legal records. constraints are free correctness: not null , unique , check , foreign key . the database enforces them for every writer, including the one you forgot. right types: date / timestamptz not strings; numeric for money, never float; text over arbitrary varchar(n) ; jsonb for truly variable attributes, not as a substitute for columns. name things plainly and consistently: snake_case , singular or plural but one choice, _at for timestamps, _id for keys.

a schema example create table store ( store_id text primary key, name text not null ); create table orders ( -- "order" is a reserved word id bigint generated always as identity primary key, order_id text not null unique, -- stable natural key order_ref text not null, -- what the customer sees store_id text not null references store, order_date date, status text not null check (status in ('paid','pending')), notes text, created_at timestamptz not null default now(), updated_at timestamptz not null default now() ); -- many-to-many through a join table create table order_item ( order_id text not null references orders (order_id) on delete cascade, product_id text not null references product, quantity int not null check (quantity > 0), primary key (order_id, product_id) );

index types (postgresql) type good for example b-tree (default) equality, ranges, sorting, prefix like 'abc%' (with c collation, or an index using text_pattern_ops ) create index on orders (order_date); composite filters on several columns; column order matters (store_id, order_date desc) covering ( include ) answering a query from the index alone (index-only scan) (store_id) include (order_ref, order_date) partial indexing only the rows you query; small and fast (id) where status = 'pending' expression queries on a computed value (lower(email)) unique enforcing uniqueness, and lookups unique (store_id, order_ref) gin full-text search ( tsvector ), jsonb containment, arrays using gin (to_tsvector('english', notes)) brin huge tables physically ordered by a column (append-only by time); tiny index using brin (created_at) hnsw / ivfflat (pgvector) approximate nearest-neighbour search on embeddings using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)

index rules of thumb index for your queries, not your columns. start from the slow query's where , join and order by . composite order: equality columns first, then the range or sort column. (store_id, order_date) serves store_id = ? and order_date > ? ; the reverse order serves it poorly. leftmost prefix: an index on (a, b, c) helps most with queries on a , a,b , a,b,c . on b alone it helps little: postgresql can still use it through a skip scan, but only when a has few distinct values. foreign keys usually need an index on the referencing column, or deletes and joins scan. every index slows writes and uses disk. drop unused ones ( pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 ). low-selectivity columns (a boolean, a status with 3 values) rarely help alone; use a partial index instead. functions on columns ( where date(created_at) = … ) skip a plain index; write a range or index the expression. build on live tables with create index concurrently , then confirm it is valid: an interrupted build leaves an invalid index.

reading a query plan explain (analyze, buffers) select order_ref, order_date from orders where store_id = '1_05' and order_date >= '2024-01-01' order by order_date desc limit 20; -- look for: -- seq scan on a big table → missing or unusable index -- rows=10 (estimated) vs actual rows=500000 → stale stats: analyze -- sort … external merge disk → work_mem too low, or index the sort -- nested loop with huge inner loops → join order or missing index -- index only scan, heap fetches: 0 → ideal -- check index validity after a concurrent build select indexrelid::regclass, indisvalid from pg_index where not indisvalid; -- slowest queries (pg_stat_statements extension) select query, calls, mean_exec_time from pg_stat_statements order by total_exec_time desc limit 10;

partitioning (one database) create table event ( id bigserial, -- fine here; generated … as identity on a partitioned table needs postgresql 17+ event_date date not null, payload jsonb, primary key (id, event_date) -- must include the partition key ) partition by range (event_date); create table event_2025 partition of event for values from ('2025-01-01') to ('2026-01-01'); create table event_2026 partition of event for values from ('2026-01-01') to ('2027-01-01'); create table event_default partition of event default; -- retire old data instantly instead of a slow delete alter table event detach partition event_2025; drop table event_2025; -- other kinds: partition by list (region) partition by hash (customer_id) why: queries that filter on the key skip other partitions (pruning); old data drops in one statement; maintenance runs per partition. when: very large tables (tens of millions of rows and up) with a natural time or category filter. small tables only get slower. cost: unique constraints must include the partition key; queries without it scan every partition.

sharding (many databases) what: split rows across separate database servers by a shard key, so each holds part of the data and load. shard key choice is the whole design: high cardinality, evenly spread, present in almost every query (tenant id, user id). hash sharding spreads load evenly but makes range queries hit every shard. range sharding keeps ranges together but creates hot shards (all of today's writes on one). directory / lookup sharding maps keys to shards in a table: flexible, but the directory becomes critical. costs: cross-shard joins and transactions become application problems; resharding is a migration project; operations multiply. try first: better indexes, read replicas, caching, partitioning, a bigger instance, archiving cold data. shard when one primary truly cannot take the writes. managed or distributed options do it for you: spanner, cockroachdb, citus (postgres), vitess (mysql). alloydb read pools scale reads only; they do not shard.

replication & scaling reads read replicas copy the primary asynchronously. scale reads; accept replica lag (a user may not see their own write). synchronous replicas confirm writes before commit: no data loss on failover, at the cost of write latency. high availability (cloud sql ha, patroni) promotes a standby when the primary fails. connection pooling (pgbouncer, hikaricp, r2dbc pool): postgres connections are expensive. size pools so instances × pool size stays under max_connections . caching (redis) for hot, read-heavy data, with a deliberate invalidation rule.

replica lag, drawn read-your-writes and replica lag a sequence diagram with three lifelines: the app, the primary database and an asynchronous read replica. 1: the app writes a change to the primary. 2: the primary confirms the commit. 3: the app reads from the replica straight away. 4: the replica has not yet received the change and returns the old value. 5: the change reaches the replica a moment later. the user did not see their own write. app primary read replica 1 update name = 'ana' 2 committed 3 select name 4 old name: not copied yet 5 async copy arrives the user did not see their own write the first bullet above, step by step. reading straight after a write? read from the primary, or use a synchronous replica and pay for it in write latency.

transactions, isolation, locking isolation prevents read committed (postgres default) dirty reads. each statement sees data committed before it began. repeatable read non-repeatable reads (and, in postgresql, phantom reads): the transaction sees one snapshot throughout. serializable all anomalies; transactions behave as if run one by one. retry on serialization failure. -- pessimistic: lock the row you will change select * from account where id = 7 for update; -- job queue: each worker claims different rows select id from job where state = 'ready' order by created_at limit 10 for update skip locked; -- optimistic: version column, fail if someone else changed it update doc set body = $1, version = version + 1 where id = $2 and version = $3; -- 0 rows → conflict, reload and retry keep transactions short. a long one holds locks and stops vacuum cleaning up dead rows.

c.h: Safe schema changes on live data
c.x: safe schema changes on live data additive first: add a nullable column, a new table, a new index (concurrently). safe and reversible. expand / contract for renames and type changes: add the new column, write to both, backfill in batches, switch reads, stop writing the old, drop it in a later release. avoid long locks: some alter table forms rewrite the whole table. set lock_timeout so a migration fails fast instead of blocking traffic. backfill in batches (by id range), committing as you go, not one giant update. version every change with a migration tool (liquibase, flyway, alembic), and never edit a migration that has already run in production. test on a production-sized copy; a change that takes seconds on a test table can take hours on a table of tens of millions of rows.

anti-patterns entity-attribute-value tables ( key , value rows for everything): no types, no constraints, painful queries. comma-separated lists in a column: use a join table or an array with a gin index. floats for money and strings for dates. no foreign keys "for speed": orphans and silent corruption cost more. n+1 queries from an orm loop: one query per row instead of one join. select * in application code: breaks when columns change, fetches what you do not need. offset pagination on deep pages: use keyset pagination ( where (date, id) < ($1, $2) order by date desc, id desc limit 20 ). unbounded growth with no retention or archiving plan.

oltp vs olap design oltp (postgres) olap (bigquery) workload many small reads/writes by key few large scans and aggregates storage row-oriented column-oriented schema normalised, constraints denormalised, nested, wide speed comes from indexes partitioning, clustering, reading fewer columns updates row by row, transactional batch loads and merge; avoid row-by-row dml

the idea: nodes and edges nodes are things: people, accounts, products, services. they are roughly the equivalent of a row in a relational database or a document in a document store. edges are the relationships between them, and can be directed (a follows b) or undirected. properties are key–value details on both, such as a person’s name or the date a payment was made. a small labelled property graph three nodes: a person named ana, a person named ben and a city named london. ana knows ben, with the property since 2019. ana and ben each have a lives_in relationship to london. :person name: ana :person name: ben :city name: london knows {since: 2019} lives_in lives_in a labelled property graph: nodes carry a label ( :person ) and properties; relationships are named, directed and can carry properties too. the query match (p:person)-[:lives_in]->(c:city) matches two of these paths. the mathematics is old: leonhard euler’s 1736 proof that no walk crosses each of königsberg’s seven bridges exactly once is regarded as the first paper in the history of graph theory.

two models labelled property graph: nodes and relationships both carry key–value properties; nodes have labels that group them; relationships are named, directed and have a start and an end node. neo4j (where cypher began) and amazon neptune (through opencypher) support this model. rdf (resource description framework): a w3c standard where everything is a triple , subject–predicate–object, such as “ana – worksfor – acme”. databases built for it are called triplestores, and it underlies many knowledge graphs and linked data. some products, amazon neptune among them, support both models.

query languages cypher: created at neo4j in 2011, largely by andrés taylor, and opened up through the opencypher project in 2015. it draws patterns like (a)-[:knows]->(b) . gql: the iso standard graph query language for property graphs, iso/iec 39075, published in april 2024. sql/pgq: part 16 of sql:2023 adds property graph queries to sql itself, narrowing the gap between relational and graph databases. gremlin: apache tinkerpop’s graph traversal language, described as playing the role for graph databases that jdbc and sql play for relational ones. sparql: the w3c query language for rdf; sparql 1.0 became a w3c recommendation in january 2008.

what a query looks like // gql / cypher style: people and the city they live in match (p:person)-[:lives_in]->(c:city) return p.first_name, p.last_name, c.name // friends of friends: two hops along the same relationship match (me:person {name: 'ana'})-[:knows]->(friend)-[:knows]->(fof) return distinct fof.name analysis: the second query adds one pattern per hop. in sql, each hop is typically another join on a link table, which is where graph databases are said to read more naturally.

graph or relational? graph database relational database following relationships graph databases typically use index-free adjacency : each node holds direct references to its neighbours, so reaching an adjacent node is typically constant time, and query time depends on how much of the graph is queried rather than the size of the graph relationships are joins through indexes; queries with many joins across many tables get complex, and joins can be expensive operating on many rows at once typically slower at the same operation over large numbers of rows typically faster at the same operation over large numbers of rows schema flexible: new kinds of node and relationship can be added without redesigning a strict schema and normalisation, which preserve data consistency and support acid transactions standard language gql since 2024; cypher, gremlin and sparql are all in use sql, the standard for relational databases, which have been the industry standard since codd’s 1970 relational model wikipedia’s summary adds a caution worth keeping: the graph model alone should not be the reason to replace an existing relational database.

where graphs are used shortest paths between two nodes, and measures such as a graph’s diameter. community detection: clusters of closely connected nodes. knowledge graphs: google introduced its knowledge graph in 2012, to answer searches with “things, not strings”. graphs for ai retrieval: microsoft’s graphrag research project used language models to extract a knowledge graph from text and used it as context for answering questions. microsoft now describes it as a research project largely in maintenance mode, and warns that indexing can be expensive (see rag ).

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) your key queries follow chains of relationships of unknown length (paths, networks, “how is a connected to b”) a graph database your queries are mostly filters, totals and reports over many rows a relational database or a warehouse you already run postgresql or another sql database and need some graph queries try graph queries in sql first (recursive queries, or sql/pgq where supported): a second database has a cost you need to link data from many sources with shared, published vocabularies rdf and sparql your data has many kinds of entity and relationship that keep changing a graph model of either kind: new data can be added without planning every future use in advance you need to be able to move between graph products a standard language, gql (iso/iec 39075) or opencypher, rather than one vendor’s extensions

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: learn to think in graphs even if you never run a graph database: many problems (dependencies, permissions, fraud rings, service maps) are graphs, and drawing them that way clarifies them. reach for a graph database when relationship queries are the core of the product. the other view: one well-run relational database covers most needs, including many graph-shaped queries through recursive sql and now sql/pgq. adding a specialised database brings another system to operate, back up and secure, and another query language for the team to learn.

the short answer our view: start with one relational database unless a requirement clearly calls for something else, and add a specialised store when that requirement appears. the other view: some teams pick a document or key-value store from the start because their data and access patterns are known to fit it; this can avoid a later migration. the table below sets out which requirements point where.

a first pass a first pass at choosing a data store a flowchart of five yes-or-no questions in a column. mostly files, images or backups: if yes, object storage. otherwise, analytics over many rows: if yes, a columnar warehouse. otherwise, search by words and relevance: if yes, a search engine. otherwise, find similar items by meaning: if yes, a vector index. otherwise, only get and set by key, very fast: if yes, a key-value store. if no to all five, start with a relational database. mostly files, images, backups? yes object storage no analytics over many rows? yes columnar warehouse no search by words and relevance? yes search engine no find similar items by meaning? yes vector index no only get and set by key, very fast? yes key-value store no start with a relational database json columns where the shape varies a first pass, as a flowchart ( analysis , not a rule). most systems answer “yes” to more than one question and end up with more than one store; the table below goes further. time series and graph stores are in the table and on graph databases, not in this first pass.

the families family what it stores, and what it is good at examples and typical uses relational tables of rows and columns, queried with sql, with acid transactions (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) postgresql (which also stores json, including a binary jsonb type) document semi-structured documents, such as json, each with its own shape; one of the main nosql families mongodb, which stores json-like documents (bson) with optional schemas key-value records stored and retrieved by a unique key, like a dictionary redis, which works on data in main memory and persists it to disk wide-column tables where the columns can vary from row to row; a two-dimensional key-value store apache cassandra (from facebook, 2008), built on ideas from amazon’s dynamo and google’s bigtable search engine an index for full-text search and relevance ranking elasticsearch, based on apache lucene time series data points indexed in time order, with high ingestion rates and heavy compression measurements from physical sensors, and other time-stamped data vector embeddings, searched by approximate nearest neighbour for similar meaning; used for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation dedicated vector databases, or postgresql with pgvector columnar warehouse a data warehouse serves reporting and data analysis; analytics databases benefit from storing data by column, while transactional ones suit rows bigquery, amazon redshift and snowflake use column-oriented formats; apache parquet is a column-oriented file format object storage blobs with metadata and a unique identifier, rather than files in folders files and other large objects with their metadata in-memory data held mainly in main memory, which gives faster and more predictable performance than disk systems where response time is critical many products now span several families: a multi-model database supports more than one data model, such as document, graph, relational and key-value, against one backend.

c.h: More than one store: polyglot persistence
c.x: more than one store: polyglot persistence martin fowler wrote in 2011 that any decent-sized enterprise would come to use a variety of data storage technologies for different kinds of data, a shift he called polyglot persistence (crediting scott leberknight with the term). he also said it comes at a cost. analysis: each extra store is another system to run, back up, secure and keep consistent with the others; on keeping copies in step, see solution architecture: a to b (the outbox and change data capture).

nosql is not one thing nosql, “not only sql”, covers several designs that store data differently from relational tables: key-value pairs, wide columns, graphs or documents. they do not need a fixed schema, which suits large and often unstructured datasets. analysis: “schema-less” usually means the schema lives in your code instead of the database, so it still needs designing and versioning.

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) changes that must happen together across several records (orders and stock, money) a relational database with transactions each record is read and written whole, and its shape varies a document store, or json columns in a relational database very high write volume, spread over many machines, with known query patterns a wide-column store fast lookups by key, where losing some data is tolerable or it can be rebuilt an in-memory key-value store, usually as a cache in front of the main store users search text and expect ranked results a search engine, fed from the main store metrics or sensor readings over time a time series database semantic search or retrieval for an ai feature a vector index; start with one inside a database you already run if it offers one analysis over large history a columnar warehouse, separate from the operational database your team already runs a database that meets the requirement use it before adding another: each extra store has a cost, as fowler noted (2011)

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: the questions that decide it are what must change together, how data is read, how much of it there is, and who will run the store at 3 a.m. popularity and brand are not on that list. a team’s existing operational experience is, because switching has a cost; the table’s last row says so. the other view: the store a team already knows well, and can operate safely, may suit better than a better-fitting store nobody can run; that familiarity reduces operational risk, and is more than preference.

set up once machine: a laptop with 16 gb ram is enough for most labs; an old pc or mini pc running linux makes a good always-on lab server. tools: git, docker (or podman), kubectl , kind or k3d , helm, python 3.12+ (3.13+ for lab 5), a jdk 21 or newer, and the gcloud cli. cloud, carefully: new google cloud accounts get free-trial credit, and bigquery has a free sandbox. set a budget alert on day one and delete what you are not using. your lab journal: one git repository with a folder per lab and a readme in each: goal, steps, numbers you measured, what broke and why. this becomes your portfolio. mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab && git init kind create cluster --name lab # a kubernetes cluster in docker kubectl get nodes

lab 1: microservices on kubernetes repo: googlecloudplatform/microservices-demo (online boutique: about ten services in several languages). kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/googlecloudplatform/microservices-demo/main/release/kubernetes-manifests.yaml kubectl get pods -w kubectl port-forward deploy/frontend 8080:8080 # open http://localhost:8080 then: delete a pod and watch it come back; scale a deployment; set a memory limit too low and read the oomkilled event; break a readiness probe. done when: you can explain, from kubectl describe and events alone, why each thing you broke failed. tabs: kubernetes , microservices .

lab 2: observability stack repo: prometheus-community/helm-charts (kube-prometheus-stack) on the lab 1 cluster; or open-telemetry/opentelemetry-demo with docker compose. helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts helm install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring --create-namespace kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/monitoring-grafana 3000:80 # or the opentelemetry demo (traces, metrics, logs across many services) git clone https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-demo cd opentelemetry-demo && make start # a bare docker compose up starts no observability backends then: write one promql alert for an error ratio, make it fire on purpose, and find the failing span in a trace. done when: an alert you wrote fires for a failure you caused, and you traced it to the line of code. tabs: observability , ops tooling .

lab 3: service mesh repo: istio/istio (its samples/bookinfo application) on a kind cluster. # after downloading an istio release and adding istioctl to path istioctl install --set profile=default -y kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled kubectl apply -f samples/bookinfo/platform/kube/bookinfo.yaml istioctl analyze then: turn on strict mtls, split traffic 90/10 between review versions, inject a delay, and write an authorizationpolicy that denies one service. done when: you can produce, then explain, a 403 and a 503 from proxy logs. tab: service mesh .

lab 4: gitops and helm repo: argoproj/argocd-example-apps , with argo cd installed on your cluster. kubectl create namespace argocd kubectl apply -n argocd --server-side --force-conflicts -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml kubectl port-forward -n argocd svc/argocd-server 8443:443 then: fork the example repo, point an argo cd application at its helm example, change a value in git and watch it roll out; change something by hand in the cluster and watch argo cd report the drift. done when: every change reaches the cluster only through a git commit. tabs: helm charts , devops .

c.h: Lab 5: a data pipeline on your laptop
c.x: lab 5: a data pipeline on your laptop repo: dbt-labs/jaffle_shop_duckdb (dbt's demo project, running on duckdb, no cloud account). git clone https://github.com/dbt-labs/jaffle_shop_duckdb cd jaffle_shop_duckdb python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate # this repo asks for python 3.13+ pip install -r requirements.txt # or: uv sync dbt build # seeds, models and tests dbt docs generate && dbt docs serve then: add an incremental model, a unit test and a test that fails on purpose; load a public dataset of your own (bigquery public datasets or the registry of open data on aws) into duckdb and model it in layers. done when: running the pipeline twice gives identical results, and a bad row is rejected and counted, not silently nulled. tabs: data engineering , dbt , data libraries .

lab 6: orchestrate it repo: apache/airflow , using the official docker compose quick start from the airflow documentation. then: write a dag that runs lab 5's dbt build daily, uses data intervals, retries, and records a run summary; backfill a week; make one day fail and rerun just that day. done when: a rerun of any single day changes nothing else, and a missing run raises an alert. tab: airflow dags .

lab 7: culvert against emulators repo: enrichmeai/culvert . its stack runs against local emulators, so no cloud account is needed. git clone https://github.com/enrichmeai/culvert pip install 'culvert[gcp]' # then follow the repository's docs to start the emulators and run a pipeline then: write a small pipeline against the blobstore and warehouse contracts, run it on the emulators, then read the conformance suite to see what every adapter must guarantee. done when: your pipeline code imports no cloud sdk. tabs: culvert , frameworks vs ai .

lab 8: events with kafka repo: the official apache/kafka docker image, plus a producer and consumer you write. docker run -d --name kafka -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:latest # pin a version once it works docker exec -it kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh \ --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic order.placed --partitions 3 then: write a consumer that is idempotent, kill it mid-batch, restart it and prove no event was applied twice; add a dead-letter topic for a poison message. done when: you can show consumer lag rising and recovering, and duplicates handled. tab: kafka .

c.h: Lab 9: RAG and an MCP server
c.x: lab 9: rag and an mcp server repos: anthropics/anthropic-quickstarts for starting points, modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk for the server, and the pgvector/pgvector docker image for search. docker run -d --name pg -e postgres_password=pw -p 5432:5432 pgvector/pgvector:pg17 pip install "mcp[cli]" anthropic psycopg then: chunk and embed a small document set, build hybrid search, answer questions with citations, write 30 golden questions and measure recall; wrap lab 5's run records in a read-only mcp server and use it from claude code. done when: your eval score is written down, and the mcp tool says "could not read" when the database is stopped. tabs: rag , mcp .

lab 10: infrastructure as code start: hashicorp's "get started with docker" terraform tutorial (local, free), then a small google cloud project behind a budget alert. then: declare a bucket, a dataset and a cloud run job in terraform; rename a resource with a moved block; import something created by hand; destroy everything at the end. done when: terraform plan shows no changes after apply, and nothing you made is left running. tabs: terraform , cloud run .

lab 11: payments in test mode start: a stripe or razorpay test account. stripe's cli forwards test webhooks to your laptop. stripe login stripe listen --forward-to localhost:8080/webhooks/stripe stripe trigger payment_intent.succeeded then: build order → checkout → signature check → webhook; replay the same webhook twice; simulate a timeout and reconcile. done when: no replay or retry can mark an order paid twice. tab: payment gateways .

lab 12: game day repo: chaos-mesh/chaos-mesh on your kind cluster, or just kubectl delete and tc by hand. then: with a friend, one person breaks something on the lab 1–3 stack without saying what; the other detects, mitigates and writes a blameless postmortem using the template on the sre tab. done when: the postmortem has at least one action that adds a guard (an alert, a test, a limit). tab: sre .

rules for lab work predict, then run: write down what you expect before each experiment; the gap is the lesson. break it on purpose: every lab includes a failure you cause and explain. measure: record latency, cost, row counts or recovery time, not impressions. use ai as the bulldozer, not the driver: let it scaffold and explain, then verify everything it claims by running it. pin versions once something works, and note them in the readme so the lab is repeatable. clean up: kind delete cluster , docker compose down -v , terraform destroy , and check the cloud billing page. write it up: a short post or readme per lab. teaching what you learned is the final test that you learned it.

c.h: Threads in Java, release by release
c.x: threads in java, release by release release what arrived what it meant 1.0 thread , runnable , synchronized , wait / notify threads built into the language from the start. early jvms used "green threads", scheduled by the jvm itself rather than the operating system; they were abandoned for native threads in later releases. 5 java.util.concurrent (jsr 166): executorservice , thread pools, future , locks, atomics, concurrent collections stop creating threads by hand; submit tasks to a pool. 7 fork/join ( forkjoinpool ) split a big job into small ones and use every core; work-stealing keeps them busy. 8 completablefuture , parallel streams compose asynchronous steps instead of blocking on each future . 9 flow (reactive streams interfaces) a standard contract for streams with back-pressure, used by reactive libraries. 19, 21 virtual threads: preview in 19 (jep 425), final in 21 (jep 444) cheap threads managed by the jvm: one per blocking task, without a reactive rewrite. 21 onwards structured concurrency, previewing since 21 (jep 453; fifth preview in 25, jep 505; seventh preview in 27, jep 533) treat a group of related tasks as one unit: they finish, fail and cancel together. 24 virtual threads no longer pin on synchronized (jep 491) old synchronized code stops blocking the carrier thread. 25 scoped values, final (jep 506) share immutable data with child tasks; a safer replacement for many uses of threadlocal . the full circle: the first jvms scheduled threads themselves, java then handed them to the operating system for twenty-five years, and virtual threads bring jvm scheduling back, this time on top of native threads. release numbers come from each class's "since" in the java api documentation and from the jeps.

c.h: Bytecode in the age of containers: should Java go fully native?
c.x: bytecode in the age of containers: should java go fully native? the slogan. “write once, run anywhere” is sun microsystems’ 1995 slogan for java: source compiles to bytecode , which runs on any system with a compatible jvm. wikipedia adds the honest footnote: in practice there can be subtle differences between jvm implementations and host operating systems. what containers changed. a container image is built for one operating system and processor architecture. docker’s answer for several architectures is a multi-platform image : a list of variants, one per platform, published under a single name. so with containers, portability moved from the runtime into the build pipeline. analysis: that makes the case for bytecode weaker than in 1995, but it does not remove it: one jar still runs unchanged on an x86 server, an arm laptop and an arm cloud machine, and only the jvm base image differs. the bigger question is not portability but what each model is good at. measure jvm (bytecode + jit) jvm + leyden aot cache graalvm native image start-up slowest: classes are loaded, linked and compiled as the app starts faster: in jep 483, spring petclinic (about 21,000 classes) started in 4.486 s on jdk 23 and 2.604 s with an aot cache on jdk 24, 42% faster fastest: graalvm says “up to 100x faster”, with no warm-up peak speed high once warm: the jit compiles with profiles from the running program the same jit; since jdk 25 (jep 515) it can start from a previous run’s profiles often lower without tuning (the quarkus team measured native throughput at about half, see quarkus ); graalvm says profile-guided optimisation brings it on par or better memory larger than native: spring boot’s documentation says native images “can run with a smaller memory footprint” similar to the jvm, plus a cache file (130 mb for petclinic) smaller footprint dynamic java all of it: reflection, proxies, loading classes at run time all of it a “closed world”: the class path is fixed at build time, and reflection, resources, serialisation and proxies must be declared to the build build compile to bytecode; one jar for every platform adds a training run adds a whole-program analysis at build time; one executable per operating system and architecture # project leyden on the ordinary jvm (jdk 25): one training run, then fast starts java -xx:aotcacheoutput=app.aot -jar app.jar # run once with a realistic workload; writes the cache java -xx:aotcache=app.aot -jar app.jar # every later start uses it # graalvm native image: compile ahead of time into one platform-specific executable native-image -jar app.jar app # spring boot and quarkus wrap this in their build plugins ./app why fully native is hard for java. jep 483 puts it plainly: “the java platform is highly dynamic.” dynamic class loading and reflection are what let frameworks discover an application’s configuration from its annotations. native image has to know every reachable class at build time, so spring boot’s native support assumes a closed world and restricts those dynamic parts (profile-specific configuration, for example, has limitations), and libraries need extra metadata. that is the trade the openjdk project’s project leyden avoids: its goal is to improve “the startup time, time to peak performance, and footprint of java programs” while keeping the ordinary jvm. jep 483 (jdk 24), jeps 514 and 515 (jdk 25) and jep 516 (jdk 26) are delivered, and jep 544, which compiles application code to native code in a training run and stores it in the aot cache, is complete for jdk 28. leyden’s opening plan (mark reinhold, 2022) works along “a spectrum of constraints” and says that “in the long run we will likely embrace the full closed-world constraint in order to produce fully-static images”. the other route into the jdk has closed: project galahad, which was to contribute graalvm technology to openjdk, was dissolved in march 2026 after oracle’s september 2025 announcement that graalvm would be detached from the java ecosystem. if this is true for you lean towards scale to zero, functions, command-line tools: start-up and memory decide the bill native image, with the native build tested in ci long-running services where throughput matters and start-up happens rarely the jvm; add an aot cache if restarts or autoscaling are slow heavy use of reflection, bytecode generation, plugins or class loading at run time the jvm, or budget time for native metadata one artefact for several architectures, or java agents and profilers attached at run time the jvm you are thinking of moving a working spring service to another framework mainly for start-up time measure first: an aot cache (jdk 25) and spring’s own native support, against the cost of a rewrite your team already ships native images successfully stay native for those services: the hard part (metadata, ci) is already paid for our view: native building belongs in the java platform, as an option next to the jvm, not in each framework. while the jdk does not offer it, every framework has to build its own: spring runs its own ahead-of-time processing, with further limits on top of graalvm’s, and quarkus moved dependency injection to build time. each solves the same problem differently, each brings its own restrictions, and teams end up migrating from spring to another framework for start-up time that the platform should give every java program. containers have not made bytecode useless (the jit and one jar for every architecture still count), but they have made fast start-up a basic need. leyden is the jdk taking that on, step by step; until it reaches the native end, measure an aot cache before rewriting a working spring service. the other view: only a framework knows which of its beans, proxies and configuration a program will really use, so build-time work in spring and quarkus is not wasted duplication but knowledge the jdk cannot have; and for a team that ships containers to one architecture and scales to zero, graalvm native image works today, so waiting for the platform has its own cost.

c.h: Who steers Java: Sun, the JCP, Apache, Oracle and OpenJDK
c.x: who steers java: sun, the jcp, apache, oracle and openjdk java is not only a language; it is a set of specifications, an open-source implementation, a test suite and a trademark, owned and steered by different groups. knowing who decides what explains why the package names changed, why there are several jdks, and why version numbers jumped. when what happened 1991 james gosling, mike sheridan and patrick naughton start the language project at sun microsystems. it is first called oak, after a tree outside gosling’s office, then green, then java. 1995–96 java is released in may 1995; java 1.0, the first public implementation, follows in 1996 with the promise of “write once, run anywhere”. 1998 the java community process (jcp) is set up: the formal way companies and individuals propose and agree changes to the platform through java specification requests (jsrs). 2006–07 sun releases its virtual machine and compiler as free software under the gpl (november 2006) and nearly all of the class library in may 2007: the start of openjdk . 2007 the apache software foundation, building its own free java (apache harmony), writes an open letter to sun because it cannot get an acceptable licence for the technology compatibility kit (tck), the test suite an implementation must pass to call itself java. 2010 oracle completes its acquisition of sun on 27 january 2010. in april, gosling leaves oracle. in december, apache resigns its seat on the jcp executive committee because oracle will not license the tck for apache’s java. 2011 apache harmony is retired. parts of it had been used for the core class library of android, which later moved to openjdk (android 7.0). 2017 oracle hands java ee, the enterprise specifications, to the eclipse foundation . because oracle owns the java trademark, it becomes jakarta ee ; jakarta ee 9 (2020) moves the api packages from javax to jakarta . 2018 onwards java moves to a feature release every six months, with long-term-support releases (11, 17, 21, 25) between them. since jdk 10, the openjdk jdk project produces every feature release; changes are proposed as jdk enhancement proposals (jeps). 2021 in google v. oracle , over android’s use of the java apis, the us supreme court rules 6–2 that google’s use was fair use, without deciding whether apis can be copyrighted. name what it is today jsr a java specification request: a formal proposal for a specification, reviewed in public and voted on by the jcp executive committee; a final jsr comes with a reference implementation and a tck. the jcp itself is described by a jsr. jep a jdk enhancement proposal: how changes to the jdk itself are proposed, reviewed and tracked on openjdk.org; the list of jeps serves as the roadmap for future releases. openjdk the free, open-source implementation of java se, where every jdk feature release is now produced; builds, commercial support and free updates are available from several organisations. tck the compatibility test kit an implementation must pass before it can be called compatible. jakarta ee the enterprise specifications (servlets, persistence and more), now run by the eclipse foundation; spring boot 3 and apache tomcat follow the jakarta package names (see spring boot ). apache the apache software foundation hosts many of the java tools you use daily: tomcat, maven and ant among them (see build tools ). our view: the history is worth knowing because it still shows up in your code: javax versus jakarta imports, the choice of which jdk build to install, and how a feature you want reaches the language (a jep, not a vote of users). the other view: for day-to-day work you need only the current lts release, a supported openjdk build and the jakarta names; the politics behind them changes little about how you write java.

c.h: The plethora of JDKs: which one to install
c.x: the plethora of jdks: which one to install java se is a specification. openjdk is the open-source code that implements it. the jdk you download is somebody’s build of that code, usually with the builder’s own patches and backports, and usually tested against the compatibility kit (the tck in the card above). wikipedia gives the reason there are so many: because oracle no longer releases updates for long-term-support releases under a permissive licence, other organisations publish their own builds. most linux distributions and package managers ship one too. build who builds it cost and licence worth knowing oracle openjdk oracle, at jdk.java.net open source (gplv2 with the classpath exception) builds of the current release only; no long-term updates (wikipedia’s table marks it “lts: no”) oracle jdk oracle jdk 25: free for all users under the no-fee terms and conditions, with updates released after september 2028 planned to move to the otn licence. jdk 17 and 21 updates are now under the otn licence, free for personal and development use only oracle’s own build, with paid support through a java se subscription eclipse temurin adoptium at the eclipse foundation (formerly adoptopenjdk, started 2017) free “to use, forever”, gplv2 with the classpath exception lts releases supported for at least four years; each release passes the java compatibility kit; paid support from other companies amazon corretto amazon no cost, “production-ready” tck certified; quarterly updates; linux, windows and macos microsoft build of openjdk microsoft quarterly updates free of charge to anyone optional support on azure azul zulu azul systems permissive licence tck tested; c.h: What happened to JNI, java.awt.Robot and MIDlets
c.x: what happened to jni, java.awt.robot and midlets three pieces of java that many engineers met early on, and what each became. then what happened today jni the java native interface is how java calls c, c++ and other native code. jep 454 lists its “tedious artifacts”: native methods in java, a c header file derived from them, and a c implementation that calls the library you want. and, as jep 472 puts it, calling native code “can lead to arbitrary undefined behavior, including jvm crashes”. project panama’s foreign function & memory (ffm) api was previewed in jdk 19, 20 and 21 (jeps 424, 434, 442) and became final in jdk 22 (jep 454), to call native libraries “without the brittleness and danger of jni”. the jextract tool generates the java bindings from a library’s c header files. still there, but discouraged. since jdk 24 (jep 472), loading native code through jni prints a warning unless native access is enabled, and ffm’s native calls are restricted in the same way. jep 472 states that it is not a goal to deprecate or remove jni, and many jdk classes, such as those for file i/o and audio, still use it inside. new code should use ffm. robot java.awt.robot , added in java 1.3, generates real mouse and keyboard events in the operating system’s input queue, “for the purposes of test automation, self-running demos, and other applications where control of the mouse and keyboard is needed”. robot.mousemove really moves the pointer. its documentation warns that platforms may restrict that access: on x window systems without the xtest extension, for example, creating a robot fails. still in the jdk (it is in the java se 25 api), and still used to test desktop apps. for web apps, browser-automation tools such as playwright and selenium do this job (see testing ). if you meant robots: lejos replaced the firmware on lego mindstorms bricks so that they could run java, with versions for the rcx (2000), nxt (2007) and ev3 (2014); robotics covers today’s tools. midlets java apps and games on feature phones. a midlet is an application for midp , the mobile information device profile of java me , which ran on the connected limited device configuration (cldc). the first midp phones launched in april 2001. apps came as a .jad description and a .jar , often downloaded over the air. by 2013 there were more than three billion java me phones, but the platform was already in decline as smartphones overtook feature phones. android runs apps written in java, but its runtime is very different from java me. largely gone from phones; emulators keep the old games playable. java’s smallest platform lives on as java card , in sim and esim cards, bank cards, identity cards and passports. the browser applet, another early java promise, was deprecated in jdk 9 (jep 289), marked for removal in jdk 17 (jep 398) and removed in jdk 26 (jep 504). what ffm looks like. one java method handle replaces the native method, header file and c wrapper: // calling c's strlen from java with the ffm api (the example in jep 454) linker linker = linker.nativelinker(); methodhandle strlen = linker.downcallhandle( linker.defaultlookup().find("strlen").get(), functiondescriptor.of(java_long, address) ); try (arena arena = arena.ofconfined()) { memorysegment str = arena.allocatefrom("hello"); long len = (long)strlen.invoke(str); // 5 } the jni warning since jdk 24 , as jep 472 shows it. adding --enable-native-access=<module> (or all-unnamed for code on the class path) at launch removes it: warning: a restricted method in java.lang.system has been called warning: system::load has been called by com.foo.server in module com.foo (file:/path/to/com.foo.jar) warning: use --enable-native-access=com.foo to avoid a warning for callers in this module warning: restricted methods will be blocked in a future release unless native access is enabled our view: the pattern across all three is the same. java keeps an old api working for years, adds a safer replacement, and then warns, deprecates and removes in public steps, each in a jep you can read. the other view: some still see that pace as too slow. jni took over twenty years to get a supported alternative, and the slow fading of applets and java me let other platforms take the browser and the phone.

the short answer most server code spends its life waiting: for a database row, an http reply, a file. the cpu is idle while it waits. our view: every change to how java handles threads has been about one thing, making that waiting cheap . the other view is in the card “our view, and the other view”. the page java has the same history as a one-table summary; this page tells it step by step, with what each step cost.

thirty years in one line six eras of java threads, 1996 to 2023 a timeline of six eras. 1996, raw threads: one java thread per operating-system thread. 2004, thread pools: reuse a fixed set of threads. 2011, fork/join: split cpu work and steal idle time. 2014, futures: chain work without waiting. 2017, reactive: a few threads that never block. 2023, virtual threads: millions of cheap threads. 1996 raw threads one java thread per os thread 2004 thread pools reuse a fixed set of threads 2011 fork/join split cpu work, steal idle time 2014 futures chain work without waiting 2017 reactive a few threads, never blocking 2023 virtual threads millions of cheap threads six eras, each answering the same question differently. the years are the java (or library) releases named in each card below.

1. raw threads java 1.0 · 1996 java shipped with threads in the platform from the start: thread , runnable , the synchronized keyword, and wait / notify on every object. concurrency was part of the language and its core library, not an add-on. thread t = new thread(new runnable() { public void run() { handle(request); } }); t.start(); early jvms used green threads , scheduled by the jvm itself. they were abandoned in java 1.3 for native threads : each java thread became a real operating-system thread. the cost: an os thread reserves a large stack (by default 1 mb on 64-bit x86 linux, 2 mb on arm64 linux) and is expensive to create and switch. a server could hold a few thousand threads, not hundreds of thousands.

2. thread pools and java.util.concurrent java 5 · 2004 java.util.concurrent (jsr 166, led by doug lea) changed everyday java. instead of creating a thread per task, you hand tasks to an executor that reuses a fixed pool. it came with future and callable , explicit locks, atomic variables, concurrenthashmap , and coordination tools such as countdownlatch . the same release brought a new java memory model (jsr 133), so these tools had firm guarantees underneath. executorservice pool = executors.newfixedthreadpool(200); future<case> f = pool.submit(() -> repository.find(id)); // shown in today's syntax case c = f.get(); // blocks this thread until the result is ready this became the classic server model behind servlets and spring mvc: one pooled thread per request , blocking while it waits. the cost: the pool size is the ceiling. with 200 threads all waiting on a slow database, request 201 queues, even though the cpu is idle.

3. fork/join java 7 · 2011 forkjoinpool tackled a different problem: big cpu-bound jobs. a task splits itself into smaller tasks, and idle threads steal work from busy ones' queues. it made multi-core machines easy to use for computation. it did nothing for waiting on i/o.

4. futures you can chain java 8 · 2014 completablefuture , together with lambdas, let you describe what happens after a result arrives instead of blocking a thread to wait for it: completablefuture.supplyasync(() -> fetchcase(id)) .thenapply(this::summarise) .thenaccept(this::send); no thread sits idle between the steps. each step runs when the previous one completes. the cost: error handling, timeouts and debugging get harder. a stack trace no longer shows the story of the request.

5. reactive reactive streams 1.0, 2015 · java 9 flow , 2017 · spring webflux, 2017 underneath, non-blocking networking had existed since nio in java 1.4 (2002): one thread with a selector can watch many sockets. netty built an asynchronous, event-driven framework on it: a handful of threads that never block, serving very many connections. reactive libraries made that model programmable. an early, widely used one was rxjava , netflix’s jvm implementation of microsoft’s reactive extensions, first published around 2013. it introduced many java developers to observable and to operators such as map , flatmap , zip and retry . rxjava 2 (october 2016) was rewritten on the reactive streams specification (1.0 in spring 2015), which grew out of rxjava 1.x and was started by engineers at netflix, pivotal and lightbend. project reactor, the library under spring webflux, follows the same specification. these libraries describe work as streams of events with backpressure , so a slow consumer can tell a fast producer to slow down. java 9 put the same interfaces into the jdk as java.util.concurrent.flow . spring framework 5.0 (2017) added webflux ; spring boot’s webflux starter runs it on netty by default. webclient.get().uri("/cases/{id}", id) .retrieve() .bodytomono(case.class) .map(this::summarise) .timeout(duration.ofseconds(5)); the cost: every layer has to be non-blocking, down to the database driver (hence r2dbc instead of jdbc). one blocking call on an event-loop thread stalls everyone, and the code reads as chains of operators instead of plain steps.

6. virtual threads preview in java 19 and 20 · final in java 21 · 2023 project loom asked a different question: what if threads were simply cheap? a virtual thread is managed by the jvm, not the operating system. when it blocks on i/o, the jvm suspends it and frees the underlying os thread (the “carrier”) for another virtual thread. you can run millions of them. try (var executor = executors.newvirtualthreadpertaskexecutor()) { executor.submit(() -> handle(request)); // plain blocking code, one cheap thread per task } thread.ofvirtual().start(() -> handle(request)); the plain, blocking style from 2004 is back, and it scales the way reactive code does. spring boot 3.2 turned it into a single setting, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true , on java 21 or later. the first versions had one notable trap. a virtual thread blocking inside a synchronized block was pinned to its carrier, which could starve the pool. java 24 (jep 491) removed nearly all of that pinning for synchronized .

7. what is arriving now java 25 (2025) to java 27 scoped values are final in java 25 (jep 506): a safer, cheaper replacement for many uses of threadlocal that suits millions of short-lived threads. structured concurrency has been in preview since java 21 and was previewed again in each release since: the seventh preview is in java 27 (jep 533). it treats a group of subtasks as one unit: start them together, and if one fails, cancel the rest and report one error. it addresses the error-handling problem that futures and reactive code never solved neatly.

was quarkus reactive by nature? underneath, yes. quarkus (1.0 in november 2019) runs on vert.x and netty , an event-loop engine like the one under webflux. but today it does not force reactive code on its users. you can write: ordinary blocking code , which quarkus runs on worker threads, off the event loop; reactive code with its mutiny library; and, on java 21 or later, virtual-thread endpoints , marked @runonvirtualthread . spring offers the same three: blocking mvc, reactive webflux, and mvc on virtual threads. more on quarkus and spring .

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: the thread did not get faster in thirty years. each step made it cheaper to keep a thread waiting, until it cost almost nothing, so for most request/response services virtual threads with plain blocking code are now the simplest choice that scales. the other view: reactive code is more than a workaround for expensive threads. backpressure, streaming and composing many events are first-class in it, and teams that need those may find a reactive stack the clearer model, with virtual threads adding little.

which model to use today model good for ( analysis ) watch out for virtual threads most request/response services that wait on databases and apis. simple code that scales. very long cpu work still needs a bounded pool. libraries that hold locks or threadlocal caches deserve a check. reactive (webflux, mutiny) streaming, server-sent events, backpressure between fast and slow parts, very high connection counts. everything must be non-blocking end to end, and debugging is harder. fixed thread pools cpu-bound work, and limiting how much load reaches a fragile downstream. pool size becomes the throughput ceiling when tasks mostly wait. your team already runs one model well stay with it unless a row above forces a change. switching has a cost. the races, deadlocks and queues underneath all of these are on concurrency , with runnable examples.

further reading java 8 lambdas by richard warburton (o’reilly) is a short, practical introduction to the functional style that step 4 relies on: lambdas, streams, collectors and completablefuture . the book’s exercises and examples are on github at richardwarburton/java-8-lambdas-exercises .

the short answer every web server answers the same question: when ten thousand clients are connected and most of them are idle or slow, who waits for them? over thirty years the answer moved from a process, to a thread, to an event loop, and now back to a thread that costs almost nothing. the same story from the thread’s side is on how java threads evolved ; the network underneath is on networking .

thirty years in one line six eras of serving many clients, 1993 to 2023 a timeline of six eras. 1993, a process per request: cgi and apache prefork. 1996, a thread per connection: java.io, servlets and tomcat. 2002, event loops: epoll, java nio and nginx. 2004 to 2011, frameworks on nio: netty, jetty and nio.2. 2009 to 2017, asynchronous all the way: servlet 3, node.js and webflux. 2023, virtual threads: blocking code that is cheap. 1993 process per request: cgi, prefork 1996 thread per connection: java.io, tomcat 2002 event loops epoll, nio, nginx 2004–11 frameworks on nio: netty, nio.2 2009–17 async servlet 3, node, webflux 2023 virtual threads blocking code, cheap six eras. the years are the releases named in the cards below.

1. a process per request 1993–1995 the early web ran programs through cgi , specified by the ncsa team in 1993: for every request, the web server started a new process, passed the request in environment variables and standard input, and sent back whatever the program printed. it was simple and fully isolated, but starting a process per request is slow. apache httpd (april 1995) kept processes around instead. its pre-forking model (later the “prefork” module) held a pool of worker processes, each answering one request at a time. the cost: one process per connection. memory, not cpu, set the number of users a server could hold.

2. java.io : a thread per connection java 1.0 (1996) · servlets (1997) · tomcat (1999) java’s original i/o, java.io , is stream-based and blocking : inputstream.read() blocks until data is available. a server built on it accepts a socket and gives it a thread: serversocket server = new serversocket(8080); while (true) { socket socket = server.accept(); // blocks until a client connects pool.submit(() -> handle(socket)); // that thread blocks on every read and write } the servlet api (1.0 in 1996–97) put a standard interface over this model, and tomcat , first released at the apache software foundation in 1999, became a widely used container, alongside jetty . threads were lighter than processes, and the code was easy to read: read the request, call the database, write the response, top to bottom. the cost: an idle keep-alive connection still holds a whole thread. in 1999 dan kegel named the problem c10k : how do you serve ten thousand clients at once?

3. readiness and event loops: nio kqueue (2000) · java 1.4 nio (2002) · epoll (2002) · nginx (2004) operating systems answered c10k with efficient readiness notification: kqueue in freebsd 4.1 (july 2000) and epoll in linux 2.5.45 (october 2002), replacing the older select and poll , whose cost grows with the number of sockets watched. instead of one thread waiting on each socket, one thread asks the kernel which sockets are ready and services only those. java got the same ability in java 1.4 (february 2002) through nio (jsr 51): channels, buffers, and a selector that watches many channels at once. selector selector = selector.open(); serverchannel.configureblocking(false); serverchannel.register(selector, selectionkey.op_accept); while (true) { selector.select(); // one thread waits for any socket to be ready for (selectionkey key : selector.selectedkeys()) { if (key.isacceptable()) accept(key); if (key.isreadable()) read(key); // never blocks: the data is already there } selector.selectedkeys().clear(); } outside java, nginx (october 2004) was built on this model: a master process and a few worker processes, each handling many connections with an asynchronous, event-driven approach rather than a thread each. it became a widely used front door for web applications, often in front of java servers. the cost: raw nio is hard. partial reads, buffer flipping, back-pressure and threading rules are all yours to get right.

4. frameworks on nio netty and apache mina (mid-2000s) · tomcat 6 nio connector (2006–07) · nio.2 in java 7 (2011) libraries took on that difficulty. apache mina and then netty , created by trustin lee, wrapped nio in event loops, pipelines of handlers and pooled buffers. netty became the networking layer under much of the java world: grpc for java, cassandra, elasticsearch, vert.x and, later, spring boot’s default server for webflux. servlet containers moved their connectors to nio too. tomcat 6.0 (betas in 2006, stable in 2007) shipped an nio connector, so an idle keep-alive connection no longer held a thread ; the old blocking connector was removed in tomcat 8.5 and 9. request processing itself still used a thread per request. nio.2 in java 7 (2011, jsr 203) added asynchronous channels and the java.nio.file api ( path , files ) that replaced most uses of java.io.file .

5. asynchronous all the way through servlet 3.0 (2009) · node.js (2009) · servlet 3.1 (2013) · spring webflux (2017) the next step was to free the thread during the request, not only between requests. servlet 3.0 (december 2009) let a request be suspended and resumed later on another thread, and servlet 3.1 (may 2013) added non-blocking reads and writes. node.js (2009) showed a whole application could live on one event loop, with every i/o call asynchronous. in java, vert.x (2011), undertow (first released 2013, 1.0 in 2014) and spring webflux (2017, on reactor, running on netty by default) followed. a handful of event-loop threads serve everything, as long as nobody blocks one of them. the cost: every library in the request path must be non-blocking, down to the database driver. one blocking call on an event-loop thread stalls every connection that thread serves.

c.h: 6. Virtual threads: blocking I/O becomes cheap
c.x: 6. virtual threads: blocking i/o becomes cheap socket rewrites in java 13 and 15 · virtual threads final in java 21 (2023) project loom took a different route. java first reimplemented its classic blocking socket classes (jep 353 in java 13, jep 373 in java 15) so they could work with a new kind of thread, then called fibers. then virtual threads (final in java 21, jep 444) made threads cheap. when a virtual thread blocks on a socket, the jvm unmounts it and resubmits it when the operation can complete; on linux, the jdk’s poller underneath uses epoll . try (var executor = executors.newvirtualthreadpertaskexecutor()) { while (true) { socket socket = server.accept(); executor.submit(() -> handle(socket)); // the 1996 code, now one cheap thread per connection } } the code from step 2 is back, and it scales like step 3. spring boot runs request handling on virtual threads with one property ( spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true ), and helidon 4 introduced a web server (helidon nima) built from the ground up on virtual threads.

the same problem, four answers model who waits for a slow client examples process per connection a whole os process cgi, apache prefork thread per connection a platform thread (the jvm’s default stack is 1 mb on 64-bit x86 linux) java.io servers, classic tomcat event loop nobody: the kernel reports when the socket is ready nginx, node.js, netty, webflux virtual thread a parked virtual thread, with an event loop underneath spring boot 3.2 and later on java 21, helidon 4 the protocols kept moving too: http/2 (rfc 7540, may 2015, since replaced by rfc 9113) put many requests on one connection, and http/3 (rfc 9114, june 2022) runs over quic on udp. each step raised the number of conversations a server holds at once.

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: underneath, it is now the same machinery: the kernel’s readiness api (epoll, kqueue) does the waiting. what changed is how much of it the programmer has to see. nio and event loops exposed it; virtual threads hide it again behind plain, blocking-looking code, which suits most services. the other view: hiding the machinery has a price. event-loop code makes concurrency and back-pressure visible in the program, and some teams prefer that explicitness, especially for streaming or very high connection counts, where it is easier to reason about than many parked threads.

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) request/response service that mostly waits on databases and apis, on java 21 or later thread per request on virtual threads streaming, server-sent events, many long-lived idle connections an event-loop server (netty, webflux, vert.x) serving static files and terminating tls in front of applications a dedicated event-loop proxy such as nginx your team already runs one model well stay with it unless a row above forces a change: switching has a cost

where you meet it android apps , where it is widely used. server-side services with spring boot or ktor, mixed freely with java in one codebase. build scripts: gradle's kotlin dsl ( build.gradle.kts ). shared code across platforms with kotlin multiplatform.

the ideas that matter null safety: string can never be null; string? can, and the compiler makes you handle it with ?. , ?: or a check. data classes: equals , hashcode , tostring and copy for free. sealed types and when : the compiler checks you handled every case. extension functions: add behaviour to a type you do not own. coroutines: asynchronous code written like sequential code (the kotlinx.coroutines library). java interop: call java and be called from it; watch nullability at the boundary, where java types arrive as "platform types" the compiler cannot check.

java, kotlin or scala? all three run on the jvm and can use the same libraries. they differ in what they optimise for. java kotlin scala first released 1995 2011 (1.0 in february 2016) 2004 (scala 3 in may 2021) created by sun microsystems jetbrains martin odersky style object-oriented, steadily adding records, pattern matching and virtual threads concise object-oriented with functional features; null safety in the type system a deep blend of object-oriented and functional programming, with a powerful type system where you meet it most enterprise back ends, spring and quarkus services android, and spring or ktor services beside java data processing (apache spark is written in scala) and functional back ends learning curve gentle; the most material and people gentle for java developers steeper; very expressive, which can also make code harder to read a practical rule: learn java first, because everything on the jvm assumes it. add kotlin for android or a more concise service codebase, and scala when you work with spark or a team that writes functional code.

c.h: A small program, and its test
c.x: a small program, and its test run with maven or gradle and the kotlin plugin. this compiles and its tests pass on the jvm. data class order(val id: string, val pence: int, val note: string? = null) sealed interface check { data class ok(val pence: int) : check data class invalid(val reason: string) : check } fun validate(o: order): check = when { o.pence <= 0 -> check.invalid("order ${o.id} has no amount") else -> check.ok(o.pence) } // an extension function: adds behaviour to a type you do not own. fun int.aspounds(): string = "£%d.%02d".format(this / 100, this % 100) fun main() { val orders = listof(order("a1", 1250, note = "gift"), order("a2", 0), order("a3", 499)) val total = orders.map(::validate).filterisinstance<check.ok>().sumof { it.pence } println("total: ${total.aspounds()}") // null safety: note is string?, so the compiler makes you handle null. orders.foreach { println("${it.id}: ${it.note?.uppercase() ?: "no note"}") } } import kotlin.test.test import kotlin.test.assertequals import kotlin.test.assertis class orderstest { @test fun `zero amount is invalid`() { assertis<check.invalid>(validate(order("a2", 0))) } @test fun `pence format as pounds`() { assertequals("£17.49", 1749.aspounds()) } }

build and tools gradle with the kotlin dsl is the most common build; maven has a kotlin plugin too. tests: kotlin.test on junit 5; mockk for mocks; kotest if you like a specification style. style: ktlint or detekt in ci. ide: intellij idea, from the same company, has the deepest support.

common mistakes !! everywhere: it turns a compile-time check back into a runtime crash. handle the null instead. trusting java types: a value from a java method may be null even if you declared it non-null. blocking inside a coroutine: a blocking call ties up the thread; use a suspending api or the io dispatcher. clever over clear: scope functions ( let , apply , also ) nested three deep are hard to read.

match (structural pattern matching) match event: case {"state": "succeeded", "rows": int(n)} if n == 0: warn("succeeded with zero rows") case {"state": "succeeded", "rows": int(n)}: ok(n) case {"state": "failed", "error": str(msg)}: fail(msg) case {"state": state}: unknown(state) case _: raise valueerror(f"bad event: {event!r}") match path.split("/"): case ["data", y, *rest] if y.startswith("year="): ... patterns match structure and types; they do not do string prefix matching. use a guard ( if ) for that.

errors, logging, context managers import logging, contextlib, time log = logging.getlogger(__name__) logging.basicconfig(level=logging.info, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s") try: load(uri) except notfound: log.warning("missing %s", uri) # lazy formatting except exception: log.exception("load failed for %s", uri) # includes traceback raise else: log.info("loaded %s", uri) @contextlib.contextmanager def timed(label): t = time.perf_counter() try: yield finally: log.info("%s took %.2fs", label, time.perf_counter() - t) with timed("orders load"): run()

concurrency # threads for blocking i/o (gcs, bq, http) from concurrent.futures import threadpoolexecutor, as_completed with threadpoolexecutor(max_workers=16) as ex: futs = {ex.submit(copy, uri): uri for uri in uris} for f in as_completed(futs): try: f.result() except exception as e: log.error("%s: %s", futs[f], e) # asyncio with structured cancellation (3.11) import asyncio async def main(): async with asyncio.taskgroup() as tg: tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch(u)) for u in urls] return [t.result() for t in tasks] asyncio.run(main()) # processes for cpu-bound work from concurrent.futures import processpoolexecutor
