which version should i learn? short answer: none in particular. learn modern javascript, meaning everything from ecmascript 2015 onward, and use what your target browsers or node.js support. ecmascript 2015 (also called es6) is the line that matters ( our view ; it is where most of today’s syntax begins). it added let and const , arrow functions, classes, modules ( import / export ), promises, iterators and for…of , template literals and destructuring. much older code you meet was written without these. since then there has been one edition a year, named by year: es2016, es2017, up to es2026. each one is small: the proposals that reached stage 4 before that year’s spec was branched, in march. to reach stage 4, a feature needs, among other things, two compatible implementations that pass the test262 conformance tests and real experience with shipping implementations, so by the time it is in an edition it is already running in at least two javascript engines. do not ask "which es version". ask "is this feature available where my code runs?" for browsers, mdn marks each feature with baseline : widely available means it has worked for at least 2.5 years in chrome, edge, firefox and safari on desktop, and in chrome, firefox and safari on mobile. typescript is javascript with types, checked before the code runs. learn it after the language, not instead of it.

what each edition added from tc39's list of finished proposals, by the year each was expected to be published. you do not need to memorise this; it shows how small the yearly steps are, and where the features you use came from. edition features you will meet es2015 let / const , arrow functions, classes, modules, promises, iterators, for…of , template literals, destructuring, map / set es2016 ** (exponent), array.prototype.includes es2017 async / await , object.values / entries , string padding es2018 rest and spread for objects ( {...obj} ), async iteration ( for await…of ), promise.prototype.finally es2019 flat / flatmap , object.fromentries , optional catch binding es2020 optional chaining ( a?.b ), nullish coalescing ( ?? ), dynamic import() , bigint , promise.allsettled , globalthis es2021 replaceall , promise.any , logical assignment ( ??= ), numeric separators es2022 class fields and #private members, top-level await , .at() , error cause es2023 copying array methods ( tosorted , toreversed , with ), findlast es2024 object.groupby , promise.withresolvers es2025 iterator helpers, new set methods, json modules and import attributes, promise.try , regexp.escape es2026 array.fromasync , error.iserror , math.sumprecise , base64 for uint8array next (expected 2027) temporal (a modern date and time api), explicit resource management ( using )

the patterns underneath every framework functions are values. you pass them, return them and store them. event handlers, callbacks, react components and hooks are all functions. closures: a function keeps access to the variables around it when it was created. mdn: closures are created every time a function is created. private state and callbacks that remember values rely on this. the event loop: one thread runs one job at a time, each to completion. slow work (network, timers, files) finishes later and queues a job. block that thread and nothing else runs until you finish, including the page’s response to the user. promises and async / await : a promise is a value that arrives later. await pauses your function, not the thread. modules: import and export . modules always run in strict mode. objects and prototypes: class is a cleaner way to write prototype-based inheritance, not a different model. immutability: make a new object or array instead of changing the old one ( {...obj} , tosorted ). some frameworks compare old and new values to decide what to redraw; a new object makes that comparison cheap and reliable ( analysis ). iterators and generators: anything you can for…of over.

c.h: What a framework is made of
c.x: what a framework is made of this mapping is analysis, to help you read any framework's docs. framework idea the javascript or web feature under it component a function or class that returns a description of the ui props function arguments, usually destructured state and hooks closures over values the framework stores for you reactivity, signals, stores the observer pattern: subscribe a function, call it on change re-rendering compare old and new values (cheap when data is immutable), or track exactly which values changed effects, data loading promises, async / await , fetch , cleanup functions routing the history api and the url code splitting dynamic import() reusable widgets without a framework web components: custom elements, shadow dom, html templates

c.h: Try it: the patterns in plain JavaScript
c.x: try it: the patterns in plain javascript save as patterns.mjs and run node patterns.mjs , or paste into a browser console. no framework, no install. // 1. closure: count keeps its own private state function counter() { let n = 0; return () => ++n; } const next = counter(); next(); next(); console.log("closure:", next()); // 3 // 2. observer: the core of every "reactive" framework function signal(value) { const subs = new set(); return { get: () => value, set: (v) => { value = v; subs.foreach((f) => f(v)); }, subscribe: (f) => { subs.add(f); return () => subs.delete(f); }, }; } const price = signal(10); const stop = price.subscribe((v) => console.log("render price:", v)); price.set(12); // render price: 12 stop(); // 3. immutability: new array, old one untouched const items = [3, 1, 2]; const sorted = items.tosorted(); console.log(items, sorted); // [ 3, 1, 2 ] [ 1, 2, 3 ] // 4. the event loop: synchronous code finishes first settimeout(() => console.log("timer job"), 0); promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("promise job")); console.log("sync code"); // sync code, promise job, timer job // 5. async/await: pauses the function, not the thread const wait = (ms) => new promise((r) => settimeout(r, ms)); async function load() { await wait(100); return { user: "ada", roles: ["admin"] }; } const { user, roles: [first] } = await load(); // top-level await, destructuring console.log(user, first, user?.length ?? 0);

a learning order that works values, types, let / const , functions, arrays and objects closures and scope the dom and events: change a page with no framework the event loop, promises, async / await , fetch modules, then a build tool (see build tools ) classes, prototypes, iterators typescript then one framework, the one your team or your target job uses our view: the framework you learn second takes a fraction of the time of the first, because you now see the patterns rather than the syntax. the other view: many people learn a framework first because jobs ask for it, and pick up the language as they go; that works too, as long as you go back and fill in the patterns above. see ui history for how the frameworks came and went.

c.h: Choosing a framework: start from the requirement
c.x: choosing a framework: start from the requirement comparisons of frameworks usually turn into preference. instead, write down what your product and your team need, and ask each candidate the same questions. check every answer in the framework’s own documentation, at the version you would use. if you need ask each candidate fast first load and search-engine indexing (public sites, shops) does it render on the server or generate static pages, and how much javascript does a page ship? a rich app behind a login (dashboards, tools) how does it manage state, forms and data loading at scale? mostly static content with a few interactive parts could plain html, a little javascript, or web components do it with no framework at all? mobile apps from the same code is there a supported way to build native or cross-platform apps? (see apps .) a product that must live for many years what is its release and support policy, who funds it, and how hard were its past major upgrades? hiring and a team that can keep it running do your current team and your local job market know it? accessibility from the start do its components and docs follow wcag patterns? (see accessibility .) an existing codebase can it be added page by page, or does it need a rewrite? two rules of thumb ( our view ): the requirement you cannot change later (hosting, long-term support, team skills) outweighs the one you can; and a choice you can explain in one sentence of requirements is better than one you explain by popularity.

common traps == converts types; use === . || replaces 0 and "" too; use ?? when only null or undefined should fall back. numbers are 64-bit floating point (ieee 754): 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is false . keep money in integer minor units (pence, paise, cents) or a decimal library. sort() changes the array it is called on; tosorted() returns a new one. a forgotten await gives you a promise, not the value. long work on the main thread blocks the ui; a web worker runs it on a background thread instead.

the short answer functional style means writing code as values flowing through functions that return new values: pure functions (same input, same output, nothing else changed), immutable data , and functions such as filter , map and sorted that take other functions as arguments. imperative style means loops and variables that change step by step. our view: functional style is the better default for transforming data , because each step can be read and tested on its own and nothing changes behind your back. imperative code is clearer where one real thing must change in place, where the work talks to the outside world, and in a few measured hot spots. the other view is at the end of the page.

c.h: The core operations, side by side
c.x: the core operations, side by side operation does python java (streams) filter keep the items that pass a test [s for s in sales if s.paid] .filter(s -> s.paid()) map turn each item into something new [s.total for s in sales] .map(sale::total) sort order by one key or several sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (r.store, -r.total)) .sorted(comparing(row::store).thencomparing(row::total, reverseorder())) group collect items under a key defaultdict(list) in a loop, or itertools.groupby on sorted data .collect(groupingby(sale::store)) reduce combine everything into one value sum(...) , max(...) , functools.reduce .maptoint(...).sum() , .reduce(0, integer::sum) flat map each item becomes several; flatten them [line for o in orders for line in o.lines] .flatmap(o -> o.lines().stream()) first n stop early itertools.islice(gen, n) , or slice a list .limit(n) , .findfirst() one pipeline: filter, map, sort, collect six sales flow left to right through four steps. filter removes the one cancelled sale, leaving five. map turns each sale into a row of store and total, still five. sort orders the rows by store, then by total biggest first. collect gathers them into a new list. the input list is never changed. 6 sales left untouched filter 5 not cancelled map (store, total) sort store, total ↓ collect new list of 5 each step takes a value and returns a new one python: sorted((s.store, s.total) for s in sales if s.status != "cancelled" …) java: sales.stream().filter(…).map(…).sorted(…).tolist() data flows through steps that each return something new. nothing is changed in place, which is what makes the pipeline easy to test and, in java, possible to run in parallel. filter before you sort. sorting is the expensive step, o(n log n); throwing away what you do not need first makes it cheaper.

c.h: Ordering: what keeps order and what does not
c.x: ordering: what keeps order and what does not sorts are stable in both languages: items with equal keys keep their relative order. python’s sorting guide guarantees it; java says “for ordered streams, the sort is stable”. that is why you can sort by a secondary key first and the primary key last. the last sort wins. sorting by store and then by total leaves the list ordered by total. use one sort with a two-part key instead (drill 06). a java stream has an encounter order if its source does (a list , an array). tolist() keeps it. a hashset or a hashmap ’s keys have no defined order. foreach on a parallel stream ignores order: the jdk calls it “explicitly nondeterministic”. use foreachordered when order matters, or better, collect. python’s executor.map works like the built-in map : results come back in input order, whichever task finishes first. order costs something in parallel. the jdk notes that order-bound operations such as limit() “may require buffering to ensure proper ordering, undermining the benefit of parallelism”, and that unordered() can help when you do not need the order.

c.h: Parallel streams: when they pay off
c.x: parallel streams: when they pay off in java, .parallelstream() (or .parallel() ) splits the work across threads. it helps only when there is enough work to share. measured on a 4-core machine, java 21, best of five runs: workload sequential parallel verdict 2,000,000 items, heavy arithmetic in map , then filter and sum 1,466 ms 441 ms 3.3× faster 2,000,000 items, the same map , then sorted().limit(10) 1,951 ms 598 ms 3.3× faster 1,000 items, light map , then sum 0.033 ms 0.180 ms 5× slower : splitting costs more than the work how a parallel stream splits the work and keeps the order a list of eight items is split into four parts. four threads each run map on their own part, at the same time. the parts are joined back in their original positions, so tolist returns the results in encounter order. below, the wrong way: four threads each add their results to one shared arraylist, which is not thread-safe, so items are lost and the order is whatever the threads happened to do. source: items 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8, in encounter order thread 1: map(1, 2) thread 2: map(3, 4) thread 3: map(5, 6) thread 4: map(7, 8) tolist(): parts joined in place: results 1 … 8, in order the wrong way: foreach(results::add) into one arraylist measured: wrong count in 19 of 20 runs, an exception in the other a parallel stream splits the source, works on the parts at the same time, and joins the results in their original order when you collect with tolist() . it cannot protect a list you change yourself from inside it. keep the steps stateless. the jdk’s advice: “the best approach is to avoid stateful behavioral parameters to stream operations entirely”. no shared counters, no shared lists. collect, do not mutate. map(...).tolist() is safe in parallel; foreach(list::add) is not (drill 05). parallel streams are for cpu work. for waiting on networks or disks, use virtual threads or a thread pool (see concurrency and how java threads evolved ). python has no parallel streams. use processpoolexecutor.map for cpu work (each process has its own interpreter) and threadpoolexecutor.map for waiting; both return results in input order. measure first. the third row above is the common case in ordinary business code.

c.h: Where the functional style needs care
c.x: where the functional style needs care one real value that many must change. a balance, the seats left on a flight, a cache. the logic can be pure, but somewhere one value changes, guarded by a lock, a transaction or an atomic update (see concurrency ). side effects. charging a card, sending email, reading the clock. keep them in a thin outer layer around a pure core, often called “functional core, imperative shell” (drill 04). single-use pipelines. generators and streams are lazy and can be read once. python silently gives an empty generator the second time; java throws “stream has already been operated upon or closed” (drill 02). deep recursion. neither cpython nor java turns recursion into a loop. cpython stops at its recursion limit (1,000 by default); a recursive sum of 5,000 items raised recursionerror here. java overflowed its stack at 100,000 levels and was fine at 10,000. use a loop when the depth comes from the data (drill 03). hot paths on large data. new values mean new allocations. in low-latency code (see banking & low latency ) or huge in-memory jobs, changing in place can matter. measure before choosing. naturally stateful algorithms. an lru cache, a visited set in a graph search, a simulation: possible functionally, usually clearer with loops and a little state. debugging long chains. a failure deep in a long pipeline gives a stack trace that is harder to read than a loop’s; the same is said of reactive code on spring boot . name the steps as small functions. java specifics. lambdas cannot throw checked exceptions through java.util.function types; break and early exit are awkward inside a stream; and a lambda that changes a field from a parallel stream brings back the lost update .

choose by requirement if this is true for you lean why you are transforming data: input in, output out, no shared state functional each step reads and tests on its own it must be easy to test, or safe to run in parallel functional (pure functions) no hidden state to set up or to race on many threads must update one shared value imperative, with a lock or transaction at that one place the state is real; guard it, do not hide it it talks to the outside world (i/o, payments, email) a pure core inside an imperative shell test the rules without the world the input is too big to hold in memory lazy pipelines (generators, streams), read once constant memory recursion depth grows with the data a loop no tail-call optimisation in cpython or java a measured hot path is slow because of copies imperative, in place, after measuring fewer allocations your team already writes in one style lean that way switching has a cost

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: write pure functions and pipelines by default for data, keep side effects at the edges, and drop to imperative code where state is real or a measurement says so. most bugs in the drills below come from mixing the two without noticing. the other view: some teams go further and use languages and libraries built for the functional style (immutable collections, effect systems, scala, haskell, clojure), handling state and side effects inside that model. it works well when the whole team is fluent; it is a larger change than adopting streams and comprehensions.

practise it: six drills each drill is a small, broken piece of real code in python and java, with tests that fail until you fix it, a prediction to make first, hints, and an explanation of the fix. about 10 to 15 minutes each, in well-rounded-engineer-labs/functional . drill what breaks 01 · the function that changed its input tax added twice: a function rewrote its caller’s list 02 · the pipeline you can only read once right order count, £0 revenue 03 · the recursion that ran out a chain 100,000 deep overflows the stack 04 · the core and the shell pricing that reads the clock and sends email cannot be tested 05 · the parallel stream that lost items items lost and order random from a parallel foreach 06 · the report sorted the wrong way filter and map right, then two sorts where one two-key sort was needed

the short answer our view: add a layer only when you can name the problem it solves for you. the other view: a team that adopts typescript, a bundler and a state library together, from a template, has one documented path from day one and does not have to retrofit types or a build later. which suits you depends on the requirements in the table below.

c.h: From source code to the browser
c.x: from source code to the browser from source code to the browser a pipeline of five boxes from left to right. source code, written in typescript and jsx, is type-checked by the typescript compiler. a transpiler such as babel or esbuild turns it into javascript the target can run. a bundler such as webpack or vite joins the modules into a few optimised files. the browser then runs plain javascript. under each box is the reason it exists. source typescript, jsx you write type check tsc catch mistakes transpile babel, esbuild run on the target bundle webpack, vite fewer, smaller files browser javascript what actually runs several steps are optional: browsers run es modules, and node.js can strip types itself the layers between the code you write and what the browser runs, and the reason each one exists. one tool often does several steps: esbuild, for example, bundles and minifies and also handles typescript and jsx.

c.h: Each layer, and why it exists
c.x: each layer, and why it exists layer what it does date or note typescript (microsoft) adds static typing with optional type annotations to javascript, designed for large applications; it transpiles to javascript released to the public in october 2012 jsx an xml-like syntax for describing ui inside javascript, created by facebook for react. it is syntactic sugar, transpiled into nested function calls; with typescript the files end in .tsx with react babel a transpiler that turns newer javascript (es2015 and later) into code older engines can run, and also transforms jsx and typescript 16 million core downloads a week in 2019 module bundler (webpack, esbuild, vite) follows the imports from an entry point, builds a dependency graph, and combines the modules into a few bundles, often minifying and removing unused code esbuild, written in go, claimed to be 10 to 100 times faster than other bundlers when it was released vite a development server, written by vue’s creator evan you, that reloads just the edited file using native es modules, and bundles for production supports typescript and jsx; no date in our sources react (meta) a library for building uis from components open-sourced at jsconf us in may 2013 react native (meta) uses react with native platform capabilities to build apps for android, ios and other platforms introduced in 2015 redux a library for managing and centralising application state, inspired by facebook’s flux and the elm architecture; created by dan abramov and andrew clark 2015

does your app need redux? redux’s own documentation says it is “not designed to be the shortest or fastest way to write code”, and that react’s built-in state system “might be all you need”. it quotes pete hunt, an early react contributor, on flux, the pattern redux grew out of: “you’ll know when you need flux. if you aren’t sure if you need it, you don’t need it.” the docs list where it helps most: a lot of application state needed in many places state that is updated often update logic that may be complex a medium or large codebase that many people work on a need to see how state changed over time react’s own documentation shows another way to share state: combining a reducer with context, built into react.

c.h: Layers you can sometimes leave out
c.x: layers you can sometimes leave out browsers run modules natively: javascript modules load with import in the browser, and an import map can tell it where bare module names live, without a bundler. node.js runs typescript files directly by stripping the types, for code that uses only “erasable” typescript syntax: enabled by default from node.js 23.6 and 22.18, and marked stable in 25.2 and 24.12. for full typescript features, its docs point to a third-party tool such as tsx . types as comments in javascript itself is a tc39 proposal at stage 1 (per its repository page, which says it is not updated regularly): an idea under discussion, not part of the language. // greet.ts type user = { name: string; visits: number }; function greet(user: user): string { return `hello ${user.name}, visit number ${user.visits}`; } console.log(greet({ name: "ana", visits: 3 })); $ node greet.ts hello ana, visit number 3 run as shown with node.js 22.23 and no build step; the second block is its real output.

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) a small page or tool, few dependencies, one maintainer plain javascript modules in the browser, perhaps with an import map: no build step code that several people maintain for years typescript, type-checked in ci many npm dependencies, or you must support older browsers a bundler and transpiler, usually through one tool such as vite shared state that many screens read and change, with complex updates a state library such as redux; otherwise react’s own reducer and context the same team must ship ios and android, and it already knows react react native (see apps for the native alternative) your team already runs a working toolchain upgrade it in place rather than switching tools: switching has a cost

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: much of the difficulty comes from adopting the whole stack on day one. starting small and adding a layer when a real problem appears keeps a front end easier to understand and to upgrade. the other view: a framework or starter template that includes the whole stack gives a team one well-trodden path, with documentation and many people who already know it, and avoids reassembling the pieces later when the app grows.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation say what typescript, jsx, a transpiler and a bundler each do run a typescript file and a plain es module read a package.json and its build scripts 2 practitioner set up typescript type-checking in ci decide whether an app needs a state library upgrade a toolchain dependency safely 3 senior choose which layers a project needs, by requirement remove a layer that no longer earns its place plan a web and react native codebase 4 expert set an organisation's front-end platform and upgrade policy weigh frameworks against a smaller custom stack keep build complexity in check across teams each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

where you meet it cloud and platform tools: docker, kubernetes, terraform, prometheus and many operators are written in go. reading go helps you debug the tools you run. see kubernetes and operators . network services and apis , where its small binaries and fast start-up suit containers. command-line tools , shipped as one file with no runtime to install.

the ideas that matter small on purpose: few keywords, one formatting style ( gofmt ), one obvious way to do most things. errors are values: functions return an error ; you check if err != nil . wrap with %w and test with errors.is . goroutines and channels: cheap concurrent functions, coordinated with channels, sync.waitgroup and mutexes. interfaces are implicit: a type satisfies an interface just by having its methods. composition, not inheritance: embed one struct in another. a strong standard library: http servers, json and testing need no framework.

c.h: A small program, and its test
c.x: a small program, and its test go run . runs it; go test -race ./... runs the table-driven test with the race detector on. both pass as written. package main import ( "errors" "fmt" "sync" ) type order struct { id string pence int } var errinvalid = errors.new("invalid order") // validate returns an error value instead of throwing: the caller must decide. func validate(o order) error { if o.pence <= 0 { return fmt.errorf("order %s: %w", o.id, errinvalid) } return nil } // total validates orders concurrently, one goroutine each, and sums the valid ones. func total(orders []order) (int, []error) { var ( wg sync.waitgroup mu sync.mutex sum int errs []error ) for _, o := range orders { wg.add(1) go func(o order) { defer wg.done() err := validate(o) mu.lock() defer mu.unlock() if err != nil { errs = append(errs, err) return } sum += o.pence }(o) } wg.wait() return sum, errs } func main() { sum, errs := total([]order{{"a1", 1250}, {"a2", 0}, {"a3", 499}}) fmt.println("total pence:", sum) for _, e := range errs { fmt.println("error:", e, "| invalid?", errors.is(e, errinvalid)) } } package main import ( "errors" "testing" ) func testvalidate(t *testing.t) { cases := []struct { name string order order wanterr bool }{ {"positive amount", order{"a1", 100}, false}, {"zero amount", order{"a2", 0}, true}, {"negative amount", order{"a3", -5}, true}, } for _, c := range cases { t.run(c.name, func(t *testing.t) { err := validate(c.order) if (err != nil) != c.wanterr || (err != nil && !errors.is(err, errinvalid)) { t.fatalf("validate(%v) = %v, wanterr %v", c.order, err, c.wanterr) } }) } }

build and tools modules: go mod init , dependencies pinned in go.mod and go.sum . built in: go build , go test (with -race and -cover ), go vet , gofmt , and benchmarks and fuzzing in the test tool. containers: a static binary fits a tiny base image. see docker .

common mistakes ignoring an error with _ : the failure is silent until it is expensive. leaking goroutines: one blocked forever on a channel nobody reads. pass a context.context and stop on cancel. data races: shared state touched from goroutines without a lock or channel. run tests with -race . a nil map write panics: make the map first.

where you meet it performance-critical services and infrastructure: proxies, databases, storage engines. fast tools for other languages: python's polars and the ruff linter are written in rust. see data libraries . systems and embedded code , and webassembly in the browser. security-sensitive code , where memory-safety bugs are the usual way in. see security .

the ideas that matter ownership: each value has one owner; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is freed. no garbage collector, no manual free . borrowing: lend a value as &t (many readers) or &mut t (one writer), never both at once. the borrow checker enforces it. no null, no exceptions: option<t> for maybe-a-value, result<t, e> for success-or-error, and ? to pass an error up. enums and match : the compiler checks every case is handled. traits: shared behaviour, like interfaces, resolved at compile time. fearless concurrency: the same rules stop data races from compiling.

c.h: A small program, and its tests
c.x: a small program, and its tests cargo run runs it; cargo test runs the two tests; cargo clippy reports no warnings. note that orders is still usable after total(&orders) , because total only borrowed it. use std::fmt; #[derive(debug, clone, partialeq)] struct order { id: string, pence: u32, } #[derive(debug, partialeq)] enum ordererror { empty(string), toolarge { id: string, pence: u32 }, } impl fmt::display for ordererror { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::formatter) -> fmt::result { match self { ordererror::empty(id) => write!(f, "order {id} has no amount"), ordererror::toolarge { id, pence } => write!(f, "order {id} is too large: {pence}"), } } } // borrows the order (&order): validating does not take ownership of it. fn validate(o: &order) -> result<u32, ordererror> { match o.pence { 0 => err(ordererror::empty(o.id.clone())), p if p > 1_000_000 => err(ordererror::toolarge { id: o.id.clone(), pence: p }), p => ok(p), } } // the ? operator returns the first error to the caller instead of panicking. fn total(orders: &[order]) -> result<u32, ordererror> { let mut sum = 0; for o in orders { sum += validate(o)?; } ok(sum) } fn main() { let orders = vec![ order { id: "a1".into(), pence: 1250 }, order { id: "a3".into(), pence: 499 }, ]; match total(&orders) { ok(sum) => println!("total pence: {sum}"), err(e) => println!("error: {e}"), } // orders is still usable here: total only borrowed it. let valid: vec<&order> = orders.iter().filter(|o| validate(o).is_ok()).collect(); println!("valid orders: {}", valid.len()); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn empty_order_is_an_error_not_a_panic() { let o = order { id: "a2".into(), pence: 0 }; assert_eq!(validate(&o), err(ordererror::empty("a2".into()))); } #[test] fn total_stops_at_the_first_error() { let orders = vec![ order { id: "a1".into(), pence: 100 }, order { id: "a2".into(), pence: 0 }, ]; assert!(total(&orders).is_err()); } }

build and tools cargo: build, test, dependencies (crates from crates.io) and benchmarks in one tool. rustfmt formats, clippy lints, rust-analyzer powers the editor. the compiler's messages are unusually helpful: read them in full, they often contain the fix.

common mistakes fighting the borrow checker with .clone() everywhere: it compiles, but hides the design question of who owns what. unwrap() in production code: it panics on an error. return a result or handle it. reaching for unsafe to get past a compile error. it does not switch off the borrow checker, but the operations it allows are no longer checked by the compiler, so their safety rests on you. expecting to be fast at it in a week. the learning curve is real; it pays back in fewer production bugs.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain ownership and borrowing use result, option and match build and test with cargo 2 practitioner write a cli or service in rust use traits, iterators and error types well keep clippy clean and the code formatted 3 senior design with lifetimes and generics write async rust and choose a runtime wrap unsafe or foreign code behind safe interfaces 4 expert lead rust adoption where safety and speed matter write libraries other languages call teach rust and review for soundness each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

what every build tool does resolves dependencies: downloads the libraries you name, and the libraries they need (transitive dependencies), from a registry such as maven central or the npm registry. runs the steps in order: compile, test, package, publish. you ask for the last step and the tool runs the ones before it. pins versions: a lockfile, a wrapper script or a version catalog, so a build next year uses the same versions as today. avoids repeated work: skips steps whose inputs have not changed. is the same in ci as on your machine. if it only builds on one person's laptop, it does not build.

a short history when tool what it brought 1976 make stuart feldman at bell labs: rules in a makefile, and a target rebuilt only when a source file is newer 2000 apache ant james duncan davidson, from the tomcat project: a java replacement for make, with xml build files 2004 apache maven jason van zyl (started 2002): conventions instead of scripts, and dependencies downloaded from a repository 2008 gradle builds on the concepts of ant and maven, with a groovy or kotlin build language; first stable release in june 2012 2010 npm isaac z. schlueter: the package manager for node.js, included in the node.js installer 2014 webpack bundles a web app's modules into files a browser loads 2015 bazel google's open-source port of its internal build tool blaze (started 2006), for large monorepos 2016 yarn started by sebastian mckenzie at facebook; rewritten in 2020 (codename "berry") 2017 pnpm zoltan kochan: one shared store on disk, linked into each project 2020 vite evan you, creator of vue.js: a fast dev server plus a production build

maven: convention over configuration a maven project is described by its pom.xml (project object model). if you follow the standard layout ( src/main/java , src/test/java ), you configure almost nothing. three built-in lifecycles: default (build and deploy), clean and site . main phases of the default lifecycle, in order: validate , compile , test , package , verify , install (into your local repository), deploy (to a remote repository). mvn verify runs every phase before verify too, so you only name the last one. plugins do the work: each phase runs plugin goals bound to it, and the bindings depend on the packaging ( jar , war , pom ). transitive dependencies are included automatically. when two versions of one library meet, maven picks the nearest definition in the dependency tree, not the newest. that surprises people: check with mvn dependency:tree . <dependencymanagement> pins versions for the whole tree, and the import scope pulls in a published bill of materials (bom), as spring boot and many cloud sdks provide. scopes: compile (the default), provided (the jdk or the container supplies it at runtime), runtime , test (only for compiling and running tests, and not passed on). the maven wrapper ( mvnw ) downloads the maven version the project declares, so nobody needs the right one installed. <project> <modelversion> 4.0.0 </modelversion> <groupid>com.example</groupid> <artifactid>orders</artifactid> <version> 1.0.0-snapshot </version> <dependencymanagement> <!-- one place for versions --> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupid>org.junit</groupid> <artifactid>junit-bom</artifactid> <version> 5.11.0 </version> <type>pom</type> <scope>import</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencymanagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupid>org.junit.jupiter</groupid> <artifactid>junit-jupiter</artifactid> <!-- no version: the bom sets it --> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </project> ./mvnw verify # compile, test, package, verify ./mvnw dependency:tree # which version won, and why

c.h: Gradle: a task graph you can program
c.x: gradle: a task graph you can program a gradle build is written in kotlin ( build.gradle.kts ) or groovy ( build.gradle ). instead of a fixed lifecycle, it builds a graph of tasks and runs the ones your request needs. three phases every build goes through: initialization (which projects are in the build), configuration (run the build scripts and work out the task graph), execution (run the selected tasks). the gradle wrapper ( gradlew ) is the recommended way to run any gradle build: it runs the declared gradle version and downloads it if needed. commit it. the daemon is a long-lived background process that hosts gradle's engine, so later builds skip the start-up cost. incremental builds: a task whose inputs and outputs have not changed is skipped as up to date. the build cache goes further: it reuses task outputs from earlier builds, on this machine or from a shared remote cache, when the inputs match. the configuration cache saves the result of the configuration phase and reuses it on the next build. version catalogs keep every dependency version in one file, gradle/libs.versions.toml , referenced as libs.… in the build scripts. android apps are built with gradle , through the android gradle plugin. # gradle/libs.versions.toml [versions] junit = " 5.11.0 " [libraries] junit-bom = { module = "org.junit:junit-bom", version.ref = "junit" } // build.gradle.kts plugins { java } dependencies { testimplementation(platform(libs.junit.bom)) testimplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter") } tasks.test { usejunitplatform() } ./gradlew build # compile, test, assemble ./gradlew build --build-cache # reuse outputs from earlier builds

maven or gradle? maven gradle build file xml ( pom.xml ): declarative kotlin or groovy: code model fixed lifecycle of phases graph of tasks versions in one place dependencymanagement and boms version catalogs and platforms choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards you build an android app gradle: android builds use it, through the android gradle plugin a large multi-module build where build time hurts gradle: up-to-date checks, the daemon and the build and configuration caches skip work you want every project to look the same, with little custom logic maven: a fixed lifecycle and conventions, configured rather than programmed the build needs real custom logic gradle: the build is code; in maven the logic goes into a plugin your team, ci templates and company plugins already use one stay with it unless a row above is a real, measured problem: switching has a cost other views: some engineers find gradle builds harder to read because the scripts are code; others find maven’s xml verbose. both are preferences. the rows above are requirements.

npm: the default for node.js package.json names your dependencies with version ranges and holds your scripts ; npm run build runs one. a script named prebuild or postbuild runs before or after it. package-lock.json is generated whenever npm changes node_modules . it records the exact tree, so the next install builds the same one. commit it. npm ci is for ci: it needs an existing lockfile, fails if package.json and the lock disagree, and never writes to either. use npm install to change dependencies, and npm ci to reproduce them. npx runs a package's command without installing it into your project. ranges: a caret allows any change that keeps the left-most non-zero number; a tilde allows only patch-level changes when the minor is given. the lockfile is what stops a range from drifting between installs. "dependencies": { "express": "^ 5.1.0 ", // 5.x.x, never 6 "lodash": "~ 4.17.21 " // 4.17.x only }

c.h: npm 12: install scripts are off by default
c.x: npm 12: install scripts are off by default install scripts ( preinstall , install , postinstall ) run code from a dependency on your machine the moment you install it, so a compromised package can act before you have run a line of your own code. npm 12, released in july 2026, changed the defaults: dependency lifecycle scripts are blocked unless the root package's allowscripts policy allows them. run npm install-scripts approve to record approvals, then npm rebuild to run the newly approved scripts. git and tarball-url dependencies are refused unless you opt in ( allow-git and allow-remote now default to none ). npm-shrinkwrap.json is no longer read: rename it to package-lock.json . on an older npm, --ignore-scripts turns install scripts off, though npm test and npm run still run the script you asked for.

yarn, pnpm and corepack yarn started at facebook in 2016. its modern version can install with plug'n'play : no node_modules folder at all, but a single .pnp.cjs loader that tells node where each package is. it can also use a normal node_modules install. pnpm keeps one content-addressable store on disk. each project's files are hard-linked or copy-on-write cloned from it, so a hundred projects using one library do not keep a hundred copies, and a new version adds only the files that changed. pnpm's node_modules is not flat: only your direct dependencies sit at the top, as symlinks. code cannot quietly import a package it never declared. tools that dislike symlinks can use nodelinker: hoisted . corepack lets a project use the yarn or pnpm version named in the packagemanager field of package.json , without installing it globally. it shipped with node.js until version 25. from 25 on, install corepack separately.

c.h: npm, Yarn or pnpm: choose by requirement
c.x: npm, yarn or pnpm: choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards nothing extra to install, the most tutorials and examples npm: it comes with the node.js installer many projects on one machine or ci runner; disk and install time matter pnpm: one content-addressable store, hard-linked into each project code must not import packages it never declared pnpm (non-flat node_modules ) or yarn plug’n’play no node_modules folder at all yarn plug’n’play a tool in your chain breaks on symlinks npm, or pnpm with nodelinker: hoisted strict control over install scripts by default npm 12 or later blocks dependency install scripts unless allowed; check the others’ current settings for your version the project already uses one keep it, and pin it with packagemanager in package.json

c.h: Bundlers: the other half of a JavaScript build
c.x: bundlers: the other half of a javascript build a package manager (npm, yarn, pnpm) fetches dependencies. a bundler turns your modules into the few files a browser downloads. a front-end build needs both. webpack (2014) builds a dependency graph of your modules and supports code splitting with dynamic import() . vite has two parts: a dev server that serves native es modules with very fast hot module replacement, and a build command that bundles for production with rolldown. typescript adds a type-check step: tsc --noemit in ci catches type errors even when the bundler only strips the types.

c.h: Habits that keep builds healthy, in any ecosystem
c.x: habits that keep builds healthy, in any ecosystem habit java node.js pin the tool itself commit mvnw or gradlew packagemanager in package.json , and a pinned node version in ci pin every dependency boms, dependencymanagement , version catalogs commit the lockfile and install with npm ci . yarn ( --immutable ) and pnpm refuse to change the lockfile on ci by default see why a version won mvn dependency:tree , gradle dependencies npm explain <pkg> , npm ls limit what runs at install add plugins and extensions deliberately, from sources you trust allow install scripts only for packages that need them make ci fast cache ~/.m2 or ~/.gradle ; gradle's build cache cache the package manager's store, not node_modules upgrade on purpose small, regular dependency updates (dependabot or renovate), each with a green build, beat one big upgrade a year

what an api is an api (application programming interface) is a contract: the operations a system offers, the inputs they take, the outputs and errors they return, and the rules for calling them. the contract is what other teams build against; the implementation behind it can change freely as long as the contract holds. public / partner / internal: who may call it, and so how strict versioning, security and documentation must be. synchronous: the caller waits (rest, grpc, graphql). asynchronous: the caller sends and moves on; the result arrives later (queues, events, webhooks). spec first: write the contract (openapi, protobuf, asyncapi) before the code; generate clients and docs from it.

rest in practice resources are nouns with urls: /orders , /orders/{id} , /stores/{code}/orders . http methods are the verbs: get reads, post creates, put replaces, patch updates part, delete removes. stateless: each request carries everything needed (including auth); no server session required. status codes carry meaning: 200, 201 created (+ location ), 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 conflict, 422, 429, 500, 503. errors as problem details (rfc 9457): type , title , status , detail . pagination with a cursor ( ?cursor=…&limit=50 ) rather than deep offsets. filtering and sorting by query parameters: ?store=1_05&from=2024-01-01&sort=-order_date . caching with etag / if-none-match and cache-control . method safe idempotent get, head yes yes put, delete no yes post no no: use an idempotency-key header patch no not guaranteed

an openapi contract openapi: 3.1.0 info: { title: shop api, version: 1.2.0 } paths: /v1/orders/{id}: get: operationid: getorder parameters: - { name: id, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: string } } responses: "200": description: the order content: application/json: schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/order" } "404": description: not found content: application/problem+json: schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/problem" } components: schemas: order: type: object required: [id, orderref, store] properties: id: { type: string } orderref: { type: string } store: { type: string } orderdate: { type: [string, "null"], format: date } problem: type: object properties: type: { type: string, format: uri-reference } title: { type: string } status: { type: integer } detail: { type: string } securityschemes: bearer: { type: http, scheme: bearer, bearerformat: jwt } security: [ { bearer: [] } ]

api styles compared style shape strengths weaknesses use for rest / json over http resources + http verbs universal, cacheable, easy to debug over- or under-fetching; loose typing unless specified public and partner apis, most web services grpc protobuf messages over http/2, generated clients fast, strongly typed, streaming both ways not browser-native; harder to inspect internal service-to-service calls graphql one endpoint; client asks for exactly the fields it needs flexible for uis; one round trip for nested data caching, query cost control, authorisation per field front ends combining many sources webhooks your server calls the client's url when something happens no polling delivery retries, signature checks, client downtime notifying partners (payments, git events) messaging / events publish to a topic; subscribers consume decoupling, buffering, fan-out eventual consistency, duplicates, debugging integration between domains, pipelines websockets / sse long-lived connection for pushes real-time updates, streaming responses connection management at scale live dashboards, chat, streaming ai output soap / xml envelope with wsdl contract strict contracts, ws-* standards verbose, legacy tooling integrating older enterprise systems file exchange csv/parquet drops on sftp or buckets simple, bulk latency, partial files, schema drift bulk data between organisations

grpc contract syntax = "proto3"; package shop.v1; service orderservice { rpc getorder(getorderrequest) returns (order); rpc streamnew(streamnewrequest) returns (stream order); // server streaming } message getorderrequest { string id = 1; } message streamnewrequest { string store = 1; } message order { string id = 1; string order_ref = 2; string store = 3; string order_date = 4; // iso date; field numbers never reused } compatibility rules: add fields with new numbers; never change or reuse a field number; reserve removed ones.

c.h: Gateway, load balancer, proxy, mesh: who does what
c.x: gateway, load balancer, proxy, mesh: who does what component job knows about gcp examples load balancer spread traffic across healthy instances; terminate tls ips, ports, hosts, paths cloud load balancing reverse proxy front a server: tls, compression, routing, caching http requests envoy, nginx api gateway single entry for apis: authentication, rate limits, routing, request transformation api keys, tokens, routes, quotas api gateway, apigee api management platform gateway plus api products, developer portal, analytics, monetisation, lifecycle consumers, apps, products, plans apigee service mesh service-to-service mtls, retries, traffic splitting, telemetry inside the platform every internal call cloud service mesh (istio) backend for frontend an api shaped for one client type that client's screens a small service on cloud run north-south traffic (clients into your platform) goes through the gateway; east-west traffic (services to each other) is the mesh's job. keep business logic out of both.

who does what, drawn north-south and east-west traffic clients outside the platform reach it through a load balancer and an api gateway: north-south traffic. inside, services call each other through the service mesh, which adds mtls, retries and telemetry: east-west traffic. a backend for frontend is shaped for one client. business logic lives in the services, not in the gateway or the mesh. mobile app partner load balancer: spread, tls api gateway: auth, rate limits north-south: into the platform inside the platform: the mesh, east-west bff for mobile orders payments stock mtls, retries, telemetry on every internal call the table above as a picture. the gateway guards the front door; the mesh handles the corridors; neither holds business logic.

api versioning and evolution additive changes are safe: new endpoints, new optional fields, new enum values clients are told to tolerate. breaking changes (removing or renaming fields, changing types or meaning) need a new version. where to version: in the path ( /v1/ ) is the most visible and the easiest to route at a gateway; headers are cleaner but harder to test. deprecate politely: announce, add deprecation and sunset headers, measure who still calls, then remove. meaning can break without a schema change: a field whose values change meaning is a breaking change even if its type is the same. contract tests in ci catch accidental breaks.

reliable integration timeouts on every call; retries only for idempotent operations, with backoff and jitter. idempotency keys for posts that create or charge. long-running work: return 202 accepted with a status url, or emit an event when done. webhooks you send: sign the payload (hmac), retry with backoff, let clients replay. webhooks you receive: verify the signature, respond fast, process asynchronously, dedupe by event id. rate limits with 429 and retry-after . correlation ids ( traceparent ) passed through every hop.

integration styles file transfer: one system writes files, another reads them. simple and still common for bulk data. shared database: several systems read and write the same tables. avoid: no system owns the schema. remote procedure call: one system calls another's api (rest, grpc). simple; couples availability. messaging: systems exchange messages through a broker. decoupled in time; more moving parts. from enterprise integration patterns (hohpe and woolf), a catalogue of messaging patterns.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain rest resources, methods and status codes call an api with curl and read its openapi spec tell sync from async integration 2 practitioner design a rest api with pagination, errors and versioning write and publish an openapi contract add timeouts, retries and idempotency keys 3 senior choose rest, grpc, graphql or events for a context design gateway, mesh and bff responsibilities run api evolution: deprecation and contract tests 4 expert set api standards and governance across the organisation design a partner and public api programme lead integration architecture across many systems each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the timeline timeline of api styles a horizontal timeline, evenly spaced and not to scale: rpc 1981, corba 1991, xml-rpc and soap 1998, rest 2000, openapi 2015, graphql 2015, grpc 1.0 2016, mcp 2024, a2a 2025. 1981 rpc 1991 corba 1998 xml-rpc, soap 2000 rest 2015 openapi 2015 graphql 2016 grpc 1.0 2024 mcp 2025 a2a evenly spaced, not to scale from remote procedure calls to agent protocols. the last two were designed for ai models and agents, rather than for programs calling programs. a selection from the table below. when what arrived the idea 1981–1984 remote procedure call (rpc) bruce jay nelson is credited with coining the term in 1981; he and andrew birrell published a paper on implementing it in 1984. calling a function on another machine as if it were local. 1991 corba the object management group’s standard for objects on different platforms and languages to call each other, with interfaces described in an interface definition language (idl). 1996 dcom microsoft’s proprietary equivalent, extending com across the network (launched in beta for windows 95 in 1996). java had its own, java rmi. 1998–2002 soa and the enterprise service bus service-oriented architecture, which can be built with web services. an enterprise service bus routes and transforms messages between services; the first commercial esb dates from 1998, and the term was first published by gartner in 2002. 1998 xml-rpc, then soap dave winer shipped xml-rpc in 1998: remote calls encoded as xml over http. soap grew from the same work into a fuller xml messaging protocol, described by wsdl documents. 2000 rest roy fielding’s doctoral dissertation described representational state transfer, the architectural style of the web: resources, a uniform interface and stateless requests. 2001 json douglas crockford specified json in the early 2000s and sent the first json message in april 2001. it became the usual body for web apis. 2010–2015 swagger, then openapi tony tam began swagger in 2010 to describe http apis; in 2015 the specification became a separate project, openapi, overseen by the openapi initiative under the linux foundation. 2015 graphql facebook started it in 2012 and open-sourced it in 2015: clients send a query against a typed schema, and the result mirrors the query’s shape. it moved to the graphql foundation in 2018. 2015–2016 grpc google had run an internal rpc system, stubby, since about 2001. in 2015 it decided to build the next version as open source: protocol buffers over http/2, with bidirectional streaming, timeouts and cancellation. grpc 1.0 followed in august 2016. 2024 model context protocol (mcp) introduced by anthropic in november 2024 to standardise how ai applications connect to tools and data; adopted by other ai vendors in 2025 and donated to the linux foundation’s agentic ai foundation in december 2025. 2025 agent2agent (a2a) introduced by google in april 2025 and now developed with the linux foundation: an open protocol for agents built on different frameworks by different companies to discover each other through “agent cards” and collaborate, using json-rpc over http(s), without exposing their internal memory or tools.

c.h: The lesson RPC and CORBA left
c.x: the lesson rpc and corba left rpc and corba aimed for location transparency : a remote call should look like a local one. but remote calls are usually orders of magnitude slower and less reliable than local ones, and can fail because of network problems. corba’s version has been criticised as a fundamental design flaw, citing waldo, wyant, wollrath and kendall’s a note on distributed computing (sun microsystems laboratories, 1994). wikipedia flags that citation as not yet verified, so the paper itself is worth reading. analysis: every later style made the network more visible in some way: http status codes in rest, explicit deadlines in grpc, and the timeouts and retries on distributed systems .

what each style changed soap and wsdl brought a formal contract and a standard envelope: a wsdl document describes the operations a service offers. analysis: its xml is heavier than json; the other view is that a strict contract and its tooling were what many enterprises wanted. rest used what the web already had: urls for resources, http methods, status codes and caching. its constraints include client and server separation, statelessness, cacheable responses and a uniform interface. graphql moved the choice of data to the client, with one endpoint and a typed schema. grpc brought back strongly typed rpc, with a binary format and streaming, for calls between services. mcp and a2a describe capabilities so that a model or an agent, not just a programmer, can discover and call them.

c.h: Protocol Buffers: the contract under gRPC
c.x: protocol buffers: the contract under grpc protocol buffers (protobuf) is google’s language-neutral, platform-neutral way of serialising structured data. google developed it for internal use (from early 2001) and released a code generator for many languages as open source. you describe messages once in a .proto file; the compiler, protoc , generates classes for each language, and grpc uses the same files to describe services. // person.proto syntax = "proto3"; message person { string name = 1; int32 id = 2; string email = 3; } the numbers are field numbers , and they are what goes on the wire, not the names. each field is written as a tag, (field_number << 3) | wire_type , followed by its value. the same record as protobuf and as json (python’s default json.dumps spacing, so compact json would be smaller), measured once on this one record: import json from google.protobuf import descriptor_pb2, descriptor_pool, message_factory # the same schema as person.proto, built in code so no protoc is needed here fdp = descriptor_pb2.filedescriptorproto(name="person.proto", syntax="proto3") msg = fdp.message_type.add(name="person") f = descriptor_pb2.fielddescriptorproto msg.field.add(name="name", number=1, type=f.type_string, label=f.label_optional) msg.field.add(name="id", number=2, type=f.type_int32, label=f.label_optional) msg.field.add(name="email", number=3, type=f.type_string, label=f.label_optional) pool = descriptor_pool.descriptorpool() pool.add(fdp) person = message_factory.getmessageclass(pool.findmessagetypebyname("person")) p = person(name="ana", id=1234, email="ana@example.com") wire = p.serializetostring() as_json = json.dumps({"name": "ana", "id": 1234, "email": "ana@example.com"}).encode() print("protobuf bytes:", len(wire), wire.hex(" ")) print("json bytes: ", len(as_json)) print("round trip: ", person.fromstring(wire).email) protobuf bytes: 25 0a 03 41 6e 61 10 d2 09 1a 0f 61 6e 61 40 65 78 61 6d 70 6c 65 2e 63 6f 6d json bytes: 55 round trip: ana@example.com run as shown with python 3 and the protobuf package (output from version 7.36.1 ); the second block is its real output. reading the bytes: 0a is (1<<3)|2, field 1 with wire type 2 (length-delimited); 03 is the length, then 41 6e 61 is “ana”. 10 is (2<<3)|0, field 2 as a varint; d2 09 is 1234, written seven bits at a time with the top bit of the first byte set to say another byte follows. 1a is (3<<3)|2, field 3; 0f is the length, 15, then the 15 bytes of “ana@example.com”. normally you would generate person with protoc ; the schema is built in code here only so the example runs without it.

changing a protobuf schema safely never change a field’s number once the message is in use: the number identifies the field in the wire format, so changing it is the same as deleting the field and adding a new one. reserve the numbers of fields you delete, and their names if you want protoc to refuse them, so nobody reuses them by accident. adding new fields is how a protobuf schema grows: the docs say it can be extended “without invalidating existing data or requiring code to be updated”. field numbers 19,000 to 19,999 are reserved for the protobuf implementation itself. more on contract evolution is on apis & integration .

protobuf or json? if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) high-volume calls between your own services, in several languages protobuf, usually with grpc a public api that browsers or scripts call json: readable without the schema you must read a message without its .proto file json: protobuf messages do not describe themselves messages larger than a few megabytes, or large numeric arrays something else: the protobuf docs say it is not a good fit rules require a formal standard not protobuf: its docs say it is not a formal standard of any organisation the right column is our reading of the protobuf documentation, not a standard. other teams weigh size and speed more, or readability more; your team already running one format counts too, because switching has a cost.

c.h: The gateway in front of it all
c.x: the gateway in front of it all as apis multiplied, a gateway in front of them took on the shared work: routing, authentication, rate limits, quotas, transformation and monitoring (more on apis & integration and apigee ). agents have produced a new kind of gateway. the right-hand column is our summary of the vendor documents listed below ( analysis ), not a standard definition: api gateway ai and agent gateway traffic it fronts requests from clients to your apis requests from apps and agents to models, to tools (often over mcp) and to other agents (a2a) what it meters usage and load also tokens and spend per model, team or user what it routes requests to the right backend service also by model and provider, with load balancing and failover between providers what it checks access and usage policies also prompts and responses, through guardrails and content filters what it translates requests and responses, on the fly existing rest or openapi apis into mcp tools that agents can call

agent gateways today each description below is the project’s or vendor’s own: azure api management has an “ai gateway” that extends its existing api gateway rather than being a separate product: it imports model endpoints as apis, manages token usage and quotas, exposes existing rest apis as mcp servers, and imports and manages a2a agent apis. apigee can expose apis as mcp tools to agentic applications, implementing the mcp server specification. amazon bedrock agentcore gateway is described as a fully managed gateway that gives agents one entry point to tools, other agents and models, taking openapi, smithy and lambda as tool sources. agentgateway , an open-source proxy, describes itself as built on mcp and a2a, with an llm gateway, an mcp gateway, an a2a gateway, guardrails, authentication and opentelemetry tracing. agent router , formerly envoy ai gateway and now an agentic ai foundation project, offers one openai-compatible api for models and mcp servers, with credentials, routing, quotas and failover kept in one place. docker’s mcp gateway runs mcp servers in isolated containers and gives ai models one gateway to reach them. analysis: the pattern repeats an old one. an agent gateway does for model and tool calls what api gateways did for service calls: one place for identity, limits, cost and audit. security for agents is on agentic ai security .

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) public or partner api, many unknown clients, cacheable reads rest with an openapi contract many front ends needing different shapes of the same data graphql high-volume calls between your own services, streaming, several languages grpc an existing soap or corba system that works and is not changing keep it, and wrap it behind a gateway or an anti-corruption layer (see solution architecture: a to b ) ai applications need to call your existing apis as tools expose them over mcp, through a gateway that already holds your auth and quotas agents from different teams or vendors must hand work to each other a2a many teams calling several model providers, and spend must be visible an ai gateway for token quotas, routing and failover your team already runs one gateway product check its ai and mcp features before adding another: switching has a cost

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: each new style added to the toolbox more than it replaced the old one. older styles keep running alongside newer ones, grpc and rest often sit side by side, and an mcp server can wrap a rest api that already existed. knowing the history makes it easier to see that an agent gateway is a familiar idea with new things to meter. the other view: agent traffic differs enough, with long-running tasks, token costs, and decisions made by a model rather than a programmer, that treating it as “just another api” misses new risks. on this view, agent protocols and gateways deserve their own design and security thinking from the start.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation place rpc, corba, soap, rest, grpc and graphql in order, and say what each changed explain why location transparency was criticised say what mcp and a2a are for 2 practitioner choose an api style for a case by its requirements wrap a legacy soap service behind a gateway expose an existing rest api as mcp tools 3 senior explain what an ai or agent gateway adds: token quotas, model routing, guardrails plan a move from an older api style without breaking clients design gateway policies for agent traffic 4 expert set an organisation's api and agent-protocol strategy choose between extending an existing gateway and adding an agent gateway govern models, tools and agents in one place each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the idea in one paragraph a graphql server publishes a schema : the types, their fields and how they connect. clients send a query to a single endpoint (usually post /graphql ) describing the shape of data they want, and get back json in exactly that shape. reads are queries , writes are mutations , live updates are subscriptions . each field is filled by a resolver function on the server, which can read from a database, another service or a cache. rest graphql endpoints many, one per resource one response shape fixed by the server chosen by the client nested data several round trips or custom endpoints one request contract openapi (optional) the schema (built in, introspectable) http caching natural for get harder: needs persisted queries or client caches errors http status codes usually 200 with an errors array; partial data possible. the graphql-over-http draft uses 4xx or 5xx when a request cannot run at all versioning /v1, /v2 evolve one schema; deprecate fields best for public apis, simple resources, caching uis combining many related entities; many client types

schema (sdl) type query { order(id: id!): order searchorders(q: string!, store: string, first: int = 20, after: string): orderconnection! } type mutation { addtolist(listid: id!, orderid: id!): savedlist! } type subscription { orderadded(store: string!): order! } type order { id: id! orderref: string! orderdate: date # custom scalar store: store! items: [string!]! similar(first: int = 10): [order!]! } type store { code: id! name: string! state: string } scalar date ! means non-null. [string!]! is a non-null list of non-null strings.

queries, variables, fragments query search($q: string!, $store: string, $after: string) { searchorders(q: $q, store: $store, first: 10, after: $after) { edges { node { ...ordercard } } pageinfo { hasnextpage endcursor } } } fragment ordercard on order { id orderref orderdate store { name } } # variables (sent separately as json): # { "q": "umbrella", "store": "1_05" } curl -s https://api.example.com/graphql \ -h "authorization: bearer $token" -h "content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"query":"query($id:id!){order(id:$id){orderref store{name}}}","variables":{"id":"123"}}' always use variables, never string interpolation into the query: it enables caching of the parsed query and avoids injection.

resolvers and the n+1 problem asking for 20 orders, each with its store , naively runs 1 query for the list and 20 more for stores: n+1 queries. batch loading (dataloader pattern): collect all the store ids requested in one execution step, fetch them in one query, and hand each order its store. per-request cache: the same store requested twice in one query is loaded once. spring: @batchmapping . quarkus: a resolver taking @source list<…> . python strawberry: dataloader . measure: log query counts per graphql request in tests.

n+1, drawn the n+1 problem and batch loading two columns for one graphql query asking for 20 orders, each with its store. on the left, the naive resolvers: one query for the 20 orders, then one query per order for its store, 21 queries in all. on the right, batch loading: one query for the orders, then all the store ids are collected and fetched in one query, 2 queries in all. naive: 1 + 20 = 21 queries batch loading: 2 queries select 20 orders select store where id = … select store where id = … select store where id = … select store where id = … … 20 times select 20 orders collect the store ids select stores where id in (…) log query counts per request in your tests to catch the left-hand shape twenty orders, two ways. the left grows with the list; the right stays at two queries however many orders you ask for.

spring for graphql // schema files: src/main/resources/graphql/*.graphqls @controller class ordergraphql { private final orderservice orders; private final storeservice stores; ordergraphql(orderservice o, storeservice s) { orders = o; stores = s; } @querymapping order order(@argument string id) { return orders.find(id).orelse(null); // null → field is null, no error } @mutationmapping savedlist addtolist(@argument string listid, @argument string orderid) { return orders.addtolist(listid, orderid); // check ownership inside } @batchmapping // one query for all stores map<order, store> store(list<order> list) { map<string, store> bycode = stores.bycodes( list.stream().map(order::storeid).collect(collectors.toset())); return list.stream().collect(collectors.tomap(o -> o, o -> bycode.get(o.storeid()))); } } // scalar date needs an implementation, here from graphql-java-extended-scalars @configuration class graphqlconfig { @bean runtimewiringconfigurer scalars() { return w -> w.scalar(extendedscalars.date); } } // test @graphqltest(ordergraphql.class) class ordergraphqltest { @autowired graphqltester tester; @mockitobean orderservice orders; @mockitobean storeservice stores; @test void returnsnullforunknownid() { tester.document("{ order(id: \"x\") { orderref } }") .execute().path("order").valueisnull(); } }

quarkus (smallrye graphql) // quarkus ext add smallrye-graphql → schema generated from code @graphqlapi public class orderapi { @inject orderservice orders; @inject storeservice stores; @query public order order(@nonnull string id) { return orders.find(id).orelse(null); } @mutation public savedlist addtolist(@nonnull string listid, @nonnull string orderid) { return orders.addtolist(listid, orderid); } // batched field resolver: adds order.store, one call for all orders public list<store> store(@source list<order> list) { return stores.inorderfor(list); } } // graphql ui in dev mode: http://localhost:8080/q/graphql-ui spring for graphql is schema-first (you write sdl); smallrye graphql is code-first (the schema comes from your classes).

python (strawberry) import strawberry from strawberry.dataloader import dataloader async def load_stores(codes: list[str]) -> list["store"]: rows = await db.stores_by_codes(codes) # one query by = {r.code: r for r in rows} return [by.get(c) for c in codes] # same order as input @strawberry.type class store: code: strawberry.id name: str @strawberry.type class order: id: strawberry.id order_ref: str store_id: strawberry.private[str] @strawberry.field async def store(self, info: strawberry.info) -> store: return await info.context["store_loader"].load(self.store_id) @strawberry.type class query: @strawberry.field async def order(self, id: strawberry.id) -> order | none: return await db.order(id) schema = strawberry.schema(query=query) # context per request: {"store_loader": dataloader(load_fn=load_stores)}

pagination: connections type orderconnection { edges: [orderedge!]! pageinfo: pageinfo! totalcount: int # optional; can be expensive } type orderedge { cursor: string! node: order! } type pageinfo { hasnextpage: boolean! haspreviouspage: boolean! startcursor: string endcursor: string } cursor-based (the relay connection convention): stable under inserts, works with keyset queries in the database. cap first on the server (e.g. max 100). make cursors opaque (base64 of the sort key and id).

errors { "data": { "order": null }, "errors": [{ "message": "not authorised to view this order", "path": ["order"], "extensions": { "code": "forbidden" } }] } a response can hold partial data plus errors; clients must check errors even on http 200. put a stable machine-readable extensions.code on every error. expected business outcomes (validation failed, not found) can also be modelled in the schema as result types ( union saveresult = savedlist | validationerror ). never leak stack traces or sql in message .

security authorise per field and per object in resolvers or the service layer; one endpoint means url-based rules cannot protect anything. limit query depth and complexity so a client cannot request similar { similar { similar … } } a thousand levels deep. cap list sizes and set timeouts per request. persisted queries (allow-list of known query hashes) for first-party clients: blocks arbitrary queries and enables get caching. introspection: consider disabling it in production for private apis; it is not a security boundary, just less help to attackers. rate limit by cost, not by request count, since one request can be cheap or enormous. batching attacks: limit the number of operations or aliases per request (aliases can repeat a login mutation hundreds of times).

performance and caching batch loaders everywhere a field fetches by key. select only needed columns: look at the requested fields (selection set) before querying. client caches (apollo client, relay, urql) normalise results by type and id; give every object a stable id . http caching needs get with persisted queries; otherwise cache in resolvers or the data layer. trace per resolver (opentelemetry) to find slow fields.

schema evolution and scale add freely: new types, new fields, new optional arguments. deprecate before removing: oldfield: string @deprecated(reason: "use newfield") , then watch usage and remove. never change a field's type or meaning in place. schema checks in ci compare against the published schema and fail on breaking changes. federation: several teams own subgraphs (orders, users, billing) composed by a router into one supergraph (apollo federation, graphql mesh). behind a gateway: apigee or another gateway can still handle authentication and rate limits in front of /graphql .

levels: what to expect 1 foundation read a schema and write queries with variables and fragments explain queries, mutations, subscriptions and resolvers tell when graphql fits better than rest 2 practitioner build a server with spring for graphql, smallrye or strawberry avoid n+1 with batch loaders; paginate with connections return useful errors and test resolvers 3 senior secure a graphql api: field authorisation, depth and cost limits, persisted queries evolve a schema without breaking clients; schema checks in ci tune performance with tracing and caching 4 expert design a federated graph across teams set graphql governance and standards for the organisation decide graphql vs rest vs grpc strategy across products each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
