c.h: Real time and near real time are different promises
c.x: real time and near real time are different promises term what it means examples ( analysis ) hard real time missing a deadline is a total system failure airbag control, industrial safety systems firm real time infrequent misses are tolerable, but a late result is worth nothing a video frame or a market price that arrives too late to use soft real time a late result is still useful, but worth less the later it is live dashboards, multiplayer game state near real time the delay that processing and network transmission add between an event and its use, such as for display a cart badge, an order status, a stock count, a notification our view: on the web, “real time” almost always means near real time, and the honest way to say it is a number: “the badge updates within two seconds for 99% of changes”. the other view: product teams use “real time” as shorthand for “no refresh button”, and insisting on the strict term can derail a useful conversation; agree the number, whatever word you use.

c.h: The journey of one cart event
c.x: the journey of one cart event change: the phone sends “add item” (a rest call or a graphql mutation) to the cart service. record: the cart service saves the cart and an outbox row in one transaction, so the change and its event cannot disagree (see the transactional outbox on architecture ). publish: a relay publishes cartitemadded to the cart-events topic, keyed by cart id: the key decides the partition, so every event for one cart stays in order (see kafka ). bridge: a push gateway (often the backend-for-frontend) consumes the topic and holds the open browser connections. browsers cannot read kafka directly ( analysis: kafka clients speak kafka’s own protocol over tcp, which browser apis do not offer). deliver: the gateway sends the event to that customer’s open connections, over sse, a websocket or a graphql subscription. show and catch up: the laptop updates the badge. if it was offline, it catches up when it reconnects. analysis: the device that made the change already knows from its own response. push is for everyone else: other tabs and devices, and changes made elsewhere, such as a price change or an item going out of stock. the journey of one cart event six numbered steps. 1: the phone sends add item to the cart service. 2: the cart service saves the cart and an outbox row in one transaction. 3: a relay publishes cartitemadded to the cart-events topic, keyed by cart id. 4: a push gateway consumes the topic and holds the open browser connections. 5: it sends the event to that customer's connections over sse, a websocket or a graphql subscription. 6: the laptop updates the cart badge, or catches up when it reconnects. phone add item 1 cart service cart + outbox, 1 tx 2 relay publish from outbox 3 cart-events key = cart id 4 push gateway holds connections 5 laptop badge updates 6 step 5 travels over sse, a websocket or a graphql subscription the six steps above, drawn. read along the top, then back along the bottom. kafka sits in the middle; the browser never talks to it directly.

c.h: From Kafka to browsers: the gateway’s three problems
c.x: from kafka to browsers: the gateway’s three problems fan-out. in a kafka consumer group, each partition is read by one consumer. if every gateway instance joins one group, an instance sees only some partitions, but the customer’s connection may be on a different instance. three ways out ( analysis ): each gateway instance uses its own consumer group, reads every event and forwards only those for customers connected to it: simple, but every instance reads the whole topic. route each connection to the instance that owns the partition of the cart it watches (events are keyed by cart id): efficient, and hard to keep right as instances and partitions move. the gateway republishes to a fan-out layer built for connections, such as a pub/sub service or a managed one (below). missed events. a connection drops, and events arrive while it is down. with sse the browser reconnects by itself after a dropped connection and sends the last event id it saw in a last-event-id header, so the gateway can resume. the graphql specification defines a subscription’s result as a stream of events, but not replay, so a common pattern is to re-run the cart query on reconnect, then follow the stream ( analysis ). who may listen. authenticate the connection, and let each customer subscribe only to their own carts. a long-lived connection outlives a short-lived token, so decide what happens when it expires. analysis: send the whole change (“item x added, new total y”) or only a signal (“cart changed, fetch it”)? a signal keeps one source of truth and makes missed events harmless, at the cost of an extra request; the whole change saves the request and needs ordering and replay to be right.

every option, side by side option how it works direction from the sources short polling the browser asks every few seconds client asks the delay is up to one interval, and most requests return nothing ( analysis ) long polling the server holds each request open until it has something, then the client asks again client asks, server waits not a true push, but it emulates one where a real push is not possible; rfc 6202 lists its known issues server-sent events (sse) one long http response carrying a stream of events, read with eventsource server to browser only reconnects by itself after a dropped connection and resends last-event-id ; without http/2, browsers allow only 6 sse connections per domain, across all tabs websocket an http handshake upgrades to a framed, two-way connection over tcp both ways rfc 6455; the browser api has no backpressure, so a fast sender can overwhelm a slow page; reconnect and replay are yours to build ( analysis ) graphql subscription a subscription operation returns a stream of results; the transport is separate server to browser (over a two-way or one-way transport) common transports: graphql-ws (websocket subprotocol graphql-transport-ws ) and graphql-sse (over sse, with single-connection and distinct-connections modes) webtransport streams and datagrams over http/3 both ways multiple and unidirectional streams, out-of-order delivery, and unreliable datagrams web push a message to the browser’s push service, handled by a service worker server to device needs an active service worker; reaches the user when the page is closed, so it is for notifications rather than keeping a page in sync managed services a cloud service holds the connections; your backend publishes to it varies aws appsync subscriptions; api gateway websocket apis (routes to lambda, http or aws services); azure web pubsub; asp.net core signalr, which falls back from websockets to sse to long polling

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards updates only flow from server to browser (a cart badge, an order status) sse the browser also sends a steady stream of messages (chat, collaborative editing, a game) websocket your front end already talks graphql and you want one schema for queries, mutations and updates graphql subscriptions, over graphql-sse or graphql-ws a delay of tens of seconds is acceptable, or traffic is small short polling: little to build or run ( analysis ) proxies or firewalls in front of your users break long-lived connections long polling, or a library that falls back to it you must reach the user when the page is closed web push you need many independent streams, unreliable datagrams, or backpressure in the browser webtransport; check browser support first you do not want to run servers that hold many open connections a managed service on your cloud your users still reach you over http/1.1 and open many tabs avoid one sse connection per tab: share one connection between tabs, or use a websocket

c.h: SSE in the browser, and on the wire
c.x: sse in the browser, and on the wire // browser: listen for cart events const events = new eventsource('/carts/me/events'); events.addeventlistener('cart', (e) => { const change = json.parse(e.data); updatebadge(change.itemcount); }); // what the gateway writes on the response. // each event ends with a blank line. id: 7f3a-42 event: cart data: {"cartid":"c-9","itemcount":3} a blank line ends each event, and the browser dispatches it then. after a dropped connection the browser reconnects and sends last-event-id: 7f3a-42 , and the gateway resumes after that event.

the same with graphql type subscription { cartchanged(cartid: id!): cartevent! } subscription { cartchanged(cartid: "c-9") { itemcount total } } the server resolves the subscription from the gateway’s kafka consumer. choose the transport separately: graphql-ws or graphql-sse. see graphql .

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: for a cart, a second or two is near real time enough. sse from a backend-for-frontend that consumes kafka, sending a “cart changed” signal and re-fetching on reconnect, is little to build and run, and recovers from dropped connections on its own. reach for websockets when the browser must send a stream too, and for graphql subscriptions when graphql is already your api. the other view: a team that already runs graphql gains more from one schema and one client than sse saves; a team with a managed websocket service on its cloud may find that cheaper to run than its own gateway; and at small scale, polling every few seconds is often the honest, boring answer that nobody has to be on call for.

the short answer picture a service that reads orders from a queue and writes each one to a database. on a quiet day the database keeps up. then a sale starts, orders arrive ten times faster, and the question nobody asked at design time suddenly matters: where do the orders that cannot be written yet go? this page is about that question. reactive , in the spring team’s words, “refers to programming models that are built around reacting to change”: network components reacting to i/o events, ui controllers reacting to mouse clicks. instead of a thread waiting for an answer, code is called when the answer arrives. back pressure is borrowed from plumbing, where it is the resistance that pushes back against flow in a pipe. in software it is a way to regulate the flow of data so that components are not overwhelmed: the slow part of a system tells the fast part to ease off. the two go together for one reason, which the spring documentation puts plainly: “in synchronous, imperative code, blocking calls serve as a natural form of back pressure that forces the caller to wait. in non-blocking code, it becomes important to control the rate of events so that a fast producer does not overwhelm its destination.” take away the waiting, and you must put the brake back on deliberately. this page goes deep on one idea. the history of how java got here is on how java threads evolved and io, nio & web servers ; spring’s choice between blocking and reactive is on spring boot .

the problem in one picture back pressure: the consumer tells the producer how much it can take a producer sends items through a bounded buffer to a slower consumer. the consumer sends a request for n more items back to the producer. if the producer cannot slow down, it has three choices: buffer, drop or fail. producer fast: 1,000 a second bounded buffer room for n items consumer slow: 100 a second items items request(n): “i can take n more” if the producer cannot slow down, it must choose: buffer (memory grows) · drop (data is lost) · fail (the error is visible) back pressure is the arrow going backwards. without it, the buffer in the middle has to absorb the difference, and an unbounded buffer is only a slower way to run out of memory. the picture is simple, and once you have seen it you will spot it everywhere. every pipeline has a slowest step: a database that takes 10 ms per insert, a partner api with a rate limit, a phone on a weak signal. whatever arrives faster than that step can handle has to go somewhere. spring’s documentation answers the obvious question, “what if a publisher cannot slow down?”, in one line: “it has to decide whether to buffer, drop, or fail.” back pressure is the fourth option, and the best one when the source allows it: ask the producer to slow down.

reactive streams: the contract back pressure only works if both sides agree on how to ask for more, and that agreement is what reactive streams provides. it began in late 2013 as an initiative between engineers at netflix, pivotal and lightbend, with contributions from red hat, oracle, twitter and others. its aim is to govern “the exchange of stream data across an asynchronous boundary” (to another thread or pool) while making sure the receiving side is not forced to buffer arbitrary amounts of data. version 1.0 for the jvm was released in april 2015 with the java api, a written specification, a test kit (tck) and examples, so that libraries from different teams can be plugged together. interface methods its job publisher<t> subscribe(subscriber) produces items, but only as many as have been asked for subscriber<t> onsubscribe , onnext , onerror , oncomplete receives the subscription, then the items, then one ending signal subscription request(long n) , cancel() the line back to the producer: “send me n more”, or “stop” processor<t,r> both of the above a processing stage that is a subscriber on one side and a publisher on the other four rules worth knowing by heart (numbered as in the specification): 1.1 : the total number of onnext signals a publisher sends “must be less than or equal to the total number of elements requested”. this one rule is back pressure. 2.1 : a subscriber “must signal demand via subscription.request(long n) to receive onnext signals”. nothing flows until someone asks. 3.9 : asking for zero or a negative number is an error, signalled with illegalargumentexception . 3.17 : a demand of long.max_value may be treated as “effectively unbounded”. requesting it is how a subscriber says “send everything”, and so turns back pressure off. into the jdk. doug lea, who leads jsr 166 (the java.util.concurrent work), proposed the interfaces for java 9, and they arrived through jep 266 as java.util.concurrent.flow : the same four interfaces nested in one class, plus submissionpublisher , a ready-made publisher. the specification’s own readme sums up the design: “since back-pressure is mandatory the use of unbounded buffers can be avoided.”

c.h: Run it: a slow subscriber slows the producer
c.x: run it: a slow subscriber slows the producer reading the rules is one thing; watching them work is more convincing. this example uses only the jdk (java 21 or later; save it as slowsubscriber.java and run java slowsubscriber.java ). the subscriber asks for one item at a time and takes 100 ms over each. the publisher has room for four unread items. submissionpublisher.submit “blocks until resources are available”, so once the buffer is full, the producing loop is held to the consumer’s pace. import java.util.concurrent.flow; import java.util.concurrent.forkjoinpool; import java.util.concurrent.submissionpublisher; public class slowsubscriber { public static void main(string[] args) throws exception { // a publisher with room for 4 unread items per subscriber try (var publisher = new submissionpublisher<integer>(forkjoinpool.commonpool(), 4)) { publisher.subscribe(new flow.subscriber<>() { flow.subscription subscription; public void onsubscribe(flow.subscription s) { subscription = s; s.request(1); } // ask for one public void onnext(integer item) { sleep(100); // a slow consumer system.out.println("consumed " + item); subscription.request(1); // ready for the next one } public void onerror(throwable t) { t.printstacktrace(); } public void oncomplete() { system.out.println("done"); } }); for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { long start = system.nanotime(); publisher.submit(i); // blocks while the buffer is full long waited = (system.nanotime() - start) / 1_000_000; system.out.println("produced " + i + (waited > 10 ? " after waiting " + waited + " ms" : "")); } } thread.sleep(1500); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { thread.sleep(ms); } catch (interruptedexception e) { thread.currentthread().interrupt(); } } } what it printed when we ran it: produced 1 produced 2 produced 3 produced 4 produced 5 consumed 1 produced 6 after waiting 96 ms consumed 2 produced 7 after waiting 97 ms ... five items go straight in (one being consumed, four in the buffer). from then on, every submit waits about 100 ms: the consumer’s speed has travelled back up to the producer. change s.request(1) to s.request(long.max_value) and the producer is no longer paced by requests; it is held only by the buffer. the other publishing method, offer , “may drop items (either immediately or with bounded timeout)” instead of blocking, with a handler to decide what to do.

c.h: When the producer cannot slow down
c.x: when the producer cannot slow down asking the producer to slow down is the best answer, but not every producer can listen. mouse movements, a sensor, a market data feed and a timer all keep coming whether you are ready or not. for those, every library offers the same four choices; only the names differ, so it helps to see them side by side. choice reactor rxjava flowable jdk kotlin flow buffer onbackpressurebuffer , bounded or unbounded, with an overflow strategy onbackpressurebuffer ; backpressurestrategy.buffer submissionpublisher ’s per-subscriber buffer; a queue in a threadpoolexecutor buffer(n) drop new items onbackpressuredrop onbackpressuredrop ; drop offer ; discardpolicy buffer(onbufferoverflow = drop_latest) keep only the latest onbackpressurelatest onbackpressurelatest ; latest discardoldestpolicy (drops the oldest queued task) conflate() fail onbackpressureerror (an illegalstateexception ) missingbackpressureexception ; error abortpolicy , the default ( rejectedexecutionexception ) none built in; the emitter suspends instead slow the caller request(n) from the subscriber request(n) submit blocks; callerrunspolicy the default: emit suspends choose by requirement , not by which operator you have seen before: if this is true for you lean towards because every item matters (payments, orders, audit events) and the source can wait slow the caller: request-based demand, a blocking submit , or callerrunspolicy nothing is lost; the cost is that the producer runs at the consumer’s speed every item matters but bursts are short a bounded buffer sized for the burst, failing loudly when it overflows absorbs the spike; the overflow error tells you the burst was bigger than planned only the current value matters (a price, a position, a progress bar) keep only the latest ( onbackpressurelatest , conflate ) old values are worthless once a newer one exists losing some items is acceptable (sampled metrics, telemetry) drop protects the consumer at a known, accepted cost overload must be seen and handled upstream (a gateway, a queue in front of a fragile system) fail fast: reject with an error the caller can retry later a clear “not now” beats a slow timeout; see load shedding on sre

c.h: Push, pull, and the hybrid in between
c.x: push, pull, and the hybrid in between there are really only two ways for data to move between a producer and a consumer, and reactive streams cleverly uses both. an iterator is pull : the consumer asks for the next item when it is ready, so it can never be overwhelmed, but it waits whenever the item is not ready yet. a callback or event listener is push : items arrive as soon as they exist, which is fast, but the consumer has no say in the rate. reactive streams is both. reactor’s reference guide calls it “a push-pull hybrid”: the subscriber pulls by requesting n items, and the publisher pushes each one as soon as it exists, up to that limit. libraries also prefetch , requesting a batch ahead of need to avoid a round trip per item, and operators can change the request on the way up (a buffer(10) that is asked for one batch may ask upstream for ten items). kafka sits firmly at the pull end. a consumer calls poll() when it is ready, max.poll.records limits how many records one call returns, and the consumer api’s “consumption flow control” section offers pause() and resume() per partition, for example to let a lagging stream catch up before reading further from one that is ahead. kafkaa slow consumer simply falls behind (its lag grows) without harming the broker.rsquo;s design notes give the reason: in a push system a slow consumer simply falls behind (its lag grows) without harming the broker.ldquo;the consumer tends to be overwhelmed when its rate of consumption falls below the rate of productiona slow consumer simply falls behind (its lag grows) without harming the broker.rdquo;, while with pull a slow consumer simply falls behind (its lag grows) without harming the broker.ldquo;the consumer simply falls behind and catches up when it can.a slow consumer simply falls behind (its lag grows) without harming the broker.rdquo; more on kafka .

back pressure across the network library back pressure stops at the edge of the process. the good news is that between machines you are not on your own: the network protocols have had their own back pressure for decades, long before any reactive library existed. layer how the receiver says “slow down” tcp every segment carries a window: “the range of sequence numbers the sender of the window (the data receiver) is currently prepared to accept”, related to its free buffer space (rfc 9293). when the receiving application stops reading, the window shrinks towards zero and the sender stops. http/2 credit-based flow control with window_update frames, per stream and per connection. the initial window is 65,535 octets, and “a sender must respect flow-control limits imposed by a receiver” (rfc 9113). it works hop by hop, not end to end, so a proxy has its own windows on each side. grpc (java) streams can switch to manual flow control: disableautorequest() , then request(1) when ready, and check isready() before sending (the grpc-java manualflowcontrol example). rsocket carries reactive streams across the network: a request_n frame means “request n more items with reactive streams semantics”. spring webflux reads and writes http bodies “through non-blocking i/o with reactive streams back pressure”, on servers such as reactor netty. analysis: this is why a slow mobile client does not need special code in a webflux endpoint. when the client reads slowly, tcp’s window fills, the server cannot write, and demand stops flowing up the reactive chain to the database query. it is also why a websocket in the browser is harder: its api has no back pressure (see real-time to the browser ).

c.h: The same idea in other languages
c.x: the same idea in other languages none of this is special to java. once you know the pattern, you will recognise it in every language that handles streams. node.js streams. write() returns false when the data buffer has exceeded highwatermark (commonly 16 kb by default) or the write queue is busy, and a 'drain' event fires once it has emptied. the node.js guide’s rule: “never call .write() after it returns false but wait for ‘drain’ instead.” pipe() does this for you. // node.js: respect write()'s answer, or memory grows without limit function copy(source, destination) { source.on('data', (chunk) => { if (!destination.write(chunk)) { // false: the buffer is above highwatermark source.pause(); // stop reading... destination.once('drain', () => source.resume()); // ...until it has emptied } }); source.on('end', () => destination.end()); } // in practice, source.pipe(destination) or stream.pipeline() does this for you kotlin flow. flows are sequential by default: the producer’s emit suspends until the collector has handled the value, which is back pressure with no protocol at all. buffer() lets the producer run ahead in a separate coroutine (by default it suspends again when the buffer overflows), and conflate() means the emitter “is never suspended due to a slow collector”, which skips to the newest value. // kotlin flow: emit() suspends while the collector is busy, so a flow is paced by default prices() .conflate() // a slow collector skips to the most recent value .collect { show(it) } events() .buffer(64) // up to 64 waiting; then emit() suspends again .collect { save(it) } rxjava. version 2 onwards split its types: flowable supports reactive streams and back pressure; observable has none and is meant for short sequences and gui events. reactor , the library under spring webflux, implements reactive streams in all its operators, with mono (0 or 1 item) and flux (0 to n). // reactor (spring webflux): name what happens when the consumer falls behind flux<reading> readings = sensor.readings() // a source that cannot slow down .onbackpressurelatest() // keep only the newest reading .publishon(schedulers.parallel()); // a blocking call, kept off the event-loop threads mono<customer> customer = mono.fromcallable(() -> legacyclient.find(id)) .subscribeon(schedulers.boundedelastic());

c.h: Blocking code has back pressure too
c.x: blocking code has back pressure too it is easy to forget, in all the talk of reactive libraries, that plain blocking code has had back pressure all along. a blocked thread is the oldest flow control there is: the caller cannot send the next request until the last one returns. the trouble used to be cost: one platform thread per waiting call. virtual threads (final in java 21, jep 444) make waiting cheap again, and jep 444 says how to limit concurrency once threads are no longer the limit: “do not be tempted to pool virtual threads in order to limit concurrency. instead use constructs specifically designed for that purpose, such as semaphores.” import java.util.concurrent.executors; import java.util.concurrent.semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.atomicinteger; public class limit { static final semaphore permits = new semaphore(20); // the service can take 20 calls at once static final atomicinteger inflight = new atomicinteger(), peak = new atomicinteger(); public static void main(string[] args) { try (var executor = executors.newvirtualthreadpertaskexecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) executor.submit(limit::callservice); } // waits for all 1,000 tasks system.out.println("peak concurrent calls: " + peak.get()); } static void callservice() { try { permits.acquire(); // wait here when 20 are already running try { peak.accumulateandget(inflight.incrementandget(), math::max); thread.sleep(50); // stands in for the remote call inflight.decrementandget(); } finally { permits.release(); } } catch (interruptedexception e) { thread.currentthread().interrupt(); } } } when we ran it, it printed peak concurrent calls: 20 and took about 3 seconds: 1,000 calls of 50 ms, 20 at a time, is 2.5 seconds of waiting plus start-up. how big should the limit be? little’s law , proved by john little in 1961, says the average number of items in a stable system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside: l = λw . with 20 permits and 50 ms per call, the most this code can sustain is 20 ÷ 0.05 = 400 calls a second. if 600 a second arrive, a queue grows without end, whatever the threading model. back pressure, a bigger limit or shedding load are the only ways out. the thread pool version. a threadpoolexecutor with a bounded queue is back pressure for tasks. its callerrunspolicy makes the submitting thread run a rejected task itself, which the jdk documentation calls “a simple feedback control mechanism that will slow down the rate that new tasks are submitted”. with an unbounded linkedblockingqueue , nothing pushes back at all.

mistakes that defeat back pressure most back pressure problems are not exotic. they come from a handful of ordinary decisions, each of which looks harmless on the day it is made. mistake what happens instead an unbounded buffer or queue “just in case” the difference in speed piles up in memory until the process dies, often long after the cause bound every queue and decide what happens when it is full requesting long.max_value everywhere rule 3.17 lets the publisher treat it as unbounded: back pressure is switched off request in batches, or let the library’s operators manage demand a blocking call on an event-loop thread every request sharing that thread stalls wrap it: reactor’s faq uses mono.fromcallable(...).subscribeon(schedulers.boundedelastic()) , which also caps how many threads blocking work can take an rxjava observable for a large or fast stream nothing pushes back; rxjava’s wiki notes that missingbackpressureexception usually surfaces at observeon , while the cause is a source that ignores requests, such as interval() use flowable with an explicit strategy treating retries as free a slow dependency gets more traffic just when it needs less (see the retry storm on distributed systems ) retry with backoff and a budget, behind a circuit breaker

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: learn back pressure as a property of systems, not of one library. ask of every queue, buffer and stream in a design: what happens when the consumer is ten times slower than the producer? if the answer is “memory grows”, the design is not finished. for most request-and-response services, plain blocking code on virtual threads with a semaphore and bounded queues gives you that answer with the least new code. the other view: reactive libraries make back pressure part of the type, end to end, from the database driver (r2dbc) to the http response, and they compose streams, timeouts and retries in one model. for streaming, server-sent events and many long-lived connections, teams that have learned the model may find it clearer than hand-placed semaphores.

choose by requirement if this is true for you lean towards request and response, mostly waiting on a database or other services blocking code on virtual threads, with a semaphore per dependency streaming results, server-sent events, very many idle connections reactive (webflux, reactor, mutiny) or kotlin flow messages between services, consumers at their own pace a log or queue with pull-based consumers ( kafka ) your team already runs a reactive stack in production stay on it: switching has a cost, and its back pressure is already end to end a library that others will plug into expose reactive streams or flow types, so any compliant library can consume it

the model concept meaning topic a named stream of records, e.g. order.placed partition an ordered, append-only log; a topic has many. ordering is guaranteed only within a partition. record key, value, headers, timestamp. the key decides the partition (same key → same partition → ordered). offset a record's position in its partition. consumers track how far they have read. broker a server storing partitions. a cluster has several. replication factor copies of each partition on different brokers (3 is typical). leader / isr one replica, the leader, takes all writes (and reads, unless consumers are set to fetch from a follower); in-sync replicas are caught-up followers. consumer group consumers sharing the work: each partition is read by one consumer in the group. max parallelism = partition count. retention records kept for a time or size, then deleted, regardless of whether they were read. compaction keep only the latest record per key; a table-like topic. kraft kafka's built-in metadata quorum, replacing zookeeper (removed in kafka 4.0). unlike a queue, reading does not remove a record. many groups can read the same topic independently, and a group can rewind to replay.

keys, partitions and groups, drawn a topic, its partitions and two consumer groups a producer sends records keyed by order id to the topic order.placed, which has three partitions. records with the same key always go to the same partition, so they stay in order. consumer group billing has two consumers: one reads partitions 0 and 1, the other reads partition 2. consumer group analytics has one consumer reading all three. each group keeps its own offsets, so both read every record and reading removes nothing. producer key = order id topic order.placed partition 0 append-only, ordered partition 1 append-only, ordered partition 2 append-only, ordered group billing consumer 1: p0, p1 consumer 2: p2 group analytics consumer: p0, p1, p2 same key, same partition, so one order’s events stay in order. inside a group each partition has one reader, so parallelism stops at the partition count. a second group reads everything again with its own offsets.

durability and delivery settings producer acks=all with topic min.insync.replicas=2 and replication factor 3: a write survives one broker failure. enable.idempotence=true (the default in modern clients): retries do not create duplicates within a partition. at-least-once consuming: process, then commit the offset. a crash between the two replays the record, so consumers must be idempotent. at-most-once: commit before processing. rarely what you want. exactly-once inside kafka (read-process-write between topics) with transactions and isolation.level=read_committed . side effects outside kafka still need idempotency. ordering: choose the key for the entity whose events must stay in order (order id, account id).

cli essentials b=localhost:9092 kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $b --create --topic order.placed \ --partitions 6 --replication-factor 3 --config retention.ms=604800000 kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $b --describe --topic order.placed kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server $b --topic order.placed \ --property parse.key=true --property key.separator=: # type: ord123:{"store":"1_05"} kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server $b --topic order.placed \ --group debug --from-beginning --property print.key=true kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $b --describe --group indexer # lag per partition kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $b --group indexer \ --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-11-01t00:00:00.000 --topic order.placed --execute consumer lag (latest offset minus committed offset) is the key health metric: growing lag means consumers cannot keep up.

spring for apache kafka # application.yml spring: kafka: bootstrap-servers: ${kafka_bootstrap} producer: acks: all key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.stringserializer value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.jsonserializer consumer: group-id: indexer auto-offset-reset: earliest key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.stringdeserializer value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.jsondeserializer # the default is string properties: spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.example.events" # spring kafka 4 (boot 4) deprecates jsonserializer/jsondeserializer for jacksonjsonserializer/jacksonjsondeserializer @service class publisher { private final kafkatemplate<string, orderplaced> kafka; publisher(kafkatemplate<string, orderplaced> kafka) { this.kafka = kafka; } void publish(orderplaced e) { kafka.send("order.placed", e.orderref(), e); } // key = order ref } @component class indexer { @kafkalistener(topics = "order.placed", groupid = "indexer") void on(orderplaced e) { index.upsert(e); // idempotent: same event twice is harmless } } // retries and a dead-letter topic for poison messages @bean defaulterrorhandler errorhandler(kafkatemplate<object, object> t) { return new defaulterrorhandler(new deadletterpublishingrecoverer(t), new fixedbackoff(1000l, 3)); }

quarkus with kafka # application.properties (quarkus-messaging-kafka) kafka.bootstrap.servers=${kafka_bootstrap} mp.messaging.incoming.placed.connector=smallrye-kafka mp.messaging.incoming.placed.topic=order.placed mp.messaging.incoming.placed.group.id=indexer mp.messaging.outgoing.indexed.connector=smallrye-kafka mp.messaging.outgoing.indexed.topic=order.indexed # the emitter below needs its own channel: a channel has one producer unless you merge mp.messaging.outgoing.reindexed.connector=smallrye-kafka mp.messaging.outgoing.reindexed.topic=order.indexed @applicationscoped public class indexer { @incoming("placed") @outgoing("indexed") public orderindexed process(orderplaced e) { return index.upsert(e); } } @applicationscoped public class publisher { @inject @channel("reindexed") emitter<orderindexed> out; // not "indexed": the method above feeds that void send(orderindexed e) { out.send(e); } } in dev and test, dev services starts a kafka-compatible broker for you.

python (confluent-kafka) from confluent_kafka import producer, consumer p = producer({"bootstrap.servers": bootstrap, "acks": "all", "enable.idempotence": true}) p.produce("order.placed", key=order_ref, value=json.dumps(evt), callback=lambda err, msg: err and log.error("send failed: %s", err)) p.flush() c = consumer({"bootstrap.servers": bootstrap, "group.id": "indexer", "auto.offset.reset": "earliest", "enable.auto.commit": false}) c.subscribe(["order.placed"]) while true: msg = c.poll(1.0) if msg is none: continue if msg.error(): log.error(msg.error()); continue handle(json.loads(msg.value())) # idempotent c.commit(message=msg, asynchronous=false) # commit after processing

the ecosystem schema registry with avro, protobuf or json schema: producers and consumers agree on schemas; compatibility rules block breaking changes. kafka connect: ready-made source and sink connectors (databases, gcs, bigquery) without custom code. debezium: change data capture from databases into kafka topics. kafka streams: a java library for stateful stream processing (joins, windows, aggregates) inside your service. flink: a separate engine for large-scale stream processing. on gcp: managed service for apache kafka runs clusters for you; dataflow and bigquery have kafka connectors.

kafka vs pub/sub kafka pub/sub model partitioned log; consumers track offsets topics and subscriptions; per-message ack ordering per partition (by key) per ordering key, when enabled replay rewind offsets within retention seek to a time or snapshot within retention capacity you size brokers and partitions (managed or self-run) serverless, scales automatically ecosystem connect, streams, schema registry, debezium native gcp integrations (bigquery, gcs, dataflow, eventarc) choose when kafka skills or tools exist; log semantics, compaction, very high throughput gcp-native, simple operations, global delivery

designing topics name by event, past tense: order.placed , order.paid . partitions: enough for peak consumer parallelism with headroom; adding later changes key-to-partition mapping. keys: the entity that needs ordering; avoid hot keys. payload: include an event id, type, version and timestamp; keep events self-describing. retention: long enough to recover from a consumer outage and replay. dead-letter topic for records that keep failing, with alerting on it.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain topics, partitions, offsets and consumer groups produce and consume with the cli read consumer lag 2 practitioner build producers and consumers in spring, quarkus or python with correct acks and commits make consumers idempotent; use dead-letter topics use a schema registry 3 senior design topics, keys and partition counts for scale and ordering run kafka connect and cdc pipelines tune throughput, latency and durability 4 expert operate kafka platforms (or choose managed) for the organisation design event-driven architectures across domains lead stream processing with kafka streams or flink each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

who is involved party role customer pays with a card, upi, net banking or wallet merchant you: the business being paid payment gateway / aggregator collects payment details securely, routes the transaction, gives you apis, checkout and webhooks (razorpay, stripe, payu, cashfree) acquirer the merchant's bank, which receives the funds card network visa, mastercard, rupay: routes card transactions between banks issuer the customer's bank, which approves or declines upi (npci) india's real-time account-to-account network; apps such as phonepe, google pay, paytm act as front ends regulator in india the rbi: rules on recurring payments, tokenisation, data storage and aggregators

card payment lifecycle authorise: the issuer checks funds and fraud and places a hold. with 3-d secure (otp or app approval) the customer authenticates. capture: the merchant confirms the charge (automatically or later, e.g. after shipping). an uncaptured authorisation expires. settle: funds move to the gateway, then to your bank account, on the gateway's settlement cycle (razorpay's standard is t+2 working days), minus fees. refund: full or partial, returned through the same route; takes days to reach the customer. chargeback / dispute: the customer disputes with their bank; you submit evidence or lose the funds plus a fee.

upi in brief intent / qr flow: your checkout opens the customer's upi app (or shows a qr); they approve with their upi pin. collect flow: you send a payment request to a upi id; the customer approves in their app. (being phased down for many use cases; check current npci rules.) real-time and irrevocable from the customer's side; refunds are separate transactions. upi autopay: recurring mandates the customer approves once, for subscriptions. pending is normal: a payment can sit in a pending state for minutes; your system must wait for the final status rather than assume failure.

standard integration flow (server-verified) create an order on your server with the amount in the smallest unit (paise) and your own receipt id. store it as created . open the gateway's checkout in the browser or app with that order id. card and upi details go to the gateway, never to your servers. checkout returns payment id, order id and a signature to your client, which sends them to your server. verify the signature on the server and fetch the payment from the gateway api to confirm amount, currency and status. webhooks ( payment.captured , payment.failed , refunds, disputes) arrive at your endpoint; verify their signature and update state idempotently. treat webhooks and api fetches as the source of truth, never the browser. fulfil only when your order is paid according to the server. reconcile daily against the gateway's settlement reports.

the flow, drawn a server-verified payment a sequence diagram with three lifelines: the browser or app, your server, and the gateway. 1: your server creates an order with the amount in paise and stores it as created. 2: the browser opens the gateway's checkout with that order id; card and upi details go to the gateway, never to your server. 3: checkout returns a payment id and a signature, which the client sends to your server. 4: your server verifies the signature and fetches the payment from the gateway. 5: the gateway also sends a webhook, which your server verifies and applies idempotently. 6: only then is the order paid and fulfilled. browser / app your server gateway 1 create order, amount in paise 2 checkout: card, upi details 3 payment id, order id, signature 4 verify signature, fetch payment 5 webhook: payment.captured paid: fulfil 6 the browser is never the source of truth the steps above as a sequence diagram. the card details never touch your server, and nothing is fulfilled on the browser’s word: only on a verified signature, a fetched status and the webhook.

razorpay: order and verification # create an order (amount in paise: 50000 = ₹500.00) curl -u "$rzp_key_id:$rzp_key_secret" \ -x post https://api.razorpay.com/v1/orders \ -h "content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"amount":50000,"currency":"inr","receipt":"order_8421"}' // verify checkout signature: hmac-sha256(order_id + "|" + payment_id, key_secret) static boolean validcheckout(string orderid, string paymentid, string signature, string keysecret) throws exception { mac mac = mac.getinstance("hmacsha256"); mac.init(new secretkeyspec(keysecret.getbytes(utf_8), "hmacsha256")); string expected = hexformat.of().formathex( mac.dofinal((orderid + "|" + paymentid).getbytes(utf_8))); return messagedigest.isequal(expected.getbytes(utf_8), signature.getbytes(utf_8)); // constant time } // webhook: hmac-sha256 of the raw request body with the webhook secret, // compared with the x-razorpay-signature header. never re-serialise the json first. // the same event can arrive more than once: dedupe on the x-razorpay-event-id header.

stripe: paymentintent and webhook import stripe stripe.api_key = stripe_secret_key intent = stripe.paymentintent.create( amount=50000, currency="inr", metadata={"order_id": "order_8421"}, idempotency_key="order_8421-create", # safe to retry ) # return intent.client_secret to the front end, which confirms the payment # webhook endpoint def stripe_webhook(request): payload = request.body # raw bytes sig = request.headers["stripe-signature"] try: event = stripe.webhook.construct_event(payload, sig, webhook_secret) except (valueerror, stripe.signatureverificationerror): # older sdks: stripe.error.signatureverificationerror return 400 if not seen_before(event["id"]): # dedupe: webhooks repeat handle(event) return 200

payment state machine created ──checkout──▶ pending ──captured──▶ paid ──refund──▶ partially_refunded / refunded │ │ │ │ ├──failed──▶ failed └──dispute──▶ disputed ──▶ won / lost └──expired──▶ expired └──timeout──▶ (stay pending; poll the gateway; never assume) allow only valid transitions; reject or log anything else. events can arrive late or out of order (a webhook before the browser callback, a failure after a success for a different attempt). decide by the gateway's fetched status. keep every transition as an append-only event with its source (webhook, api fetch, user).

the state machine, drawn payment state machine a uml state diagram. created goes to pending at checkout, or to expired. pending goes to paid when captured, or to failed. a pending payment that times out stays pending while the gateway is polled. paid goes to partially_refunded or refunded on a refund, or to disputed, which ends won or lost. created pending paid expired failed refunded disputed checkout captured expired failed timeout: stay, poll the gateway refund, full or partial dispute then won or lost the diagram above as a uml state diagram. only these arrows are allowed; anything else is rejected or logged, and a timeout never moves a payment on its own.

money-handling rules integers in the smallest unit (paise, cents) or decimal types; never floats. store the currency with every amount. compute prices and totals on the server. never trust an amount sent by the client. idempotency keys on every create, capture and refund call, derived from your own ids, so a retry cannot charge twice. webhook handlers are idempotent : dedupe by event id; applying the same event twice changes nothing. unknown is not failed: a timeout means "we do not know yet". poll the gateway before telling the customer it failed or retrying the charge. round once, at a defined step, with a documented rule (taxes, discounts, splits).

double-entry ledger create table ledger_entry ( id bigint generated always as identity primary key, txn_id uuid not null, -- groups the entries of one transaction account text not null, -- 'customer_receivable', 'gateway_clearing', 'revenue', 'gst_payable' amount_paise bigint not null, -- positive = debit, negative = credit currency char(3) not null, created_at timestamptz not null default now() ); -- every txn_id must sum to zero select txn_id from ledger_entry group by txn_id having sum(amount_paise) <> 0; -- must return nothing append only: corrections are new entries, never edits. balances are sums. this makes every rupee traceable and reconciliation possible.

subscriptions and recurring payments gateways model plans (price, interval) and subscriptions (a customer on a plan) with a mandate or saved token for charging. india: rbi e-mandate rules govern recurring card and upi payments: customer registration with authentication, pre-debit notifications, and extra authentication above a limit. check the current limits and rules; they have changed over time. handle the lifecycle via webhooks: activated, charged, payment failed, halted, cancelled, completed. dunning: retries on failed renewals, customer notices, grace periods, then downgrade or cancel. entitlements (what the user may use) are derived from subscription state in your system, updated only from verified events. proration rules for upgrades and downgrades mid-period, decided and written down.

security and compliance pci dss: use hosted checkout or the gateway's elements so card data never reaches your servers; your compliance scope stays small. card tokenisation (india): merchants may not store card numbers; saved cards use network or issuer tokens through the gateway. data localisation: rbi requires payment system data to be stored in india; confirm your gateway and your own storage comply. secrets: api keys and webhook secrets in a secret manager; separate test and live keys; rotate on staff changes. webhook endpoint: verify signatures on the raw body, reject old timestamps where provided, respond quickly, process asynchronously. fraud: use the gateway's risk tools, 3-d secure, velocity limits, and watch for card testing (many small failed attempts). tax and invoices: gst-compliant invoices with the correct rates and place of supply.

reconciliation download settlement and transaction reports from the gateway daily (api or dashboard). match each gateway transaction to your order by order id and amount. match settlements to bank credits, accounting for fees and taxes. flag mismatches: paid at gateway but not in your system (missed webhook), paid in your system but not settled, amount differences, unexpected refunds or disputes. resolve each one and record why. a rising mismatch count is an incident. run reconciliation as a scheduled job with run records, like any pipeline.

testing payments use the gateway's test mode keys, test cards and test upi ids for success, failure, 3-d secure and pending cases. replay recorded webhook payloads in automated tests; build fixtures from real test-mode events, not guesses. test duplicates, out-of-order events, timeouts and partial refunds explicitly. keep a test-mode end-to-end checkout in your release checks. never test with live keys or real cards in non-production environments.

operating payments metrics: payment success rate by method and bank, latency, webhook delay, pending count and age, refund rate, dispute rate. alerts: success rate drops, webhooks stop arriving, pending payments older than a threshold, reconciliation mismatches. support tools: look up an order's full event history; never let support edit payment state by hand. multiple gateways: routing or failover between gateways improves success rates, at the cost of more reconciliation.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain authorisation, capture, settlement, refunds and chargebacks explain the order → checkout → verify → webhook flow know why card data must never touch your servers 2 practitioner integrate a gateway with server-side verification and signed webhooks make payment calls and webhook handling idempotent model payments as a state machine; test with test-mode fixtures 3 senior design subscriptions, dunning and entitlements build a double-entry ledger and daily reconciliation own payment security, pci scope and regulatory rules (rbi) 4 expert design multi-gateway routing and payment platforms lead payments compliance and audits set money-handling standards across the organisation each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

what makes banking software different analysis, built on the sources at the end. a shop that loses an order apologises. a bank that loses or invents money breaks the law. that changes the order of priorities: correct: money is never created or lost. every movement is a balanced pair of entries (see payment gateways ), and every change can be traced to who made it and why. available: instant payment schemes run 24 hours a day, every day, so there is no longer a quiet night to take systems down. fast enough: fast enough for the scheme’s deadline and for the customer, which is usually far from the microseconds a trading system needs. the other view: some argue that speed is itself a form of correctness for payments, because a payment that misses its scheme deadline fails. both views agree on the order inside the deadline: correct first.

c.h: How a bank’s systems fit together
c.x: how a bank’s systems fit together channels: the mobile app, web banking, branches, call centres, and partners through apis. integration: gateways and messaging that connect channels to the systems of record, with limits, fraud checks and audit on the way. core banking: the system that centralises the bank’s record keeping for deposits, loans and accounts, so any branch or channel sees one record. payment schemes: connections to card networks, instant payment schemes and slower batch schemes, each with its own message formats and deadlines. ledger and reporting: the general ledger, regulatory reports, reconciliation. mainframes and cobol: cobol is used mainly in business, finance and administrative systems, and is still widely used on mainframes for large-scale batch and transaction processing; most cobol work today maintains existing applications. some ibm mainframes (z900 to system z10) execute instructions twice and compare the results, to catch hardware faults.

the layers, drawn how a bank's systems fit together five layers from top to bottom. channels: mobile app, web banking, branches, call centres, partner apis. integration: gateways and messaging with limits, fraud checks and audit on the way. then, side by side, core banking, the one record of accounts, deposits and loans, and the payment schemes: cards, instant and batch, each with its own formats and deadlines. at the bottom, the ledger and reporting: the general ledger, regulatory reports and reconciliation. channels mobile web branch call centre partner apis integration gateways and messaging: limits, fraud checks, audit records core banking one record of every account payment schemes cards, instant, batch books general ledger, regulatory reports, reconciliation the list above as layers. a payment from the app crosses every one of them, and with instant schemes the checks in the integration layer must finish within seconds.

from overnight batch to instant scheme how fast sepa credit transfer (euro) settles within one business day sepa instant (euro, since november 2017) under ten seconds; at most twenty in exceptional cases; around the clock faster payments (uk, since may 2008) typically a few seconds, not guaranteed fednow (us, since july 2023) instant, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year upi (india) see payment gateways what changes when payments are instant ( analysis ): checks that once ran in the overnight batch, such as limits, fraud and sanctions screening, now run inline within the deadline; and maintenance can no longer wait for a closed weekend.

c.h: Why the new banks got to market fast: Monzo, Revolut, Starling
c.x: why the new banks got to market fast: monzo, revolut, starling three uk-founded banks went from start-up to millions of customers in about a decade. the published record points to three reasons, and only one of them is technology. reason what happened the rules opened after the 2008 financial crisis the uk government decided to open the market to new banks. the financial services act 2012 came into force on 1 april 2013, and the prudential regulation authority set up a new bank start-up unit with a staged route: an expression of interest, then “authorisation with restrictions”, then the restrictions lifted. before that, setting up a bank with a full uk licence was extremely expensive and time-consuming, and the “big four” banks dominated. starling, founded in january 2014, received its licence in july 2016; monzo’s restrictions were lifted in april 2017. they started narrow monzo (founded as mondo in 2015) began with an app and a prepaid card, and launched its full current account in october 2017. revolut (founded in july 2015) began as an app for spending abroad at interbank exchange rates, as an e-money institution rather than a bank; it received an eu banking licence in december 2018 and a uk licence, with restrictions, in 2024. each offered one useful thing first, and became a bank later. no legacy to carry no branches (starling has none) and app-first products, which wikipedia’s article on challenger banks describes as modern practices “that avoid the costs and complexities of traditional banking”. starling built its own platform and in february 2022 set up engine, a subsidiary that offers its systems to other firms as a service. the cost of moving fast. in 2019 monzo said it had inadvertently logged 480,000 customers’ card pins, readable by its own engineers, because they were sent in the query string of an https request. in september 2022 a cyber attack on revolut exposed the personal data of over 50,000 customers, and a flaw in its us payment system lost $20 million to criminals between late 2021 and early 2022. in october 2024 the financial conduct authority fined starling £29 million for weak anti-money-laundering and sanctions controls dating back to 2017. monzo withdrew its us banking licence application in 2021, and reported its first annual profit for the year to march 2024. several of these are quality attributes (security, privacy, compliance) that growth outran; see quality attributes and security . our view: the speed came from three things together: a regulator that built a staged way in, a narrow first product, and no old systems or branches to carry. modern technology mattered, but it was one of three, and on its own it would not have produced a bank. the other view: established banks are slower partly by obligation: decades of products, data and customers to keep working, and a scale at which a mistake hurts more people. the fines and incidents above suggest the new banks meet the same pressures as they grow. sources: wikipedia’s articles on challenger banks , monzo , revolut and starling bank . we could not read the banks’ own engineering blogs from this environment, so this card says nothing about their technology choices.

c.h: ISO 20022: the language banks are moving to
c.x: iso 20022: the language banks are moving to an iso standard for electronic data interchange between financial institutions. it is a repository of message and business-process descriptions, modelled in uml and turned into concrete messages (most often xml). why engineers meet it: payment schemes and correspondent banking are moving their messages to it, so a payments system has to read and produce it, and map it to and from older formats during the move. why it helps ( analysis ): structured fields for parties, purposes and references, instead of free text, make screening and reconciliation easier to automate.

c.h: Low latency: what “low” means depends on the job
c.x: low latency: what “low” means depends on the job if you are building what matters what “fast” looks like a banking app screen the customer’s wait, every time, including the slow ones tail latency (p99) across every service in the chain, not the average an instant payment finishing every check inside the scheme’s deadline a whole journey within seconds (sepa instant: under ten), with a known budget per step a market-data or trading system reacting before the competition under a millisecond is often called “ultra low latency”, and the bar keeps moving physics sets the floor. light in a vacuum covers a kilometre in about 3 microseconds, so a trading engine 150 km from an exchange can never get a round trip under 1 millisecond, before any software runs. fibre is slower: its core has a refractive index of about 1.4475, which works out ( our calculation ) at roughly 4.8 microseconds per kilometre, or about 1.4 ms for that round trip. this is why co-location, running servers in the exchange’s own data centre, is one of the defining features of high-frequency trading.

c.h: Techniques, and what each one costs: choose by requirement
c.x: techniques, and what each one costs: choose by requirement if this is your problem consider what it costs you ( analysis ) you do not know where the time goes measure first: tracing per hop, percentiles, a profiler (see performance ) time; nothing else on this list is worth doing before it database round trips dominate keep the working state in memory and the database for durability: lmax’s trading platform runs its business logic in memory with event sourcing, and its business logic processor was reported to handle 6 million orders per second on a single thread, in its team’s own benchmark recovery by replaying events; careful design of snapshots threads wait on locks and queues single-threaded business logic fed by lock-free ring buffers (lmax’s disruptor); fewer hand-offs between threads a programming model most teams have not used garbage-collection pauses on the jvm a low-pause collector: with generational zgc (jep 439), pause times are measured in microseconds; or allocate less on the hot path some throughput and memory overhead small messages wait in the network stack turn off nagle’s algorithm with tcp_nodelay more, smaller packets on the network the kernel’s network stack itself is too slow kernel bypass, such as dpdk, which processes packets entirely in user space specialised hardware and skills; you take over what the kernel did distance dominates move closer: same region, same data centre, or co-location at the exchange money, and less freedom over where you run our view: most banking systems are slow because of too many network hops and database calls, not because of the garbage collector or the kernel. work down the table from the top. the other view: in trading, the last rows are the whole game, and teams start there because the first rows were solved long ago.

measure latency honestly percentiles, not averages: the slow requests are the ones customers remember (see performance ). coordinated omission: a load generator that waits for each response before sending the next stops sending exactly when the server is slow, so it quietly misses most of the slow periods. gil tene’s wrk2 sends at a constant rate and records into hdrhistogram to avoid it. measure end to end and per hop: the customer’s wait is the sum of every hop in the chain. test with production-like data and load, including the batch jobs and peaks of month end.

correctness under speed idempotency everywhere: retries are certain at this scale; a repeated payment message must not move money twice (see payment gateways ). exactly-once effects, not exactly-once delivery: messages may arrive twice; the ledger must apply them once. reconcile continuously: compare your ledger with the scheme’s and the bank’s, every day, and treat a mismatch as an incident. plan for the slow path: when a check cannot finish inside the deadline, decide in advance whether to reject, hold or approve, and record why.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain how channels, core banking, schemes and the ledger fit together explain why every payment step must be idempotent read p50, p99 and p99.9 and say which one customers feel 2 practitioner build a payment flow that meets an instant scheme's deadline map a message to and from iso 20022 load-test without coordinated omission 3 senior design for 24/7 operation with no batch window set and enforce a latency budget per hop choose between in-memory, lock-free and conventional designs by requirement 4 expert lead a core banking or scheme migration set resilience and latency standards across a bank design ultra-low-latency trading infrastructure each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

reactive or blocking? blocking (thread per request): each request holds a thread while it waits for a database or another service. simple to write, read and debug, with ordinary loops and try/catch. reactive (spring webflux, project reactor): a few threads handle many requests by never waiting; work is composed as a pipeline of callbacks. it scales to many concurrent slow calls, but code, stack traces and debugging are harder, and every library on the path must be non-blocking too. virtual threads changed the balance. since java 21, blocking code can use cheap virtual threads, so the simple thread-per-request style scales to high concurrency. as jep 444 puts it, virtual threads are not faster threads: they exist to provide scale (higher throughput), not speed (lower latency). measured: in our spring boot vs quarkus benchmark, with 1,000 connections to an endpoint that waits 100 ms, blocking spring served about 1,960 requests a second, the same code with virtual threads about 8,500 to 8,800, and reactive spring and quarkus about 9,400 to 9,750. our view: start blocking, and turn on virtual threads for i/o-heavy services. choose reactive when you need streaming or back-pressure, or you already have a reactive stack; do not rewrite a working blocking service for throughput alone without measuring it first. see performance . the other view: some teams choose reactive from the start, because one model covers streaming, back-pressure and many slow calls, and in the benchmark above it served the most requests.

the measurement, drawn requests a second, one benchmark a bar chart from the guide's own spring boot and quarkus benchmark: 1,000 connections to an endpoint that waits 100 ms. blocking spring served about 1,960 requests a second. the same code with virtual threads served about 8,500 to 8,800. reactive spring and quarkus served about 9,400 to 9,750. blocking spring 1,960 + virtual threads 8,500–8,800 reactive spring, quarkus 9,400–9,750 0 10,000 requests a second the measured numbers above as bars: one benchmark, one endpoint that waits 100 ms. virtual threads close most of the gap without rewriting blocking code; measure your own service before choosing.

c.h: Filters, interceptors and aspects: where the code around your code lives
c.x: filters, interceptors and aspects: where the code around your code lives some code has nothing to do with what a request is for, yet has to run for almost every one of them: checking who is calling, timing the call, adding a request id to the logs, opening a transaction, compressing the response. copy it into every controller and it soon drifts apart. java has grown three places to put this kind of code instead, and once you can see all three side by side, a lot of “spring magic” stops being magic. 1. the servlet filter: the oldest gate. filters arrived in servlet 2.3, and the interface has hardly changed since. a filter sits in front of a servlet and sees the raw request on the way in and the response on the way out. its own documentation lists the jobs it was designed for: authentication, logging and auditing, data compression, encryption. filters form a chain, and each one decides whether to pass the request on by calling chain.dofilter . this one times every request (it compiles against jakarta servlet 6, as used by tomcat 10): import jakarta.servlet.filter; import jakarta.servlet.filterchain; import jakarta.servlet.servletexception; import jakarta.servlet.servletrequest; import jakarta.servlet.servletresponse; import jakarta.servlet.http.httpservletrequest; import java.io.ioexception; // runs for every request, before any servlet or controller sees it. public class requesttimingfilter implements filter { @override public void dofilter(servletrequest request, servletresponse response, filterchain chain) throws ioexception, servletexception { long start = system.nanotime(); try { chain.dofilter(request, response); // hand over to the next filter, then the servlet } finally { long ms = (system.nanotime() - start) / 1_000_000; string path = ((httpservletrequest) request).getrequesturi(); system.out.println(path + " took " + ms + " ms"); } } } spring security’s servlet support is built on filters like this one. spring registers a single delegatingfilterproxy with the servlet container, which hands each request to filters that live as spring beans, so they can use everything else in your application. 2. the handler interceptor: a gate that knows the route. a filter runs before spring has worked out which controller will handle the request. a spring mvc handlerinterceptor runs after that decision, with three hooks: prehandle before the controller (return false and it never runs), posthandle after it, and aftercompletion once the request has finished. // spring mvc: runs around the controller method, and knows which handler was chosen public class auditinterceptor implements handlerinterceptor { @override public boolean prehandle(httpservletrequest request, httpservletresponse response, object handler) { // return false to stop here: the controller is never called return true; } } two things in spring’s own documentation are worth knowing. for @responsebody methods the response is already written before posthandle runs, so it is too late to add a header there. and spring warns that interceptors are “not ideally suited as a security layer”, because their path matching can disagree with the controllers’; it recommends spring security or another approach in the servlet filter chain, applied as early as possible. 3. the aspect: code wrapped around methods, not requests. aspect-oriented programming was developed by gregor kiczales and colleagues at xerox parc, who then built aspectj, an extension to java first released in 2001 and now an eclipse foundation project. the idea is to describe a cross-cutting concern once (the advice ) and say where it applies (the pointcut ), instead of writing it into every method. spring’s @transactional works this way. spring aop keeps it simple on purpose. it is pure java, needs no special compiler, and supports only one kind of join point: the execution of a method on a spring bean. it wraps the bean in a proxy , a jdk dynamic proxy when the bean implements an interface and a cglib subclass when it does not, and the proxy runs the advice before handing over to the real object. that one design choice explains the most common surprise. here is a small spring program, run with spring 6.2: import org.aspectj.lang.proceedingjoinpoint; import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.around; import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.aspect; import org.springframework.context.annotation.annotationconfigapplicationcontext; import org.springframework.context.annotation.bean; import org.springframework.context.annotation.configuration; import org.springframework.context.annotation.enableaspectjautoproxy; public class aopdemo { @aspect static class timing { @around("execution(* aopdemo.orderservice.*(..))") // every public method of orderservice object time(proceedingjoinpoint call) throws throwable { long start = system.nanotime(); try { return call.proceed(); } finally { system.out.printf(" [aspect] %s took %d us%n", call.getsignature().getname(), (system.nanotime() - start) / 1_000); } } } static class orderservice { public void placeorder() { system.out.println("placing order"); checkstock(); // a call on 'this': the proxy never sees it } public void checkstock() { system.out.println("checking stock"); } } @configuration @enableaspectjautoproxy static class config { @bean timing timing() { return new timing(); } @bean orderservice orderservice() { return new orderservice(); } } public static void main(string[] args) { try (var context = new annotationconfigapplicationcontext(config.class)) { orderservice orders = context.getbean(orderservice.class); system.out.println("the bean is a " + orders.getclass().getsimplename()); orders.placeorder(); system.out.println("--- calling checkstock from outside:"); orders.checkstock(); } } } what it printed: the bean is a aopdemo$orderservice$$springcglib$$0 placing order checking stock [aspect] placeorder took 984 us --- calling checkstock from outside: checking stock [aspect] checkstock took 115 us look at the first call. placeorder was timed, but checkstock , called from inside it, was not: the call went to this , the real object, and never passed through the proxy. spring’s documentation says it plainly: self-invocation “is not going to result in the advice associated with a method invocation getting a chance to run”. it is why a @transactional method called from another method in the same class runs without a new transaction ( analysis , following from the same rule). the fixes spring suggests are to restructure the code so the call goes through another bean, or to inject a reference to the proxy. aspectj’s compile-time and load-time weaving change the bytecode itself, so they do not have this limit. the modern versions of the same three ideas. in spring webflux, a webfilter plays the part of the servlet filter in a reactive application. in jakarta ee, and so in quarkus, jakarta interceptors give you an @aroundinvoke method that “interposes on business methods”, much like an aspect. and native images change the trade-off: graalvm must be told about dynamic proxies, so for a spring native image the proxies are created at build time and compiled in. if the code you want to add… put it in applies to every http request, before anything else (authentication, cors, compression, a request id) a servlet filter, or a webfilter in webflux; for security, spring security’s filter chain needs to know which controller is handling the request a handlerinterceptor applies to business methods however they are called (transactions, caching, metrics on a service) an aspect, or an annotation that spring already implements with one applies to two or three methods only plain code: call a helper, or wrap the object yourself has to work on calls inside the same class, or on fields aspectj weaving, not spring’s proxies our view: use the least invisible mechanism that does the job. filters for http, plain code when only a few methods need it, and aspects when the same rule genuinely applies everywhere, written down where the team will find it. every aspect is code that runs without appearing in the method it changes, and the self-invocation surprise shows how easily that catches people out. the other view: that invisibility is the point. aspects keep business code about the business, @transactional is used happily in a great many spring applications, and one well-named aspect is easier to change than the same five lines copied into fifty methods.
