the short answer spring began as example code in a book, shipped as one jar, and grew into a widely used way to build java services. our view: each layer was added to remove a pain the previous one left behind. the other view is in the card “our view, and the other view”. how to use spring today is on spring ; this page is how it got there.

twenty years in one line seven eras of spring, 2002 to 2022 a timeline of seven eras. 2002, the book: j2ee without ejb. 2004, spring 1.0: one jar and xml beans. 2007, annotations: autowired and component. 2009, spring 3: java configuration and the jar split into modules. 2014, spring boot: no configuration to start. 2017, spring 5: webflux and reactive. 2022, spring 6: java 17, jakarta and native images. 2002 the book j2ee without ejb 2004 spring 1.0 one jar, xml beans 2007 annotations @autowired, @component 2009 spring 3 java config, jar split 2014 spring boot no config to start 2017 spring 5 webflux, reactive 2022 spring 6 java 17, jakarta, native seven eras. the years are the release dates in the cards below.

1. a reaction to j2ee 2002–2003 in the early 2000s, enterprise java meant j2ee and ejb 2 : an application server, deployment descriptors, home and remote interfaces, and business code you could not test without the container. rod johnson’s book expert one-on-one j2ee design and development (wrox, november 2002) argued that most applications did not need all of that. it came with 30,000 lines of framework code showing the alternative: plain java objects, wired together by a container, with infrastructure kept out of the business code. readers asked to use that code. juergen hoeller and yann caroff persuaded johnson to make it an open-source project, and became co-founders. caroff suggested the name: spring , a fresh start after the “winter” of traditional j2ee. the project went public in june 2003.

2. spring 1.0: one jar, three ideas march 2004 spring 1.0 final was released on 24 march 2004. it was distributed as one file, spring.jar , alongside finer-grained module jars for those who wanted less. it rested on three ideas that are still its core: inversion of control and dependency injection. the container creates your objects and hands them their dependencies, so classes stay plain and testable. aspect-oriented programming. cross-cutting concerns such as transactions and security are applied around your code, not written inside it. templates over raw apis. jdbctemplate , hibernate support and a single transaction abstraction removed the open-try-catch-close boilerplate. <bean id="caseservice" class="com.example.caseservice"> <property name="repository" ref="caserepository"/> </bean> spring mvc was in the box too, as a simpler alternative to struts. configuration was xml , and large applications grew large xml files.

3. annotations spring 2.0 (october 2006) · 2.5 (november 2007) java 5 brought annotations, and spring moved the wiring next to the code. spring 2.0 added xml configuration based on xml schema (shorter config) and integrated with the aspectj pointcut language. spring 2.5 added @autowired , @component , @service and @controller , with classpath scanning to find them ( @repository dates from 2.0). @service public class caseservice { @autowired private caserepository repository; } the family began to grow around the core. acegi security became an official spring project at the end of 2007 and was renamed spring security (2.0 shipped in april 2008). spring web services (2007), spring batch and spring integration (2008) followed. the company behind it changed its name too: interface21 became springsource in 2007.

c.h: 4. Spring 3: Java config, and the end of spring.jar
c.x: 4. spring 3: java config, and the end of spring.jar december 2009 spring 3.0 made java 5 the baseline. it brought @configuration classes (configuration written in java, checked by the compiler), the spring expression language, and rest support in mvc. @configuration public class appconfig { @bean caseservice caseservice(caserepository repo) { return new caseservice(repo); } } it also stopped providing the all-in-one spring.jar . the framework was now a set of modules ( spring-core , spring-beans , spring-context , spring-jdbc , spring-webmvc and more), and builds pulled in only what they used. vmware bought springsource in august 2009, and spring data followed in 2010–11, bringing the repository idea to jpa, mongodb, redis and others. the new pain: each module was simple, but starting a project meant choosing compatible versions of a dozen modules and writing the same setup every time.

5. spring boot: convention over configuration spring 4.0 (december 2013) · spring boot 1.0 (april 2014) spring 4.0 added first-class java 8 support, websocket and @restcontroller . the bigger change was spring boot , which answered “how do i start?” with defaults: starters: one dependency ( spring-boot-starter-web ) brings a tested set of libraries and versions. auto-configuration: if a database driver is on the classpath, a datasource is set up for you, and you override only what you need. an embedded server: tomcat (or jetty) inside the jar; java -jar app.jar replaced deploying war files to an application server. actuator: health, metrics and info endpoints for production. @springbootapplication public class app { public static void main(string[] args) { springapplication.run(app.class, args); } } boot arrived as microservices and containers took off. spring cloud 1.0 (march 2015) paired a configuration server with integrations for netflix’s open-source tools (eureka, zuul, ribbon). spring moved to pivotal , spun out of vmware, in 2013; vmware agreed to acquire pivotal in 2019, and broadcom completed its purchase of vmware in november 2023.

6. spring 5: reactive september 2017 · boot 2.0 (march 2018) spring 5.0 made java 8 the baseline and added webflux , a second web stack built on project reactor, running on netty or undertow among others. a few threads that never block serve many connections, with end-to-end backpressure; r2dbc later did the same for databases. it also added first-class kotlin support and a functional routing model. spring mvc stayed fully supported, so teams chose per service. the threading story behind this is on how java threads evolved .

7. spring 6: java 17, jakarta and native spring 6.0 (november 2022) · boot 3.0 (eight days later) spring 6 raised the baseline to java 17 and moved from javax.* to jakarta.* , following java ee’s move to the eclipse foundation. it added first-class support for graalvm native images , through ahead-of-time processing: applications that start much faster and use less memory. observability was rebuilt on micrometer. boot 3.2 (november 2023) added a one-line switch for virtual threads , spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true , plus the simpler restclient and jdbcclient . spring modulith (first release 2022) gave a structure for well-separated modules inside one application, checked by tests, and spring ai (1.0 in may 2025) brought model clients, prompts and vector stores into the same style. spring framework 7 and boot 4 (november 2025) continue the line, with jspecify null-safety annotations across the codebase.

what stayed the same idea 2004 today dependency injection xml <bean> with <property> constructor injection, found by scanning or @bean infrastructure around code aop proxies for transactions the same proxies, plus ahead-of-time generated code for native images templates over raw apis jdbctemplate , hibernatetemplate jdbcclient , restclient , spring data repositories getting started copy spring.jar , write xml start.spring.io , one starter, no xml

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: spring grew by adding a layer each time the previous one made something tedious: xml gave way to annotations, annotations to java config, hand-picked jars to starters, and application servers to an executable jar. the single jar is gone, but plain java objects with infrastructure kept out of the way are still the point. the other view: each layer also hid more of what happens at start-up, and auto-configuration can make it hard to see why a bean exists; teams that value explicitness may prefer a smaller framework, or plain java with fewer conventions (see quarkus for one alternative).

spring boot → quarkus spring boot quarkus @restcontroller, @getmapping @path , @get (quarkus rest, jakarta rest annotations) @service, @component @applicationscoped (or @singleton ) @autowired @inject , or constructor injection @value @configproperty(name = "…") @configurationproperties @configmapping(prefix = "…") on an interface application-prod.yml %prod. prefix in application.properties jparepository panacherepository<t> or panacheentity restclient / @httpexchange @registerrestclient interface @restcontrolleradvice @serverexceptionmapper actuator smallrye health ( /q/health ), micrometer ( /q/metrics ) @springboottest, @mockitobean @quarkustest , @injectmock testcontainers @serviceconnection dev services (starts the container for you) reactor mono / flux mutiny uni / multi

cli & dev mode quarkus create app org.acme:shop-api \ --extension='rest-jackson,hibernate-orm-panache,jdbc-postgresql,hibernate-validator' quarkus ext list --installable quarkus ext add smallrye-health micrometer-registry-prometheus quarkus dev # live reload; press r to run tests, d for dev ui ./mvnw quarkus:dev # same with maven ./gradlew quarkusdev # same with gradle ./mvnw package # target/quarkus-app/quarkus-run.jar java -jar target/quarkus-app/quarkus-run.jar ./mvnw package -dnative # native binary (graalvm / mandrel) ./mvnw package -dnative -dquarkus.native.container-build=true # no local graalvm dev ui: http://localhost:8080/q/dev-ui . ship target/quarkus-app/ as a directory; the -run.jar alone is not runnable.

rest endpoint @path("/api/orders") @produces(mediatype.application_json) public class orderresource { private final orderservice svc; orderresource(orderservice svc) { this.svc = svc; } // constructor injection @get @path("/{id}") public orderdto get(@restpath uuid id) { return svc.get(id); } @get public list<orderdto> list(@restquery @defaultvalue("0") int page) { ... } @post @path("/search") public list<orderdto> search(@valid searchrequest req) { return svc.search(req); } @get @path("/{id}/raw") public restresponse<string> raw(@restpath uuid id) { return svc.raw(id).map(restresponse::ok) .orelse(restresponse.notfound()); } }

configuration # src/main/resources/application.properties quarkus.http.port=8080 quarkus.datasource.db-kind=postgresql %prod.quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://${db_host}:5432/shop %prod.quarkus.datasource.username=${db_user} %prod.quarkus.datasource.password=${db_password} quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=none # json console logs: add the quarkus-logging-json extension shop.dataset=analytics shop.stores=1_05,4_12 @configmapping(prefix = "shop") public interface shopconfig { string dataset(); @withdefault("20") int maxresults(); list<string> stores(); } @configproperty(name = "shop.dataset") string dataset; // single value profiles: dev , test , prod built in; pick another with -dquarkus.profile=staging . env vars override: shop_dataset .

data with panache // active record @entity public class order extends panacheentity { // gives long id public string orderref; public localdate orderdate; public static optional<order> byorderref(string orderref) { return find("orderref", orderref).firstresultoptional(); } } // repository style @applicationscoped public class orderrepo implements panacherepository<order> { public list<order> recent(string store) { return list("storeid = ?1 and orderdate > ?2 order by orderdate desc", store, localdate.now().minusdays(30)); } } @transactional public void save(order o) { o.persist(); } order.find("storeid", "1_05").page(page.of(0, 50)).list(); order.count("orderdate is null"); dev services: in dev and test, with no jdbc url set, quarkus starts a postgres container for you (needs docker or podman).

rest client @registerrestclient(configkey = "supplier") @path("/objects") public interface supplierclient { @get listing list(@restquery string prefix); @get @path("/{key}") uni<byte[]> fetch(@restpath string key); // reactive } # application.properties quarkus.rest-client.supplier.url=https://api.example.org quarkus.rest-client.supplier.read-timeout=10000 @inject @restclient supplierclient supplier; // fault tolerance (quarkus-smallrye-fault-tolerance) @retry(maxretries = 3, delay = 200) @timeout(10_000) @circuitbreaker(requestvolumethreshold = 10) public listing safelist(string p) { return supplier.list(p); }

threading: blocking, reactive, virtual // blocking signature → worker thread (default for non-uni returns) @get public list<orderdto> list() { ... } // reactive signature → event loop: never block inside it @get public uni<orderdto> get(@restpath uuid id) { return client.fetch(id) .onitem().transform(this::todto) .onfailure().retry().atmost(3) .ifnoitem().after(duration.ofseconds(5)).fail(); } multi.createfrom().iterable(uris) .onitem().transformtouniandmerge(this::fetch); // concurrent // virtual threads (java 21+) @get @runonvirtualthread public list<orderdto> slowlist() { return blockingdao.all(); } // force a reactive-typed method onto a worker @blocking

errors, health, metrics public class errormappers { @serverexceptionmapper public restresponse<map<string, string>> notfound(notfoundexception e) { return restresponse.status(response.status.not_found, map.of("error", "not_found", "orderref", e.orderref())); } } @readiness @applicationscoped public class suppliercheck implements healthcheck { public healthcheckresponse call() { return healthcheckresponse.named("supplier").status(reachable()).build(); } } // /q/health/live /q/health/ready /q/health/started @inject meterregistry registry; registry.counter("orders.rows.loaded").increment(n); @counted @timed // on methods

jobs & scheduling // command mode: run once, exit with a code (cloud run job, k8s job) @quarkusmain public class loadermain implements quarkusapplication { @inject loader loader; @override public int run(string... args) { return loader.load(args) ? 0 : 1; } } // java -jar quarkus-run.jar --year=2024 (or quarkus-picocli for real flags) // in-app schedule (quarkus-scheduler); cron has a seconds field @scheduled(cron = "0 15 6 * * ?", timezone = "utc") void tick() { ... } @scheduled(every = "10m", concurrentexecution = scheduled.concurrentexecution.skip) void poll() { ... }

testing @quarkustest class orderresourcetest { @injectmock orderservice svc; // quarkus-junit-mockito (before 3.31: quarkus-junit5-mockito) @test void returns404() { when(svc.get(any())).thenthrow(new notfoundexception("x")); given().when().get("/api/orders/{id}", uuid.randomuuid()) .then().statuscode(404) .body("error", is("not_found")); } } @quarkusintegrationtest // runs against the built jar or native binary class orderresourceit extends orderresourcetest {} @quarkustest @testprofile(noschedulerprofile.class) // per-test config overrides class schedulerofftest { /* tests here run with the overrides below */ } public class noschedulerprofile implements quarkustestprofile { public map<string, string> getconfigoverrides() { return map.of("quarkus.scheduler.enabled", "false"); } }

containers, kubernetes, gcp quarkus ext add container-image-jib kubernetes ./mvnw package -dquarkus.container-image.build=true \ -dquarkus.container-image.registry=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev \ -dquarkus.container-image.group=my-proj/apps # generated manifests: target/kubernetes/kubernetes.yml quarkus.kubernetes.replicas=2 quarkus.kubernetes.resources.requests.memory=256mi quarkus.kubernetes.env.secrets=db-credentials # google cloud clients come from the quarkiverse extensions, e.g. # io.quarkiverse.googlecloudservices:quarkus-google-cloud-bigquery # ...:quarkus-google-cloud-storage @inject bigquery bigquery; @inject storage storage; native images start far faster and use less memory, at a cost in throughput (the quarkus team measured native at about half), which suits cloud run and scale-to-zero. libraries that rely on reflection need native config; test the native build in ci.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation create a project and run dev mode write a rest endpoint and a @quarkustest configure with application.properties and profiles 2 practitioner use panache, rest clients and fault tolerance choose blocking, reactive or virtual-thread endpoints package as a container; use dev services 3 senior build and run native images; fix reflection issues design for kubernetes and serverless startup migrate services from spring with clear trade-offs 4 expert write quarkus extensions set framework strategy across spring and quarkus estates understand build-time processing and arc internals each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the short answer flex has gone with the flash runtime it ran on. rails and grails have not: both were still tagging new versions in 2026. our view: “faded” describes how often they are talked about more than whether they work, and many of their ideas now live in other frameworks.

then and now rails, flex and grails, 2004 to 2026 a timeline with three lanes. rails: first open-source release july 2004, version 8.0 in november 2024, and still tagging releases in 2026. grails: version 0.1 in march 2006, 1.0 in february 2008, and a version 8 tag in october 2026 under the apache software foundation. flex: given to apache by adobe in 2011, the flash player it needs deprecated in july 2017, last flex sdk release 4.16 in november 2017 and unsupported after december 2020. 2004 2008 2012 2016 2020 2024 rails open source 8.0 still tagging grails 0.1 1.0 v8 at apache flex to apache flash deprecated last sdk, 4.16 flash unsupported a timeline of the dates on this page, each from its source. rails and grails were still tagging new versions in 2026; flex’s last sdk release was in 2017, and the flash runtime it needs lost support at the end of 2020 (dashed line).

ruby on rails a server-side model–view–controller web framework in ruby, under the mit licence. david heinemeier hansson extracted it from the project management tool basecamp at 37signals and released it as open source in july 2004. what it introduced: it emphasises convention over configuration , a term hansson used to describe rails’ philosophy, and don’t repeat yourself . a model class user maps by default to a table users ; database migrations and scaffolding of views made it quick to build an application. wikipedia lists django, laravel, cakephp and grails among the frameworks it influenced. now: rails 8.0 was released in november 2024 and 8.1 in october 2025; the repository tagged v 8.1.4 in september 2026. sites that use it include github and shopify.

grails an open-source web framework for the java platform in the groovy language, following the same coding by convention idea. it was first called “groovy on rails” and dropped that name in march 2006 at hansson’s request. version 0.1 came out in march 2006 and 1.0 in february 2008. what it brought: rails-style productivity on the jvm, re-using existing java technologies, hibernate and spring, under one interface. now: it is apache grails , developed at the apache software foundation; its repository tagged v 8.0.0 in october 2026. groovy itself lives on in gradle build files and jenkins pipelines (see build tools and harness ).

adobe flex a software development kit for cross-platform rich web applications on the adobe flash platform, first developed by macromedia. user interfaces were laid out in mxml, with actionscript for behaviour, and applications needed flash player or adobe air to run. adobe gave flex to the apache software foundation in 2011. why it ended: it depended on one runtime. the iphone and ipad did not support flash player; adobe stopped developing flash player for mobile, deprecated flash in july 2017, ended support at the end of 2020, and began blocking flash content on 12 january 2021. apache flex’s latest release listed on wikipedia is 4.16.1 , in november 2017. its successor project, apache royale (formerly flexjs), compiles actionscript to javascript instead. analysis: the declarative idea survived, describing a user interface as nested components in a markup language, as jsx does today (see front-end toolchain ); the dependence on one vendor’s runtime did not.

why technologies fade ( analysis ) cause seen here the runtime goes away flex could not outlive flash player the platform shifts phones and tablets without flash; html5 took over video and interactive content the ideas are absorbed convention over configuration, migrations and scaffolding spread to frameworks in other languages, so choosing rails for them alone became less necessary attention moves on a framework can keep releasing while fewer people write about it; being discussed less is not the same as being unsupported

c.h: Choose by requirement: you maintain one of these
c.x: choose by requirement: you maintain one of these if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) the application runs in flash player replace it: the runtime has had no general support since 2020, and browsers block flash content a rails or grails application on a version that still gets fixes keep it, and upgrade on the project’s schedule; check each project’s own maintenance policy an old major version that no longer gets security fixes upgrade in steps, one major version at a time, with tests around the behaviour first (see testing ) you cannot hire or keep people who know the stack weigh a gradual move, piece by piece behind the same interface (see solution architecture: a to b ) your team knows the stack well and it meets the requirements stay: a rewrite has its own cost and risk

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: judge a framework by whether it is maintained and whether it fits your requirements, not by how often it is in the news. the ideas these three introduced are worth learning even if you never use them. the other view: attention matters in practice: fewer new tutorials, libraries and people to hire make a stack harder to staff and extend, so choosing what most teams use lowers that risk, even if an older framework still works well.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation say what convention over configuration means name what each of rails, grails and flex introduced check whether a framework is still releasing 2 practitioner read a framework's maintenance policy before upgrading upgrade a framework one major version at a time recognise a dependency on a runtime one vendor controls 3 senior decide whether to keep, upgrade or replace an older application plan a gradual migration behind the same interface weigh staffing risk against rewrite risk 4 expert set an organisation's policy for ageing stacks spot single-vendor runtime risk early carry good ideas from older frameworks into new ones each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

design thinking start with empathy: understand the people you are designing for, their goals, context and frustrations, before you decide what to build. frame the problem in their words. a well-framed problem is half solved; a badly framed one gets a polished answer to the wrong question. generate many ideas, then sketch and prototype the promising ones as cheaply as possible. test and iterate: put the prototype in front of real people, learn, and change it. repeat.

the double diamond a design process model popularised by the british design council in 2005, in four phases: discover: go wide; research the problem and the people. define: narrow down to the real problem. develop: go wide again; explore possible solutions. deliver: narrow down; test, choose and ship. two diamonds: diverge then converge on the problem, then on the solution.

ux practices engineers can use talk to users before building, and watch them use what you built. what people do often differs from what they say. usability testing with a few people finds most big problems: jakob nielsen's advice is to test with no more than five users and run as many small tests as you can afford. heuristic evaluation: review a design against a short list of usability principles, a method developed by rolf molich and jakob nielsen. personas and journeys keep real people in mind: who they are, what they are trying to do, and where it goes wrong.

good ux is good engineering clear errors: say what went wrong and how to fix it, in plain words. see apis for good error responses. fast feels good: speed is part of the experience. see performance and core web vitals on web fundamentals . consistency: the same thing looks and behaves the same everywhere. accessible by default: design for everyone from the start. see accessibility .

wcag 2.2 in one card the web content accessibility guidelines (wcag) are the w3c standard for accessible web content; wcag 2.2 became a w3c recommendation on 5 october 2023. they are organised under four principles, often remembered as pour : principle means examples perceivable people can see or hear the content, one way or another text alternatives for images, captions for video, enough contrast operable people can use it, whatever their input everything works by keyboard, no keyboard traps, targets big enough to hit understandable people can follow it the page language is declared, labels and errors are clear, behaviour is predictable robust it works with assistive technology every control exposes a name, role and value each success criterion has a level, a, aa or aaa; aa is the common target. two aa examples: normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and in 2.2 pointer targets should be at least 24 by 24 css pixels, with some exceptions.
start with semantic html native html elements come with keyboard support and the right role for free. reach for aria only when no native element does the job.

test it unplug the mouse: can you reach and use everything with tab, enter, space and the arrow keys, and always see where the focus is? use a screen reader on your own pages for ten minutes; it changes how you write markup. zoom to 200% and use a phone-width screen: does anything break or hide? automated checks (axe, lighthouse) catch a share of issues; they cannot judge whether alt text or labels make sense. do both. see testing .

it is also the law european union: under the european accessibility act, as of 28 june 2025, newly marketed products and services it covers must be accessible. many countries have similar laws for public-sector and commercial services. check the rules where your users are. beyond the law: captions help people in noisy places, contrast helps in sunlight, keyboard support helps power users. accessibility is quality.

the options approach what it is good for watch out for native, per platform swift and swiftui on apple platforms; kotlin and jetpack compose on android the best platform feel, newest features first, the deepest device access two codebases, two skill sets, features that drift apart shared logic, native ui kotlin multiplatform: share business logic, keep each platform's own ui (or share ui too with compose multiplatform) teams that want one copy of the rules but a native look newer tooling; you still need people who know each platform one ui toolkit everywhere flutter (dart), which draws its own widgets from a single codebase one team shipping the same app to several platforms fast looks the same everywhere unless you adapt it; a further language to learn web skills, native components react native: react and javascript or typescript, mapped to the platform's own ui building blocks teams that already build for the web with react a bridge layer between javascript and native code to understand and upgrade the web itself progressive web apps (installable, can work offline), or a web app inside a native shell (capacitor) reach, one codebase, no store review for every change (pwa) device apis and store presence vary by platform

how to choose start from the product, not the framework. does it need the camera, sensors, background work, or the latest platform features on day one? that pushes towards native. count the people. one small team rarely keeps two native apps equal; a shared approach often wins there. share the rules, not necessarily the screens. business logic and data code are the safest things to share; ui is where platforms differ most. try the web first if the app is mostly forms and content. a good responsive web app may be all you need. see web fundamentals .

where it is going declarative ui everywhere: swiftui, jetpack compose, flutter and react all describe what the screen should show and let the framework work out the changes. kotlin is google's preferred language for android (announced 7 may 2019), and kotlin multiplatform was declared stable in november 2023. sharing code is now a normal choice, not a compromise, for many apps; truly native work remains the right call for the most demanding ones. there is no single way out. each option trades reach, feel, cost and skills differently, and the answer can change as the app grows.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain native, cross-platform and web app options build and run a sample app on one platform know what an app store review involves 2 practitioner ship a feature on one mobile platform, with tests share business logic across platforms build an installable, offline-capable web app 3 senior choose an app architecture for a product and team design offline, sync and push notifications plan releases, versions and backwards compatibility 4 expert own mobile and desktop strategy across products lead a move between app technologies set performance, accessibility and security standards for apps each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

timeline when what why it mattered before the 1980s text terminals and command lines type a command, read the answer. still used for many engineering tasks. see linux . 1973 xerox alto an early computer with a graphical interface and a mouse. 1984 apple macintosh brought the graphical interface to a mass-market personal computer. 1985 windows 1.0 (november 1985) microsoft's graphical environment on top of dos. 1993 mosaic web browser made the web graphical and popular; pages were documents, not applications. 1995 onwards java applets programs inside the browser. browsers dropped the plug-in support they needed in the 2010s. 1996 to 2020 flash rich animation and video in the browser through a plug-in; its player was retired at the end of 2020. 1999, named 2005 xmlhttprequest, then "ajax" pages could fetch data without reloading. the term ajax was coined in february 2005. 2006 jquery smoothed over browser differences and made page scripting approachable. 2007 and 2008 the first iphone, then android touch-first phones, app stores, and native mobile development. 2010 to 2014 angularjs (2010), react (2013), vue (2014) single-page applications: the browser builds the ui from data and calls apis. 2015 react native; "progressive web app" coined web skills reach native apps; web apps learn to install and work offline. 2018 to 2021 flutter 1.0 (2018), swiftui (2019), jetpack compose (2021) declarative ui comes to mobile: describe the screen, let the framework update it.

what stays the same every generation repeats the same lessons: keep the interface responsive while work happens in the background, separate what is shown from the data behind it, make it usable by everyone (see web fundamentals for accessibility), and test it the way people use it. the tools change; those do not. checked against (wikipedia): xerox alto ; macintosh 128k ; windows 1.0 ; mosaic ; java applet ; adobe flash ; ajax ; jquery ; iphone ; android ; angularjs ; react ; vue.js ; react native ; progressive web app ; flutter ; swiftui ; jetpack compose .

levels of testing level checks speed tools unit one function or class in isolation; logic, edge cases, errors ms junit + assertj, pytest, dbt unit tests integration your code with a real database, queue or http layer seconds testcontainers, wiremock, @springboottest, @quarkustest, bigquery emulator contract producer and consumer agree on an api or schema seconds pact, spring cloud contract, schema tests, dbt contracts end to end a user journey through the deployed system minutes playwright, selenium, scripted api checks data tests the data itself: keys, nulls, ranges, freshness, row counts per run dbt data tests, assertions in pipelines non-functional load, latency, resilience, security minutes–hours k6, gatling, locust, chaos tests, zap most tests should be fast unit and integration tests; a few end-to-end tests cover the critical journeys. a suite nobody runs because it is slow protects nothing.

the test pyramid mike cohn introduced the test pyramid in his book succeeding with agile . it is a picture of how many tests to write at each level: /\ few end-to-end tests: slow, brittle, prove the critical journeys / \ /----\ some integration and service tests: real database, real http / \ /--------\ many unit tests: fast, isolated, run on every change /__________\ write lots of small, fast unit tests, some coarser-grained tests, and very few that drive the whole system end to end. the higher the level, the slower and more fragile the test, and the harder it is to tell from a failure what broke. the anti-pattern is the "ice-cream cone": mostly manual and end-to-end tests with few unit tests. the suite gets slow, flaky and expensive, and people stop trusting it. treat it as a guide, not a law. the names of the middle layers vary between teams; the shape is what matters. contract tests (see below) keep services honest without many end-to-end tests. source: martin fowler's site, the practical test pyramid .

what makes a good test fails for the right reason: write it first, or break the code on purpose, and watch it go red. a test only ever seen green is unproven. tests behaviour, not implementation: inputs and outputs, not which private method was called. refactors should not break it. one reason to fail, with a name that says what it checks: rejectsunparseabledate . arrange, act, assert: set up, do one thing, check the result. independent: no shared state or order between tests; unique test data per test. deterministic: fixed clock, fixed seed, no real network, no sleeps. covers the edges: empty, null, one, many, boundary values, bad input, the dependency being down.

tdd in one loop red: write a small failing test for the next behaviour. green: write the least code that makes it pass. refactor: clean up with the tests as a safety net. for a bug: first write a test that reproduces it and fails, then fix. the test stays, so the bug cannot return. our view: this is also a good way to brief an ai assistant: give it the failing test as the definition of done. the other view: for exploratory work, where the behaviour is not yet known, some prefer to let the assistant sketch first and write the tests once the shape is clear.

java: junit + assertj + mockito class orderdateparsertest { @parameterizedtest(name = "{0} → {1}") @csvsource({ "05-05-1959, 1959-05-05", // day-first, from one source "2024-01-31, 2024-01-31", // iso, from the others }) void parsesbothformats(string raw, localdate expected) { assertthat(orderdateparser.parse(raw)).isequalto(expected); } @parameterizedtest @valuesource(strings = {"", "31-31-2024", "yesterday"}) void rejectsunparseable(string raw) { assertthatthrownby(() -> orderdateparser.parse(raw)) .isinstanceof(illegalargumentexception.class) .hasmessagecontaining("does not parse"); } } @extendwith(mockitoextension.class) class loadertest { @mock blobstore store; @injectmocks loader loader; @test void reportsunknownwhenlistingfails() { when(store.list(any())).thenthrow(new runtimeexception("403 forbidden")); assertthat(loader.run().state()).isequalto(state.unknown); // not "0 objects" verify(store, never()).copy(any(), any()); } } this code runs on junit 5 and junit 6 alike. junit 6 needs java 17 or newer.

python: pytest import pytest from datetime import date from pipeline.dates import parse_order_date @pytest.mark.parametrize("raw, expected", [ ("05-05-1959", date(1959, 5, 5)), ("2024-01-31", date(2024, 1, 31)), ]) def test_parses_both_formats(raw, expected): assert parse_order_date(raw) == expected @pytest.mark.parametrize("raw", ["", "31-31-2024", none]) def test_rejects_unparseable(raw): with pytest.raises(valueerror, match="does not parse"): parse_order_date(raw) @pytest.fixture def fake_store(monkeypatch): store = fakestore() # a small in-memory fake beats a deep mock monkeypatch.setattr("pipeline.land.store", store) return store def test_copies_only_new_objects(fake_store): fake_store.seed(["a", "b"]) result = land(source=["a", "b", "c"]) assert result.copied == 1 and result.already_current == 2

test doubles: pick the lightest double is dummy passed but never used stub returns canned answers fake a working lightweight version (in-memory store) spy records how it was called mock pre-programmed with expectations it verifies mock what you do not own only at the boundary; prefer a fake or a real container. build stubs from captured real responses , never from a guess. a stub shaped from the docs confirms the guess. too many mocks means the test checks wiring, not behaviour.

integration tests with real dependencies // java: real postgres in docker for the test @testcontainers @springboottest class orderrepositoryit { @container @serviceconnection // testcontainers 2: org.testcontainers.postgresql (1.x: postgresqlcontainer<?>) static postgresqlcontainer pg = new postgresqlcontainer("postgres:16"); @autowired orderrepository repo; @test void upsertkeepstheexistingid() { long id = repo.upsert(sample("k1")).id(); long again = repo.upsert(sample("k1").withorderref("changed")).id(); assertthat(again).isequalto(id); // ids are never renumbered } } // http dependency: wiremock serving a captured response stubfor(get(urlpathequalto("/objects")) .willreturn(aresponse().withstatus(200) .withbodyfile("supplier/listing-page-2.xml"))); # python: testcontainers from testcontainers.community.postgres import postgrescontainer def test_load_roundtrip(): with postgrescontainer("postgres:16") as pg: dsn = pg.get_connection_url(driver=none) # postgresql://… (the default adds +psycopg2 for sqlalchemy) load_rows(dsn, rows); assert count(dsn) == len(rows)

browser tests with playwright playwright is a framework for web automation and testing that drives chromium, firefox and webkit with a single api. // tests/orders.spec.ts import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test'; // baseurl is set in playwright.config.ts test('a customer can find an order', async ({ page }) => { await page.goto('/orders'); await page.getbylabel('search').fill('k1'); await page.getbyrole('button', { name: 'search' }).click(); await expect(page.getbyrole('row', { name: /k1/ })).tobevisible(); }); // npx playwright test run the suite // npx playwright test --ui develop and debug in ui mode // npx playwright codegen <url> record a first draft of a test // npx playwright show-trace trace.zip auto-waiting: before an action, playwright runs actionability checks on the element and waits for them to pass, so tests need no hand-written sleeps. if the checks do not pass within the timeout, the action fails. retrying assertions: await expect(locator).tobevisible() and similar assertions retry until they pass or time out. remember the await . locate as a user would: the recommended locators are getbyrole , getbytext and getbylabel , which follow user-facing attributes rather than css paths that change with every redesign. locating by role gives early feedback on aria roles and accessible names, but does not replace an accessibility audit (see accessibility ). traces for failures in ci: the trace viewer steps back and forward through each action of a recorded test. a common setting is trace: 'on-first-retry' , which records only when a test is retried. apis too: playwright can call your rest api directly, without loading a page, to set up data or check a result. our view: keep end-to-end browser tests to the few journeys that matter most, and test the rest at lower levels. the other view: some teams test most behaviour through the browser because that is what users see, and accept slower suites for it.

c.h: API tests: Postman, Newman and tests in code
c.x: api tests: postman, newman and tests in code // a postman test script, run after the request pm.test('returns the order', function () { pm.response.to.have.status(200); const body = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(body.orderref).to.eql('k1'); pm.environment.set('orderid', body.id); // chain into the next request }); # shell: run the same collection in ci with newman, and write junit xml for the ci report newman run orders.postman_collection.json -e staging.postman_environment.json \ -r cli,junit --reporter-junit-export results/newman.xml postman: an api platform where you build requests into collections, keep variables in environments, and attach test scripts like the one above. newman: postman’s command-line collection runner, so the same collection runs in ci. its built-in reporters are cli, json, junit, progress and emojitrain. rest assured (java) and pytest with httpx (python): api tests written as code, next to the service they test. bruno: an offline api client that stores collections as plain-text files in a folder, so they can live in git with the code. if this is true for you it leans towards people who do not write code (testers, analysts, support) explore and share apis postman, with newman to run the same collections in ci tests should live in the service’s repository and run with its build rest assured or pytest with httpx collections must be plain-text files reviewed in pull requests, with no cloud account bruno (offline-only, collections in a folder, git for sharing), or tests in code the same test should check both the api and the page that uses it playwright, which does both your team already maintains a large postman workspace keep it, and run it with newman; switching has a cost

testing data pipelines idempotency: run the same input twice; the output must be identical (row count and content). incremental vs full: an incremental run on top of yesterday equals a full rebuild. edge data: empty partition, one row, duplicates, late rows, a new source column, a malformed date. reconciliation: rows in = rows loaded + rows rejected + rows skipped, every run. run records: assert the counters written to the ledger, not only the log line. "source down": the run must end failed or unknown, never succeeded with zero. real dialect: a sql string checked against a mock proves its shape, not that bigquery accepts it. run it on the emulator or a dry run. # dbt dbt build -s my_model+ # models + their tests, in order dbt test -s test_type:unit # logic on fixed inputs dbt test -s test_type:data # assertions on built tables

property-based testing instead of hand-picked examples, state a property that must hold for all inputs and let the tool generate hundreds, shrinking any failure to the smallest case. # python: hypothesis from hypothesis import given, strategies as st @given(st.dates(min_value=date(1950,1,1), max_value=date(2030,12,31))) def test_format_then_parse_roundtrips(d): assert parse_order_date(d.strftime("%d-%m-%y")) == d @given(st.lists(st.text())) def test_dedupe_is_idempotent(xs): assert dedupe(dedupe(xs)) == dedupe(xs) java: jqwik ( @property , @forall ). good properties: round trips, idempotency, invariants (sorted output stays sorted), and "never throws".

load and performance tests // k6: ramp to 60 searches/s and check p95 latency import http from 'k6/http'; import { check } from 'k6'; export const options = { scenarios: { search: { executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startrate: 5, timeunit: '1s', preallocatedvus: 50, stages: [{ target: 60, duration: '5m' }, { target: 60, duration: '10m' }] } }, thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500'], http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'] }, }; export default function () { const r = http.get(`${__env.base}/api/search?q=land+acquisition`); check(r, { '200': (x) => x.status === 200 }); } // k6 run -e base=https://staging.example.com search.js test against production-sized data in a production-like environment. measure percentiles (p95, p99), not averages. find the breaking point, then decide the alert threshold below it.

c.h: Choosing a load-testing tool: by requirement
c.x: choosing a load-testing tool: by requirement tool tests are written in notes from its own documentation k6 javascript, run by an engine written in go http, websockets, grpc and browser tests; thresholds in the script; agpl-3.0 licence gatling java, javascript, typescript, kotlin or scala simulations as code, an html report, and a build that fails when performance regresses; the community edition is apache 2.0 locust python tests are regular python code; run from the command line or a web ui, with results in real time apache jmeter test plans built in a gui, run headless from the command line 100% java; many protocols, including http, soap and rest if this is true for you it leans towards tests should live with a javascript or typescript codebase, with pass or fail thresholds in ci k6 or gatling the team works in java or kotlin and wants load tests in the same language as the service gatling the team works in python, or the test needs python libraries locust testers build plans without writing code, or you test protocols such as soap, jdbc or jms jmeter a licence must be permissive for how you ship or embed the tool check each licence first: k6 is agpl-3.0, gatling’s community edition apache 2.0 whichever tool, read percentiles rather than averages, and watch for coordinated omission: a load generator that waits for each reply stops sending exactly when the server is slow (see banking & low latency ). our view: send load at a fixed rate for service capacity tests. the other view: a closed loop, where each virtual user waits for its reply, models real users who really do wait, and suits journey tests.

flaky tests, coverage, ci flaky test: passes and fails on the same code. causes: time, ordering, shared state, real network, async waits. fix or delete it; never retry it into green or quarantine it forever. coverage shows what was executed , not what was checked . 100% coverage with weak assertions proves little. use it to find untested code, not as a target. mutation testing (pit for java, mutmut for python) changes your code and checks that some test fails. it measures test strength. ci runs every test on every pr, on a clean checkout. a local green and a ci red on the same commit usually mean untracked files or a different environment. never skip, disable or weaken a test to get green. if a test is wrong, fix it in its own reviewed change.

testing ai features unit-test everything around the model: prompt building, parsing, retries, fallbacks. validate structured outputs against the schema, and the values against your data. run an eval set in ci and track the score; fail the build on a regression beyond a threshold. include adversarial cases: prompt injection in documents, empty retrieval, the model refusing. mock the model in unit tests with recorded real responses; run the eval against the real model.

one we build: enrich-test-api enrich-test-api is a java test library for exercising real cloud service semantics against local emulators, so a test names no cloud provider. it is an early alpha: aws only, emulator only. it is open source (apache 2.0). it is ours, so we are not neutral: compare it with testcontainers and the other tools on this page.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation write unit tests with clear arrange-act-assert run the suite locally and read ci failures reproduce a bug with a failing test before fixing it 2 practitioner use testcontainers and wiremock for integration tests test edge cases, errors and dependency failures keep tests fast, independent and deterministic 3 senior design a test strategy across unit, integration, contract and end to end add property-based, load and mutation testing where they pay off eliminate flaky tests and slow suites 4 expert set testing standards and quality gates for the organisation build test infrastructure: environments, data, emulators measure test effectiveness, not just coverage each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the short answer our view: stop aiming for one environment that runs everything. test logic locally and fast; test each boundary with contracts and real dependencies in containers; run a small number of end-to-end checks in a short-lived cloud environment built the way production is; and treat production itself as a place you test, carefully, with canaries and monitoring. the other view is in the last card on this page.

c.h: Where each kind of check runs
c.x: where each kind of check runs where each kind of check runs four stages from left to right: your laptop, ci, a short-lived cloud environment, and production. on the laptop: unit tests, component tests with test doubles, integration tests with real dependencies in containers, and consumer contract tests. in ci: the same tests on every push, plus provider contract verification. in a short-lived cloud environment: a few smoke and end-to-end tests against the real managed services. in production: canary releases, synthetic checks, and monitoring and alerts. an arrow underneath shows that the checks added at each stage are fewer and slower, but closer to the real system. your laptop unit tests component tests (test doubles) integration tests (real deps, containers) consumer contracts ci the same tests, on every push plus provider contract verification short-lived cloud env a few smoke and end-to-end tests against the real managed services production canary releases synthetic checks monitoring and alerts most checks, fastest feedback fewer and slower, but closer to the real system where each kind of check runs. moving right, the checks added at each stage are fewer and slower, but closer to the system your users reach ( analysis ).

c.h: Why “everything end to end” breaks down
c.x: why “everything end to end” breaks down the test pyramid , from mike cohn’s succeeding with agile : many small, fast unit tests, some coarser tests, and very few high-level tests, because the higher you go, the fewer you should have. end-to-end tests are notoriously flaky, fail for unexpected reasons, need a lot of maintenance and run slowly, as ham vocke puts it in the practical test pyramid . vocke also cautions that the pyramid is overly simplistic and works best as a rule of thumb. microservices add network boundaries, so the testing strategies of a single in-process application need to be reconsidered (toby clemson, testing strategies in a microservice architecture ).

c.h: Contracts instead of a full stack
c.x: contracts instead of a full stack contract tests (martin fowler): keep testing against a test double for speed and reliability, and separately run contract tests to catch the real service changing underneath you. fowler notes they can run on their own rhythm, often once a day, and a failure need not break the build. consumer-driven contracts (ian robinson, 2006): each consumer states what it needs from a provider, and the provider tests against all its consumers’ expectations. in practice (vocke): consuming teams send their pact contract files to the provider team, which uses them in its provider tests. he calls consumer-driven contract tests “a real game changer” for autonomous teams that move fast and with confidence. analysis: two services can then be tested apart, which is what makes a team independent of a shared environment.

c.h: Local stand-ins for cloud services, and their limits
c.x: local stand-ins for cloud services, and their limits stand-in what it gives you its own caveat testcontainers throwaway instances of databases, browsers or anything that runs in a docker container, inside your tests analysis: only for what ships as a container image kind a local kubernetes cluster whose “nodes” are docker containers; usable for local development or ci designed first for testing kubernetes itself; it is not your cloud’s managed cluster google pub/sub and firestore emulators local versions for development and tests the pub/sub emulator itself warns its implementation may be incomplete or differ from the real system; google’s known limitations include no iam operations. firestore’s emulator has “notable limitations”, for example it does not mirror production’s transaction concurrency modes azurite a free local emulator for azure storage microsoft says it supports only blob, queue and table storage, and has functional differences from an azure storage account in the cloud localstack a framework to develop and test aws applications locally its open-source repository is archived and read-only as localstack consolidates into a single unified image; the company offers a free hobby plan for non-commercial use, and paid plans analysis: an emulator passing is evidence about your code, not about the cloud service. pub/sub’s emulator lists iam operations as unsupported, and none of the stand-ins above claims to reproduce your cloud’s identity, networking or quotas, so check those in a real environment.

short-lived cloud environments create an environment per pull request or per test run, built by the same helm charts and terraform as production (see helm and terraform ), and delete it afterwards. in kubernetes, a namespace isolates a group of resources within one cluster, and resource quotas divide the cluster between users, so many such environments can share one cluster. point them at real managed services, using separate small instances or test projects. this card is analysis built on the kubernetes namespace documentation, which says namespaces are intended for clusters with many users across teams. the cost is real: cloud spend and setup time per environment.

c.h: Production is part of the strategy
c.x: production is part of the strategy qa in production (rouan wilsenach): watch the behaviour of production closely, with the right monitoring and a good continuous delivery pipeline, so issues are found as they happen and fixed quickly. canarying (google sre workbook): a partial and time-limited deployment of a change, evaluated against the rest, usually on a much smaller part of production or of the users. feature flags let you ship code switched off and turn it on for a few users first ( analysis ; see devops ).

c.h: How much of each: choose by requirement
c.x: how much of each: choose by requirement if this is true for the part you are testing it leans towards ( analysis ) business logic, calculations, validation unit tests on your machine, lots of them your code talking to a database, cache or broker that ships as a container integration tests with testcontainers, on your machine and in ci a call to another team’s service consumer-driven contract tests, verified in the provider’s ci a managed cloud service whose emulator’s listed limitations do not touch what you use the emulator for fast feedback, plus a few tests against the real service identity, iam permissions, network policies, quotas a short-lived cloud environment: there is no faithful local copy a critical user journey (sign in, pay, place an order) a handful of end-to-end tests in a cloud environment, plus synthetic checks in production a risky change you cannot fully rehearse a canary or a feature flag, with monitoring and a fast rollback your team already has a shared test environment that works keep it, and add contracts to reduce how much depends on it: switching has a cost

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: fast local tests and contracts catch most mistakes cheaply, and a few real-environment checks plus careful releases catch what they cannot. chasing a perfect local copy of the cloud costs more than it saves. the other view: some teams, for example in regulated or high-risk settings, judge a full pre-production environment that mirrors production worth its cost and flakiness, and run large end-to-end suites there for the assurance it gives.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation say which tests run locally and which need a real environment explain a contract test run a dependency in a container for a test 2 practitioner write consumer contract tests and verify them in the provider's ci use an emulator and know its listed limitations add smoke tests to a deployment 3 senior design a per-pull-request cloud environment plan canary releases with automatic evaluation decide test depth per component by risk 4 expert set an organisation's test strategy across teams and environments balance test-environment cost against risk make production observability part of quality each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the short answer our view: write so that someone who was not in the room can understand what changed and why, months later. treat code review as a way to keep the code base healthy and to share knowledge, not only to catch bugs. the other view is in the card “our view, and the other view”.

writing that gets read bottom line up front (bluf) means starting a message with its key information, so the reader gets the most important part first. it is a standard in u.s. military communication and resembles the inverted pyramid in journalism: conclusions come before the material that supports them. plain language is writing designed so the reader understands it as quickly, easily and completely as possible, avoiding verbose, convoluted language and jargon. many countries require public agencies to use it. analysis: both ideas suit engineering writing, where most readers are busy and arrive looking for one answer.

commit messages git’s own documentation suggests, though it does not require, starting a commit message with one short summary line of no more than 50 characters, then a blank line, then a fuller description. git treats the text up to the first blank line as the commit’s title and uses it throughout, for example as the subject of a patch sent by email. conventional commits is a lightweight convention on top of that: each message starts with a type, such as fix: (a bug fix, a semantic-versioning patch) or feat: (a new feature, a minor version), and a breaking change is marked with ! or a breaking change: footer, which makes it easier to build tools on the history. fix: prevent racing of requests introduce a request id and a reference to latest request. dismiss incoming responses other than from latest request. remove timeouts which were used to mitigate the racing issue but are obsolete now. reviewed-by: z refs: #123 an example from the conventional commits 1.0.0 specification. its summary line is 31 characters.

the kinds of engineering writing writing what it is for what published guidance says commit message why one change was made, kept with the code for ever a short summary line, a blank line, then the detail (git documentation); optionally a type prefix (conventional commits) pull request (change) description what a change does and why, for its reviewers and for later readers of the history google’s guide: the first line is a short summary of specifically what the change does, written as an imperative sentence, able to stand alone; the rest explains what is being changed and why design proposal agreeing an approach before building it a python enhancement proposal (pep), for example, is a design document that should give a concise technical specification of a feature and its rationale architecture decision record (adr) one important decision, with its context and consequences the widely used adr template comes from a 2011 post by michael nygard. an adr is not edited later: it is amended with new information, or superseded by a new adr documentation helping people learn, do, look up or understand diátaxis separates four kinds: tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation (the picture below) review comment improving one change, and the people who make the next one the card on review comments, below

four kinds of documentation four kinds of documentation (diátaxis) a two-by-two grid. columns: study (acquiring a skill) and work (applying a skill). rows: doing (practical action) and thinking (understanding). study and doing: tutorials, a lesson where you learn by doing. work and doing: how-to guides, which help you get a task done. study and thinking: explanation, which tells you why. work and thinking: reference, facts to look up while you work. study acquiring a skill work applying a skill doing practical steps thinking understanding tutorials a lesson: learn by doing how-to guides get a real task done explanation the why, and the context reference facts to look up while you work the four kinds of documentation in daniele procida’s diátaxis, redrawn as a two-by-two grid. to place a page, diátaxis asks two questions: is it about action or understanding, and is the reader studying or working? a page that tries to be two kinds at once usually serves neither reader well ( analysis ).

what code review is for code review is a quality activity in which people other than the author examine source code. its goals include finding defects, but also sharing knowledge of the code base and its expectations with both reviewers and author. michael fagan described the first studied process, inspection , in the ibm systems journal in 1976. research cited on wikipedia’s page found that up to 75% of review comments concern evolvability and maintainability rather than functionality, and fewer than 15% of the issues discussed relate directly to bugs. for defects, capers jones’s analysis of over 12,000 projects found formal inspections discovered 60–65% of latent defects, informal ones fewer than half, and most testing about 30%; another case study found lightweight reviews could find as many bugs as formal ones, faster.

the standard google’s guide sets google’s published code review guide says the primary purpose of review is to make sure the overall health of the code base improves over time. its senior principle: reviewers should favour approving a change once it definitely improves the overall code health, even if it is not perfect. “there is no such thing as ‘perfect’ code—there is only better code.” the guide also sets expectations on size and speed. about 100 lines is usually a reasonable size for a change and 1,000 usually too large, though it gives no hard rule; one business day is the maximum time it should take to respond to a review request. research cited on wikipedia puts optimal review rates at 200 to 400 lines of code an hour; faster than a few hundred lines an hour may be too fast to find errors in critical software.

review comments google’s guide on writing review comments asks reviewers to be kind, to explain their reasoning, and to comment on the code rather than the developer. its example: less helpful: “why did you use threads here when there’s obviously no benefit to be gained from concurrency?” more helpful: “the concurrency model here is adding complexity to the system without any actual performance benefit that i can see. because there’s no performance benefit, it’s best for this code to be single-threaded instead of using multiple threads.” it suggests labelling how much a comment matters, so the author can tell a required change from a suggestion: nit: (minor polish), optional or consider: (a good idea, not required), fyi: (something to think about later). it also says to comment on what is good in a change, not only what could be better, and that fixing the change is the author’s responsibility, though direct suggestions sometimes help more.

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) a decision affects several teams, or is costly to reverse a written design proposal, reviewed before building future readers will ask why the system is this way an architecture decision record beside the code you publish versions and changelogs from the history conventional commits, so tools can read the type of each change changes take days to be reviewed smaller changes and an agreed response time, as in google’s guide the software is safety-critical, or a standard requires review a formal inspection process; wikipedia notes review is mandatory in some such contexts your team already has writing and review conventions that work keep them, and write them down: changing conventions has a cost

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: clear writing and timely review are part of the engineering work, not overhead around it. a change that nobody else can understand is not finished. the other view: review after the code is written adds waiting, and much of its value is in comments about style that tools could check; some teams prefer to put effort into automated checks, pairing while the code is written, or reviewing after merge, and keep pre-merge review for risky changes.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation write a commit message with a short summary line and a reason describe a pull request so a reviewer knows what and why read review comments as being about the code, not you 2 practitioner review others' changes within a day, labelling comments by importance keep changes small enough to review well write an architecture decision record 3 senior write a design proposal others can build from set a team's review and writing conventions place documentation in the right one of four kinds 4 expert shape how an organisation records decisions balance review effort against automated checks mentor others through review each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the method set a goal in numbers: "p95 search latency under 500 ms at 60 requests/s", "nightly load finishes in 40 minutes", "cost under ₹x per 1,000 requests". no goal, no finish line. measure the current state in a production-like environment with realistic data and traffic. find the bottleneck: the one resource or step limiting everything (cpu, memory, i/o, a lock, a query, a dependency). use traces and profiles, not intuition. change one thing that addresses it. measure again the same way. keep the change only if the numbers improved and nothing else got worse. repeat until the goal is met, then stop. then guard it with a performance test in ci. most of the gain usually comes from one or two fixes: a missing index, an n+1 query, a synchronous chain, an oversized payload. find those before tuning anything clever.

laws worth knowing little's law: items in the system = arrival rate × time in system (l = λw). 100 requests/s × 0.2 s = 20 requests in flight, so you need about 20 concurrent workers or connections. amdahl's law: speeding up a part only helps by that part's share. making a step that takes 10% of the time infinitely fast saves 10%. queueing: as utilisation approaches 100%, waiting time grows sharply, not linearly. plan for 60–70% utilisation at peak. tail amplification: if one call is slow 1% of the time, a request that fans out to 100 such calls is slow 1 − 0.99 100 ≈ 63% of the time. latency vs throughput: batching raises throughput and usually raises latency; tune for whichever the goal names.

percentiles, not averages an average hides the users having a bad time. report p50 (typical), p95 and p99 (the tail), and max. you cannot average percentiles across instances; compute them from histograms. measure at the edge the user sees (load balancer, client), and also per dependency. watch for coordinated omission in load tests: a tool that waits for slow responses before sending the next request under-reports latency. use open-model (arrival-rate) tests.

kinds of performance test test question load do we meet the goal at expected peak? stress where does it break, and how does it fail? spike what happens on a sudden 10× burst? does autoscaling keep up? soak does it degrade over hours (leaks, growing queues)? capacity how much traffic per instance, and what will growth cost? micro-benchmark is this function faster than that one? (jmh, pytest-benchmark) load-test example with k6 is on the testing tab. test against production-sized data; a query fast on 10,000 rows can be slow on 20 million.

profiling the jvm # java flight recorder: low overhead, safe in production jcmd <pid> jfr.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/rec.jfr # or at startup java -xx:startflightrecording=duration=60s,filename=rec.jfr -jar app.jar # open rec.jfr in jdk mission control: hot methods, allocations, locks, gc # async-profiler: flame graphs of cpu, allocation or wall-clock time asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f cpu.html <pid> asprof -d 30 -e alloc -f alloc.html <pid> jcmd <pid> gc.heap_info jcmd <pid> thread.print # thread dump: what is everyone waiting on? flame graph: width = time spent; look for wide plateaus near the top. containers: set -xx:maxrampercentage ; watch gc pause time and allocation rate. startup: cds/aot caches, lazy initialisation, or native images for scale-to-zero. blocking i/o: virtual threads (21+) raise concurrency cheaply; cpu-bound work still needs cores.

c.h: Tuning the JVM: collector and memory
c.x: tuning the jvm: collector and memory collector from oracle’s garbage collection tuning guide flag g1 mostly concurrent; scales from small machines to large multiprocessor ones; the default on most hardware and operating systems -xx:+useg1gc parallel (throughput) several threads speed up collection; for medium to large data sets on multiprocessor hardware -xx:+useparallelgc zgc maximum pauses under a millisecond, independent of heap size, at some cost in throughput; for low-latency applications -xx:+usezgc -xx:+zgenerational in java 21 ( -xx:+usezgc alone selects the older, non-generational zgc there) serial a single thread does all collection work; chosen by default on some small configurations -xx:+useserialgc start with the defaults. oracle’s guide says: unless you have strict pause-time requirements, run first and let the vm choose a collector; if needed, adjust the heap size; only then change the collector. size the heap in containers by percentage. by default the jvm may use 25 percent of the available memory for the heap. a setting such as -xx:maxrampercentage=75 raises that; leave room for the rest of the process (threads, metaspace, direct buffers). one change at a time, measured with the same load test before and after (see the method, above). our view: for most services, the heap size and the number of database calls matter far more than the choice of collector. the other view: for services with strict tail-latency targets, switching to zgc can be a large change, because pauses stop growing with the heap.

micro-benchmarks done right (jmh) @state(scope.benchmark) @benchmarkmode(mode.averagetime) @outputtimeunit(timeunit.microseconds) @warmup(iterations = 3) @measurement(iterations = 5) @fork(1) public class parsebench { string raw = "05-05-1959"; @benchmark public localdate parse() { return orderdateparser.parse(raw); // return the result so it is not optimised away } } hand-written timing loops on the jvm lie: no warm-up, dead-code elimination, jit effects. use jmh, and only after a profile shows the code matters.

profiling python # sampling profiler, attach to a running process, no code changes py-spy top --pid 1234 py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid 1234 # flame graph # deterministic profiler for a script python -m cprofile -o out.prof -m loader python -c "import pstats; pstats.stats('out.prof').sort_stats('cumtime').print_stats(20)" # imports and memory python -x importtime -m loader 2> imports.txt # slow imports pip install memray && memray run -m loader # allocations replace python loops over rows with vectorised work: sql in the warehouse, polars, pyarrow, numpy. threads or asyncio for i/o-bound work; processes for cpu-bound work. stream large files instead of reading them whole into memory.

where time usually goes area common cause fix database missing index, n+1 queries, fetching unused columns, lock waits explain analyze, indexes, joins or batch loads, select only needed columns ( database design ) connection pools pool too small (queueing) or too large (database overload) size from little's law; watch pool wait time service calls sequential calls, no timeouts, new connection per call parallelise independent calls, keep-alive, http/2, timeouts payloads huge json responses, no compression, no pagination paginate, compress, return only needed fields serialisation reflection-heavy mapping in hot paths profile; precompiled serialisers; smaller objects memory and gc high allocation rate, heap too small, large object churn profile allocations; reuse buffers; tune heap and collector cold starts large images, eager initialisation, jvm warm-up smaller images, cpu boost, min instances, aot/native ( cloud run ) warehouse queries full scans, skewed joins, repeated subqueries partition filters, clustering, pre-aggregation ( sql skills ) pipelines one object at a time through one container; small files parallel tasks, bulk loads, purpose-built engines (dataflow), compact files llm calls long prompts, sequential calls, large models for simple tasks prompt caching, parallel calls, streaming, smaller models where evals allow

concurrency and backpressure bound every queue and pool; an unbounded queue turns overload into an out-of-memory crash. shed load early (429/503) when saturated rather than accepting work you cannot finish in time. set timeouts shorter than the caller's, so work is not done for a caller that has given up. cloud run concurrency and max instances, and database pool size, must agree: instances × pool size ≤ database connection limit. locks and synchronised blocks serialise work; look for them in thread dumps under load.

performance as a habit performance budgets in ci: fail the build if a key benchmark or bundle size regresses beyond a threshold. track p95/p99 per endpoint after every deploy, with deploy markers on dashboards. cost per unit of work (per request, per row loaded) next to latency: faster that costs 5× may be the wrong trade. capacity reviews before expected growth or launches. write down the numbers of each investigation, so the next one starts from evidence.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation read p50/p95/p99 latency and throughput on a dashboard spot an obvious n+1 query or missing index run an existing load test and report the result 2 practitioner profile a jvm or python service and fix the hot spot write load tests with goals and thresholds size pools and concurrency with little's law 3 senior lead performance investigations end to end with evidence set performance goals, budgets and capacity plans balance latency, throughput and cost in design 4 expert own performance engineering practice across the organisation understand runtime, os and hardware effects deeply design systems for extreme scale and tail latency each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
