principles least privilege: every person, service and token gets only the access it needs, for only as long as it needs it. defence in depth: several independent layers (network, identity, application, data), so one failure is not a breach. secure by default: private unless opened, denied unless allowed, encrypted unless there is a reason not to be. never trust input: anything from a user, another service, a file, a web page or a model's output is validated before use. no secrets in code, images, logs or chat. they live in a secret manager and are injected at runtime. fail closed: when an auth or permission check cannot run, deny. a gate that opens on error is not a gate. assume breach: log and alert so that a compromise is noticed and contained quickly.

owasp top 10 (2025 edition) risk looks like prevent with a01 broken access control get /api/orders/123 returns another user's order; the server fetches a user-supplied url that points to an internal service or metadata endpoint (ssrf, now part of this category) check ownership on every request, server side; deny by default; test it. for urls: allow-list destinations, block internal ranges, separate egress a02 security misconfiguration public bucket, debug endpoints on, default passwords, open cors infrastructure as code, reviewed; secure defaults; scanners a03 software supply chain failures an old library with a known cve; a compromised dependency or build tool an sbom, dependency updates, sca scanning, components from trusted sources only, protected ci a04 cryptographic failures plain http, passwords hashed with md5, keys in the repo tls everywhere, argon2id/bcrypt for passwords, managed keys a05 injection sql built by string concatenation; shell commands with user input parameterised queries, no shell with input, allow-lists a06 insecure design no rate limit on login; reset tokens that never expire threat model at design time; abuse cases as requirements a07 authentication failures weak passwords allowed, no mfa, session never expires use a proven identity provider; mfa; short-lived tokens a08 software or data integrity failures unsigned build artefacts; deserialising untrusted data signed images, pinned dependencies, verified artefacts a09 security logging & alerting failures a breach discovered months later; logs nobody is alerted on audit logs, alerts on suspicious patterns, retained logs a10 mishandling of exceptional conditions an error path that fails open, leaks a stack trace, or leaves a transaction half done handle errors where they happen and in one global handler; fail closed and roll back; rate limits and quotas the 2021 edition numbered these differently and had ssrf as its own a10. owasp revises the list every few years; check owasp.org for the latest edition. the api security top 10 is the companion list for apis.

injection: always parameterise // java jdbc // wrong: "select * from orders where order_ref = '" + orderref + "'" preparedstatement ps = conn.preparestatement( "select * from orders where order_ref = ?"); ps.setstring(1, orderref); // spring jdbcclient jdbc.sql("select * from orders where order_ref = :order_ref").param("order_ref", orderref)... # python psycopg cur.execute("select * from orders where order_ref = %s", (order_ref,)) # never f-strings # bigquery bigquery.queryjobconfig(query_parameters=[ bigquery.scalarqueryparameter("order_ref", "string", order_ref)]) # where order_ref = @order_ref identifiers (table and column names) cannot be parameters: pick them from an allow-list. never pass user input to a shell. use the library call, or an argument list without a shell. escape output for its context (html, json, urls) to prevent xss. use the framework's templating, not string building.

authentication & authorisation authentication is who you are; authorisation is what you may do. most breaches are authorisation bugs. use oidc / oauth 2.0 with a proven provider rather than building login yourself. for browser apps, the authorisation code flow with pkce. jwts: verify the signature, issuer, audience and expiry on every request; keep them short-lived; never accept alg: none ; never put secrets in them (they are only encoded). refresh tokens rotate on use and are revocable; in browsers keep them in httponly; secure; samesite cookies. check permissions on the server for every request and every object: "is this user allowed this order?", not just "is the user logged in?". load roles from the source of truth on each authentication; do not trust roles a client sends. passwords: argon2id or bcrypt, rate-limited login, breached-password checks, mfa for admins.

spring security: a stateless api @bean securityfilterchain api(httpsecurity http) throws exception { return http .authorizehttprequests(a -> a .requestmatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitall() .requestmatchers("/api/admin/**").hasrole("admin") .anyrequest().authenticated()) // deny by default .oauth2resourceserver(o -> o.jwt(customizer.withdefaults())) .sessionmanagement(s -> s.sessioncreationpolicy(sessioncreationpolicy.stateless)) .csrf(c -> c.disable()) // only safe when auth is a bearer header, not a cookie .build(); } // object-level check in the service, not only the url rule if (!casefile.ownerid().equals(currentuserid)) throw new accessdeniedexception("not yours");

web & api hardening https only, with hsts ( strict-transport-security ). content-security-policy to limit where scripts load from; x-content-type-options: nosniff ; frame-ancestors against clickjacking. cors: list exact origins; never reflect any origin with credentials allowed. csrf: needed when the browser sends cookies automatically; use tokens or samesite cookies. rate limits on login, signup, password reset and expensive endpoints. validate request bodies (types, lengths, ranges) and reject unknown fields where it matters. errors: generic messages to the client, details to the logs. no stack traces in responses. uploads: check type and size, store outside the web root, scan if users share them.

secrets # store echo -n "$value" | gcloud secrets create db-password --data-file=- # grant one workload access to one secret gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding db-password \ --member=serviceaccount:api@p.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role=roles/secretmanager.secretaccessor # rotate: add a version, roll the workload, then disable and destroy the old one gcloud secrets versions add db-password --data-file=new.txt gcloud secrets versions destroy 1 --secret=db-password no service account json keys: workload identity federation for ci, attached service accounts for workloads. a rotation is not finished until old versions are destroyed. scan commits for secrets (gitleaks, github secret scanning). a leaked secret is rotated, not just deleted from git: history and forks keep it. never print secrets in logs, ci output, error messages or ai prompts.

cloud security on gcp iam: one service account per workload; predefined narrow roles; no owner or editor for services; grant to groups, not individuals. organisation policies: block public buckets, service account key creation, and external ips where not needed. network: private ips for databases; ingress limited to the load balancer; cloud armor in front of public apps. data: encryption at rest is on by default; cmek when you must control keys; vpc service controls around sensitive datasets. audit logs: admin activity is always on; enable data access logs for sensitive services so reads are attributable. security command center surfaces misconfigurations and threats across the project. separate projects for dev and prod; nobody's laptop has standing prod write access.

threat modelling in 30 minutes draw the data flow: users, services, stores, and the trust boundaries between them. for each boundary, ask stride questions. list the threats, rate likelihood and impact, and pick mitigations. turn mitigations into tickets and tests. stride question spoofing can someone pretend to be another user or service? tampering can data be changed in transit or at rest? repudiation can someone deny an action because nothing recorded it? information disclosure can data leak to someone not entitled to it? denial of service can someone exhaust a resource or the budget? elevation of privilege can someone gain rights they should not have?

step 1, drawn a data flow with trust boundaries a small data-flow diagram. a user's browser sends requests across the internet trust boundary to an api. the api reads and writes a database across a second boundary, and calls a payment provider across a third. each boundary is where to ask the six stride questions: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. browser api database payment provider boundary: internet boundary: data boundary: third party at each boundary ask s t r i d e, rate each threat, turn mitigations into tickets and tests step 1 of the method above: draw the flow and mark the trust boundaries. the dashed lines are where the stride questions go.

data protection & privacy know where personal data is: tag columns and datasets; keep an inventory. collect less, keep less: only what the purpose needs, with a retention period. mask or tokenise personal data in non-production environments and analytics. honour legal obligations: deletion requests, legal holds, consent. apply them on every read path, not only in one table. know the law that applies: for india, the digital personal data protection act, 2023; gdpr for eu residents. logs are data too: no personal data or tokens in log lines unless necessary and protected.

supply chain & ci pin dependencies with lockfiles; review what new dependencies bring. automated updates (dependabot, renovate) gated by tests. scan: sast (codeql, semgrep), sca (dependabot alerts, osv), images (trivy), secrets (gitleaks). pin third-party github actions to a commit sha; give workflows the minimum permissions: . protect main and deploy tags; require reviews and checks; restrict who can push release tags. sign images and generate sboms so you can prove what is running.

security testing unit and integration tests for access control: user a cannot read user b's object; an expired token is refused; a missing role gets 403. sast reads code for dangerous patterns; dast (owasp zap) probes the running app. dependency and image scans on every build. fuzzing parsers and file handlers with malformed input. penetration test before launch and after major changes, by someone independent. prove each guard red: try the forbidden action in a test and watch it fail.

c.h: Cryptography: use it, do not invent it
c.x: cryptography: use it, do not invent it know the three jobs: hashing proves something has not changed and cannot be reversed; encryption hides data and can be reversed with the key; signing proves who produced something. passwords are hashed, never encrypted, with a slow, salted algorithm. the owasp password storage cheat sheet recommends argon2id (at least 19 mib of memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1); scrypt if argon2id is not available; bcrypt (work factor 10 or more, 72-byte password limit) for legacy systems; pbkdf2 with hmac-sha-256 and 600,000 or more iterations where fips-140 is required. fast hashes such as sha-256 alone are not suitable. use a vetted library and its defaults. never write your own algorithm or protocol. random means a secure generator: securerandom in java, the secrets module in python, never math.random or random for tokens. encrypt in transit (tls 1.2 or 1.3 everywhere, inside the network too) and at rest, and keep keys in a key management service, apart from the data, with rotation.

containers and kubernetes small images: a minimal or distroless base has fewer packages to patch. scan images in ci, pin them by digest, and sign them. never bake secrets into an image ; mount them at run time from a secret manager. pod security standards define three cumulative profiles: privileged, baseline and restricted. aim for restricted, and enforce it per namespace with the label pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted . least privilege in the cluster: narrow rbac roles, no service-account token where a pod does not call the api, and networkpolicies that deny by default. # container securitycontext that meets restricted securitycontext: runasnonroot: true allowprivilegeescalation: false capabilities: drop: ["all"] seccompprofile: type: runtimedefault readonlyrootfilesystem: true # good practice too

networks and zero trust zero trust: being inside the network earns no trust. every call is authenticated and authorised, service to service as well as user to service (mtls and tokens; see service mesh ). deny by default: firewalls and security groups open only the ports and sources a service needs. control outbound traffic too: a compromised service that cannot reach the internet cannot send your data out. keep databases and internal services off the public internet; use private networking and private endpoints. protect the edge: a waf and ddos protection in front of public endpoints, rate limits on apis (see apigee ). segment: a breach in one area should not open every other one.

ai and llm security the owasp genai llm top 10 (2026 edition, published august 2026) lists the main risks for applications built on language models: llm01 prompt injection. treat every input, including retrieved documents, web pages and tool results, as possibly carrying instructions. separate instructions from data; never let content alone trigger an action. llm02 sensitive information disclosure. do not put data in a prompt that the user may not see; filter outputs; check what your provider keeps. llm03 excessive agency. give tools the least privilege they need, and require a person's approval for actions that change things. llm04 supply chain. vet models, datasets, plugins and mcp servers as you would any dependency. llm05 data and model poisoning. know where training and retrieval data come from, and who can write to them. llm06 unbounded consumption. rate limits, token budgets and timeouts per user and per job. llm07 misinformation. ground answers in sources, cite them, and evaluate; never present a guess as fact. llm08 hidden context exposure. assume the system prompt and tool schemas can be extracted: never put secrets or security rules only there. llm09 vector and embedding weaknesses. apply access control in retrieval, so a user can only retrieve what they may read. llm10 improper output handling. treat model output as untrusted input: validate, escape and parameterise it before it reaches a browser, a shell or a query. more in ai for engineers , rag , mcp and agent harness .

c.h: People: the most targeted part of any system
c.x: people: the most targeted part of any system most attacks start with a person, not a server: a convincing email, message or call. urgency is the warning sign. "pay this now", "reset my access", "send me the file": check through another channel you already trust before acting. voices and video can now be faked convincingly. use phishing-resistant sign-in where you can (passkeys or hardware security keys), a password manager with a unique password everywhere, and multi-factor authentication on every account that offers it. keep devices updated and locked, and never leave a logged-in laptop unattended. report mistakes at once, without blame. a clicked link reported in five minutes is a small incident; hidden for a week, it is a big one.

security logging and detection log what an investigator will need: sign-ins that succeed and fail, permission and role changes, admin actions, data exports, and access denied. never log secrets, tokens, passwords or full card numbers, and mask personal data. protect the logs: separate access, append-only or write-once storage, kept long enough to investigate. alert on what matters: many failed sign-ins, access from somewhere new, a sudden large export, a disabled control. see observability .

backups and ransomware a common rule of thumb is 3-2-1: three copies of your data, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy off-site. keep one copy immutable or offline, with separate credentials, so an attacker who gets in cannot delete or encrypt the backups too. a backup you have not restored is a hope. test restores on a schedule and time them. agree the targets: how much data you can lose (rpo) and how long you can be down (rto), then design to meet them.

compliance frameworks you will meet iso/iec 27001: an information security management system, certified by audit. soc 2: an auditor's report on a service organisation's controls, common with us customers. pci dss: rules for handling payment card data (see payment gateways ). data protection law: the gdpr in the eu, the uk gdpr, india's digital personal data protection act, and others where your users live. compliance is not security. a certificate shows controls existed when audited; good engineering keeps them working every day.

practise it: seven security drills the security track in the labs turns the basics on this page into short drills, each in python and java: broken code from a real kind of breach, with tests that fail until you fix it. one shared standard states the seven rules once, as a review checklist, as a block to paste into a coding agent’s instructions, and as the tests that enforce both. drill you learn owasp top 10:2025 the file anyone could read resolve a path, then check it is still inside the folder a01 the order that was not yours check access on every object, not only at login a01 the comment that ran code encode output; never build markup by joining strings a05 the password stored the fast way slow, salted password hashing; constant-time compare a04 the reset link you could guess secure randomness, single use, expiry a04, a07 the secret in the log allow-list what you log; redact the rest by name a09 the field nobody meant to change allow-list what a request may change a08

c.h: Security checklist for a pull request
c.x: security checklist for a pull request is every new endpoint authenticated, and does it check ownership of each object? is all input validated, and every query parameterised? any new secret? is it in the secret manager, not in code or config? any new permission or iam role? is it the narrowest that works? does anything new get logged that should not be (tokens, personal data)? new dependency: maintained, licensed acceptably, no known cves? what happens on error: does it fail closed? is there a test that proves the forbidden case is refused?

when something goes wrong contain: revoke the leaked key, disable the account, block the ip, take the endpoint down. preserve evidence: keep logs and snapshots before cleaning up. assess: what was accessed, since when, whose data. notify: security lead, then customers and regulators as the law requires and within its deadlines. fix the cause and add a guard (test, policy, alert) so it cannot recur.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation spot phishing; use a password manager and passkeys parameterise every query; never commit secrets check that users can only reach their own data apply the pr security checklist 2 practitioner hash passwords correctly and run containers to the restricted profile implement oauth 2.0 / oidc with a provider and validate tokens properly use least-privilege iam and a secret manager fix findings from sast, sca and image scans 3 senior threat-model a system and turn threats into tests design authentication, authorisation and audit for a product respond to and contain a security incident 4 expert own the security architecture and policies across teams lead compliance (dpdp, gdpr, soc 2) and external testing build a security culture and secure-by-default platforms each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

c.h: One idea underneath: a key pair
c.x: one idea underneath: a key pair two keys, made together. the public key can be shown to anyone. the private key never leaves its owner: not in email, not in a ticket, not in a repository. encrypt: anyone with the public key can encrypt a message, but only the holder of the private key can decrypt it. sign: the private key signs, and anyone with the public key can check that signature. this is how a server proves who it is, how an ssh key logs you in, and how a commit is marked as yours. if this is true for you key type it leans towards ( analysis ) a new ssh key for you or a service ed25519: the type github’s own instructions generate a legacy system that does not support ed25519 rsa, 4096 bits, as github suggests for that case a tls certificate for a website or service ecdsa (for example p-256) or rsa; check what your clients and ca support you want the key to need a hardware token a security-key type such as ed25519-sk

what a certificate is a certificate authority (ca) stores, signs and issues digital certificates. a certificate certifies that a public key belongs to the named subject, so others can rely on it. web certificates use the x.509 format (rfc 5280). the fields you will read most: subject and subject alternative name (san): who it is for. clients match the hostname against the san. issuer: the ca that signed it. validity: not before, not after. public key, and the issuer’s signature over all of the above.

the chain of trust your operating system or browser ships a store of trusted root certificates. roots sign intermediate cas, and intermediates sign the leaf certificate on your server. a client validates the chain from the leaf up to a root it already trusts. a certificate chain of trust three boxes left to right: a root ca certificate, which is self-signed and already in the client's trust store; an intermediate ca certificate, signed by the root; and the leaf certificate for the server's name, signed by the intermediate. the server sends the leaf and the intermediate. the client checks each signature back to the root it already trusts. root ca self-signed signs intermediate ca signed by root signs leaf certificate cn / san: shop.internal sent by the server already in the client’s trust store the client validates each signature back to the root the chain of trust. the server sends its leaf certificate and the intermediate; the client already holds the root. a missing intermediate breaks the chain. analysis: the server must send its leaf and the intermediates; the client already has the root. a missing intermediate is a common cause of “works in my browser, fails in my code”, because some clients fetch a missing intermediate themselves and many libraries do not.

c.h: A certificate signing request (CSR), step by step
c.x: a certificate signing request (csr), step by step a csr is the message you send a ca to apply for a certificate. rfc 2986 defines it in three parts: the request information (your name, your public key and any attributes), a signature algorithm, and a signature over the request information made with your private key. that signature proves you hold the private key, which never goes to the ca. # 1. make a private key and a csr, with the names the certificate must cover openssl req -new -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:p-256 -noenc \ -keyout server.key -out server.csr \ -subj "/cn=shop.internal" \ -addext "subjectaltname=dns:shop.internal,dns:api.shop.internal" # 2. check it before you send it openssl req -in server.csr -noout -verify # certificate request self-signature verify ok openssl req -in server.csr -noout -text # read the subject and the san # 3. send server.csr (never server.key) to the ca; it returns server.crt # 4. read what came back, and check it matches your key openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectaltname openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256 openssl pkey -in server.key -pubout | openssl sha256 # the two hashes must match

c.h: Your own CA, for a lab or internal services
c.x: your own ca, for a lab or internal services # a root ca (keep ca.key offline in real use) openssl req -x509 -new -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:p-256 -noenc \ -keyout ca.key -out ca.crt -days 365 -subj "/cn=lab root ca" # the ca signs the csr from the card above, keeping its san openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -ca ca.crt -cakey ca.key -cacreateserial \ -out server.crt -days 90 -copy_extensions copy # validate the chain, as a client would openssl verify -cafile ca.crt server.crt # server.crt: ok these commands were run with openssl 3.0.13 . -copy_extensions on openssl x509 -req is documented in the 3.x manual; on an older openssl, put the san in an -extfile instead. a private ca is trusted only by machines you configure to trust it; for anything the public reaches, use a public ca.

getting certificates automatically: acme acme (rfc 8555) is a protocol a ca and an applicant use to automate proving control of a domain and issuing the certificate. let’s encrypt uses it so a server can obtain browser-trusted certificates without human intervention. its default certificates are valid for 90 days. so renewal must be automatic ( analysis ): a 90-day certificate renewed by hand will expire on someone’s holiday.

c.h: Both sides show a certificate: mTLS
c.x: both sides show a certificate: mtls in mutual tls the client also presents a certificate, so each side proves who it is. service meshes issue and rotate these workload certificates automatically; see service mesh & istio .

c.h: The errors you will meet, and what they mean
c.x: the errors you will meet, and what they mean the message (from openssl) what it usually means what to check ( analysis ) unable to get local issuer certificate the client cannot build a chain to a root it trusts is the server sending its intermediate? does the client trust the root (a private ca must be added to its trust store)? hostname mismatch the name you connected to is not in the certificate the san list, not just the subject’s common name certificate has expired now is past the “not after” date renewal automation; and the clock on the client the two public-key hashes above differ the certificate was issued for a different private key which key made the csr each message was produced for real: a leaf checked without its intermediate, the same certificate checked for a name not in its san, and checked at a date after it expires ( openssl verify -attime ). supplying the intermediate with -untrusted int.crt turned the first into ok.

ssh keys # make a key pair (github's own instruction); set a passphrase when asked ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -c "your_email@example.com" # its fingerprint: what you compare when someone asks "is this your key?" ssh-keygen -lf ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub # first connection: compare the fingerprint shown with the one the service publishes ssh -t git@github.com your public key goes on the server, in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (a default file sshd checks; the authorizedkeysfile setting controls which), or into github’s settings. the private key stays on your machine. ssh-agent holds your private keys for the session, so a passphrase-protected key is unlocked once rather than for every connection. ~/.ssh/known_hosts records the host key of every server you have connected to. if a host’s key ever changes, ssh warns and disables password authentication, to prevent server spoofing or man-in-the-middle attacks. when that warning appears ( analysis ): find out why the key changed (a rebuilt server, a new load balancer) before you remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -r host . deleting the line to make the warning go away defeats the check.

c.h: Git: signing commits with your SSH key
c.x: git: signing commits with your ssh key git config --global gpg.format ssh git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub git config --global commit.gpgsign true # sign every commit # to verify locally, list the keys you trust echo "you@example.com $(cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub)" >> ~/.ssh/allowed_signers git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedsignersfile ~/.ssh/allowed_signers git verify-commit head # good "git" signature for you@example.com with ed25519 key sha256:... why sign: anyone can set user.email to any address. a signature that verifies shows the commit came from the holder of that key. github marks commits signed with gpg, ssh or s/mime as verified when it can check the signature, so add the key to your account as a signing key too. authentication and signing are separate: the same ssh key can let you push and sign your commits, but github registers it for each purpose separately: to use one key for both, you upload it twice. everyday git commands are on devops .

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: automate every certificate’s renewal, keep private keys where they were made, and sign your commits. each removes a way to be surprised: an expiry, a leaked key, or a commit that only claims to be yours. the other view: some systems cannot automate renewal (older appliances, devices in the field, partners who install certificates by hand), and for them short lifetimes add work and risk. commit signing adds setup for every engineer and machine; some teams rely on protected branches and reviewed pull requests instead.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain a key pair: what the public key and the private key are each for read a certificate's subject, san, issuer and dates make an ssh key and add its public half to a server or github 2 practitioner make a csr with the right san and check it before sending fix a missing intermediate, a hostname mismatch and an expired certificate sign git commits with an ssh key and verify them 3 senior run a private ca for internal services, and know its limits automate certificate renewal with acme set up mtls between services 4 expert set an organisation's key and certificate policy plan certificate and key rotation without outages design trust for partners and devices that cannot automate each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

c.h: What the law asks of a system
c.x: what the law asks of a system the eu’s general data protection regulation (gdpr) gives people rights over their data, including access to it, a portable copy, erasure under certain circumstances, and a challenge to decisions made solely by an algorithm. its principles include purpose limitation, data minimisation, storage limitation, and integrity and confidentiality. it also governs moving personal data outside the eu and eea. analysis: for engineers, each right becomes a capability the system must have: find everything about one person, export it, delete or anonymise it, and explain an automated decision. a design that cannot find all of one person’s data cannot honour any of these.

where personal data ends up analysis. in a service architecture it is rarely only in the service that owns it: each service’s own database, and the events it publishes. caches and search indexes built from those events (see caching and rag ). analytics and warehouse copies, and exports to partners. logs and traces that captured a field they should not have. backups of all of the above. keep a data catalogue: which service holds which personal fields, why, and for how long. it is the map every request below depends on.

c.h: Keep less of it, in fewer places
c.x: keep less of it, in fewer places data minimisation: collect and copy only what the purpose needs. tokenisation: replace a sensitive value with a token that has no meaning of its own and maps back only through the tokenisation system. services pass the token around; the real value lives in one place. pseudonymisation: transform data so it cannot be tied to a person without additional information, such as a key; the gdpr’s definition (article 4(5), as summarised by wikipedia) requires that information to be kept separately. tokenisation and encryption are both examples. anonymisation: remove what identifies people, so they can no longer be identified, directly or indirectly. combining the data with other datasets can sometimes undo it.

erasure meets retention erasure is a right to request deletion on certain grounds, and it is limited: it applies only under certain circumstances, and wikipedia notes it was made more limited than the earlier “right to be forgotten” proposal. the sources behind this page do not list the exceptions, so read article 17 itself. systems also have their own retention rules: microsoft documents, for example, that some system-generated logs are kept under its service retention policies and are not removed by a data subject delete request. analysis: the common engineering case is a request to delete data that another rule requires you to keep, such as a financial record. the usual pattern is to delete what you may, pseudonymise or anonymise what you must keep, restrict who can read it, and record which rule applied and when the kept data will go. which rule wins is a legal decision; the system’s job is to make either answer possible.

deleting across services analysis: one way to do it. record the request in one place that owns it, with an id and the time it arrived. publish one event , such as customererasurerequested , keyed by the customer, so every service that holds their data hears it (see kafka ). each service acts and confirms: it deletes or anonymises its data, then publishes its own confirmation. make each step idempotent, because the event may arrive twice. track until everyone has confirmed, chase the ones that have not, and only then report the request as done. derived copies follow: rebuild or purge caches and search indexes, and stop the person reappearing from a later replay of old events. analysis: this is a saga with no compensation step, because deletion cannot be undone (see architecture ). the hard parts are the services nobody listed in the data catalogue, and old events that would re-create the data if replayed.

the steps, drawn deleting a customer's data across services one way to do it, numbered. 1: the erasure request is recorded in the service that owns it, with an id and a time. 2: it publishes one event, customererasurerequested, keyed by the customer. 3: each service that holds their data deletes or anonymises it, idempotently, and publishes a confirmation. 4: the owner tracks the confirmations and chases the missing ones. 5: only when every service has confirmed is the request reported done, and caches and search indexes are purged too. erasure service records the request 1 event erasurerequested 2 orders support marketing 3 track 4 5: done only when all confirm; purge caches and indexes too the steps above as a picture. deletion cannot be undone, so this is a saga with no compensation: the hard part is the service nobody listed, and old events that would bring the data back if replayed.

backups and crypto-shredding crypto-shredding makes encrypted data unusable by deleting or overwriting its encryption key. it helps where the data itself is hard to reach, such as backups and copies spread across systems, because only the key needs destroying. analysis: encrypt each person’s sensitive fields with a key of their own. if no copy of that key survives (key backups, caches) and the encryption holds, destroying it makes those fields unreadable everywhere, backups included. the cost is managing many keys, and losing a key by mistake loses the data.

c.h: Keeping data in the right place
c.x: keeping data in the right place data residency is where the data is actually stored; data localisation is a requirement that it be stored within a given region. the gdpr governs transfers of personal data outside the eu and eea, so where you store and process it is a design decision, not only an operations one. analysis: choose regions per market, route each customer to their region, and check where logs, backups and support tools copy the data too (see gcp vs aws vs azure for regions).

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) many services need to refer to a person but few need the actual value tokenisation, with the real values in one vault analysts need the data’s shape, not who it describes anonymisation before it reaches the warehouse you must keep a record but stop it pointing at a person pseudonymisation, with the key held separately and access restricted data sits in backups or systems you cannot edit row by row crypto-shredding with per-person keys personal data spans many services owned by different teams an erasure event, confirmations from each service, and one tracker customers in several jurisdictions regional deployments, with routing and residency checked for logs and backups too

prove it test deletion in ci: create a person, erase them, and assert they are gone from every store you list. audit access: who read which personal data, when, and why, with a correlation id across services. report: how many requests, how long each took, and which services were slowest to confirm. this card is analysis : these are practices, not legal requirements quoted from the regulation.

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: design for erasure from the first service, with a data catalogue, tokens instead of copies, and an erasure event every service must handle. retrofitting it across dozens of services is harder than building it in. the other view: early on, a small team may keep personal data in one service on purpose, so deletion stays a single query, and add tokenisation and events only when the data starts to spread. building the full machinery before the system needs it has a cost too.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation list where personal data ends up in a service architecture explain tokenisation, pseudonymisation and anonymisation name the rights a person has over their data 2 practitioner keep a data catalogue of personal fields per service build an erasure event that every service handles idempotently test deletion end to end in ci 3 senior design for erasure and legal retention together use crypto-shredding for backups and copies plan regional deployments for data residency 4 expert set an organisation's personal-data architecture and standards work with legal and the data protection officer on retention rules audit and report on data subject requests across systems each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

how real attacks unfold mitre att&ck is a public knowledge base of attackers' tactics and techniques, based on real-world observations. its enterprise matrix (version 20.1) groups what attackers do into 15 tactics, roughly in the order an intrusion progresses: reconnaissance → resource development → initial access → execution → persistence → privilege escalation → stealth → defense impairment → credential access → discovery → lateral movement → collection → command and control → exfiltration → impact attackers rarely need anything clever. a stolen password, an unpatched server, a misconfigured bucket or a convincing email is usually enough to start. every step is a chance to stop them. defence is not one wall; it is noticing and blocking at many of these stages. use it practically: for each system you own, ask which techniques would work against it, and whether you would see them.

c.h: A brief history of attacks, and what everyone should do
c.x: a brief history of attacks, and what everyone should do security is not only a job for specialists. look at how some of the best-known attacks got in, and most began with something ordinary: software not updated, a message someone trusted, a password with nothing behind it, or a supplier everyone relied on. those are things everyone can do something about. year attack how it got in what it did 1988 morris worm holes in common unix programs (sendmail and finger); it copied itself from machine to machine across the early internet one of the oldest worms spread over the internet, and the first us felony conviction under the 1986 computer fraud and abuse act 2000 iloveyou an email attachment that seemed to come from someone you knew, then mailed itself to everyone in your address book infected an estimated 10% of internet-connected computers; about $10 billion of damage 2003 sql slammer a bug in microsoft sql server whose fix had been released six months earlier, but not applied most of its 75,000 victims were infected within 10 minutes 2010 stuxnet typically an infected usb drive, crossing into machines that were not on the internet; four previously unknown flaws damaged equipment in iran’s nuclear programme: code causing physical harm 2014 heartbleed a missing length check in openssl, a library much of the web uses for encryption; in the code since 2012 a fix came out the day it was disclosed; every site using the library had to update 2017 wannacry a windows flaw microsoft had patched on 14 march 2017; the attack began on 12 may 2017 encrypted files on more than 300,000 computers in 150 countries and demanded bitcoin 2017 equifax a website still running an old version of apache struts with a known flaw records of 147.9 million americans, 15.2 million british and about 19,000 canadian citizens 2020 solarwinds a widely used it management product, compromised in the supply chain, then installed by its customers thousands of organisations, including parts of the us federal government; undetected for months 2021 colonial pipeline a compromised password for an inactive vpn account that did not have multi-factor authentication the company halted its fuel pipeline to contain the ransomware, and paid the ransom 2021 log4shell a flaw in log4j, a java logging library used almost everywhere; unnoticed since 2013 rated 10, the highest cvss score; potentially hundreds of millions of devices 2024 xz utils backdoor a backdoor added on purpose to open-source compression software by a contributor using the name “jia tan” found by a developer, andres freund, before the affected versions were widely deployed to production systems; rated 10.0 the pattern ( analysis ): four ways in keep coming back. unpatched software (slammer, wannacry, equifax), where the fix existed before the attack. people tricked (iloveyou, and phishing in general). passwords alone (colonial pipeline). trusted suppliers and shared code (solarwinds, heartbleed, log4shell, xz utils), where one weak link reaches everyone who uses it. habit what to do which attacks it would have helped against multi-factor sign-in turn on multi-factor sign-in (a code, an app prompt or a security key, as well as the password), most of all for email, banking and work accounts colonial pipeline: one password was enough unique passwords use a different password everywhere, kept in a password manager, so one leaked password does not open your other accounts leaked passwords: wikipedia says the one used at colonial pipeline was likely found on the dark web updates install updates promptly, and turn on automatic updates for your devices and apps sql slammer, wannacry and equifax: fixes were available beforehand check the unexpected be suspicious of the unexpected: an attachment, a link, an urgent request for money or a password. check by another route (call the person, open the site yourself) before acting iloveyou, and phishing generally backups keep backups, with at least one copy that is not always connected ransomware such as wannacry. wikipedia cites a 2020 survey in which 56% of ransomware victims got their data back from backups, against 26% who paid; newer ransomware also threatens to leak data, which backups do not prevent remove the unused remove what you no longer use: old accounts, apps, browser extensions, devices still signed in colonial pipeline: the account was inactive unknown usb drives do not plug in unknown usb drives, and do not lend yours to unknown machines stuxnet crossed into machines that were not on the internet this way report quickly report quickly if you clicked something, or something feels wrong. early reporting is what limits the damage, and nobody should be blamed for it solarwinds stayed hidden for months if you build software , the same four ways in apply to your systems: keep dependencies updated and know what you ship ( quality attributes , the vulnerability loop), check access on every object, and never log secrets ( security , and the security drills in the labs ). our view: most of the damage in this history came through ordinary doors that ordinary habits close, so the basics above are worth more to most people than any specialist tool. the other view: some attacks, such as stuxnet or the xz backdoor, were built by well-resourced attackers that no personal habit would stop; defending against them is the work of vendors, open-source maintainers and governments, and blaming individuals for those would be unfair. sources: wikipedia’s articles on each attack in the table, and on multi-factor authentication , phishing and ransomware . we could not read the uk ncsc’s or the us cisa’s advice pages from this environment.

defence in depth identity first: strong, phishing-resistant sign-in, least privilege, and removing access people no longer need. keep things patched and known: you cannot protect what you do not know you have. keep an inventory of systems, software and data. segment: a breach in one place should not open everything else. assume breach: design so that one compromised laptop, account or service does limited damage. back up, offline: see "backups and ransomware" on the security page.

detect and respond collect the right signals: sign-ins, admin actions, process and network activity, cloud audit logs. detection is a craft: write rules for behaviour attackers cannot easily avoid, test them, and tune out noise, so real alerts are not drowned. have an incident plan before you need it: who leads, who decides, how you contain (isolate a machine, revoke a credential), how you communicate, and when you call in help or the authorities. learn without blame afterwards, and fix the root cause, not just the symptom.

the people and roles blue team / security operations (soc): watch, detect and respond. red team and penetration testers: attack, with written permission, to find weaknesses first. purple teaming: both sides together, turning each attack into a detection. application and cloud security engineers: help builders get it right from the start (see security ). governance, risk and compliance: policies, audits and standards (see "compliance frameworks" on the security page). threat intelligence: who is attacking whom, and how.

ethics and the law only test systems you own, or have written permission to test. scanning or probing someone else's systems without permission is illegal in many countries, whatever your intent. practise legally: deliberately vulnerable training apps, capture-the-flag events and your own home lab . report what you find responsibly: through the organisation's security contact or vulnerability disclosure programme, and give them time to fix it. security is a team sport. our view: much of the defence is ordinary engineers who patch, review, log, ask "what if this is stolen?", and report mistakes quickly.

c.h: Judging a cloud provider’s security: the Cloud Security Alliance
c.x: judging a cloud provider’s security: the cloud security alliance the cloud security alliance (csa) is a not-for-profit organisation, formed in 2008, that promotes security best practice for cloud computing. three of its outputs come up whenever a team chooses or audits a cloud service: name what it is cloud controls matrix (ccm) a framework of security controls for cloud providers and their customers, grouped into domains. providers use it to evaluate and document their controls. consensus assessments initiative questionnaire (caiq) questions built on the ccm that a customer or auditor may ask a provider. a provider answers it to document how it complies with the csa’s best practices. in ccm version 4 the questionnaire and the matrix were combined. star (security, trust, assurance and risk) registry a free public registry, launched in 2013 with the british standards institution, where providers publish their csa assessments. star level 1, self-assessment: the provider publishes a completed caiq or a report documenting its compliance with the ccm. it is free and open to any provider. star level 2, third-party assessment: an independent auditor checks the controls. star certification builds on the iso/iec 27001 management system standard plus the ccm; star attestation is a soc 2 type 2 audit with the ccm’s criteria added. continuous monitoring: google describes star as a three-step programme of self-assessment, third-party audit and continuous monitoring. one microsoft page calls this level 3; two other microsoft pages list only two levels. the matrix, the questionnaire and even the number of levels differ between sources: microsoft’s own pages give 16 or 17 ccm domains, “more than 140” or “more than 250” caiq questions, and two or three star levels, so check which version an assessment used. analysis: for an engineer, a provider’s star entry answers part of a supplier review without a new questionnaire, and the ccm is a checklist for your own side of the shared responsibility too. a self-assessment is the provider’s own word; a level 2 report is an auditor’s, and its scope (which services and regions) is what we would check first. the other way to look at it: a detailed level 1 answer on the exact control you care about can tell you more than a broad level 2 certificate that does not cover your service.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain how a typical intrusion unfolds spot phishing and report incidents quickly know that you only test systems you may test 2 practitioner map your system's exposure to common attacker techniques log the signals an investigation needs follow the incident plan during an incident 3 senior write and tune detections; run a tabletop exercise lead containment and recovery in an incident design defence in depth for a product 4 expert own the organisation's security operations and incident response run red, blue and purple team programmes build a security culture across teams each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

why agency changes the risk owasp’s top 10 for llm applications (2025 edition) puts it plainly: the impact of a successful prompt injection depends largely on the business context and on how much agency the model has . a chatbot that can only answer can be made to say something wrong. an agent with tools can be made to do something wrong: send data, change records, run commands. owasp calls the vulnerability that lets damaging actions happen excessive agency , and names three root causes: excessive functionality: tools the task does not need, such as a document reader that can also delete documents. excessive permissions: a tool connected to other systems with more rights than it needs, such as write access where read access would do. excessive autonomy: high-impact actions taken without anyone checking them. the trigger does not have to be an attacker: owasp lists hallucination from a poorly engineered prompt or a weak model alongside prompt injection, a compromised tool and, in multi-agent systems, a compromised peer agent.

prompt injection direct: the user’s own input changes the model’s behaviour, deliberately or by accident. indirect: the instructions arrive inside content the agent reads: a web page, a file, an email, a tool’s output. owasp’s example is a user asking for a web page summary, where hidden instructions on the page make the model insert an image link that sends the private conversation to an attacker’s url. invisible: injected text does not need to be readable by people, only parsed by the model, and multimodal models can carry it in images. jailbreaking is a form of prompt injection that makes the model ignore its safety rules altogether. where prompt injection enters an agent a data-flow diagram. a user sends a request to the agent, a process combining the model and its loop. inside a dashed trust boundary are the agent, its tools (also a process) and its context store. the agent calls tools; tools act on external systems and fetch untrusted content such as web pages, emails and files. that content returns through the tools as tool output, into the agent and its context: this is where injected instructions enter. controls: least privilege on tools, human approval for high-impact actions, and authorisation in the external systems. trust boundary: your application user request agent model + loop tool calls tools context / memory actions external systems authorise here, not in the model fetch untrusted content web, email, files injected instructions return as tool output and enter the agent and its context least privilege; approve high-impact a threat-model data-flow diagram of an agent: external entities (user, external systems, untrusted content) as rectangles, the agent and its tools as processes (circles), its context as a data store, and the trust boundary dashed. anything a tool returns is untrusted input to the model. owasp says it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention exists, given how models work, and that rag and fine-tuning do not fully mitigate it. so the controls below aim to limit the damage an injection can do.

the risk lists, by name owasp top 10 for llm applications, 2025: prompt injection sensitive information disclosure supply chain data and model poisoning improper output handling excessive agency system prompt leakage vector and embedding weaknesses misinformation unbounded consumption (including “denial of wallet”)

agent-specific risks: owasp’s agentic draft owasp’s agentic security initiative has a first public draft of a top 10 for agentic applications in its repository. it is a draft, so the names and order may change (owasp’s website, which may carry a later version, could not be reached when this page was checked), but it shows where the risks go beyond a single model call: risk in the draft’s words, roughly agent behaviour hijack manipulating an agent’s goals or plans towards the attacker’s aims tool misuse and exploitation tricking an agent into using its tools in harmful or unintended ways identity and privilege abuse impersonating agents, or escalating access through identity weaknesses agentic supply chain insecure models, agents, tools or artefacts unexpected code execution unsafe code run through the agent’s behaviour memory and context poisoning corrupting what the agent remembers, so later decisions go wrong insecure inter-agent communication poisoned messages or abused protocols between agents cascading failures a fault or hallucination in one agent spreading through others human-agent trust exploitation exploiting over-trust or approval fatigue in the people overseeing agents rogue agents malicious or compromised agents acting on their own

c.h: Tools and MCP: where the access lives
c.x: tools and mcp: where the access lives the model context protocol’s own security best practices name attacks that come from connecting agents to tools: confused deputy: a program tricked into misusing its own authority on behalf of someone with fewer rights. in mcp, a proxy server in front of a third-party api can be abused to get authorisation without the user’s consent. token passthrough: an mcp server that accepts a token not issued to it and forwards it downstream. the guidance is blunt: mcp servers must not accept tokens that were not explicitly issued for them. local server compromise: a local mcp server is a program running on your machine with your rights. before a one-click setup runs one, the client must show the exact command, mark it as dangerous and ask for approval; it should also run servers in a sandbox with minimal privileges. broad scopes: a token granted every scope up front turns one leak into access to everything. the guidance is progressive, least-privilege scopes. more on the protocol, and on checking a server before you install it, is on mcp .

controls that limit the damage drawn from owasp’s mitigations for prompt injection and excessive agency: control what it means in practice fewer, narrower tools offer only the tools the task needs, each with only the functions it needs. prefer a “write this file” tool over an open-ended “run a shell command” one. least privilege give tools the smallest rights in downstream systems, such as read access to one table. keep the application’s own api tokens in the application, which makes the calls, and out of the model’s prompt and context. act as the user run actions in the context of the user they are for, with that user’s permissions, for example through oauth with the minimum scope. complete mediation authorise every request in the downstream system, not by asking the model whether an action is allowed. human approval require a person to approve high-impact actions before they happen. mark untrusted content separate and label external content so it has less influence. detection services can help: microsoft’s prompt shields, for example, scan user prompts and documents for attack patterns. microsoft notes the models are trained and evaluated mainly on english, so test them with your own attacks. treat output as untrusted validate and encode what the model produces before it reaches a browser, a shell, a query or another system (owasp’s improper output handling). log, limit, test log tool calls, rate-limit actions so monitoring can catch problems before the damage grows, and red-team the agent as an untrusted user. tools apply these too. claude code’s security documentation, for example (anthropic’s description of its own product), lists a permission system that asks before sensitive operations, approval for commands that fetch from the web, a trust dialog for a new folder, a separate approval prompt for mcp servers in a project’s .mcp.json , and sandbox network isolation.

agents in an attacker’s hands in november 2025 anthropic reported disrupting an espionage campaign it assessed, with high confidence, to be run by a state-sponsored group using its claude code tool. anthropic said it believes this is the first documented case of a large-scale cyberattack executed without substantial human intervention. by anthropic’s account: the attackers jailbroke the model by splitting the attack into small, innocent-looking tasks and telling it that it worked for a security firm doing defensive testing. the agent did reconnaissance, wrote exploit code, harvested credentials and extracted data, with tools often reached over mcp. ai did an estimated 80 to 90% of the work, with people stepping in at perhaps four to six decision points per campaign. it targeted around thirty organisations and succeeded in a small number. it was not flawless: it sometimes hallucinated credentials, or claimed to have found secrets that were in fact public. this is one vendor’s account of misuse of its own product, and it says it sees only its own platform. analysis: the lesson for defenders does not depend on the vendor: attacks can now run at machine speed, so detection and response need to be automated too. anthropic itself advises security teams to try ai for soc automation, threat detection, vulnerability assessment and incident response. the other reading: this is one vendor’s account that others have not replicated, and the share of the work an ai does may differ for other attackers and tools.

frameworks to map against owasp top 10 for llm applications and the agentic draft above, for application risks. mitre atlas (adversarial threat landscape for ai systems): a public knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques and procedures aimed at ai systems, with its data published in a public repository. att&ck, its counterpart for attacks in general, is on cybersecurity . the mcp security best practices, for anything that connects agents to tools.

choose by requirement if this is true for your agent it leans towards ( analysis ) it reads untrusted content (web, email, uploads) and can also send data or call external urls break the chain: remove outbound tools, or require approval before anything leaves it acts for many different users run each action as that user, with their permissions and a narrow oauth scope; never one shared service account with wide rights it can change money, records or infrastructure human approval for those actions, and authorisation enforced in the downstream system it writes or runs code a sandbox with restricted file system and network access, and generated code reviewed like any other it installs or connects to third-party mcp servers a list of approved servers, the exact command shown before first run, and tokens issued only for each server several agents pass work to each other treat every agent’s output as untrusted input to the next, and log the whole chain cost can grow without limit rate limits and spending caps per user and per run

prove it test with attacks: put injection payloads in documents, pages and tool outputs, and assert the agent does not act on them (see rag ). review the permission map: every tool, its rights, and who approves what. audit: every tool call logged with the user, the agent and the input that led to it. this card is analysis . only the injection testing draws on owasp, which advises testing the model as an untrusted user.

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: design every agent assuming its model will at some point follow an attacker’s instructions, because owasp says no fool-proof prevention is known. what matters is what it can do when that happens: narrow tools, least privilege, approval for high-impact actions, and authorisation outside the model. the other view: approvals and narrow tools reduce what agents are useful for, and constant prompts can wear down the people answering them. the owasp agentic draft lists exploiting “over-trust or fatigue in human oversight” as a risk, and claude code’s security documentation describes allowlisting frequently used safe commands as a “prompt fatigue mitigation”. on this view, more autonomy inside a sandbox with network isolation, plus monitoring, is worth the trade: the sandbox then carries more of the safety.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain direct and indirect prompt injection with an example name the three root causes of excessive agency treat model output as untrusted input 2 practitioner give an agent only the tools and permissions its task needs add human approval for high-impact actions check an mcp server and its scopes before connecting it 3 senior design agent actions to run as the user, with authorisation outside the model red-team an agent with injected documents and tool outputs sandbox agents that write or run code 4 expert set an organisation's policy for agents, tools and approvals map agent risks to owasp and mitre atlas plan detection and response for attacks at machine speed each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

c.h: The roles and the two standards
c.x: the roles and the two standards role is example resource owner the user who owns the data a customer client the app that wants access the web app, a mobile app, a partner's server authorisation server authenticates the user and issues tokens google identity, okta, auth0, keycloak, entra id resource server the api that accepts tokens the search api, or apigee in front of it oauth 2.0 is about authorisation : giving a client an access token to call an api on someone's behalf, limited by scopes . openid connect (oidc) adds authentication on top: an id token (a jwt) that says who the user is. "sign in with google" is oidc. access token goes to apis. id token is for the client to learn who logged in; never send it to apis as an access token. refresh token gets new access tokens without a new login.

which flow for which client client flow notes web app with a server authorisation code + pkce confidential client: the server holds the secret and tokens single-page app (browser) authorisation code + pkce, ideally through a backend-for-frontend the bff keeps tokens server-side and gives the browser a secure cookie mobile / desktop app authorisation code + pkce via the system browser public client: no secret can be kept safe in the app service to service client credentials no user; the service authenticates as itself tv, cli, device without a browser device authorisation grant user approves on another device with a code workloads on gcp service account identity (google-signed tokens) no secrets at all; workload identity federation from outside gcp implicit , password do not use deprecated by current best practice (rfc 9700, oauth 2.1 draft)

c.h: Authorisation code + PKCE, step by step
c.x: authorisation code + pkce, step by step 1. client makes a random code_verifier and its hash: code_challenge = base64url(sha256(code_verifier)) 2. browser is sent to the authorisation server: get /authorize?response_type=code &client_id=shop-web &redirect_uri=https://shop.example.com/callback &scope=openid%20profile%20email%20search.read &state=random (csrf protection) &nonce=random (id-token replay protection) &code_challenge=…&code_challenge_method=s256 3. user logs in and consents; server redirects back: https://shop.example.com/callback?code=auth_code&state=random (client checks state matches) 4. client exchanges the code at the token endpoint (from the server for a web app or bff; from the device for a mobile or desktop app): post /token grant_type=authorization_code&code=auth_code &redirect_uri=…&client_id=shop-web&code_verifier=original 5. response: access_token, id_token, refresh_token, expires_in 6. client calls the api: authorization: bearer access_token pkce proves the party redeeming the code is the one that started the flow, so a stolen code is useless.

authorisation code + pkce, drawn authorisation code with pkce a sequence diagram with four lifelines: the user's browser, the client app, the authorisation server, and the api. 1: the client makes a random code verifier and keeps it, sending only its hash, the code challenge. 2: the browser is sent to the authorisation server with the challenge and a random state. 3: the user logs in and consents. 4: the server redirects back with a one-time code and the same state. 5: the client sends the code and the original verifier to the token endpoint. 6: the server checks the verifier against the challenge and returns access, id and refresh tokens. 7: the client calls the api with the access token. browser client app auth server api make code_verifier, keep it 1 2 /authorize + code_challenge, state user logs in, consents 3 4 redirect: ?code=…&state=… 5 /token + code + code_verifier 6 access, id, refresh tokens 7 bearer access token the six steps above as a sequence diagram. the verifier never travels until step 5, and only its hash went out in step 2, so someone who steals the code in step 4 cannot redeem it.

client credentials (machine to machine) curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth2/token \ -u "$client_id:$client_secret" \ -d grant_type=client_credentials \ -d scope=orders.read # → {"access_token":"…","token_type":"bearer","expires_in":3600} curl -h "authorization: bearer $token" https://api.example.com/v1/orders/123 cache the token until shortly before it expires; do not fetch one per call. prefer private-key jwt or mtls client authentication over shared secrets where supported. on gcp, prefer service account identity over client secrets.

validating an access token (jwt) fetch the issuer's keys from its jwks url (from /.well-known/openid-configuration ); cache them. verify the signature with the key matching the token's kid ; accept only the expected algorithm (e.g. rs256 or es256). never none . check iss equals your issuer exactly. check aud contains your api's identifier. check exp (and nbf ) with small clock skew. check required scopes for the operation. then check object-level permission in your own code. # python (pyjwt) jwks = jwt.pyjwkclient("https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json") key = jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token) claims = jwt.decode(token, key.key, algorithms=["rs256"], audience="https://api.example.com", issuer="https://auth.example.com/") # spring boot resource server spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com/ spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences: https://api.example.com # quarkus quarkus.oidc.auth-server-url=https://auth.example.com/ quarkus.oidc.token.audience=https://api.example.com opaque (non-jwt) tokens are validated by calling the server's introspection endpoint (rfc 7662).

scopes, claims and roles scopes limit what a client may do on the user's behalf ( orders.read ). they are about the app, not the user's own rights. claims are facts in the token: sub (stable user id), email , groups , custom claims. roles and permissions are your application's rules. load them from your source of truth; do not trust a role the client could have influenced. key users by sub plus issuer, not by email, which can change or be reused. keep tokens small; large claim sets slow every request.

tokens in browsers and apps best for spas: a backend-for-frontend does the oauth flow and keeps tokens; the browser gets an httponly; secure; samesite session cookie. avoid localstorage for tokens: any xss can read it. short access tokens (minutes) and rotating refresh tokens that are revoked if reused. mobile: store refresh tokens in the platform keychain / keystore; use the system browser, not an embedded web view, for login. logout revokes refresh tokens and ends the provider session if needed.

common mistakes accepting a token without checking audience: a token for another api works on yours. using the id token to call apis. loose redirect uris (wildcards, prefix matching): codes get sent to an attacker. missing or unchecked state : login csrf. implicit flow or tokens in urls, where they leak through logs and referrers. long-lived access tokens with no revocation. trusting scopes alone and skipping object-level checks. rolling your own authorisation server instead of using a maintained one.

beyond the basics sender-constrained tokens (dpop or mutual tls) make a stolen token useless to anyone else. pushed authorisation requests (par) send the request parameters server to server first. token exchange (rfc 8693) for a service calling another on the user's behalf. oauth 2.1 (draft) consolidates current best practice: pkce everywhere, no implicit or password grants. oauth for ai agents and mcp servers: agents act with delegated, scoped, revocable tokens, never the user's password.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain access, id and refresh tokens and scopes protect an api with a jwt resource server configuration use the authorisation code flow with pkce through a library 2 practitioner validate tokens fully: signature, issuer, audience, expiry, scopes choose the right flow per client type store tokens safely in web and mobile apps 3 senior design identity for a product: providers, bff, service-to-service, token lifetimes review oauth implementations for the common mistakes integrate gateways (apigee) and workload identity 4 expert own identity architecture across the organisation apply advanced specs (dpop, par, token exchange) lead identity incidents and provider migrations each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
