in one paragraph data engineering is building and running the systems that move data from where it is produced to where it is used, and making it correct, current, documented and affordable on the way. source systems (apps, files, apis, sensors, public datasets) produce data in their own shapes and at their own pace. analysts, dashboards, machine-learning models, ai features and products need it in a shape they can query and trust. the data engineer owns the path between them: getting it in, keeping a faithful copy, reshaping it, checking it, delivering it, and knowing at any moment whether it is right. a pipeline that runs is not the goal. the goal is data that people can rely on without asking the data engineer first.

who does what role focus typical output data engineer ingestion, storage, pipelines, platform, reliability landed raw data, loaded tables, orchestrated jobs, a working platform analytics engineer modelling data for use, mostly in sql and dbt clean, tested, documented models and metrics data analyst answering business questions queries, dashboards, reports data scientist statistics, experiments, predictive models analyses, models, experiment results ml / ai engineer putting models into products and running them features, training and inference pipelines, evals, ai features backend engineer applications that create and serve data apis and services, the source systems data engineers read from in small teams one person covers several rows. the boundaries matter less than knowing who owns each table.

the lifecycle every pipeline follows stage question it answers on gcp, for example tab generation where does the data come from, how often, in what shape, under what licence? app databases, partner files, public mirrors, event streams — ingestion how do we get a faithful copy without losing or duplicating anything? storage transfer service, cloud run jobs, pub/sub, datastream (cdc) cloud run storage where does each version live, for how long, at what cost? gcs (files), bigquery (tables), cloud sql (serving) bigquery transformation how do raw records become clean, conformed, useful tables? dbt on bigquery, dataflow (beam), managed service for apache spark (formerly dataproc) dbt serving how do consumers read it, fast enough and safely? bigquery views, postgres for an api, looker, exports, vector indexes for ai spring running underneath every stage: orchestration ( dags ), data quality and observability, security and access, data management (catalog, lineage, retention), infrastructure as code ( terraform ), and ordinary software engineering ( tests, ci, reviews ). this stage model is adapted from fundamentals of data engineering by joe reis and matt housley, a good first book on the subject.

batch vs streaming batch: process a bounded chunk (yesterday, one file, one partition) on a schedule. simple, cheap, easy to rerun. latency of minutes to a day. streaming: process events continuously as they arrive. latency of seconds, but harder: ordering, late events, state, exactly-once. micro-batch: small batches every few minutes. often the practical middle. choose by the consumer’s need: if someone must act within seconds, streaming; within minutes, micro-batch; a report read once a day, batch. our view: most reporting is fine with daily or hourly batch, so start there. the other view: building on a stream from the start avoids a rewrite if a later use case needs seconds.

etl vs elt etl: extract, transform in a separate engine, then load the result. common when the warehouse was expensive or small. elt: extract, load the raw data into the warehouse, transform there with sql (dbt). common on bigquery and similar warehouses. our view, elt where you may: you keep the raw data, so a bug in a transform is fixed by rerunning it, not by re-ingesting from a source that may have changed or gone. the other view, when etl fits: where the warehouse is expensive or small, as in the etl bullet above, transforming first means less raw data is stored and loaded. some teams also prefer to clean or remove fields, such as personal data, before they reach the warehouse. heavy non-sql work (parsing pdfs, images, large joins outside the warehouse) still goes to an engine built for it, such as dataflow or spark.

where data lives store good at oltp database (postgres) many small reads and writes by key; serving an app warehouse / olap (bigquery) scanning and aggregating billions of rows; analytics data lake (gcs) cheap storage of any file, raw and forever lakehouse (iceberg / delta on object storage) warehouse-style tables over lake files, readable by several engines vector index similarity search for ai retrieval file formats: csv and json are easy but untyped and slow to scan. parquet and orc are columnar, compressed and typed, which suits analytics. avro suits row-by-row streams with schema evolution.

c.h: Layers: each one has one job
c.x: layers: each one has one job layer also called rule raw / landing bronze, raw byte-for-byte copy of what the source published. never edited. lets you replay everything. operational / staging odp, staging the raw data as typed tables, as published. renamed and cast, not reinterpreted. foundation / conformed silver, fdp, intermediate cleaned, deduplicated, keyed, versioned, joined to reference data. structure added once, reused by many. consumable / marts gold, cdp, marts shaped for one named use: a dashboard, an api, a model's features. derivation runs one way: each layer reads only the layer below. a product that reads from a downstream serving database creates a cycle and should be refused.

modelling basics grain: what one row means ("one order", "one order line per day"). state it for every table; most bugs are grain confusion. keys: a natural key from the source and, where needed, a surrogate key you generate. never reuse or renumber a key that others store. normalised (many narrow tables, no repetition) suits oltp. dimensional (facts plus dimensions, a star schema) suits analytics. one big table is fine on bigquery for a single use. facts are events with measures (an order, a payment). dimensions describe them (store, product, date). slowly changing dimensions: type 1 overwrites; type 2 keeps history with valid-from/valid-to rows (dbt snapshots).

properties of a good pipeline idempotent: running it twice for the same input gives the same result. overwrite a partition or merge on a key; never blindly append. incremental: processes only what is new or changed, decided from evidence (a watermark, etag or ledger), not "we visited it". backfillable: any past period can be rerun on purpose. late data aware: records can arrive after their period; reprocess a lookback window. schema-change safe: a new or renamed source column fails loudly or is handled deliberately, never silently dropped. observable: every run records what it read, wrote, skipped and failed, with counts. resumable: a failure midway restarts from where it stopped, not from zero.

data quality dimension example check completeness row count matches the source; no unexpected nulls validity dates parse; codes are in the allowed set uniqueness one row per key at the stated grain consistency every store code exists in the store table freshness newest record is within the expected age accuracy values match the source on a sample the worst quality failure is a silent one: a parse that turns bad dates into null, or a monitor that reports 0 when its source was unreachable. reject or count what you cannot read, and report "unknown" rather than a confident zero.

ingestion patterns full snapshot: copy everything each time. simple; fine for small tables. incremental by watermark: fetch rows changed since the last updated_at or id. change data capture (cdc): read the source database's change log for inserts, updates and deletes (datastream, debezium). file drops: compare source and destination listings (names, sizes, etags) and copy only the difference. events: producers publish to a queue (pub/sub, kafka); consumers process at-least-once, so handle duplicates. apis: paginate, respect rate limits, keep the raw response, and record the error body when a call fails.

governance & responsibility ownership: every table has a named owner and a description. lineage: you can say which sources feed a column and which products a change will affect. access: least privilege per dataset; serving systems get read-only access. personal and sensitive data: know where it is, mask or restrict it, honour deletion requests and legal holds. licences: respect source terms; carry attribution (for example cc-by) into every published output. retention and cost: decide how long each layer is kept and who pays for scans. contracts: agree the schema and meaning of anything another team reads, and change it on purpose.

c.h: A worked example, end to end
c.x: a worked example, end to end an online shop's orders, exported daily by its stores and served to the shop's staff through a reporting api. source: two order systems (the website and the store tills) export orders as parquet and json files to object storage, partitioned by year. files are sometimes re-exported in place. ingest (land): a cloud run job compares the source bucket's listing with the gcs landing bucket and copies only new or changed objects. it records examined, copied, already-current and failed counts. raw: the bucket keeps the originals byte for byte, so anything later can be replayed. load (raw): each landed file becomes rows in bigquery tables, with run id and load time, exactly as exported. transform (analytics): dbt cleans and conforms: parses two date formats (and rejects what does not parse), computes a stable order key, deduplicates re-exported rows, joins store reference data, and runs tests. consumable (mart): a dbt model shapes exactly what the reporting api needs, with a contract on its columns. serve: a loader upserts that table into postgres on the stable key, without renumbering existing ids that links, invoices and refunds depend on. the api reads postgres read-only. orchestrate and observe: a scheduler ticks daily; an orchestrator runs each stage when its input is ready and appends every state change to a ledger, so "what happened on 2026-09-19?" has an answer. every tab in this guide appears somewhere in that path. that is why a data engineer needs breadth.

c.h: Questions a data engineer always asks
c.x: questions a data engineer always asks what does one row mean, and what is its key? what happens if this runs twice? if it fails halfway? what does this return when the source is down, and can anyone tell that apart from "no data"? how will i know it is late or wrong before a user does? who reads this table, and what breaks for them if i change it? how much does a run cost, and what makes it grow? can i rebuild it from raw if i have to?

glossary partition: a slice of a table (by date or year) that queries can skip. watermark: the point up to which data is known to be processed. backfill: deliberately reprocessing a past period. upsert / merge: insert new rows, update existing ones, by key. lineage: the graph of which data feeds which. data contract: an agreed schema and meaning between producer and consumer. freshness: how old the newest data is. scd: slowly changing dimension, how history of descriptive attributes is kept. cdc: change data capture, streaming a database's changes. dag: directed acyclic graph, the dependency order of tasks. ledger: an append-only record of every run and state change.

choosing by situation data already in bigquery: sql or dbt first; bigframes if you need a dataframe api. do not pull it out to process it. files up to a few gb on one machine: polars or duckdb; pandas if a library you need expects it. tens to low hundreds of gb on one large machine: polars (lazy, streaming) or duckdb. beyond one machine, batch: bigquery, dataflow (beam) or spark on managed service for apache spark (formerly dataproc). streaming: dataflow (beam), flink, or kafka streams inside a service. inside a java service: plain java streams for small sets; beam for pipelines; spring batch for restartable business jobs. reading and writing parquet in python: pyarrow underneath, whatever dataframe you use on top.

validation libraries pandera: schemas for pandas and polars dataframes (types, ranges, nullability) checked in code and tests. great expectations: expectation suites and data docs for pipelines. pydantic: validating individual records and api payloads in python. dbt tests: keys, relationships and accepted values in the warehouse. jakarta bean validation: record validation in java. whatever the tool: reject or quarantine what does not parse, and count it. never coerce failures to null silently.

c.h: The same task in five libraries
c.x: the same task in five libraries count orders per store since 2020 from parquet files partitioned by year. # pandas: reads into memory, eager import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet("data/", columns=["store", "year"], filters=[("year", ">=", 2020)]) # pushdown; partition columns arrive as category out = (df.groupby("store", observed=true).size() .sort_values(ascending=false)) # polars: lazy; filters and column selection pushed into the scan import polars as pl out = (pl.scan_parquet("data/year=*/*.parquet", hive_partitioning=true) .filter(pl.col("year") >= 2020) .group_by("store").agg(pl.len().alias("n")) .sort("n", descending=true) .collect()) # duckdb: sql straight over the files import duckdb out = duckdb.sql(""" select store, count(*) as n from read_parquet('data/year=*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true) where year >= 2020 group by store order by n desc """).df() # pyspark: distributed, writes results back to gcs from pyspark.sql import sparksession, functions as f spark = sparksession.builder.getorcreate() (spark.read.parquet("gs://landing/data/") .where(f.col("year") >= 2020) .groupby("store").count() .orderby(f.desc("count")) .write.mode("overwrite").parquet("gs://out/store_counts/")) # bigquery dataframes: pandas-like code, executed inside bigquery import bigframes.pandas as bpd df = bpd.read_gbq("my-proj.analytics.orders") out = df[df["order_year"] >= 2020].groupby("store_id").size()

arrow and parquet in python import pyarrow.dataset as ds import pyarrow.parquet as pq dataset = ds.dataset("data/", format="parquet", partitioning="hive") table = dataset.to_table(columns=["order_ref", "store", "order_date"], filter=ds.field("year") >= 2020) # pushdown print(table.schema) # check types before trusting them pq.write_table(table, "out.parquet", compression="zstd", coerce_timestamps="us", # many readers expect microseconds allow_truncated_timestamps=true) timestamp units are a classic trap: parquet written with nanosecond timestamps can be read wrongly or refused by some engines, especially for dates before 1970. check the schema and write the unit the reader expects.

java options java streams and collectors for in-memory work ( java tab ). apache beam (java) for pipelines on dataflow, flink or spark. spark (java/scala) on managed service for apache spark (formerly dataproc) or databricks. spring batch for chunked, restartable jobs with skip and retry policies. parquet-java and arrow java for columnar file io. jackson (json), apache commons csv or fastcsv for text formats; stream rather than loading whole files. duckdb jdbc for sql over local or remote parquet from java.

c.h: Habits that make any library fast
c.x: habits that make any library fast columnar formats (parquet) over csv and json for anything read more than once. read only the columns and rows you need (projection and predicate pushdown). lazy evaluation (polars, spark, beam) lets the engine optimise the whole plan. no row-by-row loops ( apply , iterrows ); use vectorised expressions. right types: categoricals for repeated strings, arrow-backed strings, proper dates. partition by the common filter (date, year); avoid thousands of tiny files. stream or chunk data larger than memory. push work to the warehouse when the data is already there.

correctness traps silent type coercion: integers with nulls become floats in classic pandas; ids with leading zeros become numbers. set dtypes explicitly. date parsing: mixed formats ( dd-mm-yyyy and yyyy-mm-dd ) parse wrongly or to null; specify the format and count failures. time zones: naive vs aware timestamps compared silently. joins: duplicate keys multiply rows, just as in sql. floating-point money: use decimals or integer minor units. schema drift: a new or renamed source column must fail loudly or be mapped on purpose.

project layout & dbt_project.yml models/ staging/ stg_*.sql 1:1 with sources, rename + cast only (view) intermediate/ int_*.sql joins, dedupe (ephemeral or view) marts/ fct_* dim_* what consumers read (table/incremental) seeds/ snapshots/ macros/ tests/ analyses/ # dbt_project.yml name: shop profile: my_project models: shop: +persist_docs: {relation: true, columns: true} staging: +materialized: view marts: +materialized: table +labels: {owner: data, layer: analytics} vars: start_year: 2023

model config for bigquery {{ config( materialized = 'table', partition_by = { 'field': 'order_date', 'data_type': 'date', # date | timestamp | datetime | int64 'granularity': 'month' # day | month | year (hour too for timestamp/datetime) }, cluster_by = ['store_id', 'order_ref'], # up to 4 columns require_partition_filter = true, partition_expiration_days = none, labels = {'layer': 'analytics'}, tags = ['daily'] ) }} -- integer-range partition partition_by = {'field': 'order_year', 'data_type': 'int64', 'range': {'start': 1995, 'end': 2030, 'interval': 1}}

incremental: merge {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'merge', unique_key = 'order_id', # or a list on_schema_change = 'append_new_columns',# ignore | fail | sync_all_columns partition_by = {'field': 'order_date', 'data_type': 'date'}, incremental_predicates = [ "dbt_internal_dest.order_date >= date_sub(current_date(), interval 30 day)" ] ) }} select * from {{ ref('int_orders') }} {% if is_incremental() %} where _landed_at > (select max(_landed_at) from {{ this }}) {% endif %} incremental_predicates prunes the target side of the merge. without it bigquery scans the whole destination on every run.

incremental: insert_overwrite {% set partitions_to_replace = [ 'current_date()', 'date_sub(current_date(), interval 1 day)' ] %} {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'insert_overwrite', partition_by = {'field': 'event_date', 'data_type': 'date'}, partitions = partitions_to_replace # static: cheapest ) }} select * from {{ ref('stg_events') }} {% if is_incremental() %} where event_date in ({{ partitions_to_replace | join(',') }}) {% endif %} replaces whole partitions, no row matching. leave out partitions for "dynamic" mode: dbt finds the partitions in the new data, at the cost of an extra query.

incremental: microbatch 1.9 {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'microbatch', event_time = 'order_date', batch_size = 'day', # hour | day | month | year begin = '2023-01-01', lookback = 2, partition_by = {'field': 'order_date', 'data_type': 'date', 'granularity': 'day'} ) }} -- no is_incremental() block: dbt filters each batch for you, -- and filters upstream refs that declare their own event_time select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }} dbt run -s fct_orders --event-time-start 2024-01-01 --event-time-end 2024-02-01 dbt retry # re-runs only failed batches

taskflow dag (airflow 3) from datetime import datetime, timedelta from airflow.sdk import dag, task @dag( schedule="15 6 * * *", # cron, "@daily", timedelta, asset, none start_date=datetime(2025, 1, 1), catchup=false, # default false in 3.x (true in 2.x) max_active_runs=1, default_args={"retries": 2, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5)}, tags=["orders"], ) def orders_daily(): @task def list_new(ds=none) -> list[str]: return find_objects(since=ds) @task(retries=3) def load(uri: str) -> int: return load_to_bq(uri) @task def report(counts: list[int]): print(sum(counts)) report(load.expand(uri=list_new())) # dynamic task mapping orders_daily()

branching, trigger rules, task groups from airflow.sdk import task, task_group @task.branch def choose(**ctx): return "full_load" if ctx["logical_date"].day == 1 else "delta_load" @task(trigger_rule="none_failed_min_one_success") def join(): ... @task(trigger_rule="all_done") # always runs: cleanup, alerts def cleanup(): ... @task.short_circuit def has_work(n: int) -> bool: return n > 0 # false skips everything downstream @task_group def per_store(store: str): ...

data-aware scheduling (assets) from airflow.sdk import asset, dag, task raw = asset("bigquery://proj/raw/orders") @dag(schedule="@daily", start_date=datetime(2025,1,1)) def producer(): @task(outlets=[raw]) def load(): ... load() @dag(schedule=[raw], start_date=datetime(2025,1,1)) # runs when raw updates def consumer(): @task def build(): ... build() producer(); consumer() airflow 2.4–2.10 call these dataset ( from airflow.datasets import dataset ).

reliability checklist idempotent tasks: a rerun of the same interval gives the same result. use write_truncate on a partition ( table$20250131 ) or a merge, never a blind append. no heavy work at parse time: top-level code runs on every scheduler parse. no api calls or db queries outside tasks. small xcoms: pass uris and counts, not dataframes. deferrable operators and sensors ( deferrable=true ) free worker slots while waiting. pools cap concurrency against a shared resource: pool="bq_slots" . alert on failure: on_failure_callback in default_args . pin provider versions in your composer/requirements; operator args change between majors.

airflow 2 → 3 gotchas authoring imports move to airflow.sdk ( dag , task , asset , variable ). schedule_interval and timetable args are removed: use schedule . catchup now defaults to false . context keys execution_date , next_ds , prev_ds , tomorrow_ds are removed. bash, python and empty operators live in the apache-airflow-providers-standard package. tasks no longer get direct metadata-db access; use the rest api or the sdk. subdagoperator and slas are gone; use task groups and deadline alerts (added in 3.1, marked experimental). run ruff check --select air3 dags/ to find most of these.

the five principles principle what it says the smell it fixes ( analysis ) overdone, it becomes ( analysis ) s single responsibility a class should have only one reason to change one class that prices, saves and emails; every change risks the other two dozens of one-method classes that are hard to follow o open–closed software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification: behaviour can be extended without editing their source a growing if / switch that every new case edits extension points for variations that never come l liskov substitution a property provable about objects of a type should hold for objects of any of its subtypes a subclass that throws, or quietly changes behaviour, where the parent worked rarely overdone; the usual fix is less inheritance i interface segregation no code should be forced to depend on methods it does not use a huge interface that every implementer half-fills with stubs interfaces so small that a simple idea is spread across many d dependency inversion high-level modules should not depend on low-level ones; both depend on abstractions, and abstractions do not depend on details business logic that cannot be tested without a real database an interface for every class, each with one implementation forever where they come from: robert c. martin introduced the principles in his 2000 paper design principles and design patterns ; michael feathers coined the acronym solid around 2004. the open–closed principle is bertrand meyer’s, and the substitution principle is barbara liskov’s, from 1987, formalised with jeannette wing in 1994 (see a brief history ).

c.h: Four of them in one small example
c.x: four of them in one small example // before: one class prices, applies every rule and saves. // a new discount means editing this method again. class orderservice { long totalpence(order o) { long t = o.subtotalpence(); if (o.customer().isstaff()) t = t * 80 / 100; if (o.coupon() != null) t = t - o.coupon().valuepence(); repository.save(o); return t; } } // after: a new rule is a new class, not an edit (o). interface discount { // one method; nothing to stub (i) long apply(order o, long totalpence); } record staffdiscount() implements discount { public long apply(order o, long t) { return o.customer().isstaff() ? t * 80 / 100 : t; } } record coupondiscount() implements discount { public long apply(order o, long t) { return o.coupon() == null ? t : math.max(0, t - o.coupon().valuepence()); } } class pricing { // pricing only; saving lives elsewhere (s) private final list<discount> discounts; // depends on an abstraction, not on concrete rules (d) pricing(list<discount> discounts) { this.discounts = discounts; } long totalpence(order o) { long t = o.subtotalpence(); for (discount d : discounts) t = d.apply(o, t); return t; } } money is kept in integer pence, as on payment gateways . pricing no longer saves, so it can be tested with no database (s), and with a list of fake discounts (o, d). the order the discounts run in is now the order of the list, and it changes the answer: staff then coupon turns 1000 into 700, coupon then staff into 720. the “before” version fixed that order in code; now it is a decision to make, and test, on purpose.

liskov, the classic trap a classic textbook example. a square is a rectangle in geometry, so it is tempting to make square extends rectangle . but code that sets a rectangle’s width and then its height expects the area to be width × height. a square that keeps its sides equal breaks that expectation, so it cannot stand in for a rectangle: the subtype fails the property the caller relied on. analysis: the usual way out is fewer inheritance links, not cleverer ones: make both immutable values, or give them a shared interface with no setters.

c.h: Two rules from the Gang of Four
c.x: two rules from the gang of four “program to an interface, not an implementation.” “favor object composition over class inheritance.” both are from design patterns (gamma, helm, johnson and vlissides). dependency injection is a common way to meet them: an object receives what it depends on rather than creating it, often from a framework container. martin fowler’s article of january 2004 described it, and settled on the name after discussion with other advocates of inversion of control.

c.h: Patterns by the problem they solve
c.x: patterns by the problem they solve design patterns describes 23 patterns in three groups: creational, structural and behavioural. below is a selection of the 23. the last column is analysis . if your problem is… pattern (group) in modern java or kotlin choosing an algorithm at runtime strategy (behavioural) often just a functional interface and a lambda telling many objects when one changes observer (behavioural) listeners, events and reactive streams (see javascript for the same idea in the browser) a fixed sequence of steps where some steps vary template method (behavioural) an abstract class with hooks, or a method that takes the varying steps as functions requests as objects you can queue, log or undo command (behavioural) a record per command, handled in one place behaviour that depends on the object’s state state (behavioural) a sealed type per state and a switch over it walking a collection without exposing its structure iterator (behavioural) built in: iterable and the for-each loop adding behaviour around an object without subclassing decorator (structural) java’s i/o streams are built this way making an interface you cannot change fit the one you need adapter (structural) a small wrapper class at the edge of your code offering one simple entry point to a complicated subsystem facade (structural) a service class in front of several clients standing in for another object (access checks, remote calls, added behaviour) proxy (structural) generated by frameworks more often than written by hand treating a tree of parts the same way as a single part composite (structural) menus, file trees, expression trees building an object with many optional parts builder (creational) kotlin’s named and default arguments, or a builder for java letting a subclass or caller decide which class to create factory method (creational) a static factory method, or a function that returns an implementation exactly one instance of something singleton (creational) some consider it an anti-pattern: global state that hides dependencies and makes unit testing harder. one instance managed by a dependency-injection container avoids both

when principles and patterns hurt presumptive features: fowler’s word for code built for a feature that is not needed yet. yagni, “you aren’t gonna need it”, is the counter. kent beck’s rules of simple design, as fowler states them, in priority order: passes the tests, reveals intention, no duplication, fewest elements. anti-patterns: common but counterproductive solutions; andrew koenig coined the term in 1995, inspired by design patterns .

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: learn the principles and the common patterns well enough to name them in a review, then use one when its problem is in front of you, not to make code look professional. refactor into a pattern when the second or third variation arrives. the other view: in a large codebase shared by many teams, agreeing on patterns early keeps code consistent and saves later rewrites. and in functional styles, many patterns become plain functions and modules, so some argue solid matters less outside object-oriented code.

test yourself a class formats invoices and also sends them by email. which principle does that strain? single responsibility: it has two reasons to change, the invoice layout and the way it is delivered. every new payment method means editing the same switch . which principle, and which pattern helps? open–closed; the strategy pattern, with one implementation per payment method. a readonlylist extends list and throws on add . what is wrong? it breaks liskov substitution: code written for list that calls add fails when handed the subtype. your business logic news up a database client directly. which principle would let you test it without the database? dependency inversion: depend on an interface, and pass in a real client in production and a fake in tests. which pattern are java’s i/o streams built on? decorator: each stream wraps another and adds behaviour, such as buffering.

event-driven systems services communicate by publishing events (facts about something that happened: orderplaced , orderpaid ) to a broker. other services subscribe and react. the producer does not know or wait for its consumers. term meaning event something that happened, past tense, immutable. many consumers. command a request to do something ( loadpartition ). one handler, may be refused. broker pub/sub, kafka, eventarc: stores and delivers messages. topic / subscription where events are published / one consumer group's view of them. at-least-once the usual guarantee: a message may arrive twice. consumers must be idempotent. ordering usually not global. use an ordering key (per order, per entity) when sequence matters. dead-letter queue where messages go after repeated failures, so one bad message does not block the rest. gains: loose coupling, independent scaling, new consumers added without touching producers. costs: eventual consistency, harder debugging (no single call stack), duplicates and reordering to handle, schema changes that ripple to unknown consumers.

choreography vs orchestration choreography orchestration how each service reacts to events and emits its own. no one is in charge. a central orchestrator tells each service what to do next and tracks state. analogy dancers who each know their cue a conductor with the score good for few steps, independent teams, fan-out reactions ("on landing, also index and notify") many steps, strict order, retries, compensation, a need to answer "where is this run?" risk the overall flow exists only in people's heads; cycles and lost steps are hard to see the orchestrator is a central dependency and can grow into a god service tools pub/sub, kafka, eventarc airflow, cloud workflows, temporal, step functions, a custom orchestrator with a ledger many systems mix them: orchestration inside a bounded process (a data pipeline's stages), choreography between domains (the pipeline publishes "ready"; the search team reacts).

saga: transactions across services a distributed transaction across several databases cannot use one acid commit. a saga splits it into local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails. book a paid subscription: 1. billing: create pending invoice ↺ compensate: void invoice 2. payments: charge card ↺ compensate: refund charge 3. accounts: activate plan ↺ compensate: deactivate plan 4. email: send welcome (no compensation: an email cannot be undone, so it runs last) step 3 fails → run compensations in reverse: refund (2), void invoice (1). an orchestrated saga that fails and compensates a uml sequence diagram with four lifelines: orchestrator, billing, payments and accounts. the orchestrator asks billing to create a pending invoice, then payments to charge the card, and both succeed. it asks accounts to activate the plan, which fails. it then runs compensations in reverse order: payments refunds the charge, and billing voids the invoice. orchestrator billing payments accounts 1. create pending invoice ok 2. charge card ok 3. activate plan failed compensate, in reverse: refund charge void invoice the subscription saga above as a uml sequence diagram: solid arrows are requests, dashed arrows are replies. when step 3 fails, the orchestrator runs the compensations for steps 2 and 1, in reverse order. orchestrated saga: a coordinator runs the steps and the compensations, and stores the saga's state. easier to follow and test. choreographed saga: each service listens for the previous step's event and emits its own, including failure events that trigger compensation. compensation is a new action, not a rollback: a refund is not "un-charging". some steps (an email sent) cannot be undone, so put them last. every step and compensation must be idempotent, because messages repeat. expose intermediate states ( pending , active , cancelled ): other readers will see them.

transactional outbox problem: you update your database and publish an event. if one succeeds and the other fails, they disagree. begin; update orders set status = 'paid' where id = 42; insert into outbox (id, topic, payload, created_at) values (gen_random_uuid(), 'order.paid', '{"order_id":42}', now()); commit; -- relay process (or cdc on the outbox table) select * from outbox where published_at is null order by created_at limit 100 for update skip locked; -- publish each, then update outbox set published_at = now() where id = any($1); one local transaction makes the state change and the intent to publish atomic. the relay may publish twice; consumers dedupe by event id.

idempotent consumers -- remember what you processed, in the same transaction as the effect create table processed_events (event_id uuid primary key, processed_at timestamptz); begin; insert into processed_events values ($1, now()) -- $1: the event's id on conflict do nothing; -- if 0 rows inserted: duplicate, skip the effect update accounts set plan = 'pro' where id = $2; -- $2: the account commit; prefer naturally idempotent operations: set status = 'paid' rather than balance = balance + 10 . apis take an idempotency key header so a retried post does not charge twice. batch jobs overwrite a partition or merge on a key.

cqrs & event sourcing cqrs (command query responsibility segregation): writes go to a model shaped for updates; reads come from separate models shaped for queries (a search index, a denormalised table). reads are eventually consistent. event sourcing: store the sequence of events as the source of truth; current state is derived by replaying them. full audit history and time travel, at the cost of complexity, schema versioning of old events, and snapshots for speed. append-only ledger is the lightweight version many data platforms use: one row per state change, current state from a "latest event" view. never update, never delete. use them where history and audit are the product. most crud services do not need either.

common architectural patterns pattern what it is use when / watch out layered (n-tier) controller → service → repository → database default for a service. keep controllers thin and rules in services. hexagonal (ports & adapters) domain logic in the centre; databases, apis and queues are adapters behind interfaces logic you want to test without infrastructure, or swap providers. modular monolith one deployable with enforced module boundaries our view: a sensible starting point for many teams; split later along boundaries that proved real. the other view: a team that already meets the readiness checklist on microservices (automated deploys, central logs and tracing, stable boundaries) can start with separate services and skip the later split. microservices independently deployed services owning their data many teams, different scaling needs. costs: network failures, distributed data, ops overhead. api gateway single entry point: routing, auth, rate limits many backends behind one public surface. backend for frontend (bff) a thin api per client type (web, mobile) clients with very different data needs. strangler fig route features one by one from the old system to the new replacing a legacy system without a big-bang rewrite. cache-aside read the cache; on a miss read the db and fill the cache read-heavy data that tolerates brief staleness. decide invalidation up front. circuit breaker stop calling a failing dependency for a while; fail fast prevents one slow service taking down its callers. retry with backoff + jitter retry transient failures with growing, randomised waits only for idempotent calls. cap attempts; never retry 4xx validation errors. bulkhead separate pools for separate dependencies one slow dependency cannot exhaust all threads or connections. queue-based load levelling put work on a queue; workers drain it at their pace spiky load in front of a resource with fixed capacity. sidecar a helper container next to the app (proxy, log shipper) cross-cutting concerns in kubernetes and service meshes.

consistency & trade-offs cap: during a network partition a distributed store chooses consistency (refuse some requests) or availability (answer, possibly stale). pacelc: and when there is no partition, it trades latency against consistency. strong consistency: every read sees the latest write. eventual: replicas converge, reads may lag. read-your-writes: a user always sees their own changes. exactly-once delivery is rarely real end to end; build at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing. fallacies of distributed computing: the network is not reliable, latency is not zero, bandwidth is not infinite, and the topology changes. the theory behind these, from clocks to consensus, is on distributed systems .

design review checklist who owns each piece of data, and who may write it? what happens when each dependency is slow, down, or returns garbage? which operations must be atomic, and how is that achieved across boundaries? what is retried, and is it idempotent? how do we see a request or run end to end (ids, traces, ledger)? what is the expected load, and what breaks first at 10×? how do we deploy, migrate and roll back without downtime? what is the simplest design that meets today's need?

choosing a style list the quality attributes that matter most, in order: e.g. correctness and auditability, then cost, then latency. note the constraints: team size and skills, budget, regulations, existing systems. pick the simplest style that satisfies the top attributes; resist adding patterns "for later". identify the riskiest assumption and test it with a spike or prototype. record the decision and its trade-offs in an adr.

architecture decision record # adr 0042: serve order search from postgres, not a search engine status: accepted (2026-11-12) context: 20 m orders, ~60 searches/s peak, p95 < 500 ms; team already runs postgres; no search-engine skills. decision: postgres full-text (gin) + b-tree filters on a read replica; revisit if p95 > 500 ms or relevance complaints exceed x/month. alternatives: elasticsearch (more ops, better relevance); bigquery (latency too high for interactive search). consequences: + one database to run − relevance tuning limited links: load test results, issue #… one decision per record, numbered, never edited after acceptance; supersede it with a new one. keep them in the repo.

the short answer two systems can have identical features and be completely different to live with: one is slow, leaks data and nobody dares change it; the other is quick, safe and easy to extend. the difference is in its quality attributes , also called non-functional requirements: security, performance, accessibility, observability, resilience, maintainability, privacy, cost. two habits make them real. plan them early , while they are still choices rather than rework. and write each one as an acceptance criterion with a number and a check, so that it can pass or fail like any feature. our view: a quality that has no number and no check is a wish, and wishes are the first thing cut when a deadline comes. the other view is at the end of the page.

plan early some qualities are cheap to decide on day one and expensive to add later, because they shape the structure everything else is built on: where data may live , and how long it is kept: it decides regions, backups and which services may hold personal data (see personal data across services ). who may do what : the identity and permission model runs through every endpoint and table. what you can see : request and trace ids, structured logs and an audit trail are easy to add to a new service and painful to retrofit (see observability ). accessibility : built into the design system, it is nearly free; added to fifty finished screens, it is a project (see accessibility ). how it fails : timeouts, retries and idempotency are design decisions, not patches (see microservices ). in the first week: list the qualities that matter, rank them for this system (they compete: see below), write each as a scenario with a number, and decide how each will be checked. the ranking is a decision; record it in an architecture decision record (see architecture ). from a wish to a test five steps left to right. a wish such as 'search should be fast'. a scenario that says who does what, under which conditions: 200 searches a second at peak. a criterion with a number: 95% of searches answer in under 300 ms. a check that runs automatically, a load test in ci with that threshold. a signal in production, a latency objective and an alert. below, the note that a quality you cannot measure is still a wish. a wish “search is fast” 1 a scenario 200 a second, peak 2 a criterion p95 under 300 ms 3 a check load test in ci 4 a signal objective + alert 5 plan it in the first week, check it on every change until it has a number and a check, a quality is a wish the same five steps work for security, accessibility, cost and the rest each quality goes through the same five steps. the first two happen in planning; the last three keep it true after launch.

c.h: Each quality as an acceptance criterion
c.x: each quality as an acceptance criterion the numbers below are examples to adapt , not standards; the point is the shape: a measurable statement and a way to check it automatically. quality the question an acceptance criterion, for example how it is checked security can only the right people do the right things? every endpoint except /health needs a valid token; user a cannot read user b’s orders; no known critical vulnerability in production for more than 7 days access-control tests, dependency and image scans in ci (see security ) resilience what happens when a dependency fails? if the payment provider times out, checkout answers within 3 s with a retryable error and never charges twice fault-injection tests; covered in depth on microservices , distributed systems and sre observability when it misbehaves, can we tell why, quickly? every log line carries a trace id; an alert fires within 5 minutes of the error rate passing 2% a test that forces errors and checks the alert (see observability ) accessibility can everyone use it, including with a keyboard or a screen reader? meets wcag 2.2 level aa; every journey works by keyboard alone automated checks in ci, plus a person with a screen reader for each new journey (see accessibility ) performance is it fast enough at the load we expect? 95% of searches answer in under 300 ms at 200 a second a load test with thresholds in ci (see performance , testing ) maintainability can we change it safely and quickly? modules depend only in allowed directions; the build and tests finish in under 10 minutes architecture tests (archunit and similar), build time tracked in ci (see solid & design patterns ) privacy do we keep only what we need, only where we may? a customer’s erasure request is completed in every service within 30 days an end-to-end erasure test across services (see personal data across services ) cost does it cost what we planned? cost per 1,000 orders stays under an agreed figure; an alert at 80% of the monthly budget billing export and budget alerts (see cloud cost ) a fuller vocabulary: the iso/iec 25010 quality model (2011 edition) lists eight product quality characteristics and 31 sub-characteristics, and added security and compatibility as main characteristics compared with the iso/iec 9126 model it replaced. it is a useful checklist for “what have we forgotten?”.

they compete: rank them qualities pull against each other: more security checks add latency; more resilience (replicas, retries) adds cost; heavy optimisation can hurt maintainability; strong consistency can cost availability during a partition (see distributed systems ). so rank them for each system, by requirement: if this is true for you rank higher it moves money or holds health or identity data security, correctness, auditability the public must be able to use it, whatever their abilities accessibility users wait on it in real time, or traffic comes in bursts performance, resilience many teams will change it for years maintainability, observability it runs at large scale on cloud bills you pay cost it is an experiment that may be thrown away speed of change; keep security and privacy at their minimum, never zero

secure by design secure by design treats security as a constraint on the design from the start, like performance or cost, instead of something added later through patches or extra controls. it assumes the system will be attacked, and arranges it so that a compromise is hard, contained and recoverable. the us agency cisa published “secure by design” principles for software makers in october 2023. principle what it looks like in a design assume a hostile world every input is untrusted, including from your own other services: validate at each boundary, parameterise every query least privilege each service account, database user and token can do only its job: the report service can read orders, not refund them defence in depth no single control is trusted alone: authentication at the gateway and authorisation checks in the service and row-level limits in the database small attack surface expose only what users need: no admin endpoints on the public network, unused features and ports switched off secure defaults the safe setting is the one you get without trying: private storage buckets, encryption on, multi-factor sign-in on, debug off open design, not secrecy security rests on keys and proven algorithms, not on hiding how it works (see keys, certificates & ssh ) continuous assurance controls are tested on every change and watched in production, not checked once before launch how to plan it early: threat-model the design before building (see security , “threat modelling in 30 minutes”), then turn each mitigation into an acceptance criterion and a test. for a ready-made list of verifiable security requirements, the owasp application security verification standard (asvs, version 5.0.0 , may 2025) is written exactly for this: pick the level that fits the system and use its requirements as acceptance criteria. secure by design sits beside privacy by design and zero trust, and the same habit applies to ai features (see agentic ai security ).

c.h: Vulnerabilities: a loop, not a scan
c.x: vulnerabilities: a loop, not a scan a vulnerability is a weakness that can be used to break a system’s security. most of the ones a team has to deal with are in components it did not write: libraries, base images, platforms. scanning finds them; what makes the difference is how you run the loop around the scan. the vulnerability loop a loop of six steps. know what you run: an inventory of every component, a software bill of materials. find: scanners, tests and reports from outside. identify: a cve id for the vulnerability and a cwe for the kind of weakness. prioritise: severity from cvss, likelihood of exploitation from epss, and whether your system actually exposes it. fix within the agreed time, or mitigate. verify and tell: re-scan, and disclose or notify. then back to the start, because new vulnerabilities are published every day. 1 know what you run sbom, every component 2 find scans, tests, reports 3 identify cve id, cwe type 4 prioritise cvss + epss + exposure 5 fix or mitigate within the agreed time 6 verify and tell re-scan, disclose new vulnerabilities are published every day: the loop never stops finding vulnerabilities is the easy part; scanners do it. the work is in steps 1, 4 and 5: knowing what you run, deciding what matters, and fixing it within a time you agreed in advance. term what it is cve a public id for one specific vulnerability, such as cve-2021-44228. the cve system was launched by mitre in 1999, and its ids underlie the us national vulnerability database. cwe a category of weakness (for example, improper input validation), so you can see which kinds of mistake keep recurring. cvss a 0–10 severity score from first, with bands none (0), low (0.1–3.9), medium (4.0–6.9), high (7.0–8.9) and critical (9.0–10.0). the current version, 4.0, was released in november 2023. epss also from first: the estimated probability, from 0 to 1, that a published vulnerability will be exploited in the wild. sbom a software bill of materials: the inventory of every component in what you ship, so that when a new cve appears you can answer “do we run that?” in minutes. severity is not priority. cvss measures how bad a vulnerability is in general; it is not designed for deciding what to patch first, though it is often used that way. combine it with the likelihood of exploitation (epss) and your own exposure: is the vulnerable code reachable, on the internet, holding sensitive data? agree fix times before you need them , as acceptance criteria: for example, critical and reachable within days, high within weeks, the rest in the normal update cycle. our view: the exact numbers matter less than having them written down and measured. the other view: fixed times can push teams to rush low-risk fixes to meet a clock; some prefer to triage each finding on its own exposure and set no deadline. reduce the noise at the source. fewer dependencies, slim base images and automated updates gated by tests (see security , “supply chain & ci”) mean fewer vulnerabilities to triage at all. make it easy to be told. publish how to report a vulnerability to you. coordinated disclosure, once called responsible disclosure, gives a vendor time to fix before details are published; a common industry deadline, pioneered by google, is 90 or 120 days, cut to 7 when the vulnerability is already being exploited. know your own components. without an sbom, “are we affected?” becomes a search through every repository, on the worst possible day.

c.h: Growing the architecture one slice at a time, with agents
c.x: growing the architecture one slice at a time, with agents few teams start with a clean design; most inherit code that grew. the qualities above can still be brought in step by step: one customer journey at a time, end to end, while the team keeps shipping (the strangler fig idea on architecture , rather than a big-bang rewrite). with agents now writing much of the code, each step has a second job: it gives the agent rails to work within. step what the team does why it matters more when agents write code 1. agree the words name the business capability and its terms (order, refund, shipment) and use the same names in code, tickets and conversation an agent copies whatever names it finds. a short glossary in the repository’s agent instructions (claude.md, agents.md and similar) keeps it from inventing a third word for the same thing (see agent harness ) 2. map who talks to whom draw where data flows and where trust changes: user to service, service to service, service to third party the agent itself is now on the map: what it can read, change and call is a trust boundary of its own (see agentic ai security ) 3. write the contracts down make each api, event and module interface explicit: a schema, an interface, a versioned spec a written contract is a specification an agent can build to and a contract test can hold it to; an unwritten one is a guess it will fill in (see specifications , test strategy ) 4. put the criteria in the pipeline turn the acceptance criteria above into checks that run on every change: security scans, accessibility checks, load-test thresholds, architecture tests agents produce changes faster than people can read them line by line. automated gates apply the same bar to every change, whoever or whatever wrote it, and leave reviewers the questions in the checklist above 5. make it visible add logs, metrics and traces, and set service level objectives for the journey (see observability , sre ) code nobody on the team wrote by hand is code nobody remembers; production signals are how you find out what it actually does 6. close the loop learn from incidents and telemetry, and revisit decision records when the facts change record why a decision was made, beside the code: it is what the next person, and the next agent session, reads before changing it our view: in the ai era these steps matter more, not less: the faster code is produced, the more the structure, the contracts and the gates decide whether it is any good. the other view: for a small product with one team, much of this is overhead, and a well-tested monolith with clear modules may be all the architecture it needs for years (see microservices for when splitting pays). choose the steps by the requirements in the ranking table above.

c.h: Review every change for its effect on the system
c.x: review every change for its effect on the system formatters, linters, type checkers and tests now catch most of what reviewers used to comment on, and more of the code itself is written by agents (see humans & agents ). what is left for a person is the part no tool can judge: what the change does to the system. google’s published review guide already ranks it first: the overall design is “the most important thing to cover in a review”, and a reviewer should ask whether the change makes the whole system better or more complex, and bring in someone qualified for privacy, security, concurrency or accessibility. the qualities on this page make a short checklist for any pull request, whoever or whatever wrote it: look at ask of the change purpose does the description say what changes for the user, and does the code do that and nothing else? boundaries does each rule live in the module that owns it? is any api, event or schema it changes versioned and written down? ( architecture , apis & integration ) failure what happens on bad input, a slow network or a dependency that is down? are retries safe to repeat? ( microservices ) security and privacy does it add an entry point, a permission, a secret or a new kind of personal data? does it add a dependency with known vulnerabilities? running it when it goes wrong at 3 a.m., will logs, metrics and traces show where, and can it be rolled back or switched off? ( observability ) the next change could another team, product or channel reuse this safely, or has something general been hard-wired for one case? the criteria does it still meet the acceptance criteria above: the latency, accessibility and cost numbers? is there a test that would fail if it did not? our view: leave style to the tools and spend review time on these questions; the more code agents write, the more this is the reviewer’s real job. the other view: line-by-line reading still finds bugs the checks miss, and google’s guide asks reviewers to look at every line they are asked to review. both are true; the checklist decides where the time goes first. more on the craft of review in writing & code review .

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: decide and rank the qualities in the first week, write each as a criterion with a number, and check it automatically from then on. treat security as a design constraint, and vulnerabilities as a loop with agreed fix times. the other view: some teams prefer to learn their real quality needs from production: ship something small, measure it against service level objectives (see sre ), and tighten where users actually feel pain, rather than guess numbers up front. it avoids gold-plating qualities nobody needs. it works best for performance and cost, where you can measure and adjust; it is risky for security, privacy and accessibility, where a gap can harm people before you notice it.

c.h: When code is cheap, checking it is the work: one view from industry
c.x: when code is cheap, checking it is the work: one view from industry in a november 2026 episode of the pragmatic engineer , gergely orosz talked with microsoft’s chief executive, satya nadella. the episode’s notes open with the question “what does software engineering look like when generating the code becomes cheap and verifying it is the hard part?”. several points from orosz’s summary of the conversation bear directly on the qualities on this page: topic point made in the interview what it means for qualities ( analysis ) tests models that critique generated code can reach their goal in undesirable ways, “for example, making tests pass by deleting failing tests” protect the checks themselves: a change that deletes, skips or loosens a test is a review item, whoever made it agents models are intelligent but unreliable, so treat them as “insider risks” and build a separate system to verify that agentic systems work as expected least privilege for agents, and verification that does not depend on the agent being checked (see agentic ai security ) lock-in keep the harness, memory and model decoupled to avoid lock-in, and build private evaluations to choose and upgrade models maintainability applied to ai: a boundary you can swap behind, and a test suite for the part you swap (see agent harness ) specifications specifications and verification are becoming more important acceptance criteria written before the code are the specification a person or an agent builds to (see specifications ) people microsoft and carnegie mellon university started a preceptorship, pairing experienced engineers with newer ones to build “systems thinking, taste, and judgement” the judgement this page asks for (ranking qualities, reviewing for system impact) is learned from people, not only from tools how to weigh it. it is one person’s view, given in an interview by the head of a company that sells ai tools and models, and orosz writes that “we didn’t arrive at any definite solutions” on verification. the underlying problem is not new: tests, types, reviews and staged roll-outs have always been how teams checked code they did not write themselves. what has changed is how much code arrives to be checked. our view: the qualities on this page, written as acceptance criteria and checked automatically, are the verification layer that turns cheap code into code you can trust; the cheaper the code, the more that layer is worth. the other view: some expect more of the checking itself to be done by models, critiquing code and learning from production traces; the interview treats that as promising, and also notes that it brings the problem back to verifying the models’ fixes.

c.h: From a function to a system
c.x: from a function to a system the habits that make one function good are the same ones that make a whole system good, applied at a larger scale. a clear name becomes a shared business vocabulary. a small function with one job becomes a module with one owner, so that a change stays local. checking inputs becomes security decided in the design. a useful error message becomes logs, traces and objectives that tell you what the running system is doing. our view: architecture is not a separate skill learned after clean code, but the same care carried across boundaries, failures and production. the other view: some decisions only exist at system scale (data residency, consistency across services, cost) and cannot be reached by tidying code; they need deliberate design, which is why this page starts with planning early.

practise it the labs turn several of these qualities into short, testable drills in python and java: resilience (the double charge, the retry storm, the stale read), performance (the timed data structures drills), maintainability and testability (the core and the shell), and correctness under concurrency. for security, the security drills practise seven basics, from path traversal to secrets in logs, with one standard shared by people and coding agents.

c.h: Solution architecture is not business architecture
c.x: solution architecture is not business architecture business architecture solution architecture enterprise architecture definition (sourced) holistic views of the business: capabilities, end-to-end value delivery, information and organisational structure, and how they relate to strategies, products, policies and stakeholders (wording quoted on wikipedia) a description of a discrete, focused business operation or activity and how information systems and technology support it (the open group’s definition, among several) an enterprise architecture framework is a methodology for guiding the transformation of a business from a baseline state to a target state, sometimes through several transition states the question it answers ( analysis ) what does the business do, and what must it be able to do? how will these systems change, in what order, to support that? how does the whole estate move, and what standards hold it together? typical output ( analysis ) capability maps, value streams baseline, transition and target states; interfaces; data ownership; decisions and their trade-offs roadmaps, principles, the portfolio our view: a solution architecture that only restates business capabilities, or only draws the target, is not finished. it must say how the systems change, step by step, and what runs at each step. the other view: in a small organisation one person does all three, and the lines blur; and a solution designed without the business architecture can be a fine route to the wrong place.

solution, technical and infrastructure architecture togaf, an enterprise architecture framework, models architecture in four domains: business, data, application and technology. togaf’s skills framework does not recognise a solution architect role, yet such roles are widely advertised, and the technical and infrastructure split below is common usage rather than togaf, so the same words can mean different jobs. the last column uses an invented example: keeping a shopping cart the same on every device. layer defined as (togaf, as summarised on wikipedia) decides, in practice ( analysis ) shopping-cart example ( illustrative ) business the business strategy, governance, organisation and key business processes what the business must be able to do customers expect the same cart on every device solution not one of togaf’s four domains. the open group defines it as “a description of a discrete and focused business operation or activity and how is/it supports that operation” which systems change, their interfaces, who owns which data, and the route from a to b add a cart events topic and a push gateway, in transition steps application a blueprint for the individual systems to be deployed, their interactions, and their relationship to core business processes the services and how they talk the cart service, and a backend-for-frontend that holds browser connections data the structure of the organisation’s logical and physical data assets, and the data management resources that go with them sources of truth, models, retention the cart service owns the cart; events are keyed by cart id technical (togaf: technology) the hardware, software and network infrastructure needed to support the deployment of core, mission-critical applications common usage, not togaf: many organisations split technology in two. technical: the software platform, meaning languages, frameworks, middleware and integration patterns kafka, server-sent events, the web framework infrastructure no separate togaf domain: infrastructure appears inside the technology domain’s definition common usage, not togaf: infrastructure: compute, networks, storage, hosting, regions and recovery the managed kafka cluster, load-balancer timeouts long enough for open connections, two regions our view: solution architecture cuts across the other layers. it starts from the business need, chooses the application and data changes, asks the technical and infrastructure architects for platforms that fit, and puts it all in order from a to b; gartner’s definition, which combines guidance from business, information and technical viewpoints, is similar. the other view: in organisations with strong platform teams, the solution architect mostly chooses from a catalogue that technical and infrastructure architects maintain; and in a small team one engineer holds every layer at once.

c.h: Strategic, tactical and temporary: say which one you are building
c.x: strategic, tactical and temporary: say which one you are building kind what it is for what you accept ( analysis ) when it ends ( analysis ) strategic part of the target state (b), built to last higher cost and time up front not planned; it is the destination tactical meets a real need now, inside today’s constraints (a deadline, a regulation, a contract) known shortcuts: prudent, deliberate technical debt in fowler’s terms, taken on knowingly, when the payoff for an earlier release outweighs the cost of paying it back when the strategic solution replaces it; the date and the trigger are written down temporary (transitional) exists only to help move from a to b: cartwright, horn and lewis call it transitional architecture, “software elements installed to ease the displacement of a legacy system that we intend to remove when the displacement is complete” work that will be thrown away, by design when the transition state it serves is passed analysis: the three-way split, and mapping tactical to prudent, deliberate debt and temporary to transitional architecture, are our framing, not a standard. the sources use the debt quadrant and transitional architecture, not these three labels. technical debt is ward cunningham’s metaphor (1992); fowler’s gloss is that the extra effort every later change costs because of a shortcut is the interest on the debt. sacrificial architecture (fowler) is the longer-horizon version of the same idea: deliberately accepting now that in a few years you will (hopefully) need to throw away what you are building. our view: label every component strategic, tactical or temporary, and give each tactical and temporary one an owner, an exit condition and a date. the other view: labels drift, and many “temporary” solutions become permanent; some teams refuse tactical work for exactly that reason and accept slower delivery instead.

c.h: The incremental model: A, transition states, B
c.x: the incremental model: a, transition states, b cartwright, horn and lewis, in patterns of legacy displacement , put it plainly: gradual replacement delivers benefits early and avoids the risks of a big bang, and while it runs the old and new systems operate side by side. an illustrative example, moving order handling off a legacy system: state what runs built only for this state value delivered way back a: baseline the legacy system does everything – – – transition 1 a router in front of the legacy system; all traffic still goes to legacy the router, if b will not need it a seam: you can now move traffic remove the router transition 2 new order-status service; legacy still owns the data; state changes copied to the new service the copy of events from legacy faster order tracking for customers route status back to legacy transition 3 new system owns new orders; legacy keeps old orders until they close a sync that keeps legacy reports working new orders on the new platform feature toggle sends new orders to legacy b: target new system only – legacy licence and support cost removed none needed: decommission is the last deliverable each transition state is a real production system: it must be operated, monitored and secured, and it must say which system is the source of truth for each piece of data. when you draw your own, add a “source of truth” column for each state. the example is illustrative, not a recommendation for any real system.

c.h: Short-term solutions for the transition period
c.x: short-term solutions for the transition period during the transition you need to… technique removed when ( analysis ) move features one at a time from old to new strangler fig: new pieces grow around the old system until it can be retired the last feature has moved change an interface many callers use, without breaking them parallel change (expand and contract): expand, migrate, contract the contract phase replace a component inside one codebase while still releasing regularly branch by abstraction : put an abstraction in front, build the new implementation behind it, switch the old implementation is deleted ship unfinished work safely release toggles: transitionary by nature; hodgson says they should generally not stay much longer than a week or two, though product-centric toggles may stay longer the feature is fully released change things without the old system noticing legacy mimic: the new system interacts with the legacy one so that it is not aware of any change the legacy system is gone feed the new system from the old one’s changes event interception: intercept updates to system state and route some of them to the new component the new system owns that data prove the new path under real load before users see it dark launching: call the new back end from existing traffic without users being able to tell the new path is live expose the change to a few users first canary release: roll out to a small subset before everyone rolled out to all

c.h: Choosing a migration pattern by requirement
c.x: choosing a migration pattern by requirement analysis: the rows are our mapping of requirement to pattern; the aws, wikipedia and cartwright et al. pages describe each pattern, but none of them gives this table. if this is true for the piece you are moving it leans towards its calls can be intercepted at the edge of the old system strangler fig, behind a router or gateway it sits deep inside the old system, with other code depending on it branch by abstraction (aws recommends it for components deep in the stack with upstream dependencies; it is not suitable where data consistency is involved) the new model and the old one mean different things by the same words an anti-corruption layer between them you must prove the new system gives the same answers before trusting it parallel run, comparing outputs two data stores must stay in step while both are live the transactional outbox or change data capture, not a dual write the change is low-risk and easy to reverse a canary release, then a direct cut-over analysis: most moves combine several of these. a strangler fig moves the traffic, an anti-corruption layer protects the new model, and a parallel run proves the result before the old path is switched off.

parallel run the old and new systems run side by side for an agreed period, take the same input, do the same processing, and their outputs are compared. when the new system has proved reliable, the old one is removed. cartwright, horn and lewis list it among the ways to cut over from a legacy system. the cost: running two systems at once is expensive, takes time, and can mean doing work twice. decide before you start ( analysis ): which outputs must match exactly, what tolerance applies to the rest, how long the run lasts, and which system’s answer counts while they disagree.

anti-corruption layer a mediation layer that translates one system’s domain model into another’s, so the new service is not shaped by the old one’s meanings. aws suggests it when the migrated service’s model differs from the original, when two systems with different semantics must exchange data, or when changing one to fit the other is not practical. what it costs: another component to monitor, release and run; added latency; a possible scaling bottleneck; and a single point of failure, because if it fails the service behind it is unreachable. aws says to record it as technical debt and decommission it once every dependent caller has migrated. what it buys: callers owned by other teams need not change at the same time as you.

c.h: Dual write, and the two ways out
c.x: dual write, and the two ways out a dual write is one operation that writes to two systems, such as saving to the database and then publishing an event, or writing to both the old and the new database during a migration. if one write succeeds and the other fails, the two disagree, and nothing notices unless you check. aws describes two ways out, both under the transactional outbox pattern: an outbox table, or change data capture. way out how it works fits ( analysis ) transactional outbox write the change and an outbox row in one database transaction, then publish from the outbox (see architecture ); events can arrive twice or out of order, so make the consumer idempotent your own service, where you can change the code change data capture read each committed row-level change from the database and publish it as an event. debezium does this, and only committed changes are visible, so rolled-back work never leaks out a legacy database you cannot change, or many tables at once our view: do not dual write; use one of the two above. the other view, in our experience: some teams accept a dual write for a short migration window, with a reconciliation job that compares the two stores every night, because it needs no new infrastructure. if you do, treat every mismatch as an incident, and write down the date the dual write ends.

splitting a shared database the target aws describes: database per service, where each service stores and reads only its own data, so services stay loosely coupled and each can choose its store. what it costs: cross-service transactions and queries are harder, and you run several databases. the shared-database pattern: several services use one database. aws says to avoid hot tables (single tables that several services write to) and to keep every schema change backward-compatible: drop a column or table only when no current or previous version of any service references it. aws also notes it does not reduce dependencies between teams and adds runtime coupling. queries across services: aws says that with database per service you must add another pattern for these: api composition (which cqrs can speed up) or event sourcing. analysis: a common order is: give each table one owning module while the database is still shared; stop other modules reading those tables directly, going through the owner instead; copy the data to the new store with change data capture; switch reads, then writes; and finally drop the old tables. every step before the drop can be reversed; plan the drop last, after the old tables have gone unreferenced for an agreed period.

c.h: Engineering from A to B, not just a picture of B
c.x: engineering from a to b, not just a picture of b our view: rules of thumb, not a standard. every step deploys and runs on its own, and has a way back. every step delivers something a user or the business can see, or removes a cost; otherwise ask why it is a step. data has one owner at each state. write down which system is the source of truth, and when that changes. budget for the throwaway work. transitional pieces are real engineering, then real removal. decommissioning is a deliverable, with a date and an owner, not a hope. record each choice in an architecture decision record, including which items are tactical or temporary (see architecture ).

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: a proposal that shows only the final state is a wish, not a plan. the useful document shows a, each transition state, b, what is temporary at each point and how it goes away. the other view: a clear target picture is what aligns people and wins funding, and the detailed route is often better worked out by the delivery teams as they learn; fixing every step up front can lock in a route that turns out wrong. both can hold: fix the target and the first one or two transitions, and plan the rest as you go.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation tell business, solution and enterprise architecture apart say whether a piece of work is strategic, tactical or temporary draw today's system (a) and the target (b) 2 practitioner plan transition states between a and b, each one deployable use strangler fig, parallel change or branch by abstraction for a real change write down the source of truth for each piece of data at each state 3 senior design transitional architecture and plan its removal take on tactical debt deliberately, with an owner and an exit date lead a legacy displacement without a big bang 4 expert set how an organisation plans and funds transitions, not only targets govern a portfolio of strategic, tactical and temporary work teach teams to engineer the route, not only the destination each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
