the assumptions that fail the fallacies of distributed computing are false assumptions that programmers new to distributed systems tend to make. l. peter deutsch at sun microsystems listed seven in 1994, building on earlier work by bill joy and dave lyon, and james gosling added the eighth around 1997: the network is reliable. latency is zero. bandwidth is infinite. the network is secure. topology does not change. there is one administrator. transport cost is zero. the network is homogeneous. partial failure is what makes this hard. unmesh joshi describes gray failures: a node may misbehave without going down, a network may lose a few packets or slow some messages enough that only some nodes time out, and a process may freeze (a garbage-collection pause, for example) and resume without knowing it was frozen. the cluster is then split in what it believes, with some parts stalled and others carrying on.

cap and pacelc cap (brewer’s conjecture, 2000; proved by gilbert and lynch, 2002): a distributed data store can give at most two of consistency (every read gets the latest write or an error), availability (every request to a working node gets a response, possibly not the latest data) and partition tolerance (it keeps working while messages between nodes are lost or delayed). our reading ( analysis ): partitions cannot be ruled out on a real network, so the choice is what to do during one: refuse the operation and stay consistent, or answer and risk inconsistency. pacelc adds the normal case: else , with no partition, you still trade latency against consistency. two traps: cap’s consistency is not the c in acid, and cap’s availability is not “high availability” in the everyday sense.

consistency models linearizable (herlihy and wing, 1987): operations that overlap in time still appear to take effect instantly, in a single order that respects real time. it is a strong correctness condition, and it lets a programmer reason about the system as if there were one copy of the data. eventual consistency: if no new updates are made, every read eventually returns the last value. replicas are said to converge. it is a weak guarantee, chosen for availability. base versus acid: eventually consistent stores are often described as basically available, soft state, eventually consistent, in contrast to acid transactions. weaker models in between, such as read-your-writes, are on architecture .

time and order tool what it gives you wall clock time of day. joshi notes it can jump when ntp corrects it and is not guaranteed to be monotonic, so it cannot measure a timeout; and machines’ clocks are not perfectly synchronised, so it cannot order events across them. monotonic clock the usual workaround for measuring elapsed time; joshi points out that a process pause can still distort the measurement. lamport timestamp (leslie lamport, 1978) a simple logical counter carried on messages, giving a partial order of events: if one event could have caused another, it gets the smaller number. vector clock one logical counter per process, carried on every message, so you can tell whether two events are causally ordered or concurrent. hybrid logical clock a version that increases like a counter but stays close to real date and time, so clients can ask for data “as of” a time. generation clock (also called term or epoch) a number that goes up with each new leader, so a leader that paused and came back can be recognised as out of date.

agreeing: consensus and raft consensus lets a group of machines agree on the same sequence of changes, so they can act as one replicated state machine. paxos , by leslie lamport, was first submitted in 1989 and published in 1998. raft , by diego ongaro and john ousterhout, was designed as an alternative that is easier to understand. etcd, which kubernetes uses, is built on raft. one leader at a time. each server is a leader, a follower, or, during an election, a candidate. the leader sends regular heartbeats. elections. a follower that hears nothing for its election timeout (typically 150 to 300 ms) becomes a candidate, starts a new term , votes for itself and asks the others. each server votes once per term. log replication. the leader appends each change to its log and replicates it to followers. a change counts as committed once a majority have stored it. raft server states a uml state diagram. a server starts as a follower. if it hears no heartbeat before its election timeout it becomes a candidate. a candidate that receives a majority of votes becomes the leader. a split vote starts a new term and a new election. a candidate that receives a message with a higher term becomes a follower again. follower candidate leader election timeout (no heartbeat) majority of votes message with a higher term split vote: new term raft’s server states, as a uml state diagram. a leader keeps followers in place by sending regular heartbeats; randomised election timeouts make split votes resolve quickly. raft in its basic form tolerates crashed servers, not lying ones: every node trusts the elected leader. kafka’s own metadata quorum is described on kafka .

quorums and split brain majority quorum: an update counts once a majority of nodes acknowledge it. five nodes need three, and can lose two. why a majority: two majorities always share a node, so two halves of a broken cluster cannot both make decisions. split brain: two parts of a system each believe they are in charge and change overlapping data independently, usually after a network partition. leases give a node exclusive access for a limited time; it must renew before expiry, so a crashed or paused node loses the access on its own. analysis: this is why clusters usually run with an odd number of nodes: a fourth node adds cost without letting you lose a second one. the other view: an even number is sometimes chosen when spreading nodes across zones or racks matters more than the failure count.

transactions across machines: two-phase commit two-phase commit has a coordinator ask every participant to prepare (vote), then tell them all to commit or roll back. its main weakness is that it blocks : a participant that has voted yes must wait for the coordinator’s decision, and if the coordinator fails for good, some participants never resolve, and in rare cases a person has to step in. analysis: this is why services usually prefer sagas, with a compensating step for each local transaction, over a distributed transaction (see architecture and microservices ). the other view: a saga gives up isolation between steps and needs compensation logic, so where a database or transaction coordinator already provides two-phase commit and short blocking is acceptable, it can be the simpler option.

when nodes lie: byzantine faults a byzantine fault is one where a component shows different symptoms to different observers, so others cannot even agree whether it has failed. the name comes from lamport, shostak and pease’s 1982 paper on the byzantine generals problem. byzantine fault tolerant systems can keep working with fewer than one third of their nodes faulty or malicious. analysis: inside one organisation, crash fault tolerance (raft, paxos) is usually enough. byzantine fault tolerance matters where participants may be malicious or do not trust each other. public blockchains are a related case, though wikipedia notes that their guarantees differ from classical byzantine fault tolerance (see bitcoin & blockchain ).

c.h: Living with eventual consistency: session guarantees
c.x: living with eventual consistency: session guarantees with replicas that catch up later, a user can write something and then not see it, or see a newer value and then an older one. in 1994 douglas terry and colleagues described four session guarantees : promises made to one user or one client, which are much cheaper than making every replica agree at once. guarantee the promise what goes wrong without it read your writes after you write a value, your later reads see it (or something newer) you update your address, refresh, and the old one is back monotonic reads once you have seen a value, you never see an older one a comment appears, then disappears on the next refresh monotonic writes your writes are applied in the order you made them you set a price, then correct it, and the correction is applied first writes follow reads a write you make after reading a value is applied on top of that value or a newer one a reply is stored before the message it answers common ways to provide them ( analysis ): send a user’s reads to the primary for a short time after they write; keep a user on the same replica (sticky routing); or have the client remember the version it last saw and refuse older answers. the labs drill “the stale read” ( distributed systems drills ) is the second failure above in code.

c.h: CRDTs: replicas that merge without asking each other
c.x: crdts: replicas that merge without asking each other a conflict-free replicated data type is a data structure copied across machines where any copy can be updated independently, without coordinating with the others, and the data type itself resolves any differences when the copies meet. marc shapiro, nuno preguiça, carlos baquero and marek zawirski defined the concept formally in 2011; it was first motivated by collaborative text editing and mobile computing, and is used in online chat and other systems. simple examples are a counter that only goes up (each replica counts its own increments, and the total is the sum) and a set where additions always win. our view: crdts are worth knowing because they show that “eventual” can still mean “correct”, if the data type is designed for it. the other view: many business rules cannot be expressed as data that merges automatically (a balance that must never go negative, a seat that can only be sold once), and those still need coordination or a single owner.

fencing: stopping the old leader when a leader or lock holder seems to have failed, the rest of the system cannot tell whether it has really died or is only paused, by a long garbage collection, a slow network or a suspended virtual machine. if it is only paused, it may wake up and keep writing as if it were still in charge. fencing isolates such a node from the shared resources it controlled, so it cannot do damage when it comes back. shut it out : cluster software can power the node off (known as stonith, “shoot the other node in the head”) or block its access to shared storage. make old writes harmless ( analysis ): give every new leader or lock holder a number that only goes up, have it send that number with every write, and have the storage reject any write carrying an older number than one it has already seen. the labs drill “the lock that outlived its owner” ( distributed systems drills ) is this failure, and its fix, in python and java.

patterns to know by name unmesh joshi’s catalogue, published as the book patterns of distributed systems in 2023, names recurring building blocks of distributed systems. six of its patterns, picked here as a start: pattern the problem it solves write-ahead log keep every agreed change after a crash, by persisting each state change as a command in an append-only log heartbeat notice a failed server in time, by having each one send regular “i am alive” messages majority quorum stop two groups of servers making independent decisions generation clock recognise a leader that paused or was cut off and has since been replaced lease give exclusive access that expires by itself if its holder crashes or pauses hybrid clock version data so the versions are ordered and also map to a date and time

c.h: Testing it: chaos, histories and simulation
c.x: testing it: chaos, histories and simulation approach what it asks its limit chaos engineering (netflix’s chaos monkey, 2011, disables a randomly chosen server during working hours) does the system stay available, and recover, when parts fail? unmesh joshi’s point: staying up does not show the answers are right, since a node can answer every request and still return an old value. client-history checking (jepsen) record what clients invoked and what came back, then check that history against a consistency model. finding a failure is only the first step; you must also reproduce it. even with the same fault schedule, thread, message and disk timing differ from run to run on a live cluster. deterministic simulation testing (below) run the real code against a simulated network, disk and clock, with every fault decided by one seed. the code has to be built for it, under strict rules.

deterministic simulation testing joshi names four sources of nondeterminism, each of which changes the order in which events reach the software: the system clock , thread scheduling , network timing and disk timing . simulation testing takes control of all four: time comes from ticks, not the clock. a timeout counts calls to tick() , so a pause cannot fire it early. production systems already work this way: etcd’s raft is driven by node.tick() , with election and heartbeat timeouts set in ticks, and tigerbeetle fixes a tick at 10 ms. one thread runs the protocol , so there is no scheduler to vary the order. the network and the disk are interfaces with a simulated version in tests, which can drop, delay or duplicate messages. tigerbeetle’s simulator also reorders packets, partitions the network and corrupts reads and writes. every random choice comes from a seeded generator. the same seed gives exactly the same faults in the same order, so a failure found on one run replays every time. time is fast-forwarded: the simulation runs the next tick at once instead of waiting, so a run that would take hours on a live cluster takes seconds, and thousands of runs that would add up to days finish quickly. tigerbeetle says one minute of its simulator’s time is equivalent to days of real-world testing. correctness is checked against the recorded client history, as jepsen does, not just “did it stay up”. where it comes from: joshi writes that foundationdb pioneered deterministic simulation testing for distributed databases, using a custom c++ coroutine language and a deterministic scheduler, and that it simulates at the level of byte streams. tigerbeetle , a financial transactions database, uses a single-threaded, tick-driven design, which joshi found easier to implement in java. tigerbeetle’s own documentation says its simulator, the vopr, is deterministic from a seed and the git commit, so any bug it finds can be replayed, and credits foundationdb and antithesis as its inspiration. antithesis is a commercial platform with a deterministic hypervisor, which joshi suggests when re-architecting the application is not feasible. tickloom is joshi’s java library for teaching the approach.

the rules simulation imposes to keep the core deterministic, joshi’s tickloom code follows six rules. in short (his examples are java, but the idea applies in any language): no reading the system clock directly. no unseeded randomness, including for ids. no threads, executors or standard futures in the core. no direct network or disk i/o: everything goes through the interfaces. no iterating over unordered collections such as a hashmap , whose order can differ between runs. no background thread calling back into the deterministic side. on cost, joshi argues that a single event loop with asynchronous, batched i/o often performs better for i/o-bound systems, the design redis, foundationdb and tigerbeetle use. the trade-off is that handlers must never block, and you scale across cores by running more processes.

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) you build on a managed database or kafka and do not write the replication yourself learn the guarantees it documents; test your own retries, timeouts and idempotency; use chaos tests for recovery a wrong answer costs more than a refused one (money, stock, bookings) a store that chooses consistency during a partition staying responsive matters more than every read being current (feeds, catalogues) eventual consistency, with the staleness designed for you need a leader, a lock or cluster membership an existing consensus system such as etcd, not a home-made one you are writing a consensus protocol, a replication layer or a storage engine deterministic simulation testing, designed in from the start an existing system you cannot restructure client-history checking, or simulation below the application at the hypervisor (commercial platforms such as antithesis)

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: every engineer who builds services should know the fallacies, cap and quorums well enough to read a database’s guarantees critically, and anyone writing the replication itself should design for simulation testing from the first line, because retrofitting determinism is usually harder ( our view ; hypervisor-level tools exist for when re-architecting is not feasible). the other view: most teams never write a consensus protocol. for them the strict rules of simulation are a cost with little return, and time is better spent on timeouts, idempotency, chaos tests and choosing well-tested infrastructure.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation name the fallacies of distributed computing and give an example of each explain cap and pacelc, and what each letter means explain why a five-node cluster survives two failures 2 practitioner read a database's consistency guarantees and say what they mean for your code design timeouts, retries and idempotency for partial failure explain lamport timestamps, vector clocks and generation clocks 3 senior explain how raft elects a leader and replicates a log choose consistency per use case and design for its staleness plan chaos and client-history tests for a service 4 expert design a replicated component and its failure handling build deterministic simulation testing into a system from the start set an organisation's standards for distributed correctness each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

monolith, modular monolith, microservices monolith modular monolith microservices deployables one one, with enforced internal modules many, deployed independently data one shared database one database, schema per module each service owns its data calls between parts in-process in-process through module apis over the network scaling whole app whole app per service team fit one small team one to a few teams many teams owning services end to end main cost tangling as it grows discipline to keep boundaries distributed-systems complexity and operations most systems should start as a modular monolith and extract a service only when a boundary has proved stable and there is a concrete reason: independent scaling, a different release cadence, a separate team, or different technology or security needs.

what microservices buy, and cost gains teams deploy their service without coordinating a big release. scale and tune each service for its own load. a failure can be contained to one service. different services can use different technologies where it helps. costs network calls fail, time out and add latency. no cross-service transactions: sagas and eventual consistency instead. debugging needs distributed tracing; testing needs contracts. many pipelines, deployments, dashboards and on-call rotations.

how to split services by business capability or bounded context (domain-driven design): search, carts, billing, identity. not by technical layer (a "database service" is an anti-pattern). each service owns its data and is the only one that writes it. others ask through its api or react to its events. high cohesion inside, loose coupling between: a typical change should touch one service. align with teams (conway's law): one team owns a service end to end. size by responsibility, not lines of code. too many tiny services ("nano-services") multiply network calls and operations for no gain. test the split: if two services must always deploy together, they are one service.

c.h: Monorepo or one repo per service?
c.x: monorepo or one repo per service? a monorepo is not a monolith. a monorepo stores the code of many projects in one repository; each service can still build, deploy and scale on its own. a monolith is one application. you can run microservices from a monorepo, or a monolith from many repositories. the repository decides how people change code together; the deployment decides how the system runs. monorepo one repo per service (polyrepo) change across services one atomic commit and one review for the api, its clients and their tests one pull request per repo, merged and released in the right order shared code a shared library is just a folder, used from source a published package with versions, which each service must upgrade large refactors you can see and fix every caller in one change callers in other repositories you cannot see may stay on the old version access control by default everyone can read everything grant access per repository versions some teams use one version for everything and lose per-service versions each service has its own version and release history tooling needed a build that only builds and tests what changed; ci that scales with the repo simple per repo; harder across repos (dependency updates, shared standards) clone size everything by default; partial or sparse clones fix it only the service you work on who runs very large monorepos: wikipedia names google, meta, microsoft, uber, airbnb and twitter. several had to change their tools to do it: google built its own version control system (piper), facebook (now meta) contributed to mercurial, microsoft contributed to the git client and built the virtual file system for git when it moved its windows engineers to one git repository, and twitter wrote the pants build system.

c.h: Where a monorepo fits with microservices
c.x: where a monorepo fits with microservices choose by your requirements, not by preference. read down the left column, tick the rows that are true for you, and see which way they lean. if this is true for you it leans towards why services often change together (shared api contracts, schemas, clients) monorepo one atomic commit and one review instead of ordered releases across repos you need large refactors across many services monorepo every caller is visible and fixed in the same change code must be hidden from some contributors (partners, vendors, regulated code) separate repos a monorepo gives read access to everything by default each service is versioned and released to outside users on its own separate repos per-project versions are simpler; some monorepos lose them nobody owns build tooling and ci capacity separate repos a monorepo needs a build that only builds what changed, or ci slows with every service added teams are separate organisations with little shared code separate repos little gain from atomic changes; more cost in shared tooling a few teams, mostly one domain, shared libraries either; one repo per team or domain is a common middle keeps atomic changes where they matter, and access lines where they matter conway's law (melvin conway, 1967): systems mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds them. the repository layout should match how your teams actually work together. other views: companies have moved in both directions as they grew. uber engineers gave a talk titled “monorepo to multirepo and back again” (2017). neither layout is a maturity level: the right one can change when your teams, access rules or tooling change. making it work build only what changed. a build tool that knows the dependency graph (bazel, buck, pants, please, or nx) builds and tests only the affected services. ci that rebuilds everything on every commit does not scale. deploy each service on its own. one repository, many pipelines: each service keeps its own image, version tag and rollout. a monorepo must not turn into a release-everything-together monolith. ownership per folder: a codeowners file names the team responsible for each path; owners are requested for review automatically, and branch protection can require their approval. keep clones fast: git clone --filter=blob:none (partial clone) downloads file contents only when needed, and git sparse-checkout set services/orders libs/common keeps only the folders you work on in your working tree. the required-check trap: on github, a workflow skipped by a paths filter leaves its required checks stuck as "pending", so the pull request cannot merge. a job skipped by an if: condition reports success instead. github’s advice is to avoid requiring workflows that can be skipped. so run the workflow always, decide what changed in a first job, and skip the expensive jobs with if: . make that first job a required check too: a job whose needs failed is skipped and may not block the merge. enforce the boundaries in code: a service may import shared libraries but never another service's internals. check this in the build, or the monorepo quietly becomes a distributed monolith. # .github/workflows/ci.yml : always runs, so required checks always report on: [pull_request] jobs: changes: runs-on: ubuntu-latest outputs: orders: ${{ steps.f.outputs.orders }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: { fetch-depth: 0 } - id: f run: | changed=$(git diff --name-only origin/${{ github.base_ref }}...head) if printf '%s\n' "$changed" | grep -e '^(services/orders|libs/common)/' > /dev/null then echo "orders=true" >> "$github_output"; else echo "orders=false" >> "$github_output"; fi orders: needs: changes if: needs.changes.outputs.orders == 'true' # skipped by if: reports success runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: ./gradlew :services:orders:build # .github/codeowners : who reviews which folder /services/orders/ @acme/orders-team /libs/common/ @acme/platform-team

communication style use for watch out for synchronous rest / grpc queries that need an answer now chains of calls: latency adds up and availability multiplies down asynchronous events (kafka, pub/sub) telling others something happened eventual consistency, duplicates, ordering asynchronous commands (queues) work another service should do retries, dead letters, idempotency prefer events between domains; keep synchronous calls shallow (ideally one hop). cache or replicate the data you need from other services (from their events) rather than calling them on every request. see apis & integration , kafka and graphql .

infrastructure around services service discovery: kubernetes dns names, cloud run urls, or a registry. never hard-code instance ips. api gateway at the edge for authentication, rate limits and routing ( apigee ); a backend for frontend per client type when needs differ. service mesh (istio / cloud service mesh) for mtls, retries and traffic splitting between services, without code in each one. configuration and secrets injected at runtime per environment. platform blueprint: a service template with logging, tracing, health checks, security and ci already wired, so each new service starts correct.

resilience in code (spring + resilience4j) @service class supplierclient { private final restclient http; supplierclient(restclient http) { this.http = http; } @circuitbreaker(name = "supplier", fallbackmethod = "unavailable") @retry(name = "supplier") public listing list(string prefix) { return http.get().uri("/objects?prefix={p}", prefix).retrieve().body(listing.class); } // honest degradation: "cannot see", never "nothing there" listing unavailable(string prefix, throwable t) { return listing.unknown("supplier unavailable: " + t.getmessage()); } } resilience4j: circuitbreaker: instances: supplier: slidingwindowsize: 20 failureratethreshold: 50 waitdurationinopenstate: 30s retry: instances: supplier: maxattempts: 3 waitduration: 200ms enableexponentialbackoff: true quarkus offers the same through microprofile fault tolerance ( @retry , @circuitbreaker , @timeout , @fallback ). always set a client timeout too.

microservices patterns at a glance pattern the problem it solves where to read more database per service services that share tables cannot change or deploy alone data across services, on this page saga a business transaction that spans services, without a distributed lock: local steps, each with a compensating step architecture transactional outbox saving a change and publishing its event without one succeeding alone architecture idempotent consumer messages arrive more than once architecture cqrs reads and writes need different models or different scale architecture , event sourcing api gateway and backend for frontend many services behind one public surface; clients with different needs architecture , apigee timeout a call that never returns holds a thread or connection for ever resilience in code, on this page retry with backoff and jitter transient failures; only for idempotent calls resilience in code, on this page circuit breaker callers keep waiting on a dependency that is already failing below bulkhead one slow dependency uses up every thread or connection below (from hystrix to resilience4j) rate limiter a caller, or you, sends more than the other side can take below (from hystrix to resilience4j) sidecar and service mesh the same networking, security and telemetry code repeated in every service service mesh & istio strangler fig moving from a monolith one piece at a time solution architecture: a to b

how a circuit breaker works martin fowler’s description: wrap a protected call in a circuit breaker object that monitors for failures. once failures reach a threshold, the breaker trips, and further calls return an error at once, without the protected call being made. closed: calls go through, and failures are counted. open: calls fail fast for a set time, giving the dependency room to recover. half-open: trial calls go through (fowler describes one; libraries allow a configured number); success closes the breaker, failure opens it again. alert when a breaker opens: it is a symptom someone needs to see.

the states, drawn circuit breaker states a uml state diagram with three states. closed: calls go through and failures are counted. when failures reach the threshold the breaker trips to open: calls fail at once, without calling the dependency, for a set time. when that time has passed it moves to half-open: trial calls go through. if they succeed it returns to closed; if they fail it goes back to open. closed calls pass, failures counted open fail fast, no call made half-open trial calls go through failures reach the threshold wait time passed trial calls succeed a trial fails the three states above as a uml state diagram. while the breaker is open the failing dependency gets no calls at all, which is what gives it room to recover.

from hystrix to resilience4j hystrix, netflix’s library, is in maintenance mode and no longer in active development. netflix says it keeps using it for its existing applications, uses open, active projects such as resilience4j for new ones, and is beginning to recommend others do the same. resilience4j is a lightweight fault-tolerance library designed for functional programming. it provides a circuit breaker, retry, rate limiter, time limiter (timeouts) and bulkhead, in semaphore and thread-pool forms, which wrap any function or lambda. on quarkus and other microprofile runtimes, microprofile fault tolerance gives the same ideas as annotations (see resilience in code, above). analysis: if you still run hystrix, expect to rewrite each command as a decorator or annotation. the concepts, closed, open and half-open, carry over.

c.h: Circuit breaking in code, or in the mesh?
c.x: circuit breaking in code, or in the mesh? istio’s “circuit breaking” is configured on a destinationrule and enforced by its envoy sidecars. it is not the same mechanism as a library’s breaker. envoy enforces connection and request limits at the network level, without code in each application, and each proxy decides on its own (envoy calls its limits “fully distributed (not coordinated)”). its outlier detection is passive health checking: it removes hosts that behave unlike the others, for example after consecutive errors, from the load-balancing set for a while. in code (resilience4j, microprofile fault tolerance) in the mesh (istio, envoy) what trips it failure rate or slow calls over a window, per named dependency connection and pending-request limits; outlier detection on errors per host what it isolates ( analysis ) the whole dependency, as your code calls it individual pods (ejection), or the connections to a service when it trips your fallback runs: a cached answer, a default, or an honest “unavailable” the caller gets an error (in istio’s own example, http 503) and must handle it languages ( analysis ) one library per language, and the same settings repeated per service any language, no code change, configured in one place who changes it ( analysis ) the service team, in code and configuration often a platform team, in kubernetes resources

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) the caller needs a fallback that makes business sense (cached prices, “delivery date unknown”) our view: a breaker in code, because only the application knows what a sensible fallback is services in many languages, and you want one consistent policy without changing code the mesh usually one bad pod among healthy ones mesh outlier detection, which takes that pod out of rotation a whole dependency is down, or it is an external api outside the mesh a breaker in code, around the client: the mesh guards only traffic that passes through its sidecars you do not run a service mesh our view: a breaker in code. adopting a mesh only for this has a cost (see service mesh & istio ) you need both protections both: the mesh for connection limits and pod ejection, code for timeouts and fallbacks analysis: set retries in one layer only. if the application retries three times and the mesh retries twice per attempt, one failing call can become up to nine requests, when the dependency is least able to take them. istio applies a default retry policy (two retries on connection failures and similar) even if you configure none.

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: keep timeouts and fallbacks in code, where the business meaning is, and let a mesh, if you have one, add connection limits and eject bad pods. do not adopt a mesh only to get circuit breaking. the other view: platform teams that already run a mesh often prefer one place for every network policy. keeping resilience out of application code means fewer libraries to upgrade in every service and the same behaviour in every language, and teams accept handling a 503 in exchange.

data across services database per service: separate schemas or instances; no other service reads its tables. cross-service transactions become sagas with compensating steps. reliable events with the transactional outbox , so a state change and its event never disagree. queries across services: api composition (call and combine) for small cases; a read model built from events (cqrs) for heavy ones. reporting goes to the warehouse via events or cdc, not by joining services' databases. details on architecture and event sourcing .

observability is not optional distributed tracing (opentelemetry): one trace id follows a request through every service, queue and database call. structured logs with trace id, service, version and request id on every line. metrics per service: rate, errors, duration (red) and saturation; slos on user-facing ones. health endpoints: liveness (restart me) separate from readiness (send me traffic). dependency maps from traces show who calls whom, and where latency comes from.

testing microservices unit and component tests inside each service, with its own database in a container. contract tests (pact, spring cloud contract) between consumers and providers, run in both pipelines, so a provider cannot break a consumer unnoticed. a few end-to-end tests of critical journeys in a shared environment. event schema checks with a schema registry and compatibility rules. resilience tests: kill or slow a dependency and check the caller degrades as designed.

security between services zero trust: authenticate every call, even inside the network. service identity: mtls from a mesh, or google-signed id tokens between cloud run services. user context: propagate the user's token or a signed internal token; each service still checks its own permissions. least privilege per service: its own service account, database user and secrets.

anti-patterns distributed monolith: services that must be deployed together or share a database. shared database written by several services. chatty synchronous chains: a calls b calls c calls d for one request. nano-services too small to justify their operational cost. shared libraries with business logic that force lock-step upgrades (shared infrastructure blueprints are fine). no ownership: services nobody is on call for. splitting before understanding the domain: boundaries drawn too early are expensive to move.

migrating from a monolith make the monolith modular first: enforce module boundaries and separate each module's data. pick one capability with a clear boundary and a real reason to move. put a routing layer (gateway or proxy) in front, and route that capability's traffic to the new service ( strangler fig ). move its data, with a period of syncing or dual reads, and make the new service the only writer. remove the old code. repeat only if the first extraction paid off.

readiness checklist can you deploy a service with one automated pipeline, in minutes? do you have centralised logs, metrics and tracing? can you create a new service from a template in under an hour? do teams own services end to end, including on-call? are the domain boundaries understood and stable? if several answers are no, a modular monolith will serve you better for now.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain monolith vs modular monolith vs microservices work in one service: build, test, deploy, read its logs and traces know why services own their data 2 practitioner build a service with timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and health checks use events and the outbox to integrate with other services write contract tests with consumers 3 senior draw service boundaries from the domain; decide when not to split design sagas, read models and observability across services lead a strangler-fig extraction from a monolith 4 expert set the organisation's service architecture and platform blueprint align team structure with service ownership decide when to consolidate services as well as split them each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

l: Case Studies: How Tech Companies Evolved

c.x: eight directions eight companies, 1994 to 2026 a timeline with eight lanes. yahoo: a web directory in january 1994, search from google from june 2000, the hadoop-based search webmap in february 2008, and its internet business sold to verizon in june 2017. ebay: founded as auctionweb in september 1995; by 2008 its site was partitioned by function and by data, with no distributed transactions; in 2022 it described releasing more than 3,000 dependent libraries in about two hours. amazon: first public web services in july 2002, amazon s3 in march 2006 and ec2 in august 2006. facebook, now meta: launched in february 2004, announced hiphop for php in february 2010, released the hack language in march 2014, and from february 2019 its hhvm runtime supported hack only. netflix: database corruption stops dvd shipping for three days in august 2008, chaos monkey in 2011, and a february 2016 post on completing the move to the cloud. github: the upgrade from rails 3.2 to 5.2 finishes in august 2018, a 50% load reduction from splitting its main database is reported in 2021, and weekly rails upgrades are described in 2023. shopify: founded in 2006, sharded its databases in 2014, and in 2025 described moving all its apps to react native. stack overflow: launched in 2008, questions per month peaked in 2014, bought by prosus in 2021, and by 2026 monthly questions were down by more than 99% from that peak. 1995 2000 2005 2010 2015 2020 2025 yahoo directory google search hadoop webmap sold to verizon ebay founded partitioned, no 2pc 3,000 libraries amazon web services s3 and ec2 facebook / meta launch hiphop hack hhvm: hack only netflix outage, then aws chaos monkey migration complete github rails 5.2 50% less load weekly upgrades shopify founded sharding react native stack overflow launch peak questions prosus −99% the dates in the case studies below, each from the source cited with it. eight different directions: yahoo helped build tools the whole industry used while losing its own market, ebay split one site by function and by data and gave up distributed transactions, facebook kept its php code and changed the language and runtime underneath it, amazon turned its internal services into a product, netflix moved to another company’s cloud, github kept one large rails application and changed what was underneath it, shopify split its data across databases, and stack overflow’s biggest change came from outside its architecture.

c.h: Yahoo: a pioneer that built the industry’s tools and lost its own market
c.x: yahoo: a pioneer that built the industry’s tools and lost its own market what happened. in january 1994 jerry yang and david filo, graduate students at stanford, made “jerry and david’s guide to the world wide web”, a human-edited directory organised in a hierarchy rather than a searchable index. yahoo was incorporated in march 1995, added a search engine the same year, and became the first popular online directory and search engine on the web. yahoo began using google for its search in june 2000; over the next four years it built its own search technology, partly from inktomi, which it bought for $280 million in 2002, and switched to it in 2004. its engineers were central to hadoop , the open-source system for storing and processing data across many machines that grew from google’s papers: in february 2008 yahoo launched the search webmap, a hadoop application on more than 10,000 cores whose data was used in every yahoo web search. the same month microsoft offered $44.6 billion for the company; yahoo rejected it. in 2016 yahoo disclosed two data breaches, one in 2013 affecting over a billion accounts and one in 2014 affecting over 500 million. verizon announced in july 2016 that it would buy yahoo’s internet business for $4.83 billion and completed the purchase in june 2017; in 2021 funds managed by apollo bought 90% of it. wikipedia sums it up: one of the pioneers of the early internet, whose use declined in the 2010s as it lost market share to facebook and google. our view: yahoo’s engineering helped build tools much of the industry came to run on, hadoop above all, while its own products lost users; good infrastructure did not decide the outcome. the breaches add a second lesson that ties to quality attributes : security failures came to light during the company’s sale, years after they happened. the other view: yahoo’s decline is usually explained by strategy and leadership more than engineering (wikipedia describes strategic missteps alongside the security incidents), so it is a weak guide to architecture decisions; it says more about product focus than about systems. what you can take ( analysis ): know which part of your work is the product users choose you for, and which is infrastructure others could supply; and treat security as part of what a company is worth, not only a technical risk. don’t copy it if you are tempted to conclude “build your own search” or “build your own platform”: yahoo did both, and the case does not show that either decided the outcome. sources: wikipedia’s articles on yahoo and apache hadoop . we could not read a yahoo engineering account from this environment.

c.h: Why Yahoo declined, and is it finished?
c.x: why yahoo declined, and is it finished? no single decision sank yahoo. what the sources describe is a run of choices over about fifteen years. wikipedia’s summary: “yahoo’s decline was punctuated by a series of strategic missteps and severe security incidents.” when the choice what happened 1998, 2002 did not buy google in 1998 larry page and sergey brin offered to sell their search engine to yahoo for $1 million, and yahoo declined. in 2002 terry semel negotiated to buy google for a reported $5 billion; yahoo’s final offer was $3 billion, which google rejected. wikipedia: that second miss “is widely considered one of the largest strategic errors in corporate history”. 1999–2001 bought big, at the top of the bubble yahoo grew into a web portal , a site meant to keep users inside it, and made its two biggest acquisitions in 1999: geocities for $3.6 billion and broadcast.com for $5.7 billion. its share price closed at $118.75 on 3 january 2000 and fell to $8.11 on 26 september 2001. geocities closed in october 2009. 2000–2010 did not keep control of search google powered yahoo’s searches from june 2000. yahoo switched to its own technology in february 2004, and from august 2010 its organic results came from microsoft’s bing. in ten years yahoo rented its search, built its own, then rented it again. 2004–2006 sold trust in its results a paid-inclusion programme guaranteed commercial sites a listing for a fee. marketers resisted the fees, and the public disliked that paid listings could not be told apart from organic results; yahoo scaled it back by october 2006. 2008 turned down microsoft yahoo rejected microsoft’s offer of $44.6 billion. microsoft raised it to $47 billion; yahoo held out for at least 10% more, and microsoft withdrew in may 2008. nine years later verizon paid $4.48 billion for the internet business. 2001–2012 changed leaders again and again terry semel (2001), jerry yang (2007), carol bartz (2009, fired in 2011), tim morse (interim), scott thompson (january 2012), ross levinsohn (interim, may 2012) and marissa mayer (july 2012): seven chief executives in about eleven years, each with a new direction. the largest layoff in its history, 2,000 people, came in early 2012. 2013–2017 bought audience, then lost trust under mayer, yahoo bought tumblr in 2013 for $1.1 billion in cash. in 2016 it disclosed breaches from 2013 and 2014 covering over a billion and over 500 million accounts. verizon cut its price by $350 million because of them, completing the purchase in june 2017. the best deal it made. in august 2005 yahoo paid $1 billion for 40% of alibaba. when verizon bought the internet business, what remained of yahoo inc. was renamed altaba in june 2017: an investment company holding the alibaba and yahoo japan stakes. it sold them and dissolved in october 2019. for its last years, the company’s stock market value rested more on that 2005 investment than on yahoo’s own products ( analysis ). is it finished? no, but it is smaller and private. funds managed by apollo global management bought 90% of yahoo from verizon in september 2021 (verizon kept 10%). yahoo left mainland china in november 2021 and cut about 1,000 of its 8,600 staff in 2023. it still runs yahoo mail, news, finance, sports and search, and an advertising business. our view: the common thread is that yahoo never settled what it was. it treated itself as a media portal while the web moved to search and then to social networks, and it bought and rented the core capability (search) instead of owning it. the breaches show the cost of treating security as overhead: $350 million came off the sale price. the other view: this reading leans on hindsight. in 1998 and 2002 nobody knew how valuable search advertising would become, the board could argue that in 2008 it was holding out for a fair price, and some argue that a portal company could not have turned into google or facebook whoever was in charge. seen that way, yahoo is less a lesson in mistakes than in how fast a market leader’s market can move. what engineers can take ( analysis ): know the one capability your users choose you for, and keep it in your own hands; and treat security as part of what the business is worth, because it is priced when the business is sold.

c.h: eBay: split by function and by data, and no distributed transactions
c.x: ebay: split by function and by data, and no distributed transactions what happened. pierre omidyar founded ebay as auctionweb in september 1995, as a hobby site; it took the name ebay in 1997. by 2008 its architect randy shoup described a site with over two billion page views a day, and the practices it had learned to scale it. ebay partitioned by function : selling, bidding and search ran on separate pools of application servers (“roughly 16,000 application servers into 220 different pools”), and there was “no single monolithic database”, but separate databases for users, items and purchases, “1000 logical databases in all, on 400 physical hosts”. it then split each one horizontally : user data, for example, was divided over 20 hosts, “if you can’t split it, you can’t scale it”. because listing one new item could touch “twenty or thirty different hosts”, it allowed “absolutely no client-side or distributed transactions of any kind - no two-phase commit”, and reached eventual consistency instead through careful ordering of database operations, asynchronous recovery events and reconciliation batches. its other practices were to decouple components asynchronously, move work onto asynchronous flows, put a layer of indirection in front of databases and search, and cache with care. infoq’s 2022 report on ebay recalls two of its vice-presidents, shoup and mark weinberg, describing “systemic challenges with releasing major dependencies, leading to the equivalent of distributed monoliths”, and says ebay’s engineers built a system to release more than 3,000 dependent libraries in about two hours. our view: ebay is the older, pre-cloud version of the story many companies tell about microservices: split by business function, split again by key, and treat consistency as a choice per operation rather than all or nothing. the 2022 report shows the cost that follows: once the code is split, the dependencies between the parts become the thing to manage. the other view: ebay’s scale was rare, and giving up transactions moves work into code that orders writes, retries and reconciles; most systems can keep acid transactions in one database for a long time, and should until a measured limit says otherwise (see distributed systems and database design ). what you can take ( analysis ): decide per operation how much consistency it really needs; split data along the path it is read; prefer asynchronous hand-offs between parts that can wait. don’t copy it if one database still handles your load: distributed data without distributed transactions is a lot of careful code to own. their own accounts: randy shoup, “scalability best practices: lessons from ebay” (infoq, may 2008); interview with randy shoup (infoq, june 2008, recorded at qcon san francisco 2007); “ebay’s architectural principles” (talk, infoq, february 2008); and the 2022 report, “managing complex dependencies with distributed architecture at ebay” (infoq, april 2022).

c.h: Amazon: internal services that became AWS
c.x: amazon: internal services that became aws what happened. in the early 2000s amazon pursued service-oriented architecture as a way to scale its engineering, and was frustrated with the speed of its software engineering. an engineering leader, matt round, recommended giving engineering teams as much autonomy as possible, adopting rest, standardising infrastructure, removing gate-keeping decision-makers, and continuous deployment. in july 2002 amazon launched its first public web services, opening the amazon.com platform to developers; over a hundred applications were built on it by 2004, which convinced amazon that developers were “hungry for more”. andy jassy then mapped out an “internet os” of basic infrastructure building blocks. amazon s3 storage launched on 14 march 2006, the first generally available aws infrastructure service, followed by ec2 compute in august 2006. our view: aws grew out of work to make amazon’s own engineering faster, and outside developers’ demand for the 2002 web services confirmed there was a market for it. the lesson we draw is to build the platform your own teams need, and to treat outside demand as evidence. the other view: few companies have amazon’s scale, so the same decomposition into many independent services can cost a smaller organisation more in coordination than it saves; the conditions that made it pay off at amazon may not hold elsewhere. what you can take ( analysis ): standard, automated building blocks with clear interfaces let teams move without waiting on each other. don’t copy it if you have a few teams: the coordination it removes may be smaller than the overhead it adds. their own account: werner vogels, “modern applications at aws” (all things distributed, august 2019) † .

c.h: Facebook (Meta): kept the PHP, changed the language and runtime underneath
c.x: facebook (meta): kept the php, changed the language and runtime underneath what happened. mark zuckerberg launched “thefacebook” on 4 february 2004, and facebook.com grew on a large php codebase. rather than rewrite it in another language, facebook changed what ran it. in february 2010 it announced hiphop for php , which translated php into c++ and compiled it; wikipedia says its original motivation was to save resources on facebook’s servers. it then built the hiphop virtual machine (hhvm) , a just-in-time compiler, because hiphop had hit a plateau for performance and could not support all of php; hhvm matched hiphop’s performance on facebook.com in the last quarter of 2012, and facebook deprecated hiphop in early 2013. in march 2014 facebook released hack , a php dialect with gradual static typing: “over the last year, we have migrated nearly our entire php codebase to hack, thanks to both organic adoption and a number of homegrown refactoring tools”, it wrote. type checking was incremental, so a file could be partly converted. the post gives the reason for the work: at facebook scale, “with thousands of engineers shipping new code twice a day”, errors that a dynamic language only shows at run time slowed everyone down. from hhvm 4.0, in february 2019, hhvm supported hack only. along the way facebook also built and open-sourced tools that spread far beyond it, among them the cassandra database (open-sourced in july 2008) and react (may 2013). our view: facebook treated its language as something it could change, a little at a time, instead of something to escape with a rewrite: first a faster way to run the same code, then types that could be added file by file while the site kept shipping. it is the same idea as github’s weekly upgrades, applied to the language itself. the other view: building your own compiler, runtime and language needs a scale and a team that almost nobody has, and it leaves you maintaining a language few others use (hhvm dropped php support in 2019); in our view, for most teams, adding the type hints or type checker their own language already offers costs far less. what you can take ( analysis ): when a codebase is too large to rewrite, look for changes that can be adopted gradually, with tools that do most of the work, while everything keeps running; types added file by file are one such change. don’t copy it if your language or a standard tool already gives you that path, as python’s type hints and typescript do for their languages. their own account: “hack: a new programming language for hhvm” (engineering at meta, march 2014). the hiphop and hhvm history is from wikipedia, which cites facebook’s own posts.

c.h: Netflix: to the cloud after an outage, then failure on purpose
c.x: netflix: to the cloud after an outage, then failure on purpose what happened. in august 2008 netflix’s database was corrupted and the company could not ship dvds to customers for three days, which led it to move all its data to the amazon web services cloud; netflix published “completing the netflix cloud migration” in february 2016, and by august 2016 it had closed its last physical data centre. during the migration, in 2011, netflix built chaos monkey , a tool that randomly chooses a server in production and disables it during its usual hours of activity, to move from assuming nothing breaks to treating breakdowns as inevitable. it released the code in 2012, and chaos monkey became part of a wider “simian army”, which includes chaos kong, simulating the loss of a whole aws region. netflix’s chaos monkey repository describes the idea: “exposing engineers to failures more frequently incentivizes them to build resilient services.” its circuit-breaker library hystrix is now in maintenance mode. netflix’s readme says its focus moved to adaptive approaches that react to real-time performance, and that it uses resilience4j for new internal projects. our view: the outage showed that one database was a single point of failure; testing failure in production made resilience something checked every day rather than assumed. netflix moving its own hystrix to maintenance mode shows that a company’s tools can change while the idea behind them stays. the other view: deliberately breaking production needs mature monitoring, automation and on-call practice first; without those, chaos experiments add risk, so many teams start in a test environment, or with game days, and grow from there (see test strategy and sre ). what you can take ( analysis ): find your single points of failure before an outage does, and test failure regularly, starting small. don’t copy it if you cannot yet see what your system is doing: monitoring and quick rollback come before deliberate failure. their own accounts: “completing the netflix cloud migration” (netflix, february 2016) † ; “the netflix simian army” (netflix technology blog, july 2011) † ; chaos monkey and hystrix on github.

c.h: GitHub: one Rails monolith, kept and scaled
c.x: github: one rails monolith, kept and scaled what happened. github.com has been a ruby on rails monolith since the beginning. in 2023 github wrote that it is nearly two million lines of code, that more than 1,000 engineers work on it daily, that it deploys as often as 20 times a day, and that nearly every week one of those deploys is a rails upgrade. it was not always so: in 2018 the upgrade from rails 3.2 to 5.2 took a year and a half, on a codebase then ten years old. its data followed a similar path: github.com was built around one main mysql cluster, mysql1 , and any incident there affected every feature stored on it. from 2019 github grouped tables into “schema domains”, enforced the boundaries with sql linters, and then moved them to separate clusters; by 2021 load on the hosts holding the former mysql1 data had fallen by 50%, with fewer database incidents. our view: github kept the single application and drew boundaries inside it instead, first in the data, enforced by tools, before moving anything physically. upgrading a little every week turned a year-and-a-half project into routine work. the other view: a monolith this large needs heavy investment in tooling, testing and deployment to stay workable, and teams still share one codebase and one release train; organisations that want teams to choose their own languages and release on their own may still prefer separate services. what you can take ( analysis ): draw boundaries inside the application first, and enforce them with tools; upgrade little and often instead of rarely and painfully. don’t copy it if your teams truly need independent releases and different languages: then separate services may fit better. their own accounts: “upgrading github from rails 3.2 to 5.2” (eileen m. uchitelle, september 2018); “partitioning github’s relational databases to handle scale” (thomas maurer, september 2021); “building github with ruby and rails” (adam hess, april 2023).

c.h: Shopify: built on Rails, scaled by splitting its data
c.x: shopify: built on rails, scaled by splitting its data what happened. shopify was founded in 2006. according to wikipedia, tobias lütke had built the online snowboard shop snowdevil with ruby on rails, and the platform grew from it. shopify created liquid, an open-source template language written in ruby, so shops could change their pages safely. as it grew, shopify introduced sharding in 2014 to spread its data across multiple databases, and later moved to fully isolated instances. shopify also publishes packwerk , a ruby gem “used to enforce boundaries and modularize rails applications”: it groups files into packages, controls which constants a package makes public, and is meant to help existing codebases become more modular “without obstructing development”. on mobile, shopify wrote in 2025 that over five years it had moved all its apps to react native, so the same code could serve every platform. our view: when one database became the limit, shopify split the data, first into shards and later into isolated instances, which changes how much one problem can affect. packwerk shows a second idea it has published for rails code in general: make the boundaries between parts of an application explicit and checked, before deciding whether to split it. (the sources we could read do not say how shopify applies packwerk to its own main application.) the other view: sharding and isolated instances add their own operational work, such as moving data between shards and answering questions that span them; some teams prefer one larger database for as long as it lasts, to keep that work away. what you can take ( analysis ): split data by a natural key (for shopify, the shop) when one database is the limit; make module boundaries explicit and checked by a tool, as packwerk does for rails, before deciding whether to split the code. don’t copy it if your data has no natural key that keeps most queries in one place: sharding then makes everyday queries harder. their own accounts: “e-commerce at scale: inside shopify’s tech stack” (shopify engineering) † ; “five years of react native at shopify” (mustafa ali, january 2025) † ; packwerk on github.

c.h: Stack Overflow: its own data-access library, and a change in demand
c.x: stack overflow: its own data-access library, and a change in demand what happened. jeff atwood and joel spolsky created stack overflow in 2008. it is written in c# with asp.net mvc, uses microsoft sql server, and accesses data through dapper , “a simple object mapper for .net” that was originally developed for and by stack overflow, and which its team advertises as fast; wikipedia cites sam saffron’s 2011 post “how i learned to stop worrying and write my own orm” for it. in june 2021 prosus agreed to buy the company for $1.8 billion. then the questions fell: from over 100,000 a month in 2022 to a few thousand by early 2026, and by june 2026 more than 99% below the 2014 peak. wikipedia attributes the fall to the arrival of ai coding tools and, according to some, a moderation culture seen as hostile. in the 2026 stack overflow developer survey, most respondents said they visit less often for simple questions, while a small group visit more to check answers from generative ai. our view: two lessons sit side by side. the engineering one is an inference: stack overflow built, and open-sourced, its own small data-access library instead of adopting a larger one, which we read as a choice to keep a stack its team could understand fully (saffron’s post, which we could not open, gives their own reasons). the bigger one: the largest change in the company’s recent history came mainly from outside its architecture, from ai tools and, according to some, from a moderation culture, which is a community and product choice rather than an engineering one. the other view: writing your own data-access layer is a cost few teams can justify, since well-supported general tools exist; and the decline may say less about engineering than about a product whose value, answering simple questions, moved to ai tools. what you can take ( analysis ): watch how your users’ habits change, not only your system’s metrics; a healthy system can still lose its reason to exist. a small stack you understand end to end is easier to change when that happens. don’t copy it if a well-supported general tool already meets your needs: writing and maintaining your own library then costs more than it saves. their own accounts: sam saffron, “how i learned to stop worrying and write my own orm” (march 2011) † ; dapper on github; stack overflow developer survey 2026 .

side by side ( analysis ) what forced the change what they changed what they kept yahoo search moving to google, and users moving to google and facebook its own search (2004), hadoop; then sold, in 2017 the brand and its portal services ebay load that no single server or database could carry function split into pools and databases, data split by key; no distributed transactions consistency where an operation needs it, chosen per use case amazon frustration with the speed of its software engineering teams and services with more autonomy; then infrastructure offered as a product amazon.com itself, which the services and infrastructure were first built for facebook / meta a large php codebase that cost too much to run and was hard to check before it ran the compiler, then the runtime, then the language (gradual types) the php code itself, converted gradually rather than rewritten netflix a database corruption that stopped shipping for three days all its data to aws, its last data centre closed by 2016; failure tested in production the ideas behind its tools, even as hystrix moved to maintenance mode github one database cluster whose incidents affected every feature, and a ten-year-old codebase on old framework versions data split by domain; upgrades made weekly one rails application shopify one application and its data serving ever more shops data split into shards, then isolated instances; one mobile codebase in react native not stated in the sources we could read stack overflow far fewer questions: ai tools and, according to some, moderation culture not mainly its architecture: the change was in demand c#, sql server, and its own small data-access library our view: in six of the eight cases the change followed a concrete engineering problem, and each kept something stable while it changed the rest; yahoo and stack overflow show the kind of change engineering cannot steer. the other view: these are well-documented successes; the companies that made the same moves and struggled write fewer blog posts, so lessons drawn only from success stories can mislead.

choose by requirement if this is true for you a case to read ( analysis ) one database can no longer carry the load, and some operations can wait ebay: partition by function and key; consistency chosen per operation a large codebase in a dynamic language is hard to change safely, and too big to rewrite facebook: types added file by file, with tools doing the conversion many teams are slowed by waiting on each other amazon: autonomy and service boundaries one component failing takes everything down netflix’s outage, and github’s mysql1 you want confidence that failures are survivable netflix: chaos engineering one large application works, but is slow to upgrade github: weekly upgrades and schema domains one database is the limit, and data has a natural key shopify: sharding by shop your users’ habits are changing faster than your product stack overflow: the fall in questions; yahoo: users moving to google and facebook your team already runs one well-understood application github: boundaries inside it before splitting it, since splitting has a cost (and shopify’s packwerk for rails)

levels: what to expect 1 foundation retell one company's engineering change and what caused it say what a single point of failure is, with an example find a company's own account of a change 2 practitioner explain why netflix tests failure in production explain how github drew boundaries inside one application separate what a case study shows from what it suggests 3 senior judge whether a company's approach fits your organisation's size and needs plan a change that keeps one thing stable spot survivorship bias in success stories 4 expert use case studies to argue for or against an architecture change write your own organisation's case study honestly learn from failures as well as successes each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the short answer databricks sells a platform where companies store, process and analyse their data, and increasingly build ai on top of it. it grew out of apache spark , a tool for crunching very large amounts of data across many computers, which its founders created at the university of california, berkeley. in august 2026 it closed a funding round at a $190 billion valuation, on a revenue run rate of about $7 billion a year, and it is still private. for engineers it is a good case study twice over: an open-source project that became a business, and a live example of how investors put a price on a fast-growing company (see how companies are valued ).

from spark to a company 2009: matei zaharia starts spark at berkeley’s amplab. it is open-sourced in 2010. for repeated calculations, such as training machine-learning models, it could cut the time taken by several orders of magnitude compared with hadoop mapreduce, the main big-data tool of the day. 2013: spark is donated to the apache software foundation, and seven of its creators, ali ghodsi, andy konwinski, arsalan tavakoli-shiraji, ion stoica, matei zaharia, patrick wendell and reynold xin, found databricks to commercialise it. andreessen horowitz leads a $14 million first round. 2014–2017: spark becomes a top-level apache project; databricks launches its first cloud product; microsoft offers it inside azure as azure databricks. 2023: databricks buys the generative ai start-up mosaicml, reported at $1.3 billion, and launches its data intelligence platform, joining its data platform with generative ai. 2024: it open-sources unity catalog, its tool for governing who can see and use which data. ion stoica was the first chief executive; ali ghodsi took over in 2016.

c.h: What it actually sells: the lakehouse
c.x: what it actually sells: the lakehouse companies have traditionally kept data in two kinds of places: a data warehouse , tidy and fast for business reports, and a data lake , cheap storage for everything else, including raw files, images and logs. databricks popularised the lakehouse , which combines the two. its open-source delta lake project adds reliable database-style transactions to files in a data lake. one design choice matters a lot to customers: the data stays in the customer’s own cloud storage, in open formats such as delta lake and apache iceberg, while databricks provides the computing on top. industry analysts note that this separation of storage and compute reduces lock-in. around that core it now sells tools for machine learning, vector search for retrieval (see rag ), serving models, and building ai agents. analysis: this is the argument behind the valuation: databricks sells the layer where a company’s data already lives. if ai for a company is built on its own data, the platform that holds the data is well placed to sell the ai too.

c.h: How a $190 billion valuation is worked out
c.x: how a $190 billion valuation is worked out databricks valuation at each funding round bars for five funding rounds: 38 billion dollars in august 2021, 62 billion in december 2024, over 100 billion in august 2025, 134 billion in december 2025, and 190 billion in august 2026. $38b aug 2021 $62b dec 2024 >$100b aug 2025 $134b dec 2025 $190b aug 2026 private valuations at each round, in us dollars. five times higher in five years, and the last three steps came within about twelve months. databricks has no share price, because it is not listed. its valuation is the price per share agreed in each funding round, multiplied by all its shares. the latest round, led by coatue in july 2026 and closed in august at $5 billion, set the company at $190 billion after the new money (“post-money”). blackstone, mgx, t. rowe price and sixth street growth also invested. for a fast-growing software company, investors usually reason from revenue , because profits are small or still to come. a quick way to see the price: step number valuation after the august 2026 round $190 billion revenue run rate at the time $7 billion a year valuation divided by run rate about 27 times revenue growth reported in june 2026 80% a year, on a $6.9 billion run rate a run rate takes recent revenue, often one month or quarter, and scales it up to a year. it flatters a company that is growing fast, which is exactly why investors use it: they are paying for where revenue is heading. databricks also reported positive free cash flow over the twelve months before february 2026, which supports the price. the full toolkit, from multiples to discounted cash flow, is on how companies are valued .

c.h: Will it be the biggest software IPO ever?
c.x: will it be the biggest software ipo ever? “biggest” can mean two things: the company’s value when it lists, or the money raised in the listing. for comparison, snowflake, a data-warehouse rival, raised $3.4 billion when it listed in september 2020, one of the largest software ipos. our view: if databricks lists anywhere near its last private price, it would be one of the largest software listings there has been, and its position under enterprise ai is the reason investors keep paying more for it. the other view: private valuations are set by a small group of investors and can fall when a company meets the public market; a price of about 27 times revenue assumes very fast growth continues for years. competition is fierce, from snowflake and from the cloud providers’ own data services, and ai spending may not keep rising at today’s pace. and databricks may simply choose to stay private, as it has so far. reports of new funding talks at higher valuations appear often. we include only rounds that have closed and been reported, and update this page when a new one closes.

when databricks fits, by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards you already run spark, or have large data-engineering and machine-learning workloads databricks, which grew out of spark you want your data to stay in your own cloud storage in open formats a lakehouse with delta lake or iceberg, databricks or another engine your work is mostly sql reporting on structured data, with a small team a managed warehouse may be simpler (see bigquery ) you are all-in on one cloud and want fewer vendors that cloud’s own data services; azure also offers azure databricks your team already uses a data platform stay with it unless a requirement above forces a move: migration costs time and money

c.h: What engineers can take from it
c.x: what engineers can take from it open source can be the start of a business, not the opposite of one: spark built the audience databricks sells to. academic research can become infrastructure the whole industry runs on. owning the place where data lives is a strong position when ai arrives.
