the short answer palantir sells software that pulls together an organisation’s scattered data, from databases, spreadsheets, sensors and documents, so people can analyse it and act on it. it does not collect or sell data itself; its customers bring their own. it makes money by selling that software, usually in large contracts, to two kinds of customer: governments , especially defence and intelligence agencies, and companies . what makes it unusual is how it sells: for years it sent its own “forward-deployed engineers” to sit with customers and make the software work on their problems. and how it is valued: in 2025 its stock market value passed $400 billion, on revenue of under $3 billion the year before.

from paypal to the pentagon 2003: founded in palo alto by peter thiel, alex karp, stephen cohen, joe lonsdale and nathan gettings. thiel, a paypal co-founder, said it could apply software similar to paypal’s fraud detection to other problems. karp, a former colleague of thiel’s from stanford law school, became chief executive. early money: venture capital firms showed little interest, so thiel and his fund largely paid for the initial $30 million. in-q-tel, the cia-affiliated venture firm, invested about $2 million. 2010s: its clients grew to include the cia, the nsa, the fbi and the us military, which used it in afghanistan to help predict where roadside bombs would be. 2020: it went public on the new york stock exchange through a direct public offering rather than a traditional ipo. 2023: it launched aip, its artificial intelligence platform, and reported its first profitable quarter under standard accounting rules (gaap), $31 million, after about twenty years of losses. 2024: it joined the s&p 500 and moved its listing to nasdaq.

what it sells product who uses it what it does gotham militaries, intelligence agencies, counter-terrorism analysts, some police forces joins data from many sources so analysts can find links, patterns and anomalies foundry companies and civil government, such as airbus, merck kgaa and nhs england an operating platform for an organisation’s data: integrate it, model it, build applications on it apollo palantir’s own products, and customers’ secure environments delivers and updates software continuously (ci/cd) across all of a customer’s environments aip both government and commercial customers brings large language models into customers’ private networks, so they can build ai “agents” on their own data apollo’s software-as-a-service is one of five offerings the us department of defense has authorised for its most sensitive mission-critical systems (impact level 5).

how the money comes in large, long contracts. government deals are often worth hundreds of millions: a nearly $1 billion software contract from the us navy in november 2024, a seven-year, £330 million contract from nhs england in 2023 to run its federated data platform, and a three-year, £240 million contract from the uk ministry of defence in december 2025. engineers on site. its “forward-deployed engineers” work inside the customer’s organisation to connect the data and build what the customer needs. analysis: it is expensive, but it ties the software closely to how the customer works. boot camps instead of long pilots. to sell aip faster, palantir runs five-day boot camps to onboard prospective customers. commercial growth. in the fourth quarter of 2025, revenue was $1.4 billion, up 70% on a year earlier; us commercial revenue rose 137% to $507 million, and total contract value signed in the quarter reached a record $4.3 billion. palantir revenue and net income, 2018 to 2024 revenue grows every year from 595 million dollars in 2018 to 2.87 billion in 2024. net income is a loss each year from 2018 to 2022, largest in 2020 at 1.17 billion dollars, then turns to a profit of 210 million in 2023 and 462 million in 2024. 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 $2.87b −$1.17b loss revenue net loss / profit revenue (filled) and net income (dashed below the line when a loss, solid above it when a profit), in us dollars. twenty years of losses, then profit from 2023. full-year 2025 figures are not shown because the sources we used disagree on them; the chart stops at 2024, where they agree.

how investors value it most companies are valued on their profits. palantir’s price is far ahead of its profits, so investors are paying mainly for expected growth. three numbers show the gap: measure number market value in 2025, per the economist $430 billion that value divided by 2024 earnings ($462 million) over 600 times price against expected sales, november 2025 85 times forward annual sales, the most expensive in the s&p 500 fortune noted the contrast in 2025: among the world’s most valuable companies, yet with revenue far below the $50 billion needed to join the fortune 500. compare databricks , a private company valued at about 27 times its revenue, and see how companies are valued for the methods. our view: the price only makes sense if aip turns palantir into the standard way large organisations run ai on their own data, and governments keep spending on defence software. the other view: the economist called it possibly “the most over-valued firm of all time”; at these multiples, even strong growth may not be enough, and a slowdown would hit the share price hard.

why it is controversial palantir’s customers include immigration enforcement, police forces and militaries, and its software can bring together a great deal of information about individuals. civil liberties groups have raised concerns about mass surveillance; its use for predictive policing has drawn criticism over racial bias; and the nhs contract was criticised by the british medical association and others over patient privacy and procurement transparency. the other view: alex karp disputes the surveillance characterisation, and supporters point out that palantir does not collect or store data of its own: customers bring data they already hold, and keep the rights to it. they also point to uses such as fraud detection for the us government and the nhs’s covid-19 vaccination programme. as with any powerful tool, the argument is less about the software than about who uses it, for what, and with what oversight.

c.h: Forward-deployed or self-serve? Choosing by requirement
c.x: forward-deployed or self-serve? choosing by requirement palantir’s sales model has been widely copied: the wall street journal and business insider describe a “palantir mafia” of start-ups founded by former employees. if you are building a software business, which model fits depends on what is true for you: if this is true for you it leans towards few, very large customers with messy, sensitive data forward-deployed engineers working on site customers in classified or disconnected networks deployment tooling like apollo, and certifications, before anything else many smaller customers who can set things up themselves a self-serve product with good documentation you need to prove value quickly to a sceptical buyer a short, hands-on boot camp on the customer’s own data you cannot afford engineers per customer yet self-serve first; add on-site help for the biggest accounts

c.h: What engineers can take from it
c.x: what engineers can take from it integrating messy data is where much of the value is; models are only as good as the data under them. engineers who sit with users learn what to build faster than any requirements document. who your software serves is a choice with consequences; the ethics are part of the engineering.

the idea most systems store current state and overwrite it: a subscription row says plan = 'pro' . event sourcing stores the sequence of facts instead: subscriptionstarted(basic) , planupgraded(pro) , paymentfailed , paymentsucceeded . current state is computed by replaying (folding) those events. the events are the source of truth; every other view is derived from them and can be rebuilt. term meaning event an immutable fact in the past tense, with data and metadata (who, when, causation) stream the ordered events of one entity, e.g. subscription-42 aggregate the entity that enforces business rules; rebuilt from its stream; decides which new events a command produces command a request to change something ( upgradeplan ); may be rejected event store append-only storage of streams with per-stream versions projection / read model a view built from events for querying (a table, a search index, a cache) snapshot saved aggregate state at a version, to avoid replaying long streams cqrs separate models for writes (commands) and reads (queries); event sourcing usually comes with it

when it is worth it good fits history is the product: audit trails, finance, legal records, compliance. you need to answer "what was the state on date x, and why?" several different read models from the same changes. complex domains where business events are first-class (orders, claims, subscriptions). poor fits simple crud with no interest in history. teams new to the pattern on a deadline. data that must be truly deleted on request with no workaround. apply it to the one part of the system that needs it, not the whole system.

the flow a command arrives: upgradeplan(subscription-42, pro) . load the aggregate's events (from the latest snapshot) and fold them into current state. the aggregate checks business rules and decides zero or more new events. append them with the expected version (optimistic concurrency). if someone else appended first, reload and retry. projections consume new events and update read models. queries read from the read models, which may lag slightly behind. the event sourcing flow six numbered steps. 1: a command arrives, upgradeplan for subscription 42. 2: the aggregate's past events are loaded, from the latest snapshot, and folded into its current state. 3: the aggregate checks the business rules and decides new events. 4: the events are appended with the expected version; if someone else appended first, the write is refused and the command reloads and retries. 5: projections consume the new events and update read models. 6: queries read the read models, which may lag slightly behind. command upgradeplan(42, pro) 1 load + fold events → state 2 decide rules → new events 3 append if version still n 4 projections update read models 5 queries read models 6 conflict: reload and retry may lag slightly behind the events the six steps above, drawn: along the top, then back along the bottom. the dashed arrow is optimistic concurrency: an append that finds a newer version is refused, and the command starts again from fresh events.

an aggregate in java sealed interface subevent permits started, planupgraded, cancelled {} record started(string id, string plan, instant at) implements subevent {} record planupgraded(string id, string plan, instant at) implements subevent {} record cancelled(string id, string reason, instant at) implements subevent {} enum status { active, cancelled } record subscription(string id, string plan, status status, int version) { static subscription replay(list<subevent> events) { subscription s = null; for (subevent e : events) s = apply(s, e); return s; } static subscription apply(subscription s, subevent e) { // pure: no side effects return switch (e) { case started st -> new subscription(st.id(), st.plan(), status.active, 1); case planupgraded u -> new subscription(s.id(), u.plan(), s.status(), s.version() + 1); case cancelled c -> new subscription(s.id(), s.plan(), status.cancelled, s.version() + 1); }; } list<subevent> upgrade(string newplan, instant now) { // decide if (status != status.active) throw new illegalstateexception("subscription not active"); if (plan.equals(newplan)) return list.of(); // idempotent: nothing to do return list.of(new planupgraded(id, newplan, now)); } } separate decide (rules, may reject) from apply (pure state change). apply must never fail for a stored event: it already happened.

an event store in postgres create table events ( global_position bigint generated always as identity primary key, stream_id text not null, version int not null, type text not null, data jsonb not null, metadata jsonb not null default '{}', -- user, causation_id, correlation_id recorded_at timestamptz not null default now(), unique (stream_id, version) -- optimistic concurrency ); -- load a stream select type, data, version from events where stream_id = 'subscription-42' order by version; -- append, expecting the stream to be at version 3 insert into events (stream_id, version, type, data) values ('subscription-42', 4, 'planupgraded', '{"plan":"pro"}'); -- unique violation → another writer got version 4 first → reload, re-decide, retry caution: identity values are assigned at insert, not commit, so with concurrent writers a projection reading by global_position can miss a row committed late. dedicated event stores (kurrentdb, formerly eventstoredb) or a transactional outbox with careful checkpointing handle this.

projections and read models // a projection keeps a checkpoint and is idempotent void handle(storedevent e) { tx.run(() -> { switch (e.payload()) { case started s -> db.upsert("subscription_view", s.id(), map.of("plan", s.plan(), "status", "active")); case planupgraded u -> db.update("subscription_view", u.id(), map.of("plan", u.plan())); case cancelled c -> db.update("subscription_view", c.id(), map.of("status", "cancelled")); } db.savecheckpoint("subscription_view", e.globalposition()); // same transaction }); } store the checkpoint in the same transaction as the update, so a crash never applies an event twice or skips one. to change a read model, build a new one by replaying all events, then switch reads to it. read models are eventually consistent. show users "updating…" or read their own writes from the aggregate when it matters.

evolving events events are immutable and permanent. you cannot fix old ones in place; plan their shape carefully. additive changes (new optional fields with defaults) are safe. version the event type ( planupgraded.v2 ) when the meaning changes. upcasting: convert old event versions to the current shape when reading, so the code handles one version. never rename or reuse an event type for a different meaning. name events in business language ( paymentfailed ), not technical ( rowupdated ).

snapshots, size and deletion snapshots every n events (or when replay gets slow) store state plus version; load the snapshot, then only later events. keep streams short-lived where the domain allows (one stream per billing period, not per customer forever). personal data and deletion: keep personal data out of events where possible (reference an id), or encrypt it per person and destroy the key to "forget" them (crypto-shredding). archiving: move closed streams to cold storage after their retention period.

testing: given, when, then @test void upgradeemitseventwhenactive() { var given = list.<subevent>of(new started("s1", "basic", t0)); var events = subscription.replay(given).upgrade("pro", t1); // when assertthat(events).containsexactly(new planupgraded("s1", "pro", t1)); // then } @test void cannotupgradecancelled() { var given = list.<subevent>of(new started("s1", "basic", t0), new cancelled("s1", "user", t1)); assertthatthrownby(() -> subscription.replay(given).upgrade("pro", t2)) .hasmessagecontaining("not active"); } aggregates tested this way need no database or mocks: given past events, when a command, then expected events or a rejection.

c.h: The lightweight version: an append-only ledger
c.x: the lightweight version: an append-only ledger many systems get most of the benefit without full event sourcing: an append-only table with one row per state change, and current state from a "latest event" view. never update, never delete. -- bigquery: current state of each pipeline stage from its event log create or replace view `p.ops.v_job_run_latest` as select * from `p.ops.job_run_events` where true qualify row_number() over (partition by run_date, stage order by event_ts desc) = 1; you get history, auditability and "what happened on date x" with ordinary sql. add aggregates, projections and replay only if the domain needs them.

tools kurrentdb (formerly eventstoredb): a database built for event streams, subscriptions and projections. axon framework / axon server (java): aggregates, sagas, projections and an event store. postgres with an events table: simple and often enough, with the caveats above. kafka is a good event log for distribution, and its docs offer it as a backend for event sourcing, but it lacks two things an event store usually gives you: efficient per-entity stream reads and per-stream optimistic concurrency. many systems store events in a database and publish them to kafka through an outbox.

common mistakes event sourcing the whole system instead of the part that needs history. events that mirror table changes ( customerupdated with every field) instead of business facts. side effects (emails, payments) inside apply , so a replay sends them again. querying the event store for lists and searches instead of building read models. no plan for event versioning, personal data or replay time. treating eventual consistency of read models as a bug rather than designing for it.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain events, streams, aggregates, projections and cqrs read an event stream and follow how state was built tell an append-only ledger from full event sourcing 2 practitioner implement an aggregate with decide/apply and given-when-then tests build idempotent projections with checkpoints append with optimistic concurrency 3 senior decide where event sourcing fits in a system and where it does not design event schemas, versioning and upcasting plan snapshots, replay, rebuilds and personal-data handling 4 expert lead event-sourced architectures across domains and teams choose and operate event stores at scale set standards for event modelling and governance each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the method, in order clarify requirements. functional: what users can do. non-functional: scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, cost, security, compliance. write down what is out of scope. estimate. users, requests per second (average and peak), read/write ratio, data size per item, storage per year, bandwidth. numbers decide the design. define the api. the few endpoints or events that deliver the functional requirements, with their inputs and outputs. model the data. entities, keys, access patterns ("fetch by x, list by y sorted by z"), and which store fits each pattern. draw the high-level design. clients, load balancer, services, stores, caches, queues. one request path end to end. deep-dive the hard parts. the component that is hottest, biggest or most consistency-sensitive. show how it scales and fails. find bottlenecks and failure modes. what breaks first at 10×? what happens when each dependency is down? state trade-offs. what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change it. the same steps make a good design document. start simple, and add a component only when a requirement or a number demands it.

scaling playbook, cheapest first measure. find the actual bottleneck: cpu, memory, db queries, a slow dependency. fix the query. indexes, fewer round trips, no n+1. often 10–100× for free. scale up the instance. boring and effective. make services stateless and scale out behind a load balancer. cache hot reads; add a cdn for public content. read replicas for read-heavy databases. move work off the request path to queues and workers. partition big tables; archive cold data. shard or move to a distributed database only when one primary cannot take the writes.

load balancing: sharing the traffic a load balancer sits in front of several servers and decides which one handles each request. it also watches them: a server that fails its health checks stops receiving traffic, which is why a failing check shows up to clients as a 502 or 503 (see networking for layer 4 and layer 7 balancers). how it chooses what it does fits when round robin the first request to the first server, the next to the second, and round again; can be weighted so larger servers get more requests are similar in cost and servers are alike least connections each new request to the server with the fewest active connections; can also be weighted requests vary in length, such as long downloads or streams hash the same key (a user, a session, an ip address) always goes to the same server a server holds something per key, such as a local cache or session consistent hashing keys and servers on a ring, so adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys (see distributing data above) the set of servers changes often; cdns and distributed caches use it random each request to a randomly chosen server; with many clients the load evens out the simplest option, often good enough at scale static or dynamic. round robin and random ignore how busy each server is; least connections and response-time-based methods use live load information. static methods are simpler and work well for fairly regular work such as web requests. the balancer must not be the single point of failure. load balancers are usually run in high-availability pairs, or as a managed cloud service built that way. sticky sessions (sending a user back to the same server) make servers stateful again; prefer stateless servers with session data in a shared store, so any server can take any request. dns can balance too : round-robin dns gives clients different addresses in turn, with no balancer at all, but it cannot react quickly to a failed server because answers are cached.

c.h: Service discovery: how services find each other
c.x: service discovery: how services find each other in a system of many services, instances start, stop and move all the time, so their addresses change. service discovery is how one service finds the current address of another without anyone writing it down. the rule: never hard-code an instance’s ip address. approach how it works where you meet it dns names call a stable name; the platform keeps the name pointing at healthy instances kubernetes services give each service a dns name (see kubernetes ) a platform url or load balancer call one stable address; the platform routes to whatever instances exist cloud run urls, a cloud load balancer in front of a group of machines (see cloud run ) a service registry instances register themselves; callers ask the registry, which drops instances that fail health checks consul, often where services run on virtual machines as well as kubernetes (see service mesh & istio ) a service mesh a proxy beside each service handles discovery, retries and encryption for it istio and linkerd (see service mesh & istio ) our view: use what your platform already gives you (dns names on kubernetes, urls on a managed platform) and add a registry or a mesh only when a requirement needs it, such as services spread across kubernetes and virtual machines. the other view: some teams adopt a mesh early so that discovery, retries and encryption are consistent from the start, accepting the extra moving parts.

scale up or scale out scaling up (vertical) adds cpu, memory or storage to one machine. scaling out (horizontal) adds more machines, for example going from one web server to three behind a load balancer. if this is true for you it leans towards the bottleneck is one database or stateful service, and a bigger machine is available scale up first: no change to the code, no coordination between nodes the service is stateless and traffic rises and falls scale out, and scale back in when traffic drops you need to survive the loss of a machine scale out: one machine, however large, is a single point of failure the work cannot be split (wikipedia notes that some applications do not scale horizontally) scale up, or redesign the work so it can be split you are near the largest machine you can buy or rent scale out, which usually means sharding or partitioning the data wikipedia lists the benefits of scaling up as avoiding the extra management, programming effort and coordination problems (throughput, latency, synchronisation) that come with more nodes. that is why the scaling playbook above starts with the cheapest step and keeps scaling out of the data for last.

c.h: Data locality: move the work to the data
c.x: data locality: move the work to the data moving data across a network costs time and money; moving the code is usually far cheaper. apache hadoop was built on this idea: it splits files into blocks across the machines of a cluster, then sends packaged code to the machines that hold each block, so the processing happens where the data already is. keep services near their data : an application in one region reading a database in another pays the round trip on every query (see the latency numbers above). bring data near users : cdns and caches are data locality for reads (see caching ). push filtering down : ask the database for the ten rows you need, not ten thousand to filter in the application (see sql skills ). mind the bill : cloud providers charge for data leaving a region or zone (see cloud cost ).

caching strategies cache-aside: app reads cache, on a miss reads the db and fills the cache. most common. read-through: the cache library loads from the db itself on a miss. write-through: write to cache and db together; reads always warm, writes slower. write-behind: write to cache, flush to db later; fast, but data can be lost. ttl bounds staleness; explicit invalidation on write keeps it fresher but is easy to miss. stampede: a popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the db. use request coalescing, a lock, or early random refresh. what to key on: include everything that changes the answer (user, locale, version). a missing part of the key serves one user's data to another.

rate limiting token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate up to a burst size; each request takes one. allows short bursts. the usual choice. leaky bucket: requests drain at a fixed rate; smooths traffic, no bursts. fixed window: n per minute; simple, but allows 2n across a window boundary. sliding window: counts over the last 60 s; fairer, slightly more state. where: at the gateway per api key or user; inside services to protect a fragile dependency. response: http 429 with retry-after , so well-behaved clients back off. distributed: keep counters in redis with atomic increments, or accept per-instance limits. the whole journey, the four algorithms side by side with a simulation, and failure handling: rate limiting .

distributing data replication copies data for availability and read scale. leader-follower is the common model; multi-leader and leaderless trade consistency for write availability. partitioning / sharding splits data for write scale and size. choose a key that spreads load and matches the main access pattern. consistent hashing places keys and nodes on a ring, so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/n of the keys. used by caches and distributed stores. hot keys (one celebrity, one big tenant, today's date) defeat even spreading. split them, cache them, or add a random suffix. quorums: with n replicas, reading r and writing w where r + w > n means every read set overlaps every write set, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write.

designing for failure timeouts on every network call , shorter than the caller's own timeout. retries only for idempotent operations, with backoff and jitter, and a cap. circuit breakers and bulkheads so one sick dependency cannot take down the rest. graceful degradation: serve cached or partial results, and say so. never present "could not check" as "nothing found". redundancy: multiple instances across zones; regional failover only if the requirement justifies the cost. backpressure: queues with limits; shed load early (429/503) instead of collapsing. backups you have restored, with a known recovery point (rpo: how much data you can lose) and recovery time (rto: how long you can be down).

worked example: a url shortener requirements: create a short link; redirect fast; links never change; 100 m new links/year; reads 100× writes; 99.9% available. estimates: writes ≈ 3/s average; reads ≈ 300/s, peak ~1,500/s. 100 m × 500 b ≈ 50 gb/year. api: post /links {url} → {code} ; get /{code} → 301/302 redirect. data: link(code pk, url, created_at, owner) . access pattern is lookup by code only: any key-value store or postgres works. code generation: base62 of a unique id (7 chars ≈ 3.5 trillion codes). use a sequence or id service to avoid collisions; random codes need a uniqueness check. high level: load balancer → stateless service → cache (hot codes) → database. cdn can cache redirects for popular links. deep dive: reads are the load: cache-aside with long ttl works because links are immutable. writes are tiny. trade-offs: 301 is cached by browsers (fewer hits, no click counting); 302 keeps analytics. click analytics go to a queue and a warehouse, not the redirect path.

the design, drawn a url shortener, high level two paths. the read path, which carries the load: a browser asks for a short code; a cdn may answer popular redirects; otherwise a load balancer passes it to a stateless service, which checks a cache of hot codes and only then the database, and returns a 301 or 302 redirect. the write path is small: post a url, get a code made from a unique id in base62, stored in the database. click analytics go to a queue and a warehouse, off the redirect path. read path (~300/s, peak ~1,500/s) browser cdn load balancer service cache: hot codes database on a miss redirect: 301 is cached by browsers; 302 keeps click counts write path (~3/s) post /links {url} code = base62(unique id) click analytics: queue the worked example as a picture. reads are a hundred times the writes, so the read path gets the cache and the cdn; the links never change, so a long ttl is safe.

c.h: Worked example: search over 20 M orders
c.x: worked example: search over 20 m orders requirements: keyword and filter search (store, date, product), open an order, look up its refunds. results within 500 ms at p95. data refreshed daily. a customer's erasure request must apply everywhere immediately. estimates: ~60 searches/s at peak; 20 m records, ~40 gb metadata, ~140 gb line items and notes. data flow: order-system exports → landing bucket → warehouse layers (raw → foundation → consumable) → serving postgres. the warehouse is the record; postgres is a read-optimised copy. see data engineering . serving: stateless api on cloud run; postgres with full-text (gin) and b-tree indexes on filter columns; read replica for search; cache for hot queries and order pages. stable identity: ids never renumber, because urls, invoices and refunds refer to them. loads upsert on a stable key. erasure requests: checked on every read path (search, page, api, exports) from the application database, not baked into the copy, so a new request takes effect without a reload. freshness and honesty: each result carries its source and date; when a source is stale or unreachable, the api says so rather than returning a confident empty result. scaling later: move search to a dedicated index (or add semantic search with embeddings) when relevance or load outgrows postgres; keep postgres for lookups.

more practice problems rate limiter for a public api notification service (email, push, sms) with retries and user preferences news feed or timeline chat with presence and message history file upload and processing pipeline job scheduler that runs millions of tasks reliably metrics and logging pipeline rag question-answering over company documents payment flow with a saga and idempotency keys for each: run the method above, and write the trade-offs down. the written reasoning is the skill.

the short answer it is three in the morning and a partner’s integration has a bug: a retry loop with no pause, sending thousands of requests a second at your orders api. without a rate limiter, those requests queue up behind your real customers’ requests, the database slows down, and soon nobody can place an order. with one, the partner gets a polite “not now” in milliseconds, and everyone else carries on as if nothing had happened. that is the whole job: count requests per caller, compare against a policy, and say yes or no before the expensive work starts. the difficult parts are the details: who counts as a caller, which algorithm does the counting, how many servers share one count, and what happens when the counter itself is slow or gone. the short version of the system design card is on system design ; this page takes each of those details in turn.

the path of one request it helps to follow a single request from start to finish, because each step answers one question. the path of one request through a rate limiter a client sends a request to the gateway, which works out who is calling. the rate limiter picks the policies that apply, asks the shared counter store to check and update the count in one atomic step, and decides. if allowed, the request goes on to the backend api. if not, the gateway answers 429 too many requests straight away, and the backend never sees it. client app, partner gateway who is calling? rate limiter policy + algorithm backend api the capacity counter store shared, atomic allowed check and update in one step rejected: the gateway answers 429 at once reject early, protect what is behind. a rejected request costs the gateway and the counter store a little work; it never reaches the backend it would have overloaded. the edge (a cdn or waf) absorbs volumetric attacks before anything else; a rate limiter is not the place to soak up a flood. the gateway matches the route and works out who is calling: an api key, a user and tenant from a verified token, or, for anonymous traffic, an ip address. the limiter picks every policy that applies to this caller and route (a per-user limit, a per-tenant limit, a global limit for the endpoint), and runs the algorithm each one names. the counter store checks and updates the count in a single atomic step, so two requests arriving together cannot both take the last slot. the decision goes back to the gateway: forward the request to the backend, or answer 429 itself, straight away. the limiter is a logical step, not necessarily a separate service. it can run as a plugin inside the gateway (no extra network hop), as a dedicated limiter service the gateways call, or as a library inside each application. most teams start with the first and only move when they need limits shared across many gateways or products.

what the client sees a good limiter does not just refuse; it tells the client what happened and when to try again, so well-behaved clients slow down by themselves. http/1.1 429 too many requests retry-after: 30 ratelimit-policy: "basic";q=100;w=60 ratelimit: "basic";a=0;w=30 429 too many requests was defined in rfc 6585 (2012): it “indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time”, the response should explain the condition, and it may include retry-after . retry-after , defined in rfc 9110, tells the client how long it ought to wait before a follow-up request. ratelimit-policy and ratelimit are newer header fields from the ietf http apis working group: one describes the quota policies, the other the quota available right now. in the example, q=100;w=60 is a quota of 100 in a 60-second window, and a=0 says none is left. they are still an internet-draft (revision 12 at the time of writing), so check what your clients understand before relying on them. many apis still send their own x-ratelimit-* headers. on the client side, the matching courtesy is to honour retry-after and back off with jitter (see the retry storm on distributed systems ). a client that retries a 429 immediately is the problem the limiter exists to solve.

c.h: Who is the caller? Designing the key
c.x: who is the caller? designing the key every counter lives under a key made of three parts: an identity, a scope, and the window or policy it belongs to. get the key wrong and the cleverest algorithm counts the wrong thing. key (illustrative) what it limits rate:user:123:orders one user, on one api rate:apikey:abc:global one api key, across every route rate:tenant:acme:read a whole customer organisation, on read operations rate:ip:203.0.113.7:login anonymous attempts to log in from one address prefer a verified identity. limits by ip alone hit everyone behind one corporate proxy or mobile carrier at once, and let an attacker with many addresses slip through. trust forwarded addresses only from your own proxies. the client’s address usually arrives in x-forwarded-for or the standard forwarded header (rfc 7239), and anyone can write those headers. take the address added by your own outermost proxy, not the first one in the list. give keys an expiry, so counters for callers who have gone away do not pile up for ever.

four algorithms, one simulation there are four algorithms you will meet again and again. a policy picks one of them; they are alternatives, not layers. the quickest way to feel the difference is to feed them all the same traffic. this plain python program sends 100 requests in the last second of one minute and another 100 in the first second of the next, against a limit of 100 a minute: """four rate-limiting algorithms, limit 100 requests a minute, fed the same traffic.""" def fixed_window(times, limit=100, window=60): counts, allowed = {}, 0 for t in times: w = int(t // window) # which clock-aligned minute if counts.get(w, 0) < limit: counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1 allowed += 1 return allowed def sliding_log(times, limit=100, window=60): log, allowed = [], 0 for t in times: log = [x for x in log if x > t - window] # drop timestamps older than a minute if len(log) < limit: log.append(t) allowed += 1 return allowed def sliding_counter(times, limit=100, window=60): counts, allowed = {}, 0 for t in times: w = int(t // window) elapsed = (t % window) / window # how far into the current minute estimate = counts.get(w - 1, 0) * (1 - elapsed) + counts.get(w, 0) if estimate < limit: counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1 allowed += 1 return allowed def token_bucket(times, capacity=100, rate=100 / 60): tokens, last, allowed = capacity, 0.0, 0 for t in times: tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (t - last) * rate) # refill lazily, no timer needed last = t if tokens >= 1: tokens -= 1 allowed += 1 return allowed # 100 requests in the last second of one minute, then 100 in the first second of the next burst = [59 + i / 100 for i in range(100)] + [60 + i / 100 for i in range(100)] print("200 requests within 2 seconds, across a minute boundary:") for f in (fixed_window, sliding_log, sliding_counter, token_bucket): print(f" {f.__name__:16} allowed {f(burst)}") what it printed when we ran it: 200 requests within 2 seconds, across a minute boundary: fixed_window allowed 200 sliding_log allowed 100 sliding_counter allowed 102 token_bucket allowed 103 algorithm how it works in the run above trade-off fixed window one counter per key per clock-aligned minute; reset when the minute changes 200 allowed: the limit holds per window, not per any 60 seconds simplest and cheapest, but allows up to double the limit across a boundary sliding log keeps a timestamp for every accepted request and counts the last 60 seconds exactly 100 precise, but memory grows with the limit, which hurts at high volumes sliding counter two fixed-window counters, the previous one weighted by how much of it still overlaps the last 60 seconds 102: an estimate, close but not exact two counters per key, smooths the boundary spike; assumes requests were spread evenly token bucket a bucket of up to n tokens refills at a steady rate; each request takes one; refill is computed lazily on each request 103: a full bucket of 100, plus about 1.7 tokens a second of refill allows controlled bursts up to the capacity, enforces the long-run rate; can charge expensive requests more than one token the token bucket comes from networking, where it checks that packets conform to limits on bandwidth and burstiness. its close relative, the leaky bucket, drains requests at a fixed rate instead, and the generic cell rate algorithm used in atm networks is one form of it. redis’s own documentation for incr shows the fixed-window pattern with a counter per ip per second.

many gateways, one limit here is the trap that catches almost every first distributed limiter. put three gateways behind a load balancer, give each its own in-memory counter with a limit of 100 a minute, and one user spread across them can make 300 requests. each gateway honestly thinks the user is under the limit. local counters do not add up to a global limit. the fix is a shared counter store that every gateway consults, commonly redis, though it is one option among several. sharing brings a second trap: two gateways reading the counter at 99, both comparing it with 100, and both writing 100. both requests were allowed; the limit was 100 and you served 101. the read, the comparison and the write must happen as one atomic step. -- the counter and its expiry in one atomic step (the pattern in redis's incr documentation) local current = redis.call("incr", keys[1]) if current == 1 then redis.call("expire", keys[1], 60) end return current redis’s documentation walks through exactly this. it shows a version with a race condition (a client that increments but never sets the expiry leaks the key) and fixes it with a short lua script, because redis guarantees a script’s atomic execution. if this is true for you lean towards one instance, or a rough limit per instance is good enough a local limiter: fastest, no network, nothing extra to fail the limit is a promise to customers or protects a shared backend a distributed limiter with a shared, atomic store you need both speed and accuracy a cheap local pre-check, then the global check; a common combination

when the limiter itself breaks a limiter is a dependency on the hot path of every request, so sooner or later the counter store will be slow, partitioned or down. decide what happens before it does, per route, because there is no single right answer ( analysis ): choice what happens suits fail open : allow users are not blocked by a limiter outage, but the backend is unprotected exactly when something is already wrong public read apis, ideally with a local emergency limit as a floor fail closed : reject strong protection, but a limiter failure becomes a user-facing outage login, one-time passwords, payments and other abuse-sensitive or costly operations local fallback each instance enforces a share of the global limit on its own until the store returns most production systems: rough, but bounded the other failures are quieter: a timeout with no budget (a few milliseconds, no long retries), a stale policy cache that keeps enforcing old limits, replica lag after a failover that loses recent increments, and retries that turn a slow store into a stampede.

c.h: Scaling, and several limits at once
c.x: scaling, and several limits at once hot keys. one large tenant can send all its traffic to a single counter on a single shard. the usual remedies, each a trade-off ( analysis ): partition the counter, accepting a merge step; give each gateway a lease of tokens to spend locally (say 500 of a global 10,000), accepting that leases make the global limit approximate; build a hierarchy of local, regional and global limits; or give exceptionally hot tenants dedicated capacity. several limits on one request. a request may have to pass a global limit, a tenant limit, a user limit and an endpoint limit, and it is allowed only if every one passes. the subtle bug is the partial update: the global and tenant counters are incremented, then the user limit says no, and the request has used up quota it was never given. check every limit first and commit only if all pass, or keep the counters where a single atomic script can check and update them all together.

security, and watching the limiter what it is not. a rate limiter is one layer of abuse protection. it does not replace authentication or authorisation, and it is not ddos protection: volumetric floods have to be absorbed at the edge. use tight limits on login, password reset and one-time passwords, keyed per account and per ip, so one attacker cannot try many accounts and many attackers cannot hammer one (see security ). measure it separately from the apis it protects. a healthy api can hide a sick limiter that is failing open. track requests evaluated, allowed and rejected per tenant and route, the limiter’s own latency, store timeouts and errors, fail-open activations and hot-key concentration, and alert when 429s spike for one tenant or the fallback switches on (see observability ).

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: start with a token bucket per api key, inside the gateway, with a shared atomic store once you run more than one gateway; send 429 with retry-after ; and decide fail-open or fail-closed per route before the first outage forces the decision. the other view: for many internal services a local, per-instance limit is honest enough and removes a network dependency from every request; a distributed limiter is real infrastructure, with its own failures to design for, and is worth it only when the limit is a promise or the backend is shared.

choose by requirement if this is true for you lean towards short bursts are fine, the long-run rate matters token bucket cheapest possible check, boundary bursts acceptable fixed window smoother than fixed, still cheap sliding counter exact rolling count, modest volume sliding log requests differ greatly in cost token bucket charging more tokens for expensive calls

c.h: Who writes specifications, and how they become final
c.x: who writes specifications, and how they become final body what it publishes how a document becomes final ietf and the rfc editor rfcs: the internet’s protocols and formats (http, tls, json, oauth) not every rfc is a standard: the ietf adopts some as internet standards, while many are informational or experimental. the header of each rfc says which (“category: standards track”, “informational”) w3c web standards such as wcag drafts move through the w3c process to a w3c recommendation, the finished standard whatwg the html living standard and other web platform standards a living standard: updated continuously rather than released as numbered versions ecma tc39 ecma-262, the ecmascript (javascript) language proposals move through numbered stages; at stage 4 a proposal is finished and incorporated into the specification, which is published as a yearly edition iso and iec, ieee sql (iso/iec 9075), dates and times (iso 8601), floating point (ieee 754), posix (ieee 1003) developed by the standards body’s committees and published by the body open-source foundations openapi (openapi initiative, a linux foundation project), cloudevents (cncf), opentelemetry, oci image format public repositories, working groups and tagged releases language communities java (the jls and jvms, with jdk enhancement proposals, jeps, for changes), python (peps) a proposal document is discussed, accepted and implemented; a pep is a design document with a concise technical specification and a rationale

how to read a specification learn the key words. rfc 2119 defines them: must (or required, shall) is an absolute requirement; should (or recommended) means there may be valid reasons to do otherwise, but the full implications must be understood and weighed first; may (or optional) is truly optional. capitals matter. rfc 8174 clarifies that the words carry that meaning only when they appear in capitals. a lower-case “should” is ordinary english. normative and informative. requirements are normative; examples, notes and appendices marked informative explain but do not bind. check the status and what replaced it. an rfc’s header lists what it obsoletes and updates: rfc 9110 (http semantics) obsoletes rfcs 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235 and several others, and portions of rfc 7230. quote the current one. read the table of contents first, then only the sections your question needs. few people read a spec front to back the first time.

c.h: Why it is worth the effort
c.x: why it is worth the effort our view: reading the specification for the two or three formats you use every day pays back many times. you stop arguing from blog posts, you can tell a library bug from your own, and you can write a precise bug report: quoting the section of rfc 9110 on 404 not found settles a review in one line. the other view: specifications are long, formal and written for implementers. for most daily work a good library and its documentation are enough, and time spent on the spec is time not spent shipping. go to the spec when the library and your expectation disagree.

the catalogue: languages ecma-262 , the ecmascript language specification, edited in public by tc39; proposals are tracked in its proposals repository (see javascript ). the java language and virtual machine specifications , one edition per java se release; changes to the jdk are proposed as jeps (see java ). peps , python enhancement proposals, and the python language reference (see python ).

c.h: Describing an interface: choose by requirement
c.x: describing an interface: choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards clients call you with http requests and wait for a response openapi services publish and consume messages on a broker asyncapi, with cloudevents for the envelope clients need to choose the fields they get, across related data graphql’s schema typed calls between your own services, with streaming and generated clients protocol buffers with grpc you only need to validate a json document, such as a config file or a message body json schema an ai agent must discover and call your tools mcp our view: write the description first and generate code from it, so the document is the contract. the other view: generating the description from code keeps it from drifting from what runs, and suits teams that change the api often.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation read must, should and may as rfc 2119 and rfc 8174 define them find the specification behind a format or protocol you use every day tell an rfc that is a standard from one that is informational 2 practitioner settle a disagreement by quoting the section of a spec describe an api in openapi, asyncapi, graphql or protobuf check which rfcs a document obsoletes before you cite it 3 senior choose an interface description by requirement write a specification other teams can build from track proposals that will change your stack (jeps, peps, tc39 stages) 4 expert represent your organisation in a standards body or working group set the interface and versioning standards across an organisation contribute to a specification or its conformance tests each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

where caches live layer example good for watch out for browser http cache static assets, per-user responses wrong cache-control serving stale pages cdn cloud cdn public content near users caching personalised responses by mistake gateway apigee responsecache identical api responses keys that ignore the caller's identity in-process caffeine, functools.lru_cache hot reference data, nanosecond reads each instance has its own copy; memory per instance distributed redis / memorystore shared across instances, sessions, rate limits network hop; one more system to run database buffer cache, materialised views repeated queries and aggregates refresh schedules warehouse bigquery cached results, bi engine repeated dashboard queries cache is skipped for some queries (non-deterministic functions, changed tables) model api prompt caching long, repeated prompt prefixes any change in the prefix invalidates it a cache is a copy, so every cache is a consistency decision. add one when measurements show the need, and decide up front how stale its data may be.

read and write patterns cache-aside (lazy loading): read the cache; on a miss, read the source and fill the cache. simple and the most common. read-through: the cache library loads from the source itself on a miss (caffeine loadingcache ). write-through: writes go to the cache and the source together; reads are always warm; writes are slower. write-behind: write to the cache, persist later. fast, but a crash loses writes. rarely worth it. refresh-ahead: refresh popular entries before they expire so users never wait for a miss.

c.h: Write policies by name: through, back, around
c.x: write policies by name: through, back, around the same three names appear in cpu caches and in application caches, and they answer one question: when data is written, what happens to the cache? policy on a write fits when write-through write to the cache and the backing store together data is read soon after it is written, and writes can afford to be slower write-back (write-behind) write to the cache now, to the store later writes must be fast and losing the most recent ones in a crash is acceptable (rarely, in business data) write-around (no-write allocate) write straight to the store; do not put the data in the cache until it is read much of what is written is rarely read back, such as logs or bulk imports, so it would only push useful entries out of the cache

invalidation ttl: entries expire after a set time. bounds staleness even when an invalidation is missed. every cache entry should have one. delete on write: after updating the source, delete the cache key (not update it), so the next read reloads fresh data. versioned keys: include a version in the key ( order:v3:123 , or a data version number); bump it to invalidate everything at once. event-driven: consume change events (cdc, domain events) and evict affected keys. immutable data (an issued invoice, a fingerprinted file) can be cached forever. the race to know: reader a misses and reads the old value; writer b updates the source and deletes the key; a then writes the old value into the cache. a ttl bounds the damage; versioned keys avoid it.

the race, drawn the cache invalidation race a sequence diagram with four lifelines: reader a, the cache, the source database, and writer b. 1: a asks the cache for a key and misses. 2: a reads the old value from the source. 3: b updates the source. 4: b deletes the cache key. 5: a, still holding the old value, writes it into the cache. the cache now serves the old value until its ttl expires. reader a cache source writer b 1 get key: miss 2 read: old value 3 update to new value 4 delete key 5 set key = old value stale until the ttl expires the race in the last bullet above, step by step. a’s write in step 5 lands after b’s delete, so the cache keeps an old value. a ttl bounds how long; versioned keys avoid it.

stampedes (thundering herd) a popular key expires and thousands of requests miss at once and hit the database together. single flight / request coalescing: only one caller loads; the others wait for its result (caffeine does this per key in-process). distributed lock: set lock:key 1 nx ex 10 in redis; the winner loads, others briefly serve stale or wait. stale-while-revalidate: serve the expired value while one background refresh runs. jittered ttls: add randomness so many keys do not expire at the same moment. probabilistic early refresh: refresh slightly before expiry with rising probability.

key design include every input that changes the answer: ids, filters, page, locale, user or tenant, and the api or data version. normalise inputs (sort filters, lower-case where meaning allows) so equal requests share a key. namespace keys: service:entity:version:id . never share a cache entry across users when the response depends on permissions; include the permission scope in the key, or cache only the permission-independent part. keep values small ; large values make the cache slow and evict everything else.

c.h: What not to cache, or not that way
c.x: what not to cache, or not that way errors and outages as "not found": caching an empty result because the source was down turns "cannot see" into a confident "nothing there" for the whole ttl. negative results (genuinely not found) only briefly, if at all. secrets and tokens in shared caches. personalised data in public caches (cdn, gateway) without per-user keys. data with legal effect (an erasure request, a deletion) behind a long ttl: it must take effect immediately, so check it outside the cache or evict on change. cheap queries: if the source answers in 1 ms, a cache adds complexity for little gain.

c.h: Spring Cache with Caffeine or Redis
c.x: spring cache with caffeine or redis @configuration @enablecaching class cacheconfig { @bean cachemanager cachemanager() { var m = new caffeinecachemanager("orders", "stores"); m.setcaffeine(caffeine.newbuilder() .maximumsize(10_000) .expireafterwrite(duration.ofminutes(10)) .recordstats()); // hit ratio for metrics return m; } } @service class orderservice { @cacheable(cachenames = "orders", key = "#id", unless = "#result == null") public order get(string id) { return repo.find(id).orelse(null); } @cacheevict(cachenames = "orders", key = "#o.id()") public void update(order o) { repo.save(o); } } # switch to redis shared across instances spring: cache: type: redis redis: time-to-live: 10m key-prefix: "shop:v3:" data: redis: host: ${redis_host} port: 6379 @cacheable works through a proxy, like @transactional : calling the method from inside the same class skips the cache.

python: in-process and redis from functools import lru_cache from cachetools import ttlcache, cached @lru_cache(maxsize=1024) # immutable inputs, never expires def store_name(code: str) -> str: ... @cached(ttlcache(maxsize=10_000, ttl=600)) # expires after 10 minutes def order_summary(order_id: str) -> dict: ... import json, random, redis r = redis.redis(host=redis_host, port=6379, decode_responses=true) def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict | none: key = f"shop:order:v3:{order_id}" if (hit := r.get(key)) is not none: return json.loads(hit) o = db.load_order(order_id) # raises if the db is down: do not cache that if o is not none: r.set(key, json.dumps(o), ex=600 + random.randint(0, 60)) # jittered ttl return o def update_order(o: dict) -> none: db.save(o) r.delete(f"shop:order:v3:{o['id']}") # delete after write

redis essentials set order:v3:123 '{"order_ref":"…"}' ex 600 # with ttl set lock:order:123 1 nx ex 10 # only if absent: a simple lock get order:v3:123 del order:v3:123 ttl order:v3:123 incr ratelimit:app42:202611121015 # counters, rate limits expire ratelimit:app42:202611121015 60 info stats # keyspace_hits, keyspace_misses, evicted_keys set maxmemory and an eviction policy ( allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a pure cache). avoid keys * in production; use scan . design so the system still works (slower) if redis is down; a cache should not be a single point of failure. on gcp: memorystore for redis or valkey, private ip, auth and in-transit encryption on.

http and cdn caching # fingerprinted static assets cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable # public api response, shared caches allowed, short freshness cache-control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30 etag: "v3-123-a1b2" # per-user data cache-control: private, max-age=30 # sensitive cache-control: no-store more on headers on web fundamentals . configure the cdn to vary on, or bypass for, the authorization header and cookies.

caching in the data stack bigquery cached results: identical queries reuse results for free for about 24 hours, unless tables changed or the query is non-deterministic. materialised views: bigquery keeps aggregates up to date incrementally and can rewrite queries to use them. bi engine: in-memory acceleration for dashboards. serving tables: a consumable table in postgres is itself a cache of the warehouse; it needs a refresh rule and freshness monitoring like any other cache. pipeline-level: skip work whose inputs have not changed (compare etags or content hashes) instead of recomputing.

measuring a cache hit ratio (hits ÷ requests): low ratios mean wrong keys, short ttls or data that is not reused. latency on hit and on miss. evictions and memory: constant evictions mean the cache is too small for the working set. staleness: how old served data is, against the agreed maximum. source load with and without the cache, to prove it earns its keep.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain cache-aside, ttl and hit ratio use an in-process cache for reference data read http caching headers 2 practitioner add spring or python caching with keys, ttls and eviction on write use redis safely with ttls, eviction policy and a fallback measure hit ratio and staleness 3 senior design multi-layer caching for a system with explicit staleness rules prevent stampedes and invalidation races decide what must never be cached (outages, permissions, legal effect) 4 expert set caching standards and shared cache platforms design caching for global, multi-region systems lead consistency and cost trade-offs across products each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

git you will use daily git switch -c feat/123-short-name origin/main git add -p # stage hunk by hunk git commit -m "fix: reject unparseable order dates" git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main git push -u origin feat/123-short-name git push --force-with-lease # after a rebase; never plain --force git log --oneline --graph -20 git log -s "parse_date" --oneline # commits that added/removed a string git blame -l 40,60 file.py git diff origin/main...head # what my branch changes git show <sha>:path/file # a file at a revision git stash push -m wip; git stash pop git restore file # discard local edits git revert <sha> # undo a merged commit safely git bisect start bad good # binary-search a regression git worktree add ../wt2 -b other origin/main # second checkout git reflog # find "lost" commits

branching & pr habits trunk-based: short-lived branches off main , merged within a day, behind feature flags if unfinished. one concern per pr. if the title needs "and", split it. protect main : pr required, checks required, no force pushes. commit messages say why, not only what. conventional prefixes ( feat: , fix: , chore: ) help changelogs. review for behaviour: tests that would fail without the change, error paths, what happens when a dependency is down. promote artefacts, not branches: build once, tag the image with the commit sha, deploy that same image to each environment.

github actions → gcp (no keys) name: deploy on: push: { branches: [main] } permissions: contents: read id-token: write # needed for workload identity federation concurrency: { group: "deploy-${{ github.ref }}", cancel-in-progress: false } jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - uses: actions/setup-java@v6 with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: 21, cache: gradle } - run: ./gradlew test deploy: needs: test runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: prod # environment secrets, protection rules steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v3 with: workload_identity_provider: ${{ vars.wif_provider }} service_account: ${{ vars.deploy_sa }} - uses: google-github-actions/setup-gcloud@v3 - run: | img=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/${{ vars.gcp_project }}/apps/api:${github_sha::12} gcloud auth configure-docker asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev --quiet docker build -t "$img" . && docker push "$img" echo "img=$img" >> "$github_env" - uses: google-github-actions/deploy-cloudrun@v3 with: { service: api, region: asia-south1, image: "${{ env.img }}" } the major versions shown were current in november 2026; check each action's latest release. for security, pin third-party actions to a full commit sha rather than a tag. a workflow-level paths: filter on a required check can leave a pr waiting forever; skip inside the job instead.

release strategies strategy how when rolling replace instances a few at a time default for stateless services blue/green run old and new side by side, switch traffic at once fast rollback, needs double capacity canary send a small % to the new version, watch metrics, increase risky changes with good metrics feature flag ship code dark, turn it on per user or percentage separating deploy from release expand / contract add the new schema, migrate, remove the old in a later release database changes with zero downtime every release needs a rollback you have practised. a database migration that cannot be rolled back makes the whole release one-way.

blue-green, in plain words think of a theatre with two stages. the audience watches the blue stage while the crew builds the next show on the green one. when green is ready and rehearsed, you swing the audience over in one move. if something goes wrong, you swing them straight back: blue is still standing. before the switch: green gets the same checks real users would give it, through a private url or a test route. the switch is all at once, so a fault reaches every user, but only until you switch back, which takes seconds. keep blue running until you trust green. pulling it down early leaves you with no way back. # kubernetes: a deployment per colour, # labelled version: blue / version: green. # the service's selector picks the live one. kubectl patch service shop-api \ -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}' # roll back: patch it back to "blue". # cloud run: deploy green with no traffic gcloud run deploy api --image=…:4b1c2d0 \ --no-traffic --tag=green # test https://green---api-xxxxx.a.run.app gcloud run services update-traffic api \ --to-tags=green=100 the price: for a while you run two full copies, so you pay for twice the capacity. read martin fowler's bluegreendeployment .

canary, in plain words miners once took a canary underground: if the air turned bad, the bird showed it first. a canary release works the same way. a small share of real users gets the new version, you watch closely, and only when it looks healthy do you send more. go in steps: for example 1%, then 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%, pausing at each step long enough to learn something. compare the canary with the old version running at the same time, not with yesterday: error rate, p95 and p99 latency, saturation, and one number the business cares about. decide the stop rule before you start. "roll back if errors rise above 1% for five minutes" is a rule; "keep an eye on it" is not. # kubernetes gateway api: # weights on an httproute apiversion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: httproute metadata: name: shop-api spec: parentrefs: - name: public-gw rules: - backendrefs: - name: shop-api-stable port: 8080 weight: 95 - name: shop-api-canary port: 8080 weight: 5 # cloud run: move traffic by revision gcloud run services update-traffic api \ --to-revisions=api-00042-xyz=5,api-00041-abc=95 with istio, the same weights live on a virtualservice (see service mesh ). read the gateway api guide to http traffic splitting and fowler's canaryrelease .

c.h: Choosing between them, and the hard parts
c.x: choosing between them, and the hard parts pick blue-green when you need an instant, whole switch and an instant way back, and you can afford two copies for a while. it suits releases you can test fully before users arrive. pick canary when you have enough traffic and good metrics to learn from a small slice. at 1% of 100 requests an hour you learn almost nothing, so a quiet service is better served by blue-green and a thorough test. the database is the hard part of both. old and new versions run at the same time against the same data, so every schema change has to work for both: add first, move the data, remove the old shape in a later release (expand and contract). sessions and caches: a user who bounces between versions may see two behaviours, so keep a user on one version where that matters, and make sure caches and queues can be read by both. feature flags are a separate tool. a deploy puts code on servers; a flag decides who sees the feature. used together, a canary checks the code is healthy and a flag controls the release to users. automate it once you understand it. argo rollouts and flagger run blue-green and canary steps on kubernetes with automatic analysis, and harness has both built in. do it by hand a few times first, so you know what the tool is deciding for you. whichever you pick, rehearse the rollback before you need it. the way back is the part of a release that matters most when things go wrong, and it is usually the part nobody practised.

observability logs say what happened (structured json, with a request or run id). metrics say how much and how often. traces say where the time went across services. golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. red for services (rate, errors, duration); use for resources (utilisation, saturation, errors). sli: a measured ratio, e.g. requests under 500 ms ÷ all requests. slo: the target, e.g. 99.5% over 30 days. error budget: the 0.5% you may spend on releases and incidents. alert on symptoms users feel (slo burn rate), not on every cpu spike. every alert needs an owner and a runbook. know "nothing there" from "cannot see": a check whose data source is down must report unknown, not zero or green.

incident response declare it early and name an incident lead. one channel, one timeline. mitigate before you diagnose: roll back, fail over, scale up, turn the flag off. communicate status on a schedule, even "no change". write down what you saw and did, with timestamps, as you go. review blamelessly afterwards: what happened, why the system allowed it, which guard would have caught it. track the follow-ups to done.

supply-chain & secrets no long-lived keys: workload identity federation for ci, service accounts for workloads. secrets in a secret manager, injected at runtime. never in git, images, logs or ci output. least privilege: one service account per workload, with only the roles it uses. dependency updates automated (dependabot or renovate), with tests gating them. scan code (sast), dependencies (sca), images (trivy) and committed secrets (gitleaks, github secret scanning). know what you ship: sboms and signed images (cosign) make "are we affected by cve-x?" a query, not a hunt.

measuring delivery dora metric question deployment frequency how often do we ship to production? lead time for changes commit to production: how long? change failure rate what share of deploys cause a failure? failed deployment recovery time (formerly time to restore) how fast do we recover from a failed deploy? deployment rework rate what share of deploys are unplanned fixes for a production incident? speed and stability rise together when changes are small, tested and easy to roll back.

twelve-factor, short version one codebase, many deploys; config in the environment, not the code. dependencies declared and pinned; backing services (db, queue) attached by url. build, release and run are separate steps; the same build goes to every environment. processes are stateless and disposable: fast start, graceful shutdown on sigterm . logs are an event stream to stdout; the platform collects them. admin tasks (migrations, backfills) run as one-off processes from the same release. dev and prod as similar as possible: same images, same database engine.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation use git daily: branch, commit, rebase, pr read a ci run and find why it failed roll back a deploy 2 practitioner write ci/cd workflows with caching and keyless cloud auth add structured logs, metrics and alerts take part in incident response 3 senior design release strategies (canary, blue/green, flags) define slos and alerting on symptoms improve dora metrics; lead post-incident reviews 4 expert build an internal developer platform and golden paths set delivery and reliability standards for the organisation lead culture change toward small, safe, frequent releases each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
