core objects kind use it for pod one or more containers sharing network and volumes. rarely created directly. deployment stateless apps: keeps n replicas, rolling updates, rollback. statefulset stable names and per-pod disks: databases, kafka, zookeeper. daemonset one pod per node: log shippers, node agents. job / cronjob run to completion, once or on a schedule: batch loads, migrations. service stable virtual ip and dns name in front of matching pods. ingress / gateway http routing from outside into services (gateway api is the newer model). configmap / secret configuration and credentials, as env vars or files. persistentvolumeclaim a request for durable storage. serviceaccount identity for pods (and, on gke, the link to a google service account). horizontalpodautoscaler scale replicas on cpu, memory or custom metrics. networkpolicy pod-level firewall rules. namespace a scope for names, quotas and rbac.

kubectl daily kubectl config get-contexts kubectl config use-context gke_my-proj_asia-south1_main kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop kubectl get pods -o wide kubectl get deploy,svc,ing kubectl get all -a # every namespace kubectl describe pod api-7d9f-abcde # events at the bottom kubectl logs deploy/api -f --since=10m kubectl logs api-7d9f-abcde -c sidecar --previous # crashed container kubectl exec -it deploy/api -- sh kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80 kubectl top pods # needs metrics-server kubectl apply -f k8s/ --dry-run=server # validate against the cluster kubectl diff -f k8s/ kubectl apply -f k8s/ kubectl rollout status deploy/api kubectl rollout undo deploy/api kubectl rollout restart deploy/api # new pods re-read env from secrets/configmaps (re-pull only with imagepullpolicy: always) kubectl scale deploy/api --replicas=3 kubectl get events --sort-by=.lasttimestamp kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy # built-in field docs

deployment + service apiversion: apps/v1 kind: deployment metadata: { name: api, labels: { app: api } } spec: replicas: 2 selector: { matchlabels: { app: api } } strategy: { rollingupdate: { maxunavailable: 0, maxsurge: 1 } } template: metadata: { labels: { app: api } } spec: serviceaccountname: api containers: - name: api image: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:3f2a9c1 ports: [{ containerport: 8080 }] envfrom: [{ configmapref: { name: api-config } }] env: - name: db_password valuefrom: { secretkeyref: { name: db, key: password } } resources: requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512mi } limits: { memory: 512mi } readinessprobe: httpget: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 } periodseconds: 5 livenessprobe: httpget: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 } initialdelayseconds: 20 startupprobe: httpget: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 } failurethreshold: 30 periodseconds: 2 --- apiversion: v1 kind: service metadata: { name: api } spec: selector: { app: api } ports: [{ port: 80, targetport: 8080 }]

job & cronjob apiversion: batch/v1 kind: cronjob metadata: { name: orders-load } spec: schedule: "15 6 * * *" timezone: "etc/utc" concurrencypolicy: forbid # never two runs at once startingdeadlineseconds: 600 successfuljobshistorylimit: 3 failedjobshistorylimit: 5 jobtemplate: spec: backofflimit: 0 # no automatic retries activedeadlineseconds: 3600 ttlsecondsafterfinished: 86400 template: spec: restartpolicy: never serviceaccountname: loader containers: - name: loader image: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/loader:3f2a9c1 args: ["--year=2024"] resources: { requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2gi }, limits: { memory: 2gi } } kubectl create job --from=cronjob/orders-load manual-20250131 # run now kubectl get jobs; kubectl logs job/manual-20250131

services & traffic clusterip (default): reachable inside the cluster only. nodeport : a port on every node (30000–32767). mostly a building block. loadbalancer : provisions a cloud load balancer with an external (or internal, by annotation) ip. headless ( clusterip: none ): dns returns pod ips directly; used with statefulsets. dns name: <svc>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local ; within the same namespace just <svc> . a service with no endpoints means its selector matches no ready pod: check labels and readiness. apiversion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: ingress metadata: { name: api } spec: ingressclassname: nginx # gke's own controller uses the annotation kubernetes.io/ingress.class: gce instead # ingress nginx was retired in march 2026: prefer gateway api or a maintained controller rules: - host: api.example.com http: paths: - path: / pathtype: prefix backend: { service: { name: api, port: { number: 80 } } } kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api

a request, drawn how a request reaches a pod a request from outside enters through an ingress or gateway, which routes by host and path to a service. the service has a stable name and ip and selects pods by label. a deployment keeps three replicas. two pods are ready and receive traffic. the third is failing its readiness probe, so the service sends it nothing, though it keeps running. client ingress / gateway service app=shop deployment, 3 replicas pod 1: ready pod 2: ready pod 3: not ready readiness failing: no traffic, not restarted a service sends traffic only to pods that are ready. readiness failing takes a pod out of rotation; liveness failing restarts it. a service with no ready pods has no endpoints.

requests, limits, probes requests decide scheduling: the node must have that much free. limits cap use. over the memory limit → the container is killed ( oomkilled , exit 137). over the cpu limit → throttled, not killed. set memory request = limit for steady apps. many teams leave the cpu limit off to avoid throttling. jvm: size heap from the container with -xx:maxrampercentage=75 . readiness failing removes the pod from service traffic. liveness failing restarts it. startup holds the other two off until the app has booted. never make liveness depend on a database or another service: an outage then restarts every pod. qos: guaranteed (requests = limits for all), burstable, besteffort (none set; evicted first).

debug by status status usually means pending no node fits the requests, a pvc is unbound, or a node selector/taint excludes all nodes. describe pod → events. imagepullbackoff wrong image name or tag, or the node's identity cannot read the registry. crashloopbackoff the app starts and exits. logs --previous shows why: bad config, missing secret, failed probe. oomkilled memory limit too low, or a leak. check describe → last state. createcontainerconfigerror a referenced configmap or secret key does not exist. running, not ready readiness probe failing: wrong path or port, or a dependency is down. evicted node ran short of memory or disk. kubectl debug -it api-7d9f-abcde --image=busybox:1.36 --target=api # ephemeral debug container kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash # network toolbox pod

config, secrets, scaling, safety kubectl create configmap api-config --from-literal=dataset=analytics --from-file=app.yml kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password='...' # base64, not encrypted kubectl get secret db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d # hpa kubectl autoscale deploy api --cpu=70% --min=2 --max=10 # older kubectl: --cpu-percent=70 # poddisruptionbudget: keep capacity during node upgrades apiversion: policy/v1 kind: poddisruptionbudget metadata: { name: api } spec: minavailable: 1 selector: { matchlabels: { app: api } } # networkpolicy: default deny ingress in the namespace apiversion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: networkpolicy metadata: { name: default-deny-ingress } spec: podselector: {} policytypes: [ingress] for real secrets use secret manager via the csi driver or external secrets, not values committed in yaml.

rbac & gke workload identity # pod's kubernetes sa → google service account (no json keys) apiversion: v1 kind: serviceaccount metadata: name: loader namespace: shop annotations: iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: shop-loader@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \ shop-loader@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role=roles/iam.workloadidentityuser \ --member="serviceaccount:my-proj.svc.id.goog[shop/loader]" # rbac: read-only on pods in one namespace kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n shop kubectl create rolebinding jo-reads --role=pod-reader --user=jo@example.com -n shop kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n shop --as=jo@example.com gke can also grant iam roles straight to the kubernetes principal ( principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<number>/locations/global/workloadidentitypools/<proj>.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/<ns>/sa/<ksa> ) without a google service account.

gke, helm, kustomize gcloud container clusters create-auto main --region=asia-south1 # autopilot gcloud container clusters get-credentials main --region=asia-south1 gcloud container clusters list # helm: packaged apps with values helm install redis oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts/redis \ -n cache --create-namespace -f values.yaml # check the chart's readme for where its images come from helm upgrade --install api ./chart --set image.tag=3f2a9c1 helm template ./chart | kubectl diff -f - helm rollback api 1 # kustomize: one base, overlays per env (built into kubectl) k8s/base/kustomization.yaml resources: [deploy.yaml, svc.yaml] k8s/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml resources: [../../base] images: [{ name: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api, newtag: 3f2a9c1 }] patches: [{ path: replicas.yaml }] kubectl apply -k k8s/overlays/prod autopilot: google manages nodes and you pay per pod request. standard: you manage node pools. for one-shot batch work, cloud run jobs are often simpler than a cluster.

know what you are protecting two numbers decide everything else. rpo (recovery point objective): how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. rto (recovery time objective): how long you can afford to be down. agree them with the business before choosing a design, because a shorter rto or rpo always costs more. state where it lives how it comes back cluster objects (deployments, services, config) the cluster's backing store, usually etcd re-apply from git (gitops), or restore an etcd snapshot or a velero backup application manifests and helm values your git repository re-apply. if git is the source of truth, the cluster is replaceable. see helm charts persistent data volumes, and databases inside or outside the cluster volume snapshots, database backups with point-in-time recovery secrets kubernetes secrets, or an external secret store from the external store; never only inside the cluster you are trying to recover everything around it dns, certificates, iam, container images, load balancers infrastructure as code. see terraform

c.h: Best practices that prevent most outages
c.x: best practices that prevent most outages never run naked pods: use a deployment or statefulset, so a failed pod is replaced. run more than one replica of anything that matters. spread across zones: topology spread constraints (with a topologykey such as the zone label) keep replicas apart, so one zone failing does not take them all. poddisruptionbudgets: say how many replicas must stay up during voluntary disruptions such as node drains and upgrades. tools should evict through the eviction api, which respects them. probes: readiness keeps traffic away until a pod is ready; liveness restarts a stuck container; a startup probe holds the other two off until a slow starter is up. requests and limits on every container, so the scheduler can place work and one noisy pod cannot starve the rest. version-control all configuration and keep it simple, with consistent labels.

back up: three layers etcd (self-managed clusters): take regular snapshots with etcdctl snapshot save , store them off the cluster, and encrypt them: they hold every secret. workloads and volumes: velero backs up cluster objects and persistent volumes to object storage, on a schedule, with a retention period ( --ttl ). the volumesnapshot api takes snapshots of volumes through the storage system's driver. managed clusters: the provider runs the control plane and etcd; you protect your workloads and data. each has a backup service: backup for gke, aks backup, and aws backup for eks. databases: prefer a managed database, or a database operator with its own backups and point-in-time recovery, over raw volume snapshots of a running database.

restore: the commands from the kubernetes and velero documentation. names in angle brackets are yours. # etcd (self-managed): snapshot, and restore into a new data directory etcdctl_api=3 etcdctl --endpoints $endpoint snapshot save snapshot.db etcdutl --data-dir <data-dir-location> snapshot restore snapshot.db # velero: back up on a schedule velero schedule create <schedule-name> --schedule "0 7 * * *" --ttl 720h0m0s # velero disaster recovery: make the backup location read-only, restore, then set it back kubectl patch backupstoragelocation <location> --namespace velero \ --type merge --patch '{"spec":{"accessmode":"readonly"}}' velero restore create --from-backup <schedule-name>-<timestamp> kubectl patch backupstoragelocation <location> --namespace velero \ --type merge --patch '{"spec":{"accessmode":"readwrite"}}' making the backup location read-only first stops a scheduled backup from overwriting good backups while you restore.

c.h: Four DR strategies, from cheap to fast
c.x: four dr strategies, from cheap to fast backup and restore: rebuild the cluster and restore data when disaster strikes. cheapest; slowest to recover. pilot light: a minimal copy of the core (data replicated, little else running) in another region, scaled up on the day. warm standby: a smaller but working copy runs all the time, ready to take traffic and scale. multi-site active/active: two or more regions serve traffic at once. fastest recovery; most expensive and hardest to keep consistent. these four are the categories in aws's disaster recovery whitepaper; the same ideas apply on any cloud.

c.h: A backup you have not restored is a hope
c.x: a backup you have not restored is a hope restore regularly into a scratch cluster, and time it. that time is your real rto. write the runbook a person can follow without the automation, and keep it outside the cluster. see sre . run game days: drain a zone, delete a namespace in a test cluster, lose the etcd leader, and watch what happens. watch the backups: alert when a scheduled backup fails or is late. see observability .

levels: what to expect 1 foundation run workloads as deployments with several replicas add readiness and liveness probes explain rpo and rto 2 practitioner add poddisruptionbudgets and zone spreading schedule velero or managed backups and restore one keep all manifests in git so a cluster is replaceable 3 senior choose a dr strategy against agreed rpo and rto design multi-zone and multi-region clusters run restore drills and game days 4 expert own platform resilience across clusters and regions set backup, restore and dr standards lead recovery during a major incident each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

concepts term meaning chart a package: templates, default values and metadata values inputs that fill the templates; defaults in values.yaml , overridden per environment release one installed instance of a chart in a namespace, with a name revision each install, upgrade or rollback of a release; the history helm can roll back to repository / registry where charts are published: an http chart repo or an oci registry (e.g. artifact registry) chart version vs app version version changes when the chart changes; appversion names the application it deploys

the terms, drawn a chart, its values, and a release's revisions a chart holds templates and default values. values for one environment override the defaults. helm renders both into kubernetes manifests and installs them as a release with a name in a namespace. each install, upgrade and rollback adds a revision: revision 1 installed, revision 2 an upgrade, revision 3 a rollback that restores revision 1's manifests as a new revision. chart templates + values.yaml values-prod.yaml overrides the defaults helm upgrade render + apply release shop in prod revision 1: install revision 2: upgrade revision 3: rollback to 1 a rollback is a new revision the table above as one picture. the history of revisions is what lets helm rollback take you back, and the rollback itself becomes the next revision.

chart structure shop-api/ chart.yaml # name, versions, dependencies values.yaml # defaults values.schema.json # optional: validate values templates/ _helpers.tpl # named templates (labels, names) deployment.yaml service.yaml ingress.yaml configmap.yaml hpa.yaml notes.txt # printed after install tests/ test-connection.yaml charts/ # dependency charts (vendored) # chart.yaml apiversion: v2 name: shop-api description: shop api type: application # or "library" for shared templates only version: 0.3.0 # chart version (semver) appversion: "3f2a9c1" # image tag it deploys by default dependencies: - name: common version: "1.x.x" repository: oci://asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/charts

commands helm create shop-api # scaffold helm lint ./shop-api helm template shop ./shop-api -f values-prod.yaml # render locally, no cluster helm upgrade --install shop ./shop-api \ -n shop --create-namespace \ -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=3f2a9c1 \ --atomic --timeout 5m # roll back automatically on failure # helm 4 renamed --atomic to --rollback-on-failure; check `helm version` helm list -n shop helm history shop -n shop helm rollback shop 4 -n shop helm get values shop -n shop # what was applied helm get manifest shop -n shop helm uninstall shop -n shop helm dependency update ./shop-api helm package ./shop-api # → shop-api- 0.3.0 .tgz helm push shop-api- 0.3.0 .tgz oci://asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/charts helm install shop oci://asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/charts/shop-api --version 0.3.0

templates # templates/_helpers.tpl {{- define "shop-api.fullname" -}} {{- printf "%s-%s" .release.name .chart.name | trunc 63 | trimsuffix "-" -}} {{- end -}} {{- define "shop-api.selectorlabels" -}} app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .chart.name }} app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .release.name }} {{- end -}} # templates/deployment.yaml apiversion: apps/v1 kind: deployment metadata: name: {{ include "shop-api.fullname" . }} labels: {{- include "shop-api.selectorlabels" . | nindent 4 }} app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .values.image.tag | default .chart.appversion | quote }} spec: replicas: {{ .values.replicacount }} selector: matchlabels: {{- include "shop-api.selectorlabels" . | nindent 6 }} template: metadata: labels: {{- include "shop-api.selectorlabels" . | nindent 8 }} annotations: checksum/config: {{ include (print $.template.basepath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }} spec: containers: - name: app image: "{{ .values.image.repository }}:{{ .values.image.tag | default .chart.appversion }}" resources: {{- toyaml .values.resources | nindent 12 }} {{- with .values.env }} env: {{- toyaml . | nindent 12 }} {{- end }} envfrom: - secretref: name: {{ required "secretname is required" .values.secretname }} the checksum/config annotation restarts pods when the configmap changes. required fails the render with a clear message instead of deploying something broken.

values per environment # values.yaml (defaults: safe, small) replicacount: 1 image: repository: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/shop-api tag: "" # defaults to appversion resources: requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512mi } limits: { memory: 512mi } env: [] secretname: "" # values-prod.yaml (only what differs) replicacount: 3 resources: requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 1gi } limits: { memory: 1gi } secretname: shop-api-secrets later -f files override earlier ones; --set overrides files. prefer files in git over --set . add values.schema.json so a typo in a value fails at install, not at runtime. never put secret values in values files; reference secrets created by external secrets or the secret manager csi driver.

hooks and tests # templates/migrate-job.yaml: run db migrations before an upgrade apiversion: batch/v1 kind: job metadata: name: {{ include "shop-api.fullname" . }}-migrate annotations: "helm.sh/hook": pre-install,pre-upgrade "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0" "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded spec: backofflimit: 0 template: spec: restartpolicy: never containers: - name: migrate image: "{{ .values.image.repository }}:{{ .values.image.tag | default .chart.appversion }}" args: ["migrate"] hook events: pre-install , post-install , pre-upgrade , post-upgrade , pre-rollback , pre-delete and more. migrations in a hook must be backward compatible: a rollback does not undo them. helm test shop runs pods annotated "helm.sh/hook": test to smoke-test a release. unit-test templates with the helm-unittest plugin; lint and install-test charts in ci with chart-testing ( ct ).

helm, kustomize and gitops helm kustomize approach templates + values plain yaml + patches per overlay packaging and versions yes: charts, releases, rollback no: just manifests best for distributing reusable apps; many similar services your own manifests with small per-environment differences risk template logic becomes hard to read many overlays become hard to follow gitops (argo cd, flux): the desired chart version and values live in git; a controller in the cluster applies them and reports drift. no one runs helm upgrade by hand in production. run helm diff upgrade (plugin) or the gitops diff before every production change.

chart best practices selector labels never change after the first release: kubernetes forbids changing a deployment's selector. standard labels ( app.kubernetes.io/name , instance , version , managed-by ). sensible defaults: resources, probes, security context (non-root, read-only root filesystem) on by default. keep templates boring: little logic; move complexity into values, not nested conditionals. a library chart of shared helpers is your blueprint: every service chart depends on it, so a fix reaches all of them. pin dependency versions ; publish charts to an oci registry with immutable versions. document values in values.yaml comments and the schema.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation install, upgrade, roll back and inspect a release read a chart's values and override them per environment render a chart locally with helm template 2 practitioner write charts with helpers, schema-validated values and sane defaults use hooks for migrations and helm test for smoke tests publish charts to an oci registry 3 senior design library charts as a shared blueprint for many services deliver charts with gitops (argo cd or flux) and diffs choose between helm and kustomize per case 4 expert own the organisation's deployment packaging standards run chart supply chain: signing, provenance, registries lead migrations between delivery models each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the pattern a custom resource definition (crd) adds a new resource type to the kubernetes api, such as postgrescluster or pipelinerun . users create custom resources stating the desired state ( spec ): "three postgres replicas, version 16, nightly backups". a controller watches those resources and the objects it owns, and reconciles : observe the actual state, compare it with the spec, act to close the gap, and record what it saw in status . reconcile runs again on every change and periodically, so the system heals itself when reality drifts. controllers are level-triggered : they act on the current state, not on the event that woke them. that makes them robust to missed events and restarts, as long as every reconcile is idempotent.

the loop, drawn the reconcile loop a loop of four steps around a custom resource. 1 observe the actual state of the cluster. 2 compare it with the spec, the desired state, such as three postgres replicas. 3 act to close the gap, for example create the missing replica. 4 record what was seen in status. the loop runs on every change and periodically, and acts on the current state rather than the event that woke it. custom resource spec: 3 replicas 1 observe actual state 2 compare with spec 3 act to close the gap 4 record in status again on every change, and periodically the controller’s loop. because it looks at the current state each time, a missed event or a restart does no harm, as long as each pass is idempotent.

operator or helm chart? helm chart operator does installs and upgrades a set of manifests continuously manages a system through its whole life day-2 operations none after apply backups, failover, scaling, upgrades, repair fits stateless services, most applications stateful systems (databases, kafka), complex platforms cost templates a program to build, test, secure and maintain our view: use well-tested operators (often installed with helm) rather than writing your own. write one only when you have real operational knowledge to automate and no existing operator does it. the other view: a team with real operational knowledge to automate may get more from its own operator than from a general one.

operators worth knowing cert-manager: issues and renews tls certificates. prometheus operator: prometheus, alertmanager and scrape targets as resources ( servicemonitor , prometheusrule ). cloudnativepg: postgresql clusters with replication, failover and backups. strimzi: kafka clusters, topics and users. spark operator: spark applications as resources. argo cd / flux: gitops controllers. external secrets operator: syncs secrets from secret manager into kubernetes. config connector / crossplane: manage cloud resources (gcs buckets, cloud sql) as kubernetes objects.

a custom resource definition apiversion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 kind: customresourcedefinition metadata: name: pipelineruns.data.example.com spec: group: data.example.com scope: namespaced names: plural: pipelineruns singular: pipelinerun kind: pipelinerun shortnames: [plr] versions: - name: v1alpha1 served: true storage: true subresources: status: {} additionalprintercolumns: - { name: date, type: string, jsonpath: .spec.rundate } - { name: phase, type: string, jsonpath: .status.phase } schema: openapiv3schema: type: object properties: spec: type: object required: [rundate, stages] properties: rundate: { type: string, format: date } stages: type: array items: { type: string, enum: [land, raw_load, build] } status: type: object x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields: true apiversion: data.example.com/v1alpha1 kind: pipelinerun metadata: { name: run-2026-11-12, namespace: data } spec: rundate: "2026-11-12" stages: [land, raw_load, build] # kubectl get plr -n data

go: kubebuilder and controller-runtime kubebuilder init --domain example.com --repo github.com/example/pipeline-operator kubebuilder create api --group data --version v1alpha1 --kind pipelinerun make manifests # generate crds and rbac from code markers make install run # install crds, run the controller locally func (r *pipelinerunreconciler) reconcile(ctx context.context, req ctrl.request) (ctrl.result, error) { var run datav1alpha1.pipelinerun if err := r.get(ctx, req.namespacedname, &run); err != nil { return ctrl.result{}, client.ignorenotfound(err) // deleted: nothing to do } // 1. observe: the jobs this run owns // 2. compare: which stage should run next, given spec and finished jobs? // 3. act: create that stage's job with a deterministic name // (creating it twice returns alreadyexists: idempotent) // and set an owner reference so it is garbage-collected with the run // 4. record: update status.phase and conditions via the status subresource return ctrl.result{requeueafter: time.minute}, nil }

java and python // java operator sdk @controllerconfiguration public class pipelinerunreconciler implements reconciler<pipelinerun> { @override public updatecontrol<pipelinerun> reconcile(pipelinerun run, context<pipelinerun> ctx) { // observe owned jobs, create the next stage's job if missing run.setstatus(computestatus(run, ctx)); return updatecontrol.patchstatus(run); } } // quarkus has an extension for the java operator sdk # python: kopf import kopf @kopf.on.create("data.example.com", "v1alpha1", "pipelineruns") @kopf.on.update("data.example.com", "v1alpha1", "pipelineruns") def reconcile(spec, name, namespace, status, logger, **_): next_stage = choose_next_stage(spec["stages"], status) if next_stage: ensure_job(name, namespace, next_stage) # idempotent create return {"phase": "running" if next_stage else "succeeded"} # kopf stores it under status.reconcile

rules for a good controller idempotent reconcile: running it ten times gives the same result as once. no in-memory state: everything needed is in the cluster (spec, status, owned objects), so restarts are safe. status and conditions: report ready , progressing , degraded with reasons and the observed generation. owner references so owned objects are cleaned up automatically; finalizers to clean up things outside the cluster (cloud resources) before deletion. requeue with backoff on errors; never tight-loop. leader election so only one replica acts at a time. least-privilege rbac , generated from the code. validate early: openapi schema and cel rules ( x-kubernetes-validations ) reject bad specs at the api. distinguish unknown from failed: if the controller cannot read a dependency, report that, rather than marking the resource failed or healthy.

testing and operating operators unit-test the decision logic (spec + observed state → actions) without a cluster. envtest (go) runs a real api server for integration tests; kind or k3d clusters for end-to-end tests. crd versioning: start at v1alpha1 ; add conversion webhooks when you introduce new versions; never break stored objects. metrics: reconcile counts, errors, duration and queue depth (controller-runtime exposes them). capability levels (operator framework): basic install → seamless upgrades → full lifecycle → deep insights → autopilot. aim for the level your users need. distribution: package the operator with a helm chart or olm bundle.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain crds, custom resources, controllers and reconcile use existing operators (cert-manager, cloudnativepg, strimzi) read a resource's status and conditions 2 practitioner write a crd with schema validation build a simple controller with kubebuilder, java operator sdk or kopf use owner references, finalizers and status correctly 3 senior design operators for stateful systems and day-2 operations test with envtest and real clusters; version crds with conversion decide operator vs helm vs managed service 4 expert build platform apis on kubernetes for the organisation maintain operators at high capability levels contribute to the operator ecosystem each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

what a mesh gives you capability what it means without a mesh mutual tls every call between services encrypted and authenticated with workload certificates, rotated automatically tls and certificates managed in each service workload identity and authorisation policies such as "only the frontend's service account may call get /api/*" network policies (ip-based) and code checks traffic management canary weights, header-based routing, mirroring, timeouts, retries load balancer rules or code resilience circuit breaking, outlier detection, connection limits libraries such as resilience4j in each service observability uniform request metrics, access logs and trace spans for every hop instrumentation in every service egress control only allow-listed external hosts reachable firewall and proxy rules north-south traffic (clients into the platform) is the gateway's job; east-west traffic (services to each other) is the mesh's. business logic belongs in neither.

when it is worth it good reasons many services on kubernetes, often in several languages. a requirement for encrypted, authenticated traffic between all services (zero trust, compliance). frequent canary or progressive releases. uniform telemetry without changing every service. reasons to wait a handful of services, or a modular monolith. serverless platforms such as cloud run, which already give service identity (iam) and tls. no one to own and upgrade the mesh: it is a critical system in every request path.

istio architecture control plane, istiod : turns your configuration into proxy configuration, issues workload certificates, and pushes both to the data plane. data plane, sidecar mode: an envoy proxy injected into every pod intercepts its inbound and outbound traffic. full l7 features per pod, at the cost of a proxy per pod. data plane, ambient mode: a per-node ztunnel provides l4 mtls and identity for all pods without sidecars; optional waypoint proxies add l7 features (routing, l7 authorisation) only where needed. lower overhead and no pod restarts to join. gateways: envoy deployments at the edge for ingress and egress, configured with the kubernetes gateway api or istio's own gateway resource. on google cloud, cloud service mesh offers a managed, istio-based mesh for gke and other environments.

the two modes, drawn istio's control plane and its two data plane modes at the top, istiod, the control plane, which turns your configuration into proxy configuration and issues workload certificates. below it two node pictures. sidecar mode: every pod has its own envoy proxy beside the app, with full l7 features per pod. ambient mode: one ztunnel per node gives every pod l4 mtls and identity without sidecars, and an optional waypoint proxy adds l7 features only where needed. istiod config + certificates sidecar mode: a node pod app envoy pod app envoy ambient mode: a node pod: app only pod: app only ztunnel: l4 mtls for every pod + a waypoint proxy only where l7 is needed a proxy in every pod: full l7, more overhead the same control plane drives both. sidecar mode puts a proxy in every pod; ambient mode shares one ztunnel per node and adds l7 proxies only where you need them.

install and enrol workloads # sidecar mode istioctl install --set profile=default -y kubectl label namespace shop istio-injection=enabled kubectl rollout restart deploy -n shop # pods get sidecars on restart # ambient mode istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y kubectl label namespace shop istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient # no restart needed istioctl waypoint apply -n shop --enroll-namespace # add l7 where needed istioctl analyze -n shop # check configuration for problems in production, install and upgrade istio through helm charts or your platform's managed offering, from git, with canary upgrades of the control plane (revisions).

the resources you will write resource purpose gateway + httproute (kubernetes gateway api) ingress and routing; the recommended api for new setups virtualservice istio routing rules: matches, weights, retries, timeouts, fault injection destinationrule policies for a destination: subsets (versions), load balancing, connection pools, outlier detection, tls peerauthentication mtls mode for workloads: strict or permissive authorizationpolicy who may call what: by service account, namespace, path, method, jwt claims requestauthentication validate end-user jwts at the proxy serviceentry register external services so they can be reached and controlled sidecar limit which services a sidecar knows about, to reduce memory and config size telemetry tune metrics, access logs and tracing

security: mtls and authorisation # mesh-wide strict mtls (after a permissive migration period) apiversion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: peerauthentication metadata: { name: default, namespace: istio-system } spec: mtls: { mode: strict } --- # only the frontend may call the api, and only get on /api/* apiversion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: authorizationpolicy metadata: { name: shop-api-allow, namespace: shop } spec: selector: { matchlabels: { app: shop-api } } action: allow rules: - from: - source: { principals: ["cluster.local/ns/web/sa/frontend"] } to: - operation: { methods: ["get"], paths: ["/api/*"] } --- # validate end-user jwts at the proxy apiversion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: requestauthentication metadata: { name: jwt, namespace: shop } spec: selector: { matchlabels: { app: shop-api } } jwtrules: - issuer: "https://auth.example.com/" jwksuri: "https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json" once any allow policy selects a workload, everything not allowed is denied. roll out in a test namespace first. the service still checks object-level permissions: the mesh knows which service is calling, not whether this user owns this case.

traffic: canary, retries, timeouts apiversion: networking.istio.io/v1 kind: destinationrule metadata: { name: shop-api, namespace: shop } spec: host: shop-api subsets: - { name: v1, labels: { version: v1 } } - { name: v2, labels: { version: v2 } } trafficpolicy: connectionpool: { http: { http1maxpendingrequests: 100 } } outlierdetection: # eject failing pods for a while consecutive5xxerrors: 5 interval: 10s baseejectiontime: 30s --- apiversion: networking.istio.io/v1 kind: virtualservice metadata: { name: shop-api, namespace: shop } spec: hosts: [shop-api] http: - timeout: 3s retries: { attempts: 2, pertrytimeout: 1s, retryon: "5xx,connect-failure" } route: - { destination: { host: shop-api, subset: v1 }, weight: 90 } - { destination: { host: shop-api, subset: v2 }, weight: 10 } # the same split with the gateway api apiversion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: httproute metadata: { name: shop-api, namespace: shop } spec: parentrefs: [{ name: shop-gateway }] hostnames: ["api.example.com"] rules: - backendrefs: - { name: shop-api-v1, port: 8080, weight: 90 } - { name: shop-api-v2, port: 8080, weight: 10 } put retries in one place, mesh or application, not both: retries multiplied at every layer turn a slowdown into a retry storm. retry only idempotent requests.

egress control # with outbound traffic policy registry_only, only registered hosts are reachable apiversion: networking.istio.io/v1 kind: serviceentry metadata: { name: payment-gateway, namespace: shop } spec: hosts: ["api.example-payments.com"] ports: [{ number: 443, name: https, protocol: tls }] resolution: dns location: mesh_external route egress through an egress gateway when you need a fixed exit point, central logging, or to combine with cloud nat and firewall rules.

observability with a mesh metrics for every request, such as istio_requests_total and request duration histograms, labelled by source, destination and response code. kiali draws the live service graph with health and traffic. tracing: proxies create spans, but your application must forward the trace headers ( traceparent ) from incoming to outgoing requests, or traces break at every service. access logs per proxy, tunable with the telemetry resource. # 5xx rate per destination service sum by (destination_service) (rate(istio_requests_total{response_code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum by (destination_service) (rate(istio_requests_total[5m]))

debugging istioctl analyze -a # config problems across namespaces istioctl proxy-status # is every proxy in sync with istiod? istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/shop-api -n shop istioctl proxy-config clusters deploy/shop-api -n shop istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n shop # which policies apply to this pod kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy -n shop # sidecar access log symptom usually 503 with uf / urx flags upstream failing or refusing; check the app and outlier ejection 404 nr no route: virtualservice or httproute mismatch connection reset after enabling strict a client outside the mesh still sends plain text 403 rbac: access denied an authorizationpolicy denies it (or no allow rule matches) app fails at startup calling a dependency sidecar not ready yet; hold the app until the proxy starts jobs never complete sidecar keeps the pod alive; use native sidecars or ambient mode pod has no sidecar namespace not labelled, or pod created before the label

meshes compared mesh notes it leans this way if istio most features; sidecar or ambient; large community; more to learn and operate you need the widest feature set and can staff its operation cloud service mesh google-managed, istio-based, integrated with gke and cloud monitoring you run on gke and want google to manage it linkerd simpler and lightweight, with its own rust proxy; fewer features its features cover what you need, and you want less to run cilium service mesh ebpf-based networking with mesh features, often without sidecars you already use cilium for networking, or want mesh features without sidecars consul spans kubernetes and vms, with service discovery your services run on vms as well as kubernetes analysis: the last column is read from the notes column, not from any ranking of the meshes. list the features you actually need before you compare: a team that needs few of them has more choices than one that needs the most.

adopting a mesh safely install in a non-production cluster; enrol one namespace. start with permissive mtls and observe traffic in kiali and metrics. move namespaces to strict once every client is in the mesh. add authorizationpolicies service by service, tested in ci against a cluster. move retries, timeouts and canaries into the mesh deliberately, removing duplicates from code. keep all mesh config in git, delivered by gitops, with istioctl analyze in ci. plan control-plane upgrades with revisions and canary them like any critical release.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain mtls, workload identity and east-west vs north-south traffic read virtualservice, destinationrule and authorizationpolicy resources find a pod's sidecar logs and proxy status 2 practitioner enrol namespaces and roll out strict mtls safely write authorisation policies and canary routes debug 503s and rbac denials with istioctl 3 senior decide whether a mesh is worth it, and sidecar vs ambient design zero-trust service-to-service security run mesh upgrades with revisions; keep config in gitops 4 expert own the mesh platform across clusters and environments design multi-cluster and multi-network meshes set network security strategy combining mesh, gateway and cloud controls each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

cli workflow terraform init # providers + backend terraform init -upgrade # newer providers within constraints terraform fmt -recursive terraform validate terraform plan -var-file=env/dev.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan terraform show plan.tfplan # read it before applying terraform apply plan.tfplan # applies exactly what you read terraform plan -destroy terraform plan -target=module.landing # emergency only terraform apply -replace=google_cloud_run_v2_job.loader terraform output -json terraform console # try expressions terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64 validate checks syntax and types only. a missing optional module argument or a wrong iam wiring shows up in a plan, not before.

the safe path, drawn the terraform workflow five steps left to right: init downloads providers and sets up the backend; fmt and validate check syntax and types; plan with -out writes a plan file; show prints that plan so a person reads it; apply of the plan file applies exactly what was read. a note says validate cannot see a missing optional module argument or wrong iam wiring; only a plan shows those. init providers, backend 1 fmt, validate syntax and types 2 plan -out plan.tfplan 3 show a person reads it 4 apply the file what you read 5 validate cannot see a missing module argument or wrong iam wiring: only a plan shows those the commands above in the order that keeps you safe. saving the plan to a file and applying that file means what runs is exactly what you read.

providers & backend terraform { required_version = ">= 1.7" required_providers { google = { source = "hashicorp/google", version = "~> 8.0" } # pin the major version you have tested } backend "gcs" { bucket = "my-proj-tfstate" # versioning on! prefix = "dataplatform" } } provider "google" { project = var.project_id region = var.region default_labels = { managed_by = "terraform", env = var.env } } # backend values cannot use variables; pass them at init: # terraform init -backend-config="bucket=my-proj-dev-tfstate"

variables, locals, outputs variable "env" { type = string validation { condition = contains(["dev", "prod"], var.env) error_message = "env must be dev or prod." } } variable "stages" { type = map(object({ enabled = bool args = optional(list(string), []) })) } variable "db_password" { type = string sensitive = true } locals { name_prefix = "shop-${var.env}" enabled = { for k, v in var.stages : k => v if v.enabled } } output "bucket_url" { value = google_storage_bucket.landing.url } # env/dev.tfvars env = "dev" stages = { land = { enabled = true, args = ["--max-objects=50"] } }

count, for_each, dynamic # for_each over a set or map: stable addresses by key (prefer over count) resource "google_bigquery_dataset" "layer" { for_each = toset(["raw", "analytics", "mart"]) dataset_id = each.key location = var.region } # reference: google_bigquery_dataset.layer["analytics"].dataset_id # count for on/off resource "google_cloud_scheduler_job" "tick" { count = var.clock_enabled ? 1 : 0 ... } # reference: one(google_cloud_scheduler_job.tick[*].id) # dynamic nested blocks dynamic "env" { for_each = var.env_vars content { name = env.key value = env.value } } # list of objects → map for for_each for_each = { for t in var.tables : t.name => t } with count , removing an item in the middle renumbers everything after it and terraform destroys and recreates those resources.

bigquery dataset & table resource "google_bigquery_dataset" "analytics" { dataset_id = "analytics" location = "asia-south1" delete_contents_on_destroy = false labels = { layer = "analytics" } } resource "google_bigquery_table" "orders" { dataset_id = google_bigquery_dataset.analytics.dataset_id table_id = "orders" deletion_protection = true require_partition_filter = true time_partitioning { type = "month" field = "order_date" } clustering = ["store_id", "order_ref"] schema = jsonencode([ { name = "order_id", type = "string", mode = "required" }, { name = "store_id", type = "string" }, { name = "order_ref", type = "string" }, { name = "order_date", type = "date" }, ]) } resource "google_bigquery_dataset_iam_member" "api_reader" { dataset_id = google_bigquery_dataset.analytics.dataset_id role = "roles/bigquery.dataviewer" member = "serviceaccount:${google_service_account.api.email}" } tables that dbt builds should not also be declared here; two owners fight over the schema. declare datasets and iam, let dbt own its tables.

gcs bucket resource "google_storage_bucket" "landing" { name = "${var.project_id}-landing" location = "asia-south1" storage_class = "standard" uniform_bucket_level_access = true public_access_prevention = "enforced" force_destroy = false versioning { enabled = true } lifecycle_rule { condition { age = 90 matches_prefix = ["tmp/"] } action { type = "delete" } } lifecycle_rule { condition { age = 365 } action { type = "setstorageclass" storage_class = "coldline" } } }

cloud run job + cloud scheduler resource "google_cloud_run_v2_job" "loader" { name = "${local.name_prefix}-loader" location = var.region deletion_protection = false template { task_count = 1 template { service_account = google_service_account.loader.email timeout = "3600s" max_retries = 0 containers { image = var.loader_image # pass a tag or digest, never :latest args = ["--year=2024"] resources { limits = { cpu = "1", memory = "2gi" } } env { name = "db_password" value_source { secret_key_ref { secret = google_secret_manager_secret.db.secret_id version = "latest" } } } } } } } resource "google_cloud_scheduler_job" "daily" { name = "${local.name_prefix}-daily" region = var.region schedule = "15 6 * * *" time_zone = "etc/utc" paused = var.clock_paused http_target { http_method = "post" uri = "https://run.googleapis.com/v2/projects/${var.project_id}/locations/${var.region}/jobs/${google_cloud_run_v2_job.loader.name}:run" oauth_token { service_account_email = google_service_account.scheduler.email scope = "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform" } } } the scheduler's service account needs roles/run.invoker (or run.developer for overrides) on the job.

iam: member, binding, policy # _member: adds one principal to one role. safe, composable. use this. resource "google_project_iam_member" "loader_bq" { project = var.project_id role = "roles/bigquery.jobuser" member = "serviceaccount:${google_service_account.loader.email}" } # _binding: owns the member list for one role (removes anyone else) # _policy: owns the whole policy (removes everything else, can lock you out) resource "google_service_account" "loader" { account_id = "shop-loader" display_name = "orders loader job" } # workload identity federation for github actions: no json keys resource "google_service_account_iam_member" "gh_deploy" { service_account_id = google_service_account.deploy.name role = "roles/iam.workloadidentityuser" member = "principalset://iam.googleapis.com/${google_iam_workload_identity_pool.gh.name}/attribute.repository/org/repo" } never mix _policy or _binding with _member for the same role: they overwrite each other on every apply.

modules modules/pipeline-job/ main.tf variables.tf outputs.tf versions.tf module "orchestrator" { source = "./modules/pipeline-job" name = "orchestrator" image = var.orchestrator_image service_account_email = google_service_account.orch.email args = ["--tick"] } module "jobs" { # for_each on modules (0.13+) source = "./modules/pipeline-job" for_each = local.enabled name = each.key args = each.value.args } output "job_names" { value = { for k, m in module.jobs : k => m.name } } # registry / git sources: pin a version source = "terraform-google-modules/cloud-storage/google" version = "~> 12.0" source = "git::https://github.com/org/tf-modules.git//bq?ref= v1.4.0 "

refactor without destroying # bring an existing resource under management (1.5) import { to = google_storage_bucket.landing id = "my-proj-landing" } # terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf # rename / move into a module (1.1) moved { from = google_cloud_run_v2_job.loader to = module.jobs["land"].google_cloud_run_v2_job.this } # stop managing, keep the real resource (1.7) removed { from = google_bigquery_table.legacy lifecycle { destroy = false } } # cli equivalents (no review step: prefer the blocks above) terraform state list terraform state show google_storage_bucket.landing terraform state mv 'a.b' 'module.x.a.b' terraform state rm google_bigquery_table.legacy

lifecycle, checks, preconditions resource "google_sql_database_instance" "shop" { ... lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true # plan fails instead of destroying ignore_changes = [settings[0].disk_size] # autoresize owns it create_before_destroy = false precondition { condition = var.env != "prod" || var.tier != "db-f1-micro" error_message = "prod needs a real tier." } } } # replace when something else changes (1.2) lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [terraform_data.image_rev] } # check block: warns on every plan, never blocks (1.5) check "landing_bucket_reachable" { data "google_storage_bucket" "l" { name = google_storage_bucket.landing.name } assert { condition = data.google_storage_bucket.l.versioning[0].enabled error_message = "landing bucket versioning is off." } }

safety checklist read every plan line that says destroy or -/+ (replace). a replaced database or bucket loses its data. state bucket: versioning on, uniform access, only the deploy identity can write. state holds secrets in plain text. one state per environment (separate prefix or project). workspaces suit identical copies, not dev vs prod with different shapes. pin providers with ~> and commit .terraform.lock.hcl . images by tag or digest from a variable, never :latest , so a plan shows when the image moves. no secrets in tfvars. reference secret manager; mark variables sensitive . apply from ci with workload identity federation, from a saved plan file. config is not state: after an apply, read the live resource to confirm it.

signals and what each answers signal is answers cost driver logs timestamped records of events, ideally structured json what exactly happened in this request or run? volume and retention metrics numbers aggregated over time (counts, gauges, histograms) how much, how often, how fast, trending where? number of time series (label cardinality) traces a request's path across services as a tree of timed spans where did the time go? which dependency failed? sampling rate profiles where cpu and memory go inside the code which function is slow or allocating? usually low (continuous sampling) events / run records business or pipeline facts (deploys, run outcomes) what changed, and did the job do its work? low monitoring tells you that something is wrong from questions you planned. observability lets you find out why , including for failures nobody predicted. you need both.

structured logging {"timestamp":"2026-11-12t06:15:04.120z", "severity":"error", "message":"load failed", "service":"orders-load", "version":"3f2a9c1", "env":"prod", "run_id":"r-2026-11-12", "stage":"raw_load", "object":"gs://landing/data/year=2024/part-3.parquet", "error":"400 bad request", "error_body":"invalidargument: …", "logging.googleapis.com/trace":"projects/p/traces/4bf92f…"} one json object per line; a severity field so levels work. always include service, version, environment, and a request or run id. log the evidence: the upstream error body, the input that failed, counts. a log that says only "failed" helps no one. never log secrets, tokens or unnecessary personal data. levels: error needs attention; warn is unusual but handled; info is a business event; debug is off in production.

metrics that matter counter: only goes up (requests, errors, rows loaded). graph its rate. gauge: current value (queue depth, connections, lag). histogram: distribution of values (latency); gives percentiles. red for services: rate, errors, duration. use for resources: utilisation, saturation, errors. golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. cardinality: each unique label combination is a separate series. never use user ids, request ids or urls with ids as labels. percentiles, not averages: p50 for typical, p95/p99 for the users having a bad time.

distributed tracing a trace is one request end to end; a span is one operation in it (an http call, a query), with start, duration, attributes and status. context propagation: the trace id travels in the w3c traceparent header and in message attributes across queues. sampling: keep a percentage of traces (head sampling), or keep all errors and slow ones (tail sampling in a collector). link logs to traces by writing the trace id into every log line. batch jobs: one trace per run, a span per stage or partition.

opentelemetry the vendor-neutral standard for producing logs, metrics and traces: one api in your code, an sdk that processes and exports, the otlp protocol, and an optional collector that receives, filters, samples and forwards to any backend. # java: zero-code instrumentation with the agent (http, jdbc, kafka, grpc …) java -javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar -jar app.jar # otel_service_name=shop-api # otel_exporter_otlp_endpoint=http://otel-collector:4318 # otel_traces_sampler=parentbased_traceidratio otel_traces_sampler_arg=0.1 # python: auto-instrumentation pip install opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install otel_service_name=orders-load opentelemetry-instrument python -m loader # manual span around meaningful work (python) from opentelemetry import trace tracer = trace.get_tracer("orders-load") with tracer.start_as_current_span("load_object") as span: span.set_attribute("object.uri", uri) rows = load(uri) span.set_attribute("rows.loaded", rows) # collector: receive otlp, batch, send to google cloud receivers: otlp: protocols: grpc: http: processors: batch: exporters: googlecloud: googlemanagedprometheus: service: pipelines: traces: { receivers: [otlp], processors: [batch], exporters: [googlecloud] } logs: { receivers: [otlp], processors: [batch], exporters: [googlecloud] } metrics: { receivers: [otlp], processors: [batch], exporters: [googlemanagedprometheus] }

spring boot and micrometer # application.yml management: endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,prometheus tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1 otlp.tracing.endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces # boot 4: opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint observations.annotations.enabled: true # makes @observed work (needs aspectj on the classpath) logging.structured.format.console: ecs # 3.4+ @component class loadmetrics { private final counter loaded, failed; private final timer duration; loadmetrics(meterregistry r) { loaded = counter.builder("orders.objects").tag("outcome", "loaded").register(r); failed = counter.builder("orders.objects").tag("outcome", "failed").register(r); duration = timer.builder("orders.load.duration").publishpercentilehistogram().register(r); } } @observed(name = "order.search") // timer + span in one annotation public list<order> search(string q) { … }

what is happening to jmx? if you have been around java for a while, you will remember opening jconsole, pointing it at a running jvm and browsing a tree of mbeans : heap usage, thread counts, a cache’s hit rate, even a button that cleared it. that is jmx, the java management extensions, and it is worth knowing what has become of it, because the answer is more interesting than “it died”. what it is. jmx 1.0 was defined through the java community process as jsr 3, with remote access added by jsr 160, and it has been part of standard java since j2se 5.0. resources are exposed as mbeans and registered with an mbeanserver ; connectors, usually rmi, let a remote tool read and change them. it still ships in every jdk today, in the java.management module, which also provides the interfaces for monitoring the jvm itself. what changed around it. monitoring moved to a different shape. instead of a person connecting a console to one jvm, systems now collect dimensional metrics from hundreds of short-lived containers, scraped over http by prometheus or pushed through opentelemetry, and an rmi port is an awkward thing to open in a container and an unwelcome thing to expose ( analysis ). you can see the shift in the defaults: spring boot does not enable jmx by default; you turn it on with spring.jmx.enabled=true . its metrics go through micrometer, a vendor-neutral facade, and spring boot describes micrometer’s jmx mapping as “primarily a cheap and portable way to view metrics locally”. apache kafka still exposes all its metrics through jmx (its documentation suggests firing up jconsole to browse them), but disables remote jmx by default and says you must enable security if you turn it on in production. quarkus ’s kafka guide shows how to switch off jmx mbean registration altogether. jmx as a source, with bridges. so jmx has quietly changed role: libraries still publish to it, and something else carries the numbers out. bridge what it does prometheus jmx exporter a collector that captures jmx mbean values and serves them for prometheus to scrape opentelemetry jmx metric insight part of the opentelemetry java agent: you describe the mbeans you want in a yaml file, and they are reported alongside the agent’s other metrics jolokia an agent that gives remote access to mbeans with json over http, instead of the rmi-based jsr 160 connectors for looking inside a jvm, flight recorder took over much of the job. jdk flight recorder, added to openjdk in jdk 11 (jep 328), is “a low-overhead data collection framework for troubleshooting java applications and the hotspot jvm”, and jdk 14 added event streaming so its data can feed continuous monitoring (jep 349). there is a flight recorder example on performance . if you need to… reach for look at one jvm on your own machine, now jconsole over local jmx; flight recorder for a recording monitor a fleet of services micrometer or opentelemetry metrics, scraped or exported to your monitoring system get numbers out of a library that only speaks jmx (kafka, tomcat, a connection pool) the prometheus jmx exporter or opentelemetry’s jmx metric insight change a setting at run time a secured management endpoint, or jmx with authentication and tls; never an open remote jmx port our view: jmx is not dying; it has moved down a layer. it is still the place inside the jvm where libraries publish their numbers, and that is worth knowing when a dashboard is missing something. but as the interface people use, it has been replaced by metrics pipelines and flight recorder, and new code should publish through micrometer or opentelemetry. the other view: for a single long-running server, a team that knows jconsole, and operations that need to change settings live, jmx remains simple, built in and free, and there is no need to replace something that works.

dashboards that get used one overview per service: traffic, errors, latency percentiles, saturation, last deploy marker. top-down: user-facing slos first, then dependencies, then resources. same layout for every service (a dashboard template is a blueprint). show the denominator: "12 errors" means nothing without "of 1.2 million requests". annotate deploys and incidents so changes line up with effects. delete dashboards nobody opens.

alerting page on symptoms users feel (slo burn rate, failed runs, stale data), not on causes (cpu at 80%). every page is actionable and links to a runbook. if nobody needs to act, it is a ticket or a dashboard, not a page. alert when the signal is missing: a job that did not run, a metric that stopped reporting. silence is not health. match on fields you control (a marker in the message, a structured field), not on a severity that may not be set. prove each alert fires once in a test environment before trusting it. review noisy alerts monthly: tune, fix the cause, or delete.

observing data pipelines dimension check run outcome every scheduled run recorded succeeded, failed or unknown; missing runs alert freshness newest data per source within its expected age volume row and object counts within expected ranges; reconciliation in = out + rejected schema unexpected new, missing or retyped columns detected quality test results (nulls, keys, parse failures) tracked over time cost and duration bytes, slot time and runtime per run, trended the most important rule: a check whose source is unreachable reports unknown, never zero and never green.

observing ai features log model id, input and output tokens, latency, stop reason and cost per call. trace each tool call and retrieval step as a span. track refusals, empty retrievals, citation failures and "not found" rates. sample real conversations for quality review and feed them into evals (with privacy controls).

keeping observability affordable exclude noisy, low-value logs at the router (exclusion filters) or lower their level. sample traces; keep 100% of errors and slow requests with tail sampling. watch metric cardinality; drop unused labels. route long-term logs to bigquery or gcs with retention rules instead of keeping everything hot. label resources so observability cost can be attributed to teams.

following a journey across services give every request an id, and pass it on to every service the request touches. log it with every line. give every user journey an id too, when several requests belong together, such as a multi-step form or a checkout. then you can follow the whole journey, not just one request. use the standard for tracing: the w3c trace context traceparent header carries a trace id and the caller's span id between services, so tools from different vendors can join the pieces up. opentelemetry propagates it for you. an audit trail makes rollback safe. if a journey fails halfway, you can only undo the steps you know were taken. record each step and why, then compensate in reverse order (see architecture on sagas). # a w3c trace context header: version, trace id, parent span id, flags traceparent: 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01

one trace, drawn one trace across three services a waterfall of spans over time for one request. the checkout request at the gateway is the root span and lasts the longest. inside it, a call to the orders service, which itself makes a database query. after that, a call to the payments service. every span shares one trace id, carried between services in the traceparent header, and the gateway span is the parent of the others. trace 0af7651916cd43dd… gateway: post /checkout orders: create orders: insert order payments: authorise start time → the traceparent header carries the trace id and parent span id between services one request as a trace: each bar is a span, indented under the span that called it. the longest bar is the user’s wait; the gaps show where it went.

principles 100% is the wrong target. users cannot tell 99.99% from 100%, and chasing it stops all change. pick the reliability users actually need. service level objectives make that target explicit and measurable. error budgets turn it into a decision rule: budget left, ship faster; budget spent, slow down and fix reliability. toil is reduced by engineering: automate repetitive manual work rather than staffing it. blameless postmortems: incidents are system failures to learn from, not people to blame. simplicity: every component you do not have cannot fail. no person or laptop is the mechanism: if something only works while a human watches it, it is not built yet.

sli, slo, sla, error budget term is example sli a measured ratio of good events to valid events search requests answered successfully in under 500 ms ÷ all search requests slo the target for an sli over a window 99.5% over 28 days error budget 1 − slo: the failure you may spend 0.5% of requests ≈ 3.4 hours of full outage in 28 days sla a contract with consequences, looser than the slo 99% monthly, or credits measure slis as close to the user as possible (load balancer or client), not from inside the server, which cannot see its own outages.

the budget, drawn an slo and its error budget a bar for 28 days of requests, 100 percent wide. 99.5 percent is the slo target: requests that must be good. the remaining 0.5 percent is the error budget, about 3.4 hours of full outage. below, the sla at 99 percent sits looser than the slo, so you are warned before the contract is broken. a burn rate of 1 spends the whole budget in exactly the window; 14.4 spends 2 percent of it in one hour. slo: 99.5% of requests good over 28 days error budget 0.5% ≈ 3.4 h outage sla in the contract: looser than the slo, e.g. 99% monthly, so the slo warns you first burn rate 1: the budget lasts exactly the window burn rate 14.4: 2% of a 30-day budget gone in one hour → page the table above as one bar. the budget is the failure you are allowed to spend; the burn rate says how fast you are spending it, and the alerts below fire on that rate.

choosing slis system typical slis request/response api availability (non-5xx), latency (fraction under a threshold) data pipeline freshness (data newer than x), completeness (rows reconciled), correctness (tests passing) batch job runs completed on time; runs succeeded storage durability, read/write availability and latency ai feature successful responses, latency, grounded-answer rate from evals pipeline freshness slo example sli: minutes in which the newest order_date served is < 26 h old ÷ minutes in the window slo: 99% over 28 days budget: ≈ 6.7 hours of staleness per 28 days

error budget policy budget healthy: ship at normal speed; take calculated risks. budget at risk (e.g. 50% spent early): extra review on risky changes; reliability work moves up the backlog. budget exhausted: freeze non-urgent feature releases for the service until reliability fixes land and the budget recovers. one incident ate over 20% of the budget: a postmortem with tracked actions is mandatory. agree the policy with product owners before it is needed.

alerting on slos: burn rates burn rate = how fast you are spending the budget, relative to spending exactly all of it over the window. burn rate 1 uses the budget in exactly 28–30 days; burn rate 14.4 uses 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. alert burn rate long window short window budget consumed action fast burn 14.4 1 hour 5 minutes 2% page medium burn 6 6 hours 30 minutes 5% page slow burn 1 3 days 6 hours 10% ticket both windows must exceed the threshold: the long one shows it matters, the short one shows it is still happening, so the alert stops soon after recovery. these are the starting values from google's sre workbook; tune to your traffic.

on-call sustainable load: few enough pages that each one gets real attention; track pages per shift. every page has a runbook: what it means, how to check, how to mitigate, who to escalate to. primary and secondary on rotation, with handover notes. access ready in advance: break-glass roles, dashboards, tooling; never "i need permissions" at 3 a.m. reduce pages continuously: every page should lead to a fix, a tuned alert, or an automated response.

incident response role does incident commander owns the incident, coordinates, decides; does not debug operations lead investigates and applies mitigations communications lead updates stakeholders and users on a schedule planning lead files bugs, arranges handoffs, tracks what was changed so it can be undone; often keeps the timeline too declare early; set severity; open one channel. mitigate first: roll back, fail over, disable the feature, shed load. communicate status regularly, including "no change". resolve, confirm with the slis, then hand over to the postmortem.

severity levels sev example response 1 product down or data loss or leak for many users page now, all hands, exec updates 2 major feature broken or badly degraded page now, incident roles 3 minor feature or few users affected; workaround exists business hours 4 cosmetic or internal only ticket

blameless postmortem template # incident: <title> sev: 2 date: 2026-11-12 ## summary what happened, impact, duration (2–3 sentences) ## impact users affected, slo budget spent, data affected ## timeline (utc) detection, escalation, mitigation, resolution ## root cause(s) the conditions that allowed it, not a person ## detection how we found out; how we should have ## what went well ## what went badly ## where we got lucky ## action items owner · due date · ticket — prevent, detect, mitigate ## lessons what we now know about the system ask "what made this possible?" five times, not "who did it?". turn each lesson into a guard: a test, an alert, a policy, an automation.

toil toil is manual, repetitive, automatable, reactive work that grows with the service and leaves no lasting value: restarting jobs by hand, re-running loads, copying credentials. cap it (google aims for under 50% of an sre's time) and spend the rest on engineering that removes it. measure it: log toil tasks and their time; automate the biggest first. automation must be durable: a scheduler and a job in the platform, not a script on someone's laptop or a session polling in a loop.

production readiness review slos defined, measured and on a dashboard. alerts on slo burn and on missing runs, each with a runbook; proven to fire. logs structured, traces flowing, dashboards from the template. capacity tested at expected peak plus headroom. deploys automated, with canary or rollback tested. backups exist and a restore has been tested ; rpo and rto written down. dependencies listed with their failure behaviour. security review done; secrets in a manager; least-privilege iam. on-call rotation and escalation path in place.

reliability practices progressive delivery: canaries, feature flags and automatic rollback. capacity planning: forecast from growth, load-test to find limits, keep headroom. graceful degradation: serve partial or cached results and say so. disaster recovery: multi-zone by default; multi-region when the slo needs it; rehearsed restores. game days and chaos tests: break things on purpose in a controlled way to test detection and response. dependency slos: your slo cannot exceed what your critical dependencies provide unless you add redundancy.

slos on google cloud cloud monitoring service monitoring defines services and slos (request-based or window-based) and charts budget. alert policies can use the slo burn rate directly. declare slos and alerts in terraform ( google_monitoring_slo , google_monitoring_alert_policy ) so they are reviewed and versioned. for pipelines, compute freshness and completeness slis from run records in bigquery and export them as custom or log-based metrics.

c.h: The layers, from the ground up
c.x: the layers, from the ground up layer what it really is why it matters to you buildings data centres: power, cooling, physical security, fibre. a zone is one or more of them that fail together; a region is a group of zones close enough to talk fast spread work across zones to survive a building failing; pick a region for latency and data residency servers racks of ordinary machines: cpus, memory, local disks, network cards. they fail every day at this scale design as if any one machine can disappear, because it will virtualisation a hypervisor splits one physical server into many virtual machines, each believing it has its own hardware your "server" shares a machine with strangers; isolation is the provider's hardest job network software-defined networking: your private network, firewall rules and load balancers are configuration on shared switches and fibre moving data costs money and time, especially between regions and out to the internet storage block disks attached over the network, object stores that spread copies of your files across machines and zones, managed file systems durability comes from copies in different places; every copy and every read has a price control plane the apis, identity and permissions, scheduling, quotas and billing that turn all of the above into "click to create" every console click and every terraform line is an api call; iam decides who can make it managed services databases, queues, serverless and ai services: software the provider runs for you, built from the same layers you trade control for convenience; the parts underneath still fail and still cost money

virtual machines, containers and sandboxes a virtual machine has its own operating system kernel on virtual hardware. strong isolation, slower to start. a container shares the host's kernel and isolates processes with kernel features. fast and light, but sharing a kernel means weaker isolation. providers close the gap with sandboxes. firecracker, developed at amazon web services for services such as aws lambda and now open source, uses linux kvm to run lightweight "microvms" that start fast but keep virtual-machine isolation. gvisor, open-sourced by google, is an "application kernel" that sits between a container and the host, because, in its own words, containers are not a sandbox. serverless is this underneath: someone else's servers, packed densely, started on demand, and billed by the request or the second.

scheduling: who runs where a scheduler decides which machine runs each piece of work, packing jobs tightly to use the hardware well and moving them when machines fail. kubernetes brings this idea to everyone. its own readme says it builds on google's experience running production workloads at scale with an internal system called borg. why you care: requests and limits, bin packing and preemption decide both your bill and whether your work gets evicted. see kubernetes .

what "managed" really means a managed database is still a database server on virtual machines with disks, replicas and backups. the provider patches and fails it over for you. object storage is many machines holding copies or encoded fragments of your files, with an api in front. that is why it is durable, cheap and slower than a local disk. a serverless function runs in a sandbox on a shared machine; a "cold start" is that sandbox being created for you. knowing the parts helps you ask the right questions: where are the copies, what happens when a zone fails, what is billed, and what can i take elsewhere.

shared responsibility the provider secures the cloud: buildings, hardware, hypervisors, their network and their services. you secure what you put in it: identities and permissions, your data, your network rules, your code and its dependencies, and the settings you choose. the more managed the service, the more the provider takes on, but your identities, data and settings are always yours. many cloud breaches start with a setting someone left open or a leaked credential, not a broken data centre. see security .

c.h: Follow one request through the layers
c.x: follow one request through the layers you open a web page served from the cloud. your request reaches the provider's edge and a load balancer (software on shared hardware), which picks a healthy instance in one zone. that instance is a container or virtual machine, placed by a scheduler on a physical server in a data centre. it reads from a managed database (more virtual machines, with a replica in another zone) and from object storage (copies spread across machines), writes logs and metrics (yet more storage), and every step is checked against permissions and metered for the bill. when one machine, or one building, fails, the layers above route around it, if you designed for it. try it yourself: run a small app on cloud run , then find each layer in the console: the region and zone, the revision and its instances, the logs, the iam roles, and the bill.
