c.h: Where each tends to stand out
c.x: where each tends to stand out google cloud: data and analytics (bigquery is serverless with nothing to size), global networking with a global vpc and single-ip global load balancing, kubernetes (gke), developer-friendly serverless (cloud run), and ai with gemini enterprise agent platform (formerly vertex ai). projects make isolation simple. aws: the broadest and deepest service catalogue, the largest ecosystem and talent pool, many regions, and mature options for almost every niche. more configuration choices, and more to learn. azure: enterprises standardised on microsoft (entra id, microsoft 365, windows, sql server, .net), hybrid setups (azure arc), and the microsoft data and ai stack (fabric, power bi, azure openai). all three are capable for almost any workload. the deciding factors are usually existing skills and contracts, specific services you depend on, data location, and price after discounts.

differences that bite iam thinking: gcp binds roles to principals on resources; aws writes json policies with explicit allow/deny and resource arns; azure assigns roles at a scope in a strict hierarchy. networking: a gcp vpc spans regions; aws and azure networks are regional and are joined with peering or transit gateways/hubs. isolation unit: gcp teams often use many projects; aws uses many accounts; azure uses subscriptions plus resource groups. warehouses: bigquery bills by bytes scanned or by slots with no cluster to run; redshift has provisioned clusters or serverless capacity units; fabric uses capacity units shared across workloads. discounts: gcp committed and sustained use discounts; aws savings plans and reserved instances; azure reservations and savings plans. spot or preemptible capacity everywhere for interruptible work. egress: data leaving a cloud costs money on all three; cross-region and cross-cloud traffic adds up. design data placement before choosing multi-cloud.

staying portable (where it matters) containers and kubernetes run the same on gke, eks and aks; cloud run-style serverless is less portable but simpler. terraform for all infrastructure, with provider-specific modules behind your own interfaces. open data formats (parquet, iceberg, delta) in object storage keep data readable by any engine. open protocols: postgres, kafka, opentelemetry, oidc, s3-compatible apis. dbt and sql transfer between warehouses with dialect adjustments. accept lock-in deliberately where a managed service saves real effort (bigquery, spanner, dynamodb); write down the exit cost. multi-cloud for its own sake doubles skills, tooling and egress. use it for a concrete reason: a customer requirement, a unique service, resilience against a provider-wide failure, or negotiation.

choosing for a new workload where is the data now, and where must it legally live? which managed services would save the most work (warehouse, kubernetes, ai models)? what does the team already know, and what do hiring markets offer? what identity and productivity stack does the organisation use? price a realistic workload on each calculator, including egress and support. prototype the riskiest piece on the leading candidate before committing.

the short answer our view: make cost visible to the people who make the design choices, and treat it as one requirement among several, next to reliability, security and speed. the other view is in the card “our view, and the other view”.

c.h: FinOps, and what the providers say
c.x: finops, and what the providers say google describes cloud finops (financial operations) as an operational framework and cultural practice that brings engineering, finance and business teams together to manage cloud spending and the business value it buys; rather than simply cutting costs, it sets up shared accountability for spending that varies with use. all three providers publish cost guidance in their well-architected frameworks. among google’s principles: align spending with business value, make people aware of the cost of their decisions, use only what you need, and optimise continuously. aws’s cost pillar includes adopting a consumption model and measuring the business output of a workload against what it costs to deliver.

how cloud pricing works on demand: pay for what you use, with no commitment. commitments: a lower price for agreeing to use, or spend, a minimum amount for one or three years: google’s committed use discounts, aws savings plans and azure reservations. aws and azure each say up to 72%; google publishes its rates product by product. spot capacity: spare capacity at a much lower price, which the provider can take back. google quotes discounts of up to 91% for spot vms; aws gives a two-minute warning before stopping a spot instance, and azure 30 seconds before evicting a spot vm. storage classes: colder classes cost less to keep and more to read. in cloud storage, nearline, coldline and archive have minimum storage durations of 30, 90 and 365 days. data transfer: google charges nothing for inbound data, but moving data between zones in one region is charged per gib, and leaving the cloud costs more; check each provider’s price list.

two kinds of lever two ways to lower a cloud bill a tree. the cloud bill is usage multiplied by rate. usage, how much you run, is lowered by switching off what is idle, right-sizing, autoscaling, deleting old data, and keeping data near the compute that reads it. rate, what you pay for each unit, is lowered by commitments for one or three years, spot capacity for work that can be interrupted, and a cheaper storage class for data read rarely. cloud bill usage × rate usage how much you run rate what each unit costs switch off what is idle right-size machines autoscale with demand delete old data keep data near compute commit for 1 or 3 years spot for interruptible work cheaper storage class the bill is how much you use multiplied by what each unit costs, so there are two sets of levers. azure’s well-architected framework names them usage optimization and rate optimization ; the levers listed come from the three providers’ documentation, cited on this page.

c.h: Worked example: when does a commitment pay off?
c.x: worked example: when does a commitment pay off? a commitment is paid whether or not you use it. with a discount of d , it is cheaper than paying on demand only if you use more than 1 − d of what you committed to. switching off a machine that is needed only in office hours is a usage lever with no commitment at all: aws’s cost pillar uses the example of development and test environments used eight hours a day in the working week, 40 hours of 168, and puts the potential saving at 75%. # is a commitment cheaper than paying on demand? # you pay for the commitment whether you use it or not. def cheaper_to_commit(discount, used): on_demand = used # pay only for what you use (price 1.0) committed = 1 - discount # pay the discounted price for all of it return committed < on_demand for discount in (0.20, 0.40, 0.60): break_even = 1 - discount print(f"discount {discount:.0%}: commit if you use more than {break_even:.0%};", "at 70% use:", "commit" if cheaper_to_commit(discount, 0.70) else "on demand") hours_on, hours_week = 40, 24 * 7 print(f"office-hours dev box: runs {hours_on} of {hours_week} hours,", f"so switching it off saves {1 - hours_on / hours_week:.0%}") discount 20%: commit if you use more than 80%; at 70% use: on demand discount 40%: commit if you use more than 60%; at 70% use: commit discount 60%: commit if you use more than 40%; at 70% use: commit office-hours dev box: runs 40 of 168 hours, so switching it off saves 76% run as shown with python 3; the second block is its real output. the discounts are round numbers for the arithmetic, not any provider’s price. aws gives 75%.

seeing who spends what tags and labels: aws cost allocation tags, once activated, group costs on the cost allocation report by each tag’s key and value; google cloud passes resource labels, such as a team or cost centre, to billing, so charges can be grouped by label. budgets and alerts: google warns that an alerts-only budget does not cap usage or spending; it only tells you how costs are trending. stopping spend needs an action, which can be automated, for example by disabling billing on a project, or a spend-cap budget where the service supports one. one format for cost data: focus, the finops open cost and usage specification, is an open schema for cost and usage data across clouds, saas and data centres, so bills from different providers can be compared.

cost as an engineering choice analysis: some of the largest costs are fixed by design rather than by tuning: a chatty service in another zone or region pays for every byte it moves; a copy of data kept “just in case” is paid for every month; logs kept at full detail for ever grow without limit. these are cheapest to fix while the design is still on paper. azure’s cost guidance also warns against choosing a cheaper option that weakens security, scalability, resilience or operability, because that can cost the business more later.

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) steady load that will run for a year or more a commitment, sized to the base you are confident of, with on demand above it batch or stateless work that can be stopped and retried spot capacity, with the work built to handle the notice period load that rises and falls with users autoscaling, or serverless that scales to zero, before any commitment environments needed only in working hours a schedule that switches them off data read rarely but kept for years a colder storage class, with lifecycle rules; check the minimum storage duration and retrieval cost services that call each other heavily place them, and their data, in the same region, and the same zone where resilience allows nobody can say which team owns a cost tags or labels, applied by policy, before any optimisation your team already has commitments or tooling with one provider use them first: moving has its own cost

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: engineers should see the cost of what they build, per service and per unit of business output, as aws’s pillar suggests, and design with it from the start. the other view: early in a product, speed of learning matters more than the bill, and time spent tuning cost can be time not spent finding out whether anyone wants the product; on this view, cost work waits until the spend is large enough to justify it.

c.h: What a retailer has to connect
c.x: what a retailer has to connect stores and tills: the point of sale, where a retail transaction is completed. a till that stops when the network does stops the shop, so stores need to keep selling on their own (see below). online: the website, the apps, search and recommendations. orders and stock: order management, and one view of stock across stores, warehouses and goods on the way. warehouses and delivery: picking, packing, carriers and returns. payments: cards and wallets in store and online (see payment gateways ). finance and planning: the erp, the general ledger, buying and replenishment. suppliers: often through edi, the computer-to-computer exchange of structured business documents such as purchase orders, invoices and shipping notices, in standards such as un/edifact, ansi asc x12, gs1 edi and tradacoms. customers: loyalty, marketing and service, which all want the same customer record. analysis: the hardest part is rarely one system. it is keeping stock and orders consistent between them, for example when a customer buys online and collects in a store that is also selling the same item at its tills.

c.h: Integration patterns that hold up in retail
c.x: integration patterns that hold up in retail analysis, built on the pages linked. events for things that changed: “order placed”, “stock moved”, “item sold”, published once and read by every system that cares (see kafka and event sourcing ). apis for questions that need an answer now: the price of this item, or reserving stock for this order (see apis & integration ). store and forward at the till: record each sale locally with its own unique id, and send it when the network returns. the receiving side must accept the same sale twice without counting it twice. the outbox: write the change and the event in one local transaction, then publish, so the two cannot disagree. batch where batch is fine: supplier edi files and nightly finance loads do not need to be real time. reconcile: compare till totals, orders, stock and payments every day, and treat a gap as an incident.

c.h: A worked example: click and collect
c.x: a worked example: click and collect the customer orders online. the order service, in the cloud, reserves stock at the chosen store through an api. an “order placed” event reaches the store system, which adds a pick task and takes the item out of sellable stock. the store picks the item and sends “ready”; the customer gets a message. at collection the till records the hand-over. if the store is offline, it records it locally and sends it later. the stock change flows to replenishment, which may send a purchase order to the supplier by edi. analysis: every arrow above can fail or arrive twice. give each message a unique id, make each receiver idempotent, and decide in advance what the store does when it cannot reach the cloud.

c.h: The same building blocks on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
c.x: the same building blocks on aws, azure and google cloud you need aws azure google cloud messaging and events between systems amazon eventbridge: a serverless service that uses events to connect application components azure service bus: a managed message broker with queues and publish-subscribe topics pub/sub: an asynchronous messaging service that decouples services producing messages from services processing them a private network link from your data centre direct connect: your network to a direct connect location over a fibre-optic cable expressroute: a private connection to microsoft cloud services through a connectivity provider cloud interconnect: low-latency, high-availability connections between your networks the provider’s cloud on your own premises aws outposts: aws infrastructure and apis at your site, operated by aws as part of a region azure local: azure capabilities on customer-owned machines, connected or disconnected, managed through azure arc google distributed cloud connected: for a very stable network connection, the lowest attainable latency, data too large to transfer for performance or cost reasons, or laws that require data to stay on premises some useful pieces do not line up one to one. each of these is described in its provider’s own documentation: azure arc lets you manage servers, kubernetes clusters and databases that run outside azure, on premises or on other clouds, as if they ran in azure. gke multi-cloud creates google kubernetes engine clusters in aws and azure. cross-cloud interconnect is a dedicated physical connection between google’s network and another cloud provider’s. a gateway you run yourself: azure api management’s self-hosted gateway is a container version of its managed gateway (developer and premium tiers); apigee hybrid keeps the management plane in google’s cloud and runs the runtime plane on your own kubernetes. on devices, for example in a store: aws iot greengrass is an open-source edge runtime that lets devices act on their own data locally and send it to aws. for retail search and recommendations: amazon personalize generates item recommendations from your data; google’s ai commerce search serves search and recommendations from catalogue and user-event data. this list is what we checked in each provider’s documentation. it does not prove a provider has no equivalent; check the current documentation before you decide.

c.h: Hybrid: what stays on premises, and why. Choose by requirement
c.x: hybrid: what stays on premises, and why. choose by requirement hybrid cloud is a public cloud and a private environment, such as a private cloud or on-premises machines, that stay separate but are bound together. if this is true for you it leans towards what it costs you stores must keep selling when the network drops compute in every store, holding the sales and prices it needs a fleet of small sites to update, secure and monitor law or contract says data must stay in a place you control on premises, or the provider’s on-premises offering hardware and capacity you plan for yourself; google lists limited processing capacity as a limit of its connected deployments devices in the store make large data, such as camera video process it locally and send only the results local capacity, and models to update at every site the work cannot tolerate network delay or jitter run it next to the devices same as above a mainframe or erp in your data centre runs the business and works keep it, and connect it with a private link, events and apis two ways of operating, and the skills for both seasonal peaks go beyond what you own cloud bursting: use public cloud capacity for the temporary peak data and networks designed so work can move none of the above public cloud only the least to run

c.h: Multi-cloud: when it pays, and when it costs. Choose by requirement
c.x: multi-cloud: when it pays, and when it costs. choose by requirement iso/iec 22123-1 defines multi-cloud as a deployment model in which a customer uses public cloud services from two or more providers. if this is true for you it leans towards what it costs you you need a service only one provider offers, and the rest runs elsewhere use that service on its own cloud for that job data transfer between clouds, a second identity and security setup a customer, regulator or contract requires a named provider, or a tested exit plan multi-cloud, or one cloud with a rehearsed exit keeping the exit working, not just written down you bought a company that runs on another cloud connect the two with apis and events first; decide on moving later two platforms until you consolidate, if ever your contract renewal depends on having a credible alternative the ability to move a workload, shown in practice only credible if you have actually kept it portable you must survive a whole provider failing the same system running on two clouds the highest cost here: two of everything, and the data kept in step a small team builds one product one provider some lock-in, accepted on purpose (see staying portable ) wikipedia’s summary of the sources: multi-cloud can improve resilience, reduce dependence on one vendor and help in negotiating price, and it brings more operational complexity, security risk, cost and integration work.

c.h: The costs that usually decide it
c.x: the costs that usually decide it data leaving a cloud: on google cloud, inbound data transfer has no charge (though services that process it, such as load balancers and cloud nat, may), while data leaving google cloud is priced by network tier and destination. check each provider’s network pricing for your traffic before you split a system across clouds. switching in the eu: under the eu data act, from 11 january 2024 to 12 january 2027 providers may charge only the costs directly linked to switching; from 12 january 2027 they may charge nothing for switching, data egress included. skills and tools: two clouds means two sets of identity, networking, monitoring and on-call knowledge. the lowest common denominator: code written to run anywhere cannot use what makes one provider better at a job.

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: start on one cloud. make every store able to work alone, connect the data centre you already have rather than rushing to empty it, and add a second provider only for a reason you can name from the tables above. the other view: some teams start multi-cloud on purpose, so that portability is built in from day one rather than retrofitted at great cost, and so that no single provider’s prices or outages can hold them hostage. lower switching charges under the eu data act cut the cost of moving later, which weakens the first argument for some and strengthens the case for keeping a real exit open for others.

reference architectures pattern flow fits batch elt source → storage transfer / cloud run job → gcs (raw) → bigquery load → dbt layers → marts → looker / api daily or hourly data, files and exports, most analytics streaming apps → pub/sub → dataflow (parse, enrich, window) → bigquery (+ gcs archive) seconds-level freshness, clickstreams, iot, fraud signals simple streaming apps → pub/sub → bigquery subscription events that need no transformation before landing cdc replication postgres/mysql → datastream → bigquery (merged or append) → dbt analytics on an operational database without load on it lakehouse gcs (parquet/iceberg) ← dataproc spark / dataflow; lakehouse (biglake) tables → bigquery sql open formats shared by several engines reverse etl / serving bigquery mart → export or loader → cloud sql / alloydb → api serving curated data to an application with low latency rag over documents gcs docs → parse (dataflow / cloud run) → chunks + embeddings (bigquery ml / agent platform) → vector search → model ai question answering over your corpus

choosing between similar services sql in bigquery vs dataflow: if it can be expressed in sql over data already in bigquery, use sql (dbt). use dataflow for streaming, non-sql parsing, or work before data reaches bigquery. dataflow vs dataproc: dataflow for new pipelines (serverless, beam, streaming). managed service for apache spark (formerly dataproc) for existing spark code or spark libraries. cloud run job vs dataflow: a job for simple, bounded work (copy files, call an api). dataflow when data volume needs many workers and autoscaling. managed airflow (formerly composer) vs workflows: managed airflow for many pipelines with dependencies, backfills and sensors. workflows plus scheduler for a handful of steps; much cheaper to run. dbt vs dataform: both do sql elt with tests. dataform is built into bigquery; dbt has the larger ecosystem and runs on any warehouse. pub/sub vs kafka: pub/sub is serverless and global with nothing to size. kafka gives log semantics, replay by offset, compaction and the kafka ecosystem. cloud sql vs alloydb vs spanner: cloud sql for most postgres needs; alloydb for heavier postgres workloads and analytics; spanner for global scale with strong consistency.

handy commands # pub/sub straight into bigquery gcloud pubsub topics create order-events gcloud pubsub subscriptions create order-to-bq \ --topic=order-events \ --bigquery-table=my-proj:raw.order_events \ --use-table-schema # storage transfer: one-off copy between buckets gcloud transfer jobs create gs://source-bucket gs://my-landing # managed service for apache spark, serverless (the cli is still gcloud dataproc): run a pyspark job gcloud dataproc batches submit pyspark job.py \ --region=asia-south1 --deps-bucket=gs://my-deps # dataflow: list and inspect jobs gcloud dataflow jobs list --region=asia-south1 --status=active gcloud dataflow jobs describe job_id --region=asia-south1 # datastream streams gcloud datastream streams list --location=asia-south1

iam for data, in practice one service account per pipeline component (landing, load, transform, serve), each with only its roles. dataset-level grants rather than project-wide: bigquery.dataeditor on the datasets it writes, dataviewer on those it reads. bigquery.jobuser on the project that pays for queries; this is separate from data access. bucket-level roles with uniform bucket-level access; objectviewer for readers, objectadmin only for the writer. policy tags for sensitive columns; authorised views to share a subset. serving databases get a read-only user for the api.

cost controls partition and cluster; require partition filters on large tables. set per-user and per-project custom query quotas, and maximum_bytes_billed on jobs. export billing to bigquery and build a cost dashboard by label. label every resource with team, component and environment. gcs lifecycle rules to move old raw data to nearline/coldline/archive. stop or scale down non-production cloud sql, dataproc and composer when unused. dataflow: right-size workers, use streaming engine, and set max workers. keep development windows small: a few partitions, not the full history.

c.h: Data quality and governance on GCP
c.x: data quality and governance on gcp dbt tests in the transformation layer for keys, relationships and accepted values. knowledge catalog (formerly dataplex) data quality scans for rules on tables, scheduled, with results in bigquery. knowledge catalog data profiling to see distributions, nulls and distinct counts. lineage from bigquery jobs and dataflow is recorded automatically in knowledge catalog once the data lineage api is enabled. run records of your own: every pipeline run writes what it read, wrote and rejected. sensitive data protection scans to find personal data you did not know you had.

partitioned, clustered table create table if not exists `proj.analytics.orders` ( order_id string not null, order_ref string, store_id string, order_date date, lines array<struct<sku string, qty int64>>, _landed_at timestamp ) partition by date_trunc(order_date, month) cluster by store_id, order_ref options ( require_partition_filter = true, description = 'orders, one row per order_id', labels = [('layer', 'analytics')] ); -- integer range partition partition by range_bucket(order_year, generate_array(1995, 2031, 1)) -- ingestion-time partition partition by _partitiondate limit: 10,000 partitions per table. daily partitions over 30 years (about 11,000 days) overflow it; use month or year.

the table, drawn a partitioned, clustered table the orders table from the example, partitioned by month of order_date: january, february, march and so on. inside each partition, rows are clustered, kept in order, by store_id then order_ref. a query that filters on order_date in march reads only the march partition; the others are not scanned. because the table requires a partition filter, a query without one is refused. proj.analytics.orders partition by month cluster by store_id, order_ref 2026-01 store s1 … store s2 … store s3 … 2026-02 store s1 … store s2 … store s3 … 2026-03 store s1 … store s2 … store s3 … 2026-04 store s1 … store s2 … store s3 … where order_date between '2026-03-01' and '2026-03-31': only march is scanned require_partition_filter = true: a query with no date filter is refused the example table above. on-demand pricing bills bytes scanned, and the partition filter is what keeps the scan to one month.

deduplicate with qualify -- latest version of each key select * from `proj.raw.orders` where order_year = 2024 qualify row_number() over ( partition by store_id, order_ref order by _landed_at desc ) = 1; -- latest event per entity (append-only ledger → current state) select * except(rn) from ( select *, row_number() over (partition by run_id, stage order by event_ts desc) rn from `proj.ops.job_run_events`) where rn = 1; -- whole row of the max, no window select array_agg(t order by order_date desc limit 1)[offset(0)].* from `proj.analytics.orders` t group by store_id;

merge (upsert) merge `proj.mart.serving` t using ( select * from `proj.analytics.orders` where order_date >= date_sub(current_date(), interval 7 day) ) s on t.order_id = s.order_id and t.order_date >= date_sub(current_date(), interval 7 day) -- prune t when matched and t.row_hash != s.row_hash then update set order_ref = s.order_ref, order_date = s.order_date, row_hash = s.row_hash when not matched by target then insert row when not matched by source and t.order_date >= date_sub(current_date(), interval 7 day) then delete; -- change detection hash to_hex(sha256(to_json_string(struct(order_ref, store_id, order_date)))) as row_hash farm_fingerprint(concat(store_id, '|', order_ref)) -- int64 key

dates & safe parsing parse_date('%d-%m-%y', '05-05-1959') -- errors on bad input safe.parse_date('%d-%m-%y', raw) -- null on bad input safe_cast(order_seq as int64) -- never let a parse failure hide as a null: count it select countif(raw is not null and safe.parse_date('%d-%m-%y', raw) is null) as unparsed from t; date_trunc(d, month) date_add(d, interval 1 day) date_diff(a, b, day) last_day(d, month) extract(year from d) format_date('%y%m%d', d) timestamp_trunc(ts, hour) datetime(ts, 'asia/kolkata') current_date('asia/kolkata') unix_millis(ts) timestamp_micros(n) -- calendar spine for gap finding select d from unnest(generate_date_array('2025-01-01', current_date())) d left join facts f on f.dt = d where f.dt is null;

array, struct, unnest, json -- explode select o.order_ref, i.sku, i.qty from `proj.analytics.orders` o, unnest(o.lines) i; -- comma = cross join -- keep rows with empty arrays left join unnest(o.lines) i -- build select order_ref, array_agg(struct(sku, qty) order by sku) lines from order_lines group by order_ref; array_length(a) a[safe_offset(0)] array_to_string(a, ',') 'x' in unnest(a) exists(select 1 from unnest(a) v where v > 3) -- json json_value(payload, '$.store.code') -- scalar as string json_query(payload, '$.lines') -- json fragment json_query_array(payload, '$.lines') -- array<json> on a json column, array<string> on a string lax_int64(payload.count) -- on a json column to_json_string(struct(a, b)) parse_json(s)

window functions select store, order_date, n, sum(n) over (partition by store order by order_date) as running, avg(n) over (partition by store order by order_date rows between 6 preceding and current row) as avg_7d, lag(n) over (partition by store order by order_date) as prev, n / sum(n) over (partition by store) as share, rank() over (partition by store order by n desc) as rnk, ntile(4) over (order by n) as quartile from daily; -- named window select sum(n) over w, max(n) over w from daily window w as (partition by store order by order_date); approx_count_distinct(order_ref) approx_quantiles(n, 100)[offset(50)]

load, export, external load data into `proj.raw.orders` from files (format = 'parquet', uris = ['gs://landing/data/year=2024/*.parquet']); export data options ( uri = 'gs://exports/serving/2025-01-31/*.parquet', -- one * required format = 'parquet', overwrite = true, compression = 'snappy' ) as select * from `proj.mart.serving` where _run_date = '2025-01-31'; create or replace external table `proj.raw.orders_ext` with partition columns options (format = 'parquet', uris = ['gs://landing/data/*'], hive_partition_uri_prefix = 'gs://landing/data');

scripting & procedures declare run_date date default current_date(); declare n int64; set n = (select count(*) from `proj.analytics.orders` where _run_date = run_date); if n = 0 then raise using message = format('no rows for %t', run_date); end if; begin transaction; delete from `proj.mart.serving` where _run_date = run_date; insert into `proj.mart.serving` select * from staging; commit transaction; execute immediate format('select count(*) from `proj.%s.t`', ds); create or replace procedure `proj.ops.rebuild`(d date) begin ... end; call `proj.ops.rebuild`(date '2025-01-31');

pipe syntax from `proj.analytics.orders` |> where order_date >= '2024-01-01' |> aggregate count(*) as n group by store_id |> order by n desc |> limit 10; -- other operators: select, extend (add columns), set, drop, rename, -- join, as (alias), pivot, unpivot, tablesample, call reads top to bottom in execution order. mixes freely with standard sql in the same project.

metadata & cost queries -- most expensive queries in the last day select user_email, job_id, round(total_bytes_billed / pow(1024, 4), 3) as tib_billed, total_slot_ms, left(query, 120) as q from `region-asia-south1`.information_schema.jobs where creation_time > timestamp_sub(current_timestamp(), interval 1 day) and job_type = 'query' order by total_bytes_billed desc limit 20; -- partitions and their row counts select partition_id, total_rows, total_logical_bytes from `proj.analytics.information_schema.partitions` where table_name = 'orders' order by partition_id; -- columns of a table select column_name, data_type, is_nullable from `proj.analytics.information_schema.columns` where table_name = 'orders'; -- table sizes select table_id, row_count, size_bytes / 1e9 as gb from `proj.analytics.__tables__` order by size_bytes desc;

time travel, snapshots, wildcards -- read the table as it was (up to 7 days back by default) select * from `proj.analytics.orders` for system_time as of timestamp_sub(current_timestamp(), interval 1 hour); -- undo a bad write create or replace table `proj.analytics.orders_restore` as select * from `proj.analytics.orders` for system_time as of '2025-01-31 06:00:00+00'; -- zero-copy snapshot / clone create snapshot table `proj.backup.orders_20250131` clone `proj.analytics.orders`; create table `proj.dev.orders` clone `proj.analytics.orders`; -- sharded tables select * from `proj.logs.events_*` where _table_suffix between '20250101' and '20250131';

cost & performance rules name columns. storage is columnar; select * bills every column. select * except(raw_html) drops wide ones. filter on the partition column with a constant or parameter. a filter through a function of another table's subquery may not prune. limit does not reduce bytes on a regular table. use table preview or tablesample system (1 percent) . dry-run first and set maximum_bytes_billed on jobs that could run away. cluster on high-cardinality filter/join columns; order matters, first column filters best. join big to small after filtering; pre-aggregate before joining. avoid row-by-row dml. batch into one merge: each statement is a query you pay for, and only two update, delete or merge statements per table run at once (20 more can queue; beyond that they fail). materialised views for repeated aggregates; bi engine for dashboards. execution graph in the console shows skew, spills and which stage costs the slots.

bq cli bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run 'select ...' bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --format=prettyjson --max_rows=20 \ --parameter=from_d:date:2024-01-01 \ 'select count(*) from `proj.analytics.orders` where order_date >= @from_d' bq query --nouse_legacy_sql --maximum_bytes_billed=10000000000 < q.sql bq ls proj:analytics bq show --schema --format=prettyjson proj:analytics.orders bq head -n 10 proj:analytics.orders bq load --source_format=parquet --replace \ 'proj:raw.events$20250131' 'gs://landing/events/dt=2025-01-31/*.parquet' # one partition bq extract --destination_format=parquet proj:mart.serving 'gs://exp/serving-*.parquet' bq cp proj:analytics.orders proj:backup.orders_20250131 bq mk --table --time_partitioning_field=order_date --clustering_fields=store_id \ proj:analytics.t schema.json bq ls -j -a -n 20 # recent jobs bq show -j <job_id>

services, jobs, worker pools kind runs when use it for service a request arrives (http, grpc, websocket, pub/sub push, eventarc) apis, web apps, webhooks. scales on traffic, down to zero. job someone executes it (cli, api, cloud scheduler, workflows) batch loads, migrations, nightly exports. runs n tasks in parallel, then exits. worker pool always, with no http endpoint pull-based consumers (kafka, pub/sub pull). generally available since april 2026; some options are still in preview.

container contract listen on $port (default 8080) on 0.0.0.0 , not 127.0.0.1 . jobs do not listen at all. stateless. any instance can serve any request; instances come and go. the filesystem is in memory and counts against the memory limit. write big files to gcs or a mounted volume. shutdown: the container gets sigterm , then about 10 seconds before sigkill . flush and close there. logs: anything written to stdout/stderr goes to cloud logging. jobs: exit code 0 means the task succeeded; anything else fails it (and retries it if max-retries > 0). platform: build images for linux/amd64 . an arm64 image from a mac will not start.

deploy a service gcloud run deploy api \ --image=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:3f2a9c1 \ --region=asia-south1 \ --service-account=api@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --no-allow-unauthenticated \ --cpu=1 --memory=1gi \ --concurrency=80 --min-instances=0 --max-instances=10 \ --timeout=300 \ --cpu-boost \ --set-env-vars=app_profile=prod,dataset=analytics \ --set-secrets=db_password=db-password:3 \ --labels=env=prod,team=data # build from source with cloud build + buildpacks / dockerfile gcloud run deploy api --source . --region=asia-south1 gcloud run services describe api --region=asia-south1 --format='value(status.url)' gcloud run services list --set-env-vars replaces all env vars; --update-env-vars adds or changes only the ones named.

revisions & traffic # deploy without sending traffic; reach it at a tagged url gcloud run deploy api --image=…:4b1c2d0 --no-traffic --tag=canary # → https://canary---api-xxxxx.a.run.app # shift 10% to the new revision gcloud run services update-traffic api \ --to-revisions=api-00042-xyz=10,api-00041-abc=90 gcloud run services update-traffic api --to-latest # 100% to newest gcloud run services update-traffic api --to-tags=canary=100 # roll back = send traffic to the previous revision gcloud run revisions list --service=api --region=asia-south1 gcloud run services update-traffic api --to-revisions=api-00041-abc=100 every deploy or config change creates a new immutable revision. settings live on the revision, so rolling back traffic also rolls back env vars and secrets.

traffic, drawn cloud run revisions and traffic splitting three steps. deploy with no traffic: revision 42 exists and is reachable only at its canary tag url, while revision 41 takes all traffic. shift 10 percent: revision 42 takes 10 percent and revision 41 90 percent. roll back: send 100 percent to revision 41 again. because settings live on the revision, the rollback also restores its environment variables and secrets. 1 deploy --no-traffic api-00041 100% api-00042 0% canary tag url only 2 update-traffic 90 / 10 api-00041 90% api-00042 10% watch errors and latency 3 roll back: 41 = 100 api-00041 100% api-00042 0% env vars and secrets too the commands above as three moments. a revision never changes, so moving traffic between revisions is how you release and how you roll back.

jobs gcloud run jobs deploy loader \ --image=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/loader:3f2a9c1 \ --region=asia-south1 \ --service-account=loader@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --tasks=10 --parallelism=5 \ --task-timeout=3600s --max-retries=0 \ --cpu=2 --memory=4gi \ --args=--year=2024 gcloud run jobs execute loader --region=asia-south1 --wait gcloud run jobs execute loader --wait \ --args=--year=2023 --update-env-vars=dry_run=true # overrides for this run only gcloud run jobs executions list --job=loader --region=asia-south1 gcloud run jobs executions describe loader-abc12 --region=asia-south1 gcloud run jobs executions cancel loader-abc12 --region=asia-south1 an execution's status is cloud run's word on whether the container exited 0. whether it did the right work is your job to record, e.g. a summary row or log line per run.

shard work across job tasks every task gets these environment variables: cloud_run_task_index : 0 … tasks − 1 cloud_run_task_count : the --tasks value cloud_run_task_attempt : 0 on the first try cloud_run_execution , cloud_run_job : names for logs and run records # python import os i = int(os.environ.get("cloud_run_task_index", 0)) n = int(os.environ.get("cloud_run_task_count", 1)) mine = [u for k, u in enumerate(sorted(all_uris)) if k % n == i] // java int i = integer.parseint(system.getenv().getordefault("cloud_run_task_index", "0")); int n = integer.parseint(system.getenv().getordefault("cloud_run_task_count", "1")); list<string> mine = intstream.range(0, uris.size()) .filter(k -> k % n == i).maptoobj(uris::get).tolist(); sort the input first so every task sees the same order. make each task idempotent: a retry repeats the whole shard.

scaling & cost concurrency (default 80 per vcpu when deployed with gcloud or terraform, 80 from the console; max 1000): requests one instance handles at once. set 1 only for code that is not thread-safe. min instances keep warm instances to avoid cold starts; they bill while idle. max instances cap spend and protect downstream databases (connections = instances × pool size). cpu allocation: by default cpu is only allocated during requests, so background threads stall after the response. --no-cpu-throttling keeps cpu on (instance-based billing). startup cpu boost ( --cpu-boost ) gives extra cpu while the container starts: helps jvm cold starts. cold start cuts: smaller images, lazy initialisation, cds/aot for java, quarkus or spring native images. jobs bill for the time each task runs, at the cpu and memory you asked for.

calling private services # grant the caller the invoker role gcloud run services add-iam-policy-binding api --region=asia-south1 \ --member=serviceaccount:caller@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role=roles/run.invoker # from your terminal curl -h "authorization: bearer $(gcloud auth print-identity-token)" https://api-xxxxx.a.run.app/health gcloud run services proxy api --region=asia-south1 --port=8080 # local tunnel # python: id token whose audience is the service url import google.auth.transport.requests, google.oauth2.id_token, requests aud = "https://api-xxxxx.a.run.app" tok = google.oauth2.id_token.fetch_id_token(google.auth.transport.requests.request(), aud) requests.get(f"{aud}/health", headers={"authorization": f"bearer {tok}"}) // java (google-auth-library) idtokencredentials creds = idtokencredentials.newbuilder() .setidtokenprovider((idtokenprovider) googlecredentials.getapplicationdefault()) .settargetaudience(aud).build(); creds.refresh(); string token = creds.getidtoken().gettokenvalue(); services need an id token (audience = url). google apis, including the cloud run admin api that executes a job, need an access token.

networking # who may reach the service --ingress=all # internet (still iam-checked) --ingress=internal # vpc and some google sources only --ingress=internal-and-cloud-load-balancing # put a load balancer / cloud armor in front # reach private ips (memorystore, internal services) with direct vpc egress --network=main --subnet=run-egress --vpc-egress=private-ranges-only --vpc-egress=all-traffic # everything via vpc → cloud nat gives a static egress ip # cloud sql via the built-in connector: unix socket in the container --add-cloudsql-instances=my-proj:asia-south1:shop # jdbc: jdbc:postgresql:///shop?cloudsqlinstance=my-proj:asia-south1:shop&socketfactory=com.google.cloud.sql.postgres.socketfactory # psycopg: host=/cloudsql/my-proj:asia-south1:shop a third party that allowlists ips needs all-traffic egress through cloud nat with a reserved address. without it, egress comes from shared google ranges.

secrets, config, volumes # secret as env var: read once, when the instance starts --set-secrets=db_password=db-password:3 # secret as a file: read when your code opens it --set-secrets=/secrets/sa.json=sa-key:latest # the runtime service account needs to read it gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding db-password \ --member=serviceaccount:api@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role=roles/secretmanager.secretaccessor # gcs bucket or in-memory volume --add-volume=name=data,type=cloud-storage,bucket=my-landing \ --add-volume-mount=volume=data,mount-path=/data --add-volume=name=scratch,type=in-memory,size-limit=1gi pin secret versions ( :3 ) in prod so a rotation is a deliberate deploy. with :latest in an env var, running instances keep the old value until they restart.

triggers cloud scheduler → job: post to https://run.googleapis.com/v2/projects/p/locations/r/jobs/j:run with an oauth token (see the terraform tab). cloud scheduler → service: http target with an oidc token whose audience is the service url. pub/sub push: subscription pushes to the service url with an oidc token; return 2xx to ack, anything else retries. eventarc: route events (gcs object finalised, bigquery job done, audit log entries) to a service. cloud tasks: queued http calls with rate limits and retries. workflows: run jobs in sequence, wait for each, branch on results. gcloud eventarc triggers create on-landing --location=asia-south1 \ --destination-run-service=ingest --destination-run-region=asia-south1 \ --event-filters=type=google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized \ --event-filters=bucket=my-landing \ --service-account=eventarc@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com

dockerfiles that start fast # java (spring boot jar) from eclipse-temurin:21-jdk as build workdir /src copy . . run ./gradlew bootjar -x test from eclipse-temurin:21-jre run useradd -u 1001 app user 1001 copy --from=build /src/build/libs/*.jar /app.jar env java_tool_options="-xx:maxrampercentage=75 -xx:+useserialgc" entrypoint ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"] # python from python:3.12-slim env pythonunbuffered=1 pip_no_cache_dir=1 workdir /app copy requirements.txt . run pip install -r requirements.txt copy . . user 1001 cmd exec gunicorn --bind :$port --workers 1 --threads 8 --timeout 0 app:app docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 -t asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:$(git rev-parse --short=12 head) --push . use the exec form ( ["java", …] or exec ) so your process is pid 1 and receives sigterm .

logging & health # one json object per line on stdout → structured log entry {"severity":"error","message":"load failed","uri":"gs://…","run_id":"r-42", "logging.googleapis.com/trace":"projects/my-proj/traces/abc123"} gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" and resource.labels.service_name="api" and severity>=error' --freshness=1h --limit=50 gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_job" and resource.labels.job_name="loader" and severity>=error' --freshness=1d --limit=20 # service.yaml fragment: probes spec: template: spec: containers: - image: … startupprobe: httpget: { path: /health/started, port: 8080 } failurethreshold: 30 periodseconds: 2 livenessprobe: httpget: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 } without severity , every line is logged at default, and severity-based alerts never fire.

declarative yaml gcloud run services describe api --region=asia-south1 --format=export > service.yaml # edit, then: gcloud run services replace service.yaml --region=asia-south1 gcloud run jobs describe loader --region=asia-south1 --format=export > job.yaml gcloud run jobs replace job.yaml --region=asia-south1 service yaml follows the knative serving schema; job yaml uses cloud run's own run.googleapis.com/v1 job kind. in a team, keep the definition in terraform ( google_cloud_run_v2_service / _job ) and use the cli for reading and one-off executions.

c.h: Errors and what they usually mean
c.x: errors and what they usually mean symptom usually means "container failed to start and listen on the port defined by port" app listens on the wrong port or on 127.0.0.1, crashes on boot (missing env var or secret), or the image is arm64. read the revision's logs. 403 calling a service caller lacks roles/run.invoker , sent an access token instead of an id token, or the token's audience is not the service url. 404 calling a service wrong url or region, or ingress is internal and you called from outside the vpc. 429 / "no available instance" max-instances reached with all instances at full concurrency. 503 with "memory limit exceeded" in logs oom: raise --memory , or stop writing large files to the in-memory filesystem. 504 / request cancelled request ran past --timeout . permission denied on secret runtime service account lacks secretmanager.secretaccessor on that secret. image pull denied the cloud run service agent cannot read the artifact registry repo (common across projects). job execution failed, logs empty task timed out, was oom-killed, or crashed before logging. executions describe shows the reason per task. background work never finishes cpu is throttled after the response. finish before responding, use --no-cpu-throttling , or hand the work to a job or cloud tasks.

core concepts concept meaning organisation top-level apigee container, tied to a gcp project environment a runtime context where proxies are deployed (dev, test, prod) environment group hostnames that route to one or more environments api proxy the façade clients call; it applies policies and forwards to the backend proxy endpoint client-facing side: base path, request and response flows target endpoint backend-facing side: the service url, its auth and timeouts flow ordered steps: preflow, conditional flows, postflow, on request and response policy a reusable step: verify a key, check a token, rate-limit, transform, cache shared flow a reusable sequence of policies used by many proxies (security, logging) api product a bundle of proxies and operations with quotas and scopes, offered to consumers developer / app a consumer and their registered app, which gets keys for products apigee x is the google cloud-hosted version; apigee hybrid runs the runtime in your own kubernetes clusters. apigee edge is the older generation.

proxy endpoint <!-- apiproxy/proxies/default.xml --> <proxyendpoint name="default"> <preflow name="preflow"> <request> <step><name>vk-verifykey</name></step> <step><name>sa-spikearrest</name></step> <step><name>q-perapp</name></step> </request> </preflow> <flows> <flow name="search"> <condition>proxy.pathsuffix matchespath "/search" and request.verb = "get"</condition> </flow> </flows> <httpproxyconnection> <basepath>/shop/v1</basepath> </httpproxyconnection> <routerule name="default"> <targetendpoint>default</targetendpoint> </routerule> </proxyendpoint>

target endpoint to cloud run <!-- apiproxy/targets/default.xml --> <targetendpoint name="default"> <httptargetconnection> <authentication> <googleidtoken> <audience>https://shop-api-xxxxx.a.run.app</audience> </googleidtoken> </authentication> <url>https://shop-api-xxxxx.a.run.app</url> </httptargetconnection> </targetendpoint> apigee calls the private cloud run service with a google id token from the proxy's service account, which needs roles/run.invoker . clients never reach cloud run directly; set its ingress accordingly.

common policies <verifyapikey name="vk-verifykey"> <apikey ref="request.header.x-api-key"/> </verifyapikey> <oauthv2 name="oa-verifytoken"> <operation>verifyaccesstoken</operation> </oauthv2> <spikearrest name="sa-spikearrest"> <rate>30ps</rate> <!-- smooths bursts --> </spikearrest> <quota name="q-perapp"> <interval>1</interval> <timeunit>day</timeunit> <allow count="10000"/> <identifier ref="client_id"/> </quota> <assignmessage name="am-removekey"> <remove><headers><header name="x-api-key"/></headers></remove> </assignmessage> category policies security verifyapikey, oauthv2, verifyjwt, basicauthentication, accesscontrol, cors traffic spikearrest, quota, responsecache mediation assignmessage, extractvariables, jsontoxml, xmltojson, raisefault extension javascript, servicecallout, messagelogging, flowcallout (shared flows) spikearrest protects the backend from bursts; quota enforces each consumer's allowance. use both.

products, apps and keys build a proxy and deploy it to an environment. create an api product listing the proxy (and operations), environments, quota and scopes, e.g. "shop api – standard: 10,000 calls/day". a developer registers an app and subscribes it to the product. the app gets a consumer key (and secret for oauth). the proxy's verifyapikey or oauthv2 policy checks it and loads the product's quota. analytics then report traffic, latency and errors per product, app and developer. products are how you package the same api differently: free and paid tiers, internal and partner access.

apigee vs api gateway apigee api gateway scope full api management lightweight managed gateway features products, developer portal, monetisation, rich policies, analytics, hybrid openapi-defined routes, api keys, jwt auth, quotas backends anything reachable cloud run, cloud functions, app engine and others cost subscription, or pay-as-you-go: per call plus each deployed environment by the hour per call only; the first 2 million calls a month are free choose when many apis, external consumers, governance, analytics a few apis, mostly internal or simple cloud endpoints is the older google option; new designs generally pick api gateway or apigee.

delivering proxies like code keep the apiproxy/ bundle and shared flows in git; review policy changes like code. deploy from ci with the apigee api, apigeecli or the apigee maven plugin, to dev → test → prod environments. manage organisations, environments and environment groups with terraform ( google_apigee_* resources). lint bundles with apigeelint before deploying. use shared flows as your blueprint: one security and logging flow every proxy calls, instead of copied policies. test with the trace/debug tool, and with automated api tests against each environment.

security and operations validate oauth tokens or jwts at the edge; the backend still checks object-level permissions. strip credentials before forwarding; add a trusted identity header only from apigee. use advanced api security to detect abuse and misconfigured proxies. put cloud armor in front of the external load balancer for waf and ddos protection. log to cloud logging with messagelogging; never log keys or tokens. watch latency split: total vs target response time tells you if the gateway or the backend is slow.

service map by lifecycle stage stage aws service what it is for land and store s3 object storage: the data lake's files, raw and curated stream in kinesis data streams; amazon msk (managed kafka) events and change streams change data capture database migration service (dms) copy and replicate from operational databases process (etl) glue (spark jobs, crawlers); emr and emr serverless; managed service for apache flink batch and streaming transformation open tables s3 tables (apache iceberg) tables on s3 with schema, snapshots and time travel query athena (sql on s3); redshift (warehouse, provisioned or serverless) analysis and serving orchestrate mwaa (managed airflow); step functions schedules and dependencies. see airflow dags catalog and govern glue data catalog; lake formation table metadata, and fine-grained access to it visualise quicksight dashboards

a reference architecture files and events land in an s3 raw prefix, never edited. a glue crawler or job registers the schema in the glue data catalog . glue or emr jobs write cleaned, partitioned parquet or iceberg tables to a curated prefix. athena queries the curated tables directly; redshift serves heavy, repeated bi workloads. dbt models the curated layer into products (dbt has athena and redshift adapters). see dbt . lake formation grants each team only the tables and columns it needs.

choosing between similar services athena or redshift? athena for ad-hoc sql on files, paid by data scanned. redshift for a warehouse with steady, heavy queries and many users. glue or emr? glue for serverless spark jobs without managing clusters. emr when you need control of the cluster, other engines, or long-running jobs. kinesis or msk? kinesis for aws-native streams with little to run. msk when you want kafka's api, tools and portability. see kafka . mwaa or step functions? airflow for data pipelines with many dependencies; step functions for event-driven workflows across aws services.

handy commands the aws cli calls the same apis the console does. names in angle brackets are yours to fill in. # copy a file into the lake's raw prefix aws s3 cp orders.csv s3://<bucket>/raw/orders/dt=2026-11-14/ # register its schema, then run a glue job aws glue start-crawler --name <crawler> aws glue start-job-run --job-name <job> --arguments '{"--run_date":"2026-11-14"}' # query it with athena, then fetch the results aws athena start-query-execution --work-group primary \ --result-configuration outputlocation=s3://<bucket>/athena-results/ \ --query-string "select status, count(*) from shop.orders group by status" aws athena get-query-results --query-execution-id <id-from-above> # run sql on redshift serverless without a jdbc driver aws redshift-data execute-statement --workgroup-name <wg> --database dev \ --sql "select count(*) from orders" # put one event on a kinesis stream aws kinesis put-record --stream-name orders --partition-key a1 --data <data> each operation and parameter was checked against the aws sdk's service definitions (botocore).

iam for data, in practice roles, not keys: jobs run as iam roles; people sign in through single sign-on. no long-lived access keys in code. two layers: iam decides who may call a service; lake formation decides which databases, tables, columns and rows they may read. separate raw from curated with different prefixes or buckets and different grants. block public access on every data bucket, and encrypt with kms keys you control.

cost controls athena bills by data scanned: parquet or iceberg, partitions and selecting only the columns you need cut it sharply. workgroups can cap a query's scan. s3 lifecycle rules move old raw data to cheaper storage classes. pause or size redshift and emr to the workload; serverless options bill only while they run. budgets and tags per team and pipeline, so a cost has an owner.

service map by lifecycle stage stage azure service what it is for land and store azure data lake storage (blob storage with the hierarchical namespace turned on); onelake in microsoft fabric, built on it the data lake’s files, raw and curated, with directories and file-level permissions stream in event hubs, with a built-in apache kafka endpoint events at high volume; existing kafka clients can often connect by changing only configuration change data capture data factory’s change data capture resource; mirroring in fabric read only what changed in an operational database, or replicate it continuously into onelake process (etl) data factory; azure databricks; spark in fabric; stream analytics for streams batch and streaming transformation open tables onelake tables, stored as delta parquet or iceberg tables any engine can read, without a proprietary format query fabric data warehouse; serverless sql pool in azure synapse (t-sql on files in the lake); azure data explorer for logs and time series analysis and serving orchestrate data factory pipelines; apache airflow jobs in fabric schedules and dependencies. see airflow dags catalog and govern microsoft purview (data map, unified catalog) find, classify and govern data wherever it lives visualise power bi reports and dashboards

a reference architecture files and events land in a raw directory of a data lake storage account, never edited. data factory copies from sources on a schedule; its change data capture reads only the rows that changed. spark in azure databricks or fabric writes cleaned, partitioned delta or iceberg tables to a curated area. the fabric warehouse, or serverless sql on the lake, serves sql; power bi reports read from it. purview catalogs the tables; azure roles and acls grant each team only what it needs.

choosing between similar services analysis, built on each service’s own description. fabric or separate azure services? fabric is one analytics platform covering ingestion, transformation, real-time processing, analytics and reporting, with onelake underneath. separate services (data lake storage, data factory, databricks, synapse) suit teams that already run them or want to choose each piece. fabric warehouse or serverless sql? the warehouse for star schemas and curated, governed data. serverless sql for ad-hoc t-sql on files in the lake, billed by the data each query processes. databricks or spark in fabric? databricks for a full data and ai platform in your cloud account; fabric’s spark when the rest of your work is already in fabric and onelake. data factory or airflow jobs? data factory for copying between many data stores and building transformations visually; airflow when pipelines are written as python dags. see airflow dags . event hubs or a kafka cluster you run? event hubs runs many existing kafka workloads with configuration changes only and no cluster to manage. run kafka yourself only for features or control it does not give you. see kafka .

handy commands the azure cli calls the same apis the portal does. names in angle brackets are yours to fill in. --auth-mode login uses your microsoft entra sign-in instead of an account key. # sign in az login # create the raw directory and upload a file into the lake (data lake storage) az storage fs directory create -n raw/orders -f <filesystem> --account-name <account> --auth-mode login az storage fs file upload --source orders.csv -p raw/orders/dt=2026-11-14/orders.csv \ -f <filesystem> --account-name <account> --auth-mode login # run a data factory pipeline, then check the run (the datafactory extension) az datafactory pipeline create-run --factory-name <factory> --resource-group <rg> \ --name <pipeline> --parameters '{"run_date":"2026-11-14"}' az datafactory pipeline-run show --factory-name <factory> --resource-group <rg> --run-id <run-id-from-above> # create an event hub for order events az eventhubs eventhub create --resource-group <rg> --namespace-name <namespace> --name orders --partition-count 4 # let a pipeline's managed identity read the lake's data az role assignment create --assignee <principal-id> --role "storage blob data reader" --scope <storage-account-id> # move raw data to cooler tiers as it ages az storage account management-policy create --account-name <account> --resource-group <rg> --policy @policy.json each command and option was checked against the azure cli’s own help definitions (the azure-cli and azure-cli-extensions repositories).

c.h: Identity and access for data, in practice
c.x: identity and access for data, in practice managed identities, not keys: jobs run as managed identities, which remove the need to manage credentials; people sign in through microsoft entra id. two layers: azure roles grant coarse access, such as read on a whole storage account or container ( storage blob data reader , contributor , owner ); acls grant fine access to directories and files. roles are checked first. if a role already grants access, acls are ignored, so an acl cannot narrow what a role allows. give broad roles sparingly. put groups in acls, not people: microsoft recommends security groups, so people can join and leave without rewriting acls across a directory tree. avoid account keys: shared key access is effectively super-user, and acls do not apply to it.

cost controls access tiers: hot has the highest storage cost and lowest access cost; cool and cold cost less to store and more to read (cool data should stay at least 30 days); archive is offline. lifecycle policies move blobs to a cooler tier by age: time since creation, since last change, or since last access (last access needs access time tracking turned on). serverless sql bills by data processed: you pay only for the data your queries process, and a query can read a chosen subset of columns. pause a fabric capacity you are not using; pausing can make content on it unavailable, so check what depends on it first. cost management shows where the money goes; tag resources per team and pipeline so a cost has an owner.

the short answer a neural network is layers of simple units. each unit multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up and applies a small non-linear function. training shows the network many examples, measures how wrong its answers are, and nudges every weight a little in the direction that makes the error smaller, again and again.

one neuron an artificial neuron takes several inputs, multiplies each by a weight , adds them up with a bias , and passes the total through an activation function . the weights are loosely analogous to the strengths of synapses between biological neurons. warren mcculloch and walter pitts described a simple, non-learning model of this kind in 1943. one artificial neuron inputs x1, x2 and x3 are multiplied by weights w1, w2 and w3 and summed with a bias b in a node marked sigma. the sum z passes through an activation function f to give the output y. x 1 w 1 x 2 w 2 x 3 w 3 σ bias b z f y activation one neuron: z = w 1 x 1 + w 2 x 2 + w 3 x 3 + b , then y = f ( z ). import math x = [0.5, 0.8, 0.2] # inputs w = [0.4, 0.6, -0.9] # weights b = 0.1 # bias z = sum(xi * wi for xi, wi in zip(x, w)) + b # weighted sum y = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z)) # sigmoid activation print(f"z = {z:.2f}, y = {y:.3f}") # z = 0.60, y = 0.646 run as shown with python 3; the last line is its real output.

layers a feedforward neural network three input nodes x1 to x3, each connected to all four hidden nodes h1 to h4, each of which is connected to both output nodes y-hat 1 and y-hat 2. arrows run left to right. x 1 x 2 x 3 h 1 h 2 h 3 h 4 ŷ 1 ŷ 2 input layer hidden layer output layer weights w weights w a feedforward network with one hidden layer. every arrow carries a weight; every node in the hidden and output layers is a neuron like the one above. a network is typically called deep if it has at least two hidden layers. biases are left out of the drawing. input layer: the numbers you feed in, such as pixel values or the features of a transaction. hidden layers: neurons whose outputs feed the next layer. this shape, fully connected layer to layer, is called a multilayer perceptron. output layer: the answer, such as a score per class. non-linear activations matter: with a non-linear activation function, even a few neurons can solve non-trivial problems; the universal approximation theorems show that suitable networks can, in principle, approximate any continuous function.

how a network learns predict: run training examples forward through the network. measure the error with a loss function , a single number that training tries to make as small as possible. find which way to move each weight: backpropagation applies the chain rule of calculus efficiently to get the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. rumelhart, hinton and williams’ 1986 paper in nature , “learning representations by back-propagating errors”, describes the method. take a small step: gradient descent moves each weight a little in the direction opposite to the gradient, the direction of steepest descent. the size of the step is the learning rate . repeat over many batches. stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a randomly chosen subset of the data each time, instead of the whole data set. the risk is overfitting : a model that matches its training data too closely and then fails on new data. that is why models are checked on data held back from training.

activation functions function what it does sigmoid squashes any number into the range 0 to 1 (used in the code above) relu passes positive values, turns negatives into 0; used in the 2012 alexnet image model gelu a smooth version of relu, used in the 2018 bert language model softmax turns a list of scores into a probability distribution over the possible outcomes, often on the output layer

kinds of network feedforward (multilayer perceptron): data flows one way, layer to layer, as in the diagram. convolutional (cnn): learns small filters, or kernels, that slide across the input; widely used for images. recurrent (rnn): feeds its output back in, for sequences. plain rnns suffer from the vanishing gradient problem, which limits long-range memory; the lstm , by hochreiter and schmidhuber (1997), was designed to ease it. transformer: introduced in the 2017 paper “attention is all you need” by eight researchers at google, built on the attention mechanism. many modern large language models are built on it (see llms ).

a short history year what happened 1943 mcculloch and pitts describe a non-learning computational model of neurons. 1958 frank rosenblatt describes the perceptron, one of the first implemented neural networks. 1969 minsky and papert’s book perceptrons sets out limits of simple perceptrons, such as computing xor (they already knew multi-layer perceptrons could). it is claimed that its pessimism helped turn research towards symbolic systems. 1986 rumelhart, hinton and williams publish their backpropagation paper in nature . 2012 alexnet, a convolutional network trained on gpus, wins the imagenet image-recognition challenge with a top-5 error rate of 15.3%. 2017 the transformer is introduced in “attention is all you need”.

choose by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards ( analysis ) tabular data with a modest number of rows and a need to explain decisions simpler models first (linear models, decision trees); a neural network only if they fall short images or other grid-shaped data a convolutional network, or a pre-trained model to fine-tune text, code or other sequences a transformer, usually a pre-trained one used through an api or fine-tuned (see llms ) little labelled data a pre-trained model adapted to your task, rather than training from scratch your team already runs one ml framework stay with it unless a requirement forces a change: switching has a cost these leanings are analysis , not sourced facts; the other way is to try a neural network first and measure it against a simpler model.

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: every engineer who works with ai benefits from understanding one neuron, a loss and a gradient step well enough to explain them. it makes the behaviour of large models, and the limits of what they learned, less mysterious. the other view: most engineers use models through an api and never train one. for them, time may be better spent on evaluation, prompting, cost and safety than on the mathematics of training.

the short answer neural networks are very good at one part of routing: predicting . how long will this road take at 8 a.m.? how late will this train be? they are much less trusted at the part that keeps people safe: deciding that two trains must never be on the same piece of track. so in practice the two are combined: a learned model predicts, and a well-understood algorithm or certified safety system decides. if neural networks are new to you, start with neural networks ; for networks of connected things, see graph databases .

c.h: Road routing: what Google Maps does
c.x: road routing: what google maps does google maps combines live traffic with historical patterns to predict travel times. working with google deepmind, it improved those predictions using a graph neural network (gnn), a network designed for data shaped like a graph: places joined by roads. the problem: maps’ predicted arrival times were already accurate for over 97% of trips, according to deepmind. the goal was the remaining few per cent. supersegments: roads are divided into “supersegments”, groups of adjacent road segments that share significant traffic. a first attempt trained a separate ordinary neural network for every supersegment; because supersegments vary in size, that did not scale, so the team switched to a gnn, which can model how traffic flows from one road to the next. the result: deepmind reported accuracy improvements of up to 50% in cities including berlin, jakarta, são paulo, sydney, tokyo and washington d.c. the research paper, presented at cikm 2021, reports that the deployed model cut negative arrival-time outcomes by over 40% in cities like sydney, compared with the previous production system. the predicted times then become the weights on the road graph, and a shortest-path search finds the fastest route. the neural network makes the map smarter; it does not replace the route search.

c.h: Run it: learning predicts, the algorithm decides
c.x: run it: learning predicts, the algorithm decides a small version of that split. a learned estimate of each road’s travel time (here a simple average by time of day, standing in for a neural network) feeds dijkstra’s algorithm, the classic way to find the shortest path in a graph: # learning predicts, the algorithm decides: how map routing combines the two. import heapq # 1. past trips: (road, hour of day, minutes taken). real systems learn from billions. history = [("ring", 8, 22), ("ring", 9, 20), ("ring", 14, 9), ("ring", 15, 8), ("centre", 8, 12), ("centre", 9, 13), ("centre", 14, 11), ("centre", 15, 12)] # 2. "learn" each road's travel time for a time of day. this tiny lookup by rush hour # stands in for the graph neural network google maps uses. def predict(road, hour): rush = 7 <= hour <= 9 times = [m for r, h, m in history if r == road and (7 <= h <= 9) == rush] return sum(times) / len(times) # 3. the road network, with each road's model input. two ways from home to office. roads = {"home": [("a", "ring"), ("b", "centre")], "a": [("office", "ring")], "b": [("office", "centre")], "office": []} # 4. dijkstra's algorithm finds the fastest route using the predicted times as weights. def fastest(start, goal, hour): queue, seen = [(0.0, start, [start])], set() while queue: minutes, node, path = heapq.heappop(queue) if node == goal: return round(minutes), path if node in seen: continue seen.add(node) for nxt, road in roads[node]: heapq.heappush(queue, (minutes + predict(road, hour), nxt, path + [nxt])) for hour in (8, 14): print(f"{hour:02}:00 ->", fastest("home", "office", hour)) what it printed when we ran it: 08:00 -> (25, ['home', 'b', 'office']) 14:00 -> (17, ['home', 'a', 'office']) at 8 a.m. the ring road is slow, so the route goes through the centre; at 2 p.m. the ring road is quicker. the route search never changed; only the predicted travel times did. that is the job a neural network does inside a routing system.

how trains are controlled today running trains safely is mostly about keeping them apart, and that is done with signalling and train protection systems, not learning: blocks. traditional signalling divides track into fixed blocks ; only one train may be in a block at a time. communications-based train control (cbtc) knows each train’s position more precisely by radio and uses a moving block that travels with the train, so trains can run closer together safely. the first radio-based cbtc opened at san francisco airport’s people mover in 2003. movement authority. in the european train control system (etcs), a radio block centre, specified to safety integrity level 4 (sil 4), the highest, generates the movement authorities that tell each train how far it may go. automatic train operation. driving can be automated in grades: in many systems (goa2) the train drives itself but a driver is on board, as on london underground’s victoria line; at goa4 , trains run with no staff on board at all. driverless operation is mostly used on lines with isolated tracks, where safety is easier to ensure; fully automated mainline railways are still an area of research. where neural networks fit in running a railway four layers. the safety layer, signalling, train protection and movement authority, is deterministic and certified to safety integrity level 4. operation, driving, starting, stopping and doors, is automatic and rule-based. dispatch and rescheduling, deciding which train goes first after a delay, is where learning is being researched. prediction of delays, arrival times and demand is a natural fit for neural networks. layer what it decides, and who decides it safety layer signalling, train protection, movement authority deterministic, certified (sil 4) operation driving, starting, stopping, doors (ato) automatic, rule-based dispatch and rescheduling which train goes first after a delay where learning is being researched prediction delays, arrival times, demand a natural fit for neural networks analysis: the closer a decision is to keeping trains apart, the more it relies on certified, predictable logic. learning sits in the layers that advise, plan and predict.

c.h: Where learning is being tried: Flatland
c.x: where learning is being tried: flatland the hard, unsolved part of running a railway is rescheduling : when a train breaks down, which of hundreds of trains should wait, re-route or go first? swiss federal railways (sbb) runs the densest mixed railway traffic in the world, with more than 10,000 trains a day routed over 13,000 switches and controlled by more than 32,000 signals. to open the problem to researchers, flatland , an open-source toolkit run as a challenge on the aicrowd platform and built around sbb’s problem, offers a simplified grid-world railway where many trains (agents) must reach their stations. it lets people test multi-agent reinforcement learning , where each train learns by trial and error, against traditional operations research , the planning and optimisation methods railways have used for decades. the honest result so far: in the 2020 flatland competition, the best submissions came from operations research , though participants found many promising reinforcement-learning approaches, often using graph representations of the network. the organisers concluded that machine learning has potential for the problem and that key topics still need research.

choosing an approach, by requirement if this is true for you it leans towards you need predictions from lots of messy historical data: travel times, delays, demand a neural network, often a graph neural network for networks you need the best route given known costs a classic algorithm such as dijkstra or a*, fed by those predictions a wrong decision could injure people deterministic, certified safety systems; learning may advise but not decide you must replan many vehicles after a disruption, today operations research methods, which still won the flatland benchmark you are researching what could work next reinforcement learning in a simulator such as flatland, compared against operations research

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: the winning pattern is a partnership. let neural networks predict, let proven algorithms plan, and keep certified systems in charge of safety. that is how google maps works, and how railways are likely to adopt learning. the other view: some researchers argue learned systems will eventually plan and control better than hand-built ones, as they have in games, and that insisting on old methods holds progress back. the evidence today does not yet show that on real railways.
