the short answer an agent is a model with instructions and tools, running in a loop until a job is done (see how anthropic & openai build agents ). getting that loop to run once is easy. making it a system means answering six questions: should this be an agent at all? is it built from the right parts? how do we know it works? what stops it doing harm? can we run it fast and cheaply enough? and can we see what it did? the life of an agentic system six stages from left to right: decide whether an agent is the right tool; build it from a model, tools, instructions and context; evaluate it with graders, suites and the pass@k and pass^k measures; guard it with guardrails and people in the loop; serve it, which is inference, covering speed, cost and caching; and observe it with traces, tokens and cost per task. an arrow returns from observe to evaluate: every real failure becomes a new eval task. decide agent, or simpler? build model, tools, context evaluate graders, pass@k guard limits, people serve inference, speed, cost observe traces, cost per task every real failure becomes a new eval task evaluation and inference are highlighted because this page goes deepest on them. the loop back is what makes the system improve rather than drift.

1. decide, and 2. build decide. both anthropic and openai say to start with the simplest thing that works. openai’s guide points agents at work that has resisted automation: complex judgement, rules that are hard to maintain, or lots of unstructured data; otherwise a fixed workflow or ordinary code may be enough. its latency guide puts it bluntly as a principle: “don’t default to an llm.” build. the parts are few, and each deserves care: model: start with the most capable, then try smaller ones once evals show where they still pass. tools: clear names, clear parameters and good descriptions; anthropic calls this the agent-computer interface. business rules belong inside the tool, where the model cannot argue with them. instructions: written from your real procedures, with what to do when information is missing. context: a finite resource; models recall less as it fills (“context rot”), so give the agent what it needs for this step, not everything. more on agent harness .

c.h: 3. Evaluation: how you know it works
c.x: 3. evaluation: how you know it works agents are non-deterministic: the same question can take a different path each time. so “i tried it and it worked” proves little. anthropic’s guide demystifying evals for ai agents gives the vocabulary: term meaning task one problem for the agent, with what success looks like trial one attempt at a task; run several, because results vary grader logic that scores part of the result; a task can have several transcript the full record of a trial: messages, tool calls, results (also called a trace) outcome the final state of the world: not “the agent said the flight is booked”, but whether the booking exists in the database suite a collection of tasks measuring one capability or behaviour three kinds of grader , usually combined: code-based: string matches, tests passing, checking which tools were called with which arguments, verifying the outcome. fast, cheap and repeatable. model-based (“llm as judge”): a model scores against a rubric, for things like tone or quality with many right answers. anthropic suggests grading each dimension with its own isolated judge, and calibrating judges against human judgement. human: the gold standard, and the slowest; used to calibrate the other two. two kinds of suite: capability evals ask “what can it do?” and should start with a low pass rate, giving you a hill to climb; regression evals ask “does it still do what it did?” and should pass nearly 100% of the time. capability tasks that become reliable graduate into the regression suite. getting started: anthropic says 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start. begin with the checks you already do by hand; test cases where a behaviour should happen and where it should not; start every trial from a clean environment, so leftovers from one run cannot pass or fail the next.

run it: pass@k and pass^k because results vary, anthropic uses two measures. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k tries succeeds, right for tools where one good answer is enough. pass^k is the chance that all k tries succeed, right for customer-facing agents that must behave the same way every time. this program shows how far apart they drift for an agent that succeeds 75% of the time: # pass@k: chance at least one of k tries succeeds. pass^k: chance all k tries succeed. # p is the agent's success rate on a single try, measured by running your eval. p = 0.75 print(" k pass@k pass^k") for k in (1, 2, 3, 5, 10): at_least_one = 1 - (1 - p) ** k all_k = p ** k print(f"{k:2} {at_least_one:6.1%} {all_k:6.1%}") what it printed when we ran it: k pass@k pass^k 1 75.0% 75.0% 2 93.8% 56.2% 3 98.4% 42.2% 5 99.9% 23.7% 10 100.0% 5.6% at three tries, pass^k is 42%, matching anthropic’s worked example: a 75% agent passes three runs in a row less than half the time. by ten tries the two measures tell opposite stories. choose the one that matches what your users need.

4. guard: layers, limits and people layers. openai describes guardrails as layered defence: relevance and safety classifiers, pii filters, moderation, and plain rules such as blocklists and length limits, on top of ordinary authentication and access control. limits. every loop needs an exit: a maximum number of turns or tool calls, so a confused agent cannot run for ever. spring ai, for example, caps tool calls per turn by default. least privilege. give the agent only the tools the job needs, and treat everything it reads as untrusted: text in a web page or document can carry instructions (prompt injection; see agentic ai security ).

c.h: Where a person should be involved, and why
c.x: where a person should be involved, and why a human in every step defeats the point of an agent; a human in no step is a risk. the sources agree on where people belong: where why before high-risk actions: sensitive, irreversible or high-stakes ones, such as moving money, deleting data or sending messages an undo may be impossible, and a model can be wrong or manipulated. openai recommends human oversight here until confidence in the agent grows. when the agent keeps failing past a limit on retries, handing over to a person protects the user’s experience (openai’s “failure thresholds”). at checkpoints and blockers in long tasks anthropic notes agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when they hit a blocker, rather than guessing. in evaluation people calibrate the model-based graders and read transcripts; anthropic notes human review stays crucial for checking work against the wider system’s requirements. reviewing what is learned from production real failures should become new eval tasks, and deciding what “correct” means is a human judgement. two practical rules from spring ai’s documentation: authenticate the approver , because checking that the person who decides may decide is your application’s job; and treat a deny message as input to the model, so keep it clean. analysis: keep lookups and cheap, reversible actions automatic, so people spend their attention where it changes the outcome.

5. serve: inference, speed and cost inference is running the model to produce an answer, and for an agent it happens on every turn of the loop, so its speed and cost multiply. anthropic measured agents using about 4× the tokens of a chat, and multi-agent systems about 15× . speed. measure time to first token (ttft), how long before the response starts, and stream the answer so people see progress. openai’s seven principles for latency: process tokens faster (a smaller model), generate fewer tokens, use fewer input tokens, make fewer requests, parallelise, make users wait less, and don’t default to an llm. prompt caching. agents resend the same instructions and tool definitions on every turn. with caching, a repeated prefix is read from cache instead of reprocessed. on anthropic’s api a cache read costs 0.1× the normal input price for most models (less on some), a cache write 1.25× for the default 5-minute lifetime or 2× for one hour; the lifetime refreshes free each time the cache is used, and cache hits do not count against rate limits. batching. work that does not need an instant answer, such as nightly evals or bulk classification, can go through a batch api, processed asynchronously with results within 24 hours. routing. anthropic’s routing pattern sends easy, common questions to smaller, cheaper models and hard ones to more capable models. self-hosting moves inference onto your own gpus, with techniques like batching and kv caches; see llms .

6. observe: see what it did keep transcripts. every model call, tool call and result, so a bad outcome can be traced to the step that caused it. openai’s agents sdk has built-in tracing; spring ai records spans and token-usage metrics through micrometer. measure per task, not per request: success rate, cost and time per completed task, and how often a person had to step in (more on agent harness ). anthropic notes that once evals exist, latency, token use and cost per task come almost for free. close the loop. each real failure becomes a new eval task, so the same mistake is caught before the next release.

c.h: A use case, built: an order-support agent in Spring Boot
c.x: a use case, built: an order-support agent in spring boot a customer writes in about an order. the agent looks the order up, explains its status, and can refund it. small refunds happen automatically; refunds over £100 pause until a supervisor approves. it uses spring boot 4.2 and spring ai 2.1, whose tool-call confirmation is built for exactly this. every stage above shows up in the code. the dependencies ( pom.xml , abridged): <parent> <groupid>org.springframework.boot</groupid> <artifactid>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactid> <version>4.2.0</version> </parent> <!-- ... --> <dependencymanagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupid>org.springframework.ai</groupid> <artifactid>spring-ai-bom</artifactid> <version>2.1.0</version> <type>pom</type> <scope>import</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencymanagement> <dependencies> <dependency><groupid>org.springframework.boot</groupid><artifactid>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactid></dependency> <dependency><groupid>org.springframework.boot</groupid><artifactid>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactid></dependency> <dependency><groupid>org.springframework.ai</groupid><artifactid>spring-ai-starter-model-anthropic</artifactid></dependency> <dependency><groupid>org.springframework.boot</groupid><artifactid>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactid><scope>test</scope></dependency> </dependencies> build: the tools. the model can only ask for these; the code decides what happens. the rule that a refund can never exceed what was paid lives here, where no prompt can talk around it: package com.example.orderagent; import java.math.bigdecimal; import java.util.map; import java.util.concurrent.concurrenthashmap; import org.springframework.ai.tool.annotation.tool; import org.springframework.ai.tool.annotation.toolparam; import org.springframework.stereotype.component; /** the agent's tools. the model can only ask for these; this code decides what really happens. */ @component public class ordertools { record order(string id, string status, bigdecimal total, bigdecimal refunded) {} private final map<string, order> orders = new concurrenthashmap<>(map.of( "a100", new order("a100", "delivered", new bigdecimal("40.00"), bigdecimal.zero), "a200", new order("a200", "delivered", new bigdecimal("450.00"), bigdecimal.zero))); @tool(description = "look up an order's status, total and how much has already been refunded") public string getorder(@toolparam(description = "order id, for example a100") string orderid) { order o = orders.get(orderid); return o == null ? "no order " + orderid : o.tostring(); } @tool(description = "refund part or all of an order. refunds over 100 need a person's approval.") public string refundorder(@toolparam(description = "order id") string orderid, @toolparam(description = "amount to refund, in pounds") bigdecimal amount, @toolparam(description = "why the customer is owed a refund") string reason) { order o = orders.get(orderid); if (o == null) return "no order " + orderid; // a business rule the model cannot talk its way around: never refund more than was paid. if (o.refunded().add(amount).compareto(o.total()) > 0) { return "refused: " + amount + " would exceed the order total of " + o.total(); } orders.put(orderid, new order(o.id(), o.status(), o.total(), o.refunded().add(amount))); return "refunded " + amount + " on " + orderid + " (" + reason + ")"; } } guard: the person in the loop, and the agent. a toolcallconfirmationpolicy bean marks refunds over the limit as needing confirmation; spring ai then pauses the loop before anything in that reply runs: package com.example.orderagent; import java.math.bigdecimal; import java.util.regex.matcher; import java.util.regex.pattern; import org.springframework.ai.chat.client.chatclient; import org.springframework.ai.model.tool.toolcallconfirmationpolicy; import org.springframework.context.annotation.bean; import org.springframework.context.annotation.configuration; @configuration public class agentconfig { static final bigdecimal approval_limit = new bigdecimal("100"); private static final pattern amount = pattern.compile("\"amount\"\\s*:\\s*\"?([0-9]+(?:\\.[0-9]+)?)"); /** human in the loop: a refund above the limit pauses the agent until a person decides. */ @bean toolcallconfirmationpolicy largerefunds() { return (toolcall, toolmetadata) -> toolcall.name().equals("refundorder") && amountof(toolcall.arguments()).compareto(approval_limit) > 0; } static bigdecimal amountof(string jsonarguments) { matcher m = amount.matcher(jsonarguments); return m.find() ? new bigdecimal(m.group(1)) : bigdecimal.zero; } @bean chatclient supportagent(chatclient.builder builder, ordertools tools) { return builder .defaultsystem(""" you are a customer support agent for an online shop. always look an order up before acting on it. be brief and polite. if a refund is refused or denied, explain why to the customer.""") .defaulttools(tools) .build(); } } guard and observe: limits and metrics ( application.properties ): spring.ai.anthropic.api-key=${anthropic_api_key} # guardrail against runaway loops: at most 10 tool calls in one turn. spring.ai.tools.limits.max-total-tool-calls=10 # observability: spring ai records gen_ai spans and token-usage metrics through micrometer. management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics serve: the api, with the approval step. /support/chat answers, or parks a paused reply and returns an approval id; /support/approve/{id} runs the person’s decision and lets the agent finish: package com.example.orderagent; import java.util.list; import java.util.map; import java.util.uuid; import java.util.concurrent.concurrenthashmap; import org.springframework.ai.chat.client.chatclient; import org.springframework.ai.chat.messages.assistantmessage; import org.springframework.ai.chat.messages.message; import org.springframework.ai.chat.messages.usermessage; import org.springframework.ai.chat.model.chatresponse; import org.springframework.ai.chat.prompt.prompt; import org.springframework.ai.model.tool.toolcalldecision; import org.springframework.ai.model.tool.toolcalldecisions; import org.springframework.ai.model.tool.toolcallingchatoptions; import org.springframework.ai.model.tool.toolcallingmanager; import org.springframework.ai.model.tool.toolexecutionresult; import org.springframework.ai.support.toolcallbacks; import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*; @restcontroller @requestmapping("/support") public class supportcontroller { record answer(string text, string approvalid, list<string> waitingfor) {} private record pending(list<message> conversation, chatresponse reply) {} private final chatclient agent; private final toolcallingmanager toolcallingmanager; private final ordertools tools; // demo only: production keeps pending approvals in a database, so they survive restarts. private final map<string, pending> pending = new concurrenthashmap<>(); public supportcontroller(chatclient agent, toolcallingmanager toolcallingmanager, ordertools tools) { this.agent = agent; this.toolcallingmanager = toolcallingmanager; this.tools = tools; } @postmapping("/chat") public answer chat(@requestbody string message) { chatresponse reply = agent.prompt().user(message).call().chatresponse(); assistantmessage out = reply.getresult().getoutput(); if (!toolcalldecisions.isawaitingdecision(reply)) { return new answer(out.gettext(), null, list.of()); } // the loop paused: nothing in this reply has run. park it and ask a person. string id = uuid.randomuuid().tostring(); pending.put(id, new pending(list.of(new usermessage(message), out), reply)); list<string> calls = out.gettoolcalls().stream().map(c -> c.name() + " " + c.arguments()).tolist(); return new answer("this needs a supervisor's approval before it happens.", id, calls); } @postmapping("/approve/{id}") public answer decide(@pathvariable string id, @requestparam boolean allow) { // in production, check here that the person deciding is allowed to approve refunds. pending p = pending.remove(id); if (p == null) return new answer("no pending approval " + id, null, list.of()); assistantmessage reply = p.reply().getresult().getoutput(); list<toolcalldecision> decisions = toolcalldecisions.toolcallkeys(reply).stream() .map(key -> allow ? toolcalldecision.allow(key) : toolcalldecision.deny(key, "a supervisor declined this refund.")) .tolist(); var options = toolcallingchatoptions.builder().toolcallbacks(toolcallbacks.from(tools)).build(); toolexecutionresult result = toolcallingmanager.executetoolcalls( new prompt(p.conversation(), options), p.reply(), new toolcalldecisions(decisions)); string text = agent.prompt().messages(result.conversationhistory()).call().content(); return new answer(text, null, list.of()); } } evaluate, part 1: fast, offline tests of the rules. no model, no api key, runs on every build: package com.example.orderagent; import static org.assertj.core.api.assertions.assertthat; import java.math.bigdecimal; import org.junit.jupiter.api.test; import org.springframework.ai.chat.messages.assistantmessage.toolcall; import org.springframework.ai.model.tool.toolcallconfirmationpolicy; import org.springframework.ai.tool.metadata.toolmetadata; /** fast, offline tests of the rules the model cannot override. no api key needed. */ class guardrailtest { private final toolcallconfirmationpolicy policy = new agentconfig().largerefunds(); private final toolmetadata metadata = toolmetadata.builder().build(); @test void smallrefundrunswithoutaperson() { var call = new toolcall("1", "function", "refundorder", "{\"orderid\":\"a100\",\"amount\":40,\"reason\":\"late\"}"); assertthat(policy.requiresconfirmation(call, metadata)).isfalse(); } @test void largerefundwaitsforaperson() { var call = new toolcall("2", "function", "refundorder", "{\"orderid\":\"a200\",\"amount\":300,\"reason\":\"broken\"}"); assertthat(policy.requiresconfirmation(call, metadata)).istrue(); } @test void lookupsneverwait() { var call = new toolcall("3", "function", "getorder", "{\"orderid\":\"a200\"}"); assertthat(policy.requiresconfirmation(call, metadata)).isfalse(); } @test void refundcannotexceedwhatwaspaid() { var tools = new ordertools(); assertthat(tools.refundorder("a100", new bigdecimal("50"), "test")).startswith("refused"); assertthat(tools.refundorder("a100", new bigdecimal("40"), "test")).startswith("refunded"); } } evaluate, part 2: evals against the real model. a code-based grader on the answer, and an outcome grader on the pause. each runs three times, because a 75% agent would pass once by luck: package com.example.orderagent; import static org.assertj.core.api.assertions.assertthat; import org.junit.jupiter.api.repeatedtest; import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.enabledifenvironmentvariable; import org.springframework.ai.chat.client.chatclient; import org.springframework.ai.model.tool.toolcalldecisions; import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.autowired; import org.springframework.boot.test.context.springboottest; /** * evals against the real model: slow, cost money, and non-deterministic, so each runs several * times. only runs when anthropic_api_key is set. */ @springboottest @enabledifenvironmentvariable(named = "anthropic_api_key", matches = ".+") class agentevaltest { @autowired chatclient agent; // code-based grader on the answer: the order's real status must appear. @repeatedtest(3) void answersorderstatusfromthetool() { string answer = agent.prompt().user("what is the status of order a100?").call().content(); assertthat(answer.tolowercase()).contains("delivered"); } // outcome grader: a large refund must pause for a person, every time. @repeatedtest(3) void largerefundalwayspausesforapproval() { var reply = agent.prompt().user("order a200 arrived broken. please refund 300 pounds.").call().chatresponse(); assertthat(toolcalldecisions.isawaitingdecision(reply)).istrue(); } } what we verified: the project compiles against spring boot 4.2.0 and spring ai 2.1.0 , the four guardrail tests pass, and the application context starts with the agent, tools and approval flow wired (a fifth test). the two evals were skipped in our environment because they call the real model and need an anthropic_api_key ; we have not run them, so treat their pass rate as yours to measure.

c.h: Where to put your effort first, by requirement
c.x: where to put your effort first, by requirement if this is true for you invest first in the agent can move money, delete data or contact people human confirmation for those tools, and authenticated approvers customers will see its answers directly regression evals measured with pass^k, and a human hand-off it is an internal tool where one good answer is enough capability evals measured with pass@k it runs many turns or many requests a day prompt caching, routing to smaller models, and cost per task it reads web pages, emails or documents from outside prompt-injection defences and least-privilege tools your team already runs java and spring spring ai, so the agent lives with your existing services; switching stacks has a cost

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: evaluation is the part that turns an agent demo into a product. build the eval suite with the agent, from its first real failures, and put people exactly where an action cannot be undone. the other view: early on, a few hand-checked examples may teach you more than a formal suite, and heavy guardrails can make an agent too timid to be useful. formal evals and confirmations pay off once real users and real money are involved.
where to go next the patterns behind agents: how anthropic & openai build agents engineering the loop: agent harness security in depth: agentic ai security spring itself: spring boot

who does what analysis, and our view. a useful starting split. your team may draw the lines differently; the point is to draw them on purpose. the person the agent sets the goal and says why it matters turns the goal into steps and asks when the goal is unclear decides what “done” means and what must not change does the searching, drafting, running and checking approves anything irreversible, costly, or visible to others stops and asks at those points, instead of guessing owns the result, whoever typed it reports what it did, with evidence, and what it could not do corrects it, and writes the lesson down where the next session will read it follows the written rules, and says when a rule seems to conflict with the task the other view: some teams give agents whole tasks end to end and review only the result. that can work for well-tested, reversible work; the table below helps you decide where.

how to brief an agent the goal and the why: “add a retry to the payment call, because the gateway returns occasional 503s.” context it cannot guess: the files, the error, the decision already made, what was tried. constraints: what must not change, which tools or commands are off limits, the budget. done means: the test that must pass, the output you expect, how you will check it. when to stop and ask: before deleting, deploying, spending, or messaging anyone. give it a role. anthropic’s documentation says that setting a role in the system prompt focuses the model’s behaviour and tone, and that even a single sentence makes a difference.

c.h: How an agent should report back
c.x: how an agent should report back evidence, not confidence: the test output, the command and its result, the link. what it did not do, and why: a check that could not run is “not run”, never “passed”. questions at checkpoints. anthropic’s guide to building agents: agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when they meet blockers, and it is common to include stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations. asking the person properly. the model context protocol has elicitation : a server can ask the user for more information through the client, and the user can accept, decline or cancel. the specification says servers must not use its form mode to ask for secrets or credentials. short and plain: the person reads the summary, not the log.

c.h: How much freedom to give: choose by requirement
c.x: how much freedom to give: choose by requirement if this is true of the task it leans towards easy to undo (a branch, a draft, a local file) let it run, with stopping conditions; review the result a test or check can prove it right let it run until the check passes; read the evidence hard or impossible to undo (deleting data, a deploy, a payment, an email) the agent proposes, a person approves each time the cost of an error is high, or falls on someone else a person approves at each checkpoint regulated, or decides things about people documented human oversight, required by law in some places (see below) nobody can say what “done” looks like yet work with it step by step; it is not ready to hand over automation bias is the tendency to favour suggestions from automated systems and ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct. wikipedia lists contributing factors including lack of confidence in your own abilities, a lack of other information to hand, and the wish to save time and effort on complex tasks or heavy workloads. a review that only clicks “approve” is not oversight. the law is arriving. the eu’s artificial intelligence act entered into force on 1 august 2024. high-risk uses, such as recruitment, education, critical infrastructure and justice, carry obligations that include human oversight; limited-risk uses carry transparency obligations. agents cost more and errors compound. anthropic recommends testing agents extensively in sandboxed environments, with guardrails.

c.h: Building a persona: a named agent
c.x: building a persona: a named agent a persona is a named agent with a defined job: who it is, what it is for, what it may touch, which skills it loads and which model it runs on. a name makes it easier for people to say who did what, and to give each one a narrow, testable remit. in claude code, a subagent is a file with a name , a description , a tools list, a model and a system prompt. each runs in its own context window with its own permissions. limiting its tools enforces what it may do; the model field picks the model for that agent alone (it inherits the main one if you leave it out). skills are folders with a skill.md of instructions. a skill’s body loads only when it is used, so reference material costs almost nothing until needed. a subagent can preload chosen skills with its skills field. claude code’s skills follow the agent skills open standard, which works across several ai tools. what you can do today, and what is only possible idea status in claude code (from its documentation) a named agent, say “vikram, the backend engineer”, with its own instructions and tools available. a subagent file; claude delegates to it when a task matches its description , or you call it by name with @agent-<name> one named agent carrying one skill or several available. the skills field preloads the full content of each listed skill; it can still use other skills when needed each named agent on its own model available, for claude models: model takes sonnet , opus , haiku , fable , a full model id, or inherit a script that runs many agents and cross-checks them available. dynamic workflows run many subagents from a script, and the script can name a model for each stage agents that talk to each other under a lead experimental: agent teams, disabled by default named agents on models from different vendors (one on copilot, one on a local ollama) not a claude code subagent feature. penstock’s readme describes choosing one vendor in its configuration. per-agent vendors are a possibility, not a product # .claude/agents/reviewer.md --- name: reviewer description: independent reviewer of a finished change. use before a pull request is opened. tools: read, grep, glob, bash model: sonnet skills: [house-style, security-checklist] --- you review a finished change. you do not edit files. check every claim against its source and report what you could not verify. report findings as: severity, file:line, what is wrong, the evidence. user personas are different, and both matter. in user-centred design, a persona is a semi-fictional profile of a typical user, built from interviews and surveys; alan cooper introduced the idea in software design. agent personas serve user personas: design the user persona first (see design thinking & ux ), then decide which agents help that person, and what each one must never do on their behalf.

where headworks fits headworks is enrichmeai’s own take on an agent you can hand real work to: penstock and cistern running together on your machine. what is released today, from each project’s readme at its latest release: you choose the model. penstock’s model layer is pluggable: github copilot by default, or anthropic, openai or a local ollama, switched in configuration. memory you review. penstock’s memory server, used from claude code or claude desktop over mcp, can write a draft episode of the work for you to review; its recall does not read drafts until you move one into the record and commit it. recall inside penstock’s own agent is off by default. access you grant. cistern gives the agent its own credential; you grant it read access to one folder, it is refused everywhere else, and you can revoke the grant from a terminal. a named persona built on that record is planned , not released.

inspiration: named agents to try ideas, not recommendations. each is a small, narrow agent you can build with today’s subagents and skills; try one, measure it, keep it if it earns its place. agent its job what it must never do a reviewer checks a finished change against its sources and the house rules; reports findings with evidence edit files (give it read-only tools) “vikram”, backend; “asha”, frontend each owns one part of the codebase, with that part’s skills (api conventions; accessibility and design tokens) change the other’s folders a test writer writes the failing test first, then hands over weaken or skip an existing test a docs keeper after each merge, finds the docs the change made wrong and proposes fixes merge its own proposals an on-call helper reads alerts and logs, suggests the likely cause and the runbook step run anything against production a release-notes writer drafts notes from merged pull requests and commit messages publish them a tutor explains, quizzes, and asks you to try first, for something you are learning hand over the answer before you have attempted it one habit that makes any of these better ( our view ): when a person corrects an agent, write the lesson into its instructions or a skill, so the next run starts from it.

a possibility for the future our view, not a description of anything released. teams of named agents, each with a narrow role, its own skills and a model chosen for its job, possibly from different vendors, working alongside people who set goals, approve the irreversible and own the result. a shared, reviewed record of decisions is what would let such a team learn without repeating mistakes. the other view: more agents mean more coordination, more cost and more places for errors to compound. anthropic’s advice is to find the simplest solution possible and add complexity only when it is needed. start with one well-briefed agent, and add a second only when you can say what it does that the first cannot.

the core argument writing code was never the main cost; owning it is. every copy of generated boilerplate must be reviewed, secured, tested, upgraded, debugged and understood by the next person. generation makes the cheap part cheaper and multiplies the expensive part. a framework makes each decision once, tests it once, fixes it once, and upgrades everyone together. generate per project framework / blueprint time to first version minutes minutes, once the framework exists consistency each copy differs subtly (retries, logging, auth, errors) same behaviour everywhere fixing a bug or cve find and patch n copies; some get missed patch once, release, bump versions review burden hundreds of generated lines per pr only the business-specific part security each copy may reintroduce a known hole secure defaults, tested once upgrades (java, spring, providers) n separate migrations one migration in the framework, then a version bump onboarding every repo is a new dialect learn the framework once knowledge decisions live in prompts nobody kept decisions in versioned, reviewed code and docs ai output quality model guesses your conventions from public code model extends your framework; smaller, consistent output total cost over 2 years grows with every copy mostly fixed, shared

c.h: A cost model in one line
c.x: a cost model in one line generated: n copies × (review + security fix + upgrade + drift) per year framework: build once + maintain once + n × (small version bump) with n = 15 services, 3 framework-level fixes a year, ~1 day each: generated: 15 × 3 = 45 fix-days, plus drift framework: 1 × 3 = 3 fix-days + 15 version bumps (automatable) the numbers are illustrative; the shape is the point. the gap grows with every new copy and every year.

c.h: When generation is the right call
c.x: when generation is the right call one-off scripts and investigations you will delete. prototypes and spikes to learn whether an idea works. filling a framework's slots: the business logic, the new query, its tests. codemods: ai-written scripts that apply the same change across many repos (an upgrade, a rename), reviewed once. tests and documentation for code that follows the framework. before the third repetition: the first two times, write or generate it directly; you do not yet know what to abstract.

c.h: When not to build a framework
c.x: when not to build a framework rule of three: abstract after three real uses, not one imagined future. inner-platform effect: a framework so configurable it becomes a worse version of the language or tool it wraps. business logic in shared libraries: forces lock-step releases between teams. share infrastructure concerns, not domain rules. no owner: a framework without a maintaining team decays faster than copies. escape hatches missing: teams need a supported way to do the unusual thing without forking.

c.h: What a blueprint looks like in this stack

c.h: Using AI to build the framework
c.x: using ai to build the framework collect the 3+ existing implementations; ask ai to list what they share and where they differ. decide the framework's api and its escape hatches yourself; that is the design work. let ai draft the framework code, tests and documentation against that design. review it like any critical library; add contract tests. let ai write codemods that migrate each existing project onto it, one pr per repo. point every repo's ai context file at the framework, so future work extends it instead of reinventing it.

keeping a framework healthy an owning team with a roadmap, changelog and support channel. semantic versioning ; breaking changes rare, announced, with migration guides and codemods. automated upgrades (renovate or dependabot) open version bumps in every consumer. golden path, not a cage: the easy way is the right way, and the unusual way is possible. scorecards (e.g. a scorecard plugin in a backstage catalogue) show which services are on current versions. measure adoption and time to first deploy for new services.

decision guide will this exist in more than one place for more than a few months? → blueprint . does it carry security, compliance or reliability rules? → blueprint , even for two uses. is it unique business logic? → write it (with ai help) inside the blueprint's slots. is it throwaway or exploratory? → generate , and delete it afterwards. is it the same change across many repos? → ai-written codemod , reviewed once. ai is the bulldozer; the framework is the road. build the road once and drive on it, rather than bulldozing a new track for every trip.

the files that shape it file holds claude.md (repo root, subfolders) project memory: what the system is, rules, commands, traps. loaded every session. ~/.claude/claude.md your personal preferences across projects .claude/settings.json shared permissions, hooks, environment, model settings (committed) .claude/settings.local.json your local overrides (not committed) .claude/agents/*.md subagents: specialised helpers with their own prompt, tools and model .claude/skills/<name>/skill.md skills: packaged procedures invoked by name or when relevant .claude/commands/*.md custom slash commands (the older format: now merged into skills, still works) .mcp.json mcp servers shared with the team these files are the blueprint for how agents work in your repo. keep them short, specific and current; a stale rule misleads every session.

permissions and hooks // .claude/settings.json { "permissions": { "allow": ["bash(./gradlew test:*)", "bash(git status)", "bash(git diff:*)"], "deny": ["read(./.env)", "bash(rm -rf:*)"] }, "hooks": { "pretooluse": [ { "matcher": "bash", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/guard-destructive.sh" }] } ], "posttooluse": [ { "matcher": "edit|write", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/check-edited-file.sh" }] } ], "stop": [ { "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/stop-gate.sh" }] } ] } } permission modes: default (ask), accept edits, plan (read and propose only), auto (runs everything, with background safety checks), dontask (only pre-approved tools), and bypasspermissions (isolated containers and vms only). hooks run your scripts at events (before/after a tool, on prompt submit, at stop, at session start). a hook that exits with code 2 blocks the action where the event allows it (pretooluse blocks the tool call, stop prevents stopping) and its stderr is fed back to claude. a posttooluse hook runs after the tool, so exit code 2 only feeds stderr back. use hooks for rules that must always hold (lint after every edit, block pushes to main ); use claude.md for guidance.

subagents and skills <!-- simplified example of .claude/agents/reviewer.md --> --- name: reviewer description: independent reviewer of a finished diff before a pr is opened. use at the end of every task. tools: read, grep, glob, bash model: sonnet --- review the diff against the task, claude.md and the official docs of every library it touches. report bugs, missing tests and unverified api use. do not edit files. <!-- simplified example of .claude/skills/<name>/skill.md --> --- name: release-sync description: bring a project page up to date with that project's latest release. use after a release or when a sync issue is open. --- 1. read the release tag and changelog. 2. update the version markers and the "what's new" block. 3. run the release checker until it reports 0 findings. subagents keep their own context, so a reviewer is not anchored on the builder's reasoning. skills turn a procedure that cost a debugging cycle into something every session follows.

c.h: A worked example: an autonomous build loop
c.x: a worked example: an autonomous build loop /new-issue turns an idea into a ready issue. /build-task builds it: verify docs, write a failing test, implement. hooks check every edit; a stop hook runs the full check before the turn can end. a reviewer subagent checks the finished diff independently. fix what it finds, at most three attempts , then write a blocker summary instead of looping. /compound turns what went wrong into a permanent guard (a test, hook or rule). open a pr; a human (or a gated merge skill) merges. each step is a skill, agent or hook committed to the repository, so every session follows the same loop.

claude cowork cowork applies claude's agentic loop to everyday knowledge work rather than code: it works through multi-step tasks on your files, documents and connected apps, on desktop, web or mobile (sessions can run in the cloud), and checks in with you as it goes. claude code claude cowork main users engineers anyone doing knowledge work: analysts, operations, legal, sales, founders works on repositories: code, tests, builds, git folders, documents, spreadsheets, presentations, connected apps extended by claude.md, skills, subagents, hooks, mcp, plugins skills, plugins and connectors (mcp), often packaged per role typical tasks implement a feature, fix a bug, review a pr, run a migration prepare a report from files, reconcile spreadsheets, draft documents, run a recurring brief plugins bundle skills, commands, agents and connectors for a role or team, so the organisation's way of working is installed rather than re-explained. same rules as any agent: give it a clear brief and a definition of done, limit what it can access, and review what it produces before it is sent anywhere. features and availability change frequently; check anthropic's current product documentation.

working well with claude code plan first for anything non-trivial: plan mode, read the plan, then let it build. give it a way to check itself: exact test and lint commands in claude.md. one task per session; /clear between unrelated tasks to keep context clean. worktrees for parallel sessions, so they never edit the same checkout. verify claims: ask what it ran and what the output was; "done" means a green check you can see. turn every correction into a rule in claude.md, a skill or a hook.

one we build: persona persona is memory for ai coding agents: penstock keeps what was asked, decided, refused and learned as plain files you own and, when memory is on, hands them to the model before it writes. it works with claude code over mcp. the persona that speaks from it is planned. it is ours, so we are not neutral.

the shape of it need on github in your google cloud project a place to work codespaces cloud workstations: managed development environments from a container image you define, in the browser or your own ide run an agent task an actions job a cloud run job: a container that runs to completion, with its own service account, timeout and retries start it issue, comment, schedule cloud scheduler, pub/sub messages, eventarc events, or a workflow several steps and a human approval workflow jobs and environments workflows, which can run steps in order, wait, and call your services secrets repository secrets secret manager, with iam on each secret and audit logs of every access once data access audit logs are turned on build and test actions cloud build a live preview a preview deployment a cloud run revision with no traffic and its own tagged url the model copilot, or a key in a secret gemini enterprise agent platform, formerly vertex ai (google's models and partner models in model garden), or any provider with its key in secret manager git stays: the history of the code still lives in a git repository, wherever you host it. what moves is where the agent runs, what it can reach, and who can see what it did.

why run it yourself your data stays in your project and region. useful when code or data may not leave a country or a company. one identity model. the agent is a service account with exactly the iam roles it needs, like any other workload. one audit trail. cloud audit logs record what the agent touched, next to everything else in the project. your choice of model, including models you are allowed to use under your own agreements. the trade-off: you build and run the plumbing that a hosted service gives you for free. start small.

a shared workspace, replit style # a workspace image you control, in your project gcloud workstations configs create agent-ws \ --cluster=dev --region=europe-west2 \ --machine-type=e2-standard-4 \ --container-custom-image=europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/tools/agent-ws:1 \ --service-account=agent-ws@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --idle-timeout=3600 \ --disable-public-ip-addresses gcloud workstations create alice \ --config=agent-ws --cluster=dev --region=europe-west2 gcloud workstations start alice \ --config=agent-ws --cluster=dev --region=europe-west2 bake the agent's tools (cli, language runtimes, test tools) into the image, so every workspace and every agent run starts the same. --idle-timeout is in seconds and stops idle workspaces, which saves money.

c.h: An agent task as a Cloud Run job
c.x: an agent task as a cloud run job gcloud run jobs create agent-task \ --image=europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/agents/runner:1 \ --region=europe-west2 \ --service-account=agent-runner@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --set-secrets=model_api_key=model-api-key:latest \ --task-timeout=30m --max-retries=0 # run one task and wait for the result gcloud run jobs execute agent-task --region=europe-west2 \ --update-env-vars=task="add tests for the date parser" --wait # or on a schedule, calling the cloud run api gcloud scheduler jobs create http nightly-triage \ --location=europe-west2 --schedule="0 6 * * 1-5" \ --uri="https://run.googleapis.com/v2/projects/my-proj/locations/europe-west2/jobs/agent-task:run" \ --http-method=post \ --oauth-service-account-email=scheduler@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com one container, one task, a hard timeout, and no automatic retries for work that changes things: an agent that failed halfway should be looked at, not rerun blindly.

preview what the agent built # deploy the agent's branch with no traffic, at its own url gcloud run deploy web --image=…/web:agent-1234 \ --region=europe-west2 --no-traffic --tag=agent-1234 # open https://agent-1234---web-xxxxx.a.run.app, then # move traffic only after a person has looked this is the "see it running" moment that makes replit-style tools feel good, with the same blue-green and canary steps as any release (see devops ).

c.h: Guard rails, before the first run
c.x: guard rails, before the first run a service account per agent, with only the roles its task needs. no owner or editor roles, ever. no direct path to production. the agent proposes (a branch, a preview, a plan); a person approves the merge or the deploy. secrets from secret manager at run time, never in the image, the prompt or the repository. limit the network: private workspaces ( --disable-public-ip-addresses ), egress only to what the agent needs, and vpc service controls around sensitive data. budgets and alerts on the project, and timeouts on every job, so a runaway loop costs minutes, not a month. log every step the agent takes with a run id, so a person can follow the journey and undo it if needed (see observability ). evaluate the agent on real tasks before trusting it with more (see agent harness ). one open-source option for the agent runtime itself is penstock , our headless, self-hosted harness, which runs agents from ci, slack or webhooks and can run as a container like the job above. it is ours, so we are not neutral.

building blocks account → organisation → project: the hierarchy for access control and shared resources. pipeline: stages run in order or parallel; each stage has steps. stage types: build (ci), deploy (cd), approval, custom. service: what you deploy (manifests, artefact). environment and infrastructure definition: where you deploy (dev, prod; a cluster or project). connector: a stored, permissioned link to github, gcp, a registry or a cluster. delegate: an agent running in your infrastructure that executes tasks, so harness never needs inbound access. secrets: stored in harness or referenced from google secret manager or vault. templates: versioned step, stage and pipeline templates teams reuse. triggers: start pipelines on git events, artefact pushes or schedules.

deploying safely strategies: rolling, canary and blue-green built in, with automatic rollback steps. continuous verification: compares metrics and logs (from prometheus, datadog, cloud monitoring and others) of the new version against the old, and fails the stage when they degrade. approvals: harness user groups, or jira/servicenow tickets. freeze windows: block deployments during set periods. policy as code: opa policies on pipelines (e.g. "prod deploys must have an approval stage and a verification step"). audit trail: who ran what, with which inputs, when.

harness vs github actions github actions harness strength ci next to the code; huge action marketplace cd: strategies, verification, approvals, governance at scale deployment model you script it in workflow steps first-class services, environments and strategies governance environments, rulesets, required reviewers opa policies, templates, rbac, freeze windows, audit fits small and medium teams; code-centric workflows many teams and services needing a standard, governed path to production a common split: github actions builds and tests on every pr; harness promotes the built artefact through environments.

c.h: Jenkins vs Harness: choose by requirement
c.x: jenkins vs harness: choose by requirement jenkins is the open-source automation server that began as hudson and was renamed in 2011 after a dispute with oracle; it is mit-licensed, extended by plugins, and since jenkins 2 (april 2016) builds are written as pipelines in a groovy-based language (a jenkinsfile ). harness is a commercial delivery platform with ci, cd and governance in one product, run as a service or as its self-managed enterprise edition on your own infrastructure. if this is true for you it leans towards why no licence budget, and people who can run servers jenkins free and open source; you pay in operations time instead years of jenkinsfiles and plugins that work jenkins, for now migration has a real cost; move when a requirement forces it fully offline or air-gapped either jenkins runs anywhere you install it; harness self-managed documents an air-gapped install canary and blue-green releases without writing them yourself harness blue-green, canary and rolling deployments are built in; in jenkins they are plugins and scripts you maintain central approvals, policies and audit across many teams harness governance is part of the product rather than assembled from plugins little appetite for patching servers and plugins harness (as a service), or github actions someone else runs the platform code already on github, simple build and deploy github actions see “harness vs github actions” above

c.h: Is Jenkins fading? What the numbers say
c.x: is jenkins fading? what the numbers say jenkins publishes a monthly count of installations that send it anonymous usage statistics: january of installations reporting 2019 232,746 2020 267,107 2021 279,894 2022 294,451 2023 293,726 2024 289,935 2025 267,475 2026 261,263 the peak in the series was march 2023, with 320,774 installations reporting; the latest published month, february 2026, had 248,133, about 23% lower. what this count is not: it includes only installations with usage statistics switched on (administrators can turn reporting off), and it counts servers, not how much each one builds. a company that merges ten jenkins servers into one shows up as a fall. meanwhile, hosted ci is growing: github reports 11.5 billion github actions minutes in public projects in 2025, up 35% on 2024. that counts public projects only, so it is a signal of direction, not a market share. our view, from the numbers above: jenkins is declining from its 2023 peak, not disappearing: around a quarter of a million installations still report every month. new projects increasingly start on hosted ci; existing jenkins estates are large and move slowly. the other view: the fall may partly be consolidation and opt-outs rather than teams leaving, and for self-hosted, air-gapped or cost-sensitive work jenkins remains a reasonable choice. checked against: jenkins usage statistics: total installations (monthly) ; jenkins source: usagestatistics (reporting can be switched off) ; github octoverse 2025 ; wikipedia: jenkins ; harness self-managed enterprise edition ; harness deployment concepts and strategies .

c.h: End to end: commit to production on Google Cloud
c.x: end to end: commit to production on google cloud trigger: a push or merged pull request on github starts the pipeline (webhook trigger on main ; pr trigger runs ci only). ci stage: clone, restore cache, compile and run tests (with test intelligence), run scanners, then build the image once and push it to artifact registry tagged with the commit sha. deploy to dev: a cd stage deploys that exact image to the dev environment (gke or cloud run) with a rolling strategy. verify dev: smoke tests and continuous verification against dev metrics and logs. approval: a named group approves prod (or a policy auto-approves outside freeze windows). deploy to prod: canary or blue-green with the same artefact; verification watches error rate and latency; automatic rollback on degradation. notify and record: slack/email notification, deployment recorded with who, what, which commit, and the verification result. build once, promote the same artefact. rebuilding per environment means prod runs something that was never tested.

harness ci in depth build infrastructure: harness cloud (hosted machines), your kubernetes cluster (pods per build), your own vms, or a local runner. choose by network access, cost and isolation. codebase: the repo connector and clone settings for the pipeline; each ci stage can clone automatically. run step: any shell command in a container image you choose ( eclipse-temurin:21 , python:3.12 ). test step with test intelligence: selects only tests affected by the change, and reports results in the ui (junit xml). background step: a service the build needs, such as postgres or a kafka broker, running beside the steps. build and push steps: build an image and push it to artifact registry, docker hub or another registry. caching: cache intelligence for common build tools, or explicit save/restore cache steps to gcs or s3. plugins: drone plugins and many github actions can run as steps. outputs: steps export variables for later steps and stages, e.g. the image tag.

a ci stage (shape) - stage: name: build identifier: build type: ci spec: clonecodebase: true platform: { os: linux, arch: amd64 } runtime: { type: cloud, spec: {} } # harness cloud machines execution: steps: - step: type: run name: unit tests identifier: unit_tests spec: image: eclipse-temurin:21 shell: sh command: ./gradlew test reports: type: junit spec: paths: ["**/build/test-results/test/*.xml"] - step: type: buildandpushgar name: image identifier: image spec: connectorref: gcp_bld host: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev projectid: my-proj imagename: apps/shop-api tags: [<+codebase.shortcommitsha>] field names follow harness's yaml at the time of writing; generate the stage in the editor and compare before committing.

harness cd in depth service: what you deploy: the artefact source (artifact registry image), manifests (kubernetes yaml, helm chart, kustomize) and variables. environment: dev or prod, marked pre-production or production, with environment-level overrides (replicas, urls, secrets). infrastructure definition: the exact target: a gke cluster and namespace, or a gcp project and region for serverless. deployment types: kubernetes, native helm, serverless targets, vms over ssh/winrm, tanzu, ecs, and custom deployments for anything else. google cloud run and cloud functions have their own deployment types. execution: generated from the chosen strategy, editable step by step; failure strategies say what to do on each kind of error (retry, rollback, manual intervention). rollback: a rollback section per stage, run automatically on failure or on a failed verification. input sets and overlays: saved sets of runtime inputs (which service, which tag) so one pipeline serves many services. multi-service and multi-environment deployments from a single stage.

deployment strategies in harness strategy how harness runs it use when rolling replaces pods or instances gradually; rollback restores the previous release default for stateless services canary deploys a small canary set, verifies, then rolls out fully and deletes the canary risky changes with good metrics blue-green deploys the new version as a stage set, tests it, then swaps traffic instant switch and rollback; capacity for two copies basic / custom your own steps (shell, http, terraform, approvals) targets without a built-in type

connecting harness to google cloud gcp connector with oidc (workload identity federation) where your plan supports it, so no service account key is stored. otherwise inherit credentials from a delegate running in gke with workload identity. one service account per environment with only the roles deploys need (artifact registry reader/writer, gke developer or cloud run developer, and service account user on the runtime account). delegates run inside your network (for example a gke namespace), so private clusters and services are reachable without opening inbound access. run at least two for availability. secrets referenced from google secret manager through a secret manager connector. github connector with a github app for cloning, pr status checks and webhooks.

github actions → harness mapping github actions harness workflow pipeline job stage step / action step / plugin on: push, pull_request triggers runner build infrastructure / delegate secrets and variables secrets, variables, connectors environments + required reviewers environments + approval stages + opa policies reusable workflows templates services: containers background steps matrix looping strategies (matrix, repeat, parallelism)

troubleshooting symptom check step queued, never starts no healthy delegate or build infrastructure matching the selector connector test fails delegate network egress, credentials, or the account's iam roles image pull error in deploy cluster or runtime identity lacks artifact registry read; wrong tag expression deployment times out readiness probes failing; check pod events and logs in the step output verification fails unexpectedly baseline too short, wrong metric query, or too few data points; read the analysis detail expression resolves to null wrong scope or step identifier; use the expression picker in the editor pipeline in git differs from ui remote pipeline branch selection; check which branch the run used

good practice keep pipelines, templates and input sets in git, reviewed like code. one pipeline template per deployment shape; services pass only inputs. run unit and integration tests in ci on every pr; deploy only from main . promote by artefact tag or digest; never rebuild per environment. every prod stage has verification and an automatic rollback. enforce with opa: prod needs approval, verification, and an artefact from the trusted registry. watch delegate health and versions; alert when none are connected. track dora metrics from harness deployment data.

harness as a blueprint publish account-level templates for "build a jvm service", "deploy to cloud run", "deploy to gke". teams reference the template version; a fix to the template reaches every pipeline that uses it. enforce the template with opa policies rather than reviews. keep pipelines in git (remote pipelines) so changes are reviewed like code. this is the same idea as the ai tab's blueprints card: decide once, reuse everywhere.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation run a pipeline and read its logs understand stages, steps, services and environments approve or roll back a deployment 2 practitioner build ci and cd pipelines with connectors, secrets and triggers use canary or blue-green with verification keep pipelines in git and use templates 3 senior design org-wide templates and opa policies set up delegates, rbac and environments securely integrate verification with monitoring and feature flags 4 expert own the delivery platform strategy and its governance lead migrations from other ci/cd tools measure and improve delivery (dora) across teams each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

how they fit together tool category does gcp-native alternative prometheus metrics scrapes and stores time-series metrics; promql; alert rules managed service for prometheus, cloud monitoring alertmanager alert routing groups, silences and routes prometheus alerts to people and tools cloud monitoring notification channels grafana visualisation dashboards and alerting over many data sources; loki (logs), tempo (traces), mimir (metrics) in the same family cloud monitoring dashboards fluentd / fluent bit log shipping collect, parse, enrich and forward logs to any backend the built-in logging agents on gke and cloud run dynatrace full-stack apm / observability platform auto-instrumentation, topology, traces, logs, metrics, ai root-cause analysis cloud trace, profiler, logging, monitoring together servicenow it service management incidents, problems, changes, requests, cmdb, approvals and workflow none: itsm sits above monitoring typical flow: apps emit telemetry → fluent bit ships logs, prometheus scrapes metrics (or dynatrace's agent collects all) → grafana or dynatrace shows it → alerts route through alertmanager → servicenow opens an incident, pages on-call, and tracks the change that fixes it.

prometheus: model pull model: prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints on an interval (spring: /actuator/prometheus ). exporters expose metrics for systems that do not: node_exporter (hosts), postgres_exporter, blackbox_exporter (probes). time series = metric name + labels. keep label values bounded. service discovery finds targets in kubernetes, gce and others. short-term storage locally; long-term in thanos, mimir or google's managed service. recording rules precompute expensive queries; alerting rules fire when an expression holds for a duration.

prometheus: configuration # prometheus.yml global: scrape_interval: 30s scrape_configs: - job_name: shop-api metrics_path: /actuator/prometheus static_configs: - targets: ["shop-api:8080"] rule_files: ["rules/*.yml"] alerting: alertmanagers: - static_configs: - targets: ["alertmanager:9093"] # rules/shop-api.yml groups: - name: shop-api rules: - record: job:http_5xx_ratio:rate5m expr: | sum by (job) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum by (job) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) - alert: shopapihigherrorrate expr: job:http_5xx_ratio:rate5m{job="shop-api"} > 0.02 for: 10m labels: { severity: page } annotations: summary: "shop-api 5xx above 2% for 10 minutes" runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/shop-api/high-errors" - alert: ordersloadmissing expr: time() - orders_load_last_success_timestamp_seconds > 26 * 3600 labels: { severity: page } annotations: { summary: "no successful orders load for 26 hours" }

promql you will use rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m]) # per-second rate of a counter sum by (status) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) # grouped histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m]))) # p95 latency increase(orders_objects_total{outcome="failed"}[1h]) # count over a window up == 0 # targets not scraped absent(orders_load_last_success_timestamp_seconds) # metric missing entirely topk(5, sum by (pod) (container_memory_working_set_bytes)) # top memory users always rate() a counter before summing; never sum raw counters. alert on absent() or up == 0 so a dead exporter is not mistaken for health.

alertmanager routing route: receiver: team-ticket group_by: [alertname, job] group_wait: 30s repeat_interval: 4h routes: - matchers: [ 'severity="page"' ] receiver: oncall-page receivers: - name: oncall-page pagerduty_configs: - routing_key_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/pagerduty_key - name: team-ticket webhook_configs: - url: https://integration.example.com/servicenow/alerts # creates a servicenow incident group related alerts, silence during planned work, and inhibit child alerts when the parent (a whole cluster down) is firing.

grafana data sources: prometheus, loki, tempo, cloud monitoring, bigquery, postgres and many more, in one dashboard. dashboards as code: provision from files or the grafana terraform provider; keep json in git and review changes. variables ( $service , $env ) make one dashboard serve every service: a dashboard template is a blueprint. grafana alerting can evaluate rules across data sources; pick one alerting system per signal to avoid duplicates. explore view for ad-hoc queries, and jumping from a metric spike to logs and traces of the same time window. # provisioning/datasources/prometheus.yaml apiversion: 1 datasources: - name: prometheus type: prometheus access: proxy url: http://prometheus:9090 isdefault: true

fluentd and fluent bit fluent bit: lightweight (c), the usual choice as a node agent or sidecar in kubernetes. fluentd: heavier (ruby), huge plugin ecosystem, often used as a central aggregator. pipeline: input → parser → filter (enrich, drop, mask) → buffer → output. on gke and cloud run logs are collected for you; add fluent bit when you need other destinations or self-managed clusters. mask secrets and personal data in filters before logs leave the node. # fluent bit (kubernetes node agent) [input] name tail path /var/log/containers/*.log multiline.parser cri tag kube.* [filter] name kubernetes match kube.* [filter] name grep match kube.* exclude log healthcheck [output] name stackdriver match * # fluentd <source> @type tail path /var/log/app/*.log pos_file /var/log/fluentd/app.pos tag app <parse> @type json </parse> </source> <filter app> @type record_transformer <record> env prod </record> </filter> <match app> @type stdout </match>

dynatrace oneagent: installed on hosts or via the kubernetes operator; instruments jvm, python, node, databases and more without code changes. smartscape: a live topology of hosts, processes, services and their dependencies. purepath: end-to-end distributed traces, down to code-level timing. dynatrace intelligence (formerly davis ai): detects anomalies and groups related events into one "problem" with a probable root cause. grail and dql: stores logs, metrics, traces and events together and queries them with dynatrace query language. slos, synthetic monitoring, real-user monitoring and opentelemetry ingestion. // dql example: error logs per namespace in the last hour fetch logs, from: -1h | filter loglevel == "error" | summarize errors = count(), by:{k8s.namespace.name} | sort errors desc commercial platforms trade cost for breadth and automation. instrument with opentelemetry where you can, so changing vendor later does not mean re-instrumenting.

servicenow: the itsm side record is incident something is broken now; restore service problem the underlying cause of one or more incidents; fix it for good change request a planned change to production: standard (pre-approved), normal (assessed and approved), emergency request a user asking for something (access, a new environment) cmdb ci a configuration item: a service, app, database or host and its relationships event management turns monitoring alerts into correlated alerts and incidents, linked to the affected ci. change automation: ci/cd pipelines (harness, github actions, jenkins) open and update change requests automatically, so low-risk deploys are approved by policy rather than a weekly board. keep the cmdb generated from real sources (cloud apis, terraform state, service catalogues); hand-maintained cmdbs drift.

servicenow table api # open p1 incidents curl -s -u "$sn_user:$sn_pass" -h "accept: application/json" \ "https://$instance.service-now.com/api/now/table/incident?sysparm_query=active=true^priority=1&sysparm_limit=10&sysparm_fields=number,short_description,state" # create an incident from an automated check curl -s -u "$sn_user:$sn_pass" -x post \ -h "content-type: application/json" -h "accept: application/json" \ "https://$instance.service-now.com/api/now/table/incident" \ -d '{"short_description":"orders load missing for 26h", "urgency":"2","impact":"2", "assignment_group":"<sys_id of the data platform group>", "description":"ledger shows no succeeded land since 2026-11-11 06:15 utc. runbook: …"}' use an integration user with only the roles it needs, oauth rather than basic auth where available, and dedupe on a correlation id so a flapping alert does not open fifty incidents.

choosing and combining all on gcp, small team: cloud logging, monitoring and trace with opentelemetry; little to run. kubernetes-heavy, open source: prometheus + grafana + loki + tempo + fluent bit; you operate them (or use managed versions). large enterprise, many stacks: dynatrace (or similar) for automatic coverage and root cause, servicenow for process. whatever you choose: one alerting path per signal, runbooks on every alert, telemetry defined as code, and opentelemetry at the source.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation read a grafana or dynatrace dashboard and find a service's errors look up and update a servicenow incident know what prometheus, fluent bit and alertmanager each do 2 practitioner write promql queries, recording and alerting rules configure log shipping and grafana dashboards as code connect alerts to servicenow incidents and ci/cd to change requests 3 senior design the monitoring stack and alert routing for a platform integrate dynatrace or open-source tooling with opentelemetry automate change management while keeping control 4 expert own observability and itsm tooling strategy and cost lead tool consolidation or migration across the organisation set standards for telemetry, alerting and incident process each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
