c.h: The headline: engaged, not prompting and resting
c.x: the headline: engaged, not prompting and resting ai gives every engineer a bulldozer instead of a shovel . that raises the bar, not lowers it. a well-rounded engineer does not write a prompt, accept whatever comes back, and take the rest of the day off. they decide where the bulldozer goes, prepare the ground, watch it work, check the result against evidence, and fix the road for the next person. the time ai saves is spent on what it cannot do: understanding the problem, testing assumptions, reviewing, and learning. prompting and resting engaged engineering accepts the first answer that looks plausible runs it, tests it, reads it, and checks it against the docs says "the ai wrote it" when it breaks owns every line that ships, whoever typed it uses saved time to do less uses saved time to understand more and improve the system re-explains the same context every day writes it into the repo once so every session and colleague benefits generates a new copy of the same boilerplate builds or extends the shared framework stops learning because the tool "knows" learns faster, because the tool removes the typing, not the thinking

c.h: Learn by doing, not by opinion
c.x: learn by doing, not by opinion be slow to opinion, quick to experiment. before arguing for a tool, pattern or fix, build the smallest thing that tests it: a spike, a benchmark, a query, a prototype. let the result decide. "i ran it on 10,000 real rows and p95 went from 900 ms to 120 ms" ends a debate that opinions cannot. say what you have and have not tried. "i have read about it" and "i have run it in production" are different levels of confidence; name which one you have. change your mind when the evidence does, and say so plainly. hands on the keyboard: read the code, run the command, open the log. second-hand summaries, including an ai's, are a starting point, not a conclusion. write down what you learned so the next person starts from your result, not from zero.

evidence and honesty claims match evidence. "tests pass" means you saw them pass, with the output. a check that could not run is reported as not run. say what you checked in the sentence: "no schedule in the file (searched the whole file)", not "there is no schedule". "cannot see" is not "nothing there". when a source is down, report unknown, never a confident zero. verify state, not proxies: config saying something is enabled is not proof that it is. surface bad news early: a risk raised on day one is a plan; on launch day it is an incident.

ownership you build it, you run it: care what happens after merge: deploys, alerts, users, cost. finish things: small, complete changes over large half-done ones. done means tested, reviewed, deployed and observed. leave the system better: fix the stale doc, the flaky test, the missing alert you tripped over. turn every mistake into a guard: a test, a hook, a rule, so it cannot happen twice. know when to stop: after a few failed attempts at the same problem, step back, write down what you know, and ask, rather than thrashing.

quality habits a failing test before the fix; a passing one after. read the official docs for the version you use before relying on an api. never weaken a check to get to green. review your own diff before asking anyone else to. prefer the simplest design that meets today's need, and write down the trade-off. treat security, privacy and cost as part of "working", not extras.

communication write clearly: pr descriptions that say what changed, why, and how it was verified; design docs others can build from. lead with the answer, then the evidence, then the detail. plain words and real numbers beat adjectives: "40% fewer bytes scanned", not "much faster". ask early and specifically: what you tried, what you saw, what you need. claim before you build: say what you are about to change so others do not duplicate it.

collaboration review generously and honestly: catch real problems, explain why, suggest a fix; skip personal taste. assume good intent; discuss the system, not the person, especially after incidents. teach what you know: pair, document, record the trap you hit. respect decisions once made; reopen them with new evidence, not repeated opinion. make others faster: the best contribution is often a tool, template or fix that removes work for the whole team.

breadth and curiosity learn the layer below and the layer above your own work: the database under your service, the user above your api. follow a request or a row end to end at least once: client, network, service, database, pipeline, warehouse. spend time outside your area of depth: data people learn deploys and on-call; platform people learn sql and modelling. read incidents and postmortems from your own systems and others'. keep a list of things you do not understand yet, and work through it.

attitude, knowledge, adaptability, persistence my view of what each quality looks like at work: quality looks like does not look like attitude curious, humble about what you do not know, positive about hard problems, generous with credit defensive about mistakes; "not my job"; cynicism about every change knowledge fundamentals understood deeply enough to reason from them; breadth across the stack; knows where to look and checks the source collecting tool names; answers from memory without checking; depth in one tool only adaptability picks up a new language, cloud or tool when the problem needs it; drops a favourite approach when evidence says so; adjusts to new team practices, including ai "we have always done it this way"; refusing new tools, or chasing every new one persistence (never give up) stays with a hard problem until it is solved or clearly handed over; changes approach after each failed attempt; asks for help with evidence; finishes the last 10% repeating the same failing attempt; quietly abandoning work; declaring victory before the check is green never giving up is not the same as never stopping. after a few failed attempts at the same thing, step back: write down what you tried and what you saw, change the approach, or bring someone in. the goal is never abandoned; the method is changed. the other view: sometimes the right call is to abandon the goal itself, because the problem turned out not to be worth solving, and persistence then becomes a cost.

chore or play our view: the same task can feel like a chore to one person and like play to another, and that difference may shape how much people enjoy it and, we think, how good they become at it (the next cards include evidence that cuts the other way). this card gathers what others have said about that idea; it is a way of looking at work, not a rule. mark twain wrote a scene about it. in the adventures of tom sawyer (1876), tom is made to whitewash a fence as a punishment, and persuades the neighbourhood children that it is a privilege, until they trade him their treasures for a turn. play is described as a range of intrinsically motivated activities: done for their own sake. the player can still be intently focused, especially when the play has goals, as in a game. johan huizinga’s homo ludens (1938) treated play as a separate sphere of human activity. self-determination theory (edward deci and richard ryan) names three basic needs behind self-motivated behaviour: autonomy , competence and relatedness . flow , described by mihaly csikszentmihalyi, is absorption in a task whose challenge matches your skill, with clear goals, quick feedback and the activity felt as rewarding in itself.

when rewards change the feeling the overjustification effect : offering an expected external reward, such as money or prizes, for something people already enjoy can reduce their own motivation to do it, sometimes called “crowding out”. early demonstrations include edward deci (1971) and lepper, greene and nisbett (1973). the effect seems stronger in children than in college students, but findings across studies are not entirely consistent. analysis: one way to read this is that a task can move from play towards chore when it is done mainly for the reward. the research summarised here does not say whether it moves back.

c.h: Where the idea meets its limits
c.x: where the idea meets its limits deliberate practice , studied by k. anders ericsson, is described as highly structured, cognitively effortful and without immediate rewards. ericsson wrote that it “is not inherently motivating”. our reading: getting very good often includes parts that do not feel like play. turning work into a game has critics: researcher sebastian deterding described early gamification as not fun and creating an artificial sense of achievement, and poorly designed workplace gamification has been compared to micromanagement. job crafting (amy wrzesniewski and jane dutton, 2001) describes people reshaping their own tasks to find more meaning at work; it is said to have the potential to improve quality of life at work and performance.

two ways of seeing it one view: how we frame a task, as something we chose and are curious about rather than something imposed, may change how it feels to do. the ideas above (autonomy in self-determination theory, flow, job crafting) point that way. the other view: some work is simply hard or dull, and calling it play does not change that. on this view, finishing what needs doing, and then resting, matters more than how it feels along the way.

c.h: "I'll learn it", not just "I don't know"
c.x: "i'll learn it", not just "i don't know" when you meet something new, answer with what you will do, honestly. instead of say "i don't know kafka." "i haven't used kafka in production yet. i learn quickly: i'll run it locally this week and come back with what i find." "not my area." "i don't know that part of the system yet. who owns it? i'll read the code and pair with them." bluffing an answer "i'm not sure. i'll check the docs and confirm by end of day." be exact about your current level: honesty about what you have not done is what makes "i learn quickly" believable. follow through: a promise to learn that is kept builds more trust than pretending to know. show the evidence of learning: a lab, a spike, a written summary.

behaviours with ai behaviour looks like does not look like direct the work a clear brief: goal, context, rules, definition of done, what to report "make this better" prepare the ground context files, exact test commands, guardrails, pinned docs in the repo re-explaining the project every session verify runs the tests, reads the diff, checks claims against docs and data trusting confident output own answers for every line that ships "the ai did it" protect no secrets or personal data in prompts; least-privilege tools pasting production credentials into a chat build roads extends frameworks and blueprints; writes codemods generating the same boilerplate again keep learning asks the tool to explain, then confirms by doing shipping code you could not explain stay engaged watches the run, steps in when it drifts, reviews the result prompt, walk away, merge whatever comes back

behaviours by level 1 foundation asks for help with specifics: what was tried and seen tests own changes; reports results honestly reviews ai output line by line before committing writes down what they learn 2 practitioner owns features from design to production and after proves ideas with spikes and measurements before arguing turns repeated mistakes into tests and rules gives useful, kind reviews 3 senior makes the evidence standard for the team ("what did you check?") builds the blueprints and guardrails others use, including for ai agents raises risks early and stops work that is going wrong mentors through pairing and written examples 4 expert shapes culture: blameless learning, honest status, small safe changes changes direction when the evidence says so, publicly multiplies the organisation through platforms, standards and teaching holds the line on quality when deadlines push against it

weekly self-check did every claim i made this week have evidence behind it? did i try something myself before forming an opinion on it? did i review and understand all the ai-written code i shipped? did i leave one thing better than i found it? did i turn a mistake into a guard? did i learn something outside my usual area? did i help someone else get faster?

c.h: Questions to ask in reviews and interviews
c.x: questions to ask in reviews and interviews "how do you know it works?" (looking for evidence, not confidence) "what did you try before deciding?" (looking for experiments) "what would make you change your mind?" "walk me through what the ai produced and why you kept or changed it." "tell me about something you broke and what you changed afterwards." "what happens if this dependency is down?"

the short answer if you have ever caught yourself thinking that young people today give up too easily, you are in very old company. older generations have long described the young as softer, and, as you will see below, research suggests the complaint says more about the people making it than about the young. what has changed, and is still argued over, is the world young people grow up in: less unsupervised play and risk, phones that compete for every spare minute, and more adults stepping in before small failures happen. those conditions shape how much practice anyone gets at sticking with something hard. that is why it is not their fault, and also why there is real hope in it: perseverance and resilience are built by experiences, and experiences can be chosen.

c.h: First, be careful with the claim
c.x: first, be careful with the claim before looking for causes, it is worth asking whether the thing we are explaining is real. here is what the research actually found. the complaint is very old. sociology even has a name for the “inaccurate, exaggerated and sensational characterization of young people”: ephebiphobia. each older generation tends to compare today’s young with a flattering memory of itself. researchers have tested the complaint itself. in five preregistered studies with 3,458 american adults, john protzko and jonathan schooler (2019) found that people believe today’s youth are in decline mainly on the traits where they themselves excel: well-read people think young people read less; intelligent people think they are less intelligent. two mechanisms drive it: we notice other people’s limits where we are strong, and a memory bias projects our present selves onto the young people of the past. the authors suggest this “may explain why the kids these days effect has been happening for millennia”. on self-control, children have got better, not worse. stephanie carlson and colleagues, including walter mischel, compared 840 children aged 3 to 5 from similar backgrounds who were given the marshmallow task in the late 1960s, the 1980s and the 2000s. the adults they surveyed expected today’s children to wait less. in fact children in the 2000s waited on average about 2 minutes longer than children in the 1960s (out of 10). the authors are careful to say that more research in diverse populations is needed. how much longer children waited, by decade compared with children tested in the late 1960s, children in the 1980s waited about one minute longer and children in the 2000s about two minutes longer on the marshmallow task, out of a maximum of ten minutes. extra waiting time compared with children tested in the late 1960s (out of 10 minutes) late 1960s the starting point 1980s about +1 minute 2000s about +2 minutes carlson and colleagues (2018): 840 children aged 3 to 5, from similar middle to high socioeconomic backgrounds, tested on the same task across three decades. adults surveyed expected the opposite. only the differences the study reports are drawn here. there is some evidence of strain. wikipedia’s article on generation z reports that when the covid-19 pandemic struck, the generation proved less resilient than older cohorts, while its values did not change and it stayed open to change, such as hybrid school and remote work. the famous willpower test is weaker than its reputation. in walter mischel’s original marshmallow studies from the late 1960s, children could take one treat now or wait for more. a replication with a far larger and more diverse sample found only half the original effect, and suggested that economic background, rather than willpower, explained the other half. analysis: waiting is easier for a child who has learned that promised rewards really arrive, so what looks like a trait is partly a lesson from the environment. “grit” is close to an old trait. angela duckworth’s grit, which combines perseverance of effort with consistency of interest, correlates strongly with conscientiousness, one of the big five personality traits; one large twin study found a genetic correlation of 0.86 between the two. a later meta-analysis concluded that grit’s usefulness may come mainly from its perseverance part. analysis: so the honest statement is much narrower than “young people lack perseverance”. some measures of strain have risen, the causes are argued over, and the qualities involved are shaped by circumstances at least as much as by character.

c.h: Why it is not their fault
c.x: why it is not their fault if something has changed, it is the setting young people grow up in. each of these explanations has serious supporters and serious critics, so they are shown side by side. what changed the argument, and the counter-argument childhood moved onto phones jonathan haidt’s the anxious generation (2024) argues that smartphones, social media and overprotective parenting “rewired” childhood from the late 2000s and caused a rise in mental illness. developmental psychologist candice odgers replied in nature that most studies have not found a large or consistently negative effect of social media on mental health, and that the link might run the other way, with struggling teenagers using phones more. her summary: “there are no simple answers”. less risk, less unsupervised play haidt, drawing on the idea of “antifragility”, argues that children need some adversity and challenge to handle difficulty as adults, and that “safetyism” has taken it away. psychologist peter gray’s free to learn argues that unleashing the instinct to play makes children happier and more self-reliant. others argue that home life, poverty and abuse matter far more than screens. attention became a product herbert simon observed that “a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention”. apps now compete for that attention by design, which makes boredom, the space where people practise sticking with something, rarer ( analysis ). failure became more visible and less frequent martin seligman’s research on learned helplessness , begun in 1967, showed how experiences of having no control teach animals and people to stop trying. analysis: the reverse holds too. people learn persistence from repeated, survivable struggles that end in success, and a childhood with fewer small failures offers fewer of those lessons.

how resilience is built here is the hopeful part. resilience research began with studies such as emmy werner’s forty years of following children from poor backgrounds on kauai, hawaii. about a third of the at-risk children grew into well-adjusted adults, which she put down to protective factors in their personalities, their families and their communities. since then, a handful of levers have gathered good evidence, and none of them depends on the year you were born. lever what the research says in practice mastery experiences albert bandura found that the most effective way to build self-efficacy , the belief that you can succeed at a task, is a personal experience of success. people with high self-efficacy treat hard tasks as things to master, not to avoid take on problems slightly beyond your level and finish them; keep a list of the hard things you have done seeing someone like you succeed bandura’s vicarious experience: watching someone you see as similar to you succeed at something difficult raises your belief that you can do it too pair with people a year or two ahead of you, not only with experts desirable difficulties robert bjork (1994): learning that feels harder, such as spacing practice out and testing yourself instead of re-reading, builds stronger memory treat the struggle of learning as a sign it is working, not as failure practice under stress donald meichenbaum’s stress inoculation training builds resistance to stress through skills training and exposure to stressful situations, in doses rehearse the hard thing (the demo, the on-call incident, the interview) before it counts relationships protective factors in families and communities recur throughout resilience research a mentor, a team that helps, friends outside work believing ability can grow carol dweck’s growth mindset: people who believe intelligence can be developed tend to embrace challenges and persevere. critics such as moreau and colleagues (2019) warn that overemphasising how changeable abilities are can do harm notice and praise effort and strategy, without pretending effort alone guarantees results

c.h: For engineers starting out, and for the people who lead them
c.x: for engineers starting out, and for the people who lead them turning that research into a working week looks something like this ( analysis , built from the levers above): if you are try this starting out pick one hard problem a week and stay with it for an hour before asking a person or an ai for the answer. turn off notifications while you do, and write down what you tried. the habit, not the talent, is what grows learning a new field space your practice over days, test yourself, and build one small thing end to end. one finished project is a mastery experience; ten half-watched tutorials are not leading or mentoring give stretch work with a safety net: a real problem, time to struggle, and help that arrives after the struggle, not before it. share your own failures, so that struggling looks normal a parent leave room for unsupervised play, boredom and small, recoverable failures, and keep your promises, so that waiting is worth it related pages: new ideas, familiarity & habits (how habits form, about 66 days on average), behaviours , and worried about ai? .

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: the young are not weaker. they have had fewer chances to practise being uncomfortable and coming through it, in a world built to remove discomfort and capture attention. that is not their fault, and the remedy is not lectures but experiences: small, real struggles that end in success, with people around who have been through the same. the other view: generational comparisons are mostly unreliable, the evidence on phones and mental health is contested, and many young people show great resilience, in a pandemic and in a hard job market. on this view the useful question is not “what is wrong with this generation?” but “what helps anyone, at any age, keep going?”

about the evidence psychology has been through a replication crisis, and several famous findings on willpower and mindset turned out smaller than first reported, as the marshmallow replication shows. this page states the claims that survived, names the debates where they are still live, and labels the practical advice as analysis, so you can tell which is which.

the short answer think about the last time someone showed you an idea that was truly new to you. chances are your first reaction was not delight but a small, polite doubt. that reaction is not a sign that you are closed-minded. it is how human brains are built: we like what we have seen before, we weigh losses more heavily than gains, and we prefer to keep things as they are. none of this is stupidity. most of what we do runs automatically, and that is how anyone gets through a busy day. but it has two practical consequences. a new idea has to become familiar before it can feel right, so whoever brings it needs patience as well as evidence. and a good habit, once it has formed, keeps working for you long after the motivation that started it has faded.

c.h: Zero to one, and one to n
c.x: zero to one, and one to n zero to one (2014) is peter thiel’s book with blake masters, based on masters’ notes from the startup class thiel taught at stanford in spring 2012. its central distinction is a simple one. going from 0 to 1 means creating something entirely new. going from 1 to n means copying or extending something that already works. thiel argues that real progress depends on the first, and he stresses finding “secrets”, things others have not yet seen, and building something unique rather than improving on what the crowd is doing. kind what it is what it needs 0 → 1 something that did not exist before: a new kind of product, a new method, a new market conviction before there is evidence, a thick skin for being called wrong, and a way to make the idea understandable 1 → n taking something that works to more people, places or scale: the same product in a new market, the same system for ten times the load discipline, repeatability and operations: most of engineering, most of the time thiel’s view, and the other view: thiel puts 0 → 1 first. the other way of seeing it is that most of the benefit of any invention arrives through 1 → n. the diffusion research further down shows that adoption, not invention, is usually the slow part: in a 1943 study, hybrid corn took more than ten years to spread among farmers. and incremental improvement is how most products actually get good. both kinds of work matter; they simply need different people, or the same people in different modes.

why new ideas look crazy four well-studied effects work against anything new. each is small on its own; together they explain a lot of polite indifference. effect what the research found mere exposure people come to like things simply because they are familiar with them. the effect has been shown with words, chinese characters, paintings, faces, shapes and sounds. robert zajonc, who developed the idea in the 1960s, observed that a new stimulus first brings fear or avoidance; each further exposure brings less fear and more interest, until the once-novel thing is liked. processing fluency the ease with which the brain processes information. what is easy to take in, because it is clear or has been seen before, tends to feel better than what takes effort. status quo bias given the same choices, people tend to keep whatever is framed as the current state (samuelson and zeckhauser, 1988). it is linked to loss aversion : losses tend to be treated as if they were about twice as large as an equal gain, so giving up the known feels worse than the new feels good. the semmelweis reflex the reflex-like tendency to reject new evidence because it contradicts established beliefs. it is named after ignaz semmelweis, who in 1847 introduced handwashing with chlorinated lime at vienna general hospital’s first obstetric clinic. maternal deaths fell from 18% to under 2%, yet his ideas were rejected; some doctors were offended at being told to wash their hands. they were accepted only after his death, once louis pasteur’s germ theory explained them and joseph lister acted on it. analysis: put those together and a new idea starts with three costs. it is unfamiliar, so it feels wrong. it is hard to process, so it feels doubtful. and it asks people to give up something they already have, which feels like a loss twice its real size. semmelweis had the evidence and still lost, partly because he had no explanation people could fit to what they already believed. evidence opens the door; an explanation is what lets people walk through it.

how new ideas spread anyway and yet new ideas do win, over and over. everett rogers’ diffusion of innovations (1962) describes how: people adopt in waves, from innovators and early adopters to the early majority , the late majority and finally the laggards . geoffrey moore’s crossing the chasm (1991) adds that high-tech products face a gap between the early users and the mainstream. who adopts a new idea, in order five groups adopt an innovation one after another: innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards. a gap, which geoffrey moore called the chasm, separates the early adopters from the early majority. innovators early adopters early majority late majority laggards time: each group adopts after the one before it the chasm everett rogers’ five groups of adopters (1962), with the gap geoffrey moore described in crossing the chasm (1991). the order comes from the research; the boxes are not drawn to the size of each group. rogers also lists five things people weigh before adopting something new. they read almost like a checklist for anyone proposing a new tool or design at work: what people weigh rogers’ question when you propose a new tool or design ( analysis ) advantage in what way is it better than the alternatives? measure it on their problem, not yours compatibility how well does it fit existing values, habits and tools? show it working alongside what they already use simplicity the easier it is to grasp, the faster it spreads one page, one example, one command observability can its benefits be seen, by watching someone else use it? demo it; let one team succeed in public trialability can you try it before committing? a pilot that is easy to undo notice how each of these makes the new thing a little more familiar and a little less of a loss, which is exactly what the effects in the previous card demand.

the brain on autopilot daniel kahneman’s thinking, fast and slow (2011) describes two modes of thought. system 1 is fast, automatic and unconscious; system 2 is slow, effortful and logical. (some priming studies the book cites have been questioned in psychology’s replication crisis; the two-system distinction itself is still widely used.) the brain uses up to about 20% of the body’s energy, more than any other organ, and running on the cheaper, automatic mode most of the time is how it copes ( analysis ). habits are that automatic mode applied to behaviour. william james wrote in 1890 that “any sequence of mental action which has been frequently repeated tends to perpetuate itself”, so that we act “without any consciously formed purpose”. research since then describes a habit as behaviour that, repeated in a consistent context, becomes automatic: efficient, needing little awareness, triggered by the context itself. the basal ganglia appear to remember the context that triggers a habit, and can revive it when the trigger returns. donald hebb’s 1949 theory is often summed up as “neurons that fire together, wire together”. how long it takes. in a study by phillippa lally and colleagues (2009), people took on average 66 days for a new daily behaviour to become as automatic as it would get, with a range of 18 to 254 days. so it is not 21 days, and it is not the same for everyone. if a new habit still feels like effort after three weeks, nothing has gone wrong.

c.h: “The brain is brainless; our habits make it better”
c.x: “the brain is brainless; our habits make it better” our view: most of what the brain does, it does without thinking: it repeats what it has repeated before. in that sense it is brainless, and that is not an insult but a design. automatic behaviour is what frees attention for the few things that really need it. it follows that the habits you choose decide much of what you do on any ordinary day. so choose them on purpose: a small daily practice, in the same place and at the same time, kept up for two months or more, will run on its own long after motivation has faded. the same mechanism explains the rest of this page. we like the familiar because the familiar is what our habits already handle, so a new idea feels crazy until it has been seen often enough to become one of them. the other view: calling the brain brainless undersells the automatic mode. fast, intuitive judgement is also where expertise lives: an experienced engineer’s sense that a design is wrong is system 1, trained by years of practice. and habits cut both ways. the same automaticity that keeps a good routine going keeps a bad one going, and it is what makes us dismiss the next semmelweis. habits make the brain better only when we keep checking which ones we are building.

putting it to work here is how the research above translates into everyday choices ( analysis ): if you want to do this get a new idea accepted make it familiar before you ask for a decision: show it more than once, connect it to what people already know, give an explanation as well as evidence, and offer a small trial that is easy to undo judge a new idea fairly notice your first reaction (“that’s crazy”) as unfamiliarity rather than evidence, and ask what would have to be true for it to work build a habit keep it small, tie it to the same cue (a time, a place, something you already do), repeat it daily, and expect about two months, not three weeks break a habit change the context that triggers it, because the trigger, not the intention, is what starts the routine related pages: perseverance & resilience , behaviours , ways of working , and case studies , where several companies were overtaken by ideas that first looked like toys.

the short answer you have probably heard all five of these names in a meeting, a podcast or a slide deck, usually attached to a single quotable line. that is a pity, because each of them offers something more useful than a slogan: a way of looking at work, money, evidence or knowledge that you can actually use on a tuesday afternoon. this page gives each of them a fair hearing. where we could read their own words, we quote them; where a famous line turns out to be someone else’s, we say so; and each card ends with the honest caveat, because every one of these thinkers has thoughtful critics too.

c.h: Peter Drucker: do the right things
c.x: peter drucker: do the right things peter drucker spent his career thinking about how organisations and the people in them actually get things done. in 1959 he coined the term knowledge worker , someone whose main contribution is what they know and think rather than what they make with their hands, and later in life he called knowledge-worker productivity the next frontier of management. if you write software for a living, he was writing about you, decades early. his most useful idea for engineers is the difference between being efficient and being effective. in a 1963 harvard business review article, “managing for business effectiveness”, he wrote: “there is surely nothing quite so useless as doing with great efficiency what should not be done at all.” wikiquote notes that the idea is older than drucker, with a similar line about education in 1887, but he made it famous. in the effective executive he added a line any team lead will recognise: “morale in an organization does not mean that ‘people get along together’; the test is performance not conformance.” be careful with: “culture eats strategy for breakfast.” it is everywhere with drucker’s name on it, but wikiquote lists it under misattributed . when you quote drucker, quote something he wrote. on this site: “busy is not progress” on ways of working puts the same idea into a daily routine.

c.h: Tim Ferriss: DEAL, a recipe for doing less
c.x: tim ferriss: deal, a recipe for doing less tim ferriss wrote the 4-hour workweek (2007) after running his sports nutrition company on 14-hour days, taking a three-week break abroad, and coming back with a different way of working: email once a day, small tasks outsourced. the book spent four years on the new york times best-seller list. in his own words, “the 4-hour workweek is broken into definition, elimination, automation, and liberation”, which spells deal . step what ferriss means what it looks like for an engineer ( analysis ) d efinition decide what you actually want to do, be and have, and what that costs. then find which few efforts produce most of the results, using the 80/20 or pareto principle: “20 percent of your inputs, will produce 80 percent of your desired results.” find the few features, services or tasks that matter most to users, and the ones nobody would miss e limination cut what is left, and use parkinson’s law: limit the time you give a task “so that you limit yourself to the truly important”. batch similar tasks such as email into a few fixed times, and do the one most important task before lunch. fewer meetings, notifications batched, one protected block each morning a utomation outsource and delegate; in his 2007 talk he suggested outsourcing “anything that can be done for less than $25”. he also describes testing a product idea cheaply before building it, which he later compared to what we now call a minimum viable product. scripts, ci pipelines and bots for repeated work; prototypes before platforms l iberation first, mobility: getting out of the office, even part-time, so time saved is really yours. second, deciding what to do with the time you have created. remote and flexible work, and the harder question of what to do with an hour you have won back be careful with: the title. the new york times noted that ferriss himself spends far more than four hours a week on blogging and promotion, wired faulted the book’s formulaic writing while praising its ideas on remote work, and some critics have been harsher. treat deal as a set of questions to ask about your week, not a promise about its length.

c.h: Naval Ravikant: leverage and specific knowledge
c.x: naval ravikant: leverage and specific knowledge naval ravikant co-founded angellist in 2010 and invested early in companies including uber and twitter. most people know his thinking through a long thread of short posts called “how to get rich (without getting lucky)”, which eric jorgenson collected, with naval’s permission, into the almanack of naval ravikant (2020), alongside his essays and interviews. the ideas that matter most for engineers: specific knowledge. “specific knowledge is knowledge you cannot be trained for. if society can train you, it can train someone else and replace you.” it “is found by pursuing your genuine curiosity and passion rather than whatever is hot right now”, and “will feel like play to you but will look like work to others.” leverage. “fortunes require leverage. business leverage comes from capital, people, and products with no marginal cost of replication (code and media).” capital and labour need someone’s permission; “code and media are permissionless leverage.” every engineer already holds one of the most powerful levers there is. long-term games. “play iterated games. all the returns in life, whether in wealth, relationships, or knowledge, come from compound interest.” build and sell. “learn to sell. learn to build. if you can do both, you will be unstoppable.” be careful with: survivorship. advice from someone who succeeded is shaped by the paths that worked for them; plenty of people followed similar principles without the same results ( analysis ). the ideas about learning, leverage and long-term relationships hold up well on their own; the promise in the title is the part to hold loosely.

c.h: Richard Feynman: you must not fool yourself
c.x: richard feynman: you must not fool yourself richard feynman shared the 1965 nobel prize in physics for work on quantum electrodynamics, worked on the atomic bomb during the second world war, and became known to the wider public in the 1980s as a member of the rogers commission that investigated the challenger disaster. but the reason engineers keep quoting him is a speech about honesty. in his 1974 commencement address at caltech, later published as “cargo cult science”, he warned graduates not to play down the weaknesses of their own work in pursuit of a conclusion they wanted. his line from it belongs on every engineering team’s wall: “the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.” a load test you designed to pass, a benchmark that measures the cache rather than the code, a demo that only works on your laptop: each is a small way of fooling yourself. the other line, found on his blackboard when he died in february 1988, is the best one-sentence description of learning by building: “what i cannot create, i do not understand.” it is why this guide pairs its explanations with code you can run. on this site: “from counting to algebra, the feynman way” on mathematics , from the feynman lectures on physics .

c.h: David Deutsch: good explanations, and why problems are soluble
c.x: david deutsch: good explanations, and why problems are soluble david deutsch is a physicist at the university of oxford, often described as the “father of quantum computing”: he described a quantum turing machine and specified an algorithm designed to run on a quantum computer (more on quantum computing ). since 2012 he has worked on constructor theory, which states the laws of physics in terms of which transformations are possible and which are impossible. his book the beginning of infinity (2011) argues that all progress, scientific, philosophical or cultural, comes from the search for good explanations . his test for a good explanation is one every engineer can use: it should be hard to vary . an explanation is hard to vary when every detail does real work, so you cannot change a part without breaking the whole. his example is the ancient story that the seasons happen because the goddess demeter is sad; it would work just as well if she were happy, which is exactly why it explains nothing. the modern explanation, the earth’s tilted axis as it orbits the sun, has no detail you could swap. the same test works on a postmortem. “the service failed because of high load” could explain almost any outage, so it explains none in particular. “the connection pool held 20 connections, the new query took 2 seconds, so at 10 requests a second the pool ran dry” is hard to vary, and that is why you can act on it ( analysis ). and deutsch’s optimism, that problems are inevitable but solutions exist if the right knowledge is sought, is a healthy stance for anyone staring at a hard bug.

how they fit together read side by side, the five answer different questions, which is why they are worth knowing together rather than as rival gurus ( analysis ): if you are asking… start with am i working on the right thing? drucker: effectiveness before efficiency how do i get my time back? ferriss: definition, elimination, automation, liberation what should i build my career on? naval: specific knowledge, leverage, long-term games can i trust this result? feynman: you must not fool yourself do i actually understand why it happened? deutsch: an explanation that is hard to vary

c.h: Our view, and the other view
c.x: our view, and the other view our view: read the originals, not the quote cards. each of these people said something more careful and more useful than the line that travels with their name, and the habit of checking who really said what is itself the feynman principle at work. the other view: two of the five are writers about success whose advice is shaped by their own unusual paths, and even the scientists are quoted far outside their fields. many good engineers never read any of them; the ideas matter only if they change what you do next week.

where to read more peter drucker, the effective executive tim ferriss, the 4-hour workweek (2007), and his 2007 sxsw talk, transcribed on his blog eric jorgenson, the almanack of naval ravikant (2020), free as a pdf richard feynman, “cargo cult science” (1974), and the feynman lectures on physics david deutsch, the beginning of infinity (2011) also on reading list .

c.h: feat, fix and chore: Conventional Commits
c.x: feat, fix and chore: conventional commits the conventional commits spec gives every commit message a type in front: type(optional scope): description . the point is a history a person can scan and a tool can read, for example to work out the next version number or write release notes. type use it when effect on the version (semantic versioning) feat: something a user of the code can now do that they could not before minor fix: a bug is patched: the code now does what it already claimed to do patch feat!: or a breaking change: footer existing users must change something (any type can carry the ! ) major chore: housekeeping that changes nothing a user sees: dependency bumps, tidying config none docs: refactor: test: perf: build: ci: style: what the name says. these come from the widely used commitlint convention (based on angular's), not from the spec itself none, unless marked breaking feat(search): filter results by court fix(login): stop the session expiring after 5 minutes chore: bump test dependencies refactor(api)!: rename /cases to /judgments breaking change: clients must call /judgments how to choose: ask "what would a user of this code notice?" a new capability is feat . wrong behaviour made right is fix . nothing noticeable is chore , refactor , docs or test . if a commit needs two types, it is usually two commits.

c.h: Writing a ticket someone can build from
c.x: writing a ticket someone can build from start with the why. the common user story shape is "as a <role> i can <capability>, so that <benefit>". the "so that" is the part people skip and the part that matters most. acceptance criteria: a short list of things that are true when it is done, each one checkable. "given a signed-in user, when they search for x, then they see y." context: links to the error, the log line, the screenshot, the conversation. the reader should not have to find you to start. out of scope: say what this ticket will not do, so it does not quietly grow. invest (bill wake): independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable. if it fails "small", split it. a bug ticket has steps to reproduce, what you expected, what happened, and where (version, environment, browser).

c.h: What Agile and XP actually said
c.x: what agile and xp actually said the agile manifesto (17 practitioners, 2001) values: individuals and interactions over processes and tools working software over comprehensive documentation customer collaboration over contract negotiation responding to change over following a plan extreme programming (kent beck, from the chrysler c3 payroll project) named four values in 1999: communication, simplicity, feedback and courage. respect was added in the second edition. its practices include test-first, pair programming, continuous integration, small releases, and a sustainable pace : one of its rules is simply "no overtime".

c.h: Honest updates: don't give an update and hide
c.x: honest updates: don't give an update and hide the daily scrum is meant to be under 15 minutes, to show progress toward the goal and the issues in the way . its job is to surface problems, not to perform being busy. a burndown chart is described as a publicly displayed chart of remaining work. public is the point: the real state, visible to everyone, every day. say "blocked" the moment you are, and on what. a blocker raised at 10am costs an hour; raised at the sprint review it costs the sprint. "nearly done" is not a status. say what is done, what is left, and what you are unsure about. bad news early is a plan; bad news late is an incident. teams that punish the messenger get green dashboards and red launches. show, don't tell: a link to the pr, the test run, the demo, beats a sentence about progress.

c.h: Continuous proactiveness: not every day is the same
c.x: continuous proactiveness: not every day is the same not every day is 9 to 5. an incident at night, a launch, a customer stuck on a deadline: some days need more, and a good engineer shows up for them. don’t be complacent. keep perspective: a hard day at a keyboard is not as hard as a shift in a coal mine. most of this work is safe, warm and well paid. that is a reason to give it full effort, not to coast. proactive means you see it before you are told: the alert that is noisy, the doc that is wrong, the dependency about to expire, the colleague who is stuck. but the long-run pace is sustainable. xp's "no overtime" rule is about the normal week: a team that runs every week on heroics stops noticing its own mistakes. a hard day is followed by recovery, not by another hard day. make the hard days rarer: after every late night, ask what would have prevented it, and fix that (a test, an alert, a runbook). flexible both ways: giving extra on the day it is needed earns the quiet afternoon when it is not.

c.h: Busy is not progress: do the first important thing first
c.x: busy is not progress: do the first important thing first a full calendar, a hundred messages answered, and at six o’clock the one thing that mattered has not moved. the frustration that follows is not a character flaw; it has well-studied causes, and a few habits deal with most of them. why a day fills up without moving the needle what happens what the sources say work expands parkinson’s law , from c. northcote parkinson’s 1955 essay in the economist : work expands to fill the time available for it. a day with no fixed slot for the important task lets everything else expand into it. the urgent crowds out the important the eisenhower method sorts tasks by urgency and importance, after a quote attributed to dwight d. eisenhower: “i have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. the urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.” messages and meetings are urgent; the design, the hard bug and the learning are important. every switch costs something psychologists have measured the switch cost , the drop in speed and accuracy right after changing task, since jersild’s experiments in 1927. a day cut into half-hours between meetings is mostly switching (see “why a day of meetings tires you more than a day of real work” on body, mind & nature ). we plan too much the planning fallacy (daniel kahneman and amos tversky, 1979): we underestimate how long tasks take, even when similar tasks took longer before. a to-do list of fifteen items guarantees that most will slip. no visible progress feels terrible teresa amabile and steven kramer analysed nearly 12,000 daily diary entries from professionals on complex projects over 15 years and found the progress principle : making progress in meaningful work, even in small steps, is a major driver of motivation, positive emotion and creativity. a busy day without progress is draining because progress is what was missing. a daily loop for doing the first important thing step how where it comes from 1. choose before the day starts the evening before, list the few most important tasks in order. tomorrow, work on the first until it is done, then the next the ivy lee method: six tasks, prioritised the night before, completed in order before adding more. the story goes that charles schwab paid lee $25,000 for it 2. make it a next action turn “work on the migration” into the first physical step: “write the rollback script for table x” david allen’s getting things done (2001): every project gets a desired outcome and a single next action 3. decide when and where “at 9:00, at my desk, before opening email, i write the rollback script” implementation intentions (peter gollwitzer, 1999): if-then plans that tie a goal to a cue make it more likely to happen 4. protect a block put the first block of the day in the calendar as a meeting with yourself; close chat and email during it cal newport’s deep work (2016): focused time on demanding tasks, without email and social media 5. finish before starting keep only two or three things in progress; a half-done task does not count kanban’s two core practices: make the work visible and limit work in progress 6. fix the time, not the scope give the task 90 minutes; if it is not finished, ship the part that is, and note the next action timeboxing: a fixed period with its own deliverable 7. record the win write one line at the end of the day: what moved. tomorrow’s step 1 starts from it the progress principle: small, visible wins sustain motivation the meetings themselves. before accepting one, ask what decision or output it will produce. decline, shorten or replace with a written update those that produce neither, and ask for an agenda when there is none (see writing & code review ). if you lead a team, the most useful thing you can protect is other people’s first block. our view: busyness is the default and progress is a decision, best made before the day begins: one important thing, one next action, one protected block, done before the inbox. doing that most days moves more than a heroic week now and then. the other view: for managers, leads and anyone whose job is unblocking others, meetings often are the important work, and judging a day by personal output misses that; and in some organisations the calendar is not yours to control. then the honest step is to agree with your manager which work matters most, and make that visible, rather than trying harder to fit it into the gaps. sources: parkinson’s law ; time management (eisenhower method) ; task switching ; planning fallacy ; teresa amabile ; ivy lee ; getting things done ; implementation intention ; deep work (cal newport) ; kanban (development) ; timeboxing (all wikipedia).

c.h: Why building a product still takes grinding, even with AI
c.x: why building a product still takes grinding, even with ai our view, with the evidence it rests on and the other view at the end. ai tools and skills make the typing faster. a product is more than the typing: it is the problem understood, the edge cases found, the claims checked, the users listened to, and the same thing fixed and improved again and again. that repeated, unglamorous work is the grind, and it has not gone away. the hard part is the problem, not the code. fred brooks argued in “no silver bullet” (1986) that no single technology or technique promises even a tenfold improvement within a decade, because much of software’s difficulty is essential complexity : if users need a program to do 30 different things, it must do those 30 things. tools remove accidental complexity. ai is a very strong tool for that, and the essential part still needs people to work through it. the last 10% takes the other 90%. the ninety-ninety rule, attributed to tom cargill of bell labs: “the first 90 percent of the code accounts for the first 90 percent of the development time. the remaining 10 percent of the code accounts for the other 90 percent.” a demo is the first 90%. a product people rely on is the rest. feeling fast is not being fast. in a randomised controlled trial published by metr in july 2025, experienced open-source developers took 19% longer on their tasks when using ai tools, while believing beforehand that ai would make them 24% faster and still believing afterwards that it had made them 20% faster. one study, of one group, at one point in time; but it shows why you measure instead of trusting the feeling. what the grind looked like, building this guide (first-hand): checking a claim about npm against npm’s own changelog showed that dependency install scripts are now blocked by default, which memory would have got wrong; an encyclopaedia put async/await in the wrong edition of javascript until tc39’s own list corrected it; and an independent review of each page found real mistakes before it went live. none of that was typing. all of it was grinding. what the grind actually is grind what ai helps with what still needs you understanding the problem summarising research, drafting questions talking to users, deciding what matters edge cases and failures suggesting cases, writing tests knowing which failures your users would actually hit checking claims finding sources fast opening the source, and refusing to publish what you could not check the last 10% drafting the fixes caring enough to finish: install, upgrade, docs, support doing it again remembering the steps, if you wrote them down showing up the next day, and the day after the other view: “work smarter, not harder”, and some teams do ship far faster with ai. both can be true. grinding without direction is just tiredness, and the earlier cards on this page still hold: a sustainable pace, and a hard day followed by recovery. the point is not more hours; it is that the hours spent understanding, checking and finishing cannot be skipped.

c.h: When Agile slows a company down
c.x: when agile slows a company down this card is opinion and observation from working in many teams, not a measured study. agile was meant to make teams faster. in many companies it has done the opposite, and the pattern is usually the same: the ceremonies were kept and the values were dropped. what the manifesto said what often happens instead individuals and interactions over processes and tools the process and the ticket tool become the work: estimation meetings, refinement of refinement, fields nobody reads working software over comprehensive documentation status reports and slide decks about the sprint, while nothing ships for weeks customer collaboration the team never meets a user; requirements arrive through three layers of proxies responding to change a fixed quarterly plan, renamed a "roadmap", with sprints as deadlines small, frequent releases two-week sprints that end in a release train once a quarter the way back is small: ship something real more often, put the people who build next to the people who use it, cut any meeting whose output nobody uses, and measure delivery (how often you release, how long a change takes to reach users) rather than story points.

everyday mathematics, for everyone you do not need advanced maths to live well, but a handful of ideas protect your money, your health and your judgement every day. none of this is about being "good at maths"; it is about not being fooled, including by yourself.

percentages and money up and down are not equal. a price that rises 50% and then falls 50% ends at 75% of where it started (1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75). down 20% then up 20% leaves you at 96%. percent is not percentage points. an interest rate going from 2% to 3% is up one percentage point, but up 50% in percent terms. watch which one you are being told. quick mental maths: 10% is the number with the decimal point moved one place; 5% is half of that; 15% is the two added; 1% is the point moved two places. compare unit prices, per kilo or per litre, not pack prices. the bigger pack is not always cheaper. small amounts add up: £4 a day is £1,460 a year, and £14,600 over ten years, before any interest.

c.h: Compound growth, for you and against you
c.x: compound growth, for you and against you compounding means growth on growth. £1,000 at 5% a year becomes about £1,629 after ten years if the interest is reinvested, against £1,500 if it is not. the rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years it takes to double. at 6% about 12 years (exactly 11.9); at 3% about 24 (exactly 23.4). debt compounds too. a balance at 24% a year, left unpaid, doubles in about 3 years (72 ÷ 24). pay off the most expensive debt first. inflation is compounding in reverse: at 3% a year, money left in a drawer loses half its buying power in about 24 years. start early. time does more of the work than the amount: small, regular savings started young often end up ahead of larger ones started late.

risk and chance relative risk can mislead. "doubles your risk" may mean going from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000. always ask: out of how many? base rates matter. suppose a test is 99% accurate both ways and the condition affects 1 person in 1,000. of everyone who tests positive, only about 9% actually have it, because the false positives from the 999 healthy people outnumber the true ones. expected value: multiply each outcome by its chance and add them up. lotteries and most casino games pay back less than you put in, on average, by design. streaks happen by chance. a coin that lands heads five times is not "due" tails; each toss is independent.

reading numbers in the news average or median? a few very high incomes pull the average up; the median (the middle value) is often a fairer picture of a typical person. correlation is not causation. two things rising together may share a third cause, or be coincidence. check the chart's axis. a bar chart whose axis does not start at zero can make a small difference look huge. ask for the size of the sample and who was asked. a survey of 20 people, or only of fans, says little. feel the size of big numbers: a million seconds is about 11.6 days; a billion seconds is about 31.7 years. the engineering cards below build on the same ideas: medians and percentiles, probability and estimation.

c.h: Complexity you should feel, not just know
c.x: complexity you should feel, not just know growth example n = 1 million o(1) hash table lookup 1 step o(log n) binary search, b-tree index lookup about 20 steps o(n) scanning a list or a table 1 million steps o(n log n) good sorting about 20 million steps o(n²) nested loops, a self-join without an index 1 trillion steps o(2ⁿ) trying every subset never finishes at a million items, the jump from o(n log n) to o(n²) is a factor of about 50,000: a fraction of a second becomes many minutes, and at larger sizes, days. an n+1 query pattern and a nested loop over two big lists are the usual ways it sneaks in.

numbers computers get "wrong" >>> 0.1 + 0.2 0.30000000000000004 # binary floating point cannot store 0.1 exactly >>> 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 false >>> from decimal import decimal >>> decimal("0.1") + decimal("0.2") == decimal("0.3") true # decimal arithmetic for money // java: int overflow wraps around silently int max = integer.max_value; // 2,147,483,647 max + 1 // -2,147,483,648 math.addexact(max, 1) // throws arithmeticexception instead use decimal types or integer minor units (paise, cents) for money. never compare floats with == ; compare within a tolerance. know your integer sizes: a signed 32-bit counter of milliseconds overflows in under 25 days (unsigned, about 50).

statistics that keep you honest median and percentiles beat the mean for skewed data such as latency: one slow request moves the mean, not the median. variance matters: two systems with the same average can have very different worst cases. sample size: a difference seen in 20 requests may be noise; in 20,000 it is more likely real. base rates (bayes): a 99% accurate alert for a problem that happens 1 time in 10,000 fires falsely about 100 times for each real case. correlation is not causation: two metrics rising together may share a cause. survivorship: you only see the systems, users or rows that made it through. multiple comparisons: test twenty things at 95% confidence and you should expect about one "significant" result by chance.

probability in operations # availability of dependencies in series multiplies 0.999 * 0.999 * 0.999 # ≈ 0.997 (three 99.9% services) # chance at least one of n calls is slow, if each is slow with p = 0.01 1 - (1 - 0.01) ** 100 # ≈ 0.63 # birthday paradox: random 32-bit ids collide sooner than you think import math math.sqrt(2 ** 32) * 1.1774 # ≈ 77,000 ids for a 50% chance of a collision the birthday bound is why ids are 128-bit uuids or longer, and why hash collisions are planned for, not assumed away.

linear algebra behind embeddings an embedding is a vector: a list of numbers that places a text in a space where similar meanings are close. dot product: multiply matching entries and add them up. cosine similarity = dot product ÷ (length of a × length of b): 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated. for vectors already normalised to length 1, cosine similarity and dot product are the same, which is why many vector databases normalise first. import numpy as np a, b = np.array([0.2, 0.8, 0.1]), np.array([0.25, 0.7, 0.0]) cosine = a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b)) # ≈ 0.99: very similar

c.h: Estimation: powers of two and orders of magnitude
c.x: estimation: powers of two and orders of magnitude power approx. name 2¹⁰ 1 thousand kib 2²⁰ 1 million mib 2³⁰ 1 billion gib 2⁴⁰ 1 trillion tib round to one significant figure and multiply orders of magnitude: being within 2× is good enough to choose a design. check units at every step; most estimation errors are unit errors. sanity-check against something known: a day is about 10⁵ seconds; a year about 3 × 10⁷.

c.h: Calculus made easy: rates and totals
c.x: calculus made easy: rates and totals calculus has a fearsome reputation, which is a shame, because its two big ideas are ones you already use every day without the symbols. glance at a car’s speedometer and you are reading a rate of change . look at the trip counter and you are reading a total built up from that rate. calculus is simply the careful version of those two glances. differentiation asks: how fast is something changing right now ? on a graph, it is the slope of the curve at one point, the steepness of a straight line that just touches it there (a tangent). integration asks: how much has built up altogether? on a graph, it is the area under the curve, found by adding up a great many thin slices. the same journey, seen two ways left: the car’s distance curves upward over three seconds, reaching 18 metres; a straight tangent line touches it at two seconds, and its slope, 8 metres per second, is the speed at that moment. right: the car’s speed rises in a straight line to 12 metres per second; the area under that line, shown as six thin slices, adds up to 18 metres, the distance travelled. slope at 2 s = speed = 8 m/s differentiation: the slope time (s) distance integration: the area speed area = 18 m time (s) differentiation reads the slope of the distance curve to get the speed at one moment. integration adds up thin slices under the speed line to get the distance. each undoes the other: the same 18 metres either way. the beautiful part, the fundamental theorem of calculus , is that these two are inverses: each undoes the other. before the theorem, nobody realised the two operations were related. isaac newton and gottfried wilhelm leibniz each worked out calculus independently in the late 17th century; the notation most of us use, dy/dx for a tiny change in y caused by a tiny change in x , comes from leibniz. run it. you do not need any symbols to see it work. this program follows a car speeding up steadily, uses differentiation to read its speed, then integration to add the speed back up into a distance: """differentiation and integration as everyday arithmetic: a car's journey, second by second.""" def distance(t): # metres travelled after t seconds, for a car speeding up steadily return 2 * t * t def speed_at(f, t, h=0.001): # differentiation: how fast is it changing right now? return (f(t + h) - f(t)) / h def area_under(f, a, b, steps=10_000): # integration: add up lots of thin slices width = (b - a) / steps return sum(f(a + (i + 0.5) * width) for i in range(steps)) * width for t in (1, 2, 3): print(f"after {t} s: travelled {distance(t):4.1f} m, speed {speed_at(distance, t):5.2f} m/s") speed = lambda t: speed_at(distance, t) # the speed at every moment print(f"adding up the speed from 0 to 3 s gives {area_under(speed, 0, 3):.2f} m") print(f"which is the distance the car really travelled: {distance(3) - distance(0):.2f} m") what it printed when we ran it: after 1 s: travelled 2.0 m, speed 4.00 m/s after 2 s: travelled 8.0 m, speed 8.00 m/s after 3 s: travelled 18.0 m, speed 12.00 m/s adding up the speed from 0 to 3 s gives 18.01 m which is the distance the car really travelled: 18.00 m the speed doubles from 4 to 8 m/s between the first and second second, as you would expect for steady acceleration, and adding the speed back up gives the distance the car really travelled. the tiny difference, 18.01 against 18.00, is honest: the program estimated the speed with small but not infinitely small steps, and calculus is exactly the study of what happens as those steps shrink towards zero. where engineers meet it: requests per second is a derivative of a request counter, which is why monitoring tools compute rate() over counters (see observability ); total cost is the integral of spend per hour; and training a neural network means following derivatives, the gradients, downhill (see neural networks ). if you want a gentle book, silvanus p. thompson wrote calculus made easy in 1910 for exactly this reader; it went through many reprints and was later revised by martin gardner (1998).

c.h: How to learn it as an adult engineer
c.x: how to learn it as an adult engineer learn each topic through a problem you have: statistics through your latency data, graphs through your dag, linear algebra through your embeddings. work examples by hand on paper , then check them in python. use ai as a patient tutor: ask for an explanation, then for exercises, then check your answers yourself. fifteen minutes a day beats a weekend once a year.

c.h: From counting to algebra, the Feynman way
c.x: from counting to algebra, the feynman way in chapter 22 of the feynman lectures on physics (volume i, "algebra"), richard feynman builds mathematics up from counting, so that each new idea grows out of the one before. the path, in short: counting gives the whole numbers; addition is counting on. multiplication is repeated addition; raising to a power is repeated multiplication. undo each operation and new kinds of number appear: subtraction needs negative numbers, division needs fractions, and roots need irrational and then imaginary numbers. the inverse of a power is a logarithm. put it all together and you reach euler's formula, e iθ = cos θ + i sin θ, which feynman called "our jewel" and "the most remarkable formula in mathematics". nothing has to be taken on faith: every step is a question ("what undoes this?") and its answer. our view: that is a good way to learn anything, mathematics or software; the other view: some people learn better from worked examples first. run the steps yourself: """from counting to euler's formula, one step at a time.""" import cmath, math # 1. counting gives the whole numbers. addition is counting on. print("3 + 4 =", 3 + 4) # 2. multiplication is repeated addition; powers are repeated multiplication. print("3 * 4 =", 4 + 4 + 4, "| 2 ** 10 =", 2 ** 10) # 3. undo each operation and new kinds of number appear: print("3 - 5 =", 3 - 5, " (subtraction needs negative numbers)") print("3 / 4 =", 3 / 4, " (division needs fractions)") print("sqrt(2) =", math.sqrt(2), " (roots need irrational numbers)") print("sqrt(-1) =", cmath.sqrt(-1), " (roots of negatives need imaginary numbers)") # 4. the inverse of a power is a logarithm. print("log2(1024) =", math.log2(1024)) # 5. put it together: e to an imaginary power goes round a circle. theta = math.pi / 3 print("e^(i*pi/3) =", cmath.exp(1j * theta), "= cos + i*sin:", complex(math.cos(theta), math.sin(theta))) print("e^(i*pi) + 1 =", cmath.exp(1j * math.pi) + 1, " (zero, to rounding)") checked against: the feynman lectures on physics (wikipedia; volume i, chapter 22 is "algebra") ; euler's formula (wikipedia, citing volume i p. 22-10) . the lectures are free to read at caltech's feynman lectures site .
