web3 building blocks blockchain: a replicated, append-only ledger agreed by consensus (proof of stake on ethereum), without a central operator. wallet and keys: a private key controls an account; whoever holds the key controls the assets. lost key, lost assets. smart contract: a program deployed on the chain (solidity on ethereum), public, and immutable unless designed to be upgradeable. tokens: fungible (erc-20) and non-fungible (erc-721 nfts) assets defined by contracts. gas: fees paid for computation and storage on chain. layer 2 rollups: process transactions off the main chain and post their data to it (zero-knowledge rollups also post a validity proof; optimistic rollups only produce a fraud proof if someone challenges), for lower fees. oracles: bring outside data on chain, a trust point in themselves. decentralised storage: ipfs and similar address content by its hash. defi and daos: financial services and organisations governed by contracts and token votes.

a minimal smart contract // spdx-license-identifier: mit pragma solidity ^ 0.8.24 ; /// records a document hash and who registered it, once. contract documentregistry { mapping(bytes32 => address) public registeredby; event registered(bytes32 indexed dochash, address indexed by); function register(bytes32 dochash) external { require(registeredby[dochash] == address(0), "already registered"); registeredby[dochash] = msg.sender; emit registered(dochash, msg.sender); } } tooling: foundry or hardhat to build and test, ethers.js or viem to call contracts, a testnet before mainnet, and an external audit before holding real value. deployed bugs are public and often permanent.

do you need a blockchain? do several parties need to write to shared data? do they not trust each other, or any single operator? is there no acceptable trusted intermediary (a database run by a neutral party, a regulator)? is public, permanent, tamper-evident history worth the cost, latency and loss of privacy? if any answer is no, a conventional database, an append-only ledger table, signed records or a timestamping service is simpler, cheaper and easier to correct. also weigh regulation: rules for crypto assets differ by country and change often (india, for example, taxes crypto transfers and has evolving rules). personal data on an immutable public chain conflicts with deletion rights.

c.h: The Semantic Web and linked data
c.x: the semantic web and linked data rdf: data as triples (subject, predicate, object), each named by a uri, so data from different sources joins up. vocabularies and ontologies: shared meanings (schema.org, dublin core, foaf; owl for formal ontologies). formats: turtle, json-ld (linked data in ordinary json), rdf/xml. sparql: the query language for rdf data and knowledge graphs. knowledge graphs: entities and relationships, used in search, ai grounding and data integration. for product data: schema.org's product type, with identifiers such as sku and gtin codes ( gtin13 ), gives items stable, linkable identities across shops. <!-- json-ld with schema.org, embedded in a web page --> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "product", "name": "folding umbrella", "sku": "umb-001", "offers": { "@type": "offer", "price": "12.99", "pricecurrency": "gbp" } } </script> # sparql: products in a given category, newest first prefix ex: <https://example.org/shop#> select ?p ?date where { ?p ex:incategory <https://example.org/category/umbrellas> ; ex:listedon ?date . } order by desc(?date)

how solid works piece is pod a personal data store on a solid server, self-hosted or from a provider; organisations can run pods for their users webid a uri that identifies a person or agent, pointing to a profile document solid-oidc authentication built on openid connect: the user logs in with their identity provider; apps act on their behalf access control web access control (wac) or access control policies (acp): who may read, write, append or control each resource resources files and containers in the pod, read and written over http (get, put, post, patch, delete) linked data structured data stored as rdf (often turtle) with shared vocabularies, so different apps understand the same data notifications apps can subscribe to changes in resources the key shift: apps and data are separated. a user can switch apps without losing data, and grant or revoke access per app or person.

data in a pod # a public profile document (turtle) @prefix foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> . @prefix solid: <http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#> . <#me> a foaf:person ; foaf:name "asha rao" ; solid:oidcissuer <https://login.example-provider.com> . # read it over plain http curl -h "accept: text/turtle" https://asha.pod.example/profile/card # web access control: owner has full control of a folder @prefix acl: <http://www.w3.org/ns/auth/acl#> . <#owner> a acl:authorization ; acl:agent <https://asha.pod.example/profile/card#me> ; acl:accessto <./> ; acl:default <./> ; acl:mode acl:read, acl:write, acl:control .

c.h: An app reading from a Pod (JavaScript)
c.x: an app reading from a pod (javascript) import { login, handleincomingredirect, getdefaultsession, fetch } from "@inrupt/solid-client-authn-browser"; import { getsoliddataset, getthing, getstringnolocale } from "@inrupt/solid-client"; await handleincomingredirect(); if (!getdefaultsession().info.isloggedin) { await login({ oidcissuer: "https://login.example-provider.com", redirecturl: window.location.href, clientname: "order notes" }); } const profileurl = "https://asha.pod.example/profile/card"; const dataset = await getsoliddataset(profileurl, { fetch }); // authenticated fetch const me = getthing(dataset, profileurl + "#me"); const name = getstringnolocale(me, "http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/name"); libraries: inrupt's javascript client libraries, and others for java and python. servers: the open-source community solid server for development and research; commercial servers for production.

where it fits personal data that many services need: health records, education credentials, identity documents, preferences. public-sector data sharing with citizen consent; some governments are piloting or running solid-based services. portability: users switch apps without exporting and importing. consent you can audit: access is granted per resource and can be revoked. challenges: app ecosystem still small, linked-data skills are less common, querying across many pods is slower than a central database, and pod providers must be trusted to run storage well.

one we build: cistern cistern is a self-hostable data pod with an mcp server: every request from an ai agent is checked against your rules when it is made, never from a cache, and gets a receipt naming the rule that decided it. its readme describes it as an open solid pod server. it is open source (apache 2.0). it is ours, so we are not neutral: compare it with the other solid servers on this page.

where i started i started as an electronics engineer, moved into computer hardware, and then into software. i first used computers around 1995, when most machines around me ran dos and windows was not yet common. the first languages i learned were basic and fortran; i still remember typing gwbasic at the dos prompt to start basic. we got hold of a windows 95 computer later, certainly by 1998, and we booted machines from floppy disks. by the time i started working, around 2000, most desks ran windows 95 or 98. as i remember it, windows nt was light and good for simply getting work done, but people found it plain next to 95 and 98; windows 2000 looked much better but needed more memory than nt. memory was scarce: we worked with 128 mb of ram, and 256 mb was a luxury. in my first software job, at one of the smallest startups you can imagine, our internet came over a dial-up line. java, as i remember it, was at version 1.1. we could not download the documentation, so we used javap to read a class's methods and worked out the rest. we wrote code in notepad. then we found editplus, wired it to javac and java so we could compile and run from the editor, and the coloured code alone made us feel we had arrived.

learning from the platform up we learned core java, then servlets and applets, and within two years we were building web applications. struts arrived around then: an apache project, founded in may 2000 by craig mcclanahan (started, as i remember it, as a holiday project). hans bergsten's writing on jsp was how many of us learned, and i remember puzzling over the difference between the servlet context and the page context. browsers were not standard. what we now call ajax worked through microsoft's xmlhttp object in internet explorer, so we wrote separate code for internet explorer and netscape. there was no chrome.

the ejb years at one of the biggest retail software companies of the time, we built with enterprise javabeans: stateless session beans to read data, entity beans for the database, and, in booking systems of that era, stateful session beans holding a conversation while the database held the lock on a ticket. xslt generated our screens from data, and uml and model-driven architecture promised that drawing the model would write the code.

c.h: We generated code long before AI
c.x: we generated code long before ai code generation is not new. i used database metadata to generate reusable boilerplate code, much as people use ai today, and xslt templates to turn data into dynamic screens. we generated the javascript for tree structures, pagination and web-based tutorials. the lesson has stayed with me: generating code is easy; understanding what you generate is the job.

the framework years enterprise java was hard. we wrestled with corba and its interface definitions, with two-phase commits for transactions that spanned systems, and later with enterprise service buses. then came spring, which its own documentation says came into being in 2003 as a response to the complexity of the early j2ee specifications. rod johnson had argued for simpler designs in his book expert one-on-one j2ee design and development (wrox), which is still on my shelf; as i remember it, his ideas about plain java objects were at spring's heart, and after vmware took the company over, spring became the standard choice. for many of us, it started with a single core jar. something changed in those years. many engineers learned the frameworks without ever looking at a servlet. the frameworks were good, but the foundations underneath them became invisible.

my bookshelf the first technical book i read cover to cover was hunter and crawford's java servlet programming (o'reilly). my first uml tool was magicdraw. at my first startup, from 2000 to 2002, i could not afford enterprise java with uml (arrington and rayhan, wiley). when i could, in 2003, i bought it for myself, out of love for it: it explained every layer, why dtos exist, and when a plain hash map is enough. seeing why each layer is there is what today's polished frameworks and generated answers rarely show. beside them still: java message service (monson-haefel and chappell), java enterprise best practices , javaserver pages and rod johnson's expert one-on-one j2ee design and development , packed away for a house move and going back on a shelf soon.

what worries me now i do not want to generalise, but i see a newer version of the same pattern. some new engineers go straight to ai without learning the fundamentals, or even the frameworks. they can get an answer, but they cannot always tell whether it is right, or fix it when it breaks. at the same time, much of the simple knowledge people once found on a website, and followed through themselves, is now asked of an ai, one question at a time. every one of those questions costs tokens, energy and data-centre capacity, often for something a page could answer with a click.

where this guide is going what this site can give people is a base knowledge of everything: enough to understand how the pieces fit, so they can then go deeper wherever they choose. if many people share that base, more of them can move into fields the world needs and is short of: building semiconductors, doing good science, and being knowledgeable and grounded in general. that makes for a better world. i work in it, so the guide starts with technology, alongside the personal side: health, money and good books. it is meant to grow. planned, not yet written: deeper sections on physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics, and on understanding your own body: why it responds as it does, simple exercise anyone can do, and ageing. there are many experts in each of these; the aim here is to state the established facts plainly and link to their research.

why this guide is free i would rather spend my own tokens once, building something useful, than have thousands of people spend theirs asking for the same basics. so this guide is free, and so are the frameworks we build: culvert , penstock , cistern and the others on the home page , all open source. a click is cheaper than a prompt. for what is already known, read the tab. use ai where it earns its keep: complex business logic, building frameworks, investigating a hard problem, or when you genuinely need to move fast. ai is here to stay; use it in the right context. and keep the foundations. they are what let you tell a good answer from one that only looks good. joseph aruja · start with start here

the thread through it all every era wrestled with the same four questions: how do two programs agree on a contract, where does state live, what happens when something fails, and how do we see what went wrong? the answers moved from heavy and agreed in advance, to light and flexible, and back again whenever the light way hurt. the questions never went away.

c.h: Why learning how it evolved matters
c.x: why learning how it evolved matters our view, with the ideas it rests on, and the other view at the end. tools change every few years; the problems they solve change far more slowly. knowing how we got here is how you tell a new idea from an old one with a new name, and how you choose and fix things without guessing. you recognise the pattern when it comes back. the same four questions run through every era on this page (contracts, state, failure, seeing what went wrong), and the answers swing between “agreed in advance” and “light and flexible”. when a new tool arrives, you can ask which swing it is, and what the last one learned. you know why the fence is there. chesterton’s fence (see philosophy ): do not remove something until you know why it was put up. most “legacy” code is a decision whose reason was forgotten; history is how you get the reason back. you avoid known traps. fred brooks named the second-system effect in the mythical man-month (1975), from ibm’s move to the far more ambitious os/360: after a small, clean first system, the second tends to become over-engineered, because the designer adds every idea deferred the first time. rewrites still fall into it. as george santayana put it: “those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” you judge what will last. the lindy effect is a heuristic, not a law: for things that do not wear out, such as ideas and technologies, the longer something has already lasted, the longer it is likely to keep lasting. it is a reason to learn the long-lived foundations on this guide’s foundations pages first, and to treat this year’s framework as unproven until it has survived a few years. you choose by requirement, not fashion. knowing what problem a tool was built for (see apps , build tools , ui history ) tells you whether that problem is yours. you can work with ai on old systems. models produce code in the style of every era they learned from, and many systems people rely on are decades old. knowing the history helps you recognise an outdated pattern in a suggestion, and maintain the old system with care rather than fear. new engineers are lucky ( our view ). what experienced engineers learned over 25 to 30 years, one release, outage and rewrite at a time, is now written down, explained and searchable, and ai can walk you through it. if you are ready to put in the work, you can learn in two or three years what took them decades to live through. the history on this page is that shortcut. the other view: history can turn into nostalgia (“we did this in 2005”) and into a reason to dismiss things that really are better. tools do improve. learn the why behind each change, not the trivia, and never use the past only to say no. and reading is not the same as living through it: judgement from your own incidents and mistakes still takes time, so build things and run them while you read. checked against: wikipedia: second-system effect ; wikipedia: george santayana ; wikipedia: lindy effect ; wikipedia: g. k. chesterton (chesterton’s fence) .

c.h: A look back: technology goes in cycles
c.x: a look back: technology goes in cycles the same ideas keep coming back, each time on cheaper hardware, faster networks and better tools. knowing the earlier turn of the wheel tells you what the new one will get wrong. the swing earlier then now where the computer is 1960s time-sharing: many users on one shared mainframe personal computers and client-server: a computer on every desk cloud computing: shared computers rented by the minute. its history is usually traced back to time-sharing how thin the client is terminals on a mainframe: the screen did almost nothing desktop applications, then web pages made on the server single-page apps in the browser, alongside server rendering, chosen per page contracts between programs corba (first version october 1991): an interface definition language agreed in advance json over http: light, flexible, often with no schema at all grpc: protocol buffers as the interface definition language. agreed in advance again data relational databases: sql and acid transactions nosql: scale out, give up some guarantees newsql: nosql’s scale with acid guarantees back work across several systems distributed transactions with two-phase commit (corba defined a transaction service among its standard services) the enterprise service bus orchestrating flows between systems sagas: local transactions, with a compensating step to undo each one. the idea comes from a 1987 paper, older than corba itself integration the enterprise service bus: a smart centre microservices: “smart endpoints and dumb pipes” service meshes and gateways: some of the centre returns, as infrastructure analysis, and the other view: it is less a circle than a spiral. each return happens because a constraint changed (hardware got cheap, networks got fast, operations got automated), and it comes back with lessons from the last time. the skill is to ask, of any “new” idea: what changed that makes it work now, when it struggled before?

c.h: Microservices and CORBA: not the same, but alike in places
c.x: microservices and corba: not the same, but alike in places our view, built on the facts below, with the other view at the end. microservices are not the new corba, but they share some of its problems, and a badly split system can repeat its mistakes. how alike they are depends on how the services were split. the similarities. both spread one system across a network, so both pay the same tax. peter deutsch’s list of the fallacies of distributed computing (sun, 1994), which begins “the network is reliable” and “latency is zero”, applies to both. fine-grained synchronous calls between services that share a database and release together recreate distributed objects: a distributed monolith . the differences. corba’s location transparency , treating a remote object like a local one, is the part most criticised. the 2014 article by james lewis and martin fowler that named microservices does the opposite. it defines them as independently deployable services organised around business capabilities, and says remote calls are more expensive, so remote apis need to be coarser-grained. done that way, it is an organisational choice, not a remote-object technology. was corba bad technology? not as simply as its reputation says. wikipedia’s account of it notes that much of the criticism of corba stems from poor implementations of the standard rather than the standard itself. it also records real problems: early versions defined the interface language but not the format on the wire, so different vendors’ products could not talk to each other until corba 2; design by committee; and location transparency. our view: many of its ideas were right and came back under other names, such as interface definitions in grpc. why sagas came back. two-phase commit is a blocking protocol: if the coordinator fails permanently, participants that have voted can wait for ever. across independently deployed services that is too fragile, so the work becomes a saga of local steps, each with a compensating step to undo it (see “rest, long journeys, and sagas” further down this page). are we only surviving because of modern tools? partly. container platforms, service meshes, retries, circuit breakers and distributed tracing absorb pain that earlier teams carried by hand. but the same tools make failure visible and recovery automatic, which is an improvement, not just a mask. a one-question test ( our view ): can one team deploy one service on a tuesday afternoon without coordinating with anyone else? if not, the system has the costs of distribution without the benefit, and the tools are keeping it alive. the other view: many teams would do better to start with a modular monolith and split only when team size or scaling demands it (see microservices ). others point out that at large scale, with many teams, independent deployment is the only thing that keeps them moving at all. both are true for different requirements. checked against: wikipedia: common object request broker architecture ; wikipedia: fallacies of distributed computing ; james lewis and martin fowler: microservices (2014) ; wikipedia: cloud computing (history) ; wikipedia: thin client ; wikipedia: grpc ; wikipedia: newsql ; wikipedia: two-phase commit protocol ; wikipedia: compensating transaction (sagas) ; wikipedia: enterprise service bus .

c.h: Distributed objects: everything agreed in advance
c.x: distributed objects: everything agreed in advance corba , from the object management group, let programs in different languages call each other's objects across a network. you wrote the contract in an interface definition language and generated client stubs and server skeletons before anything could talk. java rmi did the same between java programs, more simply, and java could load the classes it needed over the network. application servers such as weblogic wrapped this with transactions, security and pooling. powerful, and heavy. what it taught us: a remote call is not a local call. it can be slow, fail halfway, or never answer.

c.h: Enterprise JavaBeans: the beans we lived with
c.x: enterprise javabeans: the beans we lived with session beans held business logic. stateless ones served any caller and were pooled, so they suited reads and simple operations. stateful ones kept a conversation with one client across calls. stateful session beans and database locks were how some booking and ticketing systems held a seat while a customer finished: the bean kept the conversation, the database kept the lock. entity beans represented rows in the database, with the container managing how they were loaded and saved. they were heavy and slow to work with, and plain java objects mapped by tools such as hibernate, and later jpa, replaced them. message-driven beans consumed messages from a jms queue or topic, bringing event-driven work inside the application server. what it taught us: the ideas (stateless services, conversations, transactions, messaging) were right; the weight was not. spring, and later ejb itself, kept the ideas and dropped the ceremony.

models, uml and generated screens uml , which appeared in 1997, gave teams one language for drawing systems: class diagrams, sequence diagrams, use cases. grady booch, james rumbaugh and ivar jacobson brought their methods together into it. model-driven architecture , from the object management group, went further: draw the model, then generate the code from it. it worked well for some layers and poorly for the rest. xslt transformed xml into html, so screens could be generated from data and templates rather than written by hand. what it taught us: generating code from a model is powerful when the model is the truth, and painful when people edit the generated code. the same lesson applies to ai-generated code today.

c.h: The early web: stateless by design
c.x: the early web: stateless by design http forgets you between requests. to remember who you were, pages carried state in hidden form fields , in the url (url rewriting) and, increasingly, in cookies. html was standardised in the mid-1990s, but browsers still differed: code checked whether it ran in internet explorer or netscape, and what we now call ajax worked first through microsoft's xmlhttp object. caching mattered because bandwidth was precious on dial-up: browsers and proxies kept copies, and pages said how long a copy stayed fresh. what it taught us: statelessness scales, and every bit of state has to live somewhere on purpose.

pages made on the server cgi scripts started a new process for every request. php began in 1994 as rasmus lerdorf's "personal home page" tools and grew into a language for building web pages on the server. java servlets and jsp ran inside a long-lived server, handling many requests without starting a process each time. struts , an apache project founded in may 2000, brought the model-view-controller pattern to java web applications.

c.h: Runtimes get fast, and get company
c.x: runtimes get fast, and get company java began by interpreting bytecode, which was slow. just-in-time (jit) compilers, which compile the busiest code to machine code while the program runs, made it fast, and the jvm's hotspot became the standard approach. microsoft's c# and .net arrived in the early 2000s with many of the same ideas: a managed runtime, garbage collection and code compiled just in time. what it taught us: a good runtime lets you write simpler code and still go fast, and ideas spread quickly once they work.

c.h: Integration: buses, services and lighter ways
c.x: integration: buses, services and lighter ways soap web services brought back contracts agreed in advance, written in wsdl, with generated clients, much as corba had done. enterprise service buses put routing, transformation and orchestration into one large central product. lighter tools followed. apache camel implemented the patterns from hohpe and woolf's enterprise integration patterns as a library. spring came into being in 2003, by its own account, as a response to the complexity of the early j2ee specifications. what it taught us: one big central hub becomes the bottleneck and the single point of failure.

rest, long journeys, and sagas rest , which roy fielding described in his doctoral dissertation, used the web's own design (resources, urls, standard methods, caching) instead of a custom remote-call layer. without distributed transactions, a long piece of work becomes a journey of steps. if it fails halfway, you undo the completed steps in reverse order, which only works if you recorded every step you took. this idea is old. it was described as the "saga" in a 1987 database paper by hector garcia-molina and kenneth salem, long before microservices made the word popular again. see architecture .

c.h: One runnable JAR: from app servers to "java -jar"
c.x: one runnable jar: from app servers to "java -jar" for years a java web application was a war file deployed into a separate application server. then frameworks started shipping the server inside the application: one file you start with java -jar . dropwizard (first published to maven central in december 2011) bundled an embedded jetty server with jersey, jackson, logback and metrics, and its getting-started guide builds the whole application as a "fat jar". as i remember it, that was the first time many of us ran a service this way, before spring boot (1.0 in april 2014) made the idea mainstream. how the fat jar is built: the maven shade plugin unpacks every dependency into one archive. its servicesresourcetransformer merges the meta-inf/services files so libraries such as jersey and jackson do not overwrite each other's, and its manifestresourcetransformer sets the main-class , so java -jar app.jar server config.yml just works. why it mattered: one file to build, copy and run made services simple to deploy, and fitted containers perfectly a few years later. see docker and spring boot . checked against: maven central: dropwizard-core, first release dated 22 december 2011 ; maven central: spring-boot, first release dated 1 april 2014 ; dropwizard readme and getting-started guide ; the transformer classes inside the maven-shade-plugin artefact.

c.h: Why Spring lasted, and how it helped Java
c.x: why spring lasted, and how it helped java rod johnson released the first version of spring with his book expert one-on-one j2ee design and development in october 2002, as a lighter way to build enterprise java than enterprise javabeans; it was released under the apache licence in june 2003. many of the tools in the table below faded. spring did not, and the reasons are worth learning: it solved the real pain. plain java objects, dependency injection, and transactions set up by configuration rather than by the ejb container. ordinary code became easy to write and to test. it kept changing with the platform. annotations instead of xml, spring boot's runnable jar and sensible defaults (1.0 in april 2014), then a sixth major version of the framework (november 2022) that moved to a java 17 baseline and the jakarta namespace. it adopted new java features rather than fighting them. see spring boot . it integrated rather than replaced. it worked with the libraries people already used (hibernate, messaging, web frameworks) instead of asking them to throw everything away. it stayed open and backward-compatible enough that a team could upgrade step by step over the years, without rewrites. how that helped java: when enterprise java was heavy, spring made it productive again, and when cloud and containers arrived, spring boot made java a natural fit for small runnable services. keeping millions of developers productive on the jvm gave java time to modernise itself: faster releases, records, virtual threads. (the reasons above are this guide's analysis; the dates are sourced.) checked against (wikipedia): spring framework ; spring boot .

replaced by modern tools many tools from those years did not fail; the problems they solved moved somewhere else. a few we used every day: then what it did now, mostly why it moved on osgi (osgi alliance founded 1999) dynamic modules inside one jvm: bundles with declared dependencies, loaded and replaced while running, plus a service registry. eclipse is built on it. separate services in containers; the java platform module system (java 9, 2017) for module boundaries isolation moved between processes instead of inside one; bundle manifests and class loading were hard to live with. the osgi work moved to the eclipse foundation at the end of 2020. google guice lightweight dependency injection injection built into the main frameworks, such as spring boot frameworks now do injection plus configuration, servers and data access. guice is stable rather than gone: its last two releases came out together in may 2023, the second moving it to the jakarta namespace. ear and rar files an ear bundled modules for an application server; a rar held a resource adapter connecting the server to enterprise systems (jakarta connectors) one runnable jar or container image per service; client libraries, rest and messaging for integration no application server, nowhere to deploy them. they remain where websphere-style servers remain. war files are still used with servlet containers. putty and its connection managers (putty from 1999) ssh from windows, with saved sessions; add-ons gave it tabs openssh built into windows 10 since version 1803; windows terminal (announced 2019), which has tabs windows ships ssh itself. putty is still maintained by simon tatham; it is simply no longer the only way. logs on a shared network drive every server wrote files to a mapped drive; you searched them by hand logs, metrics and traces sent to a central platform: a cloud logging service or an open-source stack, often through opentelemetry hundreds of short-lived containers cannot share a drive, and you need search, alerts and one view across services. syslog started the idea of sending logs elsewhere in the 1980s. see observability . the lesson: learn the problem a tool solves, not just the tool. the problem stays when the tool is replaced. checked against (wikipedia unless stated): osgi ; java platform module system ; maven central: guice releases ; ear ; jakarta connectors ; putty ; openssh ; windows terminal ; syslog ; cncf (opentelemetry) .

c.h: Microservices, cloud, and seeing what happens
c.x: microservices, cloud, and seeing what happens microservices split systems into small services that each own their data. they brought back every distributed-systems problem at once, now spread across many teams. for years, failures were hard to follow from one service to the next. observability caught up: logs, metrics and traces, and a shared trace context passed with every call (the w3c traceparent header). see observability . the cloud turned servers into something you rent by the minute and declare in code.

the people behind the ideas we remember the famous product launches and forget many of the people whose ideas we use every day. a few worth knowing, and reading: the "gang of four" , erich gamma, richard helm, ralph johnson and john vlissides, wrote design patterns: elements of reusable object-oriented software , which gave us a shared vocabulary: factory, observer, strategy, adapter. martin fowler wrote refactoring (its second edition with kent beck) and patterns of enterprise application architecture , and has explained ideas such as continuous integration and microservices to a generation of engineers. he calls the gang of four's book "the best book ever written on object-oriented design". kent beck developed extreme programming, and test-driven development within it, in the late 1990s. grady booch, james rumbaugh and ivar jacobson created uml. gregor hohpe and bobby woolf wrote enterprise integration patterns . roy fielding described rest. hector garcia-molina and kenneth salem described sagas. and thousands of open-source maintainers whose names most of us never learn, whose work runs in almost everything we build. before you ask an ai to explain a pattern, read the person who named it. the original is usually clearer, and it tells you why. start with fowler on the gang of four , extreme programming and test-driven development .

who named it? test yourself recalling a name fixes it better than reading it again. answer each one before you open it. who called the null reference a “billion-dollar mistake”? tony hoare, who introduced it in algol w in 1965. kotlin’s null safety is one answer to it. why does adding people to a late project make it later, and who said so? fred brooks, in the mythical man-month : new people need time to learn the project, and every extra person adds lines of communication. your services end up shaped like your teams. whose law is that? melvin conway’s, from 1967. whose dissertation defined rest? roy fielding’s, in 2000. who described sagas, and when? hector garcia-molina and kenneth salem, in 1987, long before microservice designs reused the idea. what does the “l” in solid stand for, and who is it named after? the liskov substitution principle, after barbara liskov. solid itself comes from robert c. martin’s 2000 paper on design principles; the acronym was coined around 2004 by michael feathers. who created both linux and git? linus torvalds. whose paper gave us the relational model? edgar f. codd’s, in 1970. who gave us logical clocks and paxos? leslie lamport. who are the gang of four? erich gamma, richard helm, ralph johnson and john vlissides, authors of design patterns (1994). come back in a week and try again: recall spread over days lasts longer than one long session (see body, mind & nature ).

and now, ai ai can generate the code that each of these eras made us write by hand: the stubs, the boilerplate, the glue. but the four questions have not changed: contracts, state, failure, and seeing what went wrong. people who know this history recognise an old problem in a new form, and do not mistake generated code for understanding. see ai for engineers . dates here are given where we could check them against the project's own record; elsewhere the page speaks in eras rather than years.

health and habits the 4 pillar plan , dr rangan chatterjee (2017). a doctor's plan for health built on four everyday pillars, small changes made consistently. the 5 am club , robin sharma (2018). owning the start of your day before the world asks for it. the everyday hero manifesto , robin sharma (2021). doing ordinary work, every day, to a high standard. atomic habits , james clear (2018). change by small steps: build a habit by making it small and easy, and aim to get about 1% better each day. psycho-cybernetics , maxwell maltz (1960). how your self-image sets the limits of what you attempt, and how to change it. see body, mind & nature .

mind and character as a man thinketh , james allen (1903). a short book on the power of thought: by working patiently on our thoughts we can remake our lives and change our circumstances. old enough to be free to read: it is on wikisource . meditations , marcus aurelius. private notes on stoic philosophy, written by a roman emperor to himself, much of it while on military campaign. nearly two thousand years old and still practical: control what you can, accept what you cannot, do your duty well. see philosophy and being a good human .

money, work and building the almanack of naval ravikant , compiled by eric jorgenson (2020). naval ravikant's thinking on wealth, judgement and happiness, gathered from his talks and writing. zero to one , peter thiel with blake masters (2014). building something new rather than copying what exists; it grew out of thiel's startup class at stanford. i will teach you to be rich , ramit sethi (2009, updated 2019). a beginner's guide to managing money, written for people starting out. the psychology of money , morgan housel (2020). why behaviour matters more than intelligence when it comes to money.

thinking and science the beginning of infinity: explanations that transform the world , david deutsch (2011). progress comes from good explanations, and there is no limit to how far it can go. see science & method .

c.h: Why a reading list on an engineering site
c.x: why a reading list on an engineering site technology changes every year; these ideas have lasted far longer. looking after your health, mastering your own thinking, being careful with money and valuing good explanations make a better engineer and a better person. if ai saves you an hour, spend some of it on a chapter of one of these. suggest a book through the ask-on-github link at the end of any page. checked against (wikipedia): rangan chatterjee ; robin sharma ; atomic habits ; psycho-cybernetics ; as a man thinketh ; meditations ; naval ravikant ; zero to one ; i will teach you to be rich ; the psychology of money ; the beginning of infinity .

cistern a self-hostable data server built on the solid specifications. apps and ai assistants ask permission instead of taking copies: the owner writes the rule, cistern enforces it on every request, and every allow and deny gets a receipt. java, apache 2.0. the cistern page · source and issues

penstock a self-hosted agent harness. with database storage, every model call and tool call is written to an audit log the owner reads back, and its pod tool reads from a cistern pod only what was granted. java, spring boot. the penstock page · source and issues

culvert a cloud-agnostic data-pipeline framework: pipelines are defined once against a language-neutral contract set and run on any cloud by swapping adapters. java and python, apache 2.0. the guide's culvert page teaches the ideas. the culvert page · source and issues

enrich-test-api java integration tests for cloud code, on local emulators: a test asks for a bucket or a queue and gets one, backed by a container the library started, so no cloud account is needed. an alpha, and its page says so. java 17, apache 2.0. the enrich-test-api page · source and issues

learning from them the learning pages use neutral examples on purpose, so they teach the idea rather than a product. when you want to see an idea in a real codebase, these projects are where to look: agent harness and penstock, solid and cistern, data engineering and culvert, testing and enrich-test-api. headworks shows penstock and cistern running together. questions about a project go to that project's issues.

the idea pipelines are defined once against a language-neutral contract set (sixteen contracts plus a metrics record: blobstore , warehouse , source , sink , jobcontrolrepository and eleven more), realised as java interfaces and python protocols. adapters implement the contracts for each cloud, and every adapter must pass the same conformance suite , or it is not an adapter. swap the cloud, keep the logic. layer is your business logic written once; depends only on the contracts, never on a cloud sdk the contracts java interfaces and python protocols from one spec cloud adapters swappable implementations that pass the shared conformance suite this is the "framework, not generated boilerplate" argument from the frameworks vs ai tab made concrete: one contract and one test suite instead of a hand-written cloud integration in every pipeline.

design choices java owns beam: the dataflow/beam execution layer is java; legacy python beam is not carried forward. the two languages deliberately do different jobs. dbt, reused: transformation is sql and macros, packaged once; there is deliberately no java transform module. local-first: the whole stack runs against emulators, so you can develop and test without a cloud account. no silent defaults: warehouse.loadfromuri requires a loadoptions , because a defaulted write disposition let a re-run silently double its data. honest failure: reconciliation runs before the target is written, so a failed load cannot be reported as succeeded. not a replacement for beam, airflow or dbt: they are engines, and culvert is a framework around them.

install (python) # core contracts only, no cloud sdks pip install culvert # + bigquery, gcs, pub/sub, secret manager, observability pip install 'culvert[gcp]' # + airflow-side dag factory / operators / sensors, or dbt pip install 'culvert[orchestration]' pip install 'culvert[transform]' # + stageclaim on postgresql pip install 'culvert[postgres]' # test fixtures, and the conformance suite for your own adapters pip install 'culvert[tester]' pip install 'culvert[contract-tests]' # gcp + orchestration + transform pip install 'culvert[all]' # adapters are discovered through entry points from data_pipeline_core import autoconfig blob_store = autoconfig.discover().first("blob_store") # -> gcsblobstore, when culvert[gcp] is installed python 3.10 or newer.

what runs where contract gcp aws azure blobstore gcs s3 skeleton warehouse bigquery athena roadmap source · sink pub/sub sqs roadmap jobcontrolrepository bigquery dynamodb · athena roadmap observability cloud monitoring cloudwatch roadmap secrets secret manager secrets manager roadmap gcp is the full implementation; aws has the java adapter family; azure has a blob storage skeleton and is otherwise roadmap. jobcontrolrepository also has a postgresql implementation.

features worth knowing job control: run state through jobcontrolrepository on bigquery, dynamodb, athena or postgresql; a read-only culvert command line ( runs , run , entities , failures , adapters ). stageclaim (postgresql): one stage of one unit for one period cannot start twice. inputreadiness (postgresql): names each expected input that is missing, failed or still running, rather than counting rows. orchestration: a cloud-neutral dag model rendered to airflow/composer or cloud run jobs, with stage gates and a concurrency ceiling. schema files: an entity's columns, types, required flags, classification, masking, ranges and allowed values in yaml or json, loaded with the same rules in java and python. blobstore.head(uri) : size, version token and metadata without reading the object, for loaders that must be idempotent by object version. bigquerywarehouse.merge() : upserts with one merge and refuses a key that is not a target column.

status, stated plainly released in both languages on maven central and pypi, under apache 2.0 (the earliest releases were mit). ran end to end on a real gcp project (cloud run to bigquery, event-driven) before release; that run caught eight production-only bugs every local test had passed. culvert is pre-1.0: read the changelog's upgrade notes before moving between versions. a book on its design is in progress. pin a version in your build, and verify any api against that version's sources, not against main .

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain contracts, adapters and the conformance suite install culvert with the right extras or add the maven artifacts use an adapter through auto-discovery instead of a cloud sdk 2 practitioner write pipeline code against blobstore, warehouse and job control use loadoptions, head() and merge() for idempotent loads run and test against emulators locally 3 senior design pipelines whose logic is cloud-neutral add an adapter that passes the conformance suite use stageclaim, inputreadiness and orchestration gates 4 expert shape the contract spec and its evolution lead adoption across teams and clouds contribute adapters for new clouds (azure) each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
